units.la: {the woodcut initial} Vm iam multos annos, de THOMAE ERASTI Medici, ac Philosophi, nostra tempestate clarissimi, Tractatu quodam à pluribus rogitarer; quem de Ecclesiastica Disciplina, déque Excommunicatione scripsisse illum dictitabant; cuius etiam in manibus multorum eiusdam argumenti Theses, nescio quas, manu-scriptas, vidisse se se affirmabant; quae quidem Theses à viris & doctis & pijs, atque partium studijs alienis, mirum in modum probarentur; Ego his cognitis, animum ad hanc rem adiungere coepi; ponereque in perquirendo libro quantum poteram diligentiae, operae, atque industriae. Quem vbi nondum euulgatum, sed delitescentem inter alias huius viri schedas, tineis & blateis escam, comperissem; quòd autore vita functo, Haeredes eius nō eam, quae par fuisset, rationem haberent: elaboraui, ac denique perfeci, vt pretio Haeredibus depenso, Liber cui extremam Auctor manum imposuerat, in meam deueniret potestatem. Hunc postea, vbi primum per tempus licuit, diligenter typis meis excudendum tradidi. Quod autem operaepretium fecerim, hactenus animi pendeo. Illud quidem certè mihi minimè dubium bium est, complures fore, qui studijs partium magis quàm veritati addicti, meum hoc institutum accusabunt, reprehendent, ac miris denique modis exagitabunt: quasi ego auaritia inductus & rerum nouarum studio, Ecclesiae statum, his praesertim iniquis temporibus; tanta rerum omnium perturbatione, bellicis tumultibus, malorum colluuie, & doctrinarum labyrinthis; satis superque iactatum; nouo dogmate nouisque contentionibus exagitandum adhuc magis proposuerim. Quae quidem res, magnum sanè mihi dolorem, grauémque sollicitudinem allatura fuisset; nisi me laborantem erexisset, atque consolata fuisset ipsa veritas; cui accedebat auctoritas praecipuorum nostri temporis Theologorum; quorum etiam Epistolas ad libri calcem adiecimus: ac denique quòd à quam plurimis etiam alijs eruditis viris, & veritatis amantibus, hoc scriptum, summis extolli laudibus viderem. Quamobrem, etiamsi mihi in odium offensionémque incidere cuiusquam, acerbum erat; tamē ne veritas per me diutiùs oppressa diceretur, neque tanto bono pios omnes defraudarem, quos multo iam tempore libri huius editionem vehementer expetisse intelligebam; nil moratus paucorum odium, peruersámque imperandi cupidinem, qua maximè hoc genus hominū flagrat; operi me summo studio accinxi, praestitiúque quod videtis. Igitur vos, qui procul à liuore, & maleuolentia, rectum animi sensum in iudicando sequimini, nostram hanc diligentiam, & bonis omnibus gratificandificandi studium æqui boníque consulite : nostríq; patrocinium defensionémque aduersus maleuolos, & obtrectatores libenter suscipite : quo nobis animũ faciatis, alios deinceps, in vestrum commodum, libros bonos, typis nostris excudendi. Qua quidem in re dabimus operam, ne diligentiam officiúmque nostrum desideretis. Interim fruimini doctrina tanti viri ; summas immortali Deo gratias agentes, quod is tales operarios in messem suam extruserit, qui in colligendis denique frugibus, non autem dissipandis, omnem curam, diligentiam, operam, ac studium collocant. Valete foelicifsimè.
units.tr: For many years I have been asked by many people about a certain treatise by THOMAS ERASTUS, physician and philosopher, most distinguished in our time, which they kept saying he had written on Ecclesiastical Discipline and on Excommunication. Some also declared that they had seen in the hands of many people some theses, I know not what, in manuscript, on the same subject, and that these theses were marvellously approved by learned and pious men who were free of party zeal. When I learned this, I began to apply my mind to the matter and to take as much care, effort and diligence as I could in seeking out the book. When I found it, not yet published but lying hidden among the other papers of this man, food for moths and bookworms, because after the author's death his heirs had not taken the care that was fitting, I worked hard and finally arranged that, once payment had been made to the heirs, the book to which the author had put the final touch came into my hands. Afterwards, as soon as time allowed, I diligently handed it over to my press to be printed. Whether I have done something worthwhile, I still hold in suspense. This much at least is certainly not doubtful to me: many people, more devoted to party interests than to truth, will accuse me, rebuke me and finally harass me in all sorts of ways, as if I, led by greed and a fondness for novelty, had set out to stir up the state of the Church, already tossed about enough, especially in these unfavourable times of such general upheaval, warlike tumults, a flood of evils and labyrinths of doctrine, with a new dogma and new contentions. This would indeed have caused me great grief and heavy anxiety, had not truth itself raised me up as I laboured and consoled me. To this was added the authority of the chief theologians of our time, whose letters we have also appended at the end of the book; and finally, that I saw this writing greatly extolled with the highest praise by very many other learned men and lovers of truth. Therefore, although it was bitter for me to incur the hatred and offence of anyone, yet, lest truth be said to have been suppressed by me for longer, and lest I defraud all the pious of so great a good, whom I knew had for a long time earnestly desired an edition of this book, I paid no heed to the hatred of a few or to the perverse lust for domination with which this sort of men burns above all. I set myself to the work with the greatest zeal and produced what you see. Therefore you, who far from envy and ill will judge with an upright mind, take kindly to this our diligence and, for the good of all, consider it with fairness and goodwill; and gladly take up our protection and defence against the malicious and the detractors. In this way you will encourage us to print other good books for your benefit in the future. In this matter we will take care that you do not find our diligence and duty wanting. Meanwhile, enjoy the teaching of so great a man, giving the highest thanks to the immortal God, who has sent into his harvest such workers, who devote all their care, diligence, effort and zeal not to scattering but to gathering in the crops. Farewell, most happily.

units.la: T ne miretur aliquis, in haec nostra scripta incidens, quae me causae impulerint, adeóque permouerint, vt hanc disputationem de Excommunicatione mouerim; originem & occasionem motae disceptationis, breuiter & verè exponam. Anni exacti sunt plus-minus sexdecim, ex quo nonnulli febre quadam excommunicatoria, (quam titulo disciplinae ecclesiasticae ornabant, & sanctam atque à Deo praeceptam Ecclesiae, contendebant) correpti sunt, quam vehementer toti Ecclesiae maximè afficare cupiebant. Rationem eius hanc esse aiebant, vt certi Presbyteri Ecclesiae totius nomine sederent, & qui ad coenam digne, vel indignè accedere possint, iudicarent. Mirabar eos tum haec agitare consilia, cùm neque excommunicandos, neque excommunicatores idoneos haberemus. Etenim vix trigesima populi pars doctrinam intelligebat, & approbabat: coeteri omnes hostes nobis erant infestissimi: adeò vt nullus mente praeditus non prospiceret, periculosam multitudinis scissionem necessario ex ea re consequuturam. Proinde non hoc mihi tunc videbatur quaerendum, quo modo è societate Ecclesiae aliqui exturbarentur: sed contrarium potius agendum iudicabam, vt quo modo plurimi ad veritatis cognitionem adducerentur, inque Ecclesiam includerentur, ratio iniretur. Quos verò praeesse oportuisset, neque aetate & vsu, neque ingenio & iudicio, neque moribus & auctoritate tantùm caeteris praestabant, vt rem tantam cum dignitate sustinere posse ꝟiderentur. Quocirca cum absque pernicie & euersione Ecclesiae obtineri non posse ꝟiderem, quod ꝟehementer illi cupiebant, monui soepius, ꝟt rem accuratè perpenderent, nec temerè aliquid inchoarent, cuius eos deinde frustrà poeniteret. Etsi autem in sacris literis præceptam excommunicationem tunc opinabar, modum tamen, quem nobis proponebant, mandatum in eis non reperiebam. Quare cum modum nobis liberum reliquisse ꝟideretur Christus, de ꝟia & ratione, quae nostris rebus esset aptior, minúsque turbarum secum traheret, ipse quoque sedulò cogitabam. Quod eò faciebam studiosiùs, quo exitiosiorem Christianitati hanc rem non olim tantùm, sed etiam hodiè fuisse obseruaueram.
units.tr: Lest anyone be surprised to find himself reading these writings of mine, I will briefly and truthfully set out what causes moved me to write this disputation on excommunication, and the origin and occasion of the controversy. About sixteen years ago some people were seized by a certain excommunicatory fever, which they dressed up under the title of church discipline, and which they insisted was holy and commanded by God for the Church. They were very eager to impose it on the whole Church. Its purpose, they said, was that certain elders should sit in the name of the whole Church and judge who might come to the Lord's Supper worthily or unworthily. I was amazed that they were pursuing such plans then, since we had neither people fit to be excommunicated nor fit excommunicators. Indeed, scarcely a thirtieth part of the people understood and approved the doctrine, and all the rest were our most bitter enemies. So no one with sense could fail to see that a dangerous split of the multitude would necessarily follow from the business. Therefore it did not seem to me then that the question should be how some people might be thrown out of the fellowship of the Church. I judged that the opposite should be done: a method should be found by which very many might be brought to the knowledge of the truth and included in the Church. Those who ought to have presided did not stand out from the rest so clearly in age and experience, in talent and judgement, in character and authority, that they seemed able to sustain so great a matter with dignity. Therefore, since I saw that what they so vehemently desired could not be obtained without ruin and overthrow of the Church, I often warned them to weigh the matter carefully and not to begin anything rashly, which they would afterwards regret in vain. Although at that time I supposed that excommunication was commanded in Holy Scripture, I did not find in it the mandate for the method they were proposing to us. Therefore, since Christ seemed to have left us free to choose a way and method better suited to our situation and bringing less disorder with it, I too thought about this diligently. I did so the more eagerly because I had observed that this matter had been ruinous to Christianity not only in former times but even today.

units.la: Dum in hac ꝟersor cogitatione, & quid ꝟeteres super hac rescripsissent, exquiro, infirmioráque apud eos omnia cóperio, quàm mihi persuaseram, de tota re non nihil dubitare coactus sum. Consului mox etiam Scholasticos, apud quos nihil inueni melius. Ab his ad <bl>Re-</bl> <bl>centiores</bl> me contuli. Sed ne apud hos quidem exactius & firmius aliquid deprehendi: imò manifeste eos inter se in quibusdam dissentire animaduerti: quod me multò reddidit attentiorem. Ergò reliquis interpretibus ad sacras literas redi: atque inter legendum pro captu meo diligenter notaui, quid dissentaneum ꝟel consentaneum receptae opinioni esset. In qua re non ꝟulgariter me adiuuit contemplatio status <bl>Reipublicae</bl> & Ecclesiae Iudaicae. Sic enim apud me cogitabam: Deus ipse testatur Deut. 4. populum suum statuta, & leges habere tam iustas & sapientes, ꝟt cum illis nullarum gentium instituta, nullius Reipublicae sanctiones, nullae ordinationes, tiones, quantumuis sapienter excogitatae, contendere possint. Proinde necesse est, ut praeclarissimè, sapientissimeque disposita sit Ecclesia, quae ad Iudaicae formam proximè accedit. At in hac ita fuerunt constitutae res à Deo, ut duo diuersa de moribus iudicia, Politicum, & Ecclesiasticum, nusquàm reperiantur. Quid igitur prohibet, quominùs nunc quoque Ecclesia, cui clementissimus Deus Christianum largitus est Magistratum, una gubernatione contenta esse possit?
units.tr: While I was turning this over in my mind, and inquiring what the ancients had written on this subject, I found everything among them weaker than I had persuaded myself, and I was forced to have some doubts about the whole matter. I soon consulted the Scholastics too, but found nothing better among them. From them I turned to more recent writers. But I did not find anything more exact or firm among these either; indeed I noticed that they clearly disagreed among themselves on certain points, which made me much more attentive. So I returned to Holy Scripture, leaving the other interpreters, and as I read, I noted carefully, as far as my capacity allowed, what was inconsistent with or consistent with the accepted opinion. In this matter the consideration of the state of the Jewish commonwealth and Church helped me not a little. For I reasoned thus: God himself testifies in Deuteronomy 4 that his people had statutes and laws so just and wise that the institutions of no nation, the sanctions of no commonwealth, and no ordinances, however wisely devised, could compete with them. Therefore the Church, which comes closest to the Jewish form, must necessarily be arranged most excellently and wisely. But among the Jews, things were so established by God that two different judgements about morals, the civil and the ecclesiastical, are found nowhere. What then prevents the Church, to which the most merciful God has given a Christian magistrate, from being content with a single government?

units.la: Contuli deinde cum uiris bonis, pijs, & doctis cogitationes meas, eósque, ut non obiter tantùm causam expenderent, hortatus sum. Videri enim mihi minimè necessarium, ut duo ponantur capita in uno visibilis Ecclesiae corpore, quorum imperia, decreta, & gubernationes diuersae sint bactenus, ut unius rectio alterius curationi non sit subiecta, sed utriusque gubernatio in suo genere summa exstat. Equidem Senatum Ecclesiasticum sive Presbyterium, sic uolebant ordinari, ut summum ius haberet uitia puniendi, in ipsis etiam Magistratibus: attamen poenis non corporalibus, sed prohibitione Sacramentorum priuata primùm, deinde, si parùm sic proficeretur, solenni & publica. Ego uerò putare me dixi, unum à Deo constitutum Magistratum, flagitiosos non minus hodie coërcere omnes posse, quàm olim potuerit. Exemplo mihi proponebam illustrissimum Salomonis Regnum, quod Ecclesiae Christi in hac terra regnantis, veluti quidam typus esset. Neque sub hoc, neque sub Mose, vel Iudicibus, vel aliis Regibus, vel optimátum vocata procuratione duo nos ita discrepantia iudicia inuenire. Natura negat, (inquit Musculus) in eodem populo duas authenticas gubernationes, quarum una non sit alteri subiecta. Non sum ab illis, quibuscum contuli, parùm adiutus : partim quia nonnulla quàm ego rectiùs obseruarunt, partim quia de alijs quibusdam exactiùs cogitandi occasionem praebuerunt.
units.tr: Then I conferred my thoughts with good, pious and learned men, and urged them to weigh the case not merely in passing. For it seemed to me by no means necessary that two heads should be set up in one body of the visible Church, whose commands, decrees and governments have hitherto been different, so that the rule of one is not subject to the care of the other, but the government of each stands supreme in its own kind. Indeed, they wished the ecclesiastical senate or presbytery to be ordained in such a way that it would have the highest right to punish vices, even in the magistrates themselves. Yet the penalties were to be not bodily but first private, by prohibition from the sacraments, and then, if this did little good, solemn and public. I for my part said that I thought the one magistrate instituted by God could restrain all wrongdoers today no less than it could in former times. I set before myself as an example the most illustrious kingdom of Solomon, which was, as it were, a certain type of the Church of Christ reigning on this earth. Neither under this king, nor under Moses, nor under the judges, nor under other kings, nor under a government called aristocratic, do we find two such discordant judgements. Nature denies, says Musculus, that in the same people there are two authentic governments, one of which is not subject to the other. I was not helped as much as I might have been by those with whom I conferred, partly because some of them observed things more rightly than I did, and partly because they gave me occasion to think more exactly about certain other matters.

units.la: Interim quietum me continui : nec cum quoquam hac de re contendi, à quo non pronocarer. Pronocatus etiam moderatissimè semper respòdi: propterea quod neque Vtile, neque necessarium videbatur Ecclesias nostras hac disputatione turbare, dum nemo illis palam formulam iflam administrationis obtrudere sciretur. Illi verò qui longè putant esse suauius ac dulcius imperare, quàm parere, non sic quiuerunt, sed quibuscunque potuerunt arti-bus (quod postea cognoui) sanctissimo Principi conati sunt persuadere, vt aliquid tale conaretur in Ecclesias nostras inuehere. Ac nisi obstitissent alia quaedam, forte persuasuri fuerat. Quibus interim cōuitys me (quèsibi nō consentire, & ne voti compotes fierent, operâ da re non nesciebant) vbique prosciderunt, nõattinet hoc loco referre.
units.tr: Meanwhile I kept myself quiet and did not dispute about this matter with anyone who did not challenge me. When I was challenged, I always answered with great moderation, because it seemed neither useful nor necessary to disturb our churches with this disputation, so long as no one was known to be openly forcing that system of government upon them. But those who think it far more pleasant and sweeter to command than to obey did not rest, but, by whatever arts they could (as I later learned), tried to persuade the most holy Prince to attempt something of this kind against our churches. And had certain other things not stood in their way, perhaps they would have succeeded in persuading him. Meanwhile they tore me to pieces everywhere with insults, because I did not agree with them and they knew well enough that I was working to prevent them from getting their way; it is not worth reporting these here.

units.la: Accidit deinde, vt Anglus quidam, qui propter rem Vestiarium, ex Anglia ferebatur excessisse, Doctoris titulo cuperet insigniri, & de adiaphoris ac vestibus disputationem proponeret. Hanc Theologi admittere noluerunt, ne scilicet Anglos offenderent, (tametsi quaedam in posterioribus quoque thesibus de hac re continentur) vt autem nostrae res turbarentur, pro nihilo, vt videtur, duxerunt. Quare inter alias hanc thesim proposuit, oportere in quauis rectè instituta Ecclesia hanc seruari procurationem, in qua ministri cum suo delectu ad eam rem Presbyterio ius teneant, quosuis peccantes, etiam Principes excommunicandi. Quanquam metuebam decertationem hanc non frustra institutam fuisse, sperabam tamen nihil aliud fore, quàm ordinariam disputationem, quales non ad decidendas controuersias, fias, sed ad inuentutem exercendam, & ad dyudicanda ingenia eorum, qui publicos petunt honores, institutae sunt. Itaque nec ego aliquid monere Volui, nec propter negotia, interesse potui. Hortatus quoque sum alios, quos contrà disputaturos videbam, vt maiorem haberent Ecclesiae rationem, quàm imprudentiae paucorum. Disputauit nihilominus Vnus atque alter: quos fi deinde Vnà mecum non vocauissent profanos, Satanicos, Diabolicos, turbatores, hostes pietatis, phanaticos, &c. nil aliud, quàm ordinaria disceptatio fuisset.
units.tr: Then it happened that a certain Englishman, who was said to have left England because of the vestiarian controversy, wished to be honoured with the title of Doctor and proposed a disputation on adiaphora and vestments. The theologians were unwilling to admit this, no doubt so as not to offend the English (although certain points on this matter are contained in the later theses too). But they seem to have thought little of stirring up our affairs. Therefore, among other theses, he proposed this one: that in any rightly constituted Church this arrangement ought to be kept, in which the ministers, with their own choice for that purpose, have the right in the presbytery to excommunicate any sinners whatever, even princes. Although I feared that this dispute had not been instituted without reason, I hoped nevertheless that it would be nothing more than an ordinary disputation, of the kind instituted not to decide controversies, but to exercise the young and to test the talents of those who seek public honours. So I neither wished to advise anything, nor was I able to attend because of my affairs. I also urged others, whom I saw were going to dispute against it, to have greater regard for the Church than for the imprudence of a few. Nevertheless one or two did dispute; and had they not then called us together as profane, satanic, diabolical, disturbers, enemies of piety, fanatics, and so on, the whole thing would have been nothing more than an ordinary debate.

units.la: Equidem, quod ad me attinet, sanctè affirmare possum, me nunquam induxisse in animum meum de hac re, & controuersia aliquid scribere, priusquam eos tam intemperanter publicè, priuatimque agere audiui, & vidi. Quippe putaui diutius silere, nil esse aliud, quàm veritatem prodere. Quia Verò tunc eram praeter solitum occupatissimus (propter milites, qui tunc, anno videlicet 1568. cum Duce Casimiro &c. ex Gallia Varijs morbis affecti, redibant) cogitationes meas frustillatim, vt in tantis negotijs, quouis tempore quaelibet occurrebat, annotaui. Quas licet perturbatè congessissem nulloque ordine certo, propter dictam causam distribuissem, partim dum transcribebantur, partim mox atque transcriptae fuerant, nonnullis quorum iudicio plurimum tribuebam, & à quibus me nõ vulgariter amari non sine causa quidem, & false tamen, credebam, examinandas, iudicandasque dedi: simúlque rogaui, vt si quid non rectè affirmatum, firmèue probatum inuenirent, melioribus rationibus liberè confutarent. Si nihil aliud, hoc saltem impetraturum me sperabam, vt visis argumentis nostris mitescerent aliquatum, & non sine argumentis abipsis dissentire, cogitarent. Vnus ex duobus primis, quibus-
units.tr: For my part, I can solemnly affirm that I never brought into my mind to write anything on this matter and controversy until I had heard and seen them acting so intemperately, in public and in private. Indeed I thought it would be betraying the truth to keep silent any longer. But since at that time I was unusually busy (because of the soldiers who were then returning from France with Duke Casimir, etc., afflicted with various diseases, in the year 1568), I jotted down my thoughts piece by piece, as each occurred to me at any time amid such great affairs. Although I had collected them in a confused way and, for the reason mentioned, had arranged them without any fixed order, partly while they were being copied out and partly as soon as they had been copied, I gave them to some men whose judgement I valued highly, and by whom I believed I was loved not ordinarily, and indeed rightly, though falsely as it turned out, to be examined and judged. At the same time I asked that if they found anything not rightly affirmed or firmly proved, they should freely refute it with better arguments. If nothing else, I hoped to obtain this much: that, having seen our arguments, they would grow somewhat milder and would consider dissenting from them not without arguments of their own. Of the two first men with whom I had decided to confer particularly, one

units.la: cum decreueram praecipuè conferre, de quatuor partibus, tres Vidit, ac legit, priusquàm omnia descripta suissent. De quibus sententiam rogatus, postmodum se disturum promittebat, Vbi totum perlegisset. Obiter tamen de fermento nescio quid proponebat, ac Veteris Ecclesiae consensum magni aestimandum putabat: demum alia quaedam talia adferebat, ex quibus facillimum mihi erat de sententia animoque eius iudicare. Intellexi eodem fere tempore hunc ipsum de Excommunicatione Tractatu scripsisse, in quo sententiam communem probaret. Quo cognito dubium non erat, quid responsurus esset. Noram enim eum ab eo, quod semel affirmauisset absque periculi metu non discessurum. Itaque cum haec ipsa, quae opponebat, in parte postrema confutata essent, alteri totum obtuli: quo mihi amiciorem Viuere neminem putabā. Is non tantum fastidiosè (nescio Vtrum admonitus prius fuerit) librum à me accipiebat, sed aperte negabat se legere velle: etsi Vrgerem, inuitum hoc se adigi, affirmabat. Reliqui ei nihilominus per aliquot dies, & quanto studio, quantisque precibus potui, Vt perlegeret, mihique suum de eo iudicium exponeret, oraui. Quod cum frustrà me ab eo flagitare certis argumentis cognoscissem, post dies plus minus duodecim ab eo repetiui, Vt aliorum iudicia exquirerem. Caeterum, quia scriptum illud longius erat, quàm Vt breui tempore à pluribus perlegi posset, in thesis quasdam contraxi: quo facilius pluribus communicari posset. Cecidit consilium hoc in parte non infoeliciter. Nam & complurium per Germaniam clarissimorum & summorum Theologorum sententias perspexi, quod Vnicè cupiebam: & sic inter studiosos fuerunt, Vt, qui me rogante legere noluerant, contra suam Voluntatem deinde legere coacti sint. Vt porrò constaret omnibus, me praeter nudam ve‐ ritatem nihil quaerere aliud, Praefationem praefixi, in qua duo haec petiui: Primum quidem, ut omnes diligen‐ ter singula examinarent, & ad sacrarum literarum tru‐ tinam expenderent, ac si me in errore esse viderent, ab eo me liberarent, quò ipse quoque alios liberare possem. Pollicitus sum ex toto corde (testor Deum cordium scru‐ tatorem) me ei, qui errorem mihi monstrasset, coràm Deo & hominibus gratias acturum. Quoniam autem futurum praenuntiebam, quod postea accidit, rogaui se‐ cundo loco, ut si quid reprehendere constituissent, illis modis ac locis facerent, quibus & mea interpretari, & iniustè damnata, iustè tueri mihi liceret. Etsi enim me constantissimum sibi amicum, & ad omnia officia para‐tissimum experti semper fuissent, vix tamen sperare ex antegressis poteram, eos sic mecum acturos, ut cum ipsis ego egeram. Nec opinione mea sum falsus. Etenim ex amicissimis, ut stultè credideram, hostes mihi repente facti sunt, adeò, ut ne alloquio quidem suo dignarentur amplius, quantumuis nec dicto, nec facto eos vllo per omnem vitam lesissem, sed optimè de eis mereri semper studuissem, quod adhuc facere cogito. Deo interim gra‐ tias agebam, quòd in re tali potius, quàm alia quapiam, de fide & beneuolentia eorum periculum facere conti‐ gisset.
units.tr: When I had decided to confer with him chiefly about four parts of the work, he saw and read three of them before everything had been copied out. Asked for his opinion on these, he promised to give it once he had read the whole thing through. In passing he put forward something about leaven and insisted that the consensus of the Early Church deserved great weight. Eventually he added certain other such points, from which it was very easy for me to judge his view and his mind. I learned at about the same time that he himself had written a treatise on excommunication, in which he defended the common opinion. Once I knew this, there was no doubt what he would reply, for I knew that he would not abandon what he had once affirmed without fear of danger. So when these same objections had been refuted in the last part, I gave the whole book to another man, whom I thought the most friendly of anyone living to me. He not only accepted the book from me with disdain (I do not know whether he had been warned beforehand), but openly said that he did not want to read it. Although I pressed him, he declared that he was being forced to do this against his will. Nevertheless, for several days I kept asking him, with all the zeal and entreaties I could muster, to read it through and set out his judgement of it for me. When I learned by certain signs that I was asking him in vain, about twelve days later I asked him again, this time to let me seek the judgements of others. Since that writing was longer than could be read through quickly by many people, I drew it up into a set of theses, so that it could be shared more easily with many. This plan turned out not unhappily in part. For I came to know the opinions of several most distinguished and eminent theologians throughout Germany, which was my one great desire; and among the students, those who had refused to read at my request were afterwards compelled to read against their will. So that it might be clear to everyone that I seek nothing but the bare truth, I prefaced the work with a Preface, in which I asked two things. First, that everyone should examine each point diligently and weigh it in the scales of Holy Scripture, and if they saw me to be in error, that they should free me from it, so that I might in turn free others. I promised with my whole heart (I call God, the searcher of hearts, to witness) that I would give thanks before God and men to whoever showed me my error. Since I foretold what later came to pass, I asked, secondly, that if they resolved to find fault with anything, they should do so in the ways and places in which I might be allowed to explain my own words and to defend what had been unjustly condemned. For although they had always found me their most constant friend and most ready for every kind of service, I could hardly hope from past experience that they would deal with me as I had dealt with them. Nor was I mistaken in my expectation. For those who, as I had foolishly believed, were my closest friends suddenly became my enemies, to such an extent that they no longer deigned even to speak with me, although I had never harmed them in word or deed throughout my whole life, but had always striven to deserve well of them, as I still intend to do. Meanwhile I gave thanks to God that in such a matter I had put their faithfulness and goodwill to the test rather than in some other matter.

units.la: Non quieuerunt interim: sed postquàm se per Ma‐ gistratum frustrà viderunt tentauisse, Theses ex stu‐ dioforum manibus extorquere, aliud auf sunt: nempè sub specie legum, quae nullibi extant, petierunt, ut, quemadmodum Theologi in dogmata & iura aliorum nihil tentent, ità etiam aliis professoribus mandaretur, ut à Theologorum schola abstineant. Si fuisset hoc ante annos sexaginta petitum, tolerabile videri poterat: nunc quo modo ferri possit, iudicent alij. An solis illis, qui pro aliquot centenis florenis annuis Theologiam docent, dicendum est, Scrutamini Scripturas. : Probate Spiritus num ex Deo sint. Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete? & quae huius generis alia legimus? Putauì communem esse doctrinam Theologiam Christianorum omnium, ideóque publicè eam vbique doceri. Quid aliud petunt, cum, vt ab eorum schola sic abstineamus, petunt, quo modo ipsi in iura, & dogmata aliarum facultatum nihil tentent? Non puto eos hoc velle, vt non audiamus eorum praelectiones, aut in locum illum non intremus discendi gratiâ: praesertim cum propter meas theses modestissimè propositas id petierint. Quis quaesò illis Medicinae, Philosophiae, Linguarum, & Iuris studio interdixit? An quia haec ipsi studia non curant, nos Theologiae studium negligere similiter debemus? Si non plus incommodi ex ignoratione Sacrarum litterarum, quàm ex insciria illarum rerum acciperemus, gratificari ipsis forte possemus. Facilè vicerint, si contradicere statutis eorum nulli concessum sit. Idem iam olim Romanenses à nobis petierunt, ac paulò meliore iure petierunt. At ego neutris gratificari possum, dum aliud me iubet Seruator meus Christus.
units.tr: They did not rest in the meantime. But after they saw that they had tried in vain, through the magistrate, to wrest the theses out of the hands of the students, they tried something else: under the guise of laws that exist nowhere, they demanded that just as theologians attempt nothing against the doctrines and rights of others, so too the other professors should be ordered to keep away from the school of the theologians. If this had been demanded sixty years ago, it might have seemed tolerable; how it can be borne now, let others judge. Or must it be said that only those who teach theology for some hundreds of florins a year are told, "Search the Scriptures" and "Test the spirits, whether they are of God", "Prove all things; hold fast to what is good", and whatever other sayings of this kind we read? I had thought that the theology of all Christians was a common doctrine, and that it should therefore be taught publicly everywhere. What else do they seek, when they ask us to keep away from their school, just as they themselves attempt nothing against the rights and doctrines of other faculties? I do not think they want us not to hear their lectures, or not to enter that place for the sake of learning; especially since they asked this on account of my theses, which were proposed most modestly. Who, I ask, has forbidden them the study of medicine, philosophy, languages and law? Or because they themselves do not care for these studies, must we likewise neglect the study of theology? If we suffered no more harm from ignorance of Holy Scripture than they do from ignorance of those subjects, perhaps we could gratify them. They would easily win if it were granted to no one to contradict their rules. The Romanists once demanded the same of us, and with a somewhat better right. But I can gratify neither side, while my Saviour Christ commands me otherwise.

units.la: Nihil interim me mouet, quod dicunt, dedecere me Theologica tractare: meque sic exîstimationi meae parum recte consulere: forte quia sine mercede veritatem inquiro. Etenim si stipendio conductus Theologica docerem, nihil secundum ipsos, ab officio, & munere meo in hac parte alieni facerem. Ego vero nihil aliud cupio, quàm veritatem intelligi, Deum glorificari, & me pudefieri potius, quàm vt veritas prematur. Non frustra dixit alicubi Christus, illos credere non posse, qui mutuaam gloriam quaerunt, neglecta Dei gloria.
units.tr: Meanwhile I am not moved by their saying that it is unbecoming for me to treat theological matters, and that in this way I look poorly after my own reputation, perhaps because I seek the truth without reward. For if I taught theology for hire, by their own account I would do nothing alien to my office and calling in this respect. I, for my part, desire nothing else than that the truth be understood, God be glorified, and that I be put to shame rather than that the truth be suppressed. Christ rightly said somewhere that those cannot believe who seek glory from one another and neglect the glory of God.

units.la: Ergo cum ne hoc quidem ex sententia cecidissFet, conceptumque odium continere non possent, argumentis oppugnare coeperunt: quae non sine atrocibus criminationibus, quamuis opportunitate oblata, proposuerunt. Quae etsi mihi à pluribus indicarentur, facile tamen, pacis causa, contempsi, & speraui futurum, ut, cum impetus ille animi languescere coepisset, atque ira aliquantulum deferbuisset, aequiores nobis redderentur. Verum tamen nimis falsus hic etiam sum. Etenim post quintum fere menses, neque de odio aliquid remiserunt, neque impugnare nostra partim conuitijs, partim calumniis, partim nescio quibus ratiunculis sophisticis, desiterunt. Quam ob rem Theses centum sub incudem revocavi, quas redegi ad septuaginta quinque, & suo ordine collocavi, quae de principio, non ubi oportebat posuerant, sed ubi occurrerant. Exposui in ijsdem nonnulla planius: & probaui etiam quaedam firmius: denique operam dedi, ut veritatis amantibus, plene satisfacerem, quod in scripto tam breui, hoc à me praestari potuit.
units.tr: So when not even this had gone as they wished, and they could not contain the hatred they had conceived, they began to attack us with arguments, which they put forward, though seized upon as an opportunity, not without savage accusations. Although these were pointed out to me by many people, I easily disregarded them for the sake of peace, and I hoped that when that rush of feeling had begun to subside and their anger had somewhat cooled, they would become more fair towards us. But in this too I was far too mistaken. For after about five months they neither relaxed their hatred nor ceased to assail our arguments, partly with abuse, partly with calumnies, partly with I know not what petty sophistical reasonings. For this reason I called my hundred theses back to the anvil, and reduced them to seventy-five, and set them in their proper order, since they had been placed not where they belonged but where they happened to occur. In these I explained some points more plainly, and also confirmed certain points more firmly; finally I took care to satisfy fully those who love the truth, so far as this could be done in a writing so brief.

units.la: EXPLICATIO
units.tr: EXPLICATIO

units.la: Grauissimæ quæstionis, utrum excommunicatio, quatenus religionem intelligentes, & amplex- antes, à Sacramentorum vsu propter admissum [illegible, ~10 letters] facinus arcet, mandato nitatur Diuino, an excogitata sit ab hominibus?
units.tr: A most weighty question: whether excommunication, insofar as it keeps from the use of the Sacraments those who understand and embrace the religion, on account of an admitted [illegible] crime, rests on divine command, or whether it was devised by men?

units.la: Thesis prima.
units.tr: First thesis.

units.la: Excommunicationis nomen videtur ex 1. ad Corinth. cap. 10. desumptum esse: atque significare à communione illa, quæ ibidem corpus Christi nominatur. Sanè Excommunicatio nunc ab omnibus fere definitur exclusione è societate & communione fidelium.
units.tr: The name "excommunication" seems to be taken from 1 Corinthians 10 and to signify exclusion from that communion which is there called the body of Christ. Indeed, excommunication is now defined by almost everyone as exclusion from the fellowship and communion of the faithful.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Est autem duplex fidelium societas, interna scilicet ac spiritualis, & externa seu visibilis, ac politica. Quam recentes quidam Pontificij tertiam comminiscuntur, nec apte fingitur, nec ad præsentem causam pertinet.
units.tr: The fellowship of the faithful is twofold: internal, that is spiritual, and external or visible, that is political. The third kind, which some recent Papists have invented, is both poorly conceived and irrelevant to the present question.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Tantum verò inter vtramq; discrimen est, vt, qui in altera continetur, non etiam comprehendatur necessariò in altera. Nam vt membrum Christi esse potest, qui iniustè ex visibili aliqua Ecclesia eiectus est, aut inter infideles habitareue cogitur: ita qui in visibili coetu numerantur, non omnes etiam membra viva sunt Christi. Ex quo sequitur, discrepare res illas posse, quæ vni nos coniungunt, non alteri: & ab vna nos abiungunt, non ab altera.
units.tr: There is so great a difference between the two that a person who belongs to the one is not necessarily included in the other. For a man may be a living member of Christ even though he has been unjustly cast out of some visible Church, or is forced to live among unbelievers; and conversely, not all who are counted in the visible assembly are living members of Christ. From this it follows that the things which join us to the one may not join us to the other, and the things which separate us from the one may not separate us from the other.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Ac membra quidem Christi efficimur, id est, internae spiritualiq; Christi, & fidelium societati coniungimur, per solam fidem, quae per charitatem est efficax: & ex eadem hac per solam infidelitatem excidimus. Proinde non potest nos huic inserere, aut ex eadem excludere, nisi qui fidem viuā nobis donare, eandémque nobis iterùm auferre potest.
units.tr: We are indeed made members of Christ, that is, joined to Christ and to the spiritual fellowship of the faithful, through faith alone, which is effective through love; and by unbelief alone we fall away from that same fellowship. Therefore no one can insert us into it, or exclude us from it, except the one who can give us living faith and take it away from us again.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Externae verò visibilisq; ecclesiae consortes reddimur, eiusdem fidei professione, eiusdémque doctrinę approbatione, deniqe eorundem Sacramentorum vsurpatione. In quo tria haec insunt: is tantisper, dum ei insunt, inter membra externi fidelium coetus computatur: etiamsi ad internam spiritus & mentis communionem non pertingat.
units.tr: We become partakers of the external and visible Church by professing the same faith, by approving the same doctrine, and finally by partaking of the same Sacraments. Three things are involved in this: a person is counted among the members of the external assembly of the faithful for as long as these things are present in him, even though he does not attain to inward communion of spirit and mind.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Ergo qui ex Ecclesiae communione externa eijcitur, (id est, qui excommunicatur) vel ab omnibus hisce tribus: vel à duobus: vel ab vno tantùm remouetur. Sed à duobus primis, nempe à confessione fidei, & à Christianae doctrinae approbatione (sub qua volo comprehendi etiam verbi seu doctrinae auditionem) repelli nullus debet: quin potius huc inuitandi & quauis ratione adducendi sunt omnes.
units.tr: Therefore, one who is cast out of the external communion of the Church (that is, one who is excommunicated) is removed either from all three of these, or from two, or from only one. But no one ought to be repelled from the first two, namely the confession of faith and the approval of Christian doctrine (under which I wish to include also the hearing of the Word or doctrine); on the contrary, all are to be invited to these and brought to them by every means.

units.la: Quocirca relinquitur, vt, qui excommunicatur, à sola (ex tribus commemoratis) Sacramentorum participatione prohibeatur. Huic, vtrum inseparabiliter cohaereat priuati commercij negatio, an separari possit, postea considerabimus. Alias poenas non pertinere ad substantiam excommunicationis huius, certum est. Etenim possunt eandem etiam non excommunicatis infligi, & excommunicatis non infligi.
units.tr: It follows, then, that the one who is excommunicated is forbidden only the participation in the Sacraments (from the three mentioned). Whether the denial of private fellowship necessarily adheres to this, or can be separated from it, we will consider later. That other penalties do not belong to the substance of this excommunication is certain. For they can be inflicted on those who are not excommunicated, and not inflicted on those who are.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Itaque malè Pontificij praeter hanc excommunicationem (quam ipsi minorem appellarunt: ac sola Sacramentorum negatione recté definierunt) aliam insuper addiderunt, quam maiorem & Anathema vocarunt: atque contra apertam scripturam interdictione Templorum, priuati commercij, & actus cuiusuis liciti definierunt. Quoniam Apostolus in 1. Corinth. 14. palàm ostendit, neque Ethnicos, neque alios quoslibet à Diuini verbi auditione, lectione, gratiarum actionibus ac precibus Christianorum prohibitos fuisse.
units.tr: Accordingly the Papists have wrongly added, besides this excommunication (which they themselves called the lesser, and rightly defined as the denial of the Sacraments alone), another, which they called the greater and "anathema," and which they defined as the interdiction of temples, of private fellowship, and of every lawful act, contrary to the plain Scripture. For the Apostle shows plainly in 1 Corinthians 14 that neither heathens nor any others were forbidden to hear the divine Word, to read it, or to join in the thanksgivings and prayers of Christians.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Ex dictis liquet, excommunicationem nihil aliud esse, quàm publicam & solennem Sacramentorum, praesertim coenae Dominicae (quam priuatim Apostolus communionem (κοινωνίαν) appellat: vt de principio dictum fuit) interdictionem, praeeunte Seniorum cognitione: quò peccantes resipiscant, rursusque ad Sacramentorum perceptionem admittantur.
units.tr: From what has been said it is clear that excommunication is nothing other than the public and solemn interdiction from the Sacraments, especially from the Lord's Supper (which the Apostle calls, privately, communion [κοινωνίαν], as was said at the beginning), by the judgment of the elders going before, so that sinners may repent and be readmitted to the reception of the Sacraments.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Hic iam oritur quaestio, vtrùm aliquis propter commissum peccatum, aut vitam impurè actam, siquidem, vsurpare Sacramenta cum caeteris Christianis cupiat, ab eorundem vsu & perceptione sit remouendus? Quaestio de eo proponitur, qui eandem fidem nobiscum profitetur: Ecclesiae per Baptismum insertus est: atque in doctrina ab eadem non dissentit, (vt in 5. posuimus) sed in sola vita & moribus errat. Hoc ergò quaeritur, vtrùm in sacris litteris vel mandatum vel exemplum aliquod exstet, quo tales iubeantur aut docentur à Sacramentis submoueri?
units.tr: Here now arises the question: whether anyone, on account of a sin committed or a life lived impurely, should be removed from the use and reception of the Sacraments, if indeed he desires to partake of the Sacraments with other Christians? The question is put concerning one who professes the same faith with us, has been received into the Church through Baptism, and does not dissent from its doctrine (as we laid down in the fifth thesis), but errs only in his life and morals. The question, therefore, is this: does any command or example exist in the holy writings by which such persons are ordered or taught to be kept away from the Sacraments?

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Responsio nostra est, nullum exstare: sed contraria potiùs tum exempla, tum praecepta passim in Biblijs occurrere. Etenim apud Mosen lib. Exodi cap. 12. & 23. & 34. Num. 9. Deut. 16. scriptum legimus, ter debere coràm Deo singulis annis comparere omnem masculum circumcisum: videlicet in festo Azymorum, Hebdomadum, & Tabernaculorum. Nam & peregrinos (modò essent circumcisi) iubebat lex celebrare Pascha vnà cum Iudaeis. Mandatur etiam immundis, & peregrè profectis, vt eodem die secundi mensis, eodémque modo cum Iudaeis Pascha edant. Additur quoque capitis poena afficiendum esse illum, quicunque Paschae celebrationem neglexerit: qui, scilicet, neque peregrinetur, neque immundus sit. Quocirca voluit ac iussit Deus, omnes circumcisos celebrare Pascha: nec vel ab hoc Sacramento vel ab alijs ritibus, ceremonijs, ac sacrificijs quenquam exclusit, immundis exceptis.
units.tr: Our answer is that none exists; rather, in the Bibles, examples and precepts to the contrary occur everywhere. For in Moses, in the book of Exodus chapters 12, 23 and 34, in Numbers 9, and in Deuteronomy 16, we read that every circumcised male was to appear before God three times a year, namely at the feast of Unleavened Bread, of Weeks, and of Tabernacles. For the law also commanded strangers (provided they were circumcised) to celebrate the Passover together with the Jews. It is also commanded that the unclean and those who had gone on a journey should eat the Passover with the Jews on the same day of the second month and in the same manner. It is further added that the penalty of death is to be inflicted on anyone who neglects the celebration of the Passover, namely one who is neither on a journey nor unclean. Therefore God willed and commanded that all the circumcised should celebrate the Passover, and he excluded no one, except the unclean, from this Sacrament or from the other rites, ceremonies and sacrifices.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: In Leuitico diuersa imperantur Sacrificia pro diuersitate peccatorum (siue per ignorantiam & errorem, siue voluntate, & studio commissorum) quibus eiusmodi peccata expiarent, qui ea admisissent. Similiter iubet Deus Deut. 14. fine exceptione malorum, Omnibus, vt decimas suas Hierosolymis edant coràm Domino: causamque addit, vt sic discant timere Dominum Iehouam omnibus diebus suis. Erant ergo Sacramenta incitamenta ad pietatem: & proinde ab ijs nemo arcebatur, sed ad ea magis inuitabantur omnes.
units.tr: Leviticus prescribes various sacrifices according to the variety of sins, whether committed through ignorance and error or wilfully and deliberately, by which those who had committed such sins might make atonement. Likewise God commands, Deut. 14, without exception of the wicked, that all people should bring their tithes to Jerusalem before the Lord, and he adds the reason, that they may thus learn to fear the Lord their God all their days. The sacraments, then, were incentives to godliness, and therefore no one was barred from them, but all were rather invited to them.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Equidem nullum vnquam propter dictam causam legimus apud Indæos à Sacerdotibus, Leuitis, Prophetis, Scribis, Pharisæis, prohibitum vehire ad sacrificia, cæremonias, & Sacramenta. Sacerdotum principes, & Pharisæi pro pessimis habuerunt Christum, & Apostolos: at nusquam hoc tentauisse vel viuo vel mortuo Christo inueniemus, vt à sacrificijs & Sacramentis à Deo institutis eos repellerent. Sed nec Publicanum aliquem Iudæum, nec alium circumcisum improbè viuentè à templo & cæremonijs abegerunt. Non enim nesciebant, hoc sibi per legem non licere. Christum reprehenderunt quidem apud Matt.9.quòd cum Publicanis ederet ac biberet. At quòd cum eis in templo oraret: quòd sacrificijs & ritibus interesset: quòd cum his alijsq; omnibus Hierosolymam ad pascha celebrationē aliásq; solemnitates quotannis ascenderet: nusquam, & nunquam ei exprobrarunt. Quemadmodum etiam Sadducæos crudelissimos nebulones & sceleratissimos hæreticos adeò non conati sunt à ceremonijs suis repellere, vt eos, ad summi sacerdotij honorem conscendere permitterent. Quanto interim odio alteri alteros prosequerentur ex Iosepho, & act. Apost. patet. Obuijs vlnis amplexati fuissent (si eis licuisset) occasionem hanc vlciscendi suos hostes.
units.tr: Indeed, we never read that for this reason any man was prohibited by the Jewish priests, Levites, prophets, scribes or Pharisees from coming to the sacrifices, ceremonies and sacraments. The chief priests and the Pharisees regarded Christ and the Apostles as the worst of men, yet we never find that either while Christ was alive or after his death they tried to drive them away from the sacrifices and sacraments instituted by God. Nor did they expel from the temple and the ceremonies any Jewish publican or any other circumcised man who lived wickedly. For they did not fail to know that this was not permitted to them by the law. They did indeed find fault with Christ, Matt. 9, because he ate and drank with publicans. But that he prayed with them in the temple, that he attended the sacrifices and rites, that he went up to Jerusalem every year with these and all others for the celebration of the Passover and other solemn feasts, this they never once reproached him for. Likewise they did not try so much as to drive the Sadducees, cruel scoundrels and most wicked heretics, away from their ceremonies, but allowed them to rise to the honour of the high priesthood. Meanwhile, how great the hatred with which they pursued one another is clear from Josephus and the Acts of the Apostles. They would have embraced with open arms, had it been lawful, the opportunity to take revenge on their enemies.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Quinimò ne potuissent quidem malos à Pascha tis esu arcere: cùm non coram Sacerdotibus, sed in priuatis domibus ederetur: vt Christum quoque cum Discipulis suis celebrauisse postremum Pascha legimus. Fungebantur tunc omnes quodammodo Sacerdotis munere, vt de pascha loquens Philo Iudaeus, his verbis testatur: [Greek text illegible, ~40 letters]. Quod si in vna domo pauciores essent, quàm vt liberum agnum peredere possent, ex vicinis alios sibi quisque adiungere iubebatur, Exodi. 12. vt totum absumerent. Ratio similis in circumcisione obseruata fuisse videtur: nisi quòd non oportuit Hierosolymis tantùm circumcidi infantes, sicut pascha ibi celebrandum erat. Non memini enim me legere, sacerdotis praesentiam ad eam rem fuisse necessariam.
units.tr: Indeed they could not even have kept the wicked away from eating the Passover, since it was eaten not in the presence of priests but in private houses, as we read that Christ also celebrated his last Passover with his disciples. All of them then in a way performed the office of priest, as Philo the Jew attests in these words when speaking of the Passover: [Greek text illegible in the scan]. But if there were fewer people in one house than could eat a whole free lamb, each was ordered to join others from the neighbours, Exod. 12, so that they might consume it entirely. A similar arrangement seems to have been observed in circumcision, except that infants did not have to be circumcised only at Jerusalem, as the Passover had to be celebrated there. For I do not remember reading that the presence of a priest was necessary for that.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Idem praecursor ille Christi Iohannes Baptista constanter observauit: cùm ad se venientes Pharisaeos, & Sadducaeos (quorum mores praeclarè nouerat: unde progeniem Viperarum eos palàm nominabat) vnà cum Publicanis, aliisque cunctis baptizaret. Math. ac Luc. 3. cap. quò poenitentia prioris vitae ducti seipsos emendarent, itaque venturam Dei iram effugerent. Parùm verisimile est, hunc tantum virum, tot sceleribus coopertos, imò resurrectionem mortuorum impiè publicéque negantes, admissurum suisse, nisi sciisset à lege neminem talium excludi. Lex enim neminem arcet circumcisum, praeter leprosos aut immundos, vt antè dictum est.
units.tr: That same forerunner of Christ, John the Baptist, consistently observed the same practice: when he baptized those who came to him, Pharisees and Sadducees (whose manners he knew well, which is why he openly called them a brood of vipers), together with the Publicans and all the rest. Matt. and Luke 3. chapter. He did this so that, led by repentance of their former life, they might amend themselves and so escape the wrath of God that was coming. It is hardly credible that this great man would have admitted such people, steeped in so many crimes, and indeed men who impiously and openly denied the resurrection of the dead, unless he knew that by the law none of such people was excluded. For the law excludes no one who is circumcised, except lepers or the unclean, as was said above.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Porrò immunditia haec, erat legalis ceremonia, non erat vitae morúmq; impuritas. Quippe non qui peccatü admisisset, aut scelus perpetrasset, immundus erat: sed qui sunus, cadauer, excrementû, gonorrhoea vel menstruis laborantem, aliúdue simile attigisset, immundus erat. Hanc ob causã noluerunt praetorium ingredi Pharisaei, cùm Christû Pilato traderent occidendû, ne impedirètur Pascha ederé. Certè non sic figurauit Mosaica immunditia nostra flagitia, vt, quemadmodum illa inquinati arcebantur à Tabernaculo & consuetudine aliorum, ita haec significârit Sacramentorum negatione seu ex visibili Ecclesia exclusione coercenda, puniendáque esse: quod ex sequentibus clarissimè liquet. Primò, non puniebantur tunc celerati eadem poena cum immundis, dum vigeret illa legis immunditia, & sceleratorum simul magna effet turba. Quomodò ergo verisimile fuerit post sublatas, seu deletas hasce ceremonias, sic punienda significauisse? Secundò pugnauisset fecum Moses apertè, dum, quos per ceremonias indicabat pellendos, eos reipfa ad templum & ceremonias admittebat. Certum namque est, à Tabernaculo & coetu aliorum nullum propter vitiofitatem morum depulsum: fi iuxta legis præscriptum nec cadauer tetigisset, nec alia ratione consimili seipsum contaminauisset. Proindè figuram immundorum gerentes puniuisset, ac reipfa immundos impunitos (quod ad hanc pœnam spectat) reliquisset. Sic rem eandem simul negasset ac affirmaffet. Tertiò, erat impuritas legis qualitas & macula quædam corporis, cùm scelera sint operationes, atque in actione consistant. Causa namque radixque scelerum congenita nobiscum est, nec ab hominibus punitur, dum nullos profert fructus: alioquin omnes excommunicandi effent homines. Quippe non liberabimur ab hac animorum labe, quantifper in hac vita mortali superftites erimus. Altera verò macula corporis existens impuritas, feclufione à conuictu aliorum punitur: etiamsi fructum nullum ediderit, fiue, qui maculatus est, nihil contrà legem egerit. Opera seu peccata immundorum, fi, quatenus immundi erant, contra legem aliquid admitterent, instar aliarum transgressionum à magistratu coercebantur. Quarto confitentur aduersarij non quaelibet peccata excommunicatione vindicanda esse, cùm quamlibet immunditiam lex iubeat punire exclusione à Tabernaculo & sacrificijs publicis. Quarenon omnia scelera poterant figurare. Quintò non potest quisquam inuitus peccans excommunicari: cùm frequentissimè homines immundi fierent inuiti, &c. absque culpa sua, imò magno suo cum dolore. Quae culpa hacrebat in eo, cui noctu nolenti ac dormienti femen forte profluxisset? cuius vxori praeter spem menses crupiffent? cui liberi, vxor, parentes, moriebantur? aut alia talia vsu veniebant? Quod autem voluntaria finr flagitia, propter quae à Sacramentis depellendos esse aliquos nonnulli opinantur, nullius eget probatione. Sexto constituta fuit poena multo grauior hominem contra & praeter voluntatem suam occidenti, quam dierum aut septimanarum aliquot depulsio à Sacramentis: quae grauissimae ferme immunditiei poena erat. Quoniam igitur peccatum inuoluntarium, ac proinde leuissimum, acerbiore poena castigabatur, quàm foeditissima impuritas legalis, facile apparet, huius poenam non esse transferendam ad punienda flagitia. Septimo perspicpè euenieḃat, vt sanctissimus atque integerrimus quisque immundus fieret, & à Templi aditu & sacrificiorum visu arceretur, dum scelerosissimus aliquis ad eadem, nemine impediente, admitteretur. Quod si eadem debebat esse in Ecclesia Dei utrorumque poena, multo magis hic, quàm ille, arcendus fuerat. Octauo constat Deum nullo vel loco vel tempore absolutè prohibuisse omnem impuritatem legis. Quia enim voluit aliquos adesse morientibus: & aliàs morbo immundo infectis: item qui mortuos sepelirent: denique etiam, qui immundos purgarent (qua ratione ipsos etiam inquinari contingebat. Num. 19.) hoc etiam voluit, vt non omnis immunditia legis caueretur. At flagitia Deus omnia & omnibus: & semper prohibuit: nec vllo vel tempore vel loco flagitiose agere permisit. Nonò, mandat Deus, vt scelera igne, gladio, laqueo, lapidibus, plagis, multa, carcere, aliisque poenis similibus reprimantur: impuros iuxta legem aqua lustrari, ac similibus aliis rationibus purgari praecipit. Decimò non fuit pro scelerato damnatoque reputatus, qui iuxta legis definitionem factus fuisset, immundus, adeoque ad mortem vsque talis permansisset: vt cum feminae menstruis laborantes, aut viri gonorrhoea affecti, vel lepra, morerentur. At qui sic viuit, vt etiam moriens Excommunicatione dignus iudicari à viris bonis ac iustis possit, non poterit non improbus & impius censeri. Vndecimò, non habuit locum legis immunditia, praeterquam vno in populo & certo quoda tempore. At scelera vbique pullularunt apud omnes gentes, omni loco & tempore. Quoqirca cùm & punita sint & punienda iudicata fuerint scelera, cùm apud gentes alias, tum apud Iudaeos, priusquam legis impuritas introducta fuerit, aliud certè significauit, quàm flagitiosorum poenam; hanc multò certè leuiorem, quàm qua Dei voluntati satisfiat. Duodecimò, purgabatur vnusquisque certo temporis aut dierum spacio, certis quibusdam vsurpatis ceremoniis, qualisqualis animo esset, hoc est, siue volens siue nolens immundus fa& ctusfuisset. At à sceleribus nullus liberatur, nisi ex animo doleat, acverè serio; cupiat melior esse ac fieri. Decimotertiò, erat vnusquisque suo iudicio purgatus, (exceptis leprosis cum aliis paucis quibusdam) nec opus habebant iudicibus aut senioribus, qui, vtrum purificati essent, aut non essent, decernerent. De excommunicatis aliter censent adversarii. Etenim Seniorum suorum iudicio standum in hac parte volunt: non eorum affirmatione, qui se poenitere peccatorum afferunt. Decimoquartò sanus & mundus pronunciandus erat, quisquis à vertice vsque ad pedis plantam totus erat leprosus, sic vt vniuersi corporis cutis vnius esset coloris. Contrà verò, qui in parte vna vel pluribus solum secedatam eutim habebat, impurus habebatur. In sceleratis longissimè alia est ratio. Non enim qui totus est sceleribus coopertus (quomodo sus in coeno volutata tota lutulenta est) melior eo est, qui honestatis ac pietatis vmbram aliquam retinuit. Decimoquintò, nihil imperatur leprosis, quod pro emundatione sui moliantur, sed tantùm iubentur se ostendere sacerdoti: vt is pronuntiet, vtrùm purificati sint, an non sint. Sceleratis autem hoc praecipitur, vt vitam corrigant, animisque dolorem bonis sanctisque operibus testatum faciant. Decimosextò, permulti teddebantur impuri ex contactu illarum rerum, quibus alij purificabantur, & dum alios repurgabant, Num. 19. At nullus meretur excommunicari per id, quo alios sceleribus ac vitijs inquinatos studet sanare ac purgare. Quod si respondere figuram contendas, omnes illos excommunicandos concedere te oportet, qui per hanc poenam alios in viam revocare conantur. Decimoseptimò non interdicebatur immundis iuxta legem Sacramentis omnibus.
units.tr: Moreover, this uncleanness was a legal ceremony, not an impurity of life and morals. Indeed, a man was not unclean because he had committed a sin or perpetrated a crime. He was unclean if he had touched a corpse, dung, one suffering from a discharge or from menstrual flow, or anything else of the kind. For this reason the Pharisees refused to enter the praetorium when they were handing Christ over to Pilate to be put to death, lest they should be prevented from eating the Passover. Certainly the Mosaic uncleanness did not represent our wickedness in such a way that, just as the unclean were kept away from the Tabernacle and from the company of others, so this uncleanness signified that sinners were to be restrained and punished by the denial of the sacraments or by exclusion from the visible Church. This is made very clear by what follows. First, those who were ceremonially unclean were not punished with the same penalty as the wicked while that legal uncleanness was in force, and the number of the wicked was large. How then is it likely that, after these ceremonies were abolished or annulled, they would have signified that sinners should be punished in this way? Second, Moses would have contradicted himself openly, since he admitted to the temple and to the ceremonies those whom, by the ceremonies, he indicated should be driven out. For it is certain that no one was thrust out of the Tabernacle and the company of others because of the wickedness of his morals, provided that, according to the law's prescription, he had not touched a corpse or defiled himself in some similar way. Therefore he would have punished those who bore the likeness of the unclean, and would really have left the truly unclean unpunished (so far as this penalty is concerned). Thus he would have denied and affirmed the same thing at once. Third, legal impurity was a quality and a certain stain of the body, whereas wickedness consists in deeds and in action. For the cause and root of wickedness is innate in us, and it is not punished by men as long as it produces no fruits; otherwise all men would have to be excommunicated. Indeed we shall not be freed from this stain of the soul for as long as we survive in this mortal life. But an impurity that is a stain on the body is punished by exclusion from the company of others, even if it has produced no fruit, or even if the one who is stained has done nothing against the law. The works or sins of the unclean, if as unclean they committed anything against the law, were restrained by the magistrate like other transgressions. Fourth, the adversaries confess that not every sin is to be avenged by excommunication, since the law commands that every uncleanness be punished by exclusion from the Tabernacle and the public sacrifices. Therefore not all wickedness could be signified by this. Fifth, no one who sins against his will can be excommunicated, since men very often became unclean against their will, and without fault on their part, indeed with great grief. What fault clung to the man in whom seed had flowed out at night while he was asleep and unwilling? To whom, beyond expectation, had his wife's periods come? For whom did children, wife, or parents die, or other such things happen? That the sins which some think should exclude people from the sacraments are voluntary needs no proof. Sixth, a much heavier penalty was laid down for a man who killed another against and beyond his will than the exclusion from the sacraments for some days or weeks; this was almost the most severe penalty for uncleanness. Since therefore an involuntary sin, and consequently a very light one, was punished more harshly than the most foul legal impurity, it is easy to see that this penalty ought not to be transferred to the punishment of crimes. Seventh, it very often happened that the most holy and blameless man became unclean and was kept from the entrance of the Temple and from the sight of the sacrifices, while the most wicked man was admitted to them without anyone hindering him. But if the penalty of both were to be the same in the Church of God, the one should have been kept away much more than the other. Eighth, it is clear that God did not absolutely forbid all legal impurity at any place or time. For just as he willed that some be present at the dying, and at others infected with an unclean disease, and those who buried the dead, and finally even those who purified the unclean (by which means they too were sometimes defiled, Num. 19), so he also willed that not every legal uncleanness be avoided. But God forbade all crimes, in all persons and always; nor did he allow anyone to act wickedly at any time or place. Ninth, God commands that crimes be restrained by fire, sword, noose, stones, blows, fines, prison, and other similar penalties; and he orders the unclean to be cleansed by water according to the law and to be purified by other similar means. Tenth, a man who became unclean according to the definition of the law, and remained so until death, was not regarded as wicked and condemned, as when women suffering from menstrual flow, or men affected with a discharge or leprosy, died. But one who lives in such a way that, even at his death, he can be judged worthy of excommunication by good and just men, cannot but be considered wicked and impious. Eleventh, legal uncleanness had its place only among one people and at a certain time. But wickedness has sprung up everywhere among all nations, in every place and at every time. Wherefore, since wicked deeds have been punished and have been judged worthy of punishment, both among other nations and among the Jews before the legal impurity was introduced, it certainly signified something other than the punishment of wrongdoers, and a punishment much milder than that by which the will of God is satisfied. Twelfth, each person was cleansed in a certain space of time or days, by certain ceremonies in use, whatever his state of mind, that is, whether he had become unclean willingly or unwillingly. But no one is freed from sins unless he grieves from the heart, and truly in earnest, and desires to be and become better. Thirteenth, each person was cleansed by his own judgment (except lepers and a few others), and they had no need of judges or elders to decide whether they were purified or not. The adversaries think otherwise about the excommunicated. For they want the judgment of their elders to be followed in this matter, not the affirmation of those who say they repent of their sins. Fourteenth, a man was to be pronounced sound and clean if he was wholly leprous from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot, so that the skin of his whole body was of one colour. On the contrary, one who had only a spot or several spots of leprosy was regarded as unclean. In the case of the wicked the reasoning is quite different. For one who is entirely covered with crimes (as a pig wallowing in mud is wholly filthy) is not better than one who has kept some shadow of honesty and piety. Fifteenth, nothing is enjoined on lepers to undertake for their own cleansing, but they are only ordered to show themselves to the priest, so that he may pronounce whether they are purified or not. But to sinners this is commanded: that they correct their lives and show their grief of soul by good and holy works. Sixteenth, very many were made unclean by contact with those things by which others were purified, and while they cleansed others they were themselves defiled (Num. 19). But no one deserves to be excommunicated for that by which he strives to heal and cleanse others who are stained with wickedness and vices. And if you insist that this is a figure, you must concede that all those should be excommunicated who try by this penalty to call others back to the way. Seventeenth, the unclean were not, according to the law, forbidden all the sacraments.

units.la: Num. 19. bus. Quippè ritus patrios omnes priuatos custodire, Sabbathum seruare, festum expiationis, quo præcipuè Christi operum fructus exprimebatur, celebrare, sub pœna capitis cogebantur, Leuit. 16. & 23. Non enim pro condemnatis & deploratę salutis hominibus (vt suprà dixi) habebantur. Vtrùm alia sit excommunicatorum secundùm aduersariorum sententiam ratio, non est cur pluribus tentem ostendere. Decimo octauò contaminabant legaliter immundi vestes, domos, loca, homines, quibuscum agebant. Vitiosi autem nec templum, nec res alias, nec homines, præterquàm vitijs communicantes inquinabant. Non est infectum Templum quoties introductę fuerunt adulterę, Num. 5. & Ioh. 8. Telonius quoque seu Publicanus non fœdauit sua præsentia cùm ascenderet cum Pharisæo comprecatum. Luc. 18. Certè Pharisæus qui cum improbum existimabat præsentia, non se putauit contaminari. Cùm Iudas in templo abiceret nummos proditionis, non legimus Templum ab eo sordidatum suisse: nec inuenimus Pharisæos hac de re quæstos: qui in prætorium tamen ingredi noluerant, ne immundi redderentur. Quod si vel mensibus, vel profluuio muliebri laborans femina, vel qui funus curauisset, aut cadauer etiam inuitus attigisset, in templo conspectus fuisset, immunda suissent omnia: nec licuisset vel sacrificare, vel alium cultum exercere, antequàm fuisset repurgatum. Eodem modo non maculauit cœnam vltimam Iudas suis facinoribus: quod tamen accidisset, si vel ipse vel alius ex Discipulis rem mortuam tetigisset. Demùm fuit immunditia legis figura distortæ corruptæque; nostræ naturæ, quæ nisi sanguine Christi purissimo abluta purificataque fuerit, in cœlum non intromittetur. Etenim sicut Tabernaculum significauit cœlum, depulsio ab hoc, damnationem seu exclusionem è cœlesti Ierusalem, ita purificatio per aquam communem vel lustralem, emundationem per mortem Christi præfiguravit. Non igitur fuit qualitas operis figura, sed qualitatis, seu depravati ingenij nostri: nec præmonstrauit quomodò scelera essent coercenda (hoc enim apertis & explicatis verbis docuit Moses) sed quę futura esset conditio nostra in altera vita, scilicet in cœlesti regno, quod terra Chanaan adumbrabat: quæ omniaex 21.cap. Apocal. manifestè satis perspiciuntur. Augustinus aducrsus Donatistas scribens putauit significare hæreticorum exclusionem. Ex multis & magnis inter vtramque impuritatem differentiis etiam cæcus videat, non sic potuisse alteram figurare alteram, quomodò aducrsarii contendunt.
units.tr: Num. 19. For they were bound, under pain of death, to keep all the private rites of their fathers, to observe the Sabbath, and to celebrate the feast of atonement, in which especially the fruit of Christ's works was expressed (Leuit. 16 and 23). For they were not regarded (as I said above) as men condemned and of hopeless salvation. Why the adversaries' view of the excommunicated should be otherwise, there is no need for me to try to show at greater length. Eighteenth, the legally unclean made clothes, houses, places, and the men with whom they dealt unclean. But the vicious did not defile the Temple, other things, or men, except those who shared their vices. The Temple was not defiled whenever adulteresses were brought in (Num. 5 and John 8). The tax collector, or publican, did not defile the place by his presence when he went up with the Pharisee to pray (Luke 18). Certainly the Pharisee, who thought the presence of a wicked man to be a pollution, did not think himself contaminated. When Judas threw down the money of betrayal in the temple, we do not read that the Temple was soiled by him, nor do we find the Pharisees questioned about this matter, although they had refused to enter the praetorium lest they become unclean. But if a woman suffering from menstrual periods or a flow of blood had been seen in the temple, or one who had attended a funeral, or who had touched a corpse even against his will, all things would have been unclean, and it would not have been lawful either to sacrifice or to exercise any other worship until it had been cleansed. In the same way Judas did not defile the Last Supper by his crimes; yet it would have been defiled if either he or another of the disciples had touched a dead thing. Finally, the uncleanness of the law was a figure of our nature, distorted and corrupted, which will not be admitted into heaven unless it is washed and purified by the most pure blood of Christ. For just as the Tabernacle signified heaven, and exclusion from it signified damnation or exclusion from the heavenly Jerusalem, so purification by common or lustral water prefigured cleansing through the death of Christ. Therefore the quality of the deed was not the figure, but the quality or depraved disposition of our nature; nor did it foreshadow how wickedness is to be restrained (for Moses taught this in plain and explained words), but what our condition would be in the other life, namely in the heavenly kingdom, which the land of Canaan foreshadowed. All these things are seen clearly enough from Apocal. 21. Augustine, writing against the Donatists, thought it signified the exclusion of heretics. Even a blind man can see, from the many great differences between the two kinds of impurity, that the one could not have figured the other in the way the adversaries contend.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quanquàm præter dictam exceptionē Moses aliam nullam ponat, attamen ad aliam obiectionem, quæ ex verbis Mosis strui posset, respondebo: Sic enim forte arguetur aliquis: Iudaei per Mosen iussi sunt Pascha sine fermento edere: quod Paul. in 1.Corin.5.interpretatur spurcitiam vitæ. Consentaneum igitur videri alicui possit, vt cœna Domini, quæ Paschati successit, exclusis facinorosis celebretur.
units.tr: Although Moses lays down no other exception apart from the one mentioned, I will answer another objection that could be built from the words of Moses. For someone might argue as follows: the Jews were commanded through Moses to eat the Passover without leaven, which Paul in 1 Corinthians 5 interprets as the uncleanness of life. It might therefore seem fitting to someone that the Lord's Supper, which succeeded the Passover, be celebrated with the wicked excluded.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Respondeo primùm quidem parùm verisimile esse, Deum apertis verbis aliquid mandare, & idem eodem tempore figuratè rursus prohibere. Præcipit apertè, mandato aliquoties repetito vt omnis masculus (exceptis immundis & haerentibus in via) Pascha celebrent. Non igitur per figuram fermenti voluit aliquos alios absterrere. Erant tunc mali satis multi præsentes, vt non fuerit opus per fermentum eos figurare. Nec minùs in sensus incurrebât flagitiosi, quàm fermentum. Proindè cùm figurae non proponantur rerū præsentium, & in sensus æquè incurrentium, (præsertim si ipsis figuris notiores sint ac frequëtiores res figuratæ) frustra hîc figura quaeritur. Deindè nostiubet Moses illum à Paschatis esu arceri, qui fermentū ederit: sed occidi iubet. Quare facinorosi non à cœna arcendi, sed capite pleƈtendi fuerint: quam ego consecutionem haud aegrè admiseto & vt fiat opto. Nihil enim desidero magis, quàm vt seuerissima in ecclesia morum disciplina seruetur: sed quam Deus instituit, non quam finxerunt homines. Tertiò, licebat Iudaeis fermentum edere toto anno (exceptis septem illis diebus Azymorū) quos cum paschatis esu inchoabant. Si ad coenam Domini accommodare velis, concedere oportet, vt toto anno impurè viuatur, tantùm tempore celebrationis coenae Dominicae à sceleribus caucatur. Quartò loquitur Moses hîc tantùm de Pascha te, non de aliis Sacramentis. Proinde à sola domini caena, non à Baptismo forent prohibendi facinorosi. Quintò non comparat Apostolus festum Iudaeorum cum coena Domini, sed cum tota nostra vita. Nos dicit esse Azymos (vt qui Christi sanguine abluti & ab omni fermento expurgati simus.) Ideóque conuenire ait, vt in Azymis sinceritatis & veritatis, non in fermento malitiae viuamus. Longè differunt fermentum simpliciter dictum: & fermentum malitiae seu veritatis. Sic sumptum aut positum fermētum nullus nescit esse figuratū sumptum. Sensus analogicus seu figuratiuus, dicunt Scholastici, non est argumentatiuus. Certè quidquid per fermentum intelligamus, non hinc potest Excommunicatio contra apertum Dei praeceptum stabiliri aut fulciri.
units.tr: I answer, first, that it is hardly likely that God would expressly command something and at the same time figuratively forbid the same thing. He commands openly, repeating the command several times, that every male (except the unclean and those on a journey) celebrate the Passover. Therefore he did not wish, by the figure of leaven, to frighten some others away. There were then plenty of wicked people present, so there was no need to represent them by leaven. Nor were the shameless less open to the senses than leaven was. Therefore, since figures are not proposed for present things that are equally open to the senses (especially if the figured things are better known and more frequent than the figures), the figure is sought here in vain. Next, Moses orders that the one who eats leaven be barred from eating the Passover, but he orders him to be killed. Therefore the shameless should not have been barred from the supper but put to death. I do not reluctantly admit this consequence, and I wish it to happen. For I desire nothing more than that the most severe discipline of morals be kept in the Church; but it must be the discipline God instituted, not the one men have invented. Third, the Jews were allowed to eat leaven all year, except for those seven days of unleavened bread, which they began with the eating of the Passover. If you wish to apply this to the Lord's Supper, you must concede that one may live impurely all year, provided one abstains from crimes only at the time of celebrating the Lord's Supper. Fourth, Moses here speaks only of the Passover, not of the other sacraments. Therefore the wicked should be barred from the Lord's Supper alone, not from baptism.
