Fifth, the Apostle does not compare the Jewish feast with the Lord's Supper, but with our whole life. He calls us unleavened (as those washed in Christ's blood and cleansed of all leaven), and therefore says it is fitting that we live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, not in the leaven of malice. Leaven simply so called is very different from the leaven of malice or of truth. No one fails to know that leaven taken or placed in this sense is taken figuratively. The analogical or figurative sense, the Scholastics say, is not argumentative. Certainly, whatever we understand by leaven, excommunication cannot be established or supported from it against the plain command of God.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Attamen mentionem, inquiat aliquis, hîc facit Paulus Paschatis. Sed hoc ad rem nostram quid facit? Quasi verò nomen hoc, Pascha, in nouo Testamento pro coena Domini positum sit. Christus, inquit Apostolus, est Pascha nōstrum immolatus pro nobis: non coena eius. Sensus est, sicut Iudæi suum festum Azymorum ab agni esu inchoantes tantùm, per totam deinde septimanam infermentata ederunt: Sic & vos, qui in Christum credere incepistis, eiusque sanguine purgati & Azymi redd.ti estis, totam reliquam septimanam, hoc est, totum vitae spacium, purè castéque transfigere debetis.
units.tr: Yet, someone will say, Paul here makes mention of the Passover. But what does this have to do with our matter? As if this name, Passover, were used in the New Testament for the Lord's Supper! "Christ," says the Apostle, "is our Passover, sacrificed for us": not his supper. The sense is this: just as the Jews, beginning their feast of unleavened bread only with the eating of the lamb, then ate unleavened bread for the whole week, so you also, who have begun to believe in Christ and have been cleansed by his blood and made unleavened, ought to spend the whole remaining week, that is, the whole span of life, purely and chastely.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Iam quòd neque in alijs veteris Testamenti voluminibus aliquid reperiatur diuersi, vel ex hoc solo intelligitur, quòd iuxta Mosis instituta ac leges viuendum posteris fuit: Contraq; ea instituere nihil licuit, quod ad cultum Dei pertineret. Equidem Iudices pij, Sacerdotes, Prophetæ, ac Reges nullos à Sacramentis & sacrificiis abegerunt: sed summo potius studio vniuersos ad ea inuitarunt. Nota est faustissimi Regis Iosiæ historia 2. Par. 34. qui conctos Israelitas (quos nuper Diis alienis seu Dæmonibus thura adolevisse non nescicbat:) & præter hos, illos quoque qui propter breuitatem temporis mundari non poterant, ad Paschæ celebrationem conuocauit. Ex quo loco etiam perspicitur, Sacramenta, incitamenta seu inuitamenta esse ad pietatem: Et horum frequenti vsu potius, quàm priuatione homines reddi meliores: siquidem recte & fideliter simul docceantur;
units.tr: That nothing different is found in the other books of the Old Testament can be understood from this alone: posterity was to live according to the institutions and laws of Moses, and it was not lawful to establish anything contrary to them that pertained to the worship of God. Indeed, pious judges, priests, prophets and kings never drove anyone away from the sacraments and sacrifices, but with the greatest zeal invited all to them. The history of the most blessed King Josiah is well known (2 Chron. 34), who summoned to the celebration of the Passover all the Israelites (whom he knew had recently burned incense to foreign gods or demons), and besides these, also those who could not be cleansed because of the shortness of time. From this passage it is also clear that the sacraments are incitements or invitations to piety, and that men are made better by the frequent use of them rather than by being deprived of them, provided that they are taught rightly and faithfully at the same time.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Quamobrem non poterit excommunicatio ex capit. 1. Esaiæ. Psal. 50. & similibus alijs comploribus locis, in quibus dicitur, Deum nolle sacrificia & oblationes malorum defendi. Quippe in talibus omnibus locis reprehenditur Deus abusum: quod præclarè se Dei voluntati satisfecisse putarent, si externa ista perfecissent, quomodocunque tandem animus affectus esset. Deinde non iubet vel Prophetam, vel per hunc alium quendam, malos à sacrificijs & ceremonijs repellere: sed se non auditurum eos indicat, nisi etiam vitam corrigant. Alia est ratio externæ in Ecclesia politiæ: & alia voluntatis Dei erga nos nostra vel probantis vel improbantis. Postremò, ex ijsdem locis eòdem præcisè modo demonstrabitur, nemini malo licere inuocare nomen Domini. Sed nec laudare Deum, nec gratias ei agere licebit: quoniam ministros & seniores interdicere facinorosis omnia hæc oportebit. Nam similiter in impijs hęc auersatur Deus: vt ex citatis & similibus omnibus locis manifestum est. Quòd si hoc est absurdum, etiam illud absurdum est. [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: Therefore excommunication cannot be drawn from chapter 1 of Isaiah, Psalm 50, and other similar passages, in which it is said that God does not want sacrifices and offerings of evildoers to be defended. Indeed, in all such places God rebukes the abuse: people thought they had satisfied God's will splendidly if they had performed these external things, however their mind was disposed. Next, he does not command either a prophet, or anyone through him, to drive the wicked away from sacrifices and ceremonies; he merely indicates that he will not listen to them unless they also correct their lives. The arrangement of external polity in the Church is one thing; God's will toward us, approving or disapproving of ours, is another. Finally, from the same passages it will be demonstrated in exactly the same way that no wicked man may invoke the name of the Lord. But neither will it be lawful to praise God or give thanks to him, since ministers and elders will have to forbid all these things to the shameless. For likewise God turns away from the impious in these matters, as is clear from the cited passages and all similar ones. If this is absurd, then that is absurd too. [illegible, about 40 letters]

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Ne illud quidem nobis aduersatur, quod in lib.r. Esdræ cap.10. legitur. Etenim res illa politica fuit: ad Sacramenta non pertinet. Nam magistratus, non sacerdos Esdras solus (qui tamen erat pars Magistratus. Nam Iosepho teste, regebantur optimatum gubernatione: licet Ducem haberent) edictum promulgauit, vt sub poena confiscationis bonorum, & exclusionis, non à Sacramentis & sacrificijs, sed à populo, qui ex captiuitate redierat, omnes intrà triduum Hierosolymis adessent. Non hic quærimus, vtrùm Magistratus ius habeat hoc vel illo modo puniendi: sed an sacerdotes potuerint dissolutè & turpiter viuentes à sacrificijs remouere? Non potuit hoc Esdras contra mandatum Dei facere. Adde, quòd hanc poenam, remotionem scilicet à Sacramentis, Moses non iussit illis infligi, Deut.7. qui alienigenas duxissent vxores. Et quomodo Esdras punire legis transgressores debuerit, cap.7. eiusdem libri habetur: morte, exilio, corporis cruciatibus, multatione bonorum, vinculis seu carcere. Denique longè aliud erat ex illorum cotu, qui ex captiuitate redierant, excludi, quàm à templo & sacrificijs arceri. Constat enim ex ca.12. Exo. & Num.9. etiam peregrinos ad Pascha tatis celebrationem admissos suisse: modo circumcisi essent. Tunc etiam plurimi ex illis, qui vel in Iudæa permanserant, vel ex incolis deserta impuritate Gentilium ad Iudæos transfierant, vnà cum cæteris omnibus Pascha concelebrârunt: vt in fine cap.6. eiusdem libri scribitur. Hi tales à sacrificijs, templo, vel ceremonijs non prohibebantur: quamuis in illorum numero, qui ex Babylone redierant, nequaquam recensèrentur. Sic & sacerdotes aliquos à sacerdotij munere amouerunt, propterea quòd genealogias suas docere non possent, vt ex cap. 2. Esdræ liquet. Ex omnibus patet impossibile esse, vt hinc iuratur Excommunicatio.
units.tr: Nor does that passage from the first book of Ezra, chapter 10, stand against us. For that matter was a political one: it does not pertain to the sacraments. For it was the magistrate, not the priest Ezra alone (who nevertheless was part of the magistracy, for according to Josephus they were governed by an aristocracy, although they had a leader), who issued the edict that, under penalty of confiscation of goods and exclusion, not from the sacraments and sacrifices but from the people who had returned from captivity, all should be present at Jerusalem within three days. Here we are not asking whether the magistrate has the right to punish in this or that way, but whether priests who lived dissolutely and shamefully could have been removed from the sacrifices. Ezra could not have done this against the command of God. Add that Moses did not order this penalty, namely removal from the sacraments, to be inflicted on those who had taken foreign wives (Deut. 7). And what punishment Ezra ought to have inflicted on transgressors of the law is set out in chapter 7 of the same book: death, exile, torture of the body, confiscation of goods, chains or prison. Finally, it was quite different to be excluded from the company of those who had returned from captivity than to be barred from the temple and the sacrifices. For it is clear from Exodus 12 and Numbers 9 that even strangers were admitted to the celebration of the Passover, provided they were circumcised. Then also very many of those who had remained in Judea, or who had gone over to the Jews from the inhabitants, abandoning the defilement of the Gentiles, celebrated the Passover together with all the others, as is written at the end of chapter 6 of the same book. Such people were not prohibited from the sacrifices, the temple or the ceremonies, although they were by no means counted among those who had come back from Babylon. Thus also they removed some priests from the priestly office, because they could not show their genealogies, as is clear from chapter 2 of Ezra. From all this it is plain that what is here urged as excommunication is impossible.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Superest vnica illa è Synagogis eiectio, qua nonnulli sibi mirè placent: dum pro Excommunicatione afferenda producunt, quæ Ioh. 9. & 12. & 16. de hac re scribuntur. Sed multiplex ac vera hic quoque suppetit responsio. Nomen Synagogæ, aliquando significat locum, vt quando Iesus in Synagogam introijsse, inque ea docuisse scribitur: aliquando vero concionem sine conuentum, siue is in ipsa Synagoga haberetur, siue alibi: vt cùm Pharisaei primos accubitus in coenis, & primos locos in Synagogis appetiuisse legūntur. In eodem hoc significato (vel vtroq; simul) ponitur Math. 10. & 23. Cùm Christus pios in Synagogis, flagris cædendos prædicit: Et Math. 10, Marc. 13, Luc. 12. & 21, quibus in locis publicum iudicium significat, in quo significato sæpè à 70. Interpretibus hoc nomen positum est: vt deinde monebimus opportuniore loco. In prædictis proxime locis, vt Math. 10. & Mar. 13. aperte ... sic pònuntur, ac si idem per vtrumque intelligi debeat: in cæteris locis ... mox adduntur ... vt Luc. 21. (pro quibus idem Euangelista cap. 12. posuerat ...) Marc. 13. & Math. 10. Ex locorum collatione manifestißimè demonstratur, Euangelistas siue Christum his postremis locis nihil aliud intellexisse per nomen ... quàm iudicia Iudæorum, quae à consessu plurium exercebantur: sicut Gentilium iudicia nominibus ... & ... exprimuntur: quibus fere vnus præterat aliquis: aut si plures administrarent, vnius nomine administrabant. In his conuentibus siue Synagogis, virgis, flagris, pugnis caedebantur nocentes iudicati, Math. 10. 23. Act. 22. & 26. & 2. Corinth. 11. quem locum ex Deut. 25. quibus facile intelligit. Ex tali Synagoga eiectio, erat politica quaedam ignominia & poena, adeoque veluti localis quaedam relegatio: vt ex 4. cap. Lud. coniicimus. Ad Sacramenta non potest traduci, quae in templo (quod vnicum erat) & Hierosolymiis (excepta circumcisione atque aliis quibusdã) duntaxat celebrabantur. Haud dissimilis videtur poena fuisse illi, de qua proxime dictum est in explicatione sententiae apud Esdram scriptae. Synagogae tales in singulis fuisse vrbibus, nullus est qui nesciat. Ergo sive pro loco, sive pro ipsa concione nomen Synagogae accipi dicatur apud Ioh. nostrae sententiae nullain parte repugnat. Quod si maxime negetur politicum fuisse, (saltem hoc constaret) ad religionem pertinuisse. Ego autem hic non disputo, vtrum qui prauè de religione vera sentit, excommunicandus sit. Etenim Pharisaei, inquit Ioh. 9. conspirauerant in hoc, vt si Synagoga illi eiicerentur, qui Iesum haberent pro Christo. Ac quod in Synagoga esse honor tantum, & ex ea eiici, ignominia fuerit, ex eo videtur posse colligi, quod Ioh. 12. scribitur principes quosdam Iudaeos (in quorum numero fortasse Nicodemus ille quoque fuit) in Christum credidisse, at non aulos fuisse confiteri propter Pharisaeos: ne ab eis e Synagoga eiicerentur: atque addiitur ratio haec: Magis enim gloriam hominum, quam Dei dilexerunt. Praeterea constat publicanos circumcisos non suisse admissos in Synagogas: quomodo in praesentia de Synagoga disputamus: Etenim Pharisaei ne colloqui quidem sustinebant cum illis: Christumque hoc nomine sugillabant, quòd familiariter cum eis ageret. Ad eosdem, hos ad Pascha, templum, sacrificia, non admissos fuisse, nullus sanae mentis, opinor, affirmabit. Quocirca longissimè differunt ex Synagoga excludi, & a Sacramentis & ceremoniis a Deo institutis repelli, vt ex omnibus iam dictis constat, & ex 5. cap. Act. clare perspicitur. Quippe discipuli acriter a Synagoga obiurgati, nihilominus in templo quotidie docebant. Ex quot Synagogis fuit eiectus Paulus Apostolus? Hunc tamen nunquam Iudaei reprehenderunt, quòd in templum ingressus fuerit, & pro se atque aliis oblationem fieri curarit. Ad extremum hoc etiam licet addere, quam maxime doceri posset, e Synagoga excluexcludere, & à Sacramentis arcere, eadem apud Pharisæos fuisse (id quod nullo vnquam tempore verum fuisse, esse,fore, demonstrabitur) fecissent nihilominùs hoc, quemadmodum alia multa, contrà manifestum Mosis præceptum: ideóque factum eorum non imitari, sed damnare cogeremur. Non enim exemplis, sed legibus viuendum est nobis: nec imitandum quicquam cum lege Dei pugnans, nisi confundere omnia velimus. Exempla bonorum & bona, non malorum aut mala damnatáue expetamus. Haec ideò tam multis, attamen breuiter attigi, quia hoc argumento sibi quidam mirificè blandiuntur, cùm interim seipsos atque alios fallant.
units.tr: There remains that one kind of expulsion from the synagogues, in which some take great pleasure, since they bring forward in support of excommunication what is written about this matter in John 9, 12 and 16. But there is a manifold and true answer here too. The word "synagogue" sometimes means a place, as when it is written that Jesus entered the synagogue and taught in it. At other times it means an assembly or gathering, whether it was held in the synagogue itself or elsewhere, as when the Pharisees are read to have sought the first couches at feasts and the first seats in the synagogues. The word is used in this same sense (or in both senses at once) in Matthew 10 and 23, where Christ foretells that the godly will be beaten with whips in the synagogues; and in Matthew 10, Mark 13, and Luke 12 and 21, where it signifies a public court of judgment. In this sense the Seventy often used the word, as we will point out later in a more suitable place. In the passages just cited, such as Matthew 10 and Mark 13, the words are placed as though the same thing must be understood by both; in the other passages they are added ... as in Luke 21 (where the same evangelist had put ... in chapter 12), Mark 13 and Matthew 10. From comparing these places it is most clearly shown that the evangelists, or Christ, in these last passages understood by the name ... nothing other than the judgments of the Jews, which were carried out by the assembly of many men, just as the judgments of the Gentiles are expressed by the names ... and ...; over these one man for the most part presided, or if several administered them, they administered them in the name of one. In these assemblies or synagogues, those judged guilty were beaten with rods, whips and fists, as in Matthew 10 and 23, Acts 22 and 26, and 2 Corinthians 11, which one easily understands from Deuteronomy 25. Expulsion from such a synagogue was a certain civil disgrace and punishment, and so a kind of local banishment, as we conjecture from chapter 4 of Lud. It cannot be transferred to the sacraments, which were celebrated only in the temple (which was the one temple) and at Jerusalem (except circumcision and some other things). The punishment seems to have been not unlike that which was mentioned just above in explaining the sentence written in Ezra. That there were such synagogues in individual cities, no one is ignorant. Therefore, whether the name of synagogue in John is taken to mean a place or the assembly itself, it in no way conflicts with our opinion. But even if it is most strongly denied that it was civil, it would at least be granted that it pertained to religion. Yet I am not here disputing whether one who thinks wrongly about the true religion ought to be excommunicated. For the Pharisees, says John 9, had agreed together that if anyone confessed Jesus to be Christ, he would be cast out of the synagogue. And that to be in the synagogue was only an honour, and to be cast out of it a disgrace, may be gathered from John 12, where it is written that certain leading Jews (among whom perhaps Nicodemus was also one) believed in Christ, but did not dare to confess it because of the Pharisees, lest they be cast out of the synagogue; and this reason is added: "For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God." Moreover, it is established that circumcised publicans were not admitted into the synagogues, which is the matter we are now discussing concerning the synagogue. For the Pharisees would not even bear to converse with them, and they reproached Christ on this account, because he associated with them familiarly. That they were not admitted to the Passover, the temple, or the sacrifices, no one of sound mind, I think, will affirm. Therefore, being cast out of the synagogue and being repulsed from the sacraments and ceremonies instituted by God are very far apart, as is clear from all that has been said already and is plainly seen in Acts 5. Indeed, the disciples, though sharply rebuked by the synagogue, nevertheless taught daily in the temple. From how many synagogues was the apostle Paul expelled? Yet the Jews never found fault with him for entering the temple and arranging for an offering to be made for himself and others. Finally, we may add this as well: even if it could be most fully taught that to exclude someone from the synagogue and to keep him from the sacraments were the same thing among the Pharisees (which will be shown never to have been true at any time, past, present or future), they would nevertheless have done this, as many other things, against the plain command of Moses; and so we would be compelled not to imitate their deed but to condemn it. For we must live not by examples but by laws, and nothing that fights against the law of God is to be imitated, unless we wish to confuse everything. Let us seek the examples and the good deeds of good men, not the evil or the condemned deeds of bad men. I have touched on these points at such length, yet briefly, because certain men flatter themselves greatly with this argument, while in the meantime they deceive themselves and others.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Manet igitur hoc firmum, immobile,& inconcussum, in veteri Testamento nullum fuisse propter delicta morum à Sacramentis remotum: sed ad eorundem celebrationem cunctos secundùm legem à pijs sacerdotibus, Prophetis, Iudicibus, Regibus, tandémque ab ipso quoque antecursore Christi clarissimo & sanctissimo Iohanne Baptista, fuisse inuitatos magis quàm repulsos.
units.tr: It therefore stands firm, fixed and unshaken that in the Old Testament no one was ever excluded from the sacraments on account of moral offences; rather, all were invited, according to the law, to their celebration by the godly priests, the Prophets, the Judges, the Kings, and finally by John the Baptist himself, the most famous and most holy forerunner of Christ, and were admitted rather than rejected.

units.la: XXIIII.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Cœterùm Sacramenta veterum & nostra, quod ad res significatas attinet, eadem sunt, vt in 1.Cor.10. Paulus clarè ostendit. Quarè nisi legem Mosis hac in parte vel abolitam vel mutatam constet, contrarium inducere nulli homini licebit.
units.tr: Moreover, the sacraments of the old covenant and ours are the same as regards the things signified, as Paul plainly shows in 1 Cor. 10. Therefore, unless it is established that the law of Moses has been either abolished or changed in this respect, no one will be permitted to argue the contrary.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Vt enim aduersus Anabaptistas firmissimo hoc rectè vtimur argumento, quia circumcisioni Baptismus succedserit, & Christus infantes nullibi baptizari vetuerit, non mi-nùs nūs nobis licere nostros infantes baptizare, quàm Iudæis suos licuerit circumcidere: Ita hīc etiam non minūs firmiter possumus hoc pacto ratiocinari: Paschatis esui successit cœna Dominica. At Paschatis negatione vitia non puniebantur, nec propter hæc vlli arcebantur: sed potius omnes, masculi præsertim, ad eius celebrationem inuitabantur à lege. Quæ cùm nullibi legatur antiquata & abolita, ne cœnæ quidem Dominicæ negatione punienda sunt, aut hoc nomine reijciendus aliquis fuerit. De veteri Testamento satis multa: nunc ad Christum & apostolos, id est, ad nouum Testamentum descendere nos conuenit.
units.tr: For just as we rightly use this very firm argument against the Anabaptists, that baptism has succeeded to circumcision, and Christ nowhere forbade infants to be baptized, so it is no less lawful for us to baptize our infants than it was lawful for the Jews to circumcise theirs. In the same way, we can reason just as firmly in this matter: the Lord's Supper has succeeded to the eating of the Passover. But by the denial of the Passover, vices were not punished, nor were any men on account of them shut out; rather, all men, males especially, were invited by the law to its celebration. Since this is nowhere read to have been abolished or annulled, men are not to be punished by the denial of the Lord's Supper either, nor is anyone to be rejected on this ground. Enough has been said about the Old Testament; now it is fitting that we descend to Christ and the apostles, that is, to the New Testament.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Christus seruator ac Dominus noster eodem modo nulli vsu Sacramentorum interdixisse legitur: quinimò nec Apostolis alicubi iussisse, vt tale quid facerent, inuenimus. Etenim non venit in hunc mundum Christus, vt legem solueret, sed vt eam impleret atq; perficeret. Proindè cùm iuberet lex omnes Pascha celebrare præter immundos, prohibere ipse nulli voluit.
units.tr: Likewise, we read that Christ our Saviour and Lord forbade no one the use of the sacraments; indeed, we find that he nowhere commanded the apostles to do any such thing. For Christ did not come into this world to dissolve the law, but to fulfil and perfect it. Therefore, since the law commanded that all should celebrate the Passover except the unclean, he himself was unwilling to forbid it to anyone.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Constat etiam, Christum nullos vnquam reprehendisse, quòd Sacramentis vtérentur, & frequenter adessent: in templo, & Sacrificijs: sed vt recté eadem iuxta Dei voluntatem atq; legem vsurparent, solummodò monuisse. In idem semper templum ingressus est cum Pharisæis, Sadducæis, Publicanis aliisq; cunctis, malis pariter & bonis: ijsdem eum his Sacrificijs astitit: eadem cum vniuerso populo Sacramenta vsurpauit: eodem quoque baptismate à Ioanne baptizatus est, quo nequissimi illi iam nominati baptizati sunt.
units.tr: It is also established that Christ never reproached anyone for using the sacraments and frequently attending them, in the temple and at the sacrifices; he only admonished them to use these rightly, according to the will and law of God. He entered the same temple with the Pharisees, the Sadducees, the publicans and all others, evil and good alike; he was present at the same sacrifices with them; he partook of the same sacraments with the whole people; and he was baptized with the same baptism by John, by which those most wicked men just named were baptized.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Hac eademdecaufa Iudam quoque proditorem suum à postremi agni esu non arcuit, sed vnà cum 12. discipulis suis discubuit. Quanquam verò sunt, qui probare conentur, Iudam nouae Christi coenae non interfuisse (quod perdifficile, ne dicam impossibile, fuerit ex sacris literis clarè ostendere) sed prius abijse, quàm à Christo institucretur: nullus tamen puto negare audebit, eum iuxta legem ad Pafchatis esum admissum fuisse. Quo posito immotum perstat argumentum nostrum. Etenim siuè antè alterius coenae institutionem exierit, siue non exierit, (quod est probabilius, & à pluribus semper creditum) hoc semper constat, cum primae adfuisse, aque secunda non iusum else aperte abstinere. Quinetiam nullibi legitur à Christo iusus exire, vt nouae coenae non interesset. Quod si ergo exijt, sponte sponte exijt, nec ob eam causam exijt. Nos autem quid Christus fecerit, quaerimus, non quid Iudas egerit. Sufficit nobis, quòd Christus eum non iusit à sua coena abstinere.
units.tr: For this same reason he did not keep his traitor Judas from eating the last Passover lamb, but reclined together with his twelve disciples. Although there are some who try to prove that Judas was not present at the new supper of Christ (which would be very difficult, not to say impossible, to show clearly from the sacred letters), but left before it was instituted by Christ, yet I think no one will dare to deny that he was admitted to the eating of the Passover according to the law. Granted this, our argument stands unshaken. For whether he went out before the institution of the other supper or did not go out (which is more probable, and has always been believed by most), this always remains certain: that he was present at the first, and that he was plainly not forbidden to abstain from the second. Moreover, nowhere is it read that Christ ordered him to depart so that he would not take part in the new supper. But if he went out, he went out of his own accord, and not for that reason. We, however, are asking what Christ did, not what Judas did. It is enough for us that Christ did not order him to abstain from his supper.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Friuolum & leue est, quod pro excusatione adfertur, crimen non fuisse publicum, ideóque non debuisse amoueri. Quippe cum Pharisæis iam pactus precium fuerat. In ipsa quoque coena Christus discipulis aperuit, publicúmque fecit: quo magis exemplum fuisset statuendum. Postremò, vt aliquid hoc fit, saltem pro fure ante notus erat. Et quanquam talis esset, nihilominus ministerium ei commisit Dominus: potestateque Daemones eijciendi, aegros sanandi, aliáque miracula faciendi ornauit: denique omnibus annis, quibus cum Christo fuit, Pafchatis celebrationi eum, sicut caeteros, adhibuit. An non satis argumenti hoc est, eum non velle, vt flagitiosi negatione Sacramentorum puniantur? Certè maius quiddam est, malum in ministerium cooptare, quàm ad coenam talem quempiam admittere. Vtrumque Iudae contigisse à Christo videmus.
units.tr: The excuse offered, that the crime was not public and therefore he ought not to have been removed, is trifling and weak. Indeed, he had already agreed with the Pharisees for a price. Moreover, in the supper itself Christ revealed it to the disciples and made it public, so much the more should an example have been set. Finally, whatever the case, he was at least known beforehand as a thief. And even though he was such a man, the Lord nevertheless entrusted the ministry to him, adorned him with the power of casting out demons, healing the sick and performing other miracles; and in short, throughout all the years in which he was with Christ, he admitted him, as he did the others, to the celebration of the Passover. Is this not enough evidence that he did not wish the wicked to be punished by the denial of the sacraments? Certainly it is a greater thing to admit someone to the ministry who is evil than to admit such a man to the supper. We see that both happened to Judas from Christ.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Obseruandum illud quoque est, quòd discipuli in ipsa coena prima inter se contendere coeperunt de eminentia & dignitate, attamen eam ob causam nullus ex ipsis remotus est. Quinimò iussit ac voluit vt O mn i s ex calice biberent (par ratio est calicis & panis: quod ad hanc rem attinet) teste Math.26.cap. quod Marc.14. factum testatur. Quid aliud his verbis voluisse Christus credi potest, quàm confirmare ea, quae per Mosen Deus olim praeceperat? vt videlicet à publica & solenni ista gratiarum actione nullus excluderetur baptizatus, qui interesse vellet? Ex quo apparet nullum à mensa Domini remouendum, qui Christi doctrinam amplectitur, ac se doceri à Christo patitur.
units.tr: It is also to be observed that the disciples, at that very first supper, began to dispute among themselves about pre-eminence and dignity; yet no one of them was on that account removed from the table. Indeed, Christ commanded and willed that all should drink from the cup (the case of the cup and of the bread is the same, as far as this matter is concerned), as Matthew 26 records, and Mark 14 testifies that this was done. What else can Christ be believed to have intended by these words, than to confirm what God had long ago commanded through Moses? Namely, that no one who was baptized and wished to take part in this public and solemn thanksgiving should be excluded. From this it appears that no one who embraces the doctrine of Christ, and allows himself to be taught by Christ, is to be removed from the Lord's table.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Non vult angustioribus in his terris finibus regnum suum circumscribi Christus (de externo loquor) inter Christianos, quàm voluerit olim concludi & definiri inter Iudaeos. Proinde sicut iussit Deus omnes circumcisos externè participare eisdem Sacramentis ac ceremonijs, sceleratos autem gladio alijsque poenis coerceri plectíque mandauit: Ita vult hic etiam Christus omnes baptizatos seu Christianos, rectè puréque de Religione sentientes, ijsdem externis ceremonijs & Sacramentis vti: flagitiosos autem à magistratu morte, exilio, carcere, alijsque poenis talibus puniri. Huc spectare videntur similitudines illae, retis, nuptiarum, zizaniae.
units.tr: Christ does not wish his kingdom to be confined within narrower limits in these lands among Christians (I speak of the external kingdom) than God once wished it to be shut up and defined among the Jews. Therefore, just as God commanded that all the circumcised should externally share in the same sacraments and ceremonies, but that the wicked should be restrained and punished with the sword and other penalties, so Christ here also wills that all the baptized, or Christians, who think rightly and purely about religion should use the same external ceremonies and sacraments, but that the flagitious should be punished by the magistrate with death, exile, imprisonment and other such penalties. To this point seem to look those comparisons of the net, the wedding feast, and the tares.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Apud Apostolos, Paulum inprimis, haud pauciora, nec minùs plana & firma argumenta inuenimus. Primùm mum hoc est,quod nullo in loco reperiuntur Excommunicationem hanc vel docuisse vel exercuisse Apostoli. Quod argumentum per fe inualidum indissolubile redditur, fi cogitemus, eos Mosaicarum legum, quas non aboleuisset Christus,ad mortem vsque obferuantiffimos fuisse: vt vel ex vaico cap.21. & vltimo Act. cognoscere vnusquisque potetrit. Quocirca nunquam tentauerunt vel tentare voluerunt à nostris Sacramentis, (quae à veterum Sacramentis,signis tantùm & significandi tempore differunt) aliquem arcere, qui fe Christianum esse, & de doctrina recte sentire prositeretur. Nusquam enim contra Mosis praecepta aliquid fecerunt aut docuerunt, quae sublata à Christo non fuiffent, sed non minore studio legem deindè feruarunt, atque ante mortem Christi seruauerant: vt loco nuper citato testantur Apostolorum principes. Quippè gentibus tantum permiserunt fine lege Mosis viuere, non Iudaeis ad Christum conuersis: quod diligenter hic propter fequentia etiam notandum est. Et quod ad substantiam doctrinae attinet, nihil à Mose & Prophetis abhorrens docuerunt. Quoniam fi aliter docuissent, non fuisset eorum doctrina scripturis iudicata consentanea à Berrhoenfibus. Act.17.
units.tr: Among the Apostles, and above all Paul, we find no fewer arguments, and none less plain or firm. The first is this: nowhere do we find that the Apostles taught or practised this excommunication. This argument is weak in itself, but it becomes unanswerable if we consider that they were most strict observers of the laws of Moses, which Christ had not abolished, even to the point of death, as anyone may learn from Acts 21 and the last chapter of Acts. For this reason they never tried, nor wished to try, to keep from our sacraments (which differ from the sacraments of the ancients only in their signs and in the time of their signifying) anyone who professed to be a Christian and held sound doctrine. They never did or taught anything against the precepts of Moses that Christ had not abrogated. Rather, they kept the law afterwards with no less zeal, as they had kept it before Christ's death, as the chief of the Apostles testify in the passage just cited. They permitted only the Gentiles to live without the law of Moses, not the Jews converted to Christ; this must be carefully noted here because of what follows. As for the substance of doctrine, they taught nothing at odds with Moses and the Prophets. For if they had taught otherwise, their teaching would not have been judged by the Bereans to agree with the Scriptures. Acts 17.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Dicam aliquid amplius, pro sententia Mosis, quae eadem etiam nostra est, plurima: pro diuersa opinione nulla apud Paulum inueniri argumenta. Quippe in 1. ad Cor. 8. neque illos exclusit Apoft. qui adhuc aliquid putabant esse idola: neque Gnofticos illos elatos & tumidos, qui palàm Idolothytis in ipso εἰδωλείῳ, id est, {y}templo, vel certè triclinio ad folenne publicúmque idolorum epulum deftinato, cum profanis impijsque idolorum cultoribus vescebantur: id quod Deus per Mosen aperte vetuit Exod.34. per Apoft. Act.15. denique per Iohan.2. cap. Apoc. Non fuit minùs graue peccatum hoc, quàm fi quis hodiè interesse Pontificiae auderet Missae: quod ex 10. eiusdem epistolae cap. vnicuique colligere promptum est. Quoniam hoc in loco citato probat Paulus, illos tales non minùs declarare facto illo suo, se socios & κοινωνούς esse Diaboli, quàm coenae Dominicae vsurpatione testentur, se mystici corporis Christi membra esse.
units.tr: I will add something more. For the opinion of Moses, which is also ours, there are very many arguments; for the opposite opinion no arguments are found in Paul. Indeed, in 1 Cor. 8 the Apostle did not exclude those who still thought that idols were something, nor those proud and puffed-up Gnostics who openly ate meat offered to idols in the idol-temple [εἰδωλείῳ] itself, that is, in the temple or at least in the dining hall set apart for the solemn public feast of idols, along with profane and impious worshippers of idols. God clearly forbade this through Moses, Exod. 34; through the Apostles, Acts 15; and finally through John, Rev. 2. This sin was no less grave than if anyone today dared to attend the Mass of the Papists. This can easily be gathered for oneself from chapter 10 of the same epistle. For in the passage cited, Paul proves that by that deed such people bear witness no less that they are partners [κοινωνούς] of the Devil than, by their partaking of the Lord's Supper, they testify that they are members of the mystical body of Christ.

units.la: XXXIIII.
units.tr: XXXIIII.

units.la: Deinde cap.10. sic ratiocinatur Paulus. Quemadmodum Deus non pepercit olim res malas appetentibus: Idololatris: stupro se inquinantibus: Christi tentatoribus & murmuratoribus: tametsi eodem cum caeteris omnibus Baptismate baptizati fuissent, eundemque cibum spiritualem edissent ac potum bibissent: sic ne vobis quidem, quicunque talibus estis contaminati vitijs, parcet, quantumuis similiter de vno omnes pane edatis, & de eodem omnes poculo cum omnibus sanctis bibatis. Ex his perspicitur, primùm quidem, nostra & veterum Sacramenta eadem esse (quod ad rem internam seu coelestem attinet) aliàs argumentum Apost. nullum foret. Deinde liquet vtrobique multos flagitiosos & quidem publicè notos admissos fuisse. Tertiò illud etiam constat, neminem iustum esse abstinere quomodo excommunicati abstinere iubentur. Apostolus non dicit, illos tales arcendos esse: sed à Deo sic praedicit puniendos, vt veteres puniti fuerint. Etenim partem eorum Moses cum Leuitis trucidauit, Exod. 32. partem Deus igne, serpentibus, gladio, terrae hiatu, consumpsit: quod etiam Corinthijs vsu-uenit. Quoniam multos eorum morbis tunc conflictatos, multos etiam mortuos fuisse affirmat.
units.tr: Then in chapter 10 Paul reasons thus: just as God of old did not spare those who lusted after evil things, namely idolaters, those who defiled themselves with fornication, those who tempted Christ, and murmurers, even though they had been baptized with the same baptism as all the others and had eaten the same spiritual food and drunk the same spiritual drink; so he will not spare you either, whoever among you are stained by such vices, although you all eat of the one bread and drink of the one cup with all the saints. From this it is plain, first, that our sacraments and those of the ancients are the same (as far as the inward or heavenly reality is concerned); otherwise the Apostle's argument would be nothing. Second, it is clear that on both sides many wicked people, and indeed people publicly known for their sins, were admitted. Third, this also is established: no one is just in abstaining in the way the excommunicated are ordered to abstain. The Apostle does not say that such people are to be kept away, but that God foretells they will be punished as the ancients were punished. For Moses slew part of them with the Levites, Exod. 32; God consumed part of them by fire, by serpents, by the sword, and by an opening of the earth; this also happened to the Corinthians. For he affirms that many of them were then afflicted with diseases, and many died.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Sequente capite neque rixosos & Sectarios, neq; in ipsa celebratione coenae factos ebrios, alijsque scelcribus pollutos,ab vsu eius imperat abiungi. Huius certè interdictionis nullo verbo meminit: cùm longè minora corrigat,vt quod quisquc domi edere debeat. Quomodò hoc in loco potuisset hanc rem tacere, si eam approbauisset, necessariamque Ecclesiae putauisset? Sciebat Apost. aliter legem iubere : aliumque in Ecclesia Sacramentorum vsum esse: quàm vt eorum negatione morum vitia punirentur. Ideo mandat, vt vnusquisque seipsum probet: non hoc praecipit, vt alij alios examinent ac probent. Hortatur praeterea omnes,vt digne studeant edere, ne quis sibi iudicium edat: Indignè edentes nequaquam iubet arceri, sed castigatione Domini interminatur. Edentium genus diuidit per oppositas differentias in duas species, in eos scilicet, qui digne edunt, & eos, qui indignè edunt: neutros iubet non edere, sed omnes cupit digne edere.
units.tr: In the following chapter he does not command that the quarrelsome and sectarians, nor those who became drunk during the celebration of the Supper itself, nor those polluted by other crimes, be cut off from its use. Certainly he makes no mention of any such prohibition, though he corrects matters far less serious, such as that each person should eat at home. How could he have kept silent about this matter here, if he had approved of it and thought it necessary to the Church? The Apostle knew that the law commanded otherwise, and that the use of the sacraments in the Church was not meant to punish the vices of morals by denying them. Therefore he commands that each one examine himself; he does not prescribe that some examine and test others. He further exhorts all to take care to eat worthily, lest anyone eat judgment upon himself. He does not command that those who eat unworthily be kept away, but threatens them with the Lord's chastisement. He divides the eaters, by opposed distinctions, into two kinds: those who eat worthily and those who eat unworthily. He orders neither kind to refrain from eating, but wishes all to eat worthily.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Postmodùm in secunda Epist. cap.12. & 13. non minatur illis,quos post admonitionem non poenituerat impuritatis,libidinis,& impudicitiae, quam patrauerant, amotionem à mensa Domini: sed pro authoritate potestateque à Deo sibi tradita, rigidè duriterque se in eos animaduersurum ostendit: quod in suis scriptis saepè fecit: interdictionem Sacramentorum, de qua praesens est quaestio, nullibi docet: neque vel presbyteris vel aliis vllis hoc vt faciant imperat. Quòd si hoc modò coercere facinorosos voluisset, iussisset eos à Sacramentis, vsque ad emendationem, amoueri:praesertim cùm antea in eadem ecclesia Seniores ordinasset 1.Cor.6. & coenae celebrationem correxisset. Sed haec de re posteà plura dicemus fortasse.
units.tr: Afterwards, in the second Epistle, chapters 12 and 13, he does not threaten those who, after admonition, did not repent of the uncleanness, lust and impurity they had committed with removal from the Lord's table. Instead, by the authority and power given him by God, he shows that he will proceed against them sternly and harshly. He often did this in his writings. Nowhere does he teach the prohibition of the Sacraments, which is the question at hand, nor does he command this of elders or of anyone else. But if he had wished to restrain wrongdoers in this way, he would have ordered that they be kept from the Sacraments until they amended their lives, especially since he had earlier appointed elders in the same church (1 Cor. 6) and had corrected the celebration of the Supper. But perhaps we shall say more about this matter later.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Sicut in Sacramentorum celebratione nullam videmus Excommunicationis mentionem fieri, sic neque in eorundem institutione aliquid huiusmodi deprehenditur. Sed nec in finium & vsus eorum explicatione meminit ipsius scriptura. At si ad hunc etiam finem data Ecclesiae fuissent, vt essent scelerum aut sceleratorum poenae quaedam, alterutro in loco mentio eius aliqua facta fuisset. Coenae Dominicae fines, propter quos instituta fuit, hi sunt: vt solenniter celebremus mortem Domini, publicéque gratias ei agamus pro liberatione nostri: vt admoneamur & testemur nostra praesentia, nos cibum & potum vitae alium nullum habere, quàm Christum crucifixum, & sanguinem ipsius pro nobis effusum: vt declaremus nos poenitere vitae anteactae: cogitare de meliore: amplecti doctrinam Christianam: membra Christi esse: ad ecclesiam ipsius pertinere: in qua piè & sanctè desideremus viuere deinceps ac mori. An haec aliquem facere alicubi scriptura prohibuit? At aliqui, inquies, saepè redierunt ad ingenium: & nihilo meliores sunt redditi. Respondeo illum, qui sic in praesentia cogitat, vt iam dixi, impulsore spiritu sancto, à scriptura non repelli. Vtrùm & quandò tandem fit perseueraturus in sancto illo propósito, nouit Deus. Nostrum est semper bene sperare de omnibus, etiamsi saepè falsi fuerimus: & praeterea Deum ex animo comprecari, vt illum & nos simul in bono confirmet. Interim obiurgandus & admonendus est, qui maleagit, vt seipsum probet, ne iudicium sibi edat & bibat, vti Apost. docet.
units.tr: Just as we see no mention of excommunication made in the celebration of the Sacraments, so nothing of this kind is found in their institution. Nor does Scripture itself mention it in explaining their ends and use. Yet if they had been given to the Church also for this purpose, so that they might be punishments of crimes or of criminals, some mention of it would have been made in one place or the other. The ends for which the Lord's Supper was instituted are these: that we solemnly celebrate the death of the Lord and publicly give thanks to him for our deliverance; that we be reminded, and by our presence bear witness, that we have no other food and drink of life than Christ crucified and his blood poured out for us; that we declare that we repent of our former life, think of a better one, embrace Christian doctrine, are members of Christ, and belong to his Church, in which we desire to live and die piously and holily from now on. Does Scripture anywhere forbid anyone to do these things? But some, you will say, have often returned to their former disposition and have been made no better at all. I reply that the one who thinks in this way in the present, as I have already said, impelled by the Holy Spirit, is not repelled by Scripture. God knows whether and when at last he will persevere in that holy purpose. It is always our duty to hope well concerning all, even though we have often been mistaken, and besides, to pray to God earnestly that he may confirm both him and us together in good. Meanwhile the one who behaves wickedly must be rebuked and admonished to examine himself, lest he eat and drink judgment on himself, as the Apostle teaches.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Postremò, an sunt Sacramenta vel authoritate & dignitate verbo praestantiora? vel vsu magis necessaria? Absque verbo qui seruarentur nulli fuerunt: absque Sacramentis, praesertim absque coena, seruatos ac seruari potuisse multos (qui tamen non contemnerent) nullus dubitat. Haud aliter sensisse videtur Apost. quandò non ad baptizandum, sed ad praedicandum verbum missum fuisse scripsit. An non pleriq; omnes visibilia verba dicunt esse? atque oculis proponere, quae verba auribus significant? Cur ergo à verbo neminem, à Sacramentis, præsertim à coena Domini, aliquos arcere studemus? idque contrà, vel saltem citrà expressum Dei mandatum? Quia, inquiunt, verbum omnibus, Sacramenta solis conuersis instituta sunt. Scio: nec ego de Turcis, aut non conuersis loquor: sed de vocatis à Deo in Ecclesiam suam, & huc insertis: doctrinam probantibus: & Sacramentis rite vti externè saltem cupientibus.
units.tr: Lastly, are the sacraments superior to the Word in authority and dignity, or are they more necessary in practice? No one has been saved without the Word. Yet no one doubts that many have been saved, and could be saved, without the sacraments, especially without the Lord's Supper, though they did not despise them. The Apostle seems to have thought the same when he wrote that he was sent not to baptize but to preach the Word. Do not almost all people say that the Word is visible? Do they not set before the eyes what the Word signifies to the ears? Why then do we strive to keep people from the Word, and especially from the Lord's Supper, and to exclude them from the sacraments? And we do this against, or at least without, any express command of God. "Because," they say, "the Word was instituted for everyone, but the sacraments only for converts." I know that. I am not speaking of Turks or of unconverted people, but of those called by God into his Church and joined to it, who profess the doctrine and desire at least outwardly to use the sacraments rightly.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Firmè hucusque demonstrauì, neque apud Christum, neque apud Apost. huius facinorosorum castigationis, aut potiùs coercitionis, verbum aut exemplum exstare. Quocirca cùm nec vetus nec nouum Testamentum hanc puniendi rationem imperárit, sed contrarium in utroque saepè occurrat, merito putamus, humanum potiùs inuentum esse Excommunicationem (quatenùs propter vitae morumque scelera homines ab vsu Sacramentorum repellit) quàm diuinam quandam legem. Itaque consequens nunc esse videtur, vt, quae aliter sentientes pro se adducunt, inspiciamus, & nihil habere in probando virium demonstremus.
units.tr: I have now firmly shown that there is neither word nor example, either in Christ or in the Apostles, for this punishment, or rather restraint, of wrongdoers. Therefore, since neither the Old nor the New Testament prescribes this method of punishment, but often presents the opposite in both, we rightly think that excommunication (insofar as it keeps people from the use of the sacraments on account of the crimes of their life and conduct) is a human invention rather than some divine law. It seems the logical next step, then, to examine what those who think otherwise bring forward in their favour, and to show that it has no force in proof.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Praeceptum, inquiunt, exstat apud Math. 18. cap. & in Epist. D. Pauli: exemplum autem in 1. Cor. 5. cap. reperitur: item in 1. Timoth. 1. De his ordine agemus: & primùm de loco qui apud Math. habetur.
units.tr: They say there is a precept in Matthew 18 and in the Epistles of St Paul, and an example in 1 Corinthians 5, and likewise in 1 Timothy 1. We shall deal with these in order, and first with the passage in Matthew.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: Propositum Christi non fuit in hoc capite nouam gubernationem, aut exercendae Excommunicationis formam instituere, sed Discipulos erudire, quomodò in depellendis priuatis iniurijs offensionem caucrent. Quoniam enim qui ius suum mox persequuntur apud Magistratum (præsertim Gentilem & profanum, quali tum suberant Iudaei) sæpenumero infirmos offendunt, primùm eos hortatur, vt condonent potiùs iniurias, quàm in qualibet causa ad Magistratum accurrant. Hac in parte nil aliud facit, quàm quod mandatum Mosis 19. Exodi (quod Syracides cap. 28. itidem 19. fusius repetiuit) in memoriam reuocat. Deinde præcipit, si forte ad Magistratum deferre causam cogantur, ne fratres suos Iudæos apud Romanos accusent, priusquàm proprij Magistratus auxilium frustrà implorauerint: si modò scandalum euitare velint. Præceptum simile tradit Corinthijs Apost. in 1. ad Cor. 6. (qui locus præsentis est velut expositio quaedam) ne videlicet temerè inter se litigent Christiani apud Gentiles. Ergo genuinus huius loci & cap. sensus talis est: Cùm frater, hoc est, Iudæus, iniuriam tibi facit, solus eum tibi reconciliare studeto. Si solus nihil profeceris, duobus aut tribus alijs assumptis idem tentato. Si ne sic quidem te liberare ab iniuria poteris, Synedrio, id est, tui populi aut tuae religionis Magistratui indicato. Quòd si hunc etiam audire nolit, sic aduersus eum citrà cuiusquam offensionem agere poteris, quomodò aduersus Publicanum aut Gentilem iniurium tibi inferentem (qui ad aliud quàm Romanorum Tribunal se pertrahi non patiuntur) ageres.
units.tr: Christ's purpose in this chapter was not to establish a new government or a form for exercising excommunication, but to instruct his disciples how to avoid giving offence in settling private injuries. For those who at once pursue their right before the magistrate (especially a heathen and profane one, such as the Jews then were under) often give offence to the weak. So he first urges them to forgive injuries rather than rush to the magistrate in every case. In this he does nothing more than recall the command of Moses in Exodus 19, which Jesus the son of Sirach (chapter 28) repeated more fully. Then he commands that, if they are at last forced to bring the case before the magistrate, they should not accuse their Jewish brothers before the Romans until they have implored in vain the help of their own magistrate, if they wish to avoid scandal. The Apostle gives a similar precept to the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 6, which passage is, as it were, a kind of exposition of the present one: that Christians should not wrangle among themselves before the heathen. Therefore the true sense of this passage and chapter is this: When your brother, that is, a Jew, does you an injury, make it your concern to be reconciled to him alone. If you achieve nothing alone, take two or three others with you and try again. If you cannot free yourself from the injury even so, report it to the Sanhedrin, that is, to the magistrate of your own people or your own religion. But if he refuses even to hear this, you may then proceed against him without giving offence to anyone, just as you would against a publican or a heathen who wronged you (those who will not allow themselves to be dragged before any tribunal but that of the Romans).

units.la: XLII.
units.tr: XLII.

units.la: Hanc esse propriam & legitimam huius loci interpretationem, ex tota orationis serie, præsertim vero ex conclufione, atque circumstantijs omnibus, manifestè ostenditur. Primùm non de grauibus & publicis sceleribus ad religionem patriosque ritus attinentibus (quorum coercitio penès Synedrium erat) disserit hoc loco Christus: sed de priuatorum iniurijs, quorum remittendorum potestas penès quemuis est, loquitur. Euidenter, quod dixi, hoc probat, quòd tota oratio in singulari numero contexitur. Si peccauerit frater Tuus in Te (ἁμάρτῃ) corripe Eum inter Te & ipsum solum: Dic Ecclesiae: fit tibi &c. Eodem modo Luc. quoq; 17. loquitur, si frater Tuus ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σε. Et mox, si septies vno die peccet in Te, ac reuersus ad Te dicat, se poenitere, remittito Ei. Non possumus ut εἰς interpretari, in Ecclesiā. Quippè cùm postea dicit, dic Ecclesiæ, si ensus foret, O Ecclesia, dic Ecclesiæ. Neque idem significare potest, quod, te conscio. Nam neq; verborum orationisq; natura, neq; circumstantiæ hoc patiuntur. Additur enim mox, inter te & ipsum solum. Quomodò ergo, si me conscio, & non in me priuatim & solum peccauit, solus solum cogor monere, non potiùs vnà cum illis, in quos peccauit proprie obiurgare eum iubeor? At Christus non concedit, vt primò cum aliis eum adeam. De iniuria ergo loquitur mihi priuatim à fratre meo facta. Quomodò etiam Luc. verba huic interpretationi congruunt, cùm dicit, si reuersus fuerit ad te, remitte ei? An etiam hic dicemus, ad te, positū esse pro, te conscio? Sed quid significabit tunc remittere ei? An hic etiam dicere oportebit, esto conscius remissionis? An Prodigus Luc. 15. peccans in coelum, conscio coelo peccauit? Quomodò in fratres malè faciendo peccemus, ex 1. Cor. 8. patet, sed huius loci ratio est alia. Certè oratio & verba non sinunt nos de aliis, quàm priuatis iniurijs exponere: quas ipse possis poenitenti remittere. Quòd si non suaspontè eum poeniteat, hoc agere debes, vt poeniteat. Secundò probat idem, quod Apostoli aliter verba Christi non intellexerunt, vt ex Petri interrogatione patet, cùm sic quaeris: satisne est, si fratri meo in me septies peccanti, toties remisero? Non ignorabat Petrus iniuriam, quae ad Ecclesiam aut ad plures alios pertineret, se solum remittere neque posse neque debere. Tertiò probat vox, Titum. Non dicit Christus, sit nobis, sit Ecclesiae, sit aliis: sed sit tibi soli, qui ab eo iniuriam passus es vel pateris, velut Publicanus. Christus etsi omnes ex aequo Apostolos alloquatur, iubet nihilominus, iniuriosum illi soli velut Publicanum haberi, qui ab eo laesus fuit: idque post Ecclesiae admonitionem. Proinde non de illis rebus loquitur, quae ad totam Ecclesiam, siue ad alios plures spectant: sed quae, adsingulos pertinent. Quartò loquitur de talibus peccatis, quæ toties remittere fratribus debemus, quoties illi se poenitere dicunt. Et hanc transactionem seu remis_sionē inter solos duos factam litem omnem finire, apertè in his verbis dicitur, <bl>ἀλλ᾽ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐὰν ὑμῶν ἀμφοτέρων</bl> &c. At graue facinus, quod ad plures totàmue Ecclesiam pertinet, non poterit ab vno solo remitti. Notandum hîc obiter est, aduerbium <bl>ἀλλ᾽</bl>, quo se idem iam antè dixisse indicat, tametsi alijs verbis vsus fuerit. Quintò, loquitur Christus de eiusmodi peccatis, quorum, qui ea commisit, non pudet: quæue coram quouis non sit negaturus. Si de alijs grauioribus, & ad Ecclesiam aliósue plures spectantibus loqueretur, locum testes non haberent. Nullus enim tale factum, si occultum sit, coràm testibus confitebitur. At in omnibus, de quibus hîc sermo est, gradus à Christo positi seruandi sunt. Quocirca de priuatis iniurijs, ad alios nihil pertinentibus, loquitur. Sextò loquitur de talibus, quæ Ecclesia, de qua hîc loquitur Christus, non punit, sed iniuriosum verbis duntaxat castigatum dimittit. Frustrà enim diceretur, si non audierit Ecclesiam, siquidem peccatum publica pœna coercere posset. Septimò, probat idem luculentè admodùm parabola mox sequens, qua docetur, Deum non remissurum illis peccata sua, quicunque fratribus suis poenitentibus non remittunt ex animo iniurias citrà mulctā & poenam. At Ecclesia sic non debet, vt illi aiunt, remittere, sed à Sacramentis, saltem ad tempus, arcere: dum Presbyteris ad hanc rem delectis poenitentiam suam probent. Ergo non volet septies in die remittere dicentibus se poenitere: sed volet argumenta videre, de quibus hîc Christus nihil dicit. Non vult alia argumenta quàm confessionem erati: quam qui non simulat, non redibit in die septies. Perspicuè ex his demonstratur, Christum in hoc 18.Math.cap. non de erroribus Excommunicatione vindicandis, sed de Ieuibus & priuatis iniurijs, earumque componendi modo differere: ideóque ad excommunicationis negotium non pertinere. Si vel sola conclusio Christi in fine capitis infpiciatur, ablata erit omnis dubitatio.
units.tr: That this is the proper and legitimate interpretation of this passage is clearly shown from the whole course of the discourse, and especially from its conclusion and all its circumstances. First, Christ does not in this place discuss grave and public crimes touching religion and the ancestral rites (whose punishment lay with the Sanhedrin), but speaks of injuries done to private persons, whose remission lies in the power of anyone. The fact that the whole discourse is framed in the singular number proves clearly what I have said. "If your brother sins against you" (ἁμάρτῃ), "go and reprove him between you and him alone"; "tell it to the Church," and so on. Luke 17 speaks in the same way: "if your brother sins against you" (ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σε). And soon after: "if he sins against you seven times in one day, and returns to you and says he repents, forgive him." We cannot interpret "against you" as "in the Church," because he afterwards says "tell it to the Church"; if it meant "O Church, tell the Church," the sentence would be absurd. Nor can it mean the same as "with your knowledge," for neither the nature of the words and sentence nor the circumstances allow it. For immediately it is added, "between you and him alone." How, then, if he sinned in my presence and not against me privately and alone, am I bound to admonish him alone and alone? Should I not rather be ordered to rebuke him properly together with those against whom he sinned? But Christ does not permit me to go to him first with others. He is therefore speaking of an injury done to me privately by my brother. And how does the passage of Luke agree with this interpretation, when it says, "if he returns to you, forgive him"? Shall we say here too that "to you" stands for "with your knowledge"? But then what would "to forgive him" signify? Must we say here too: "be aware of the forgiveness"? Did the Prodigal in Luke 15, sinning against heaven, sin with heaven's knowledge? That we sin against our brethren by wronging them is plain from 1 Corinthians 8, but the reasoning of this passage is different. Certainly the discourse and the words do not allow us to speak of anything but private injuries, which you yourself may forgive the penitent. If he does not repent of his own accord, you ought to act so that he does repent. Secondly, the same is proved by the fact that the Apostles did not understand Christ's words otherwise, as is plain from Peter's question: "Is it enough, if my brother sins against me seven times, that I forgive him as often?" Peter did not doubt that an injury affecting the Church or many others could not be forgiven by himself alone, nor ought to be. Thirdly, the word "brother" proves it. Christ does not say "let him be to us, to the Church, to others," but "let him be to you alone, you who have suffered or are suffering an injury from him, like a publican." Although Christ addresses all the Apostles alike, he nevertheless commands that the one who wronged him be regarded as a publican by that person alone who was harmed by him, and that after the Church has admonished him. Therefore he does not speak of those matters which concern the whole Church or many others, but of those which concern individuals. Fourthly, he speaks of such sins as we ought to forgive our brothers as often as they say they repent. And that this agreement made between only two ends the whole dispute is clearly stated in these words: "But I say to you that if both of you..." and so on. But a grave crime which concerns many or the whole Church cannot be remitted by one person alone. It should be noted in passing that the particle "but" (ἀλλ᾽), by which he shows that he has already said the same thing before, though in other words. Fifthly, Christ speaks of sins of such a kind that the one who committed them is not ashamed of them and would not deny them before anyone. If he were speaking of other, graver sins touching the Church or many others, there would be no witnesses to the matter. For no one will confess such a deed before witnesses if it is secret. But in all the cases under discussion here, the steps which Christ has laid down must be observed. Therefore he is speaking of private injuries which concern no one else. Sixthly, he speaks of such matters as the Church, of which Christ is speaking here, does not punish, but dismisses the wrongdoer with a verbal rebuke only. For it would be pointless to say "if he does not hear the Church" if a public penalty could restrain the sin. Seventhly, the parable that immediately follows proves the same very clearly. It teaches that God will not forgive their sins to those who do not from the heart forgive their brothers' injuries when they repent, without any fine or penalty. But the Church, as they claim, ought not to forgive in this way, but to keep the offender from the sacraments, at least for a time, until he proves his repentance to the elders appointed for this purpose. Therefore it is not the Church's will to forgive seven times a day those who say they repent; it wishes to see proofs, of which Christ says nothing here. It wants no proof but the confession of the wrong, and whoever does not feign this will not come back seven times in a day. These points clearly show that in Matthew 18 Christ is not speaking of defending the Church against errors by excommunication, but of slight and private injuries and the manner of settling them. Therefore it does not pertain to the business of excommunication. If the conclusion of Christ at the end of the chapter alone is considered, all doubt will be removed.

units.la: XLIII.
units.tr: XLIII.

units.la: Qui opinatur Christum in hoc loco & cap. Excommunicationem instituisse, ostendere cogitur, in quibus verbis mandatum hoc comprehensum sit. Si demonstrare non poterit contineri, frustra dicet hic eam mandari. Ergo vel in his verbis inest, Dic Ecclesiae: vel cum dicitur, sit tibi velut Publicanus: vel in illis, quaecunque ligaueritis. At omnia haec nihil tale complecti certissimis argumentis probabo. Quocirca cum in aliis nullis quaeri possit, frustra in hoc capite quaeritur.
units.tr: Whoever holds that Christ instituted excommunication in this place and chapter is bound to show in which words this command is contained. If he cannot demonstrate that it is contained, he says in vain that it is commanded here. Therefore it lies either in these words, "Tell it to the Church," or when it is said, "let him be to you as a publican," or in those, "whatever you shall bind." But I will prove by the most certain arguments that all of these contain nothing of the kind. Wherefore, since it cannot be sought in any others, it is sought in vain in this chapter.

units.la: XLIIII.
units.tr: XLIIII.

units.la: Verba Christi, Dic Ecclesiae, hoc tantum probant, posse eum qui iniuria affectus est a fratre suo, ac frustra reconciliari cum eo studuerit, de iniuria queri apud Ecclesiam sive Ecclesiae Rectores aut praesides. Praeterea quod Ecclesia eadem ius & potestatem habeat iniurium hominem obiurgandi & monendi, vt iniurius esse desinat. Non plus potestatis tribuitur hic Ecclesiae, quam testibus ante datum est: si vnum hoc excipias, quod sine testibus causa non defertur ad Ecclesiam. An non igitur inepta fuerit ratiocinatio haec, Ecclesia ius habet illum, qui alios iniuria afficit, obiurgandi: Ergo ius habet eum excommunicandi, siue a Sacramentis arcendi? At vero, inquiat aliquis, Ecclesia non habet ius poenis corporalibus aut gladio plectendi nocentes: proinde prohibitione Sacramentorum punire cogitur. Respondeo, non sequi connexum hoc, etiamsi verum esset, quod antecedit (falsum esse antecedens de visibili Ecclesia acceptum, totum vetus Testamentum, omnium saeculorum historia, nostrimet oculi & sensus, nobis demonstrant) neque probari vnquam poterit ista recte cohaerere. Non potest punire gladio, ergo arcere debet a communibus Sacramentis eandem religionem profitentes.
units.tr: The words of Christ, Tell it to the Church, prove only this: that a man who has been wronged by his brother, and has tried in vain to be reconciled to him, may complain of the injury before the Church, or before the rulers or presidents of the Church. Further, they prove that the Church has the same right and power to rebuke and admonish the wrongdoer, so that he may cease to do wrong. No more power is given to the Church here than was given to witnesses earlier, except this one point: that a case is not brought before the Church without witnesses. Would not this reasoning be absurd? The Church has the right to rebuke one who wrongs others; therefore it has the right to excommunicate him, that is, to bar him from the sacraments. But, someone will say, the Church has no right to punish wrongdoers with bodily penalties or the sword; therefore it is forced to punish them by withholding the sacraments. I reply that this inference does not follow, even if the premise were true. (That the premise is false, when it is understood of the visible Church, is shown to us by the whole Old Testament, the history of all ages, and our own eyes and senses.) Nor can it ever be proved that these propositions rightly hang together: "It cannot punish with the sword; therefore it must bar from the common sacraments those who profess the same religion."

units.la: XLV.
units.tr: XLV.

units.la: Si respondeat, qui diuersum sentit, hoc verba illa velle, sit tibi velut Publicanus & Ethnicus: respondebo ego salsum esse. Quippe nulla oratione, nulla persuasione, nullis argumentis in sempiternum demonstrabitur, hanc orationem Christi, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, eandem esse cum hac, sit excommunicatus, siue à Sacramentis exclusus. Etenim Christi ætate Publicani circumcisi, siue Iudæi essent, siuè Gentiles, non arcebantur à Sacrificijs, templo, cæremoniijs & Sacramentis. Sanè videtur Christus cum Ethnico ideò coniunxisse Publicanum, ne quis istam Sacramentorum interdictionem, hic iuberi arbitraretur. Quomodò potuissent secundùm legem arceri à Templo & cultu Diuino, cùm vectigalium redemptorem esse peccatii non esset? nec à Deo vspiam prohibitum inueniretur? Christus certè nullo in loco vetuit. Ioannes Publicanis interrogantibus quid facere necesse haberent, vt salui fierent, non mandat vt officiū deserant, sed ne plus exigant, hortatur, quàm constitutum fuerat, Luc. 3. Christus quoque Principi Publicanorum Zachæo non præcipit muneris huius abdicationem: nec isto nomine ipsum reprehendit Luc. 19. Nec de illo, qui in Templū ascenderat oratum, & Christo iudice iustus domum redierat, legimus quòd Publicanus esse desierit. Luc. 18. Sed nec alios illos, qui Deum laudabant & prædicabant, Luc. 7. & 15. & Christo atque Apostolis erant charissimi, mutauisse conditionem reperimus. Summatim dicam, sacras literas, hoc est, Deum nullo tempore & loco Publicanos hoc nomine condemnare aut vituperare, quoad Publicani sunt, hoc est, vectigalium redemptores: quod omnes sani mecum libenter confitebuntur. Quo posito, sic argumetor. Deus nullum Publicanū, quia Publicanus, condemnat in sacris literis. Quem porrò Deus non damnat, is eon potest ex lege Dei excommunicari. Nullus igitur Publicanus potuit iure Diuino prohiberi ab aditu Templi & cultu diuino. Pergo iam, sic concludens. Nullus Publicanus ex lege potuit damnari seu excommunicari. At Christus non audientem Ecclesiam, de qua ibi loquebatur, iubet habere vt Publicanum. Ergo iubet pro eo haberi, qui ex lege Dei non potuit haberi execrabilis: hoc videlicet nomine, quia Publicanus sit. Quod Excommunicatores dicunt verba haec, sit tibi velut Publicanus, idem significare, ac si dixisset, sit tibi qualis Publicanus est Pharisæis, absurdum, falsum, & impossibile est. Non enim est credibile, Christum in eo loco, in quo decreuit rem adeo magni momenti, adeoque vtilem & necessariam (vt dicunt aduersarij) Ecclesiæ instituere, voluisse Regulam, quæ seruanda deinceps ab omnibus esset, ab impio facto improbissimorum hominum sumere. Deinde probatum iam fuit, nullum vnquam apud Iudæos fuisse excommunicatum: quomodo nunc de hac re disputamus. Denique pugnant omnia verba Christi cum eorum interpretatione. Etenim Christus hic non de Pharisæis (aut cum his) loquitur, sed cum discipulis agit: & de ratione cauendi scandala disserit. Hoc dicit, si iniurius homo Ecclesiam non vult audire, sit tibi, quomodo Publicanus, scilicet tibi est: non quomodo Pharisæis est. Caeterum constat Publicanos Christo & Discipulis ac religiosis omnibus non fuisse exosos: certè non habuerunt pro dignis Excommunicatione, sed cum eis quotidie edebant ac vniebant. Quod vero Ethnicum & Publicanum coniungit, cogit nos fateri, Christum de re quapiam loqui, quae vtrisque communis esset. At hi in Templum ingredi poterant, non illi. Quare de excommunicatione hic nihil dixit Christus. Longe ergo aliud significant verba haec, Sit tibi tanquam Publicanus, quàm haec, sit tibi tanquam Excommunicatus. Sensus ergo huius loci hic est: Si Ecclesiam non audiat, poteris (in hac causa) sine offendiculo cuiusquam sic cum eo agere, ac si cum Ethnico vel Publicano negotium tibi esset. Qui cum talibus controuerliam habebat, cogebatur apud Romanum Magistratum causam suam disceptare: (de ethnicis constat: de Publicanis ex eo patet, quòd Romanorum iurati effent ministri contra suam gentem: quodq; à Pharisæis & principibus Iudæorum, qui eos pro deploratis & nebulonibus habebant, nihil æqui poterant expectare) quod Christus nulli permittit aduersus fratrem Iudaeum, priusquàm eo modo reconciliationem requisierit, qui ab ipso est propositus, & olim fuerat in lege præscriptus. Hùc excusatio Pauli Act. vltimo pertinet: scilicet non se appellauisse Caesarem, nisi coactum: nec vt Iudaeos accusaret, sed vt seipsum à vi & iniuria defenderet. Si quid habebat Christianus aduersus fratrem apud Cor. iubet Apost. vt coram delectis arbitris tentet transfigere: non statim litiget coram profano magistratu. Quòd si Christianus cum Ethnico negotium haberet, quis dubitat, quin apud Gentilem magistratum ius suum persequi potuerit? Eodem modo si quis Seniorum in Ecclesia iudicium & sententiam contemneret, poterat, qui laedebatur iniuriamue patiebatur, ad Gentilem Magistratum prouocare, sine offensione proximi.
units.tr: If someone who thinks otherwise should reply that these words mean "let him be to you as a tax collector and a Gentile," I shall answer that this is false. No argument, no persuasion, and no proof will ever show that this saying of Christ, "let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector," is the same as this one, "let him be excommunicated, or shut out from the sacraments." In Christ's time, tax collectors were not barred from the sacrifices, the temple, the ceremonies, and the sacraments, whether they were circumcised Jews or Gentiles. It seems that Christ joined the tax collector with the Gentile precisely so that no one would suppose that the prohibition of the sacraments was being enjoined here. How could they have been excluded from the temple and divine worship under the law, when being a collector of taxes was not a sin? Nor would one find it forbidden by God anywhere. Certainly Christ forbade it in no place. When tax collectors asked John what they must do to be saved, he did not order them to give up their office, but urged them not to exact more than had been fixed (Luke 3). Christ did not command Zacchaeus, the chief of the tax collectors, to give up his post, nor did he rebuke him on that account (Luke 19). Nor do we read that the man who went up into the temple to pray, and who went home justified in the judgment of Christ, ceased to be a tax collector (Luke 18). Nor do we find that those others, who praised and proclaimed God (Luke 7 and 15), and were most dear to Christ and the Apostles, changed their condition. To sum up, I say that Holy Scripture, that is, God, at no time and in no place condemns or reviles tax collectors under that name, so far as they are tax collectors, that is, collectors of taxes. All sensible people will gladly agree with me on this. This being established, I argue thus: God condemns no tax collector in Holy Scripture simply because he is a tax collector. Whomever God does not condemn, that person cannot be excommunicated by the law of God. Therefore no tax collector could by divine right be barred from entrance to the temple and from divine worship. I proceed to conclude as follows: no tax collector could be condemned or excommunicated by the law. But Christ commands that one who does not hear the Church, of which he is speaking there, be held as a tax collector. Therefore he commands that he be held as one who, by the law of God, could not be held accursed, namely for this reason, that he is a tax collector. When the excommunicators say that the words "let him be to you as a tax collector" mean the same as if he had said "let him be to you as tax collectors are to the Pharisees," this is absurd, false, and impossible. For it is not credible that Christ, in the place where he decided to institute something of such great moment, and so useful and necessary to the Church (as our opponents say), would have wished to take as the rule to be kept by all thereafter an example from the wicked deed of the most wicked men. Moreover, it has already been shown that no one was ever excommunicated among the Jews, and so we are now disputing about this matter. Finally, all the words of Christ contradict their interpretation. For Christ is not speaking here of the Pharisees (or with them), but is addressing his disciples, and is discussing the manner of avoiding offences. He says: if a wicked man will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a tax collector is to you, that is, as he is to you, not as he is to the Pharisees. Moreover, it is clear that the tax collectors were not hateful to Christ, his disciples, or all the pious; certainly they did not regard them as worthy of excommunication, but ate and drank with them every day. Yet the fact that he joins the Gentile and the tax collector compels us to admit that Christ is speaking of some matter common to both. But the latter could enter the temple, and the former could not. Therefore Christ said nothing here about excommunication. These words, "let him be to you as a tax collector," therefore mean something quite different from "let him be to you as one excommunicated." The sense of this passage, then, is this: if he will not hear the Church, you may (in this matter) deal with him without offence to anyone, just as if you had a dispute with a Gentile or a tax collector. Those who had a controversy with such people were compelled to plead their case before the Roman magistrate. (That this was so for Gentiles is certain; for tax collectors it is clear from the fact that they were sworn servants of the Romans against their own nation, and because they could expect nothing fair from the Pharisees and the leaders of the Jews, who regarded them as abandoned and worthless.) Christ allows no one to do this against a Jewish brother before he has sought reconciliation in the manner he has proposed here, and which had been prescribed of old in the law. To this belongs the excuse of Paul in the last chapter of Acts, namely that he had appealed to Caesar only when compelled, and not in order to accuse the Jews, but to defend himself from violence and wrong. If a Christian had anything against a brother, the Apostle in Corinthians orders him to try to settle it before chosen arbiters, and not to go to law straightaway before a profane magistrate. But if a Christian had a dispute with a Gentile, who doubts that he could pursue his right before a Gentile magistrate? In the same way, if anyone despised the judgment and sentence of the elders in the Church, the one who was harmed or suffered wrong could appeal to the Gentile magistrate without giving offence to his neighbour.

units.la: XLVI.
units.tr: XLVI.

units.la: Clarior euadet tractatio, si quae & qualis fuerit illa Ecclesia, cui iussit dicere, consideretur. In cuius rei declaratione hoc pro initio & fundamento pono, quod ab omnibus probatum iri confido, & à nemine negatum scio: Christum scilicet de Ecclesia loqui, quae tum esset. Quomodò namque iussisset eos Ecclesiae dicere, quae nullibi reperiebatur? & de cuius constitutione nihil adhuc audierant? Si nouam fundare Ecclesiam, aut nouam gubernandi formam Apostolis incognitam voluisset, mutilam valdè tradidisset institutionem. Quippè neque qui sint illa Ecclesia, neque ex quibus & quomodo colligenda, neque modum iudicij poenásque docuit: neque de omnibus peccatis locutus est, vt iam probaui: & illi, ipsi, qui ex hoc loco Excommunicationem exstruunt, confiteri nobiscum coguntur: dum de occultis duntaxat erratis hîc agi palàm afferunt. Vbi noui aliquid instituit Christus, nihil omisit eorum, sine quibus consistere res illa non potuisset. Hic tantùm iubet Ecclesiæ dicere: quam si non audiat, permittit eum veluti Publicanum haberi ab accusatore: poenam propterea nullam addit. Lucas cùm in hunc locum incidisset, ne illa quidem singillatim commemorat, quae Math. recensuit: reliqui Euangelistæ mentionem nullam faciunt: non taciturí rem tantam & tam necessariam, si tum primùm à Christo institutam cognouissent. Adde, quòd Apostoli Christum non moriturum ritusq; Iudaicos non mutaturum persuasissimû habebant: quodque nullo verbo, nullo signo aut indicio declararunt, se Christi doctrinam non satis percipere: aut quasi inusitatum aut incognitû aliquid audirent, vel interrogare voluisse vel admiratos fuisse. Hoc solùm mirabatur Petrus, quòd toties fratri iuberetur ignoscere. Proindè non acceperunt haec verba Christi de noua gubernationis forma ipsis incognita: sed se doceri crediderunt (& rectè quidem) quandò sibi liceret Iudæum fratrem apud prophanû magistratum accusare absque offendiculo.
