Hodiè quoque non temerè videas Iudæum cum Iudæo apud Christianum magistratum litigare.
units.tr: The treatment will become clearer if we consider what kind of Church it was that he told them to address. To declare this, I lay down as a beginning and foundation a point that I trust all will accept and that I know no one denies: namely, that Christ was speaking of the Church as it then existed. For how could he have told them to speak to the Church if it was nowhere to be found, and they had heard nothing yet of how it was constituted? If he had wanted to found a new Church, or a form of government unknown to the Apostles, he would have handed down a very incomplete instruction. He taught neither who the members of that Church are, nor from whom and how it is to be gathered, nor the manner of judgment and the penalties. Nor did he speak of all sins, as I have already shown. And those very men who build excommunication on this passage are forced to agree with us, since they openly claim that only secret faults are being dealt with here. Where Christ instituted something new, he omitted nothing without which the matter could not have stood. Here he only bids them tell the Church; if the offender does not listen, he allows him to be regarded by the accuser as a publican, and adds no penalty. When Luke came to this passage, he does not even recount individually the things Matthew listed; the other evangelists make no mention at all. They would not have kept silent about so great and necessary a matter if they had known that it was first instituted by Christ at that time. Add that the Apostles were thoroughly persuaded that Christ would not die and would not change the Jewish rites; and by no word, no sign or indication did they show that they had failed to grasp Christ's teaching, or that they wished to ask about something as unusual or unknown, or were amazed at it. Peter alone wondered that he should be ordered to forgive a brother so often. Therefore they did not take these words of Christ as concerning a new form of government unknown to them, but they believed (and rightly so) that they were being taught that they might accuse a Jewish brother before a profane magistrate without giving offence. Even today you may see a Jew litigating with a Jew before a Christian magistrate without any scruple.

units.la: XLVII.
units.tr: XLVII.

units.la: Ergo non pertinet ad omnes hoc mandatum, interroget forte aliquis? sed ad illos solos qui sub impio magistratu degunt? Respondeo priorē partem de tentanda reconciliatione antequā veniatur ad iudicem ad omnes Christianos pertinere: posteriorem hunc habere locum quandò sub magistratu non Christiano degunt pij. Idcircò Paul. Corinthios quoque hortatur, vt aliquos ex suo ordine eligant, qui lites dirimant, ne cogantur coràm profano magistratu litigare. Quis dubitat Corinthijs, si qui stare delectorum iudicio nollent, vel si iniuriosus propter horum sententiam nihilo fieret melior, licuerit demùm ad Romanum Gentilemque magistratum venire? Equidem Paulus, cum se à Iudaeis iniquè premi cerneret, Caesarem appellauit, Act. 25. Quod factum vt excusarit apud Iudaeos Romae degentes vltimo cap. Act. indicatur. Planius intelliget ac certius videbit omnia haec, qui locum Leuit. 19. Eccles. 19. & 1. Cor. 6. cum hoc capite Math. diligenter conferre tentabit: & quàm aperte omnia sibi respondeant, obseruabit: inprimis verò qui Pauli & Christi verba de postrema parte attentè notabit; quae quia sub Mose & Ecclesiastico non habebant locum (quòd nulli tunc extero principi sic parerent, vt Romanis deinde parucrunt) ab utroque hoc meritò omissa fuerunt.
units.tr: Does this command therefore not apply to everyone? Someone may perhaps ask: is it only for those who live under an impious magistrate? I answer that the first part, concerning the attempt at reconciliation before one comes to the judge, applies to all Christians; the latter part has its place only when the godly live under a non-Christian magistrate. For this reason Paul also urges the Corinthians to choose some from among their own number to settle their disputes, so that they are not compelled to litigate before a profane magistrate. Who doubts that, if some were unwilling to abide by the judgment of the chosen men, or if the wrongdoer became no better because of their sentence, the Corinthians would have been allowed in the end to come before the Roman, that is, Gentile, magistrate? Indeed, Paul, when he saw himself unjustly oppressed by the Jews, appealed to Caesar (Acts 25). That this act was justified before the Jews living at Rome is shown in the last chapter of Acts. He who attentively compares Leviticus 19, Ecclesiasticus 19 and 1 Corinthians 6 with this chapter of Matthew will understand all these things more plainly and see them more clearly; and he will observe how openly they agree with one another. Above all, let him carefully note the words of Paul and Christ concerning the last part. Because under Moses and in the Ecclesiastical order this part had no place (since they did not then submit to any foreign prince in the way they later submitted to the Romans), both of them rightly omitted it.

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: Et hactenus quidem, vt opinor, facilè conuenit omnibus, nempè Christum de Ecclesia loquutum, quae in rerum natura seu in Iudaea tunc exstaret: at mox diuaricantur sententiae, cùm quid per Ecclesiae nomen intellexerit Christus, inquiritur. Quippè aliquando pro tota concione seu multitudine ponitur: nonnunquam verò pro Senatu siue Senioribus, qui eam gubernabant, accipitur. Hoc modo vsurpata reperimus nomina Hebraica significantia Ecclesiam & concionem siue congregationem (quae Septuaginta nomine ἐκκλησία expresserunt) Num. 35. Iof. 20. Psal. 82. atque alibi. Porrò Christum hoc in loco per Ecclesiam, non multitudinem vel turbam, sed Iudaicum senatum. (συνέδριον, πρεσβεῖα, συναγωγὴ) intelligere nos voluisse, argumenta sunt valida. Primum est, quòd constat Christum formam iudiciorum & gubernationis, quae secundùm leges administrabatur, non nouasse: nec contrà ea, quae Moses iubente Deo recté sanxerat, aliquid secisse, aut discipulis permisisse. Iusserat autè Moses causas tales proponere dijudicandas, non turbae, sed cuiusque loci senatui siue τῷ συνεδρίῳ: quod in singularum vrbium por-tis. tis initio confidere folebat. Si contrà hoc Mosis institutum hic aliquid instituere cogitauisset Christus, fuissent eare non leuiter offensi discipuli : qui per omnem vitam legis obferuantiffimi fuerunt. Cogitent apud fe singuli, quos Pharifæi triumphos acturi fuissent, fi verè Chriftum arguere huius criminis potuissent : quod scilicet contrà doctrinam Mosis populum aduersus magistratum incitauisset ? Quem poterant illustriorem prætextum optare, ipsum vt seditiosum accusandi, quàm fi probau.ffent, eum contrà Dei prælinitionem tentauisse populù aduersus magistratum armare? testium examinationes permittere? potestatem ad fe vocandi, quos vellent concedere? caufas cognoscendi ac iudicandi facultatem tradere? Alterum est quod Christus ei Ecclesiæ iussit dicere, quæ poteftatem habet accusatum ad fe vocandi, causam audiendi, testes examinandi. (ideò enim in fecunda admonitione iubet nos duos aut tres adiungere, vt factum idoneè probetur) & demùm pronunciandi seu iudicandi. Hæc autem à turba & multitudine fieri non posse, nisi certos quosdam eligat qui omnia moderentur, nullus ignorat. (Valdè pusillum oportet cœtum esse, qui absque Senatoribus per fe res & causas tales possit expedire. Hac de causa rectè aliqui iudicarunt, hoc præceptum Christi, fi de tota concione seu turba accipiatur, locum habere non posse, nisi cum ex valdè paucis Ecclesia constat.) Proindè cùm, qui hoc modo præsunt, nihil aliud sint, quàm Senatus fiue συνέδριον quoddam, rursus efficitur, Christum non turbæ, sed Synedrio iussisse indicari. At verò populus Christi tempore non habuit potestatem eligendi sibi magiftratum & principes. Quocircà per Ecclesiam Iudaicum senatum nos intelligere oportet: quemadmodum discipulos intellexisse ex supra di£tis constat. Ergò fi per Ecclesiam intelligamus ipsam turbam, Ecclesiæ dicere oportebit, quæ ius habeat eligendi sibi senatum talem, qualis erat tunc Iudaicæ Ecclesiæ senatus. Nostræ autem Ecclesiæ non habent potestatem talem senatum eligendi, qualis erat Synedrium Iudaeorum: imò apud Iudaeos quoque non habuit eam facultatem populus ætate Christi: vt paulò ante dixi. His iam addamus, quòd scriptura, cùm de turba loquitur, ferè vtitur nominibus, populi, multitudinis, turbæ, Filiorum Israel, aut idem significantibus alijs, vt cùm in tota Synagoga, vel in tota congregatione aliquid dictû factúmue scribitur. Taceo quòd hic loquendi modus hodiè etiam vsitatus est. Quippe Imperio aut Reipub. indicauisse diximus, quod Imperatori alijsque Imperij Rectoribus aut Reipub. Senatui exposuimus. A Republica donatos diximus, qui ab eius Senatu donum acceperunt. Huiusmodi phrases tam sunt vsitatæ, vt nirum sit à tam paucis in hoc loco obseruatum fuisse. Summa est. Christus non mutauit morem fui temporis, nec in iudicijs aliquid mutauit: sicut discipuli nullam mutationem aut nouationem suspicari videntur. Quamobrem Synedrio dicete iussit, priusquàm ad profanum magistratum itetur.
units.tr: So far, I think, all agree without difficulty: that Christ spoke of the Church that then existed in the nature of things, or in Judaea. But opinions diverge once one inquires what Christ understood by the name of the Church. For sometimes it is used for the whole assembly or multitude, but sometimes it is taken for the senate or the elders who governed it. In this way we find Hebrew names used that signify the Church and the assembly or congregation (which the Seventy rendered by the name [ἐκκλησία]), in Numbers 35, Joshua 20, Psalm 82, and elsewhere. Moreover, there are strong arguments that in this place by "Church" Christ meant not the multitude or crowd, but the Jewish senate ([συνέδριον], [πρεσβεῖα], [συναγωγή]). The first is that it is established that Christ did not change the form of judgments and government which was administered according to the laws; nor did he do anything, or permit his disciples to do anything, contrary to what Moses had rightly ordained at God's command. Moses had ordered that such cases be brought for judgment not before the crowd, but before the senate of each place, [τῷ συνεδρίῳ], which they were accustomed to assemble at the gates of each city. If Christ had intended to institute something new here, contrary to this institution of Moses, the disciples, who were most observant of the law all their lives, would not have been lightly offended. Let each consider with himself how the Pharisees would have triumphed, if they could truly have accused Christ of this crime: that he had stirred up the people against the magistrate, contrary to the teaching of Moses. What more illustrious pretext could they have wished for in order to accuse him as seditious, than if they could prove that he had tried, contrary to God's ordinance, to arm the people against the magistrate, to permit the examination of witnesses, to grant to himself the power of summoning whomever they wished, and to hand over the power of examining and judging causes? The second is that Christ ordered them to tell that Church which has the power to summon the accused, to hear the case, to examine the witnesses (for this is why in the second admonition he bids us add two or three, so that the deed may be properly proved), and finally to pronounce or judge. Nobody is unaware that these things cannot be done by a crowd and a multitude, unless it chooses certain men to manage everything. (The assembly would have to be very small indeed that could settle such matters and cases on its own without senators. For this reason some have rightly judged that this precept of Christ, if it is taken of the whole assembly or crowd, cannot hold, unless the Church consists of very few.) Therefore, since those who preside in this way are nothing other than a senate or a certain [συνέδριον], it again follows that Christ ordered the matter to be reported not to the crowd but to the Sanhedrin. But in Christ's time the people did not have the power of choosing for themselves magistrates and rulers. Therefore we must understand the Jewish senate by the Church, as is clear from what was said above that the disciples understood. Thus, if we understand by the Church the crowd itself, it would have to be said that the Church has the right to elect for itself a senate such as the senate of the Jewish Church was at that time. But our Churches do not have the power to elect a senate such as the Sanhedrin of the Jews was; indeed, among the Jews too, the people in Christ's age did not have that power, as I said a little earlier. To these let us add that Scripture, when it speaks of the crowd, mostly uses the names people, multitude, crowd, sons of Israel, or other words with the same meaning, as when it is written that something was said or done in the whole synagogue or the whole congregation. I say nothing of the fact that this way of speaking is still in use today. Indeed, we say that something was reported to the Empire or the Commonwealth, when we have set it out before the Emperor and the other rulers of the Empire or the Senate of the Commonwealth. We say that those were given gifts by the Commonwealth who received a gift from its Senate. Such phrases are so common that it would be strange if so few had noticed this in the present passage. In sum: Christ did not change the custom of his time, nor did he change anything in judgments, just as the disciples seem to suspect no change or novelty. Therefore he ordered that it be told to the Sanhedrin before one went to the profane magistrate.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: Cæterùm constat ex sacris literis & historijs, Synedrium illud legitimum fuisse magistratum: atque ius gladij tempore Christi adhuc retinuisse & exercuisse. Demonstrant hoc primùm, quae in historia Passionis Christi leguntur. Deindè alia quoque testimonia. Emittit armatos ad comprehendendum Iesum: Testes contrà eum examinat secundùm præceptum legis: vt videri volebat: Iubet Christum coràm se iudicio sisti: Vinctum tradit Pilato, publicè prius à se condemnatum: Stephanum palàm condemnat, occidíque iubet: Apostolos in carceres abduci publicos imperat: eosdem caedi mandat, habito super hac te consilio publico: Paulo mandatum dat potestatemque ex alijs vrbibus pios Hierosolymam vinctos pertrahendi, vt ibidem occiderentur: Act. 24: ipsimet Iudaei & iudices, siue τὸ συνέδριον explicatissimis verbis. hoc affirmat per Tertullum Oratorem, cùm Paulum apud Felicem accusantes sic loquitur Tertul-lus, ὃν ᾧ ἐκρατήσαμεν, ᾧ καὶ τὸν ἡμέτερον νόμον ἠθελήσαμεν κρίνειν. Iuxtà nostram legem, inquit, voluimus eum condemnare: nisi Lysias eum (vt additur) nobis per vim eripuisset è nostris manibus. Act. 23. ait Paulus ad Pontificem, tunc sedes vt secundùm præscriptum legis me iudices, & contrà legis voluntatem me iubes percuti? Post Act. 26. idem fatetur coràm Agrippâ Rege & Festo, se multos sanctos Hierosolymis atque alibi carceribus inclusisse: potestate huius rei à sacerdotum principibus accepta: se item sententia & suffragio suo eos occidisse: per omnes quoque Synagogas cruciatibus & poenis coegisse ad blasphemiam: deniq; ἐξωσίας καὶ ἀπειληθῆναι à principibus sacerdotum accepisse similiter in exteris vrbibus, & inter has Damasci, pios tractandi. Sciebant, opinor, Agrippa & Festus vtrùm haec Synedrio liceret facere, an non liceret. Nisi hæc potestas penès ipsum fuisset, non absoluissent Paulum suis sententijs: vt mox faciunt. Quippè non minus fuisset Pauli peccatum contrà Cæsarem, quàm Pharisæorum.
units.tr: Moreover, it is clear from the sacred writings and from history that that Sanhedrin was a lawful magistrate, and that in the time of Christ it still held and exercised the power of the sword. This is shown first by what is read in the history of Christ's Passion, and then by other testimonies. It sends out armed men to seize Jesus. It examines witnesses against him according to the precept of the law, as it wished to appear. It orders Christ to be brought before its own judgment. It hands him over, bound, to Pilate, having first publicly condemned him itself. It openly condemns Stephen and orders him to be killed. It commands the apostles to be led off to public prisons, and orders them to be beaten, after holding a public council on the matter. It gives Paul a commission and power to drag the pious, bound, from other cities to Jerusalem, so that they might be killed there (Act. 24). The Jews and their judges, or the Sanhedrin itself, state this in the clearest words through the orator Tertullus, when, accusing Paul before Felix, he speaks thus: whom we seized, and whom we wished to judge according to our law [ὃν ᾧ ἐκρατήσαμεν, ᾧ καὶ τὸν ἡμέτερον νόμον ἠθελήσαμεν κρίνειν]. According to our law, he says, we wished to condemn him, unless Lysias, as is added, had snatched him from our hands by force. In Acts 23 Paul says to the high priest, "Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and do you order me to be struck contrary to the law?" Then in Acts 26 the same man confesses before King Agrippa and Festus that he had shut many saints in prisons, at Jerusalem and elsewhere, with power received from the chief priests; that he had likewise put them to death by his vote and sentence; that he had also forced them, through all the synagogues, by tortures and punishments, to blaspheme; and finally that he had received from the chief priests authority and commission [ἐξωσίας καὶ ἀπειληθῆναι] similarly in foreign cities, and among these Damascus, to deal with the pious. Agrippa and Festus, I suppose, knew whether this was lawful for the Sanhedrin to do or not. Unless this power had rested with it, they would not have acquitted Paul by their sentences, as they soon do. For Paul's offence against Caesar would have been no less than the Pharisees' offence.

units.la: Non leuius enim peccat, qui illicita facit, permissu & iussu eorum, quorum non est iubere ac permittere, quàm qui talia iubent. At neutri accusantur: sed Paulus diserte absoluitur: tanquam nihil vinculis dignum admiserit. Sed nec Pilatus dixisset Ioh. 18. tollite eum vos, & secundùm legem vestram iudicate eum: si non habuissent hanc facultatem. Ergo cùm sibi non licere aiunt interficere aliquem, intelligendum hoc est de die festo, propter metum populi: vt Augustinus exponit: vel de mortis genere, quo Christum affici optabant: vt Chrysostomus interpretatur. Huic sententiæ verba Iohannis sine medio consequentia pulchrè consonant. Facta hæc sunt, inquit, vt adimpleretur, quod dixerat Iesus, significans qua morte esset moriturus. Huc etiam spectat, quod 26. Math. Christus ait, se alijs temporibus capi ab eis non potuisse, cùm in Templo subinde sedens doceret: quia scripturam oportuerit adimpleri. Tum igitur coeperunt eum, cùm propter instans festum, & populi metum. Math. Marc. 14. occidere non poterant. Quare cum viuentem ferre diutius nollent, nec occidere ipsis integrum esset, consequens erat, vt Romanis traderetur: vt sic euenirent omnia, quomodo Math. 20. discipulis praedixerat euentura: quod Ioh. primum verba, deinde Augustus & Chrysostomus innuunt. Eodem illa quoque turbae vociferatio pertinet, crucifige, crucifige eum. Math. 27. Marc. 15. Luc. 23. Ioh. 19.
units.tr: For he who does unlawful things with the permission and command of those who have no right to command or permit them sins no less than those who order such things. Yet neither side is accused; rather Paul is plainly acquitted, as if he had committed nothing worthy of chains. Nor would Pilate have said in John 18, "Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law," if they had not had this power. Therefore, when they say that it is not lawful for them to kill anyone, this must be understood either of the festival day, on account of fear of the people, as Augustine explains, or of the kind of death by which they wanted Christ to be put to death, as Chrysostom interprets. The words of John, which follow immediately, agree beautifully with this opinion: "These things were done," he says, "that what Jesus had said might be fulfilled, signifying by what death he would die." To this also refers what Christ says in Matthew 26, that at other times they could not seize him, while he sat teaching in the Temple from day to day, because the Scripture had to be fulfilled. Then, therefore, they began to seize him, since the festival was at hand and they feared the people, and so they could not kill him (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Therefore, since they were unwilling to keep him alive any longer, and it was not open to them to kill him, it followed that he should be handed over to the Romans, so that everything would come about as he had foretold to his disciples in Matthew 20. John indicates this first in words, and then Augustine and Chrysostom in meaning. The crowd's shout, "Crucify, crucify him," also pertains to this (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19).

units.la: L.
units.tr: L.

units.la: Liquet ex his, non esse verum, quod a nonnullis affirmatur, Synedrium potestatem gladij seu ius occidendi nullum habuisse: ac Stephanum ab eo per tumultum lapidibus obrutum fuisse. Potestatem habuisse, indissolubilibus argumentis probaui. Per tumultum non fuisse occisum Stephanum, ex eo pater, quod accusatus est coram confessus: quod testes auditi, quanquam falsi: quod extra urbem eductus: quod ijdem testes lapides primi in eum iecerunt secundum legis mandatum: vt ex depositione vestium ad pedes Pauli perspicue intelligi poterat. Idem hoc ex historia aeque dilucide probatur. Permiserunt Romani omnibus populis, nominatim autem Iudaeis, intra & extra Iudaeam habitantibus, in rebus ad religionem pertinentibus, suis vti legibus, suisque ritibus & moribus liberè viuere, teste Iosephus lib. Antiq. 14. cap. 12. 16. & 17. iuxta distinctionem exemplarium Graecorum. Et in 12. quidem cap. Strabonem citat authorem de Cyrene urbe scribentem, habuisse ibi principem, qui causas eorum audiret: Respub. non aliter curaret, ac si perfectae reipub. princeps esset. Faciunt huc etiam, quae Act. 18. cap. de Gallione Corinthiorum praefecto legimus. Recitat idem auctor lib. 16. cap. 4. & 5. quomodo Herodes Iudaeis per Asiam ab Agrippa impetrauerit, vt secundum priuilegia a Romanis iam ante concessa viuere ipsis deinceps etiam liceret. Commemoro haec ideo, quòd Herodem Synedrium occidisse, potestatemque ei omnem eripuisse aliqui objiciunt: quasi non fuerint alij in locum occisorum substituti. Quomodò Herodes illis facultatem de rebus ad religionem pertinentibus iudicandi & decernendi secundùm legem ademisset Hierosolymis, qui Asiaticis eandem conseruare & procurare studuit? Deinde non sub Herode vel Archelao docuit Christus, sed sub Pilato. Sanè Iudæi ipsum quoque Pilatum coegerunt signa militaria, quæ clam in vrbem curauerat importari, iterum ex vrbe tollere, ne contrà praeceptum Dei imagines in vrbe ferrent. Seruarunt hanc sibi potestatem ad excidium vsque vrbis, quod oratione Iosephi, quam ad obsessos habuit, clarissimè intelligitur. Romani, inquit, lib. de bello Iudaico 5. cap. 26. tributum petunt, quod maiores nostri patribus eorum persoluere soliti sunt. Quod si impetrauerint, neque vrbem diripiunt, neque sacra omnino tangunt. Concedunt autem vobis familias liberas & possessiones vestras tenere: legesque sacras saluas manere patiuntur. Eadem haec post captam ferè vrbem ipsemet Titus Iudæis dixit lib. de bello Iud. 6. apud Iosephum cap. 34. Ergo siue sacram siue Iudaicam historiam consulamus, certo certius constat, Synedrium, cui Christus iusit dicere, ius gladij siue necandi potestatem habuisse, praesertim eos, qui contrà religionem aliquid fecisse sent. Nam in politicis rebus & causis iniuriarum, vbi lex nihil certi statuisset, non ambigo, quin ad se Romani vel omnia vel certè pleraque rapuerint sibique vsurpârint: vt ex historia facilè auimaduertimus: & ex cap. 18. Act. illustri coniectura colligimus.
units.tr: It is clear from these things that what some affirm is not true, namely that the Sanhedrin had no power of the sword or right of killing, and that Stephen was overwhelmed with stones by it in a tumult. I have proved by indissoluble arguments that it had the power. That Stephen was not killed in a tumult is evident from the fact that he was accused before the council and gave his defence; that witnesses were heard, though false; that he was led outside the city; and that the same witnesses first cast stones at him according to the command of the law, as could be clearly seen from the laying down of garments at the feet of Paul. The same is proved just as clearly from history. The Romans allowed all peoples, and the Jews by name, both those living within Judaea and those living outside it, to use their own laws and to live freely by their own rites and customs in matters pertaining to religion. Josephus attests this in the Antiquities, book 14, chapters 12, 16 and 17, following the division of the Greek copies. In chapter 12 he cites Strabo as an author writing about the city of Cyrene, saying that there they had a ruler who heard their causes, and that the commonwealth cared for them no differently than if it had a complete prince. What we read in Acts 18 about Gallio, prefect of the Corinthians, also supports this. The same author recounts in book 16, chapters 4 and 5, how Herod obtained from Agrippa, for the Jews throughout Asia, that they might thereafter also be permitted to live according to privileges previously granted by the Romans. I mention these things because some object that Herod killed the Sanhedrin and took away all its power, as if others had not been substituted in place of the slain. How could Herod have taken away from them at Jerusalem the faculty of judging and decreeing according to the law in matters of religion, when he strove to preserve and secure the same for the Asians? Next, Christ taught not under Herod or Archelaus but under Pilate. Indeed, the Jews even compelled Pilate himself to remove again from the city the military standards which he had secretly had brought in, lest they carry images in the city contrary to God's precept. They kept this power for themselves right up to the destruction of the city, which is clearly understood from the speech of Josephus that he gave to the besieged. "The Romans," he says in the book on the Jewish War, book 5, chapter 26, "ask for tribute, which your ancestors were accustomed to pay to their fathers. If they obtain it, they neither plunder the city nor touch the sacred things at all. They allow you to keep your families free and your possessions, and they suffer your sacred laws to remain intact." Titus himself said the same things to the Jews after the city had almost been taken, in the book on the Jewish War, book 6, in Josephus, chapter 34. Therefore, whether we consult sacred or Jewish history, it is more certain than certain that the Sanhedrin, to which Christ ordered that the matter be reported, had the right of the sword or the power of killing, especially over those who had done something contrary to religion. For in political matters and causes of injury, where the law had established nothing certain, I do not doubt that the Romans seized for themselves either everything or most things and usurped them, as we readily notice from history and gather from the clear conjecture of Acts 18.

units.la: LI.
units.tr: LI.

units.la: Non pugnat cum dictis, quòd ex Iudaeis aliqui Albino dicunt apud Iosephum, lib. Antiq. 20. cap. 7. non licuisse Pontifici Synedrium absque permissione sua convocare. Etenim quid aliqui fecerint, historicè narrat: factum non laudat. Deinde non debuit tempore interregni, dum scilicet Festo mortuo Albinus in itinere adhuc esset, antequam nouus praeses potestatem ei confirmauisset, cogere iudicium ad rem tanti momenti agendam. Curauit enim Iacobum fratrem Domini, qui vulgò vocabatur Iustus, interfici: quòd, cùm charus esset omnibus, plurimi iniquissimè tulerunt. Fuerat etiam nuper creatus Pontifex, necdum à Romanorum praefecto confirmatus. Auidissimè eum arripuisse hanc interregni occasionē ostendit Eusebius 2. Eccles. hist. cap. 23. Sed quid hoc ad rem nostram? An ideò Archelaus in Testamento sui patris Herodis, Rex appellatus (idque concessione Caesaris) Rex non fuit, quia nomen regis admittere, regiamque potestatem exercere noluit, priusquàm à Caesare esset confirmatus? Idcone Magistratus vrbis alicuius quae principem habet, quales in Germania multae sunt, Magistratus verus & legitimus non est, quia mortuo principe suorum priuilegiorum confirmationem à successore petere cogitur? Quòd enim Pontifex habuerit potestatem conuocandi iudices Synedrij, confirmatione prius accepta, ex eo liquet, quòd non dicunt Albino, hoc ei simpliciter non licuisse: sed tantùm eum non debuisse inscio Albino fecisse.
units.tr: Nothing here contradicts what has been said, namely that some of the Jews told Albinus, as Josephus relates in the Antiquities, book 20, chapter 7, that the high priest might not convene the Sanhedrin without his permission. For Josephus simply narrates what some men did; he does not praise the deed. Moreover, during the interregnum, that is, after Festus had died while Albinus was still on his journey and before the new governor had confirmed the high priest's authority, the high priest ought not to have summoned a court to deal with a matter of such importance. He did indeed have James, the brother of the Lord, who was commonly called the Just, put to death, and because James was dear to everyone, very many took it extremely badly. Moreover, the high priest had only recently been appointed and had not yet been confirmed by the Roman prefect. Eusebius, in the second book of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 23, shows that he eagerly seized this opportunity of the interregnum. But what has this to do with our question? Was Archelaus not king, though he was called king in the will of his father Herod (and this with Caesar's consent), because he was unwilling to accept the title of king and exercise royal power until he had been confirmed by Caesar? Or is the magistrate of some city that has a prince, of which there are many in Germany, not a true and lawful magistrate, because when the prince dies he is compelled to seek the confirmation of his privileges from his successor? For that the high priest had the power to convene the judges of the Sanhedrin, once he had received confirmation, is clear from the fact that they do not say to Albinus that this was simply not permitted to him, but only that he ought not to have done it without Albinus's knowledge.

units.la: LII.
units.tr: LII.

units.la: Demonstratum est nunc solidissimè, Dic Ecclesiae, non aliud significare, quàm dic populi tui Magistratui (seu qui eiusdem tecum sit religionis) antequam apud profanum Magistratum cum fratre tuo litiges: vt Apostl. Paulus in 1. ad Cor. 6. cap. vbi propter hanc causam arbitros ex suo ordine eos iubet eligere, pulcherrimè exponit. Quis autem dubitat, hoc locum habere non posse, vbi magistratum Deus nobis largitur pium?
units.tr: It has now been most solidly demonstrated that "Tell it to the Church" means nothing other than "Tell it to your people's magistrate" (that is, to one of the same religion as yourself) before you go to law with your brother before a secular magistrate. The apostle Paul, in 1 Corinthians chapter 6, where for this very reason he bids them choose arbiters from their own order, sets this out most beautifully. But who doubts that this cannot apply where God grants us a pious magistrate?

units.la: Equidem Augustinus in 2. cap. lib. de fide & operibus, aperte satis indicat, se existimauisse excommunicationem visibilis gladij vicem supplere debuisse illo tempore, quo Ecclesia eo caruit. Quippè factum Mosis in transgressores gladio animaduertentis: & Pinehae adulteros occidentis praesignificasse aut praefigurasse scribit malorum coercitionem per degradationem & excommunicationem: illo videlicet tempore, quo in Ecclesia visibilis gladius fuerit cessaturus. Memini recentiores quosdam scribere: ideò Iudaeos hunc morem obseruasse excommunicandi (quod falsum esse indissolubilibus rationibus, argumentis, actestimoniis probaui) quia gladius ipsis fuisset ereptus. Id si verum esset, sequeretur locum ei non esse in Ecclesia, quae ius gladij retinet: quemadmodum neque iudices & arbitros nunc necesse habemus nobis creare praeter legitimos magistratus. Certo igitur certius est, Ecclesiam apud Math. nihil minus significare, quàm Senatum Ecclesiasticum: qui potestatem obtineat à Sacramentis arcendi.
units.tr: Indeed, Augustine, in the second chapter of his book on faith and works, indicates quite plainly that he thought excommunication ought to take the place of the visible sword at the time when the Church lacked it. For he writes that the deed of Moses, who punished transgressors with the sword, and of Phinehas, who slew the adulterers, prefigured or foreshadowed the restraint of evils by deposition and excommunication, namely at that time when the visible sword was to cease in the Church. I recall that some more recent writers have claimed that the Jews observed this custom of excommunicating because the sword had been taken from them (which I have proved to be false by indissoluble reasons, arguments and testimonies). If this were true, it would follow that there is no place for it in the Church, which retains the right of the sword, just as we now have no need to create judges and arbiters for ourselves apart from the lawful magistrates. Therefore it is most certainly the case that in Matthew the Church signifies nothing less than an ecclesiastical senate which holds the power of excluding men from the sacraments.

units.la: LIII.
units.tr: LIII.

units.la: Obijci duo adhuc nobis possunt: quomodò aliquis possit Ecclesiam non audire, si magistratus sit, ac ius gladij possideat? Item, quomodò, quae deligando & soluendo dicuntur, causae aptentur? Ad prius est iam ante responsum: Iudaeos non habuisse tunc potestatem de quibusuis rebus iudicandi: sed pertinebant omnes propè controuersiae, quae ad religionem non attinebant, ad Romanorum iudicia. Si ergo in talibus rebus quis Synedrij authoritatem negligeret, concedit ei, qui laeditur, Christus, vt ius suum persequatur apud Gentiles: ac si cum Gentili vel Publicano disceptandum ei foret. Addo, quòd multae tales caussae occurrant, quas Lex speciatim non punit: aut nulla certa poena prohibet: quo tempore facilè contingit, vt reus verbis castigatus dimittatur. Quod si ergo nondum desistat iniurius esse, poterit, qui abeo offenditur, ius suum persequi, atque apud Ecclesiam siue Magistratum instare, vt poenas luat petulantiae suae. Etsi haec quoque responsio vera est, tamen videtur mihi prior, instituto Christi, temporibus, locis, ac reliquis circumstantijs, magis consentanea esse.
units.tr: Two objections may still be raised against us: how can someone not hear the Church if he is a magistrate and possesses the right of the sword? And again, how are the things said to be bound and loosed to be fitted to causes? To the first, an answer has already been given: the Jews at that time did not have power to judge concerning all kinds of matters, but almost all controversies that did not concern religion belonged to the Roman courts. If, therefore, in such matters someone disregarded the authority of the Sanhedrin, Christ grants to the injured party that he may pursue his right before the Gentiles, just as if he had to contend with a Gentile or a publican. I add that many such causes occur which the Law does not punish specifically, or which no fixed penalty forbids; at such times it easily happens that the offender is dismissed with a verbal rebuke. But if he does not yet cease to act unjustly, the one who has been offended may pursue his right and press the matter before the Church or the magistrate, so that he may pay the penalty for his wantonness. Although this answer too is true, it seems to me that the former is more in keeping with the institution of Christ, with the times, places and the remaining circumstances.

units.la: LIIII.
units.tr: LIIII.

units.la: Ad alterum aeque facilis est responsio. Nam cum loquendi hic modus & verba prope eadem hic repetantur, quae 16.cap.Math. Christus dixerat, necessarium prorsus est, vt si non idem omnino, simile tamen aliquid significent. At ligare & soluere apud Math.16. aliud nihil significant, quàm Euangelium annunciare: quo, qui ei credit, à peccatis & morte solutus fit. Proinde hic quoque aliud non significant, quàm orare fratrem, vt ab iniuria desistat ac pietatem potius colat: propterea quòd hoc Deo sit gratum: & contrà mandatum ipsius facientem puniturus sit. Qui fratrem hoc modo ab inferenda iniuria dehortatur, vt simul ei voluntatem atque iram Dei proponat, is, si persuaserit, eum lucratus est, hoc est, soluit: si non persuaserit, manet ira Dei super ipso: quemadmodum super illo manet vel non manet, qui auditae Euangelij praedicationi vel credit, vel non credit. Vt autem prompti & faciles simus ad ignoscendū poenitentibus, elegantissima illa parabola nobis persuadere tentauit Christus: ex qua propositi ipsius in hoc loco ratio facillimè perspicitur.
units.tr: The answer to the other point is just as easy. For since this manner of speaking, and the very words here repeated, are almost the same as those Christ had used in Matthew 16, it must necessarily be that, if they do not mean exactly the same thing, they mean something similar. But "binding" and "loosing" in Matthew 16 mean nothing other than to announce the Gospel, by which whoever believes it is loosed from sins and death. Therefore here too they mean nothing other than to beg a brother to desist from injury and rather cultivate piety, because this is pleasing to God, and because he will punish the one who acts contrary to his command. He who dissuades a brother in this way from inflicting injury, while at the same time setting before him the will and the wrath of God, has, if he persuades him, won him, that is, has loosed him; if he does not persuade him, the wrath of God remains upon him, just as it remains or does not remain upon the one who either believes or does not believe the preaching of the Gospel when he hears it. And so that we may be ready and easy in forgiving the penitent, Christ tried to persuade us by that most elegant parable, from which the reason for his purpose in this place is most easily seen.

units.la: LV.
units.tr: LV.

units.la: Miror supra modum, quomodò in praesenti loco ligare & soluere aliqui exponant, pro arcere à Sacramentis, atque ad eadem admittere: cùm in totis Bibliis nusquam reperiantur verba illa pro hac re posita: nec Apostoli vnquàm ostenderint vllo verbo aut signo, se ita Christi verba intellexisse. Exstat Christi mandatum, vt ab illis, qui Euangelium nollent recipere, excusso priùs pedum pulvere, exirent, Math. ac Luc. 10. quod etiam factum scimus, Act. 13. & 18. Vt autem verbo credentibus, & in Christum baptizatis, Religionémque & doctrinam amplexantibus, quia non responderet vita doctrinae, Sacramenta negarent, nullo in loco vel ipsis mandatum, vel ab ipsis factum reperimus: vt abundè neruosèque suprà monstratum fuit. Hic autem sufficit monere, nunquam futurum, vt ex sacris literis ostendatur, ligare, pro eo positum esse, quod est, à Sacramentorum perceptione credentes arcere: aut soluere, idem significare, quod est, propter flagitium à Sacramentis amotum, ad eadem iterùm admittere: & hoc modo veluti Ecclesiae iterum inserere.
units.tr: I am greatly surprised that some explain "to bind" and "to loose" in this passage as meaning to keep people from the sacraments and to readmit them to them. Those words are nowhere used in that sense in the whole of the Bible, and the Apostles never showed by any word or sign that they understood Christ's words in that way. There is Christ's command that they should leave those who would not receive the Gospel, after first shaking off the dust from their feet (Math. and Luc. 10), and we know this was also done (Act. 13 and 18). But we nowhere find that believers who accepted the word, who were baptized into Christ and embraced the religion and doctrine, were denied the sacraments because their life did not match their teaching, either by a command given to the Apostles or by any action of theirs. This has been shown fully and forcefully above. Here it is enough to warn that it will never be shown from the Holy Scriptures that "to bind" stands for keeping believers from receiving the sacraments, or that "to loose" means the same as readmitting to the sacraments those who were removed from them for a scandal, and so grafting them back into the Church.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Sic ergo firmè & verè probatum est, Christum cap. 18. Math. non de exclusione à Sacramentis, sed de priuatarum iniuriarum pia transactione compositioneque differrere. Viderunt idem hoc etiam alij: vt Augustinus in Sermon. 16. de verbis Domini super Mathaeum. Et compilator ille Chrysostomi Theophilactus (quem nemo dubitat hanc sententiam, vt alia fere omnia, à Chrysostomo habuisse.) Inter recentiores Theologos plurima in huius capitis explanatione scribit D. Iohannes Brentius, nostrae sententiae admodùm consentanea.
units.tr: Thus it has been firmly and truly proved that Christ, in Matth. chap. 18, was speaking not of exclusion from the sacraments but of the pious settling and composing of private wrongs. Others have seen this too, such as Augustine in Sermon 16 on the words of the Lord in Matthew. So did that compiler of Chrysostom, Theophylact, whom no one doubts had this opinion, as he had almost all his others, from Chrysostom. Among more recent theologians, Dr. John Brenz writes much in explanation of this chapter, very much in agreement with our view.

units.la: LVII.
units.tr: LVII.

units.la: Postulat nunc res, vt factum Apostoli Pauli in 1. Cor. 5. describptum, ad excommunicationem hanc non pertinere demonstrem. Primùm constat Apostolum Mosaicae legis obseruantissimum fuisse: & contrà eam nihil fecisse, vt ipse de seipso testatur Act. 25. Quinimò ex Act. cap. 18. & 21. apparet, cum caeremonias etiam legis quasdam, vnà cum caeteris Apostolis obseruauisse: atqui idò male audisse à Iudaeis, non quòd Gentes docuisset legis obseruationem non esse necessariam, sed quòd Iudæis hoc fuisset conatus persuadere: cùm omnes in Iudaea fideles nihilominus legem seruarent. Caeterùm quis nescit Christum legem Mosis de celebrando pascha te pro ea parte, qua iubet omnes circumcisos adesse, non mutauisse? Proinde, neque hunc, qui incestum commiserat, neque alium quempiam, qui vellet inter Christianos numerari, à coena Domini arcuit. De Iudaeis certum est, vt qui non fuissent hoc passuri contra legem & inueteratum morem suum fieri: Gentiles autem quis credat deteriore fuisse hac in re conditione?
units.tr: The matter now requires me to show that the deed of the Apostle Paul described in 1 Cor. 5 does not pertain to this excommunication. First, it is established that the Apostle was most observant of the Mosaic law and did nothing against it, as he himself testifies in Act. 25. Indeed, from Act. chaps. 18 and 21 it appears that he observed certain ceremonies of the law together with the other Apostles. He was therefore ill spoken of by the Jews, not because he taught the Gentiles that observance of the law was not necessary, but because he tried to persuade the Jews of this, when all the faithful in Judea nevertheless kept the law. Moreover, who does not know that Christ did not change the law of Moses about celebrating the Passover, in so far as it commands all the circumcised to be present? Therefore he did not exclude from the Lord's Supper either this man, who had committed incest, or anyone else who wished to be counted among Christians. As for the Jews, it is certain that they would not have allowed this to be done contrary to the law and their long-standing custom. As for the Gentiles, who would believe that their condition in this matter was worse?

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: Si tradere Satanae aliud non fuisset, quàm interdictio Sacramentorum ad resipiscentiam vsque, cur se tanto studio, tamque exquisitis verbis Paulus excusauisset Corinthijs, & quasi deprecatus esset cap.2.&7.post.Epist? Deindè cur Corinthij fuisent tam magna tristitia affecti, vt qui iam scirent hanc in Ecclesia rationem coercendi malos suisse, manere, exercerique debere? Potius propter exemplum sibi datum, quod deinde ipsi sequerentur, gaudere debuissent. Si aliud nihil fuit, quàm inuitatio ad poenitentiam, salutaréque contrà damnationem remedium, cur tristati, & non potius gauisi fuerunt? Christus asserit angelos Dei super vnius peccatoris conuersione plus gaudere, quam super 99. iustis. Ex quo sequitur, Corinthios non fuisse spiritu Christi praeditos, si tantum ex eo conceperunt dolorem, quòd Apostolum id vnum & solum agere viderunt, vt errantem fratrem reuocaret in viam: & periclitantem seruaret. Quis non perspicit aliud fuisse, quod Apostolus molichatur? Tertiò, quid opus erat Apostolum scribere ἐχμίλιμοι ὑ. ἐχμιλοῦν? aut quomodò huius eum facti quouismodo poenitere potuit, si vbique & in omnibus Ecclesijs obseruari voluit? ac nihil aliud fuit, quàm remotio à Sacramentis ad tempus aliquod solum, siue ad resipifcentiam vsque tantum? Quartò, quid opus erat, vt tanta diligentia Corinthij apud Apostolum pro illo misero intercederent, quem mox, vbi resipuisset, iterum in societatem suam recipiendum scirent? Porrò quod pro eo seriò rogarint ex his Apostoli verbis euidens est: cui condonatis vos, ego etiam condono: si quid enim condonaui, cui condonaui, propter vos condonaui in conspectu Christi. Quintò legimus cap.2. sic se excusantem, quod periculum facere voluerit obedientiæ ipsorum: & cap.7. quod sic voluerit paterefieri studium eorum pro ipso. Quomodò haec dixisset, aut scripsisset, nisi maius aliquid mandauisset, quàm flagitiosum illum à Sacramentis repellere? Sextò, quo pacto conuenire verba haec ostendemus, ἐκ τοιούτου ... ? Multam seu damnum, seu detrimentum ex sua cos tristitia nullum passos fuisse, ait: quod moerore suo misero & infelici illi veniam impetrauerint. Hoc si factum non fuisset, damnum fuisset perpessi: nempè amisissent illum. Si tantum erat arcendus à Sacramentis donec resipisceret, cuius quaesò rei damnum passuri fuissent? Septimò, nō loquitur ibi Paulus de coena, sed de tota Christiana vita. Proinde non è coena excludi, sed è medio eum vult tolli: ne parum fermenti totam corrumpat massam. Congruit hoc verbis Apostoli, & figurae fermenti: Excommunicatio neque verbis Apostoli, neque Mosis aptari facilè potest. Oftauò notandum est, quod non scribit simpliciter, vt collecti eum in nomine domini, siue iuxta mandatum Christi, Satanae tradant, aut à Sacramentis arceant: sed ego, inquit, absens corpore, spiritu autem praesens, decreui in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, collectis vobis cum meo spiritu, & cum virtute Domini nostri Iesu Christi, hunc tradere Satanae &c. Manifestè indicans opus esse ad hanc rem virtute Domini nostri Iesu Christi: ideoque maius aliquid esse, quàm ad tempus à Sacramentis remouere. Adde, quod se decreuisse hoc facere scribit (etsi non fine ipsis statuerit facere: forte quia aberat) non autem Ecclesiae praecipit, vt per se sola hoc faciat: quasi non.
units.tr: If delivering him to Satan meant nothing more than forbidding him the sacraments until he repented, why did Paul excuse himself to the Corinthians with such zeal and such careful words, almost as if he were pleading with them (ch. 2 and 7 of the second letter)? Further, why were the Corinthians so greatly saddened, when they already knew that this was the method of restraining wicked people in the Church, that it had always remained in force and ought to be practised? They should rather have rejoiced at the example set before them, which they were then to follow. If it was only an invitation to repentance and a healing remedy against damnation, why were they saddened and not rather glad? Christ asserts that the angels of God rejoice more over the conversion of one sinner than over ninety-nine righteous persons. It follows that the Corinthians were not endowed with the Spirit of Christ, if they felt such grief only because they saw the Apostle doing this one thing alone, namely calling back a straying brother onto the path and saving him from peril. Who does not see that the Apostle was aiming at something else? Thirdly, why was it necessary for the Apostle to write that the man should be taken away from among you [ἐξαρθῆ ἐκ μέσου ὑμῶν]? And how could he ever have regretted this act in any way, if he wished it to be observed everywhere and in all the Churches? Was it anything other than removal from the sacraments for some time only, until he repented? Fourthly, why was it necessary for the Corinthians to intercede so diligently with the Apostle on behalf of that wretched man, when they knew that he would soon be received back into their fellowship once he had repented? That they earnestly asked on his behalf is clear from the Apostle's words: "To whom you forgive anything, I forgive too; for if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sakes in the sight of Christ." Fifthly, we read in ch. 2 that he excuses himself for wishing to test their obedience, and in ch. 7 that he wished their zeal for him to become known in this way. How could he have said or written these things, unless he had commanded something greater than merely keeping that disgraceful man away from the sacraments? Sixthly, in what way these words can be reconciled with "from such a one" [ἐκ τοιούτου] ... I will show. He says that they suffered no great loss or damage from their sorrow, because by their grief they obtained pardon for that wretched and unhappy man. Had this not happened, they would have suffered loss, namely of losing him. If he was to be kept only from the sacraments until he repented, what loss were they in danger of suffering? Seventhly, Paul is not speaking there about the Lord's Supper, but about the whole Christian life. Therefore he does not want the man excluded from the Supper so much as removed from the midst, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump. This agrees with the Apostle's words and with the figure of leaven. Excommunication cannot easily be fitted either to the Apostle's words or to Moses'. Eighthly, it must be noted that he does not simply write that they should gather in the name of the Lord, or according to Christ's command, and hand him over to Satan or keep him from the sacraments. Rather he says: "I, indeed absent in body but present in spirit, have determined, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together with my spirit and with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver this man to Satan," and so on. This plainly indicates that the matter requires the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore that it is something greater than removing someone from the sacraments for a time. Add that he writes that he has determined to do this (though he did not determine to do it without them, perhaps because he was absent), and does not command the Church to do this by itself alone, as if it were not...

units.la: • fi non Ecclesiae, sed Apostoli haec fuerit potestas: quae certè non sunt ofcitanter praetereunda. Vlrimò nusquam legimus Apostolum vni aut pluribus mandauisse, vt se aut viuo aut mortuo aliquem Satanae traderent ad carnis interitum: vt qui sciret hoc esse Apostolicę potestatis proprium, alijsque nullis conuenire. Nam vt sanandi, ita etiam percutiendi facultatem habuerunt: vt ex 5. & 13. cap. Act. apparet. Hac de causa nullos ordinauisse legunturApostoli, qui hanc potestatem exercere iuberentur. Quocirca passim scribit Apostolus se cum authoritate venturum: asperum & rigidum, futurum: pro potestate sibi à Deo tradita acturum: aut cum virga se venturum: peccantes sibi per Epistolam notari praecipit: presbyteris hoc nullo in loco imperat: vt dubium non sit, hanc potestatem Apostolis, non alijs concessam tunc fuisse. Hûc spectat, quod in 1. ad Tim. 1. de Hymenaeo & Alexandro scribit, se (Non Ecclesiam: Non presbyteros: Non alios quosdam) ipsos Satanae tradidisse.
units.tr: • If this power belonged not to the Church but to the Apostle, these points certainly must not be passed over carelessly. Ninthly, we nowhere read that the Apostle commanded one or several persons to deliver anyone to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, whether he himself were alive or dead; as if he knew this to be a power proper to the Apostles and not fitting for anyone else. For they had the power of healing and likewise of striking, as appears from Acts 5 and 13. For this reason we read that the Apostles appointed no one who was ordered to exercise this power. Accordingly, the Apostle writes everywhere that he will come with authority, that he will be harsh and severe, that he will act according to the power given him by God, or that he will come with a rod, and he orders those who sin to be marked by him through a letter. He never commands the elders to do this in any place. So there is no doubt that this power was then granted to the Apostles and to no others. To this belongs what he writes in 1 Tim. 1 about Hymenaeus and Alexander: that he (not the Church, not the elders, not certain others) delivered them to Satan.

units.la: LIX.
units.tr: LIX.

units.la: Ex circumstantiis atque argumentis euidenter ostendi, aliud fuisse Satanae tradere, quàm à Sacramentis arcere: quod nunc ex ipsis etiam verbis & proprietate naturáque sermonis clarius adhuc commonstrabo. Primùm non dicit Apostolus, cur non interdixistis huic scelerato vsu coenae? Sed hoc dixit, cur non luxistis, hoc est, cur non luctu & precibus vestris à Deo petiuistis potius, vt hunc quacunque ratione tolleret è medio? Sic interpretatur hunc locum Augustinus lib. 3. contra Parmen. Sed luctum, inquit, vt tolleretur, id est, vt lugentium dolor ad Deum ascenderet, & ipse tolleret hoc opus de medio eorum, sicut ipse sciret. Exponit eodem modo, quae de luctu idem Apostolus cap. 12. scripsit. Cum Augustino & veritate illi quoque faciunt, qui Apostolum alludere putant ad locum lib. 1. Reg. cap. 21. Ex quo loco conijcimus hunc apud prisco Iudaeos morem fuisse obseruatum, vt enormia scelera lcra lera per ieiunia, preces, luctumque publicum inuestigarentur & punirentur inuenta secundùm leges. Quarè cum gladio careret Ecclesia, hortatus eos fuit, vt à Deo hoc impetrarent, vt è medio tolleretur: quod longe aliud fuit ab eo, quod nos vocamus, aliquem excommunicare. Praeterea, quo quaeso authore idoneo monstrabitur vnquàm, ἐξαιρεῖν ἐκ μέσου τινὸς, idem esse, quod à Sacramentis arcere? E medio sublatus is dicitur duntaxat proprie, qui interficitur. Nam etsi qui in exilium agitur, profligatus è medio aliorum dici possit, nec vsitatè tamen, nec proprie hoc Graecis dicitur: aut saltem in Sacris literis positum non inuenitur. Quod si ex consortio fidelium iussit extrudi, quid publico luctu opus fuit? Deinde fuisset ad Gentiles ablegandus. At obstat, quod additur, vt anima salua fit ἵνα πνεῦμα σωθῇ: quae extra Ecclesiam salua esse non potuit. Si à Sacramentis duntaxat priuatoque commercio amotum dicas, non fuit è medio eorum sublatus. Nullus enim, puto, vnquam monstrabit, Apostolum eum iussisse à solis Sacramentis & priuato conuictu societateque Christianorum arceri. Proinde asuitur hoc Apostoli verbis: quod ipse nunquam cogitauisse poterit docere. Sanè nullus, opinor in sacris literis earumque interpretibus antiquioribus versatus dubitat, quin hanc sententiam, adeóque verba haec Apostolus ex Mosis Deut. mutuatus fuerit. Ponitur autem à Mose pro occasione, pro re alia nulla, in citati libri cap. 17. 19. 21. 22. 24. In his omnibus locis eadem verba habentur, cùm 13. cap. pro ἐξαρεῖτε posuisset eodem sensu & mente ἀφανίζετε. Impossibile igitur est, vt è medio tollere, hoc loco significat, excommunicare: vt nunc intelligitur Excommunicatio. Tertiò videtur ex textu probari illum miserum tunc non perseuerauisse in illo scelere. Nam dicit ὅτι ἐχρῆν τοῦτο ἀνῆκες: Et τὴν ἐντὸς ἕαυτ ἐκ κατεχήσαντα: quae fecisse eum probant, at facere non docent. Sic ergo infligere ei poenam voluisse videtur propter patratum facinus, quomodò Deus fieri iussit, & Magistratus bonus facere solet. Sanè cùm dixit, vt anima fit salua, sciuisse videtur. detur, cum poenituisse facti. Quomodo enim deeo, deca ius animo erga scelus tantum nondum constaret, hoc scribere potuisset? Quarto ait se decreuisse [illegible, ~12 letters] τῶν τοιούτων τῷ σελαχὶς ἐλεσμὸν τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἵνα πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου. An quid verbum [illegible, ~10 letters] significet necdum scitur? Quis vnquam vel apud prophanum scriptorē, vel in sacris literis hoc verbum sic positum reperit, vt hīc ponitur, vt non idem significaret, ac concedere, permittere, siue dedere? Praecedit persona dans: sequitur persona, cui datur: & quod datur, etiam persona est: postremò adjicitur hoc quoque, cur & in quem finem detur. Sermo est talis, ac si ego dicerem, me filium tradere praeceptori, vel ad institutionem, vel ad castigationem. Quis hominum dubitabit sic loquentem, filium suum praeceptoris potestati permittere, vt cum vel instituat, vel castiget? Qui exempla videre cupit inspiciat cap. 1. ad Timoth. 1. Act. 27. 28. Math. 5. & 18. 27. Marc. 13. Ioan. 19. Simillimum est, quod Math. 24. habetur. [illegible, ~8 letters] Et Mar. 15. [illegible, ~8 letters] 2. Pet. 2. de malis loquens angelis, ait, [illegible, ~10 letters] In lib. Iob cap. 2. alloquitur Deus Satanam his verbis: ἰδοὺ παραδίδωμί σοι αὐτὸν· μόνον τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ διαφύλαξον. An non hi loci docent, tradendos esse, vt affligantur, occidantur, condemnentur? Summa est, in sempiternum nullus oftendet, talem phrasim positam esse pro eo, quod est, à Sacramentis arcere: nisi interitus carnis & interdictio Sacramentorum sint res eadem. Quintò impossibile est, vt nomen hoc, ὀλέθρος, in nouo testamento ostendatur positum pro exstinctione cupiditatum carnis. Etenim vbicunque reperitur, pro morte reperitur vel animae vel corporis scriptum: siue homen carnis additum sit, siue non sit. Posset etiam dicere, nullum authorem Graecum exstare, qui sic vsurparit, quomodo aliquos exponere indicaui: sed de sacris nobis sermo est. Vsus eo est Apostolus in 1. ad Thess. cap. 5. & in 2. Epistola ad eosdem cap. 1. deniq; in 1. ad Tim. vltimo. Nomen verbale, vt ficvocè, ὀλέθρευσις in 1. Cor. 10. & participium ὀλεθρευόμενον in 11. ca. ad Hebræos scriptum legitur (quemadmodum cōpositū ἐξολεθρευθήσεται ex
units.tr: I have shown from the circumstances and arguments that to deliver someone to Satan is one thing, and to exclude him from the Sacraments is another. I will now show this more clearly from the words themselves and from the force and nature of the language. First, the Apostle does not say, "Why did you not forbid this wicked man the use of the Supper?" He says, "Why did you not mourn," that is, "why did you not rather seek from God, by your grief and prayers, that he would take this man out of the midst by whatever means?" Augustine interprets the passage this way in book 3 against Parmenian: "But mourning," he says, "that he might be taken away, that is, that the grief of those mourning might ascend to God, and that he himself might remove this work from their midst, as he knew how." He explains in the same way what the same Apostle wrote about mourning in chapter 12. Those also agree with Augustine and with the truth who think the Apostle alludes to the passage in 1 Kings, chapter 21. From that passage we may conjecture that among the Jews of old this custom was observed: enormous crimes were investigated through fasting, prayer and public mourning, and, once discovered, were punished according to the laws. Therefore, since the Church lacked the sword, he urged them to obtain from God that the man be taken out of the midst. This was something very different from what we mean by excommunicating someone. Moreover, on what suitable authority will it ever be shown that [ἐξαιρεῖν ἐκ μέσου τινὸς] means the same as to bar someone from the Sacraments? Someone is properly said to be taken out of the midst only when he is killed. For although a man driven into exile might be said to be cast out from the midst of others, this is neither commonly nor properly said in Greek, or at least it is not found so used in the sacred writings. But if he had ordered the man to be thrust out of the fellowship of the faithful, what need was there for public mourning? Furthermore, he would have had to be sent away to the Gentiles. But there is an objection in the added words, that the spirit may be saved [ἵνα πνεῦμα σωθῇ], since it could not be saved outside the Church. If you say he was removed only from the Sacraments and private intercourse, then he was not taken out of their midst. For no one, I think, will ever show that the Apostle ordered him to be shut out only from the Sacraments and private conversation and fellowship with Christians. So this is being read into the Apostle's words, something he could never have meant to teach. Certainly no one versed in the sacred books and in the older interpreters doubts, I think, that the Apostle borrowed this sentiment, and indeed these very words, from Moses in Deuteronomy. Moses uses the phrase for a particular occasion and for no other matter, in chapters 17, 19, 21, 22 and 24 of the book cited. In all these places the same words occur, although in chapter 13 he had used [ἀφανίζετε] in the same sense and meaning in place of [ἐξαιρεῖτε]. It is therefore impossible that "to take out of the midst" should here mean "to excommunicate," in the sense in which excommunication is now understood. Thirdly, it seems to be proved from the text that the wretched man had not persevered in that crime at that time. For it says [ὅτι ἐχρῆν τοῦτο ἀνῆκες] and [τὴν ἐντὸς ἕαυτ ἐκ κατεχήσαντα]. These words prove that he had done the deed, but they do not teach that he is still doing it. So he seems to have wished to inflict punishment on him for the crime committed, as God commanded and as a good magistrate usually does. Certainly, when he said that the spirit might be saved, he seems to have known that the man had repented of the deed. For how could he have written this if his mind toward the crime were still unsettled? Fourthly, he says that he has decided [illegible] to deliver such a one to Satan for the [illegible] of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. But whether the word [illegible] means this is not yet known. Who has ever found this word, in a profane writer or in the sacred books, used as it is used here, in a sense other than granting, allowing or giving up? The giving person comes first, then the person to whom something is given, and what is given is also a person; finally, the reason and the end for which it is given is added. The sentence is like saying, "I hand my son over to a teacher, either for instruction or for correction." Who among men will doubt that one who speaks so means that he entrusts his son to the teacher's authority, so that he may either instruct or correct him? Whoever wishes to see examples should look at 1 Tim. 1, Acts 27 and 28, Matt. 5 and 18, Luke 27, Mark 13, John 19. Most similar is what is found in Matt. 24. [illegible] And Mark 15. [illegible] In 2 Pet. 2, speaking of the wicked angels, he says [illegible]. In the book of Job, chapter 2, God addresses Satan in these words: [ἰδοὺ παραδίδωμί σοι αὐτὸν· μόνον τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ διαφύλαξον]. Do not these passages teach that people are handed over to be afflicted, killed, or condemned? In short, no one will ever show for all time that such a phrase is used to mean "to bar from the Sacraments," unless the destruction of the flesh and the prohibition of the Sacraments are the same thing. Fifthly, it is impossible to show that this noun [ὀλέθρος] is used in the New Testament for the extinguishing of the desires of the flesh. For wherever it is found, it is written for the death of the soul or of the body, whether or not the phrase "of the flesh" is added. One could also say that no Greek author exists who uses the word in the way I have indicated some people explain it, but we are speaking of the sacred books. The Apostle uses it in 1 Thess. chapter 5, in the second Epistle to the same people chapter 1, and finally in the last chapter of 1 Timothy. The verbal noun [ὀλέθρευσις] is found written in 1 Cor. 10, and the participle [ὀλεθρευόμενον] in Hebrews chapter 11, just as the compound [ἐξολεθρευθήσεται], taken from Deuteronomy, occurs in Acts 3. All of these signify destruction or death.

units.la: Deuter.sumptum 3.Act.ponitur)& passim interitum,seu mortem,omnia significant. ἐξολεθρεύω apud septuaginta Interpretes frequenter occurrit:ac passim fere Pagninus cōuertit, excindē di verbo.Hoc certum est,mortem vbique ipsis significare.Scio apud Apostolum σωζέω ad Ro.8.& ῥυπέω ad Col.13. demùm σωρέω ad Gal.5.&.6. pro occisione carnis affectuum poni: at ἀλλοτρίου aut ἀλοσρεύω nec apud sacros nec profanos auctores sic reperitur vsurpatum. Quinimò neque hoc nomen θάνατος in nouo Testamento in hoc significato me legisse memini. Friuolum ergo est, quod dicitur, Paulum affectus carnis hic distinguere contrà spiritum: quum mortem carnis seu corporis opponat saluti animae spiritūsue: vt verborum natiua significatio, Pauli institutum, orationis series, circumstantiae, & verbum σωτηρίας sic probant, vt veritatis amantes amplius nihil desiderent. Sextò, declarant idem haec verba, vt spiritus saluus sit in die Iesu, hoc est, in die Iudicij. Equidem clarè demonstrant, ipsum de misero illo, vt de morituro loqui. Septimò, & vltimò probat nomen τῆς ὀλεθρίας non fuisse illum à sacramentis reiectum. Quippe in sua natiua significatione positum videtur, scilicet pro increpatione, correctione, comminatione, obiurgatione, vt etiam verterunt interpretes: non autem pro poena seu multa. Ratio duplex praeterea est. Prima, quòd in sacris literis nusquam pro poena ponitur sacramentorum interdictio: altera quòd ipsa verba satis docent, pro obiurgatione poni: qua eum non vnus aliquis, sed plurimi corripuerunt. Etenim Paulus in 12.Epist.cap.3.scribit ἰκανὸν τῷ τοιούτῳ ἡ ἐπιτιμία αὕτη ἡ ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων. Absoluit eum à sola comminatione, quae ab Ecclesia siue à pluribus fuerat professa, fore vt Diabolo traderetur excarnificandus: hanc ergo solam adhuc expertus fuerat. Non enim ex parte solummodò absoluit: sed omnino. Dum ergo obiurgationem & comminationem sufficere ait,plura cum perpessum non fuisse simul indicat. Verbum ἐπιλυέω legimus Mat. 16.17.19.20.& apud alios Euangelistas, apud Paulum in 2.ad Timoth. 4. ἀνέχου, ἐπιλυσιν, παρακλησιν. In quibus omnibus locis pro increpatione semper, pro poena nunquam positum est.
units.tr: And everywhere they signify destruction or death. [ἐξολεθρεύω] occurs frequently among the Seventy, and Pagninus usually translates it with the verb "to destroy utterly." This much is certain: everywhere they signify death. I know that in the Apostle [σωζέω] in Rom. 8, [ῥυπέω] in Col. 1, and finally [σωρέω] in Gal. 5 and 6 are used for the putting to death of the affections of the flesh. But [ἀλλοτρίου] or [ἀλοσρεύω] is not found used in this way by either sacred or profane authors. Indeed, I do not remember having read the noun [θάνατος] in the New Testament in this sense. It is therefore frivolous to say that Paul here distinguishes the affections of the flesh from the spirit, since he sets the death of the flesh or body against the salvation of the soul or spirit. The natural meaning of the words, Paul's purpose, the sequence of the sentence, the circumstances, and the word [σωτηρίας] prove this so clearly that lovers of truth could desire nothing more. Sixthly, these same words, that the spirit may be saved in the day of Jesus, that is, in the day of judgment, show the same thing. Indeed they clearly demonstrate that he is speaking of that wretched man as one about to die. Seventhly and lastly, the word [τῆς ὀλεθρίας] proves that he was not rejected from the Sacraments. It seems to be used here in its natural sense, namely for rebuke, correction, admonition or reproof, as the translators also rendered it, and not for punishment or a fine. There is also a twofold reason. The first is that in Sacred Scripture the prohibition of the Sacraments is nowhere put for punishment. The second is that the words themselves sufficiently show it means reproof, since he was rebuked not by one man but by very many. For Paul writes in the twelfth Epistle, chapter 3: [ἰκανὸν τῷ τοιούτῳ ἡ ἐπιτιμία αὕτη ἡ ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων]: "Sufficient for such a one is this rebuke given by the majority." He releases him from mere admonition, which had been professed by the Church, or by many within it, and which was to be followed by his being handed over to Satan to be tormented. So he had experienced only this up to that point. For he absolves him not in part only, but altogether. Therefore, when he says that rebuke is sufficient, he indicates at the same time that the man had not suffered more. We read the verb [ἐπιλυέω] in Matt. 16, 17, 19, 20, and in the other Evangelists, and in Paul in 2 Tim. 4: [ἀνέχου, ἐπιλυσιν, παρακλησιν]. In all these places it is always used for reproof, and never for punishment.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: Verùm hic quæri potest, si ἐπιλήψια duntaxat persensit, quo pacto dicetur Satanæ ad excruciandum interficiendumque traditus fuisse? Duplex est responsio. Veteres aliqui dicunt, eum traditum quidem fuisse, vt vel morbo vel alia ratione torqueret, paulatimque eum sic conficeret: liberatum autem ab Apostolo iterum fuisse, priusquam res eo vsque perduceretur. Quæresponsio si vera est, significare potuit ἐπιλήψια poenam. Etsi verò tolerari eam posse non inficior, aliam tamen verbis Apostoli non magis conuenientem adferam. Non statuerat D. Paulus hunc hominem tradere Satanae per se solum, sed voluit hoc fieri congregata ad eam rem tota Ecclesia. Iam cùm Ecclesia tanta infelicem illum mœstitia affici cerneret, vt moerore tantùm non absorberetur, distulit hanc rem, dum tentaret Apostoli mentem, an veniam ei posset impetrare. Interim comminata est, se facturam officium, si nihil impetrauisset. Sic ille miser multis mensibus afflictus fuit: donec Apostolum condonauisse poenam cognouit. Sic ferè fuisse rem gestam ex posteriore Epistola videtur aperte satis colligi posse.
units.tr: But here someone may ask: if Paul meant only reproofs [ἐπιλήψια], how can it be said that the man was handed over to Satan to be tormented and destroyed? There is a twofold answer. Some of the ancients say that he was indeed handed over, so that Satan might torment him with a disease or in some other way and gradually wear him down, but that Paul freed him again before things went that far. If this answer is true, then reproofs [ἐπιλήψια] could signify punishment. Yet although I do not deny that this can be tolerated, I will offer another explanation that fits Paul's words better. Paul had not decided to hand this man over to Satan on his own, but wished it done with the whole Church gathered for the purpose. Now, since the Church saw that the unhappy man was so afflicted with sorrow that he was almost swallowed up by grief, Paul put the matter off while he tested the apostle's mind, to see whether he could obtain pardon for him. In the meantime Paul threatened that he would carry out the duty if he obtained nothing. So that wretched man was distressed for many months, until he learned that the apostle had remitted the punishment. It seems clear enough from the later Epistle that this is roughly how the matter was carried out.

units.la: LXI.
units.tr: LXI.

units.la: Ex omnibus iam dictis, & aliis quæ adduci poterunt, sic est aperte solideque demonstratum, hanc Satanæ traditionem longè aliud fuisse ab eo, quod hodie appellant excommunicare, siue à Sacramentis depellere, vt negari à nullo veritatis amante ac intelligente possit. Ex veteribus paulò supra dixi aliquos ita hunc locum exposuisse: inter quos Augustinus fuit, cuius testimonium anteà produxi. Extat huius viri aliud praeterea testimonium in lib. 1. De verbis Domini in monte. Ante hunc Athanasius sic interpretatus est: & post hunc Chrysostomus: ac demum huius Compilator Theophilactus.
units.tr: From all that has been said, and from other points that could be brought forward, it is clearly and soundly shown that this handing over to Satan was something quite different from what people today call excommunication, that is, exclusion from the sacraments, so that no lover and understander of the truth can deny it. I said a little earlier that some of the ancients explained this passage in this way, among them Augustine, whose testimony I cited before. There is another testimony from this man in the first book of De verbis Domini in monte. Before him Athanasius interpreted it this way, and after him Chrysostom, and finally Theophylact, the compiler of his work.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: Iam & alios locos, quos pro se adducunt, qui à nobis dissentiunt, inspiciamus, breuiter tamen. In Apostoli Pauli sententia ad Timoth. qua presbyteros in doctrina & verbo laborantes duplici honore dignos præ alijs esse ait, roboris aliquid ac firmamenti ponunt. Putant enim ex hoc loco probari, aliquos fuisse presbyteros, qui non essent docendo occupati: sed his aliud munus tribuunt: nempe censendi mores, peccatores obseruandi, monendi pertinaces, compresbyteris suis, hoc est, Ecclesiae indicandi, & cum his excommunicandi illos, qui Ecclesiam non audierint.
units.tr: Now let us briefly look at the other passages that those who dissent from us bring forward in support of their view. They place some weight and strength on Paul's statement to Timothy, in which he says that elders who labour in teaching and the Word are worthy of double honour above others. They think this passage proves that there were some elders who were not occupied with teaching, but were given another office: namely, to judge morals, to watch over sinners, to admonish the stubborn, to report to the Church together with their fellow elders, and along with these to excommunicate those who would not listen to the Church.

units.la: LXIII.
units.tr: LXIII.

units.la: Nos verò ex scriptis Apostolorum Petri & Pauli liquere putamus, ministrum, Episcopum, & presbyterum, (si hoc nomine officium & munus, non ætas, significetur) eundem fuisse tempore Apostolorum. Proinde nullus tunc fuit presbyter, qui non doceret etiam: nisi forte hoc nomine illos etiam comprehendi quis velit, qui in 1. Cor. 6. Iudices & Arbitri litium causarumque constituuntur. At de his in præsentia nobis sermo non est, cum officium eorum longè aliud fuerit. Nostram sententiam, quam veram esse satis constat, confirmant Hieronymus in 1. cap. Epist. ad Titum, & Ambrosius: nisi quòd hic primum ex presbyterorum ordine scribit Episcopum fuisse nominatum. Ergo talis est orationis Paulinæ forma, ac si diceret: Ego omnes ministros & pastores amo, maximè verò illos, qui indefesso studio intentiGimaque cura oues suæ fidei concreditas pascunt: Omnes studiosos diligo, eos inprimis, qui dies ac noctes student. Cum sic loquor, non id dico, aliquos pastores esse qui non pascant, aut studiosos, qui non studiant: sed alios alijs esse magis sedulos, neque munere suo diligentiores affirmo. Hanc esse genuinam mentis ac verborum Apostoli interpretationem, probant primùm quidem verba mox sequentia, de mercede. Non enim verisimile est, idem fuisse vllo tempore constitutum in Ecclesia præmium Ministris, & non docentibus presbyteris. Etenim illi duplex, hi vnum & simplex munus obiuissent: ac nihilominus dicit Apostolus vtrosque duplici honore dignos esse. Deinde producit Apostolus testimonium de boue triturâte: quo alibi ministris verbi sustentationem debēri ostendit. Postremò confirmat participium κοπιῶντες, quo hic vtitur. Etenim κοπιᾷν vel κοπιάζω non tantum significat operor, sed operando seu laborando defatigor: siue magno studio, cura, labore, aliquid ago. Hinc Graeci κάματον vocant, quod Latini lassitudinem nominant. Sicut differunt ἐργάζεσθαι, κοπιᾶν, πόνειν: sic etiam differunt ἐργάζεσθαι, κοπιᾶν vel κοπιάζειν, & πονεῖν. Frequenter occurrit hoc verbum in nouo Testamento, semperque sedulitatem, diligentiam, & defatigationem consignificat. Mat. 11. Venite ad me omnes. & Luc. 5. tota nocte. Ioh. 4. Erat autem Iesus. In prima Cor. 4. Colaphis caedimur & Ephe. 4. Qui furabatur, & in 1. Thes. 5. Rogamus autem vos fratres ἐιδέναι τοὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν, καὶ προϊσταμένους & hic locus egregiè praeclaréque alterum illum in 5. cap. ad Tim. in cuius expositione versamur, declarat. Reperitur praeterea ad Tim. 4. & 1. ad Cor. 15. & alibi.
units.tr: We, however, think it is clear from the writings of the Apostles Peter and Paul that minister, bishop and presbyter (if these names signify office and function, not age) were the same in the time of the Apostles. Therefore there was then no presbyter who did not also teach, unless perhaps someone wishes to include under this name those who are appointed as judges and arbiters of lawsuits and disputes in 1 Cor. 6. But we are not speaking of these now, since their office was quite different. Our view, which is sufficiently certain to be true, is confirmed by Jerome on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus, and by Ambrose, except that Ambrose first writes that a bishop was chosen from the order of presbyters. So the form of Paul's words is as if he said: I love all ministers and pastors, but especially those who feed the flock committed to their faith with unwearied and intent care. I love all who are zealous, above all those who study day and night. When I speak in this way, I do not say that there are some pastors who do not feed the flock, or some students who do not study, but I affirm that some are more diligent than others and more careful in their office. That this is the genuine meaning of the Apostle's mind and words is shown first by the words that follow, about the reward. For it is not likely that the same reward was ever established in the Church for ministers and for presbyters who do not teach. For the one would have performed a double office, the other a single and simple one, yet the Apostle says that both are worthy of double honour. Next, the Apostle brings forward the testimony about the ox treading out the grain, by which he shows elsewhere that support is owed to ministers of the Word. Lastly, he confirms this by the participle kopiōntes [κοπιῶντες], which he uses here. For kopiān or kopiazō [κοπιᾶν, κοπιάζω] means not merely to work, but to be worn out by working and labouring; that is, to do something with great zeal, care and toil. Hence the Greeks call it kamaton [κάματον], which the Latins call weariness. Just as ergazesthai, kopiān and ponein [ἐργάζεσθαι, κοπιᾶν, πονεῖν] differ from one another, so too kopiān or kopiazein and ponein differ. This word occurs frequently in the New Testament, and always carries the sense of diligence, care and exhaustion. Matt. 11: "Come to me, all of you"; Luke 5: "all night long"; John 4: "Now Jesus was"; 1 Cor. 4: "we are beaten with fists"; Eph. 4: "let him who stole"; and in 1 Thess. 5: "We beg you, brothers, to know those who labour among you and are over you" [εἰδέναι τοὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν, καὶ προϊσταμένους]. This passage clearly and admirably explains that other one in the fifth chapter of 1 Timothy, which is the subject of our exposition. It is also found in 1 Tim. 4, in 1 Cor. 15, and elsewhere.

units.la: LXIIII.
units.tr: LXIIII.

units.la: Christus, inquiunt insuper, vetuit margaritas abijcere porcis: & sancta dare canibus.
