Respondeo, Christum de illis loqui, qui margaritas contemnunt, ac pedibus calcant: & conuersi nos laniant: hoc est, de Euangelij hostibus: de quibus nos nequaquam agimus. Loquimur vtique non de aliis, quàm Christianis in doctrina recte institutis, eamque approbantibus, & sacramentis eisdem cum caeteris participare desiderantibus, tametsi non sic, vt eos decebat, vixerint. Praeterea loquitur hic Christus, non de sacramentis, sed de doctrina Euangelij canibus & porcis, hoc est, nolentibus & conculcantibus non proponenda. (Huc etiam non incommodè refertur parabola de margarita. Mat. 13. Vbi regnum coelorum simile facit Christus mercatori preciosam margaritam ementi.) Quocirca nullo modo ad praesens nostrum institutum facit.
units.tr: Moreover, they say, Christ forbade casting pearls before swine and giving what is holy to dogs. I answer that Christ is speaking of those who despise the pearls and trample them underfoot, and turn and tear us to pieces; that is, of enemies of the Gospel, with whom we are in no way concerned. We are speaking, certainly, of none other than Christians rightly instructed in doctrine, who approve it, and who desire to share the same sacraments with the rest, although they have not lived as they ought. Moreover, Christ is speaking here not of the sacraments but of the doctrine of the Gospel, which is not to be offered to dogs and swine, that is, to those who are unwilling and who trample it underfoot. (The parable of the pearl also relates to this, not inappropriately. Matt. 13, where Christ likens the kingdom of heaven to a merchant seeking fine pearls.) Therefore it has no bearing at all on our present purpose. ## LXV.

units.la: LXV.

Quod deinde aiunt D. Paulum Timotheo praecipere, vt peccantes coràm omnibus arguat,non inficiamur : sed ad causam nostram pertinere negamus. Nolo iam alia adferre multa,quae id probent, sed vnum hoc dicam, nullum hominem probaturum vnquam, in conspectu aut praesentia Ecclesiae aliquem corripere vel arguere, idem esse, quod à sacramentis arcere. Si eadem esse non demonstrabis, strustrà objicies nobis: Quis Apostolum hic de interdictione sacramentorum cogitasse docebit? Non agit etiam de peccatis publicè siue palàm perpetratis : sed peccantes, inquit, id est, in peccando perseuerantes, in omnium conspectu argue, quò & iş qui peccauit, & cum ipso caeteri timeant peccátaque fugiant. Non hîc discrimen ponitur leuium & grauium peccatorum: multo minus publicorum & occultorum,siue omninò, siue ex parte publica dicas. Obiectio, vt semel dicam, plusquàm plumbea est: & instar cerae ad ignem veritatis dissluit, inque fumum abit. Quinimò verba Pauli oppugnant. excommunicationem, dum peccantem coràm alijs iubet reprehendi: & non iubet excommunicari. Addit vt caeteri timeant, quasi diceret, si noleꝰt ille resipiscere, saltem alij meliores hinc efficientur. Significat hoc loco vox, peccantem, non illum, qui iam desijt peccare : sed in peccando perseuerantem : & post admonitionem non resipiscentem. Hunc,inquam, ἀμαρτάνοντα coram alijs obiurgare & increpare imperat : excommunicari non mandat.
units.tr: That they further say the Apostle Paul instructs Timothy to rebuke those who sin before all, I do not deny; but I deny that it pertains to our cause. I do not wish now to bring forward many other arguments that prove this, but I will say this one thing: no one will ever prove that to rebuke or reprove someone in the sight or presence of the Church is the same as to exclude him from the sacraments. If you do not demonstrate that they are the same, you will object to us in vain. Who will teach that the Apostle here was thinking of the exclusion of anyone from the sacraments? He is not speaking of sins committed openly or publicly either, but he says: rebuke those who are sinning [ἀμαρτάνοντα], that is, those who persevere in sinning, before all, so that both the one who has sinned and the rest with him may fear and flee from sin. Here no distinction is made between light and grave sins, much less between public and secret ones, whether you say this absolutely or in its public aspect. The objection, to say it once for all, is more than leaden: it melts like wax before the fire of truth and goes up in smoke. Indeed, Paul's words actually oppose excommunication, since he bids that the one who sins be reproved before others, and does not bid that he be excommunicated. He adds that the others may fear, as if he were saying that if the sinner is unwilling to repent, at least others may be made better by this. The word "sinning" here means not one who has already ceased to sin, but one who persists in sinning and does not repent after admonition. I say that he commands that such a one who is sinning [ἀμαρτάνοντα] be rebuked and reproved before others; he does not command that he be excommunicated.

units.la: LXVI.
units.tr: LXVI.

units.la: Apostolus, inquiunt, hactenùs iubet flagitiosos vitari, vt ne communem quidem cibum nos cum eis capere permittat: multò minùs voluit nos Coenam Dominicam cum eijsdem concelebrare. Nego connexum hoc. Etenim plurimùm omninò differunt priuatae familiaritatis prohibitio, & sacramentorum negatio: nec qui illam vetat, haec etiam negat. Illa poena quaedam est politica, haec sacra est. Illa praecepta nonis est, haec mandata non est. Illius & finis & caussa à D. Paulo exposita est, huius neque finem neque caussam reperimus expressam: imò neque ipsa res in sacris literis imperata vel nominata etiam inuenitur. Ac quòd altera sine altera fuerit esseque possit, Pharisaei suo facto probarunt: qui, vt caeteris volebant videri sanctiores, ita cum Pubhcanis vitae commercium nullum habebant. (An idem omnes alij fecerint, nunc me legisse non recordor.) At à Sacrificijs, templo, pascha te, alijsque Sacramentis nullus in aeternum ostendet eosdem exclusos fuisse: siquidem circumcisi essent, nec à Iudaismo defecisent. Hodie quoque multis in locis à conuictu aliorum arcentur quidam mali feriati, quibus tamen ideò Sacramentis nemo interdicit. Ex quo illud etiam perspicitur, politicam potiùs esse poenam priuati conuictus negationem, quàm Ecclesiasticam: nec haberi posse pro traditione Satanae, quam aliqui putant Excommunicationem esse. Iubet Apostolus bonis, vt malorum societatem fugiant, quo pudefacti resipiscant: non interdicit malis bonorum conuictu, si qui eos admittere velint ad suam familiaritatem. In conuictu priuato confabulantur homines de quibusuis rebus: nec is tantum non corrigitur, qui peccauit, si post peccatum aequè charum se omnibus esse putet, verumetiam caeteri facilius corrumpuntur. Quod si quis se vitari ac fugi videat, non potest non cogitare cur id fiat: ac de meliore vita instituenda consilium capere, ne inuisus sit, quibus antea erat gratus. Proinde sicut priuati commercij negatio nos à vitijs & impuritate abster ret: ita familiaris conuictus eadem in nobis alit ac fouet. Longè diuersissima est ratio perceptionis & negationis Sacramentorum. Etenim frequens horum vsurpatio nequaquam sic alit & confirmat vitia, vt priuata familiaritas. Nam in templis, vbi ea administrantur, nõ de priuatis aut vanis rebus agitur, sed verbum Domini proponitur. Ibi cum audiunt homines Christum pro se mortuum esse, ac pro eo beneficio publicam à nobis gratiarum actionem sibi postulare, nec dignum esse conuiuium, qui se non recte explorarit, sed iudicium sibi comedere omnes, quicunque indignè se inter conuiuas ingerant, omnino coguntur, qui accedere ad mensam Domini apud se decernunt, cogitare, quid ibi fiat, quid Deus velit, & quomodo vitam sic deinceps instituant, vt ea Deo placere possit: qualisqualis antè vnusquisque fuerit. Hoc inuitamento qui priuatur, semper deterior, nullo modo melior, redditur: cuius rei causla tamen, Deus tot sacrificia, caeremonias, oblationes, institutisse imperauisseque videtur. Sanè Apostolus nusquam iussit illos tales, quibuscum familiaritet viuere bonis non permittitur, à Sacramentis arcere. Et cum alibi per epistolam sibi illiusmodi homines indicari praecipit, senioribus non imponit hoc, vt excommunicent eos, siue à Sacramentis arceant. Quae omnia manifestissime probant, plurimùm illos falli, qui Excommunicationem hic ab Apostolo vel approbatam vel significatam opinantur.
units.tr: The Apostle, they say, so far commands that wicked men be avoided that he does not even permit us to take a common meal with them; much less did he wish us to celebrate the Lord's Supper together with the same men. I deny this connection. For the prohibition of private familiarity and the denial of the sacraments differ greatly, and he who forbids the one does not for that reason deny the other. The former is a kind of civil penalty; the latter is a sacred one. The former is a precept of nature; the latter is not a commandment. The purpose and the cause of the former is set out by St Paul; of the latter we find neither purpose nor cause stated, indeed the thing itself is not even enjoined or named in Holy Scripture. That the one can exist without the other, and that it has been so, the Pharisees proved by their conduct: they wished to seem holier than others, and so had no social dealings at all with the publicans. (Whether all others did the same, I do not now recall having read.) But no one will ever show from the sacrifices, the temple, the Passover, or the other sacraments that the same people were excluded from them, since they were circumcised and had not fallen away from Judaism. Even today in many places certain wicked men are shunned by others in social intercourse, and yet no one forbids them the sacraments on that account. From this it is also plain that the denial of private company is rather a civil penalty than an ecclesiastical one, and that it cannot be regarded as the delivering over to Satan, which some think excommunication is. The Apostle bids the good to flee the fellowship of the wicked, so that they may be shamed into repentance; he does not forbid the good to keep company with the wicked, if any of the wicked wish to be admitted to their familiarity. In private company men chat about all manner of things; nor is he alone not corrected who has sinned, if after his sin he thinks himself as dear to everyone as before, but the others are also more easily corrupted. But if someone sees that he is avoided and shunned, he cannot help but wonder why this is done, and take counsel to live a better life, lest he become hateful to those to whom he was formerly pleasing. Therefore, just as the withdrawal of private fellowship keeps us back from vices and impurity, so familiar company nourishes and fosters the same in us. The reasoning concerning the receiving and the denial of the sacraments is entirely different. For the frequent use of these does by no means nourish and confirm vices in the way that private familiarity does. For in the temples, where they are administered, the talk is not of private or vain matters, but the Word of the Lord is set forth. There, when men hear that Christ died for them, and that for this benefit He demands from us public thanksgiving, and that whoever has not rightly examined himself is not a worthy guest, but that all who thrust themselves unworthily among the guests eat judgement upon themselves, they are necessarily compelled, those who resolve to approach the Lord's table, to consider what is done there, what God wills, and how they may so order their lives from then on that they may be pleasing to God, whatever each one was before. He who is deprived of this invitation is always made worse, never better; and yet for this very cause God seems to have instituted and commanded so many sacrifices, ceremonies and oblations. Certainly the Apostle nowhere commanded that those with whom good men are not permitted to live in familiarity be kept back from the sacraments. And when elsewhere he orders such men to be pointed out to him by letter, he does not impose on the elders that they excommunicate them or keep them from the sacraments. All of these things most clearly prove that those are greatly mistaken who think that excommunication is here either approved or signified by the Apostle.

units.la: LXVII.
units.tr: LXVII.

units.la: Attamen Ecclesiam non decet malorum communione polluì,aiunt: idcirco necesse est, vt à bonis indisimulanter mali separentur. Ego sic respondeo, malos non posse bonos inquinare in vsu caeremoniarum à Deo institutarum: quantisper mores ingeniumque eorum non sequuntur. Etenim neque Prophetae, neque sancti Reges ac Iudices, neque Ioannes Baptista, neque Christus ipse, neque ipsius deinde Apostoli contaminati sunt, cùm in eodem templo cum deploratissimae vitae hominibus eisdem adstarent sacrificijs,eademque cum ipsis sacramenta vsurparent. Non maculauit Christum Viperarum illa progenies, cum à Ioanne eodem cum ipsis Baptismate tingeretur. Non inquinauit vel Christum & Apostolos, vel coenam vltimam, sua praesentia Iudas: quamuis & fur esset, ac de Christo tradendo cogitaret, pecuniamque accepisset. Apostolus Paulus non iubet vt in celebratione vsurpationeque sacramentorum alius alium examinemus, & num aliquis adsit, qui nos foedare posset, circumspiciamus: sed hoc mandat, vt vnusquisque, non alios, sed seipsum exploret.
units.tr: Yet, they say, the Church ought not to be polluted by communion with the wicked; therefore it is necessary that the wicked be separated without pretence from the good. I answer thus: the wicked cannot defile the good in the use of ceremonies instituted by God, so long as the good do not follow their morals and disposition. For neither the Prophets, nor the holy kings and judges, nor John the Baptist, nor Christ Himself, nor the Apostles after Him, were defiled when they stood at the same sacrifices in the same temple with men of most abandoned life, and used the same sacraments with them. That brood of vipers did not stain Christ, when He was baptized by John with the same baptism as they. Judas, by his presence at the last supper, did not defile either Christ and the Apostles or the supper itself, although he was a thief, was planning to betray Christ, and had taken the money. The Apostle Paul does not command that in the celebration and use of the sacraments we examine one another, and look round to see whether anyone is present who could defile us; but he commands that each one examine not others, but himself.

units.la: LXVIII.
units.tr: LXVIII.

units.la: Probatum à me est hucusque efficaciter & verè, nullum circumcisum ante Christum à Caeremonijs & sacra‐ mentis à Deo per Mosen institutis, propter peccata morum & vitae prohibitum fuisse: ac ne licuisse quidem hoc alicui facere, simul est ostensum. Monstratum deinde est rationibus & sacrarum literarum euidentibus testimonijs, neque Christum, neque Apostolos aliud vel docuisse vel fecisse. Insuper hoc etiam docui, quae aliter sentientes pro se adferant, patrocinari eorum sententiae non posse. Quocirca nihil impedire nunc amplius video, quo minus recte vereque concludam, Excom‐ municationem hanc, quae Christianos propter solam vitae impuritatem à sacramentis arcet, praeceptam à Deo non esse: sed ab hominibus inuentam & excogitatam. Quippe tantum abest, vt ea in sacris literis fundata sit, vt potius prohibita ex eis doceri posit.
units.tr: I have hitherto shown effectively and truly that no circumcised person before Christ was forbidden, on account of the sins of his conduct, from the ceremonies and sacraments instituted by God through Moses; and at the same time it was shown that it was not even lawful for anyone to do this. It was then demonstrated, by arguments and by clear testimonies of the sacred letters, that neither Christ nor the Apostles taught or did anything different. Moreover, I have also shown that the arguments which those who think otherwise bring forward for their own side cannot support their opinion. Wherefore I now see nothing to prevent me from concluding rightly and truly that this excommunication, which keeps Christians from the sacraments on account of the impurity of life alone, was not commanded by God, but was devised and invented by men. Indeed, it is so far from being founded in the sacred letters that rather it may be shown from them to be forbidden.

units.la: LXIX.
units.tr: LXIX.

units.la: Ergóne damnas, inquiat aliquis, tot sanctos Episcopos: qui mox post Apostolorum tempora coeperunt facinorosos ex‐ communicare? Respondeo, aliud esse dogma impugnare, & a‐ liud hominem. Complures aetate nostra viri docti & pij vete‐ rum errores catholicos, vt sic vocem, expenderunt & consu‐ tarunt: Limbum patrum apud Inferos: Ignem purgatorium: Diuorum intercessionem: Exorcismum in Baptismo: caeliba‐ tum sacerdotum: Vnctionem in Baptismo & morte: orationes pro defunctis: & in praesente causa satisfactiones: quorum neminem tamen accusatum memini, quod propterea antiquos damnauisset. Si hanc excommunicationem vt legem à Deo promulgatam Ecclesijs obtrudi voluerunt, non laudo: tamen interim studium & voluntatem eorum plurimum laudem ac probem. Studuerant enim hoc pacto, cum alia eis ratio commodior nulla occurreret, petulantiam hominum malorum coercere. Plerique etiam, vt fieri hodie quoque vide‐ mus, publicum illum receptum que ab omnibus morem secu‐ ti sunt: nec vnquam in mentem eis venit inquirere, vtrum consentanea res scripturis esset.
units.tr: Are you condemning, someone may say, so many holy bishops, who soon after the times of the Apostles began to excommunicate wicked offenders? I answer that it is one thing to attack a doctrine and another to attack a man. Many learned and pious men in our own age have weighed and debated the old errors of the Catholics, if I may so call them: the limbo of the fathers in the underworld; the purgatorial fire; the intercession of the saints; exorcism in baptism; the celibacy of priests; anointing in baptism and at death; prayers for the dead; and, in the present matter, satisfactions. Yet I do not recall that any of them was accused of having condemned the ancients on that account. If they wished this excommunication to be forced upon the churches as a law promulgated by God, I do not approve; yet meanwhile I greatly praise and commend their zeal and good intention. For they had striven, since no other more convenient method occurred to them, to restrain the wantonness of wicked men. Many, as we still see done today, followed that public and generally accepted custom, and it never came into their minds to inquire whether the thing agreed with the Scriptures.

units.la: LXX.
units.tr: LXX.

units.la: De origine huius excommunicationis certi nihil adferre nunc possum, nisi quod paulo ante bis centesimū Christi annum talc quid primum factum tentatūmue comperio. Per annos plures centum & 50. nullum à Sacramentorum participatione amotum reperio propter vitam impurè actam. Qui in Patrum lectione & historia exercitati fuit, certora fortasse indicare poterunt. Qui attentè legere volent, quae Socrat. lib.5.Eccles. hist.cap.19. scripta reliquit, circa Nouati tempora hanc Excommunicandi consuetudinem in Ecclesiam introductam non grauatè sibi persuadere patientur, puto. Sozom. tamen lib. 7,cap. 16. aliam huius instituti causam comminiscitur. Sed & Victorem Romanum Episcopum circa annum Dom. 200. legimus Coenae vsum interdixisse iniurias condonare nolentibus. Ante hoc tempus solis haereticis, & à Religione exorbitantibus communionem negatam obseruatū. Sed vt ut hoc habeat, illud certè satis constat, ideo in Ecclesiam inuectam fuisse excommunicationem, vt in ea esset aliqua vitiorum coercitio & poena. Deinde cum iam gladium obtineret Ecclesia, id est, cum Magistratus fuissent facti Christiani, mansit' nihilominus haec potestas penès Episcopos: partim quia ordinatio diuina credebatur: partim quia ægrè gladium hunc spiritualem (propter quem timebantur à summis Regibus) deponebāt. Facilè namq; alijs persuadebant, quod facilius ac libentius ipsi credebant, scilicet Christum huius rei auctorem esse. Opinionem confirmauit superstitio, salutem Sacramentis adscribens. Quippe scriptum creditumq; fuit, quosdam mori non potuisse, priusquam Coenae participes facti fuissent. Itaq; vel propter hunc errorem valdè metuerunt homines Excommunicationem: vel ab Excommunicatione natus est hic error. Facilè namq; crediderunt imperitiores in Sacramentorum vsurpatione vitam, in negatione autem mortem esse positam: quando malos horū negatione, vt extrema summaq; poena plecti viderunt.
units.tr: I can now offer nothing certain about the origin of this excommunication, except that I find something of this kind was first done or attempted shortly before the two-hundredth year of Christ. For more than 150 years I find no one removed from participation in the sacraments on account of a life lived impurely. Those practised in reading the Fathers and in history may perhaps be able to point out more certain facts. Those who will read carefully what Socrates left written in book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 19, I think will not reluctantly allow themselves to be persuaded that this custom of excommunicating was introduced into the Church around the time of Novatus. Sozomen, however, in book 7, chapter 16, invents another cause for this institution. But we also read that Victor, Roman bishop around the year of the Lord 200, forbade the Lord's Supper to those unwilling to forgive injuries. Before this time it was the observed practice to deny communion only to heretics and to those who had strayed from religion. But however that may be, this is quite certain: excommunication was brought into the Church so that there might be some restraint and punishment of vices. Then, when the Church already held the sword, that is, when the magistrates had become Christians, this power nevertheless remained in the hands of the bishops: partly because it was believed to be a divine ordinance, and partly because they reluctantly laid down this spiritual sword, on account of which they were feared by the greatest kings. For they easily persuaded others of what they themselves more easily and gladly believed, namely that Christ was the author of this institution. Superstition confirmed the opinion by ascribing salvation to the sacraments. Indeed it was written and believed that certain people could not die before they had become partakers of the Lord's Supper. Therefore either men feared excommunication greatly on account of this error, or this error arose from excommunication. For the less learned easily believed that life was placed in the use of the sacraments and death in their denial, since they saw wicked men punished by this denial as with the extreme and heaviest penalty.

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Caeterum administratores, quantum coniectura licet consequi, initio videntur fuisse Seniores illi, de quibus in 1. Cor. 6. legimus (quiq; vicem gerebant in Ecclesia Magistratus) vna cum ministris. Tota deinde potestas haec penes Episcopos manssit: qui causas omnes cognoscebant: lites componebant: ius dicebant: ac huiusmodi omnia administrabant: vt ex Augustino de his laboribus conquerente, & illius temporis historia perspicimus. Ambrosius certe affirmat, tunc in Ecclesia Seniores illos, sine quibus in Ecclesijs nihil fieri solitum esset, locum habuisse, cum Episcopis adhuc carerent. Ex Apostolo autem liquet, eos praefe sse suo muneri debuisse, quantisper sub impio Magistratu Ecclesia premeretur. Ex quo illud etiam intelligitur, sicut sub pio magistratu cessauit eorum munus, ita sub eodem excommunicationem quoq; cessare debuisse: etiamsi eam illi prius exercuissent. Notare interim oportet, hos Seniores loco Magistratus fuisse, & res politicas tractauisse: non autem Senatum Ecclesiasticum, (quem hodie discriminant a politico) fuisse. Aperte enim dicitur eos debuisse tractare lites, & res ad victum & vitae vsum pertinentes.
units.tr: Moreover, as far as conjecture allows us to infer, the administrators at first seem to have been those elders of whom we read in 1 Cor. 6, who took the place of the magistrate in the Church, together with the ministers. Afterwards all this power remained in the hands of the bishops, who examined all causes, settled disputes, pronounced judgment, and managed all matters of this kind; as we perceive from Augustine complaining of these burdens, and from the history of that time. Ambrose certainly affirms that in that period those elders, without whom nothing used to be done in the churches, held a place when there were as yet no bishops. From the Apostle, however, it is clear that they ought to have kept to their office for as long as the Church was oppressed under an impious magistrate. From this it is also understood that, just as their office ceased under a godly magistrate, so excommunication too ought to have ceased under the same conditions, even if they had previously exercised it. Meanwhile it must be noted that these elders took the place of the magistrate and dealt with civil affairs; they were not a Ecclesiastical Senate (which today people distinguish from the civil one). For it is plainly said that they ought to have handled disputes and matters pertaining to food and the conduct of life.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Fructus quos Ecclesiae peperit, vix multis libris explicentur: verbibus certe paucis non possunt comprehendi. Primum hoc perfecit, vt Sacramentis salutem homines adscribere ceperint. Sic enim argumentabantur: Negatio Sacramentorum adfert interitum: Ergo eorundem perceptio vitam largitur. De eo quod antecedit ambigere non poterant, dum maxima poena illos affici audiebant, adeoq; Satanae tradi putabant, quibuscunq; negata fuissent. Hinc aliqui non potuisse mori crediti sunt absq; coenae participatione: vt paulo supra dixi, (Auxerunt errorem, magnae, multae, longae gæ illæ satisfactiones & caeremoniæ. Item illud inprimis, quòd duntaxat agentibus animam permiserunt vsum Coenæ: vt ne fine cibo animę necessario hinc abirent. Quod si non contigisset, damnatus putabatur, cui hoc accidisset. Quasi vero Deus ex animo poenitentibus non remittat peccata vitámq; reddat, nisi Seniores illi Coena Dominica dignum iudicauerint. Quid potest hoc errore horribilius excogitari? Deinde hoc etiam perfecit, vt cunctì ferè crediderint in potestate hominis esse coelum aperire & claudere, cuicuilibuisset. Sic Theodosius Iunior prandere noluit, quia petenti Monacho negauisset quod petierat, eámq; ob rem ab eodem fuisset excommunicatus.
units.tr: The fruits that the Church has borne can hardly be set out in many books, and certainly cannot be grasped in a few words. First, it brought it about that men began to attribute salvation to the sacraments. For they argued thus: the denial of the sacraments brings death; therefore their reception gives life. They could not doubt the first premise, since they heard that the greatest punishment fell on those who were denied them, and they thought that whoever was refused them was handed over to Satan. Hence some were believed unable to die without taking part in the Lord's Supper, as I said a little above. Those great, numerous and long satisfactions and ceremonies increased the error. Above all there was this: they allowed the use of the Supper only to those who were at the point of death, so that the soul would not depart from here without the food it needed. If this did not happen, the person to whom it had not happened was thought to be damned. As if God does not forgive the sins of those who repent from the heart and restore them to life, unless those elders have judged them worthy of the Lord's Supper! What could be devised more horrible than this error? Next, it also brought it about that almost everyone believed it was in the power of a man to open and shut heaven for anyone he chose. Thus Theodosius the Younger refused to dine, because he had denied a monk what he asked for, and for that reason he had been excommunicated by him.

units.la: Quanquàm vero Episcopus vrbis Constantinopolitanæ ei diceret, inualidam esse talem exclusionem, acquiescere tamen noluit, priusquàm ille tandem eum absoluisset, qui eum ligauerat. Sic senior ab Ambrosio coactus est per 8. menses abstinere templo & concionibus. Peccauerat ille quidem, at multò leuius Ambrosio: id quod ex historia Nicephori, & Chron. D. Philippi Melanth. Vnusquisq; non destitutus iudicio cognoscere poterit. Hac ratione perfecta deniq; est, vt Romanus pontifex sibi totum subegerit Occidentem: ac Principes, Reges, Imperatores suę coegerit libidini inseruire. Et propter excommunicatos Imperatores & reges aliquot centena millia hominum trucidata sunt in Imperio Germanico. Religione insuper pro atbitrio suo mutauit & conspurcauit: dum huius fulminis metu nemo contrà eius statuta & leges hisce ausus est. Et sanè qui recte volet rem expédere, nihil aliud Deum illum fortitudinum apud Danielé significasse comperit, quàm Excommunicationem: siue à Sacris, præsertim verò à Coenæ Dominicę vsu prohibitione. Hæc enim Excommunicatio verè Deus fuit, & hodiè quoq; est, fortitudinū: quo Pont. Rom. sibi omnia subiecit: atq; alij nunc sibi similiter subijcere imperia quorūlibet studeunt. Sed spero agnitū forte sallsum hunc Deū minúsq; deinceps Ecclesiæ nociturū. Postremò re eo perduxit, vt pleriq; omnes crederent, quos æterna vita iudicauisset indignos, illos diuina gratia excidisse: & contra quoscunq; saluos esse cuperet, saluos omnino fore. An speramus nostrae aetatis homines meliores aut continentiores esse antiquis? Fallitur qui credit: & nec scripturas bene examinauit, nec vsum rerum aliquem habet.
units.tr: Yet although the bishop of Constantinople told him that such an exclusion was invalid, he would not be reconciled until at last the one who had bound him absolved him. Likewise Theodosius the Elder was compelled by Ambrose to abstain from the church and from sermons for eight months. Indeed he had sinned, but far less gravely than Ambrose. Anyone who is not lacking in judgement can learn this from the history of Nicephorus and from the Chronicle of Philip Melanchthon. Finally, by this means it was accomplished that the Roman pontiff subjected the whole of the West to himself, and forced princes, kings and emperors to serve his lust. And on account of excommunicated emperors and kings, some hundreds of thousands of men were slaughtered in the German Empire. Moreover, he changed and corrupted religion as he pleased, since through fear of this thunderbolt no one dared to act against his decrees and laws. And indeed, whoever wishes to judge the matter rightly will find that the god of fortresses which Daniel mentions signified nothing other than excommunication, that is, the prohibition from the sacraments, and especially from the use of the Lord's Supper. For this excommunication truly was, and is even today, the god of fortresses, by which the Roman pontiff subjected everything to himself, and now others eagerly seek to subject to themselves kingdoms of whatever kind. But I hope that this false god will at some point be recognised and will harm the Church less from now on. Finally, he brought matters to the point where almost everyone believed that those whom eternal life had judged unworthy had fallen from divine grace, and that whoever he wished to be saved would certainly be saved. Do we hope that the men of our age are better or more self-controlled than the ancients? He is mistaken who believes so, and he has neither examined the Scriptures well nor has any experience of affairs.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Non video cur hodie non debeat Magistratus Christianus idem facere, quod in Repub. Iudaeorum facere a Deo iussus est. An putamus nos Reipub. & Ecclesiae formam meliorem constituere posse? In 4. cap. Deut. legimus propter iudicia & statuta, quae populo Israelitico Deus dederit, omnes gentes admiraturas & praedicaturas sapientiam & intelligentiam eorum. At illi caruerunt hac Excommunicatione: ac potestas coercendi spurcos & facinorosos penes Magistratum fuit: cuius erat non modo hos ex praescripto legis Dei punire, verumetiam religionem omnē externam constituere. Quippe non Aaron, sed Moses hoc fecit: Deo sic iubente. Quam deinde potestatem ad Iosuam, non ad Eleazarum translatam scimus: Iosuae praecipit Deus, non Eleazaro, vt secundo curaret Israelitas circumcidi: nec iussit excipere eum quenquam: tametsi plurimi inter eos essent pessimi. Idem mox Pascha quoq; iussit celebrari, ac Iordanum transijssent: nec legimus eum aliquem repulisse propter vitam non satis pie honestéq; actam. Ad huius imperium arca Dei portabatur, & ad religionem pertinentia fiebant: Vt ex lib. toto Iosuae manifestum est. Samuel & Heli cum vtrumq; munus administrarent, vt sacerdotes offerebant, vt iudices Reipub. pariter cum Religione ordinabant. Et veteris quidem Testamenti summis sacerdotibus licuit etiā politiam gubernare: quòd Christi Regis & Sacerdotis typum gererent: nostris autem dictum est, Vos autem non sic. Vide 1. Pet. 5. quod huc etiam pertinet.
units.tr: I do not see why a Christian magistrate today should not do the same thing that God commanded the magistrate to do in the commonwealth of the Jews. Do we think we can devise a better form for the commonwealth and the Church? In Deuteronomy 4 we read that the peoples of all nations, on account of the judgments and statutes which God gave to the people of Israel, would admire and proclaim their wisdom and understanding. Yet they had no excommunication, and the power of restraining the impure and the criminals lay with the magistrate. It was his task not only to punish these men according to the prescription of God's law, but also to establish all external religion. Indeed, it was not Aaron but Moses who did this, at God's command. We know that this power was afterwards transferred to Joshua, not to Eleazar: God ordered Joshua, not Eleazar, to have the Israelites circumcised a second time, and he did not order anyone to be excluded, although many among them were very wicked. Likewise, soon after they had crossed the Jordan, he ordered the Passover to be celebrated, and we do not read that he rejected anyone because of a life not lived piously and honourably enough. At his command the ark of God was carried, and the matters pertaining to religion were carried out, as the whole book of Joshua makes clear. Samuel and Eli, when they administered both offices, offered sacrifices as priests and likewise set up the judges of the commonwealth along with religion. Indeed, under the Old Testament the chief priests were permitted to govern the state as well, because they bore the type of Christ the King and Priest; but to ours it has been said, "But you shall not be so." See 1 Peter 5, which also pertains to this.

units.la: LXXIIII.
units.tr: LXXIIII.

units.la: Ad reges peruentum vbi fuerit, æquè manifesta res est. De Dauide nullus dubitat: quem omnia ministeria & ossicia disposuisse constat. Legat qui vult 1. Paralip. à 22. cap. vsq; ad 27. Templum deinde non æddificauit solum,sed inaugurauit etiam Rex Salomon: non sacerdos. Hûc illustris illa de Iosaphato historia ex 19. cap. lib. paral. 2. pertinet: quę diligenter expensa præclarè caussam hanc illustrat: necnon Regis sanctissimi Ezechiae: denique totum vetus Testamentum. Proinde si Respub. & Ecclesia illa sapientissimè fuit fundata,ordinata,instituta, non poterit non ea laudari, quae quantum circumstantiae, ac res præsentes patiuntur, proximè ad illius formam accedit. Vbicunque igitur magistratus est pius & Christianus, ibi alio nullo est opus,qui alio nomine ac titulo vel gubernet vel puniat: quasi nihilà profano magistratu pius differet. Omnium reuera nocentissimus error est (inquit D. Wolfgangus Musculus in locis suis communibus de Magistratu: ex quo proximè dicta transcripsi) quod plerique de Magistratu Christiano haud aliter sentiunt,quàm de dominatu profano: cuius potestas tantum in profanis sit agnoscenda. Ergo si non modo potestatem obtinuit pius magistratus Religionem ex præcepto Sacrarum literarum constituendi, ministeria officiaque disponendi (cuius rei causa iubet Moses electum in Regem, librum legis siue scripta Mosis propria sua manu transcribere: & in illis se continenter exercere) sed & vitia eodem modo puniendi, frustrà de noua iudicij forma nunc aliqui apud nos cogitant: quae Magistratum ipsum quoque redigat in ordinem aliorum subditorum. Etenim iudicium illud Ecclesiasticum de moribus (de doctrina consuli à Magistratu semper debent in ea exercitatiores) in sacris literis nullo in loco reperitur imperatum.
units.tr: Where we come to kings, the matter is equally clear. No one doubts this about David, who is known to have arranged all the offices and duties of ministry. Let whoever wishes read 1 Chronicles, from chapter 22 to chapter 27. Moreover, it was not only the priest but King Solomon who built the Temple and also dedicated it. Here belongs that famous story of Jehoshaphat in chapter 19 of 2 Chronicles, which, when carefully weighed, illustrates this cause clearly; so too does the story of the most saintly king Hezekiah; and in short the whole Old Testament. Therefore, if that commonwealth and Church were founded, ordered and instituted most wisely, it cannot but be that the arrangement which comes as close as present circumstances and conditions allow to its form is to be praised. Wherever, then, there is a pious Christian magistrate, there is no need of any other person who governs or punishes under another name or title, as if a pious magistrate would differ in anything from a secular one. Indeed, as Wolfgang Musculus, in his Common Places on the Magistrate (from which I have just copied the things said above), says, it is a most harmful error that most people think of a Christian magistrate no differently than of a secular lordship, whose power is to be recognised only in secular matters. Therefore, if the pious magistrate has obtained not only the power to establish religion according to the precept of the Sacred Scriptures and to arrange ministries and offices (for which reason Moses commands that the one chosen as king should copy out the book of the law, or the writings of Moses, in his own hand, and continually exercise himself in them), but also the power to punish vices in the same way, then some among us are in vain now devising a new form of judgment, which would reduce the magistrate himself too to the rank of the other subjects. For that ecclesiastical judgment on morals (on doctrine, the magistrate should always be consulted by those more experienced in it) is nowhere commanded in the Sacred Scriptures.

units.la: LXXV.
units.tr: LXXV.

units.la: At in illis Ecclesijs, quae sub impio magistratu degunt, (videlicet Pontificio vel Turcico) eligi debent viri graues & pij, iuxta praeceptum Apostoli, qui inter litigantes arbitrentur: controuersias componant: aliáq; huius generis faciant. Spurcos & foedos homines ijdem vnà cum ministris admonere, obiurgareq; debent: ac si nihil proficiant, vel priuati commercij negatione, vel publica reprehensione, vel aliqua tali notatione alia punire, (seu potius reuocare ad frugem poterunt: à Sacramentis à Deo institutis, accedere cupientes, arcere non poterunt. Quis enim corda iudicat praeter Deū? Fieri potest, vt ex publica concione suscitatus igniculus aliquis sit, quem fouere quouis modo cum pietate non pugnante minimè sit inutile: sed prorsus fructuosū. Et quomodo quaeso te, non sit absurdum, adeóq; impiū, aliquem à publica & solenni gratiarum actione & commemoratione mortis Domini arcere, qui se in corde suo impelli, sentiat, vt cum Ecclesia eandem concelebret, eiusdem se membrum esse velle declaret, deniq; displicere sibi, anteactam vitam suam testari publicè velit? Finis.
units.tr: But in those churches which live under an impious magistrate (namely a Papist or Turkish one), men who are grave and godly should be chosen, according to the Apostle's precept, to arbitrate between litigants, settle disputes, and do other things of this kind. These same men, together with the ministers, ought to admonish and rebuke foul and filthy persons; and if they accomplish nothing, they may punish them by denying them private dealings, by public reproof, or by some other such mark of censure (or rather, they may call them back to a sober life). But they cannot bar from the sacraments instituted by God those who desire to come to them. For who judges hearts except God? It may happen that a little spark is kindled by a public sermon, and to foster it in any way that does not conflict with piety is by no means useless but altogether fruitful. And, I ask you, how would it not be absurd, and even impious, to bar from the public and solemn thanksgiving and the remembrance of the Lord's death someone who feels himself moved in his heart to join with the Church in celebrating it, wishes to declare that he wants to be a member of the same body, and finally wishes to testify publicly that he is displeased with his former life? The end.

units.la: Non fuerit fortasse praeter rem, si auctarij aut corollarij vice addam, quę ab omnibus Imperij ordinibus Laicis hac de re anno 1523. in Comitijs Norinberg. decreta, Romanoq; Pontifici oblata fuerunt. Quippe hoc pacto patebit, ante annos plus minus 46. coepisse Theologos de hac disputatione cogitare: nec esse nos primos, qui istæc mouemus. Equidem non puto quenquam esse vel mediocriter rerū Germanicarū gnarum, qui horum aliquid putet credatue inscijs Theologis tunc vel decretum vel à Pontifice petitum. Caeterum quo res esset clarior, placuit Germanicum exemplar in ipsis scriptum Comitijs, cum Latino, quod Pontifici missum est (Ac Matth. Flac. Illyricus cum lib. suo de Sectis & Dissensionibus Papistarum anno 1565. Basileae iterum excudi fecit)conferre:& ex vtriufq; collatione Decretum integrum proponere. Ergo inter onera centum,quæ Norinbergæ,quàm Wormatiæ biennio ante factum fuerat,distinctius expressa sunt, trigesimum quartum sic habet.
units.tr: It may perhaps not be beside the point if, by way of an addition or corollary, I add what the lay orders of the Empire decreed on this matter at the Diet of Nuremberg in 1523 and presented to the Roman Pontiff. For in this way it will be plain that theologians began to think about this dispute some forty-six years ago, and that we are not the first to raise these questions. Indeed, I do not think anyone who knows German affairs even moderately well would suppose that either a decree or a petition to the Pope was made at that time without the knowledge of the theologians. Moreover, so that the matter may be clearer, I have chosen to compare the German text written at the Diet itself with the Latin copy that was sent to the Pope (Matthias Flacius Illyricus, in his book on the Sects and Dissensions of the Papists, had it printed again at Basel in 1565), and from the comparison of the two to set out the decree in full. Accordingly, among the hundred grievances that had been more distinctly set out at Nuremberg, as had been done two years earlier at Worms, the thirty-fourth reads as follows.

units.la: Item Christiani complures Romę,& in alijs quoq; locis, per Archiepiscopos,Episcopos,eorúmue sacros Iudices ob caussas profanas & bona temporalia excommunicantur: eóq; multæ infirmæ conscientiæ affliguntur:inq; desperationem inducuntur. Sic propter pecuniam, ac res fluxas, & sæpenumerò propter caussas admodũ leues, aliqui, præterquàm quod iacturam faciunt honoris & bonorũ,contra iuram mádataq; Diuina in discrimĕ salutis animę corporisq; cõijciuntur:cum nemo tamen excommunicari, aut pro excommunicando haberi debeat, sacris testantibus literis, nisi qui hæreseus est conuictus. Quocirca orăt sacri Imperij ordines Laici Pōtificiam Sanctitatē vt pro eo,ac pium Religiosūq; patrē decet,hæc Excommunicationis onera Romæ seu in Romana Curia prorsus abroget:atq; alibi quoq; passim apud Archiepiscopos,Episcopos,eorúmq; iudices tolli curet:ac deniq, mandet,vt nullus vllam aliam ob caussam, quàm ob manifestum conuictum s. hæresios crimen ad religionem pertinentis, excommunicetur, aut pro excommunicando reputetur. Omninò enim nullus alioquin vel propter bona temporalia,vel alia humana delicta, excepta infidelitate seu hæresi à Deo eiusq; Ecclesia submoveri separariue debet. Huc etiã pertinet,quod Iohan.Stumpfius in Chronico Heluet.lib.2.de Germania,cap.29.scribit, Sacerdotes per Sueuiam circa annum Domini 1245. (cum aduersus Imperatorem Fridericum 2.& eius filium Conradum Papæ instinctu Henricus Landtgrafius Turingiæ,& post huius morte Wilhelmus Comes Hollandiæ electi suissent)constanter cùm alia, tum hoc docuisse,Nemini mortalium sub hoc sole petestatem concessam esse Christianis Spiritualia officia cultum s. Dei prohibendi. Hac de causa eos Missas cõtinenter celebrauisse refert, tametsi Papa interdixisset, Excommunicatosq; pronunciasset.
units.tr: Likewise, many Christians at Rome and in other places are excommunicated by archbishops, bishops, and their sacred judges, on account of worldly causes and temporal goods; and by this many weak consciences are afflicted and driven into despair. Thus, for money and fleeting things, and very often for quite trivial causes, some people, besides suffering the loss of honour and goods, are cast into danger of the salvation of soul and body, contrary to the divine laws and commands; yet, as the holy letters bear witness, no one ought to be excommunicated or regarded as excommunicable except one who has been convicted of heresy. Wherefore the lay orders of the holy Empire pray that His Papal Holiness, as befits a pious and religious father, should utterly abolish these burdens of excommunication at Rome or in the Roman Curia, and should see to it that they are removed elsewhere throughout the archbishops, bishops, and their judges, and finally command that no one be excommunicated, or regarded as excommunicable, for any cause other than the manifest conviction of the crime of heresy pertaining to religion. For no one, on any other ground, whether for temporal goods or other human offences, apart from unbelief or heresy, ought to be removed or separated from God and His Church. To this also pertains what Johannes Stumpf writes in his Chronicle of Helvetia, book 2, concerning Germany, chapter 29: that around the year of the Lord 1245, when Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, had been elected against the Emperor Frederick II and his son Conrad at the instigation of the Pope, and after Henry's death William, Count of Holland, the priests throughout Swabia constantly taught, among other things, this: that no mortal under this sun has been granted power to forbid Christians the spiritual offices of the worship of God. For this reason, he reports, they continued to celebrate Masses, although the Pope had forbidden it and pronounced them excommunicated.

units.la: IN THESIVM (QVAE DE EX- COMMVNICATIONE POSITÆ FVERANT) CONFIRMATIONEM, PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: ON THE CONFIRMATION OF THE THESES CONCERNING EXCOMMUNICATION: A PREFACE.

units.la: PRincipio reprehendis nostram definitionem, quod nec à quibus feratur sententia, nec quibus de rebus, satis explicet. Ego in disserendi artibus ita sum versatus, Deo est gratia, vt, quomodo res quæ exsistit, cuiusq; naturâ intelligo, definienda sit, non prorsus nescîam. At in re ficta definienda, quid mirum, si aliquorum opinioni non satisfacere videor? Caeterùm, vt priusquam in hoc certamen descendam, recte intelligatur, de qua re agatur, tria praemonere te volo. Primum, nos de externa tantum visibilis Ecclesiae Excommunicatione, quae ab hominibus exercetur, disputare. Alterum, nos hanc praecipuè oppugnare, quoad eos, de quibus nos loquimur, à Sacramentis arcet. Quippe si quis per excommunicationem poenam aliam intelligat, vt priuati conuiétus & commercij interdictionē aut huiusmodi rei alius prohibitionem, (quae tamen sacrosanctis literis non aduersetur,) cum hoc mihi lis non erit. Ergo cum illis mihi res est, qui Sacramentorum negatione coercere peccatores iubent. Tertium est, nos de illis solis loqui peccatoribus, qui doctrinâ intelligunt, probant, amplectuntur: peccata sua se agnoscere verè atq; odisse aiunt, & Sacramentis secundum institutionem Christi, cum Ecclesia vti cupiunt. Horum trium te meminisse semper velim, etiamsi non semper ego adiecero. Nunc ad rem venio.
units.tr: First you find fault with my definition, on the ground that it does not sufficiently explain by whom the sentence is pronounced or about what matters it is pronounced. I have so far practised the arts of disputation, thanks be to God, that I am not wholly ignorant of how a thing that exists, and whose nature I understand, ought to be defined. But when the thing to be defined is a fiction, is it any wonder that I seem not to satisfy some people's opinion? However, before I enter upon this contest, I want to warn you of three things, so that it is rightly understood what the matter is. First, we are disputing only about the external excommunication of the visible Church, which is exercised by men. Second, we attack it chiefly insofar as it keeps from the sacraments those of whom we speak. For if anyone understands by excommunication some other penalty, such as the interdiction of private company and business, or some other prohibition of this kind (which does not, however, conflict with the holy letters), there will be no dispute between me and him. My quarrel is with those who command that sinners be restrained by the denial of the sacraments. Third, we speak only of those sinners who understand the teaching, approve it and embrace it, who say that they truly recognise and hate their sins, and who wish to use the sacraments with the Church according to the institution of Christ. I would have you remember these three points always, even when I do not repeat them. Now I come to the matter.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De Excommunicationis definitione.
units.tr: On the definition of excommunication.

units.la: E Excommunicatione, de qua inter nos controuersamur, in sanctis scripturis nullum exstat mandatum, sed commentum est purè humanum. Quocirca cum de executoribus controuersia sit, in definitionibus autem ambigui nihil poni conuēniat, intactam hanc partem merito reliqui. Etenim Pontificij hoc ius solis sacerdotibus, praecipuè autem Episcopis tribuunt. (Qui mos multis in Ecclesia veteri seculis perdurauit.) Alij toti Ecclesiae adscribūt. Nonnulli Presbyterio suo adiudicant. Eth orum alii qui Presbyteros illos à tota Ecclesia eligi oportere contendunt. Alij Magistratui, vbi is Christianus est, hanc potestatem authoritatémque deferunt. In hac sententiarum diuersitate, cum ex scriptura lis dirimi nequeat, ideóque difficile sit dictu, cuiusnam partis rationes anteponendae sint argumentis aliarum partium, in definitione mea iure omisi. Feci nihilominus mentionē Seniorū, partim vt Excommunicatorum, partim vt causam examinantium: in quo, praeter Pontificios, cunctos alios vos conuenire videbam. Qui enim totam Ecclesiam volunt Excommunicare, non negāt expedire, vt quidam Seniores quasi praemansum cibum Ecclesiae offerant.
units.tr: Concerning the excommunication about which we are disputing, there is no command in the holy Scriptures; it is a purely human invention. Therefore, since there is a controversy about who should carry it out, and since nothing ambiguous ought to be placed in a definition, I rightly left this part untouched. For the Papists assign this right to priests alone, and especially to bishops (a custom which lasted through many centuries in the ancient Church). Others ascribe it to the whole Church. Some adjudge it to their own eldership. And some of them, those who contend that these elders must be chosen by the whole Church, assign it to others. Still others grant this power and authority to the magistrate, where he is a Christian. In this diversity of opinions, since the dispute cannot be settled from Scripture, and so it is hard to say whose reasons should be preferred to the arguments of the other parties, I rightly omitted it from my definition. Nevertheless I did mention the elders, partly as those who excommunicate and partly as those who examine the case; in this, I saw, you all agree with me, apart from the Papists. For those who want the whole Church to excommunicate do not deny that it is useful for certain elders to offer, as it were, the food already chewed to the Church.

units.la: Ratio par est alterius reprehensionis. Nam cum Excommunicationem hanc scriptura nesciat, ab eámque causam non definiat, propter quae peccata homines à Sacramentis arceri debeant, noluí ego me inter dissentientes arbitrum constituere. Quippe alij tantū graviora scelera Excommunicatione vindicanda putant: alij quodlibet peccatum, quod ex sententia Presbyterorum non corrigatur, censuram hanc merērī exīstimāhr.
units.tr: The reasoning is the same for the other objection. For since Scripture says nothing of this excommunication, and does not define for what sins people ought to be kept from the sacraments, I did not wish to make myself judge among those who disagree. Indeed, some think that only more serious crimes are to be punished by excommunication; others think that any sin which is not corrected by the judgement of the elders deserves this censure.

units.la: Ergò cum definitionis partes controuersia carere oporteat, haec autem & controuersia sint maximè, nec decidi ex scripturis res posset, non debui ego in definitione ponere. Quoniam enim res ipsa confīcta est ab hominibus, necessarium est, vt rationes quoque sint confectae, quae ab omnibus partibus ad probandum adferuntur. Quare aeque firma sunt argumenta omnia: nec facilè possunt alia aliis rectè praeferri. Quod autem reliquum fuit in hac re, de quo intelligentes viderentur non posse dubitare, huius perinde, ac si res ipsa exsisteexsisteret, definitionem arte ac methodo inuestigaui. Primum posui nominis definitionem omnibus concessam. Mox quàm multas res inter se perspicuè differentes haec comprehenderet, notaui: & quantum earum discrimen essetindicaui. Post haec, an omnibus conuenire posset Excommunicatio vestra, consideraui. Postque internae & spirituali cômunioni aptari non posse ostendi, externae solum modò congruere demonstraui. Hanc cum in tribus potissimum partibus consistere declarauissem, atque à duabus ex his neminem repelli debere monstrauissem, conclusi tandem in 8.Thesi, Excommunicationem, (si quidem in scripturis fit praecepta) aliud esse non posse, quàm solennem exclusionem à Sacramentorum communione &c. Hanc si tu definitionem veris argumentis (seruatis hypothesibus vestris) refellere poteris, praemium tibi victoriae Leporinum statuo caseum. Hanc Excommunicationem, quam vos ministerij externi partem facitis, dico aliis rebus nullis definiri posse, quàm interdictione Sacramentorum. Etenim aliae poenae huic accidunt, quae ad ipsius substantiam non pertinent: cum & haec sine illis, & illae sine hac esse possint.
units.tr: Therefore, since the parts of a definition ought to be free of controversy, and since these are above all controversial, and the matter cannot be decided from Scripture, I ought not to have put them into the definition. For since the thing itself has been devised by men, it is necessary that the reasons too should be devised, and these are brought forward by all sides in support. So all the arguments are equally firm, and one cannot easily be rightly preferred to another. As for what remained in this matter, about which those who understood would seem not to be able to doubt, I looked into its definition by method and art, just as if the thing itself existed. First I put down a definition of the name, which is granted by all. Next I noted how many clearly different things this definition would cover, and I indicated how great the difference between them is. After this I considered whether your excommunication could fit all of them. Then I showed that it cannot be applied to internal and spiritual communion, and I demonstrated that it fits only external communion. When I had declared that this consists chiefly of three parts, and had shown that none ought to be repelled from two of them, I concluded at last, in the eighth thesis, that excommunication (if indeed it is prescribed in the Scriptures) can be nothing other than the solemn exclusion from communion in the sacraments, and so on. If you can refute this definition with true arguments, keeping your own hypotheses, I will set a Leporine cheese as the prize of victory for you. I say that this excommunication, which you make a part of the external ministry, cannot be defined by any other things than the interdiction of the sacraments. For other penalties attach to it which do not pertain to its substance, since it can exist without them and they without it.

units.la: Nec tua descriptio aliud continet, nisi quod hanc potestate assignas Senioribus: at nullo argumento. Deinde quod conscia dicis Ecclesia fieri: at non consentiente sententiamque dicente. Quicquid publicè fit, hoc conscia Ecclesia fit: tametsi concinente ipsa nequaquam fiat. Quamobrem verba sunt tantum, res subest nulla. Tertiò quod explicatè ego nominaui interdictionem sacramentorum: hoc tu sub eiectione è societate visibilis Ecclesiae tegis. Ego verò illos, de quibus sermo nobis est, ex societate externa Ecclesiae aliter eijci non posse ostendi, quàm sacramentorum negatione.
units.tr: Nor does your description contain anything beyond the fact that you assign this power to the elders, but with no argument. Next, you say that it is done with the knowledge of the Church, but not with its consent and pronouncing its judgement. Whatever is done publicly is done with the knowledge of the Church, even though it is by no means done with its agreement. So these are only words, and there is no substance behind them. Thirdly, where I explicitly named the interdiction of the sacraments, you cover this with the expulsion from the fellowship of the visible Church. But I have shown that those of whom we speak cannot be cast out of the external fellowship of the Church in any other way than by the denial of the sacraments.

units.la: Clarè igitur vides recto & bono consilio me in mea definitione omisisse, quae tu malè infersisti. Quippe si dixissem sententiam esse ab Ecclesia latam, damnauisses id tu. Nam Iohannes Morellus Gallus propter librum editum, in quo contendit ius Excommunicandi non esse penès Presbyteros, sed penes Ecclesiam, à vestro Presbyterio excommunicatus, & liber publicè exustus, ac lectione eius omnibus sub graui poena interdictū fuit. Facta hæc ita sunt die 6. Sept. temb. anni 1563. teste scripto istic edito, in quo prædicta continentur. Hanc autem sententiam, quae à vobis tam atrociter, vt ille conquestus fuit, damnata est, ab illis defenditur, quibusdam mihi lis adhuc fuit. Si à ministro posuissem ferri debere, vnà tecum illi, qui priorem probauissent; me reprehendissent. Si affirmassem ad Presbyteros hoc munus pertinere, te quidem habuissem suffragatorem, at ambos illos aduersarios. Cum mihi demonstraueris, quae ex recitatis tribus opinionibus vera sit, sciam tunc, quid me facere conueniat. Similis est ratio alterius accusationis. Sed tempus est, vt tuam expendamus descriptionem.
units.tr: You see clearly, then, that I rightly and wisely left out of my definition what you have wrongly brought in. Indeed, if I had said that the sentence was passed by the Church, you would have condemned that. For John Morellus, a Frenchman, on account of a book he published, in which he contended that the right of excommunicating belongs not to the elders but to the Church, was excommunicated by your eldership, and the book was publicly burned, and reading it was forbidden to all under heavy penalty. These things were done so, on the 6th of September in the year 1563, as attested by a written account published there, in which the aforesaid things are contained. Now, that this sentence, which by you was condemned so savagely, as he complained, is defended by some people is still a matter of dispute for me. If I had said that it ought to be pronounced by the minister, I would have had those who approved the former view, together with you, reproaching me. If I had asserted that this office belongs to the elders, I would indeed have had you as a supporter, but both of those opponents against me. When you show me which of the three opinions I have recited is true, then I shall know what I ought to do. The reasoning for the other accusation is similar. But it is time we weighed your description.

units.la: Excommunicatio, inquis, est sententia, qua Seniores in Dei nomine congregati, legitima præeunte cognitione, consciáque Ecclesia, pronunciant quempiam, qui se à Deo alienarit, eiectum quoque videri ab externae Ecclesiae societate tantisper, dum Ecclesiae, quoad eius fieri poterit, constituerit, cum esse Deo reconciliatum. Hanc tu descriptionem tuam paulò post his fere verbis interpretaris. Vt nil aliud fit Excommunicatio in terris, quàm declaratio alterius occultioris factae in caelis: ex qua videlicet merito colligatur, eum, qui in caelis non habeatur pro Christi membro, indignum esse, qui inter fideles in terris censeatur. Addis haec quoque. Nec debuisti, quod praecipuum erat, praetermittere, ipsam videlicet ab interiore Christi societate seclusionem in coelis factam: cuius consequens & appendicem esse dico Excommunicationem in terris factam: adeo vt nisi illa praecesserit, ista quoque irrita merito censeatur. Cum hac descriptionis tuae declaratione pulchrè congruit Petrus Lombardus lib.4. dist. 18. Nec est inconueniens, vt quemadmodum res est à Pontificis ad vos deriuata, ita explicationem quoque ab eisdem mutuemini. Verùm Lombardo caeterisque scholasticis, qui deinde vnà tecum non omnes Magistri sui sententiam probauerunt, absque scriptuiris licuit loqui: tibi, qui diuersum profiteris, non licet.
units.tr: "Excommunication," you say, "is a sentence by which elders, gathered in the name of God, after lawful examination and with the knowledge of the Church, pronounce that someone who has alienated himself from God is also to be regarded as cast out from the fellowship of the external Church for as long as, so far as it can be done, he has not been reconciled to God in the Church." You afterwards explain this description of yours in nearly these words: "Excommunication on earth is nothing other than the declaration of another, more hidden, exclusion made in heaven, from which it is rightly inferred that one who is not held to be a member of Christ in heaven is unworthy to be counted among the faithful on earth." You add this too: "Nor ought you to have omitted what was the principal thing, namely the exclusion from the inner fellowship of Christ made in heaven itself; I say that excommunication made on earth is its consequence and appendage, so that unless the former has gone before, the latter too is rightly judged void." Peter Lombard, Book 4, distinction 18, agrees well with this explanation of your description. Nor is it inappropriate that, just as the thing itself has been derived from the Papists to you, so you should also borrow the explanation from the same source. But Lombard and the other schoolmen, who afterwards did not all approve the opinion of their master, were allowed to speak without Scripture; you, who profess the opposite, are not allowed to.

units.la: Ergo miror hoc primum, quod me in definitione putas mentionem debuisse facere interioris à Deo in caelis factae exclusionis, cum audieris me in Thesibus de sola externa Excommunicatione agere, eamque ab occultiore illa diligenter distinxisse. An quae distinxi prius, ne confunderentur, mox in definitione permiscere iterum debui? Recte autem vere q; me discreuisse, arbitror neque te neque alium quempiam dubitaturum. Differentiam hanc Lutherus etiam praeclarè vidit. Nam in 3. cap. Ioelis tom. Latin. 4. sic scribit. Duplex est Excommunicatio, Politica seu externa & visibilis, qua Ecclesia vtitur contra notorie facinorosos. Alia occulta & inuisibilis, non hominum, sed ipsius Dei est. Vides hunc virum affirmantem Ecclesiam politica tantum Excommunicatione vti? Idem in serm. de Excommunicat. tomo Germ. 1. duplicè ait esse communionem, externam & internam, sicut duę quoque res sint in Sacramentis, signum videlicet ac signatum. Internam, quae & inuisibilis sit ac spiritualis, in corde esse, cum quis per veram fidem, spem & charitatem insertus est in Christi sanctorumque communionem. Hanc (addit) nec dare nec auferre vllus homo potest, adeoq; nec Angelus nec vlla creatura, sed solus Deus per suum spiritum infundit in hominis cor Sacramento credentis. Ita huc nulla Excommunicatio pertingit praeter solam infidelitatem aut peccata, quibus seipsum excommunicat. Probat hoc mox verbis apost. ad Rom. 8. Quis nos separabit &c. Hanc externam Excommunicationem cum tu affirmes consequens & appendicem esse illius, quae in caelis facta est, confiteri nobiscum cogeris, humanam à Diuina aliam esse. Cur ergo à me postulas, vt de ea, de qua mihi controuersia cum nemine est aut fuit, & de qua me non disceptaturum ostendi, in definitione ponam? Si ab alterutro hac in re peccatum est, certè à te peccatum est, qui descriptioni humanae Excommunicationis alleuisti Diuinam.
units.tr: Therefore I am first surprised that you think I ought to have mentioned in the definition the inward exclusion made by God in heaven, since you have heard me say in my Theses that I treat only of external excommunication and have carefully distinguished it from that hidden one. Should I have mixed together again in the definition what I had first distinguished so that they would not be confused? I think that neither you nor anyone else will doubt that I distinguished them rightly and truly. Luther also saw this difference clearly. In his commentary on the third chapter of Joel (Latin tome 4) he writes: "Excommunication is twofold: political or external and visible, which the Church uses against those notoriously guilty of wrongdoing; the other is hidden and invisible, and belongs not to men but to God himself." Do you see that this man affirms that the Church uses only political excommunication? In his sermon on excommunication (German tome 1) he likewise says that communion is twofold, external and internal, just as there are two things in the sacraments, namely the sign and the thing signified. The internal communion, which is invisible and spiritual, is in the heart, when someone is grafted by true faith, hope and love into the communion of Christ and the saints. He adds that no man can give or take this, nor indeed any angel or any creature, but God alone pours it into the heart of the man who believes in the sacrament, through his Spirit. So no excommunication reaches this inward communion except unbelief alone, or the sins by which a man excommunicates himself. He proves this at once with the words of the Apostle to the Romans 8: "Who shall separate us," and so on. Since you affirm that this external excommunication is a consequence and appendix of that which was made in heaven, you are forced to confess with us that human excommunication is other than divine. Why then do you demand that I put into the definition something about which I have no dispute with anyone, and about which I have shown that I will not argue? If either of us has erred in this matter, it is certainly you who have erred, since in describing human excommunication you have mixed in the divine.

units.la: Grauius peccatum est, quod declaratio, qua tumetipse tuam explanas definitionem, cum eâdem non conuenit. Quoniam in explanatione scribis, nihil aliud eam esse, quàm declarationem occultioris in cœlis factae, ex qua colligatur, eum, qui in cœlis sit exclusus, etiam in terris excludendum esse. At in definitione dicis, eam esse sententiam Seniorum, qua pronunciant aliquem ab externa Ecclesiae societate abscissum esse. Plurimum certè differunt hae duae orationes. Excommunicatio est declaratio iudicij Dei in cœlis facti: & Excommunicatio est sententia Seniorum, qua quis excluditur è societate externa fidelium. Si responderas ex illa declaratione hanc sequi, respondebo ego vicissim, aliud esse id, ex quo aliquid sequitur, abeo, quod ex illo sequitur: nec illius declarationem posse vlla ratione vocari definitionem huius. Ostendam etiam paulò post, non posse humanam Excommunicationem ex Diuina rectè colligi.
units.tr: A graver fault is that the explanation by which you yourself unfold your definition does not agree with it. For in the explanation you write that it is nothing other than a declaration of the hidden excommunication made in heaven, from which it follows that the one who is excluded in heaven must also be excluded on earth. But in the definition you say that it is the sentence of the elders by which someone is pronounced cut off from the external fellowship of the Church. These two statements differ very much. Excommunication is a declaration of the judgment of God made in heaven; and excommunication is the sentence of the elders by which someone is shut out from the external fellowship of the faithful. If you should answer that the one follows from the other, I shall answer in turn that the thing from which something follows is one thing, and the thing which follows from it is another; and the declaration of the one cannot in any way be called the definition of the other. I shall also show a little later that human excommunication cannot rightly be inferred from the divine.

units.la: Tertiò haud rectè ponis veluti confessum, ius scilicet ferendae sententiae seu Excommunicandi penès Presbyteros esse. Nam Pontificij ad Sacerdotes suos hoc pertinere dicent: scripturaeque exemplis opinionem suam probare conabuntur. Solus Petrus, inquient, Ananiam & Saphiram, Simonémque Magum excommunicauit. (Nam ex tua sententia fuit Excommunicatio.) Solus Paulus Elymam Magū excommunicauit: Solus Alexandrum & Hymenæum Satanae tradidit: Soli sibi scelestos indicari per epistolā iubet. Solum se cum authoritate venturū scribit: & pro potestate sibi à Deo tradita poenas à nocentibus sumpturum affirmat. Solus Corinthium decreuerat Satanae tradere, tametsi congregata Ecclesia vellet fieri. Hanc consuetudinem multis seculis in Ecclesia viguisse addent. Et quamuis aliqui Episcopis Presbyteri fuerint additi, non plus tamen eos habuisse imperij, quàm Consiliarij habere solent. Haec & similia illiprose adducent: tu pro Presbyteris tuis quid adferes?
units.tr: Thirdly, you wrongly assume as agreed that the right of pronouncing sentence, that is, of excommunicating, belongs to the presbyters. For the Papists will say that this pertains to their priests, and they will try to prove their opinion by examples from Scripture. Peter alone, they will say, excommunicated Ananias and Sapphira, and Simon the Magician (for according to your view that was an excommunication). Paul alone excommunicated Elymas the Magician; Paul alone handed Alexander and Hymenaeus over to Satan; he alone orders the wicked to be pointed out to him by letter; he alone writes that he will come with authority, and affirms that he will exact punishment from the guilty by the power given him by God. He alone had decided to hand the Corinthian over to Satan, although he wished it to be done with the Church assembled. They will add that this custom flourished in the Church for many centuries. And although some presbyters were added to the bishops, they had no more power than counsellors usually have. These and similar arguments they will bring forward against that man. What will you bring forward in defence of your presbyters?

units.la: Quomodò etiam hæc verba tua defendes? Ius enim Excommunicandi ante Papisticam illam tyrannidem nunquàm quàm penès vnum fuisse comperietur, sed penès Presbyterium: & quidem non exclusò penitùs populo. Hæc tua qua ratione fis cùm nunc dictis conciliaturus, ipse videris. Ego Ambrosium solum excommunicauisse lego Theodosium: imò iam tum Seniores illos non amplius fuisse ait. An tunc Papistica tyrannis obtinuerat? Saltem Petri & Pauli temporibus nondum huc vsque excreuerat. Non ignoro Ruffinum ita loqui, ac si cum alijs Ambrosium Theodosium exclusisset. Sed mos & consuetudo illius temporis, ipsa res gesta, & scriptores alij omnes, quod dixi, comprobant. Huc facit nominihil hist, de Theodosio iuniore apud Theodor. lib. 5. cap. 37. Adde quòd in tota historia Ecclesiastica de vestro Presbyterio nihil reperitur: quantum inter legendum ipse obseruaui. Præter paucula illa, quæ apud Tertull. Cyprianum, & Augustinum de Iudicibus nescio quibus legimus, nihil ego de Presbyterorum vestrorum consessu vidi: nisi forte excidit (Ambrosium de re alia loqui, alibi indicaui) Historia certè Orientis aliter canit. Quare si aliquid huius fuit, in sola Africa fuit.
units.tr: And how will you defend these words of yours? For it will be found that the right of excommunicating was never anywhere except in the hands of one man before that Papist tyranny, but in the presbytery; and indeed the people was not wholly excluded. How you will reconcile these things with what you have now said, you yourself must see. I read that Ambrose alone excommunicated Theodosius; indeed, Rufinus says that already at that time those elders were no longer in existence. Had the Papist tyranny already prevailed then? At least in the times of Peter and Paul it had not yet grown to that point. I am not unaware that Rufinus speaks as if Ambrose had excluded Theodosius together with others. But the custom and practice of that time, the event itself, and all the other writers confirm what I have said. What is said in history about the younger Theodosius in Theodoret, book 5, chapter 37, has some bearing here. Add that nothing about your presbytery is found in the whole ecclesiastical history, as I myself have observed in my reading. Apart from those few passages in Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine where we read about certain judges, I have seen nothing of a council of your presbyters, unless perhaps I have overlooked something (I have indicated elsewhere that Ambrose speaks of another matter). The history of the East certainly sings a different tune. So if anything of this kind existed, it existed only in Africa.

units.la: Quartò dicis conscia Ecclesia ferendam esse à Presbyteris sententiam, cùm ex aliorum quorundam opinione dicere debeares consentiente simulq; suffragante. Producent hi exempla Act. 1. & 14. & 15. cap. Idem Christum voluisse dicent. 18. cap. Math. Idem Paulum in 1. Cor. 5. docuisse contendent. Demùm longo tempore in vetustissima Ecclesia morem hunc seruatum fuisse affirmabunt. Si in magna turba non posse obseruari obijcias, negabunt illi, & factum fuisse, fieriq; posse docebunt. Non enim necessarium esse, vt singuli sententias dicant, sed sufficere, si is, qui aliquid habet, dicere liberè possit, vt de prophetantib. Paul. 1. Cor. 14. scribit. Si rursus obijcias, incommoda nascitura ex multitudine malorum, respondebunt ab homine hoc dici, se verò Dei præscriptum sequi: qui longè homine melius ventura ex re qualibet mala præuiderit. Pro Presbyteris certè nihil tale proferre poteris. Nam si ad 18. Math. caput confugias, plus id sibi, quàm tibi, patrocinari clamitabunt. Addent se, adferre testimonia aperta: te citare vnsi idéque dubium: ac dubijs & controuersis locis non esse probandam rem litigiosam. Ingenuè dico, si alterutri locus hic patrocinaretur, magis horum, quam tuam sententiam confirmaret. At suo loco, Deo volente, luculentè ostendam, cum neutris seruire.
units.tr: Fourthly, you say that the sentence is to be pronounced by the presbyters with the consent of the congregation, whereas, according to the opinion of certain others, you ought to have said that it is pronounced with the consent and support of the people. These men will bring forward examples from Acts 1, 14 and 15. They will say that Christ wished the same, in Matthew 18. They will argue that Paul taught the same in 1 Corinthians 5. Finally, they will affirm that this custom was observed for a long time in the most ancient Church. If you object that it cannot be observed in a great crowd, they will deny it, and will teach that it has been done and can be done. For it is not necessary that each individual should give his opinion, but it is enough if the one who has something to say can speak freely; as Paul writes of those who prophesied, 1 Corinthians 14. If again you object the inconveniences that will arise from the multitude of evil men, they will reply that this is said by a man, whereas they follow God's prescription, who foresees far better than man what will come out of any evil thing. Certainly you can bring nothing of this kind forward for your presbyters. For if you take refuge in Matthew chapter 18, they will loudly claim that it defends them rather than you. They will add that they bring forward clear testimonies, whereas you cite one passage that is doubtful, and that a disputed matter ought not to be proved from doubtful and controverted passages. To speak frankly, if this passage defended either side, it would confirm the opinion of these men more than yours. But in its proper place, God willing, I will show clearly that it serves neither.

units.la: Quintò non explicas quando & quomodo peccator satisfecisse Presbyteris videri possit. At vbi leges nullæ sunt certæ, Presbyteriqué ex arbitrio suo agent, non poterit non esse perniciosa hæc potestas. Scio (vt alia nunc sileam) Sodomitam alicubi statim ab Ecclesia (id est, à Presbyteris) absolutum: vbi fortasse alius quispiam qui in templo vel sputauisset solùm, longè fuisset tractatus asperiùs. Quam duriter tractarint veteres illi miseros afflictosque peccatores, nullus hodiè nescit. In summa, nisi leges ponantur hac de re, pœnæ tales erunt semper, qualis erit quouis tempore Presbyterorum illorum affectus: hoc est, miserabilis erit tyrannis. His adde, quod huius tu criminis verè reus es, cuius me immerito insimulasti: nempe non dicis in tam longa tua descriptione quibus de rebus ferenda sit hæc sententia.
units.tr: Fifthly, you do not explain when and how a sinner may be seen to have satisfied the presbyters. But where there are no fixed laws, and the presbyters act at their own discretion, this power cannot fail to be harmful. I know (to pass over other examples) that somewhere a sodomite was absolved at once by the Church (that is, by the presbyters), whereas perhaps someone else who had merely spat in the temple would have been treated far more harshly. Nobody today fails to know how harshly those ancient men treated wretched and afflicted sinners. In short, unless laws are laid down on this matter, the penalties will always be such as the feeling of those presbyters happens to be at any time; that is, it will be a wretched tyranny. To these add that you are truly guilty of the very fault of which you wrongly accused me: namely, in your so long description you do not say in what matters this sentence is to be pronounced.

units.la: Quippè à Deo se alienarit oportet, quisquis Presbyteris vestris talis iudicabitur. Sed hæc ferri adhuc poterant: qui sequuntur errores longè sunt grauissimi.
units.tr: Indeed, whoever is judged such a person by your Presbyters must thereby have alienated himself from God. But these points could still be tolerated; the errors that follow are far more serious.

units.la: Sextò, veluti concessum ab omnibus audaCter sumis, Deum alicubi imperasse, (locum autem non indicas,) scelere aliquo contaminatos, à conciliabulo quodam Presbyterorum solenni ritu proclamari debere à Deo in cœlis lata sententia excommunicatos. Debet vnusquisque sic declarari à Deo exclusus, quomodo sacræ literæ docent. Faciunt hoc cùm alij, tum verò inprimis Ministri, cum publicè priuatimque omnibus & singulis iram & iudicium Dei contrà peccata ante oculos ponunt: & quæ quoslibet sceleratos pœna maneat (nisi redeant in viam, Deoque reconcilientur) exponunt.
