By an argument drawn from the unclean under the law, you wish to show that the greater excommunication, which forbids every lawful act and consigns the excommunicated to eternal damnation, rests on Scripture. Were the unclean under the law regarded as damned? Were they forbidden every lawful act? Were they kept from all the sacraments? It is not so. Even if one of the unclean died, no one doubted his salvation on that account, since even the holiest man could die so, for instance while suffering from a gonorrhoea, lying beside a corpse. Likewise a woman suffering from her monthly courses or from another flux, or a leper. Were not even the unclean compelled, on pain of death, to celebrate the sacrament of atonement with mourning? Were they not bound to observe the Sabbaths? But of these things later; now let us weigh your points. I do not recall having argued in this way, namely that because legal uncleanness was something external, it could not signify the impurity of life and morals. Your argument in this passage seems to be this: those polluted by crimes were more impure than those polluted under the law. Therefore, since the latter were kept from the sacred rites, those contaminated by vices ought much more to be repelled. Even if God had commanded that both be punished in the same way and not differently, it would certainly follow that those more impure should be kept from the temple more than the less impure. Your reasoning is similar to this, as will be very clearly seen later: a charcoal-burner, or some other dirty man who by his filth defiles those who touch him, is less pure than a drunkard, a thief or a murderer. Therefore men dressed in clean clothes will flee a thief much more, lest by contact with him they stain their garments, than a charcoal-burner. Certainly, to protect our clothes, we avoid a charcoal-burner whose garments are covered with coal dust much more than a thief dressed in clean garments. Moreover, I will show most clearly later that these arguments are alike.

units.la: Et quorsum, ais, sacrificia illa pro peccatis, nisi ut publica essent resipiscentiæ testimonia? Ego vicissim quaero ex te, quorsum hoc adducas argumentum? Statuisti probare excommunicationem maiorem niti scripturis, & veteris hoc argumento: qui sic peccarunt apud Iudæos, ut certa peccato poena nulla esset constituta à Deo, ij iussi ab eodem sunt isliusmodi peccata, certis expiare sacrificijs: ergo licet peccatores ab omni legitimo actu prohibere. Ecquis haec patienter in tam gravi causa audiat a te cum authoritate dici? An erat excommunicatus, qui, quoties & quando vellet, ad templum ire poterat, vt sacrificium Deo pro commisso a se peccato offerret? Hoc ipse, quod ad expiandum peccatum iubetur adferre sacrificium, non excluditur a sacramentis, sed ad ea inuitatur. Nam omnia haec sacrificia erant vera Sacramenta. Quomodo ergo ad stabiliendam Excommunicationem tu haec producis? Quomodo aditu templi prohibitos fuisse? aut exemplo eorum Maiorem Papae Excommunicationem astruere tentas? At saltem oportebat tales, inquis, in signum poenitentiae sacrificare. Concedo, sed ad rem nostram quid hoc attinet? Quin & apud nos idem fit. Sicut enim illa sacrificia declarabant offerentem peccauisse, & peccati poenitere: sic qui ad coenam apud nos accessurus est testificatur, prius se poenitere peccatorum, gratia Dei egere, inque morte Christi salutem sibi quaerere, adeoque sic affectum esse vt Christo dignam velit deinceps vitam viuere. Ergo quocunque vertas argumentum tuum nihil probat.
units.tr: And to what end, you say, were those sacrifices for sins, unless they were public testimonies of repentance? I in turn ask you: to what end do you bring up this argument? You undertook to prove that the greater excommunication rests on Scripture, and you bring this argument from the old law: those who sinned among the Jews, when God had fixed no certain punishment for the sin, he commanded to atone for such sins by certain sacrifices; therefore it is lawful to bar sinners from every lawful act. Who would patiently hear such things said with authority by you in so grave a matter? Was he excommunicated who could go to the temple whenever and as often as he wished, to offer a sacrifice to God for the sin he had committed? The very man who is commanded to bring a sacrifice to atone for sin is not shut out from the sacraments but invited to them. For all those sacrifices were true sacraments. How then do you bring these things forward to establish excommunication? How do you prove that they were barred from the entrance of the temple? Or do you try by their example to establish the greater excommunication of the Pope? But, you say, such people ought at least to sacrifice as a sign of repentance. I grant it, but what does this have to do with our question? Indeed the same thing happens among us. For just as those sacrifices showed that the one offering had sinned and repented of his sin, so the one who is about to come to the supper among us testifies that he first repents of his sins, seeks the grace of God, and seeks his salvation in the death of Christ, and is so disposed that he wishes thereafter to live a life worthy of Christ. Therefore, however you turn your argument, it proves nothing.

units.la: Ob schismata, hoc est, gravia offendicula inquis sunt eiecti e Synagogis homines, id est, a sacris omnibus conuentibus prohibiti sunt: qui mos a Christo reprehensus minime probari manifeste potest. Nam si in priuatis negotijs aliquoi manifestis delictis iubet Ecclesiae rebellem haberi velut Ethnicum & Publicanum, multo magis id voluit fieri in publicis criminibus. Post haec multis probas Ethnicis nefas fuisse templum ingredi: Iudaeosque cum illis vitae confuetudinem nullam habuisse: quae minime erat necesse probare. Nihil enim in sacris literis aperte scriptum probationis eget apud vos. Respondeo breuiter, salsissimum esse, quod dicis ἀποσυνάγωγοι fieri, idem significasse ac a conuentibus riubusque sacris omnibus prohiberi. Interpretatio haec non est scripturae, ideoque a me non recipiatur. In sempiternum non docebis ex sacris literis, non licuisse illis, qui ex Synagoga aliqua fuissent eiecti, ingredi gredi in templum Hierosolymitanum, consuetáque ibi cum caeteris celebrare Sacramenta. Quare merae nugae sunt, quae hoc loco profers. Quid sit aliquem vt Ethnicum & Publicanum habere, cum ad 18. Cap. Matth. peruentum fuerit, exponam: & probabo ibidem,te verba haec pessimè interpretari.
units.tr: Because of schisms, that is, grave stumbling-blocks, you say, men were cast out of the synagogues, that is, forbidden all sacred assemblies. That custom, which Christ rebuked, cannot clearly be proved at all. For if in private matters Christ commands that a rebel against the Church, for some manifest offence, be regarded as a heathen and a tax-collector, much more did he wish this to be done in public crimes. After this you prove at length that it was an offence for heathens to enter the temple, and that the Jews had no social intercourse with them. This was hardly necessary to prove. For nothing written plainly in the holy letters, among you, needs proof. I reply briefly that it is most absurd, what you say, that to be put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγοι] means the same as being barred from all assemblies and sacred gatherings. This interpretation is not Scripture's, and so I do not accept it. You will never teach from the holy letters that those who had been cast out of some synagogue were not allowed to enter the temple at Jerusalem and there celebrate the sacraments along with the others. So the things you bring forward in this place are mere trifles. What it is to have someone as a heathen and a tax-collector I will explain when we come to chapter 18 of Matthew, and I will prove there that you interpret those words very badly.

units.la: Paulus optimus Christi interpres prohibet cum nomine tantum fratribus cibum capere, 1. Cor. 5. Cuius loci sensum vt quis in omnes formas conuertat, nunquàm probabiliter, nedum necessariò euicerit, dignos conuenientibus ijs, qui ad fidei confessionem spectabant, habitos suisse, quibuscum priuatae vitae vsus nefarius censeretur. Quae de haereticis ex 3. cap. Epist. ad Titum allinis, ad nos non pertinent. Ego mihi persuasi, me veritatis amatoribus, quos agnitum errorem reuocare non pudeat, perfacile demonstraturum esse, ex hoc loco id non sequi, quod tu sequi opinaris. Primum quidem non dicit Paulus non admittendos tales, si quidem admitti cupiant ad auditionem verbi, ad preces, ad caenam Dominicam, denique ad legitimos & à Deo praeceptos ritus actúsque alios. Quod si de excommunicatione loqui voluisset, longè breuius & apertius dixisset, arcete eum à Sacramentis: aut tradite enim Satanae, vt vos hanc rem exponitis. At non hoc iubet, sed ne commiscentur (hoc enim est συναναμίγνυσθαι.) id est, imperat ne familiariter & coniunctissimè cum talibus viuant. Causae huius rei duae sunt: vna, vt, qui peccauit, pudefiat ac corrigatur. Nam qui se ab aliquibus vitari videt praeter morem, hoc ipso scelcris argüi se intelligit, siqueque pudefactus vitam emendat. Altera, quod ex familiari malorum conuictu, qui boni sunt, corrumpuntur: & ab aliis tales iudicantur, quales ij sunt, quorum arctiore societate vtuntur: qui autem mali sunt, hoc ipso in malo confirmantur. In Sacramentorum vsu contraria modo eueniunt omnia. Quippe horum frequens vsus nec vtentem, nec spectantes aut praesentes reddit deteriores: sed augentur magis in vtrisque spiritussanƈti dona. Sunt enim adminicula quædam infirmitatis nostræ, & inuitamenta ad pietatem cultumque Dei. Hinc fit, vt horum negleƈtio neque pudefaciat praue agentes, neque negligentes reddat meliores, sed eosdem deteriores efficiat.
units.tr: Paul, the best interpreter of Christ, forbids eating with those who are brothers in name only, 1 Cor. 5. No one could ever probably, let alone necessarily, prove, by turning the sense of that passage in every direction, that those were meant who were regarded as worthy of companionship with those who belonged to the confession of faith, and with whom the wicked practice of private life would be judged a fault. What is said about heretics in the third chapter of the Epistle to Titus does not pertain to us. I was persuaded that I should easily demonstrate to lovers of the truth, who are not ashamed to retract an error once recognised, that what you suppose follows from this passage does not follow. First, Paul does not say that such people are not to be admitted, if indeed they desire to be admitted to hearing the word, to prayers, to the Lord's Supper, and finally to the other lawful acts and rites commanded by God. But if he had wished to speak of excommunication, he would have said much more briefly and plainly: keep him from the sacraments, or deliver him to Satan, as you explain the matter. But he does not command this; he says that they should not mingle (for this is what συναναμίγνυσθαι means), that is, he commands that they not live with such people in familiar and very close fellowship. There are two reasons for this: one, that the one who has sinned may be shamed and corrected. For one who sees himself avoided by some people contrary to custom understands that he is convicted of wickedness, and if he is shamed he amends his life. The other is that by familiar association with the wicked, the good are corrupted, and others judge them to be such as those are with whom they have close fellowship; and those who are wicked are confirmed in wickedness by this very fact. In the use of the sacraments, everything happens in the opposite way. For the frequent use of these does not make the one using them, nor those who watch or are present, worse; rather the gifts of the Holy Spirit are increased in both. For they are certain helps to our weakness, and incitements to piety and the worship of God. Hence it comes about that neglecting them neither shames those who act wickedly, nor makes the negligent better, but makes the same people worse.

units.la: Secundò, discrimen est longè maximum interea, quæ Deus toti Ecclesiæ instituit, quæque ab omnibus vult obseruari: & ea quæ priuatis pro loco & tempore præcipit seruanda aut fugienda. Etenim hæc illis nihil derogant, quando non pugnant interse, sed simul ab eodem seruari possunt. At non pugnare, Sacramentis cum aliquo vti, & societatem eius priuatam, præsertim arƈtiorem, fugere, certo est certius. Etenim non me iubet Deus cum omnibus Ecclesiæ membris ϲωνευχαλγνωσω, at sacramentis ab ipso institutis, iubet me cum Ecclesiæ membris omnibus vti. In sacramentorum præterea vsurpatione iubeor meipsum explorare, non alios: at in conuiƈtu & sodalitate priuata intueri debeo alios, vt & lucrer eos, si praui sint, & consuetudine eorum ipse non deprauer. Præcepit Deus, vt sceleribus inquinatos propter prædiƈtas causas vitem in rebus & negotijs priuatis: in publicis à Deo ordinatis ritibus vitare eos non me iubet. Adde quod manifestè imperat Paulus, ne talem hostis loco habeamus, sed velut fratrem instruamus, 2. Thes.3. vultergo, vt in rebus ad cultum Dei & salutem proximi speƈtantibus eum non perinde vitemus, atque in ijs, quæ ad priuata commercia attinent. Immò ne conuiƈtum quidem prohibet, si ἀδελφὸν quam istic præcipit, inseruiat: sanè non vult excommunicare eum non vult, quem velut hostem habere vetat.
units.tr: Second, there is a very great difference between what God has instituted for the whole Church and wants observed by everyone, and what he commands his people to observe or avoid as private individuals, according to place and time. The latter do not detract from the former, since they do not conflict with one another and can both be kept by the same person. Now, not to conflict means that to partake of the sacraments with someone, and to avoid private fellowship with him, especially a closer fellowship, is quite certainly consistent. God does not command me to feast together [συνευωχεῖσθαι] with all the members of the Church, but he does command me to use the sacraments he has instituted together with all the members of the Church. Moreover, in using the sacraments I am commanded to examine myself, not others; but in private company and fellowship I ought to look at others, so that I may gain them if they are wicked, and not be corrupted myself by their company. God commanded that we avoid in private affairs and dealings those who are polluted by crimes, for the reasons already given; but in public rites ordained by God he does not command me to avoid them. Add that Paul clearly commands that we not regard such a person as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother (2 Thess. 3). He wills, therefore, that in matters bearing on the worship of God and the salvation of our neighbour, we do not avoid him in the same way as in matters belonging to private dealings. Indeed, he does not even forbid eating with him, if he commands that such a person be treated as a brother [ἀδελφὸν] there. Certainly he does not wish to excommunicate the one whom he forbids us to regard as an enemy.

units.la: Tertiò constat, Apostolum, vt qui seƈta Pharifæus suisset, non ignorasse Iudæorum mores. Norât itaque Publicanos à plerisque omnibus Iudæis, inprimis autē à Pharisæis sic fuisse deuitatos, vt nō modò à familiaritate consuetudineque eorum abstinerent, verumetiam cibum cum illis capere religionem esse putarent: & nihilominus neque à templo, neque ab alio cultu prohibitos fuisse.
units.tr: Third, it is clear that the Apostle, who had been a Pharisee, was not ignorant of the customs of the Jews. He knew that tax collectors were shunned by almost all Jews, and especially by the Pharisees, to such an extent that they not only abstained from familiarity and social intercourse with them, but even thought it a matter of religion not to eat with them; and yet they were not barred from the temple or from other worship.

units.la: Quod cum hoc etiam loco Apostolus iubeat, facilè liquet, ad consuetudinem vitæ priuatam pertinere hoc eius præceptum, non ad Ecclesiasticos actus. Non tantum debetis, inquit, arctiorem talium societatem vitare, sed etiam conuictum. Quod hactenus tenendum monet Apostolus vt suo prius exemplo Christus nos docuit, quatenus is non inferuiat correctioni fratris. Quocirca non potest vlla ratione ostendi, Apostolum existimasse ita inter se duo hæc connexa fuisse, vt alterum sine altero esse non posset. Dum igitur alterum iubet, alterum non iubet, nemo vtrumque eum iubere voluisse affirmare debet. Hoc factum Iudæorum ita tuam interpretationem refellit, vt solum sufficeret veritatem quærentibus possit.
units.tr: Since the Apostle commands this in the present passage as well, it is easily seen that this precept concerns the private conduct of life, not ecclesiastical acts. You must avoid, he says, not only the closer fellowship of such people but also their table company. The Apostle reminds us that this must be held to, just as Christ first taught us by his own example, insofar as the latter does not serve the correction of a brother. Therefore it cannot be shown by any reasoning that the Apostle thought these two things so connected that one could not exist without the other. Since he commands the one and does not command the other, no one ought to affirm that he wished both to be commanded. This fact of the Jews refutes your interpretation so thoroughly that it would be enough for those seeking the truth.

units.la: Quartò affirmat expresse Paulus in Actis coram Festo, & aliàs quoq;, se contrà legem Mosis nihil peccasse. Quinetiam Iudæi nullius eum transgressionis accusarunt, quàm quod Græcos in Templum introduxisse mentiebantur. Ceterum Lex Mosis iubet omnes Pascha concelebrare mundos secundùm legem: nec excipit moribus inquinatos, sed & Christus ad agni esum Iudam admisit: & cum in eius locum coenam suam instituret, omnes iussit ea vti discumbentes, id est, Christi discipulos se profitentes (Repræsentarunt enim discipuli totam Ecclesiam) dicens, bibite ex hoc omnes. Hac de causa ex Corinthiorum coena nullos, etsi permulti essent mali, exclusit. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuè patet, firmeque probatur, Paulum, dum bonis mandat, ne arctiore societate cum flagitiosis viuant, peccatoribus visu Sacramentorum, si modò vti cum alijs optassent, non interdixisse. Quippe semel contrà Mosis Christique legem id egisse videretur.
units.tr: Fourth, Paul expressly declares in Acts, before Festus, and elsewhere too, that he had committed no offence against the law of Moses. Indeed, the Jews accused him of no transgression other than having, as they falsely claimed, brought Greeks into the Temple. Moreover, the law of Moses commands that all who are clean according to the law celebrate the Passover, and it does not exclude those whose conduct is polluted. Christ also admitted Judas to the eating of the lamb, and when he instituted his supper in its place, he bade all who reclined to partake of it, that is, all who professed themselves Christ's disciples (for the disciples represented the whole Church), saying: drink of this, all of you. For this reason he excluded none from the Corinthians' supper, even though there were very many wicked people among them. From all these things it is plainly evident and firmly proved that Paul, when he charges the good not to live in closer fellowship with the wicked, did not forbid sinners the sight of the sacraments, if they wished to partake with others. Otherwise he would seem to have acted against the law of Moses and of Christ.

units.la: Postremò quid est opus longa expositione, cum ipsemet Apostolus suo facto se exponat? Certè in eadem Epistola recensét magnum Catalogum vicioforum hominum, quorum nullum iubet à coena Dominica remoueri. Quid potest exspectari clarius & certius? Quorum cap. 5. priuatum commercium iubet fugere: eosdem paulò post 11. cap. ipse non modo ad coenam Domini admittit, verumetiam mandat, vt seipsum vnusquisque exploret, qualesqualesalij sint. Aliud est malorum fugere consuetudinem, & aliud Sacramentis à Deo donatis cum caeteris vti. Hic cum Deo nobis res est: ibi cum hominibus. Hic suam vnusquisque conscientiam Deo probare debet: qualis aliorum sit, quaerere non debet. Si enim nefas esset cum improbis caenam Domini edere, non iussisset Apostolus vnumquemque seipsum probare, sed iussisset nos alios probare, ne pollueremur. Eodem spectat, quod mox addit, indignè edentem iudicium sibi edere, non alijs. Ergo vt huius loci sensum in omnes formas conuertas, nūquàm tamen vel ipsomet Paulo interprete ac Iudice tuae opinioni suffragabitur, sed de hoc loco posteaiterum disseretur.
units.tr: Finally, what need is there for a long explanation, when the Apostle himself explains his own practice? Certainly in the same Epistle he lists a great catalogue of vicious men, none of whom he commands to be removed from the Lord's Supper. What could be expected to be clearer and more certain? In chapter 5 he commands us to avoid private association with them, and shortly afterwards, in chapter 11, he himself not only admits the same people to the Lord's Supper, but also commands that each one examine himself, however others may be. It is one thing to flee the company of the wicked, and another to share with others in the sacraments given by God. Here we have to do with God; there, with men. Here each person must approve his own conscience before God; what others are like he need not ask. For if it were wrong to eat the Lord's Supper with the wicked, the Apostle would not have bidden each one to prove himself, but would have bidden us to prove others, lest we be polluted. To the same effect is what he adds soon after, that the one who eats unworthily eats judgement to himself, not to others. Therefore, although I should turn the sense of this passage into every shape, it will never support your opinion, not even with Paul himself as interpreter and judge; but this passage will be discussed again later.

units.la: Nunc ad solutiones tuas ad quatuor argumenta illa, quibus me putas maiorem Papistarum excommunicationem confutare voluisse, venio. Libet tamen prius monere, me non accusauisse, quia gradus fecerunt, quod etiam vos facitis. Species plures non esse ex meis Thesibus liquet. Nam si excommunicatio est prohibitio rei alicuius propter quam is, cui negata est, non exististimetur porrò membrum esse exterioris Ecclesiae, sola Sacramentorum negatio vocari poterit excommunicatio. Quoniam quae praeterea possunt nobis negare homines, accidentia eius sunt, ad substantiam non pertinent. D. Lutherus etiam in article ad Concil. Mantuan. indictum ait, Maiorem excommunicationem, vt Papa nominat, pro poena politica tantum habemus. Idem, nisi fallit memoria, repetiuit in admonit, ad Ecclesiast. Augustae Anno 1530. in Comitijs collectos. Deinde non hoc reprehendi, quod vnam dicunt alteram graviorem esse: sed quod maiorem interdictione templorum & actus cuiuslibet liciti definierunt. Miror vehementer, cur tibi libuerit meam sententiam oppugnare, cum eandem mecum probes. Scribis enim te censere aliter de simplici verbi auditione: a qua ne cum quidem putes arcendum esse, qui Satanae traditus esset. Sane ego in Thesibus nullam rem aliam damnati nominatim, vt ex probatione mea patet. Perperam ergo Papistæ ab auditione verbi ac templis depellunt excommunicatos, quod ego volebam.
units.tr: Now I come to your answers to those four arguments by which you think I wished to refute the greater excommunication of the Papists. Yet I should first like to point out that I did not accuse them of making degrees, which you also do. That there are not several kinds is clear from my Theses. For if excommunication is the prohibition of something on account of which the person to whom it is denied is no longer considered a member of the external Church, then the mere denial of the sacraments can alone be called excommunication, since whatever else men can deny us is accidental to it and does not pertain to its substance. Dr Luther also says, in the article prepared for the Council of Mantua, that we hold the greater excommunication, as the Pope names it, only as a civil penalty. If my memory is not failing, he repeated the same in his admonition to the preachers at Augsburg, gathered at the Diet in the year 1530. Furthermore, what is blamed is not that they say one is more grievous than the other, but that they defined it as the greater exclusion from the temples and from every lawful act. I marvel greatly why you chose to attack my opinion, since you approve the same thing as I do. For you write that you judge differently about the mere hearing of the word, from which you think not even one delivered to Satan should be barred. Indeed, in my Theses I named no other thing as condemned, as is clear from my argument. Therefore the Papists wrongly drive the excommunicated away from the hearing of the word and from the churches, which is what I was contending against.

units.la: 1. Sed age, postquam sic pruris contradicendi studio, vtrum am-ipsiusmet sententiam euertere non dubites, quod tuarum rationum pondus sit expendamus. Argumentum meum hoc est. Ab auditione verbi Deiseu concionibus publicis, lectione eiusdem ac precib', nullus arcendus est, qui interesse cupiat, vt ex 1. Cor. 14. cap. manifeste probatur. Peccant igitur Papistæ, cum maiorem excommunicationem horum prohibitione definiunt. Respondes, profanos admissos fuisse: at vel ἀποσυναγώγους factos à Iudæis, vel Satanæ traditos à Christianis, ad eos conuentus, qui communis fidei professionis causa instituti erant, admissos fuisse negas absque respispicentiæ testimonio.
units.tr: 1. But come, since you are so eager to contradict, let us weigh how much weight your arguments carry, and whether you hesitate to overturn your own opinion. My argument is this. No one who desires to attend should be barred from the hearing of God's word, that is, from public sermons, from its reading, and from prayers, as is clearly proved from 1 Cor. 14. Therefore the Papists sin when they define the greater excommunication by the prohibition of these things. You reply that the profane were admitted, but you deny that those who had been put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυναγώγους] by the Jews, or delivered to Satan by Christians, were admitted to those assemblies that were instituted for the sake of the common profession of faith, without a sign of repentance.

units.la: Simili vbique fœlicitate disputas, hoc est, fortiter affirmas, at timidè probas: Nego tibi è Synagogis eiectos ad templum & sacrificia ritusque alios à Deo per Mosen institutos non fuisse admissos. Scriptura contrarium planissimè tradit in exemplo Matthæi, & Publicani apud Lucam cap. 18. necnon in historia Adulteræ apud Iohan. 8. denique in Christi Apostolorumque suorum, inprimis autem Pauli historia. Vndè ergo tu opinionem tuam probabis? An idem fuerunt Synagoga & Templum? At ipse tu hic dicis profanos in Synagogam admissos vt ex aliquot Lucæ testimonijs coniicias: quum in Templum ingredi profanos nefas esset. Quomodo ergo si idem non fuerunt, eiectos ex Synagoga etiam eiectos ex Templo fuisse affirmas? Quomodo etiam profani homines, qui temet-ipso affirmante in Synagogas intromittebantur, non etiam in Templum ingredi sinebantur, si eadem erat huius & illarum ratio? Imò quomodo probabis tu, ex vna Synagoga eiectos, ex alijs (Nam plures erant Synagogæ non tantum in diuersis vrbibus, sed nonnunquam in vna eademq; vrbe) etiam fuisse exclusas? Ex scriptura oppositi colligimus, quod tum probabimus, cum quid ex Synagoga expellere significet, explicabimus. An à Christianis post Apostolos aliqui traditi sint Satanæ, nostra non interest quærere: qui hoc solum inquirimus, quid scripturæ mandent aut vetent. Si facere tentarunt, absq; scripturis tentârunt. Nullí enim in omnib' sanctis scripturis locus reperitur, qui hoc præcipiat. Fuit enim Apostolis extra ordinem concessa traditáque à Deo ista potestas. Proinde quæ de moribus Ecclesiæ veteris profers, ad nos non pertinent, qui scripturæ duntaxat testimonia postulauimus.
units.tr: You argue with the same success everywhere: that is, you affirm boldly but prove timidly. I deny to you that those who had been expelled from the synagogues were not admitted to the Temple, to sacrifices, and to the other rites instituted by God through Moses. Scripture teaches the contrary most plainly, in the example of Matthew and the tax collector in Luke 18, in the story of the adulteress in John 8, and finally in the history of Christ and his Apostles, and especially of Paul. How, then, will you prove your opinion? Were the synagogue and the Temple the same thing? But you yourself say here that the profane were admitted to the synagogue, as you gather from several testimonies of Luke, whereas it was unlawful for the profane to enter the Temple. How then, if they were not the same, do you affirm that those cast out of the synagogue were also cast out of the Temple? And how could profane men, who by your own assertion were admitted into the synagogues, not be allowed to enter the Temple, if the reason for this and for those was the same? Indeed, how will you prove that those expelled from one synagogue were also excluded from others (for there were many synagogues, not only in different cities, but sometimes in one and the same city)? From Scripture we gather the opposite, and we shall prove it when we explain what it means to expel someone from the synagogue. Whether some were delivered to Satan by Christians after the Apostles is no concern of ours, since we seek only what Scripture commands or forbids. If they attempted this, they attempted it without Scripture, for no passage in all the holy Scriptures is found that commands it. For this power was granted and given by God to the Apostles beyond the ordinary course. Therefore what you bring forward about the customs of the ancient Church does not concern us, since we have asked only for the testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: Causas cum adducis, cur profani potius, quàm in vita lapsi admitterentur, actum agis. Cum enim res ipsa non exstiterit, frustrà causas eiusdem recensés. In quare illud etiam notabis, te de illis loqui, qui pabulum, id est, verbum (& Sacramenta) aspernentur, cum passim nos de appetentibus loqui videas. Quare iterum extra terminos procurris. Quid opus est vetare, quod iam ante auersatur aliquis? Persuadendus magis est talis, vt appetere incipiat. Sic neque distinctionem hanc potuit cogitasse Apostolus, quàdo Christianos iubet familiaritatem fratrum vitiosorum fugere, commercium cum profanis concedit. Quibus tu argumentis ostendes, μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι, & μὴ συνηδεῖν cum aliquo in eum finem, vt pudefactus resipiscat, idem significare, atque lapsum à verbi dei auditione, omniq; actu legitimo, (in quorum numero illos etiam complector, qui ad communem fidei ἐξομολόγησιν pertinebant) prohibere? Cum rogas quinam communes cum Ecclesia preces habeant, qui vita se parum dignos Christianis gesserint? ego vicissim rogo, quinâ Deus permitti voluerit Publicano in Templum ingredi Luc. 18? An non melior descendit Pharisæo? Qui tu scis, imò qui audes cogitare, non habere eum pium animum tunc, quando cum cæteris cupit Deum orare? Quocirca multò magis interrogandus videris, qui prohibere tu alicui audeas Deû inuocare, ei gratias agere pro suis beneficijs, peccatorû culpâ deprecari, & pænitentiâ declarare? Omnia hæc præstat Ecclesia, qui tametsi deliquerit ac grauè scelus admiserit, ex verbo Dei cupit instrui, & vnâ cum alijs vult Deum comprecaricui cum ipse etiam putes verbi auditione non esse interdicendum, frustra ab aliis conuentibus distinguis. Nos enim in Ecclesijs nostris alios nullos habemus: neq; iubentur in scripturis ij, de quibus nos loquimur, à precationibus statarum horarum arceri, vt exemplū Publicani docet. Quamobrem nuda verba fundis, praeterea nihil facis.
units.tr: You bring up reasons why the profane rather than the lapsed were admitted, but that is beside the point. Since the thing itself does not exist, you are vainly listing its causes. Note also that you speak of those who spurn the food, that is, the word and the sacraments, whereas everywhere we see you speaking of those who desire them. So again you run outside the bounds. What need is there to forbid what someone already shrinks from? Such a person should rather be persuaded to begin to desire. Nor could the Apostle have had this distinction in mind when he bids Christians flee the familiarity of wicked brothers yet permits commerce with the profane. By what arguments will you show that μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι and μὴ συνηδεῖν [do not mingle with, do not share in], when done with the aim that the shamed may repent, mean the same as excluding the lapsed from hearing the word of God and from every lawful act (and among these I include those who belonged to the common confession of faith [ἐξομολόγησιν])? When you ask what common prayers those who have behaved unworthily of Christians can have with the Church, I in turn ask: by whom did God wish the publican to be allowed to enter the temple (Luke 18)? Did he not go down more justified than the Pharisee? How do you know, or rather how do you dare to think, that he did not have a pious heart then, when he wished to pray to God along with the others? Therefore you should be asked much more sharply: who are you to forbid anyone to call upon God, to give thanks to him for his benefits, to plead for pardon for his sins, and to declare his repentance? The Church does all these things. Although it has sinned and committed a grievous crime, it desires to be instructed from the word of God and wishes to pray to God together with the others. Since you yourself think the hearing of the word should not be forbidden, you vainly distinguish it from other gatherings. For in our churches we have no others. Nor are those of whom we speak commanded in the Scriptures to be kept from prayers at the stated hours, as the example of the publican teaches. Wherefore you pour out bare words and accomplish nothing else.

units.la: Illud supra modum miror, quod prohibitionē vnius eiusdemq; fidei confessionē publicam probare audes. Itaque certum est omnino præconceptam opinionem defendere, vt illa etiam à te excommunicatis velis negare, quæ Deus ne à se quidem excommunicatis negat, aut negare alios iussit? Ecquid dicent homines, cum te hucusq; progressum intelliget, vt potius interdicere hominibus confessione fidei in publico velis, quàm de imperio illo vestro aliquid remittere? At idē veteres, inquies fortasse, fecerunt. Nos autem non quid hi fecerint, sed quid rectè fecerint, quaerimus. Si enim aliquid probandum fuerit, quia veteres fecisse constet, permulta alia vos iniusté accusauistis. Christus hominem in suo nomine Dæmonia eijcientem noluit à suis discipulis prohiberi, quantumuis suo se nollet comitatui adiungere: sed addit, illum pro se esse, quisquis nō aduersarius ipsius esset, Lucæ ac Marci 9. cap. Cur ergo tu Christum confiteri volentem vetabis id publicè cum cæteris facere, etiamsi fuerit lapsus? Vis dicā, quod sentio? si ex sacris literis hanc tuā sententiam rectam esse firmiter probes, impiam esse pronunciabo.
units.tr: What I marvel at beyond measure is that you dare to prove the prohibition of public confession of one and the same faith. Is it certain, then, that you are defending an opinion conceived beforehand, so that you would deny to the excommunicated what God does not deny even to the excommunicated, or has not ordered others to deny? What will men say when they learn that you have advanced so far that you would rather forbid men the public confession of faith than give up anything of that dominion of yours? But, you will perhaps say, the ancients did the same. We, however, ask not what they did but what they did rightly. For if something is to be approved merely because it is established that the ancients did it, you have unjustly accused many other things. Christ would not have the man who cast out demons in his name hindered by his disciples, even though he did not wish to join their company; but he adds that whoever is not against them is for them (Luke and Mark, chapter 9). Why then will you forbid the lapsed man who confesses Christ to do this publicly with the others? Shall I say what I think? If you firmly prove from the sacred letters that your opinion is right, I shall pronounce it impious.

units.la: Quæ sequuntur argumenta tria, non adduxi ego, vt Papistas docerem excommunicationē malè definire prohibitionem templorum & actus cuiusuis liciti æque Deo imperati: sed notaui ea mihi, vt supra dixi, memoriæ causa, quò, cum res postularet, ostenderem excommunicationem non esse abscissione salutis definiendā. Quomodò enim sequeretur: Papistæ concedunt à communione mentis & spiritus neminē arceri posse, sed censura Ecclesiastica notatos ab externa solùm societate Ecclesiæ prohiberi: ergo non rectè prohibuerunt templum. An non interdictio templi res externa quoq; est, & particula quædam externæ societatis? Item cùm dico
units.tr: I did not adduce the three arguments that follow to teach the Papists that excommunication is wrongly defined as the prohibition of temples and of any lawful act equally commanded by God. As I said above, I noted them for the sake of memory, so that, when the matter required it, I might show that excommunication is not to be defined as the cutting off of salvation. For how would it follow that: the Papists concede that no one can be kept from communion of mind and spirit, but that those marked by ecclesiastical censure are kept only from the external fellowship of the Church; therefore they did not rightly forbid the temple? Is not the interdiction of the temple also an external thing, and a certain part of external fellowship? Likewise, when I say

units.la: Doctores eorū non plus fuisse ausos tribuere clauib', quàm quòd sint potestas expellendi ex societate externa Ecclesiæ, quomodo potuisset ex eo concludere, perperā aliquos ab aditu templorū prohibitos? Item cum sic ratiocinatus sum: si tradi Satanæ esset eijci ex Ecclesia, extra quam nulla est salus, (extra visibilem salutē esse quis negeat?) non dixisset Apostolus de Corinthio illo, se ita eum tradere voluisse, vt spiritus esset saluus, cum sic inquā collegi, quomodo potuisse concludere, ergo Papistæ malè definiunt excōmunicatione maiorem templorum interdictione? Tuum fortasse fuerit sic argumetari, non meū. Vides igitur quantum vbique à scopo aberres, quámque imprudenter disputes?
units.tr: Their teachers did not dare to attribute to the keys more than that they are the power of expelling from the external fellowship of the Church. How could you conclude from this that some were wrongly barred from entering the temples? Likewise, when I reasoned thus: if to be handed over to Satan were to be cast out of the Church, outside which there is no salvation (for who would deny that there is no salvation outside visible salvation?), the Apostle would not have said of that Corinthian that he wished to hand him over so that his spirit might be saved. When I, I say, reasoned in this way, how could you have concluded: therefore the Papists wrongly define excommunication as the greater interdiction of temples? Perhaps it would be yours to argue like that, not mine. Do you see, then, how far you stray from the goal everywhere, and how carelessly you dispute?

units.la: Quanquam verò huc non pertinent, ne tamen querare nos aliquid intactū reliquisse, age quid dicas hic quoq; videamus. Ad primum sic respondes. Cum Ecclesiæ iudiciū nihil sit aliud quàm promulgatio sententiæ in cœlis decretæ, efficitur alienos omninò à regno cœlesti decerni, qui ritè in terris ex communione Ecclesiæ eijciuntur. De hoc argumēto quia copiosè iam suprà dixim', hoc tantùm dicā, in præsentia, tibi præter quatuor illas propositiones, quarū probatione supra, cum ad syllogismū tuum de Ebrioso respondērem, requirebamus, hanc quintam insuper demonstrandam esse scripturis, si aliquid dixisse velis, nempe rectè dici Ecclesiam illis abscindere salutē excōmunicando, qui ab æterno sunt electi à Deo. His omnib' superaddere te oportebit, constare vestris Presbyteris, quinā tandem sint electi: Nisi enim hoc sciatis, falsa erit vestra promulgatio seu declaratio: sicut in Manasse Rege falsa fuisset.
units.tr: Although these matters do not pertain here, lest you complain that we have left anything untouched, come, let us see what you say here too. To the first point you respond thus: since the judgment of the Church is nothing other than the publication of a sentence decreed in heaven, it follows that those who are rightly cast out of the communion of the Church on earth are decreed to be wholly aliens from the heavenly kingdom. I have already spoken at length above on this argument, so for now I will say only this: besides those four propositions, the proof of which we demanded above when I was answering your syllogism about the drunkard, you must also demonstrate from Scripture this fifth proposition, if you wish to have said anything, namely that it is rightly said that the Church cuts off salvation by excommunicating those who have been elected by God from eternity. To all these you will have to add the demonstration that your presbyters know who the elect truly are. For unless you know this, your publication or declaration will be false, just as it would have been false in the case of King Manasseh.

units.la: Ad secundū hæc ferè dicis. Vt externum iudiciū accedens ad interius iudiciū conscientiæ auget vulnus non prorsus exulceratio, ita ad obligationē vulneris interni si accedat totius Ecclesiæ acclamatio, magis recreatur conscientia tristitiæ onere fatiscens. At quid hæc, oro te, ad rē faciunt? An ideo malè Papistas notaui? An ideo salutis negatione excōmunicatio definienda? Quicquid faciat illa Ecclesiæ acclamatio, non tamen est aliquid pro præcepto Dei obtrudendū Ecclesiæ, quod non præcepit. Ad vltimum negas consequi, quod dico. Posse enim quempiâ ex cœtu ciuiũ expelli ciuitatisfiq; iure re ipsa ad tempus priuari, qui tamé postea, cum veniam petit, restituatur. Simile hoc tuũ non est spiritussanđi. Magistratus ius hoc habens potest aliquem ciuitate priuare vel omninò vel ad tempus. Et qui sic priuatur, pro eo tempore revera priuatus est. Doce tu Presbyterium hanc habere potestatem: & quib' ipsum negauit salutē, eos ideo salute revera excidisse, quia ipsum eam negauerit. Hoc cum perfeceris, de dissimili ista tua similitudine amplius agemus.
units.tr: To the second point you say roughly these things: just as an external judgment added to the inner judgment of conscience increases the wound, though it does not altogether make it an ulcer, so if the acclamation of the whole Church is added to the obligation of the inner wound, the conscience, fainting under the burden of sorrow, is more refreshed. But what, I ask you, does this have to do with the matter? Did I therefore mark the Papists wrongly? Is excommunication therefore to be defined by the denial of salvation? Whatever that acclamation of the Church does, nothing should be thrust upon the Church as a precept of God which God has not commanded. Finally, you deny that what I say follows. For someone may be expelled from the assembly of citizens and really deprived of the right of citizenship for a time, yet be restored afterwards when he seeks pardon. Your comparison is not like the Holy Spirit's. A magistrate who has this right can deprive someone of citizenship either entirely or for a time, and one who is so deprived is really deprived for that time. Teach, then, that the presbytery has this power, and that those to whom it denied salvation have really fallen from salvation because it denied it. When you have done this, we shall deal further with your dissimilar similitude.

units.la: Hucusque definitionem excommunicationis nostrā, & quę in doctrina Pontificiorũ de hac re accusauimus, ita defendimus, vt etiā ineruditi perspicere possint, euanidas, ridiculas, & sibi non constantes esse tuas reprehensiones. Tuam è contrā descriptionem & Pontificiorũ propugnatione non inanem duntaxat, sed etiam plurimis iisdemq; fœdis erroribus referta esse apertissimè demonstraui. Superest igitur, vt, quæ contra secundam Thesium partem, in qua probamus excommunicationem neq; verbo neq; exemplo scripturarum niti, excogitastis, deinceps examinemus. Sequar autem ordinem quē vobis in oppugnandis nostris seruare placuit, quo lector facilius nostra cum nostris comparare conferreq; possit.
units.tr: Thus far we have defended our definition of excommunication, and what we have accused in the Papists' doctrine on this matter, so well that even the unlearned can see that your reprehensions are fading, ridiculous, and inconsistent with themselves. On the other hand, I have clearly demonstrated that your description and defence of the Papists is not merely empty but also stuffed with very many and the same foul errors. It remains, therefore, that we examine what you have devised against the second part of our Theses, in which we prove that excommunication rests neither on the word nor on the example of Scripture. I shall follow the order you have chosen to observe in attacking our points, so that the reader may more easily compare and set our arguments beside yours.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Defensio argumentorum, quæ contra Excommunicationem at- tuli ex Testamento veteri.
units.tr: A defence of the arguments which I brought against excommunication from the Old Testament.

units.la: Rimum argumentum nostrum inter ea, quæ ex Testamento veteri prompsimus, & pro confutāda excōmunicatione desumpsimus, tale est. Scriptura illos, de quibus nos loquimur, nec à Sacrificijs arcet, nec à Sacramentis alijs vllis: imò sub pœna capitis mandat, vt vniuersi mares circumcisi, Iudæi & peregrini, quicunq; immunditia legis non sunt inquinati, nec peregrè absunt, ter quotannis coràm Deo Hierosolymis compareant, & Sacramenta paschatis, Hebdomadarū, & Tabernaculorū cōcelebrent. Quocirca non potuerunt runt Presbyteri aut Sacerdotes præter immundos lege quæquam arcere. Audiamus bellam refutationem tuam. Aut non intelligimus, inquis, argumentum, aut vix est dignum responsione: quoniam extremum extremo iungit præterito medio. Vocat Deus quosuis peccatores ad regnum cœlorum & clamat nihilominus Apostolus sceleratos non habere partem in regno Dei. Vocat ergo ad resipiscentiam: quod & ista nostra disciplina facimus. Ac publicæ pœnitentiæ testimonium, quod requirimus, verbo Dei continetur. Qui enim potuit quispiam offerre pro peccato oblationem, qui sese peccasse palam non fateretur? Hactenus tu. An tu in medio huius argumenti inveniendo laboras? Putavi rem mihi esse cum viro qui hac in re mihi nō facessteret negotium. Medium hoc est. In sacris literis non tantum non invenire aliquos à Sacramentis propter solam vitæ turpitudinē abactos esse, sed contrarium potius probari. Hoc medio monstravi excommunicationē non esse iuris diuini, si vetus testamentū consulam*. Est ergo hoc argumentū nostrū. Quod in sacris literis non reperitur præceptū, cuiusq; contrarium inuenitur mandatū, id non est mandatum Dei. At excōmunicatio sic habet. Ergo excōmunicatio est cōmentum humanū. Minorē probaui ex lib. Exod.12.23.&43. Num.9. Deut. 16. quibus in locis præcipitur omnibus maribus circumcisis sub pœna excidij, vt coram Domino ter quotannis comparerent: nec excipit quenquam ex prædictis, præter immundos lege, & à patria absentes. Sic igitur habet Lex. Quisquis iuxta legē est mundus, nec ita proculabest, quin ad constitutum tempus adesse Hierosolymis possit, is, si præfinito die vnà cum alijs non concelebret Pascha coram Domino, exterminabitur. Si autem immundus sit eo die, aut peregrē absit, celebrent illi tales idem Pascha eodem die sequentis mensis.
units.tr: The first argument that I drew from the Old Testament, and used to refute excommunication, runs as follows. Scripture keeps those of whom we speak away neither from the sacrifices nor from any other sacraments. On the contrary, under penalty of death it commands that all circumcised males, Jews and strangers alike, who are not defiled by the uncleanness of the law and are not far away from home, appear three times a year before God at Jerusalem and jointly celebrate the sacraments of the Passover, the Weeks and the Tabernacles. Therefore the elders or priests could keep away no one except those who were unclean by the law. Let us hear your fine refutation. "Either I do not understand the argument," you say, "or it hardly deserves an answer, since it joins the extreme to the extreme and skips the middle. God calls all sinners to the kingdom of heaven, and yet the Apostle declares that the wicked have no part in the kingdom of God. So God calls them to repentance, and our discipline does the same. The testimony of public repentance, which we require, is contained in the Word of God. For how could anyone offer a sacrifice for sin who did not openly confess that he had sinned?" So far you. Or are you labouring to find the middle term of this argument? I thought I had to do with a man who would not make trouble for me on this point. The middle term is this: in the sacred writings we find not only that no one was cast out from the sacraments for the mere baseness of his life, but rather that the contrary is shown. By this middle term I have shown that excommunication is not of divine right, if we consult the Old Testament. So our argument is this: what is not found as a precept in the sacred writings, and whose contrary is found as a command, is not a command of God. But excommunication stands thus. Therefore excommunication is a human invention. I proved the minor premise from Exodus 12.23 and 43, Numbers 9, and Deuteronomy 16. In these places it is ordained that all circumcised males, under penalty of being cut off, should appear before the Lord three times a year, and it excepts none of those mentioned except the unclean by the law and those absent from home. The law therefore stands thus: whoever is clean according to the law, and is not so far away that he cannot be present at Jerusalem at the appointed time, if on the fixed day he does not celebrate the Passover before the Lord together with the others, shall be cut off. But if he is unclean on that day, or is away from home, such persons shall keep the same Passover on the same day of the following month.

units.la: Hanc Dei constitutionem, quæ ad externum cultū spectat, non debuisti cōparare cum interna vocatione qua Deus nos ad spirituale regnum vocat. Akterutrū fatearis oportet, te vel argumetū non intellexisse, quod in responsione aliquo modo significas, vel dissimulauisse. Etenim est impossibile, vt homo literatus & in sacris literis vel mediocriter versatus hic tergiuersetur. Audiamus ergo praeclaram tuam ratiocinationem. De vocat omnes peccatores ad regnum coeleste: quod tamen permulti non possidebunt, teste scriptura, Ergo Moses in praedictis locis moribus immundos vult ab eu Paschatis arceri. Quibus medijs & machinis coniunges tu ista extrema? Hoc vero est praecipitem ruere, non progredi per medium. Scriptura docet nos, Deum vocare omnes homines ad possessionem regni coelestis, sed per fidem efficacem in Christum. Eadem dicit, permultos non possessuros hoc regnum, quia ad Deum vocantem eo modo, quo vocat, volunt accedere. Hic nulla pugna est, fateor. Proba ergo nunc apud Mosen similiter inueniri duo haec mandata: nempe, Mundi secundum legem omnes (nisi procul à patria absint) pascha concelebrent: &, Non omnes iuxta legem mundi Pascha celebrent, sed illi tantum, qui moribus quoque mundi sunt. Primum extat: secundum si exstare ostenderis, ad argumentum te nostrum aliquid dixisse minimè inficiabimur. Non vides te Mosi, cum, quod ipse nusquam dixit, vis eum dixisse, apertam contradictionem, quae nulla effugi interpretatione possit, affingere?
units.tr: This constitution of God, which concerns external worship, you ought not to have compared with the inward calling by which God calls us to the spiritual kingdom. You must admit one of two things: either you have not understood the argument, though in your reply you somehow indicate that you have, or you have dissembled. For it is impossible that a man who is learned and moderately versed in the sacred writings should evade the point in this way. Let us hear, then, your splendid reasoning. "God calls all sinners to the heavenly kingdom, which nevertheless very many will not possess, as Scripture witnesses. Therefore Moses in the places cited wants the morally unclean kept from the Passover." By what means and what machinery will you join these extremes? This is indeed rushing headlong, not proceeding by the middle way. Scripture teaches us that God calls all men to possess the heavenly kingdom, but through an effective faith in Christ. The same Scripture says that very many will not possess this kingdom, because they are unwilling to come to God when he calls in the way he calls. Here there is no dispute, I grant. Now prove that these two commands are likewise found in Moses: namely, that all who are clean according to the law (unless they are far from home) celebrate the Passover; and that not all who are clean according to the law celebrate the Passover, but only those who are also clean in their conduct. The first stands. If you show the second, we will by no means deny that you have said something to our argument. Do you not see that you are attributing to Moses a plain contradiction, which no interpretation could escape, because you wish him to have said what he nowhere said?

units.la: Ergo alterutrum fateraris oportet, aut Mosen contradictoria sensisse, aut te nihil ad argumentum respondere. Etenim iubet omnes mares Pascha celebrare, illis solis exceptis, qui vel secundum legem immundi essent, vel in itinere procul à patria abessent. Moses dicit omnes: & solummodo immundos & absentes excipit, alios nullos (Aegrotantium, & qui adesse alias non potuerunt, mentionem facere nihil opus fuit.) Tu vero etiam indecorè viuentes exceptos dicis. An hoc non est in Mosis sententia contradictionem ponere? Negari porro non potest, quin multi inter Iudaeos omni tempore fuerint moribus impuri, qui nihilominus iuxta legis consuetudinem essent mundi: hoc est, qui earum rerum nihil aut fecissent, aut passi fuissent, propter quas immundi possent censeri. At impium est dicere, Deum per Mosen contradictoria simul praecepisse. Verum igitur illud est,te nihil attulisse,ac argumeti vim non satis percepisse. Si excipias,sub Mose nullos fuisse sceleratos,nihil effeceris. Primū enim non probabis ita rē habere. Quī enim in tanta hominū multitudine nulli fuisset sceleratī?(Si dubitas, inspice Psal.95.& ca.3.Epist.ad Hebraeos.) Deinde sub Iosua,Iudicibus,Regibus,qui poteris ostendere verū esse? At cōstat his omnib° tēporib°nullū fuisse à Sacramētis repulsū,qui iuxta legē mundus esset,qualibuscunq; moribus esset praeditus.
units.tr: So you must admit one of two things: either Moses held contradictory views, or you are making no answer to the argument. For he commands all males to celebrate the Passover, excepting only those who were unclean by the law or were on a journey far from home. Moses says "all", and excepts only the unclean and the absent, and no others. (There was no need to mention the sick, or those who could not otherwise be present.) But you say that those who live unbecomingly are excepted as well. Is this not to set a contradiction in the mind of Moses? Nor can it be denied that among the Jews at all times there were many morally impure who were nevertheless clean according to the custom of the law: that is, who had not done or suffered those things for which a person could be counted unclean. But it is impious to say that God through Moses commanded contradictory things at once. The truth, then, is this: you have brought nothing, and have not sufficiently grasped the force of the argument. If you say that under Moses there were no wicked men, you will have achieved nothing. For first you will not prove that this is so. How could there have been no wicked men in so great a multitude? (If you doubt it, look at Psalm 95 and the third chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews.) Then under Joshua, the Judges and the Kings, how will you be able to show that it is true? Yet it is established that in all these times no one who was clean according to the law was repelled from the sacraments, whatever his manner of life.

units.la: At resipiscentiam requirebat Lex,ais. Non inficior: nec inficiatus vnquam fui. Hoc solum negaui semper, & constanter adhuc nego, oportuisse eum, qui peccauisset, certo ad hanc rem ordinato Presbyterio satisfacere. Vnusquisque suo arbitrio,non alieno,& propria conscientia,non Sacerdotū,iudicabatur mundus & immundus: demptis Leprosis. At offerebat,inquis, oblatione pro peccatis,& hoc ipso se peccasse fatebantur. Respondeo primū, in peccatoris fuisse positum voluntate, (nullo eum ante oblatione à templo & Sacrificijs repellente) expiare suum peccatū quando vellet: neque cogebatur hac in re,sicut dixi Presbyterorū exspectare iudicium. Excipis hic, Dominū, dum ad sui cultum quosuis inuitet, non abrogare leges alibi de Presbyterorum munere sancitas. At ego velim ex te audire, quonam in loco istae de munere Presbyterorum leges decretae positaeque fuerint? Deinde qui sic peccauerat,non erat Excommunicatus,cum posset ire sacrificatum pro peccato suo cum libuisset, nemine eum ad tempus aliquod repellente. Quod si etiā expiare peccatū statim nollet,non ob id iubebatur emanere. Tertiò non valebat hoc in scelerib° quę Lex nominatim plectebat. Nulla enim Lex iubet Sacrificium certum offerri pro expiatione homicidij voluntarij,adulterij,aliorūmq; talium scelerum: sed gladio Magistratus coerceri haec facinora iubētur.
units.tr: But the Law required repentance, you say. I do not deny it, nor have I ever denied it. This alone I have always, and constantly still do, deny: that the one who had sinned was bound to make satisfaction to a Presbytery specially appointed for this purpose. Each man was judged clean or unclean by his own judgment, not another's, and by his own conscience, not by the priests', except for lepers. But, you say, he offered a sacrifice for sins, and by that very act confessed that he had sinned. I answer, first, that it lay in the sinner's own will (no one repelling him from the temple and the sacrifices beforehand) to expiate his sin whenever he wished; nor was he compelled in this matter, as I have said, to await the judgment of the elders. Here you object that the Lord, when he invites anyone to his worship, does not abrogate laws elsewhere enacted concerning the office of the elders. But I should like to hear from you where those laws about the office of the elders were decreed and laid down. Next, the man who had sinned in this way was not excommunicated, since he could go to sacrifice for his sin whenever he liked, with no one repelling him for any period. And if he was not willing to expiate the sin at once, he was not for that reason ordered to be cut off. Thirdly, this did not hold for those crimes which the Law punished by name. For no law commands a particular sacrifice to be offered for the expiation of voluntary homicide, adultery, and other such crimes; rather, these deeds are ordered to be restrained by the sword of the magistrate.

units.la: Quarto,non minus profitetur se peccatorem,imò multò magis,qui ad coenam Domini apud nos accedit,si modo recte sit institutus, & praescriptum Ecclesiae ordine obseruet, quàm qui Sacrificium pro peccato aliquo offerebat. An tu Coenam Domini professionem publicā esse oblitus es,qua, qui ad eam adit, testatur se peccatorem esse, nec aliam rationem habere, qua à peccatis suis liberari valeat, quàm sacrificium Christi in cruce peractum? An tibi excidit, oblationè pro peccato figurauisse oblationē Christi in cruce factam? Cur, si horum meministi, peccatorem ad Cœnam ire volentē, hoc est, oblationē pro peccatis suis offerre cupientē, siue testificari volentē se peccauisse, & morte Christi peccata sua deleta credere, contra expressum Dei mandatum impedis?
units.tr: Fourthly, he who comes to the Lord's Supper among us professes himself no less a sinner, indeed much more so, if only he has been rightly instructed and observes the order prescribed by the Church, than the one who offered a sacrifice for some sin. Have you forgotten that the Lord's Supper is a public profession, by which whoever approaches it testifies that he is a sinner and has no other means of being freed from his sins than the sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross? Or has it escaped you that the offering for sin foreshadowed the offering of Christ made on the cross? If you remember these things, why do you, against the express command of God, hinder the sinner who wishes to come to the Supper, that is, who desires to offer for his sins, or wishes to testify that he has sinned and believes his sins to have been blotted out by the death of Christ?

units.la: Dixi secundò sacerdotes ne potuisse quidē arcere malos ab esu Paschatis, cum in domibus patres familias cum suis ederēt. Respondes primum, Solennis omnium sanctificatio indicebatur. Deinde immundi deprehensi nominatim à Paschare prohibebantur: vt ex Esdrae. 6. & 2. Paralip. 23. cap. liquet. Similis tui vbique es, id est, nihil probas, tametsi multa dicas. Quis dubitauit aut negauit, quin se omnes parārent ad edendū Paschā? certè Pharisaei ob eam rē Christū occidere, & in Praetorium introire noluerunt. Quid ergò generalis & solennis purificationis indictio ad rem nostram facit? Quis probet hac ratiocinatione? Iubebātur ante Pascha omnes se purificare, quò Pascha edere possent: Ergo Presbyteris quibusdā ad hoc electis potestatē excludendi habētibus, satisfacere iubebantur. De purificatione & immunditia Legis, nō de turpitudine morū ista sunt accipienda. Etenim scelera longè grauiùs, quā interdictione Festorū, à quib' forte mali se optauisset excludi, plectebantur. Sic & loca scripturae à te adducta, velis, nolis, cogeris interpretari. Proinde inania verba fundis: ad rē nihil dicis. In Ecclesijs nostris simile quiddā fit, dū se pridiē quā cœna celebratur, Ministro indicāt accessuri, & publicè respōdēt ad tria illa capita, quae suo loco recitabimus. Simile est, quod immūdos dicis mēsē differre coactos, vt se purgaret. Quippe pleriq; ad vesperā erat purificati, plurimi die septima. Deus diem mēsis, quo exierant ex Ægypto, voluit memorabilē esse: nec alio die voluit huius rei memoriam celebrari. Quare cū propter immunditiam aliqui non possint hoc praestare die illo mensis primi, ne eos simpliciter arcere ab hoc Sacramēto videretur, iußit vt secundi mensis eodem die celebrarent. Debebat hoc exemplum vos monere, vt nulli cupienti temerè negaretis Coenae communionem: cum Deus extra ordinem maluerit Pascha illos edere, qui die praefinito non potuissent, quàm vt toto anno careret.
units.tr: I said secondly that the priests could not even have kept evil people from eating the Passover, since the heads of families ate it with their households at home. You reply, first, that a general sanctification was proclaimed for all. Second, that the unclean who were caught were expressly forbidden to take part in the Passover, as is clear from Ezra 6 and 2 Chronicles 23. You are like yourself everywhere: you prove nothing, though you say a great deal. Who has doubted or denied that everyone prepared to eat the Passover? Certainly it was for that reason that the Pharisees refused to enter the Praetorium and wished to put Christ to death. What, then, does a general and solemn call to purification have to do with our question? Who would prove a point by this reasoning? Everyone was ordered to purify himself before the Passover so that he could eat it; therefore certain chosen elders, who held the power of exclusion, were to be satisfied. Those passages must be understood of ritual purity and uncleanness under the Law, not of moral corruption. For wicked men were punished far more severely than by exclusion from the feasts, by which they might perhaps have wished to be shut out. So also the passages of Scripture you cite, whether you like it or not, you are forced to interpret in this way. Therefore you pour out empty words and say nothing to the point. In our churches something similar happens: on the day before the Lord's Supper is celebrated, those who intend to come notify the minister and publicly answer to those three heads which we shall recite in their place. Similar is what you say, that the unclean were compelled to postpone the meal until they had purified themselves. Indeed, most were purified by evening, and very many on the seventh day. God willed that the day of the month on which they had come out of Egypt should be memorable, and he willed that the memory of this event be celebrated on no other day. Hence, since some could not do this on that day of the first month because of uncleanness, lest they should seem to be simply barred from this sacrament, he ordered them to celebrate it on the same day of the second month. This example ought to warn you not to deny the communion of the Supper rashly to anyone who desires it, since God preferred that those who could not on the appointed day should eat the Passover outside the ordinary time, rather than that they should go without it for the whole year.

units.la: Tertium argumentum hoc est. Nec ante nec post Christum vlli vnquam legimus propter vitam inhonestam vel ab ipso Mose, vel à Sacerdotibus, Leuitis, Prophetis, Pharisaeis, Scribis, vel ab alijs vllis, interdictum Templo, Sacrificijs & Sacramentis à Deo institutis. Tu de solis Prophetis respondes dicens: nempe quia gubernacula rerum non tenebant: nec vllos habuerunt sibi magis infensos, quàm Sacerdotes & Seniores populi. Ego non de solis Prophetis locutus sum, sed praenominatis omnibus. Proinde hic etiam respondes, vt soles. Quanquam sufficere potuisset, si de Prophetis duntaxat hoc dixissem. Etenim si hac in re fuisset à Sacerdotibus peccatum, indicauissent aliquando, sicut alia ipsorum peccata accusarunt. At nihil vnquam tale reprehenderunt. Quod si tàm infensos habuerunt Sacerdotes & Seniores, mirum est, quod non aliquando conati sunt eos excommunicare: siquidem à Lege Mosis facultatem acceperant hoc faciendi. Quippe optimus hic fuisset praetextus, & valde plausibilis excusatio.
units.tr: The third argument is this. Neither before nor after Christ do we read that anyone at all was forbidden the Temple, the sacrifices, or the sacraments instituted by God on account of a dishonourable life, whether by Moses himself, or by the priests, Levites, prophets, Pharisees, scribes, or any others. You answer only concerning the prophets, saying: of course, because they did not hold the reins of government; and yet they had no more hostile enemies than the priests and the elders of the people. I did not speak only of the prophets, but of all those I named. Therefore here too you answer as you usually do. Yet it would have been enough, had I said this only of the prophets. For if the priests had sinned in this matter, they would at some point have pointed it out, just as they accused one another of other sins. But they never reproved anything of this kind. And if the priests and elders were so hostile, it is strange that they never tried to excommunicate them, since they had received from the Law of Moses the power to do so. Indeed, this would have been an excellent pretext and a very plausible excuse.

units.la: At dum populo & Sacerdotibus exprobrant, inquis, quod suis sceleribus templum polluerent, satis indicarunt, quid facturi fuerint, si administrationi praefuissent. Quaeso te an contra Mosis Legem aliquid facturos fuisse putas? At secissent, si propter solam vitae turpitudinem aliquos à Sacramentis repulissent. In scriptis eorum nusquam reperies propter hanc rem Sacerdotes aut alios reprehensos. Quomodo ergo facturos ipsos fuisse probabis, quod perperam ab alijs praetermisum nullo loco questi sunt. Quomodo mores praui polluerent Templum nomenque Dei, paulò post fusè explicabimus. Citas deinde 1. cap. Esaiæ & Psal. 51. At hi loci tuæ opinioni nulla in parte patrocinantur. Quis enim sic est rudis, qui argumentationem hanc probet? Deus aspernatur impiorum sacrificia: Ergò Prophetæ aut Sacerdotes habuerunt potestatem facinorosos amouendi à Sacramentis. Item Dauid lauari se postulat à caede: Ergo Sacerdotes facultatem arcendi à Sacramentis à Mose acceperunt. Item homicidij culpam, cuius author nesciretur, solenni ritu deprecari tenebantur, in quorum finibus cadauer inuentum suisset Deut.21. Ergò Seniores erant à Deo ordinati, qui certos quosdam Deo sacrificare volentes à sacrificando prohiberent. Item qui incōsideratè iurauit, venire debet ad templum cum oblatione pro peccato. Ergò qui sciens peierauit à quibusdam Senioribus arcebatur à Sacramentis dum ipsis satisfecisset. An hisce futilibus rationibus creditur um aliquē eruditum tibi persuasisti? Taceo quod falsum est, non fuisse in templum admissum, qui inconsideratè iurasset, sine oblatione pro peccato. Aliud est non admitti ad templum: & non remitti peccatum. Multa de poenitentia subinde dicis, de qua nulla inter nos est disputatio. Nunquam enim dubitauì an poenitentiam à nobis flagitet Deus. Hoc disputamus, an oporteat resipiscentiam Presbyteris probari ad hanc rem delectis?
units.tr: But, you say, when they reproached the people and the priests for polluting the Temple by their crimes, they sufficiently indicated what they would have done had they been in charge of the administration. I ask you, do you think they would have done anything contrary to the Law of Moses? Yet they would have done so if they had repelled some from the sacraments on account of the baseness of life alone. You will nowhere find in their writings that priests or others were rebuked for this. How, then, will you prove that they would have done it, when they never complained about it, though it was neglected by others? How wicked morals polluted the Temple and the name of God we shall explain at length a little later. Then you cite the first chapter of Isaiah and Psalm 51. But these passages do not support your opinion in any way. For who is so unlearned as to accept this argument? God rejects the sacrifices of the wicked; therefore the prophets or priests had the power to remove evildoers from the sacraments. Likewise David asks to be washed from bloodguilt; therefore the priests received from Moses the power of keeping people away from the sacraments. Likewise, the guilt of a homicide whose author was unknown had to be expiated by a solemn rite in the district where the corpse was found (Deut. 21); therefore the elders were ordained by God to prohibit certain persons from sacrificing who wished to sacrifice to God. Likewise, whoever swore rashly must come to the Temple with an offering for sin; therefore whoever swore knowingly and falsely was kept from the sacraments by certain elders until he had made satisfaction to them. Do you really think that any learned person can be persuaded by such trifling arguments? I say nothing of the fact that it is false that anyone who swore rashly was not admitted to the Temple without an offering for sin. It is one thing not to be admitted to the Temple, and another for sin not to be forgiven. You often say many things about repentance, a matter on which there is no dispute between us. For I have never doubted whether God requires repentance of us. What we dispute is whether it is fitting for elders chosen for this task to be satisfied of repentance.

units.la: Quartum hoc est, Pharisaei à Sacramentis neque indignè viuentes arcuerunt, neque Sadducaeos haereticos remouerunt. Si hoc, inquis, negemus, quomodo probaueris? Nisi mox adderes probabile esse, diceré te parum attentè scripturas legisse. Addis deinde, non mirum esse quod mutuò sese fouerint Hypocritae. At qui Apost.acta, & Iosephi historiam attentè legit, merito ridebit tuam responsionem. Quod ipse quoque vidisse videris, cum aliam adfers: nempe alteros non potuisse pellere alteros, quia non sint potestatis nomina, sed sectarum. Verum hoc est, sed tamen ijdem illi Christi tempore in potestate fuerunt & Sacerdotio fungebantur, vt ex sacris literis pariter & historia Iosephi clarissimè patet. Ergo ne hic quidē habes, quod dicas. Nec in sacris literis, nec in historia Iudaica inuenimus huius rei mentionem fieri, tametsi alteri alteros capitali odio prosequerētur. Deus bone, quam fuissent laetati, si sciuissent aliquid sibi tale per legem licere? Sed quid si Magistratus, (quaeris sub fine) non faciat officium in reprimendis sceleratis? Posset em & ego ex te quaerere, Quid si Presbyterii non faciat officium, aut Tyrannidem exerceret? Cogétne Magistratus? At excommunicabit eum. Sed ego respondebo tibi, etiamsi mihi tu non respondeas. Facient Ministri, quod fecerunt Prophetæ. Admonendus, hortandus, rogandus, increpandus, terrendus ex verbo Dei. Si ne tunc quidem fungatur suo munere, committenda res Deo erit. Impiè namque subditus ratiocinetur: Magistratus non fecit officium: Itaque ego pro ipso hac in parte accipiam imperium. Perinde hoc fit, ac si seruus argumentetur: Dominus male satisfacit familiae: Ergo me Dominum, illum autem seruum fieri oportet.
units.tr: The fourth argument is this: the Pharisees did not keep from the sacraments those who lived unworthily, nor did they remove the heretical Sadducees. If we deny this, you say, how will you prove it? Unless you were at once to add that it is probable you have read the Scriptures too carelessly. Then you add that it is no wonder that the hypocrites supported one another. But anyone who reads the Acts of the Apostles and the history of Josephus carefully will rightly laugh at your answer. You seem to have seen this yourself when you offer another: namely, that they could not drive out one another, because they were not names of offices but of sects. This is true, but nevertheless those same men were in power at the time of Christ and held the priesthood, as is clear both from the sacred writings and from the history of Josephus. So you have nothing to say even here. Neither in the sacred writings nor in Jewish history do we find any mention of this matter, although the sects pursued one another with deadly hatred. Good God, how glad they would have been, had they known that the Law allowed them anything of this kind! But what if the magistrate, as you ask at the end, does not perform his duty in punishing the wicked? For I too could ask you: what if the eldership does not perform its duty, or exercises tyranny? Will the magistrate compel them? But he will excommunicate him. I shall answer you, even though you do not answer me. The ministers will do what the prophets did: they must admonish, exhort, ask, rebuke, and terrify from the Word of God. If even then the magistrate does not fulfil his office, the matter must be committed to God. For a subject reasons impiously if he thinks: the magistrate has not done his duty, so in this respect I shall take authority for myself. It is just as if a servant were to argue: the master manages the household badly; therefore I must become the master and he the servant.

units.la: Quintum est. Totum Synedrium extremè oderat Christum & Apostolos. At tantum abest, ut à templi aditu eos prohibere conati fuerint, ut nec Matthæum Publicanū, nec Paulum, cui prae cæteris infensi inimicique erant, excludere aliquando tentárint. Ad hoc primò respondes. Imò disertissimè testatur Iohan. duobus locis conuenisse inter Iudaeos, ut qui Christum confiterentur, è Synagoga eijcerentur: nedum ut Christo ipsi parceretur. At è Synagoga eijci, erat Excommunicari: quod quam recte tu neges, suo loco dispiciamus. Secundò, mirabiliter conseruati à Deo fuerunt. Tertiò, duo fuerunt Publicanorum genera, vnum Gentilium, alterum Iudaeorum. Illos penitus aucrsabantur: horum congressum solo odio, nullo iure, fugiebant: cum Lex neque tributa neque tributorum exactores per sedamneti. De Synagoga postea dicendum erit: nunc tantum dicam te in sempiternum non esse probaturum Synagogam & templum, vel eiectionem ex illa & ex hoc eadem fuisse. Synagogae erant multæ, Templum vnum. In Synagogis non celebrabantur Sacramenta & Sacrificia, de quibus loquimur: at in Templo celebrabantur. In Synagogam etiam admittebantur profani, ut tu ais: in Templū nefas erat talē ingredi.
units.tr: The fifth argument is this. The whole Sanhedrin utterly hated Christ and the Apostles. Yet they were so far from trying to keep them away from the entrance to the Temple that they never even attempted to exclude Matthew the publican, or Paul, against whom they were especially hostile and inimical. To this you first reply: indeed John testifies most clearly in two places that the Jews had agreed that whoever confessed Christ should be cast out of the synagogue; much less was Christ himself spared. But to be cast out of the synagogue was to be excommunicated; how rightly you deny this we shall examine in its place. Second, they were wonderfully preserved by God. Third, there were two kinds of publicans, one of the Gentiles and the other of the Jews. They utterly abhorred the former, and avoided the company of the latter out of mere hatred, not by any right, since the Law permitted neither tributes nor tax-collectors. We shall speak of the synagogue later; for now I say only that you will never prove that the synagogue and the Temple, or expulsion from the one and from the other, were the same. There were many synagogues, but one Temple. The sacraments and sacrifices of which we are speaking were not celebrated in the synagogues, but they were celebrated in the Temple. Also, profane persons were admitted into the synagogue, as you say; but it was unlawful to enter the Temple in such a state.

units.la: Quod mirabiliter seruatos dicis Apostolos cum Christo, concedo: at non fuisse eos propterea tentaturos, si potentiam hanc tenuissent ex eo non consequitur. Saltem alicubi ex probauissent ipsis, quod contra Legem ingrederentur in Templum. Etenim minora obiiciunt, quod non lauarent manus: quod Christus cum peccatoribus ederet: quod sanasset in die Sabbathi aliquos. Item cum Paulo obiiciunt, cum Templum profanasse, quia Graecum introduxerit, non addunt hoc etiam, quia ipse secundum Legem ingredi non debuerit. In summa, chorda semper oberras eadem: id est multa falsa dicis, quorum nihil probare potes. Nihil fermè adhuc vidi te dignum, nisi quòd hîc fateris Publicanos circumcisos non fuisse à Templo & Sacrificijs exclusos: quod plerique hactenus fortiter negarunt. An etiam in Iudea fuerint Ethnici Publicani, nostra hoc loco nō interest quaerere.
units.tr: That the Apostles were wonderfully preserved along with Christ, you say, I grant; but it does not follow from this that they would not have attempted it had they held this power. At least you should have shown somewhere that they were reproached for entering the Temple contrary to the Law. For they object to smaller matters: that he did not wash his hands, that Christ ate with sinners, that he healed some people on the Sabbath. Likewise with Paul, they object that he profaned the Temple because he had brought in a Greek, but they do not add that he himself ought not to have entered according to the Law. In sum, you always strike the same string: that is, you say many false things, none of which you can prove. I have hardly seen anything worthy of you so far, except that here you admit that circumcised publicans were not excluded from the Temple and the sacrifices, which most have hitherto stoutly denied. Whether there were also Gentile publicans in Judea is not a question we need to pursue here.

units.la: Haec mea ex veteri testamento deprompta argumenta vix refutatione ais indigere. Benè dicis: non enim refutari vel possunt vel debet argumeta vera.
