Eiusmodi certè sunt, qualiacunque tibi videantur esse, in quibus dissoluendis tu per omnem reliquam vitam tuam, sicut video, frustrà laborabis: Sed iudicent pij ac docti.
units.tr: These arguments of mine, drawn from the Old Testament, you say hardly need refutation. You speak well, for true arguments can neither be refuted nor should be. Such arguments are certainly of this kind, however they may seem to you, and in trying to dissolve them you will, as I see, labour in vain for the rest of your life. But let the godly and the learned judge.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: Chapter IV.

units.la: Defensio Argumentorum ex nouo Testamento acceptorum.
units.tr: Defence of the Arguments Taken from the New Testament.

units.la: X nouo foedere primum hoc adfers. Iohannes Baptista, dixi, omnes ad se venientes vt baptizarentur, etiam Pharisaeos & Sadducaeos, quos tamen Viperarum progeniem esse affirmat, baptizauit: neminem repulsò. Quorsum hoc, ais, aduersus nos torquès? Non enim debuit eos Iohannes tanquàm excommunicatos repellere: cum non sit priuatae authoritatis quempiam excommunicare. Quid audio? An tam citò oblitus es quid probandum suscep…
units.tr: From the New Testament you first bring forward this. John the Baptist, I said, baptized all who came to him to be baptized, including the Pharisees and Sadducees, whom he nevertheless calls a brood of vipers; he refused no one. "What is the point of this twisting against us?" you say. "John ought not to have repelled them as excommunicated persons, since no private individual has the authority to excommunicate anyone." What is this I hear? Have you forgotten so quickly what you undertook to prove…

units.la: Statui ostendere in nouo etiam foedere nec verbum nec exemplū exstare vestrae Excomunicationis: sed contraria potius tu praecepta tu exempla inueniri. Primo loco propòsui Ioānis Bapt. propter ordinē tēporis. Is non repulit quenquā, qui se cuperet ab eo baptizari, dicens: ego externū symbolū administro, in corda nō intueor: sed alius me sequitur qui & igne baptizabit, & paleā à tritico separabit. Hic ventilabrum in sua habet manu: non ego. Proinde, vt me simulatione poenitentiae fallatis, illum non falletis. Ex quo intelligimus Ministrorum non esse negare Sacramenta petentibus: ac iudicium Deo permittendum esse, verum qui se poenitere profitetur, simulet, an vere & sincere agat.
units.tr: I undertook to show that in the New Testament there is neither a word nor an example of your excommunication, but that you will find rather the opposite precepts and examples. In the first place I put John the Baptist, for the sake of the order of time. He repelled no one who wished to be baptized by him, saying: "I administer an outward sign; I do not look into the heart. But another follows me, who will baptize with fire and will separate the chaff from the wheat. He has the winnowing fan in his hand, not I. Therefore, if you deceive me with a pretence of repentance, you will not deceive him." From this we understand that it is not for ministers to deny the sacraments to those who ask for them, and that judgment must be left to God, who sees whether the one who professes repentance is only pretending or is acting truly and sincerely.

units.la: Quam vero alienum est, quod dicis, Iohannem non debuisse sceleratos illos arcere, siquidem Deus facere aliquos iusserat? Quo in loco dixit Deus, hanc rem esse publicae authoritatis, non priuatae? Si esset Excommunicare hoc, quod vos dicitis, exempla priuatae haberemus Excommunicationis: publicae nullum. Petri & Pauli a vobis citatur exempla: praeter haec nulla habetis. Presbyterij exemplum vbi tandem latet reconditum? Sane Paulus etiam Corinthium tradere voluit Satanae: sed in praesentia totius Ecclesiae. Et cum Apostoli priuati homines fuerint, qui licuit ipsis Excommunicare, & non licuit Iohanni? Si dicas Deum dedisse hanc potestatem illis, non huic, demonstrandus est locus, in quo istud contineatur. Certe non minus a Deo fuit Iohannes missus, quam Apostoli. Res mira est. Cum Prophetas, Iohanne, alios, dicimus neminem excommunicasse, priuatis non licuisse dicis. Cum publicae exclusionis exemplum petimus, priuatorum exempla producitis: quae ad causam tamen vestram non pertinent. Cogita tandem, quaeso, quam facile affirmes, & nunquam probes.
units.tr: How far from the mark is what you say, that John ought not to have kept those wicked men away, since God had commanded some to be made? In what place did God say that this matter belongs to public authority and not to private? If what you call excommunication were this, we would have examples of private excommunication, but of public excommunication none. You cite the examples of Peter and Paul; besides these you have none. Where at last is the example of the eldership hidden away? Certainly Paul also wished to hand over the Corinthian to Satan, but in the presence of the whole Church. And since the apostles were private men, why was it lawful for them to excommunicate and not lawful for John? If you say that God gave this power to them and not to him, the passage in which this is contained must be shown. Surely John was sent by God no less than the apostles were. It is a remarkable thing: when we say that the prophets, John among them, excommunicated no one, you say that private persons were not permitted to do so. When we seek an example of public exclusion, you produce examples of private persons, which nevertheless do not bear on your cause. Consider at last, I beg you, how easily you assert and never prove.

units.la: Argumentum meum septimo loco a te adductum, tale fuit. Sicut firmiter concludimus, infantes nostros baptizari debere, quia baptismus circumcisioni successit, & Deus nullo in loco infantes noui foederis excipi iussit: ita firme quoque argumentamur, impuros moribus non esse a coena depellendos, cum hac in parte Christus Legem Mosis mutasse non legatur. Respondes, Coenam non vni agno Paschae, sed omnibus sacrificijs successisse: meque probare debere, quosuis sine delectu ad Pascha admissos. Quippe immundos exclusos fuisse constat, ais. At Moses immunditiam non distinguit: & sacrificia pro peccato ad quoduis peccatum pertinuerunt. Ex his concludis, peccati conuictos ad publicam reconciliationem vsq; ab Ecclesia alienos fuisse. Non pugno, quin Coenam omnibus Sacrificijs dicas succeßisse: at precipuè agni Paschatis esui respondere, mirum si neges. An non contra te hoc facit? Certè à Sacrificijs pro peccatis nulli arcebatur, sed cogebatur ab ea persoluenda. His ergo si succeßisset Coena Domini, non poteritis ab ea depellere vti ea rectè volentem, saltem externè. Ad Pascha lege immundos fuisse admissos, nunquam dixi aut scripsi: at moribus immundos exclusos non fuisse dixi, & dicam deinceps, donec ostensum aliud mihi fuerit. Sic certè probaui, vt tu nihil potueris refellere. Falsum quoq; est, Mosen non distinxisse immunditiam legis & morum. Miror qui audeas ista scribere, cum vtrisq; differentes constituerit poenas. Immundum lege, iubet à Templo & ceremonijs arceri: immundum moribus vel iubet puniri à Magistratu, vel iubet ad Templum venire, vt ibi mundetur. An hoc non est distinguere? Falsum non minus est, quod ais, Sacrificia pro peccato ad quoduis peccatum pertinuisse. Nā pro illis facinoribus, quae nominatim Lex iubet certa poena coerceri, nulla sunt imperata Sacrificia: sed pro alijs leuioribus, quibus poena constituta nulla erat. Vbi enim legisti apud Mosen homicidium, adulterium, Idololattriam, blasphemiam, certo Sacrificij genere expiari potuisse? Falsissimum est illud etiam, quod ex falsis falsè concludis, conuictos peccati ab Ecclesia alienos fuisse, siquidè per hoc intelligis ad Templum & Sacrificia non fuisse admissos, vsq; ad publicam reconciliationem. Etenim qui sic peccauerunt, non poterant à peccato liberari, nisi ad Templum & Sacrificia venirent. Cogebantur potius ad ea quàm arcerentur. Miserabilis certè disputator es, dum teipsum subinde oppugnas.
units.tr: My argument, which you brought forward seventh, was this. Just as we firmly conclude that our infants ought to be baptized, because baptism succeeded circumcision, and God nowhere commanded that infants be excluded from the covenant of the New Testament, so too we argue firmly that men impure in their morals are not to be driven away from the Lord's Supper, since in this respect Christ is not read to have changed the Law of Moses. You reply that the Supper succeeded not to the one paschal lamb but to all sacrifices, and that I must prove that all sorts of people without distinction were admitted to the Passover. Indeed, you say, it is established that the unclean were excluded. But Moses does not distinguish uncleanness, and sin-offerings pertained to every sort of sin. From this you conclude that those convicted of sin were kept away from the Church until public reconciliation. I do not contest that you may say the Supper succeeded all sacrifices; but that it corresponds especially to the eating of the paschal lamb, it is strange if you deny. Does this not tell against you? Certainly no one was kept away from the sin-offerings, but each was compelled to pay them. If the Lord's Supper had succeeded to these, you could not drive from it anyone who wished to approach it rightly, at least outwardly. I have never said or written that the unclean were admitted to the Passover by the Law; but I have said that the morally unclean were not excluded, and I will go on saying so until something else is shown to me. Certainly I have proved this so well that you have been unable to refute anything. It is also false that Moses did not distinguish the uncleanness of the Law from that of morals. I am amazed that you dare to write such things, since he appointed different penalties for each. For the one unclean by the Law he commands to be kept away from the Temple and the ceremonies; for the one unclean in morals he either commands punishment by the magistrate, or commands him to come to the Temple to be cleansed there. Is this not to distinguish? It is equally false that you say sin-offerings pertained to every sin. For for those crimes which the Law names and orders to be punished by a fixed penalty, no sacrifices were prescribed; they were prescribed for other lighter offences, for which no penalty had been established. For where have you read in Moses that murder, adultery, idolatry or blasphemy could be expiated by a particular kind of sacrifice? Most false too is what you conclude, falsely from false premises, that the convicted of sin were kept away from the Church, if by this you mean that they were not admitted to the Temple and the sacrifices until public reconciliation. For those who sinned in this way could not be freed from sin unless they came to the Temple and the sacrifices. They were compelled to come to them rather than kept away. You are indeed a wretched disputant, while you keep attacking yourself.

units.la: Respondes secundò, Christum alios nullos habuisse conuiuas, quàm suos discipulos: in quo tibi vt vbiq; aliàs constas. Primum enim certum est, Christum cum duodecim discubuisse discipulis: quo vos argumento contra Anabaptistas stas, seu nouos Donatistas, rectè adhùc vti fuistis. Non interfuiffe Iudam institutioni Coenæ multò difficilius probabitis, quàm nos contrarium fimus declaraturi. Sed & frustra monstraueritis. Nam interfuisse eum quotannis agni Paschalis esui nihilominus concedere cogeremini. Tertiò figurarunt Discipuli in illa coena totam Ecclesiam exteriorem, non tantum sanctos & electos. Qua de causa bibere ex poculo omnes iussit. Quartò, vt maxime concedamus, Iudā non adfuisse, nihil tamen ex eo probabis. Etenim non sequitur: Iudas exijt ante vltimæ Coenæ institutionē, Ergo Chriftus legē Dei per Mosen hac in parte sustulit: cum verbū de hac re nullū extet scriptū. Proinde hīc etiā frustra laborafti.
units.tr: Secondly you reply that Christ had no guests other than his disciples, in which you agree with yourself, as you do everywhere else. For first it is certain that Christ reclined with the twelve disciples; by this argument you were rightly accustomed to argue against the Anabaptists, or the new Donatists. You will find it much harder to prove that Judas was not present at the institution of the Supper than we shall find it to declare the opposite. But even if you did prove it, you would have laboured in vain. For you would be forced to concede nonetheless that he took part in eating the paschal lamb each year. Thirdly, the disciples in that supper represented the whole outward Church, not only the saints and the elect; for this reason he bade all of them drink from the cup. Fourthly, let us grant as much as you like, that Judas was not present; yet you will prove nothing from this. For it does not follow: Judas went out before the institution of the last Supper; therefore Christ abolished the law of God given through Moses in this respect; since no word on this matter is written anywhere. Therefore here too you have laboured in vain.

units.la: - Octauo loco hoc recitas. Argumenta quæ olim aduersus Donatistas valuerint, hodieq; contra Anabaptistas seipsos feparantes valent, etiam contra eos valent, qui alios à fe remouent. Quid huic, inquis, iudicio à Presbyterio legitimè, conscia Ecclesia, pronunciato, cōmune est cum voluntaria, ac proinde seditiosa secessione, corpus Christi, id est, Ecclefiam lacerante? Respondeo, quæ ad institutum nostrum pertinent, communia sunt omnia: nisi quod illi fe vltrò feparant, vos autem inuitos eijcitis. Vtrumq; fine mandato Dei fit. Nego enim tibi Deum velle aut voluisse, vt sub pio Magiftratu Ecclesia hoc pacto repurgetur. Hoc ex scripturis proba, & contenti erimus. Multa de dissimilitudine adfers Donatistarum & vestrae opinionis: de qua ego nihil propofui. Non enim nescio quædam esse dissimilia. Hoc volui, vos ijsdem argumentis, quibus Donatistæ suam secessionē probarunt, vestram excommunicationem probare: ac proinde quæ contra Donatistas adferantur, contra vos etiam militare. Huc vfq; vos comparo: non in omnibus eadem, sentire dico. Vbi locos scripturæ, quos Donatistæ olim & hodie Catabaptiftæ pro fe adferunt, docebis non etiā à vobis pro veftrę causæ defensione adferri, dimidium huius argumenti expugnaueris. Si deinde oftēdas, solutiones, quas olim Auguftinus, & hodie alij attulerunt, non rectè posse quibufdā vestris argumētis sic opponi, vt ex scripturis diuersum à vobis monstrari nequeat, euiceris alteram partē. Aliud est argumenta gumenta redte primum interpretari, & deinde firmè refutare: & rursus aliud est, nugas oratorie amplificare, atq; appellatione fratris claudere.
units.tr: Eighthly, you cite this: the arguments which once availed against the Donatists, and today avail against the Anabaptists who separate themselves, also avail against those who remove others from themselves. "What is common," you ask, "between this judgment, pronounced lawfully by the eldership with the consent of the Church, and a voluntary and therefore seditious secession, which tears apart the body of Christ, that is, the Church?" I answer: everything that pertains to our purpose is common, except that the others separate themselves of their own accord, while you cast out those who are unwilling. Both are done without the command of God. For I deny that God wills, or ever willed, that under a godly magistrate the Church be purged in this manner. Prove this from the Scriptures, and we shall be content. You bring forward many points about the dissimilarity between the Donatists and your opinion, of which I have proposed nothing. For I am not ignorant that some things are dissimilar. My purpose was to show that you prove your excommunication by the same arguments by which the Donatists proved their secession, and therefore that what is brought against the Donatists also tells against you. I compare you with them thus far; I do not say that you are the same in all points. If you show that the passages of Scripture which the Donatists once, and the Anabaptists today, bring forward for themselves are not also brought forward by you in defence of your cause, you will have overthrown half of this argument. If you then show that the solutions which Augustine once, and others today, have offered cannot rightly be opposed to some of your arguments in such a way that the contrary cannot be shown from Scripture, you will have conquered the other part. It is one thing to interpret the arguments rightly in the first place and then to refute them firmly; and it is another thing to amplify trifles with rhetoric and to close the matter with the appellation "brother."

units.la: Audiamus nonum. Christus cum discipulis suis in idem Templū ingressus est cum Pharisæis & Sadducæis hominibus sceleratissimis, eadem cum eis aliisq; omnibus Sacramenta vsurpauit: eodem etiam baptismate cum ipsis à Iohanne baptizatus est: nec eos alicubi iusiit à Dei cultu excludi: nec se suósq; ideo cesuit maculari. Ad hæc quid tu? Pro more tuo nugas profers. Dicis mala conscientiam vnius non polluere integritatē alterius: iustam seueritatem non debere in crudele degenerare sæuitiam. Quid hæc ad Rhombum? Concludēsne ex his, ergo Christus aliquos arcuit à Sacramentis? Non arbitror. Quid ergo? Ego enim hoc argumento ostendere vtrumq; hoc volui: & Christū nullos excōmunicauisse: & bonos in vsu Sacramentorū non pollui præsentia malorum. Dicis, quis illos à Sacris arcuisset? Respondeo, Christus, si mandatū Patris habuisset. Nam vt ementes & vendentes expulit, sic & à Sacramentis arcere non iuisset. Et sicut in alijs rebus abusum reprehendit: sic etiam in hac causa aliquando eos taxauisset: aut monuisset salte quid facto opus esset. At verò perlepidū tuum argumentū audire operæprecium est. Si pater eum voluisset fungi munere Leuitico, quid facturus fuerit indicauit eiectione mercantiū & vēdentiū. Rectè sanè, non fuerat passurus, vt ista fierent. Hinc tu consequi opinaris, eum mundos secundum legem, qualesqualesesent moribus, aditu templi contra legem prohibiturū fuisse? Dicam tibi: magistratum fuerat hortaturus, quod etiam fecit, vt prauos iuxta præscriptum Legis castigaret.
units.tr: Let us hear the ninth. Christ entered the same Temple with his disciples, together with the Pharisees and Sadducees, most wicked men. He partook of the sacraments with them and with all the others, and he was baptized with them by John in the same baptism. Nor did he ever order them to be excluded from the worship of God, and he did not think that he and his people would be defiled by them. To this, what do you say? As is your custom, you bring forward trifles. You say that the evil conscience of one man does not pollute the integrity of another, and that just severity should not degenerate into cruel savagery. What has this to do with Rhombus? Do you conclude from this that Christ therefore excluded some from the sacraments? I think not. What then? I wanted to show by this argument two things: that Christ excommunicated no one, and that good men are not polluted in their use of the sacraments by the presence of the wicked. You say, who would have kept them from the sacred things? I answer, Christ, if he had had the Father's command. For just as he drove out the buyers and sellers, so he would not have ordered them kept from the sacraments. And just as he rebuked abuse in other matters, so in this matter too he would at some time have censured them, or at least advised what needed to be done. But it is worth hearing your very charming argument. If the Father had wished him to exercise the Levitical office, he showed what he would do by the expulsion of the merchants and sellers. Rightly so: he would not have allowed these things to happen. From this do you suppose that he would have forbidden entry to the temple, contrary to the Law, to those who were clean according to the Law, whatever their morals? I tell you: he would have exhorted the magistrate, as he also did, to punish the wicked according to the prescription of the Law.

units.la: Decimo loco de Iuda agis. Hunc ego à Christo non fuisse repulsū dixi, multò minus alium ab eo remotum esse. Et cū respondeatis vos, crimē eius fuisse occultū, dixi ego à Christo in ipsa Coena fuisse patefactum. Ad hæc ita tu. Christus vni Iohanni patefacit. Hoc autem nemini præterea tunc suisse indicatum, ex eo liquet, quod scribitur eos non cognouisse, cur ei discedenti diceret, Quod facis, fac citò. Deinde non patefecit Christus factum aliquid, sed futurum. Ad haec non respondererin, nisi tui vbiq; similis esses. Falsum est, Christum hoc vni Iohanni patefecisse. Nam cum singuli interrogarent, nunquid ego is sum, Iudae respondit, tu dixisti. Iohanni autem clarius addito signo patefecit. Quanquam hoc signum alij videantur dicere omnibus datum fuisse. Ac solent, quae vni dicta fuerunt, aliquando pluribus tribui ab Euangelistis, & e contra. Falsum & hoc est, Euangelistas dicere, accumbentes non intellexisse Iudam eum esse, qui Christum esset perditurus. Hoc dicitur, eos non intellexisse, quid his verbis sibi Christus voluisset, cum dixit, Quod facis, cito fac. An quia haec non perceperunt, etiam illa verba non intellexerunt, quibus Iudae interroganti, an ipse is esset, respondit dicens, Tu dixisti, siue tu ille es? De facto & futuro non est cur disputemus. Nam consilium hoc, praesertim cum pactus iam fuisset, dignum acerbissima erat poena. Postremo si Christus neq; in suos, neq; in publice notos malos hanc potestatem exercuit, constat cum nullu excomunicasse. Verum alijs mandarit aliquid huiusmodi, tunc scia, cum testimonium produci consuexero.
units.tr: In the tenth place you deal with Judas. I said that he was not rejected by Christ, much less that someone else was removed from him. And when you reply that his crime was hidden, I said that it was revealed by Christ at the Supper itself. To this you say: "Christ revealed it to John alone." But that this was not indicated to anyone else at that time is clear from the fact that it is written that they did not understand why he said to Judas as he departed, "What you do, do quickly." Next, Christ did not reveal something already done, but something to come. You would not have replied to these points unless you were everywhere like yourself. It is false that Christ revealed this to John alone. For when each of them asked, "Is it I?", he answered Judas, "You have said it." But to John he revealed it more clearly, by adding a sign. Although others seem to say that the sign was given to all. And what was said to one is often attributed by the evangelists to several, and conversely. It is also false that the evangelists say the men reclining at table did not understand that Judas was the one who would betray Christ. It is said that they did not understand what Christ meant by these words, "What you do, do quickly." But if they did not grasp these, did they also not understand those words by which he answered Judas, who asked whether he was the one: "You have said it," or "you are he"? About what was done and what is to come there is no reason for us to dispute. For that plan, especially since he had already made the bargain, deserved the most bitter punishment. Finally, if Christ exercised this power neither over his own people nor over men known publicly as wicked, it is clear that he excommunicated no one. But if he ordered something of this kind to others, you will know it when you have produced the testimony.

units.la: II Christus cum omnes iussit de pane illo edere, & de poculo bibere, neminem exclusit: nec ab alijs excludi iussit aliquem, qui se suum profiteatur discipulum. Respondes, te id concedere: sed negare satis idoneum esse refipiscentiq testimonium in ijs qui iam antea Ecclesiam fefellerint coenam Domini postulare, in vna morte Christi remissionem peccatorum quaerere, membrum Christi se profiteri, & quae alia publice testantur, qui in oculis Ecclesiae Coenam petunt. Negas etiam vos fumere vobis imperium in conscientias hominum: tametsi nullum refipiscentiae testimonium vobis satis idoneum sit, nisi quod vos prescribitis. Deus certe Ecclesiam voluit concrentam esse in veteri testamento, si quis Sacrificium pto commissio peccato ad altare adferret: nec iussit quenquam plura postulare. Cur non ergo & vos multo illustriore confessione contenti estis? Iussit etiam Deus Luc. 17. vt dicenti, poenitet me, saepius in uno die remittamus: & hanc transactionem in coelis ratam fore pollicetur: vobis autem ea non satis est. An inclementiores Deo esse vultis? An non omnes nos saepè Deo mentimur? Certè ut tum, quum Deo pollicemur, nos deinceps aliquid fugituros, sic serio cogitemus, postea tamen non sicut decretum nobis erat, fugimus. Rogo ne velis nimis esse oculatus iudex in iudicandis hominum cogitationibus. Qui ad Coenam accedit tunc salte bene cogit, quicquid postea fit cogitaturus. Speremus de omnibus meliora: Et Deo iudicium permittamus de conscientijs.
units.tr: II. When Christ ordered all to eat of that bread and drink from the cup, he excluded no one, nor did he order anyone to be excluded by others who professes himself to be his disciple. You answer that you concede this, but deny that a testimony of repentance is sufficient for those who have previously deceived the Church and now ask for the Lord's Supper: that they seek remission of sins in the death of Christ alone, profess themselves members of Christ, and whatever else they publicly attest, those who ask for the Supper in the sight of the Church. You also deny that you assume rule over men's consciences, although no testimony of repentance is sufficient for you unless it is the one you prescribe. Surely God wished the Church in the Old Testament to be content when anyone brought a sacrifice to the altar for a sin committed; nor did he order anyone to demand more. Why then are you not content with a much clearer confession? God also commanded, Luke 17, that when one says "I repent," we should forgive him again and again in one day, and he promises that this settlement will be ratified in heaven. But for you that is not enough. Or do you wish to be more unmerciful than God? Do we not all often lie to God? Surely, just as when we promise God that we will shun something in future we think it seriously, and yet afterwards we do not flee as we had resolved, so too... I ask you not to be too sharp-eyed a judge in judging men's thoughts. He who comes to the Supper at least thinks well at that time, whatever he will think afterwards. Let us hope better things of all, and let us leave the judgment of consciences to God.

units.la: Duodecimum hoc est. Apostolus non remouet à Coena Idolothytis in ipso Idoleo vescentes: tametsi peccatum esse prorsus grauissimum iudicet. Respondes, nihil potuisse apertius dici, quàm cum dicit, eos non posse poculum Domini, & poculum Daemoniorum bibere: quo manifestè indicet, non posse illum ad Coenam Domini accedere, qui idolorum sacris communicet. Paulus dehortari voluit aliquos, ne sua libertate contra charitatem abuterentur: sed ut Idolothyta, si non propter suam propriam, saltem propter infirmorum periculum vitarent. Vtitur autem hoc argumento. Qui sacrificijs vescitur, declarat se koinonos, id est, membrum siue socium & participem esse aræ: ut vel ex Israelitarum externis patet Sacrificijs. Ergo si de Idolorum sacris editis, probatis vos ex societate Idololatrarū esse, saltem externè. At ijdem de poculo Domini bibistis: eóq; demonstraftis vos ad communionem & consortium Ecclesiae Christi pertinere. Ergo cum in duabus pugnantibus societatibus simul esse non possitis, æquum fuerit vos Idolorum sacra fugere. An hic Apostolus illos excommunicat, siue à Coena Domini abstinere iubet, qui Idolothyta cum Idololatris comederant? Minimè omnium: imò argumento à Coenae communione ducto auocare eos studet ab esu De astris immolatorū. Quocirca ré his verbis concludit: Nolo autè vos socios & consortes fieri Daemoniorum. Non dicit, nolo vos ad mensam Domini venire: nec iubet eos, nescio quibus Presbyteris poenitentiam suam probare: sed ne amplius id faciant persuadere eis conatur. Idem hoc agit Apostolus in 2. Epist. cap. 6. multis verbis, citans ex Esaie cap. 52. testimonium. Non iubet eos exire e medio fidelium, sed iubet se seiungere ab infidelibus: sicut hic non imperat eis a Coena Domini abstinere, sed idola & idolothyta fugere, & Coenâ Domini solâ vsurpare imperat. Queris hic, cur Apostolus potius dixerit poculû, quàm, sanguinem: & Mensam, quàm corpus: putasq; eû hoc ideo fecisse, vt externa Coena actione cum eius fructu coniugeret. Verior causa est, quod in hac parte, seu in hoc argumento potissimum de externa communione agit: ideo externa potius nominauit symbola, quà res interiores. Probant hoc, primum quidem, ipsum propositum. Deinde verba eius. Aspicite Israelem secundùm carnem. Tertiò, quod qui Idolothytis vescebantur persuasi erant, nihil inter ea cibosq; alios esse discriminis. Quæ praeterea hic dicis, ex recitatis à me facile refelluntur.
units.tr: The twelfth point is this. The Apostle does not remove from the Supper those who eat things sacrificed to idols in the idol's temple, although he judges this to be a most grievous sin. You reply that nothing could have been said more plainly than when he says they cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons, by which he clearly indicates that one who shares in the rites of idols cannot come to the Lord's Supper. Paul wished to dissuade some from abusing their liberty against charity, but he wanted them to avoid idol-offerings, if not for their own sake, at least for the danger to the weak. He uses this argument: whoever eats of sacrifices declares himself koinonos [κοινωνός], that is, a member, partner and sharer of the altar, as is clear even from the external sacrifices of the Israelites. Therefore, if by eating things sacrificed to idols you prove yourselves to belong to the fellowship of idolaters, at least outwardly, then since you also drink from the Lord's cup, you show that you belong to the communion and fellowship of the Church of Christ. Therefore, since you cannot be in two fighting fellowships at once, it would be right for you to flee the rites of idols. Does the Apostle here excommunicate those who had eaten idol-offerings with idolaters, or order them to abstain from the Lord's Supper? By no means. Rather, by an argument drawn from communion in the Supper, he strives to call them away from eating what has been sacrificed to idols. Therefore he ends the matter with these words: "I would not have you become partners and sharers with demons." He does not say, "I do not want you to come to the Lord's table," nor does he order them to prove their repentance to certain elders; he tries to persuade them not to do this any more. The Apostle does the same thing in 2 Cor. chap. 6, with many words, citing a testimony from Isaiah chap. 52. He does not order them to go out from the midst of the faithful, but orders them to separate themselves from unbelievers. Just so, here he does not command them to abstain from the Lord's Supper, but to flee idols and idol-offerings, and commands them to partake of the Lord's Supper alone. You ask here why the Apostle said "cup" rather than "blood," and "table" rather than "body," and you think he did this so that he might join the external action in the Supper with its fruit. The truer cause is that in this part, or in this argument, he deals chiefly with external communion; so he named the outward symbols rather than the inner realities. This is proved first by the very purpose of his argument, then by his words: "Look at Israel according to the flesh." Thirdly, because those who ate idol-offerings were persuaded that there was no difference between these and other foods. What else you say here is easily refuted by what I have recited.

units.la: Argumentum 13, sic habet. Apostol. Paul. in 1. ad Cor. 10. cap. sic ratiocinatur.
units.tr: Argument 13 runs thus. The Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians chapter 10 reasons as follows.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus non pepercit olim res malas appetentibus: Idololatris: stupro se inquinantibus: Christi tentatoribus: & murmuratoribus: tametsi eodem cum caeteris omnibus baptisinate baptizati suisset, eundemq; cibum spiritualem edissent, ac potum bibisfent: Sic ne vobis quidem, quicunq; talibus estis contaminati vitijs, parcet, quantumuis similiter, de vno omnes pane edatis, & de eodem omnes cum alijs sanctis poculo bibatis. Ex his perspicitur, primum quidem, nostra & Veterum Sacramenta eadem esse, quod ad rem internam seu coelestè attinet: aliàs enim argumentum Apostoli nullum foret. Deinde liquet vtrobiq; multos flagitiosos, & quidem publicè notos admissos fuisse. Tertiò illud etiam constat, neminem iussum esse abstinere, quomodo excommunicati iubentur. Apostolus non dicit illos tales arcendos esse, sed à Deo sic praedicit puniendos, vti Veteres puniti fuerunt. Etenim partem eorum Moses cum Leuitis trucidauit, Exod. 32. parte Deus igne, serpentib9, gladio, terrę hiatu cosupsit: quod etiâ Corinthijs vsuenit. Quoniâ multos corû morbis tunc conflictatos, multos etiâ mortuos fuisse affirmat. Ad hæc respondes primùm, me potius debuisse nostra Sacramenta comparare cum illis merè sacris epulis, quàm cum Manna & aqua Petræ, quæ etiam alendo corpori seruierunt. Deinde, vt multi ex ijs, qui Sacramentis pasti sunt, mali fuerint, an ideo nullus fuerit excommunicationis vsus? An oblatio pro peccato requisita non fuit, quia multi ad Aram accedebant sanguine manus habentes plenas? Quis collegerit ideo cessandum ab officio, quia sæpè maior pars vincit meliorem? Postremò, Paulus Corinthios nullos illorum criminum reos arguit, sed vt tales non euadant, veterum exemplo commonefacit. Vis dicam, quod sentio? Tui vbiq; similis es. Ego quomodo Apostolus argumentatus fuerit indicaui: tu me Sacramenta nostra cum Manna & aqua Petræ comparare non debuisse respondes. Apostolum monere debuisses: me, qui eius argumentationem propono, excusatum pij habebunt, spero. Sed nubis etiam fecit mentionem: non aquæ & Mannæ tantum. An & nubes ac mare alendo corpori erant necessaria? Deinde quo in loco scripsi ego nullum excommunicationis vsum futurum fuisse, (pono iam velut concessam à Deo) vbi mali sint multi? Aut vbi scripsi oblationem pro peccato requisitam non fuisse, quia plurimi ad Aram accederet mali? Aut quomodo dictum scripturæ mue à me ostendes, ideo à Dei præcepto discedendum, quia pars maior vincat meliorē? Si ad Aram multi accedebant cum sanguinolentis manib*, quomodo erant excommunicati? Quorsum ista dicas, teipsum puto nescire. Oblatio pro peccato erat mandata: Excommunicatio mādata non est: Nec ego in hoc argumento aliud ago, quā vt docea Paulo malos ibi non fuisse à Sacramentis abactos. Cū postremò dicis, Paulū non peragere reos illorū criminū Corinthios, nihil aliud facis, quàm animum tuum prodis. Sic enim in ambabus Epistolis queritur de huius Ecclesiæ deformatione, vt, qui legit, præter te tuorumq; similes aliquot, nullus sit affirmaturus, quod tu affirmas.
units.tr: Just as God did not spare, in former times, those who craved evil things, namely idolaters, those who defiled themselves with fornication, those who tempted Christ, and those who murmured, although they had all been baptized with the same baptism as the rest, had eaten the same spiritual food and drunk the same drink, so he will not spare you either, whoever you are who are defiled by such vices, even though you all eat of one bread and drink from the same cup with the other saints. From this it is plain, first, that our Sacraments and those of the Fathers are the same as far as the inward and heavenly thing is concerned; otherwise the Apostle's argument would be pointless. Second, it is clear that in both cases many scandalous men, and indeed men notorious in public, were admitted. Third, it is also certain that no one was ordered to abstain, as excommunicated persons are ordered to. The Apostle does not say that such men are to be shut out, but that they are foretold to be punished by God, just as the men of old were punished. For Moses slew part of them with the Levites (Exod. 32), part God consumed by fire, by serpents, by the sword, and by the opening of the earth; and this also happened to the Corinthians, since he says that many of them were then afflicted with diseases and many had died. To this you reply, first, that I ought rather to have compared our Sacraments with those mere sacred feasts than with the manna and the water from the rock, which also served to nourish the body. Second, if many of those who were fed with the Sacraments were wicked, does it follow that there was no use of excommunication? Was not the sin offering required because many came to the altar with hands full of blood? Who would conclude that the office must cease because the greater part often overcomes the better? Lastly, Paul does not accuse the Corinthians of being guilty of those crimes, but reminds them, by the example of the men of old, that they must not escape such punishment. Shall I say what I think? You are everywhere like yourself. I have shown how the Apostle argued; you answer that I ought not to have compared our Sacraments with the manna and the water from the rock. You ought to have admonished the Apostle; I hope that the godly will excuse me, who am setting out his argument. But he also mentions the cloud, not only the water and the manna. Were the cloud and the sea also necessary for feeding the body? Further, where did I write that there would be no use of excommunication (I now suppose it granted by God) where there are many wicked men? Or where did I write that the sin offering was not required because very many came to the altar wicked? Or how will you show from Scripture that one must depart from God's command because the greater part prevails over the better? If many came to the altar with bloody hands, how were they excommunicated? I think you do not know yourself what you mean by these things. The sin offering was commanded; excommunication is not commanded. Nor in this argument am I doing anything other than showing that, in Paul's view, the wicked were not cast out from the Sacraments there. Finally, when you say that Paul does not accuse the Corinthians of those crimes, you do nothing but betray your own mind. For in both Epistles he complains of such a deformity of this Church that anyone who reads them, apart from yourself and a few like you, would not be likely to affirm what you affirm.

units.la: Ad id quod dixi, Deum sceleratos in Ecclesia veteri puniuisse corporalibus poenis, non exclusione à Sacramentis: quas etiam Corinthijs, nulla excommunicationis mentione facta, minetur Apostolus: sic respondes. An hinc efficitur, nullum iam tum fuisse spiritualibus πνευματικοῖς locum? Respondeo nullum fuisse, si per πνευματικῶς intelligas vestras excommunicationes. Fateberis idem tu quoq; mecum, si cum animo veritatis cupido pacatóq; nostra haec perlegere poteris. Equidem argumentum ex Apostoli verbis sumptum permanet integrum. Apostolus non minatur depulsionem à Coena Domini indignè eam vsurpantibus, sed Diuinam castigationem, morbos & mortem: Ergo non censuit indignè edentes interdictione Coenae plectendos. Frustra in hac voce delitescis. Quam enim Paulus πνευματικῶς, vbi de respiscente Corinthio loquitur, sufficere ait, ea non à Presbyteris tuis, sed ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων facta fuit. Fratri etiam in nos delinquenti πνευματικῶς Christus Luc. 17. iubet: nullibi autem censuram vestram sic vocatam docebis. Cum insuper dixi Apostolum nullius meminisse exclusionis à Sacramentis: respondes, cum alio in loco eiusdem epistolae doceat, quomodo cum talibus agendum sit. At locos illos nihil tale docere ex supradictis liquet: & ex sequentibus planiùs adhuc liquebit.
units.tr: To what I said, that God in the old Church punished the wicked with bodily penalties, not with exclusion from the Sacraments, penalties which the Apostle also threatens to the Corinthians without any mention of excommunication, you reply thus: Does it follow that there was then no place for spiritual [πνευματικοῖς] penalties? I answer that there was none, if by spiritually [πνευματικῶς] you understand your excommunications. You will concede the same as I do, if you can read these things through with a love of truth and a calm mind. Indeed, the argument taken from the Apostle's words stands whole. The Apostle does not threaten exclusion from the Lord's Supper for those who partake of it unworthily, but divine chastisement, sickness, and death. Therefore he did not judge that those who eat unworthily were to be punished by being barred from the Supper. You hide in vain behind this word. For the thing which Paul calls spiritually [πνευματικῶς], where he speaks of the Corinthian who repented, and says was sufficient, was done not by your elders but by the majority [ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων]. Likewise Christ commands, in Luke 17, that a brother who sins against us be dealt with spiritually [πνευματικῶς]; but you will nowhere show that your so-called censure is called by this name. Moreover, when I said that the Apostle makes no mention of any exclusion from the Sacraments, you reply that in another place of the same Epistle he teaches how such people are to be dealt with. But it is clear from what has been said above that those passages teach nothing of the kind, and it will become clearer still from what follows.

units.la: Quartum & decimum hoc ponis. Paulus iubet, vt vnusquisq; seipsum probet, atq; sic de pane Domini edat. Ergo non putauit necessarium, vt alieno iudicio, sed vt proprio stemus hac in parte. Consecutionem hanc putas esse mirabilem, quod minimè miror; cum tuo palatui non sapiat hic cibus. At ego consecutionem facilè hoc ipso probabo iustam & probam esse: quo tuas obiectiones ad rem non pertinere docebo: Bonum ciuem, apud se considerare decet, inquis, quae sunt vires suę cum ad functionem vocatur: at non est idcirco ἀνωμαλία reijcienda. Item, debet vnusquisq; consulere propriam conscientiam an rectè vixerit: at non ideo nullae sunt iudicum partes. Item, explorare quisq; debet an sit in fide: sed non ideo non sunt erudiendi rudes. Item, debet etiam, qui deliquit, cogitare an verè resipuerit, at non ideo nullae sunt Presbyterorum partes.
units.tr: You put this as the fourteenth point. Paul bids each one prove himself, and so eat of the Lord's bread. Therefore he did not think it necessary that we stand in this matter by another's judgment, but by our own. You think this inference is remarkable, which does not surprise me at all, since this food does not taste good to your palate. But I shall easily prove by this very inference that it is just and sound, and I shall show that your objections have nothing to do with the point. A good citizen, you say, ought to consider with himself what his powers are when he is called to a office; but for that reason no irregularity [ἀνωμαλία] is to be rejected. Likewise, each one ought to consult his own conscience whether he has lived rightly; but for that reason there are no parts for judges. Likewise, each one ought to examine whether he is in the faith; but for that reason the ignorant are not to be taught. Likewise, the one who has sinned ought also to consider whether he has truly repented; but for that reason there are no parts for the elders.

units.la: Nam si ita sit, cur Paulus 2.Cor. 13. minatur se potestate sua à Deo accepta vsurum, nisi resipiscentes inuenìat? quod absque prædicatione fieri non potuit. Quod facere vbique soles, hic etiam facis: longè præter causam excurris.
units.tr: For if it were so, why does Paul in 2 Corinthians 13 threaten that he will use the power given him by God, unless he finds them repenting? This could not be done without preaching. You do everywhere what you are wont to do; here too you run far beyond the matter.

units.la: Si verè sic possemus loqui in tuis similibus, quomodo Apostolus loquitur, aliquid videretis nobis dicere. Tunc enim veracesset hæ orationes: Bonus ciuis, qui seipsum explorauit, functionem recte suscipiet: nec opus habet, vt ab alio præterea probetur. Qui suam vitam explorauit, probus est: nec examinari amplius habet opus. Sic enim Paulus loquitur. Quoniam inter vos multi Coenam indignè sumunt, non di iudicantes corpus Domini, ideo multi apud vos morbis affliguntur: & nonnulli etiam mortui sunt: quod ne vobis in posterum vsu-ueniat, vos ipsos prius explorate, & sic de pane hoc edite, deque poculo Domini bibite. Apostolus de eo loquitur, quod ad cuiusque conscientiam pertinet, quódque alius nullus potest iudicare: tu autem similia adducis, quæ alij possunt ac debent iudicare. Verum idoneus sim ad hanc vel illam functionem suscipiendam: item an aliquid contra leges perpetrarim: Item an capita doctrinæ rectè intelligam: iudicare etiam alij possunt. At num verè me peccatorum pœnitet & an firmiter in Dei misericordia propter Christi mortem acquiescam, nullus præter me potest scire: id quod Hypocritas nos satis docent. Primum igitur in hoc peccas, quod similibus toto cœlo dissimilibus arbitraris te nostra infirmare.
units.tr: If we could truly speak about your like in the way the Apostle speaks, you would seem to us to be saying something. For then these statements would be true: a good citizen who has examined himself will undertake his office rightly, and has no need to be tested further by another. Whoever has examined his life is upright, and has no need to be examined any more. For this is how Paul speaks: Since many among you eat the Lord's Supper unworthily, not discerning the body of the Lord, therefore many among you are afflicted with sickness, and some have died; so that this may not happen to you in future, examine yourselves first, and then eat of this bread and drink of the Lord's cup. The Apostle speaks of what pertains to each one's conscience, which no other person can judge; but you bring forward similar things which others can and ought to judge. For whether I am fit to undertake this or that office, and likewise whether I have committed any offence against the laws, and whether I rightly understand the heads of doctrine, others can also judge. But whether I truly repent of my sins, and whether I firmly rest in God's mercy for the sake of Christ's death, no one but myself can know; the hypocrites teach us this well enough. Therefore you err first in this, that you think your cases are wholly unlike these, and yet you suppose that they weaken ours.

units.la: Deinde, quod exïstimas nos hanc Pauli sententiam veluti Propositionem generalem propösuisse, cum nos vt particulare, imò vt singulare præceptum à Paulo propositum sciamus, aliisque proponamus. Non sic accipimus Apostoli verba, ac sr vniuersalem sonarent propositionem, hoc modo: Quicunque iubentur in re qualibet seipsos probare, non habent opus vt præterea probentur ab alijs. Apostolus hic de sola Coena loquitur, ac dicit: probet vnusquisque semetipsum, vt sic digne edat de hoc pane. Contra huiusmodi propositiones frustra adducuntur exempla de alijs rebus. Si fïlsum probare voles, hoc probare te oportebit: cum qui seipsum probauerit, nihilominus non posse de pane Domini edere, nisi probatus quoque sit a quibusdam presbyteris. Hoc tu nae tunc quidem probabis, cum flumina sursum currere caeperint, atque ignis instar glaciei frigefaciet. Quod enim Apostoli sententia haec sit, omnes illos, qui seipsos probauerint, digne ad mensam Domini accessuros, sine alius cuiusquam examinatione vlteriore ex ipsius verbis ita potest ostendi, vt impossibile sit pium hominem tergiuersari. Etenim si nosipsos dijudicaremus, inquit Apostolus, non corriperemur a Domino. An non aperte hic dicit Paulus, omnes nos, si nos-ipsos exploremus eo modo, quo ipse intellexit, non puniendos esse, hoc est, digne manducaturos? Nam soli indigne edentes a Deo puniuntur. Apage ergo cum tuis nugacibus similibus, quibus oppugnare mentem Apostoli nequicquam tentas.
units.tr: Second, you think that we have set forth this saying of Paul as a general proposition, whereas we know that it was proposed by Paul as a particular, indeed a singular, precept, and we propose it to others as such. We do not take the Apostle's words as if they sounded like a universal proposition, in this way: Whoever is bidden to prove themselves in any matter has no need to be proved by others besides. The Apostle here speaks only of the Supper, and says: let each one prove himself, so that he may eat worthily of this bread. Against propositions of this kind, examples drawn from other matters are brought in vain. If you wish to prove something false, you will have to prove this: that one who has proved himself nevertheless cannot eat of the Lord's bread unless he has also been approved by certain elders. You will prove this only when rivers begin to run uphill and fire, like ice, begins to chill. For that this is the Apostle's meaning, namely that all those who have proved themselves will approach the Lord's table worthily, without any further examination by anyone else, can be shown from his own words in such a way that it is impossible for a godly man to evade it. For, as the Apostle says, if we judged ourselves, we would not be corrected by the Lord. Does not Paul plainly say here that all of us, if we examine ourselves in the way he himself understood, shall not be punished, that is, shall eat worthily? For only those who eat unworthily are punished by God. Away then with your trifling comparisons, by which you vainly try to attack the mind of the Apostle.

units.la: Postrema instantia ex 2. Corinth. 13. manifeste contra te facit. Quippe non mandat ibi Apostolus, vt ab aliis examinemur, sed ait: pertentate vosipsos num in fide sitis: explorate vosipsos. An non cognoscitis vos ipsos, quod Iesus Christus in vobis regnet? Cognoscitis certe, nisi reprobi estis. Paulo post addit: Haec vobis absens scribo, ne praesens cogar, rigide duriterque agere iuxta potestatem mihi a Domino traditam. At hoc inquis, absque praedicatione fieri non potuit. Quid hoc ad rem? An idcirco sequetur a seipso exploratum non posse vti Coena Dominica, sed exspectare cum oportere, dum presbyteris videatur idoneus? Vehementer fallor, si non saltem incipis tibi displicere, dum vbique te hallucinari vides.
units.tr: The last objection, from 2 Corinthians 13, tells clearly against you. The Apostle does not there command that we be examined by others. He says: "Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ reigns in you? Surely you know it, unless you are reprobate." A little later he adds: "I write these things to you while absent, so that when I am present I may not have to deal sharply and severely, according to the authority the Lord has given me." But you say this could not be done without preaching. What does that matter? Will it follow that a man cannot examine himself and use the Lord's Supper, but must wait until the elders judge him fit? I am much mistaken if you do not at least begin to be displeased with yourself, since you see yourself going astray on every side.

units.la: Pro 15. Argumento haec adfers. Non iubet Apostolus, vt qui indignum se intelligit, a Coena abstineat: sed operam dare iubet, vt digne accedat, iudicium-que sibi non comedat. Nunquam ais, concesserimus Paulum volnisse, vt etiam qui se indignos sentirent, indigne potius ad Coenam accederent, quàm ab ea abstinerent. Hoc enim esset homines praetextu obedientiae ad mandati transgressionem impellere: quum grauius etiam peccet, qui indigne accedit, quàm qui abstinet. Tot rursus hic propemodum errata sunt, quot verba. Apostoli tempore ne per somnium quidem cogitabat aliquis se à Coena abstinere deberet: sed non minus sibi celebrandam Coenam putabant omnes, atque orandum sibi intelligebant. Apostolis aliquando in mentem venisse, vt aliquibus de Ecclesia sacramentis vti cupientibus eadem negarent, a nullo vnquam homine ex sacris literis demonstrabitur. Caeterùm cum non satis perpenderent aliqui mysterij magnitudinem, necdistinguerent inter hunc cibum & alios, monet eos Paulus, vt rectius rem apud se expendant, ne à Domino castigentur: sicut iam castigatos esse aliquos viderent. Non iubet igitur abstinere aliquos à Coena: sed posito hoc, quod pro more omnes accederent, hortatur vt omnes digné accedere studeant. Oratio prorsus talis est, ac si illos, qui conciones publicas non satis attentè audiunt, sic horter. Non decet vos verbi Dei praedicationem sic audire, ac si historia aliqua solum recitaretur. Qui enim sic audit, poenas dabit Deo graues: propterea quod non distinguit inter verbum coelestè, & historica hominum scripta. Huic, inquam, non prohiberem frequenter interesse concionibus: sed docerem, quomodo rectè eas audire deberet. Quocirca siue tu concedas, siue neges, verum tamen semper fuit, est, erit, quod hac in parte dixi.
units.tr: You bring forward this in reply to my fifteenth argument. The Apostle does not order the one who understands himself to be unworthy to abstain from the Supper; he orders him to take care to approach worthily, and not to eat judgment upon himself. You never say: "We have conceded that Paul wished even those who felt themselves unworthy to approach the Supper unworthily rather than abstain from it." For this would be to drive men, under the pretext of obedience, into breaking the command, since the one who approaches unworthily sins more gravely than the one who abstains. Here again there are almost as many errors as there are words. In the Apostle's time no one so much as dreamed that he ought to abstain from the Supper; all thought that the Supper must be celebrated by them no less, and understood that they must pray. That the Apostles ever thought of denying the sacraments of the Church to some who wished to use them will never be shown from the sacred letters by any man. But since some did not weigh sufficiently the greatness of the mystery, and did not distinguish this food from others, Paul warns them to consider the matter more carefully among themselves, lest they be chastised by the Lord, as they saw some already chastised. He therefore does not order some to abstain from the Supper; but, taking it as granted that all approached as was customary, he urges all to strive to approach worthily. The whole manner of speaking is just as if I were to exhort those who do not listen attentively enough to public sermons thus: "It is not fitting for you to hear the preaching of God's word as if some story were merely being recited. For whoever hears in that way will pay a heavy penalty to God, because he does not distinguish between the heavenly word and the historical writings of men." To such a person, I say, I would not forbid frequent attendance at sermons; I would teach him how he ought to hear them rightly. So whether you grant it or deny it, what I have said on this point has always been true, is true, and will be true.

units.la: At homines sic impelluntur obedientiæ praetextu ad mandati transgressionem. Nego tibi hoc sequi. Ex dictis potes facillimè perspicere, cur negem. Nam vt non impellit ad mandati transgressionem, qui hortatur aliquem, vt rectè audiat conciones: rectè oret: rectè praestet eleemosynas: ita neque is tale quid facit, qui instruit, quomodo quis vti Coena digné posit. Si ipsa ad Coenam accessio esset mala, aliquid diceres. At non Coenae vsurpatio, sed mala vsurpatio mala est. Non orare malum est, sed non orare ex fide malum est, ac Deo displicet. Non Sacrificium offerre Deo, reprehenditur, sed hoc accusatur, quod non eo modo offerrent, quo iufcerat sibi offerri. Semel dicam omnia: Nullus actus à Deo praeceptus malus est: sed malum est, quod huic contra Dei mentem vel additur vel demitur. Proinde qui iubet aliquem facere, quod Deus fieri praecepit: ac simul monet, vt vicio nullo Dei institutum deformet, is ad mandati tranfgrefsionem neminem impellit. Vides quàm etiam hic procul à mente absis Apostoli?
units.tr: "But men are thus driven, under the pretext of obedience, into breaking the command." I deny that this follows. From what has been said you can see very easily why I deny it. Just as he does not drive anyone to break a command who exhorts him to hear sermons rightly, to pray rightly, and to give alms rightly, so neither does he do any such thing who teaches how someone may use the Supper worthily. If approaching the Supper itself were evil, you would have something to say. But it is not the use of the Supper that is evil, but the evil use of it. Not to pray is bad, but not to pray in faith is bad and displeases God. Offering sacrifice to God is not blamed; what is blamed is that they did not offer it in the manner in which it had been commanded. To say everything in a word: no act commanded by God is evil; what is evil is whatever is added to it or taken from it contrary to God's intention. Therefore he who bids someone do what God has commanded to be done, and at the same time warns him not to spoil God's institution by any fault, drives no one to break the command. Do you see how far you are, even here, from the mind of the Apostle?

units.la: Ad 16. venio. Deus non vult pauciores apud Chriftianos inter membra externae suae Ecclesiae censeri, quàm voluerit pro talibus haberi inter Iudaeos. At omnes circumcifos voluit pro membris Ecclesiae haberi, tametsi interim flagitiosos à magistratu seuerissimè iuberet puniri. Ergo nunc omnes vult baptizatos, rectéque de religione sentientes pro membris externae Ecclesiae haberi: tametsi non minus nunc velit facinorosos gladio coerceri. Respondes, sic Deum voluisse Iudaeos omnes eadem sacra participare, vt tamen nonnullos, nisi refipiscentiam testarentur, excluderet. Saepè iam dixi falsum esse, quod Deum dicis alios à sacrorum vsurpatione repulifle, quàm immundos. At his non erat resipiscentia aliqua praecepta, cum saepe fine sua culpa immundi fierent: sed purificatio erat mandata, quae certo fere dierum intervallo perficiebatur, five moribus effent meliores five deteriores factí. Taceo quod non ex alieno arbitrio pendebat purgatio, sed ex suo cuiusq; , dummodo ritu Moßs purgarentur. Soli leprosi Sacerdoti se indicare cogebantur. Quod dicis, non omnia peccata fuiffe capitalia, concedo. At illa fuerunt, propter quae vos excommunicatis, vel omnia vel pleraque. Magistratus non capitalia solum, sed & alia punit: nec morte tantummodo, sed virgis etiam, carcere, mulcta, exilio fontes plectit. In summa, frigidum est quicquid in medium adducis.
units.tr: I come to the sixteenth. God does not wish fewer among Christians to be counted as members of his external Church than he wished to be held as such among the Jews. Yet he wished all the circumcised to be held as members of the Church, although meanwhile he most severely ordered the wicked to be punished by the magistrate. Therefore now he wishes all who are baptized, and who think rightly about religion, to be held as members of the external Church, although he no less wishes criminals to be restrained by the sword. You reply that God so willed that all the Jews should share the same sacred rites, yet still excluded some of them unless they gave evidence of repentance. I have often said that it is false that you say God repelled others from the use of the sacred things than the unclean. But for these there was no command of repentance, since they often became unclean without their own fault; rather a purification was commanded, which was completed after a fairly fixed interval of days, whether they became better or worse in their morals. I say nothing of the fact that the purification depended not on another's judgment but on each person's own, provided they were purified by the Mosaic rite. Only lepers were compelled to show themselves to the priest. As to what you say, that not all sins were capital, I grant it. But those were the sins on account of which you excommunicate, all or most of them. The magistrate punishes not only capital crimes but others too; and not only with death, but also with the rod, prison, fine, exile, and so on. In sum, whatever you bring forward on this is cold.

units.la: Postremo loco collocas, quod dixi, huc spectare fimilitudines Retis, Nuptiarum, Zizaniae, Palear & tritici. Illae similitudines, ais, de vniuersali repurgatione loquuntur, quae particulari, five ciuili, five ecclesiastice non officit. Extra dubium puto esse, Christum hisce parabolis nihil voluisse tollere de potestate magistratus erga sontes. Loquitur de Ministris tantum. Et in parabola de nuptijs, ut ex Augustino supra citaui, palàm dicitur, non inuitatores, sed ipsum Dominum veste nuptijs non congruente indutum iusssse eijci: inuitatores autem in mandatis habuisse malos & bonos in domum introducendi. In ea, quae de Zizania est, manifestè vetat ministris Zizaniam, quam à tritico praeclarè distinguere norant, euellere. Sic in Palea & Tritici parabola Iohannes, cum Pharisaeos ad se venientes, ut baptizarentur, vidisset, dixerit dicit, se aqua baptizare, nec posse videre verum serió an fictè peterent baptismum; at Dominum esse, qui ventilabrum in manu sua habeat, quem non sint decepturi. Sed ad haec satis multa.
units.tr: Lastly, you place here what I said, that the similitudes of the net, the wedding, the tares, and the chaff and the wheat bear on this question. Those similitudes, you say, speak of a universal purging, which does not hinder a particular one, whether civil or ecclesiastical. I think it is beyond doubt that Christ in these parables wished to take nothing away from the magistrate's power over the guilty. He speaks only of ministers. And in the parable of the wedding, as I cited above from Augustine, it is plainly said that it was not the inviters but the Lord himself who ordered the man wearing a garment unsuitable for the wedding to be cast out; the inviters, however, had the command to bring both bad and good into the house. In the parable of the tares, he plainly forbids the ministers to uproot the tares, which they knew well how to distinguish from the wheat. So in the parable of the chaff and the wheat, John, when he saw the Pharisees coming to him to be baptized, said that he baptizes with water and cannot see whether they seek baptism seriously or feignedly; but it is the Lord who has the winnowing fan in his hand, and they will not deceive him. But enough of these matters for now.

units.la: Sicut in prima parte clarè aperteque docui, nostram definitionem ac Pontificiorum accusationem immeritissimò à te reprehendi, tuam autem definitionem ac reprehensiones multis ac magnis erroribus scatere ita in secunda parte haec sic retudi plumbeas tuas obiectiones, quas contra aliquot argumenta nostra (Nam & pluta & aptius disposita propositimus) vibrasti, ut non modo illae sa illa permaneant, sed nulla ne minima quidem labecula respersa tinctaue apparcant. Attigisse illae superficiem nostrorum videntur nonnullis, ut audio: at si attentè considerabunt, quomodo sordes, quas eis allinere affricareque studuisti, abstererimus, perfacilè videbunt, si non caeci sunt redditi, pristinum ipsa candorem suum recepisse. An idem tu de tuis reprehensionibus affirmare possis, iudicent omnes pij & eruditi. Testor Deum, me nihil magis optare, quàm ut omnino plurimi utriusque partis argumenta legere, expendere, iudicare velint ac possint. Te quoque iudicem meorum ferrem, nisi verbis & factis declarasses, te defensionem vestrae illius excommunicationis non magis deserere posse, quàm doctrinae vestrarum Ecclesiarum. Summa omnium eorum quae obijcis, haec est: oportere peccatores poenitere ac resipiscere: quod & nos dicimus. At non hoc venit in controuersiam: neque hoc negauimus unquam. Hoc quaeritur, an scilicet Deus mandárit, vt, qui lapsus est in crimen aliquod, non ante sit pro resipiscente habendus, quàm causam suam probauerit quibusdam Presbyteris ad hoc ordinatis: vt videlicet iudicent, vtrum eos, qui deliquerunt, serió poeniteat, an potius simulent. Hoc probandum tibi erat. Deinde hoc etiam Deum presbyteris vestris imperasse poenitentiam simulantes, aut in bono proposito non perfistentes per sententiam ab eis solenniter latam à sacramentis depellere. Sed tempus est, vt ad sequentia pergamus.
units.tr: As I taught clearly and openly in the first part, our definition and the accusation of the Papists have been most undeservedly found fault with by you, while your definition and your reprehensions abound with many great errors. So in the second part I have so beaten back your leaden objections, which you hurled against some of our arguments (for we put forward both more and better-arranged ones), that not only do those arguments remain, but they appear not even slightly stained or tinged with any spot. Those objections seem, as I hear, to have touched the surface of our arguments for some people; but if they consider carefully how we have wiped away the filth you strove to smear and rub on them, they will very easily see, if they have not been blinded, that the arguments have recovered their original brightness. Whether you could say the same of your reprehensions, let all the pious and learned judge. I call God to witness that I desire nothing more than that very many people from both sides be willing and able to read, weigh and judge the arguments. I would take you too as a judge of my arguments, were it not that you have declared by word and deed that you can no more abandon the defence of that excommunication of yours than the doctrine of your Churches. The sum of everything you object is this: that sinners ought to repent and return to their senses, which we too say. But this is not what is in controversy, nor have we ever denied it. What is asked is whether God has commanded that one who has fallen into some crime should not be regarded as repentant before he has proved his cause to certain elders appointed for this purpose, namely so that they may judge whether those who have offended repent seriously or rather feign it. This you had to prove. Next, you had to prove that God has also commanded your elders to remove by a solemn sentence from the sacraments those who feign repentance, or who do not persevere in a good purpose. But it is time to proceed to what follows.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CAP. V.

units.la: Confutatio Argumentorum D. Bezae, quae pro excommunica- tione ex Testamento veteri attulit.
units.tr: Refutation of the arguments which Beza brought forward from the Old Testament in support of excommunication.

units.la: N tertia parte argumenta ex veteri Testamento quatuor legi, (plura necdum vidi, vt qui ad proxima semper respondeam) quibus excommunicationem studes probare: nec foelicius te hic agere video, quàm supra egeris, licèt meliora sperauerim. Saepe enim contigit, vt, qui aliena parum cōcinnè refutaret, sua pulchrè probaret. Te verò, quantum adhuc vidi, tui semper similem esse perspicio: vt me plane ostensurum spero. Ergo primum tuum argumentum hoc est. Arbor vitae Adamo Sacramentum fuit filij Dei, à quo beatitas eius omnis pendebat. Igitur cum ab eius arboris esu prohibitus fuit, ad tempus à Deo excommunicatus fuit, donec scilicet resipisceret. Primum desidero in te hic, vt & alibi, attentionem & memoriam. Tu in tua descriptione supra receptisti, (at de me nihil dicam) te de excommunicatione disputaturum, quàm Seniores quidam in nomine Domini congregati exerceant: quaeque hic in terris declaret ac promulget eam, quae facta sit in coelis: nunc autem exemplum mihi adfers eius, quod Deus in Paradyso egit. Aut ergo non ad rem nostram hoc pertinet, túque propositi tui oblitus es: aut descriptionem supra nobis attulisti non rectam, vtrum feceris, male feceris. Secundò, si posses ostendere Deum eodem modo dixisse, Quisquis indecorè viuit, à Sacramentis arcetôr: quoquomodo Adamo dixit: Si de hac arbore ederis, morte morieris, Paulò propius ad rem accederes. Quod cum probare non posis, quantum à scopo absis, ipse vides, opinor. Tertiò,non vetuit Deus Adamo sacrificijs vti: sed ipsi,vt tu etiam ais, sacrificia imperauit. Caeterum nos de sacramentis omnibus, non vno aliquo solo agimus. Quartò , non fuit ad idem sacramentum iterum post poenitentiam admissus: ac proinde non potest illius priuatio comparari cum priuatione nostrorum, ad quæ resipiscentes rursus admittuntur. Nec excusat, quod absoluutus sit alio conuenientiore instituto. Vos enim absoluendo ad eadem reducitis à quibus depulistis. Fuerunt conuenientiora constituta post Adami lapsum sacrificia,fateor. Etenim significabant reparationé amissæ faelicitatis post irrogatā poenam,nempe mortem. At hoc ad rem nostram nihil facit. Quintò cum arbor vitæ sacramentum fuerit vitæ, quam propter Christum ipsum posidebat,ac nos possessuri sumus, non negauit ei Deus sacramenta significantia reparationem illius vitæ & beatitatis in Christo. Illud habuit solus cum sua vxore: posteriora magis cömunia & similia habuit cum nostris:ac proinde comparatio nō cum illo,sed cum his facienda fuerit. Sextò non dicit scriptura Adamum expulsum fuisse ex Paradyso, vt resipisceret,nec ideo dicit exclusum ne sacramēto se vitæ consolaretur:sed ideo eiectum dicit,ne pœnam, quam meruerat, effugeret. Postremò, vt alia omittam omnia,disputamus nos de excommunicatione humana,non diuina : & de prohibitione sacramentorum quæ Deus Ecclesiæ suæ per Mosen & per Christum tradidit. Ab his neminem ex illis,de quibus loquimur, arcendum credemus & dicemus, quantisper ex sacris literis non fuerimus aliter edocti. Deus cum Adamo & posteris eius sic egit,vt rectum & iustum ei visum fuit:ac deinceps quoque cum omnibus hominibus sic agit. Nobis non licet facere in hac visibili militia. Ecclesiæ præter-id quod mandatum nobis est in sacrosanctis scripturis. Idcirco facilè tibi dedero, vt hanc exoulsionem Adami ex Paradyso, cum Augustino voces excōmunicationem nem, (Non enim libenter de nominibus rixati velim) modo eam toto genere ab ista differre memineris, de qua nos inter nos disceptamus. Videsne, quàm sis sterilis & inanis in primo tuo argumento?
units.tr: In the third part you bring four arguments from the Old Testament (I have not yet seen more, since I always answer what is nearest to hand) by which you try to prove excommunication. I see that you do no better here than you did above, though I had hoped for better. It often happens that a man who refutes another's views clumsily proves his own neatly. As far as I have seen of you, however, you are always the same, and I hope to show this plainly. So your first argument is this: the tree of life was a sacrament of the Son of God for Adam, and all his blessedness depended on it. Therefore, when he was forbidden to eat of that tree, he was excommunicated by God for a time, namely until he repented. Here, as elsewhere, I ask you first for attention and memory. In your description given above you undertook (I say nothing of myself) to discuss excommunication as certain elders gathered in the name of the Lord exercise it, and as they declare and promulgate here on earth what has been done in heaven. Now, however, you bring me an example of what God did in Paradise. Either this has nothing to do with our question and you have forgotten your own purpose, or the description you gave us above was not correct. Whichever you did, you did it badly. Second, if you could show that God said in the same way, "Whoever lives unseemly is kept from the sacraments," as he said to Adam, "If you eat of this tree, you will surely die," you would come a little closer to the point. Since you cannot prove this, you see for yourself, I think, how far you are from the mark. Third, God did not forbid Adam to use sacrifices; rather, as you also say, he commanded him to offer sacrifices. Moreover, we are not dealing with one sacrament only, but with all the sacraments. Fourth, Adam was not readmitted to the same sacrament after his repentance; therefore his deprivation cannot be compared with the deprivation of our people, who are readmitted after they repent. Nor does it help that he was absolved by another and more suitable arrangement. For you, in absolving people, restore them to the very things from which you cast them out. I grant that after Adam's fall more suitable sacrifices were appointed, for they signified the restoration of the happiness lost after the penalty, namely death, had been inflicted. But this has nothing to do with our question. Fifth, since the tree of life was a sacrament of the life which he possessed through Christ himself, and which we are going to possess, God did not deny him sacraments signifying the restoration of that life and blessedness in Christ. He had that one only together with his wife; the later sacraments were more common and resembled ours. Therefore the comparison must be made not with that one but with these. Sixth, Scripture does not say that Adam was expelled from Paradise so that he might repent, nor does it say he was shut out so that he would not console himself with the sacrament of life. It says he was driven out so that he would not escape the punishment he had deserved. Finally, to pass over all the rest: we are disputing about human excommunication, not divine, and about the exclusion from the sacraments which God handed down to his Church through Moses and through Christ. We do not believe, and will not say, that anyone of those we are speaking of ought to be kept from them, unless we have been taught otherwise from the holy Scriptures. God dealt with Adam and his posterity as seemed right and just to him, and he still deals in this way with all men. We may not do this in this visible warfare of the Church, beyond what has been commanded us in the holy Scriptures. Therefore I will readily grant you that this expulsion of Adam from Paradise may be called excommunication, with Augustine (for I would not gladly quarrel about names), provided you remember that it differs in its whole kind from the excommunication we are disputing about among ourselves. Do you see how barren and empty you are in your first argument?

units.la: Cainum, inquis secundò, non tantum à facie sua Deus expulit, sed & simul ab externo cultu prohibuit. Ergo eum excommunicauit excommunicatione maiore, imò maxima. Prima pars antecedentis vera est: sed tibi non patrocinatur. Tu enim mecum de longè alia excommunicatione disputas, puto. Valde miror tene nunc quidem tuam descriptionem reuocauisse in mentem. Vbi Seniores congregati? Vbi Ecclesiæ consensus? Conscientia Caini eundem excommunicauit, non Conciliabulum Seniorum tuorum. Alteram partem Antecedentis tibi pernego, & pernegabo semper, dum ex sacris literis probaueris. Locum profer, in quo iuflerit Cainum & posteros suos porrò non sacrificare. Augustini testimonium sino esse hominis testimonium: at ego diuinum à te exspectabam. Ego in Caini posteris non audeo dicere nullos fuisse bonos: & sacrificia alia habuisse, quàm habuerunt posteri Sethi: quamuis non pari fortasse animo vtrique ea vulgò vsurparent. Non audeo etiam affirmare, posteros Sethi fuisse aut omnes aut plerosque bonos: imò videor mihi contrarium posse demonstrare. Omnes nos non à Caino, sed à Sethi posteris, nempe à Noa ortum habemus. Ergo Cainum cum suis sinamus: & de hisce, id est, de Ecclesia Dei externa loquamur. In hac mali longè plures fuerunt, quàm boni (quod neque tu inficiaberis, spero) quorum tamen nullus offendi poterit à sacramentis exclusus: illis, inquàm, quæ in Dei Ecclesiæ inerant. Vides iterum, quàm sis infoelix probator?
units.tr: Second, you say, Cain was not only driven from the face of God, but was also forbidden external worship. Therefore God excommunicated him with the greater excommunication, indeed the greatest. The first part of the premise is true, but it does not help you. I think you are arguing about a quite different excommunication. I am greatly surprised that you have now remembered your description. Where are the elders gathered? Where is the consent of the Church? Cain's own conscience excommunicated him, not your council of elders. I deny the second part of the premise altogether, and I shall always deny it until you prove it from the holy Scriptures. Produce a passage in which God commanded Cain and his posterity not to sacrifice any longer. I expected divine testimony from you, but you offer the testimony of a man, Augustine. I dare not say that among the posterity of Cain there were no good people, or that they had no other sacrifices than the posterity of Seth had, although they perhaps did not use them with the same disposition. Nor do I dare to affirm that the posterity of Seth were all or most of them good; indeed I seem to be able to show the contrary. We are all descended not from Cain but from the posterity of Seth, namely from Noah. Therefore let us leave Cain and his people aside, and speak of the external Church of God. In that Church the wicked were far more numerous than the good (which I hope you will not deny), yet none of them could be excluded from the sacraments that were in the Church of God. Do you see again how unfortunate a prover you are?

units.la: At Lutherus, inquis, Cainum dixit excommunicatum, expectabam vt etiam Caluinum adderes. Si D. Lutherus hoc dixit, vsus est hoc nomine non proprie, quomodo nos de Excommunicatione disceptamus. Sed esto, sic dixerit. An propterea me credere iubes? Cur ergo non in alijs quoque eidem tu similiter credis? Hoc scio, D.Lutherum, si viueret, non petiturum, vt hac in re ipsi crederem, cum prorsus mihi persuadeam, eum hoc in loco nomine excommunicationis liberius vsum fuisse. Ex Aben Ezra Iudaeo testimonium cum adscriberes, tuum potius somnium aliquod addidisses. Facilius enim tibi, quàm Iudaeo sine scripturis loquenti credidero.
units.tr: But Luther, you say, called Cain excommunicated; I expected you would add Calvin too. If Dr. Luther said this, he used the word not in its proper sense, as we are disputing about excommunication. But grant that he said so. Are you bidding me to believe it on that account? Why, then, do you not believe the same man in other matters as well? I know this much: if Dr. Luther were alive, he would not ask me to believe him in this matter, since I am quite persuaded that in this place he used the word excommunication rather loosely. When you cite the Jew Aben Ezra as a witness, you have added some dream of your own. I would more easily believe you than a Jew speaking without Scripture.

units.la: Argumentum tuum tertium, (quarto loco à te positum fuit) tale est. Ex verbis Num.19. scriptis efficitur, immundos, de quibus ibi agitur, à reliquorum commercio per septimanam exclusos fuisse: & nisi rite prius expiati fuissent, quàm se alijs miscerent, ex numero Israelitarum exterminatos, id est, non alio loco habitos fuisse, quàm quo habebantur incircumcisi. De prima & secunda parte nunquam dubitaui. Vtrunque enim scriptura dicit: & causa mox plenius intelligetur. At quod exscindi & exterminari idem significent hoc loco, quod, pro incircumciso haberi, neque tu, neque alius quisquam in sempiternum probabit. Dicam audacter. Si ex Hebraea lingua, quam non intelligo, Septuaginta interpretes recte & proprie sunt interpretati, (in primo loco legimus ἐκτεμνέσθω, in secutido ἐξολοθρευθήσεται) nimium audax & indiffimulanter malus est, qui negat idem significare, ac interfici vel occidi. Quod si ergo idem hoc intelligis per haec verba, pro incircumciso haberi, recte sentis, at male loqueris: & causam tuam nulla in re meliorem facis. Quis enim consecutionem hanc concedat: Moses monuit tales occidione deletum iri, Ergo probauit Excommunicationem Allobrogicam? Si aliter sentis, & hoc sciens & prudens facis, nefariè facis. Nec aliud hic respondere volo.
units.tr: Your third argument (which you placed fourth) is this: from the words of Num. 19 it follows that the unclean, of whom it speaks there, were shut out from the company of the rest for seven days; and unless they had first been properly purified before mixing with others, they were cut off from the number of the Israelites, that is, they were regarded as no other than the uncircumcised.
