I have never doubted the first and second parts; Scripture says both, and the reason will soon be understood more fully. But that to be cut off and to be destroyed mean the same here as to be regarded as uncircumcised neither you nor anyone else will prove for all eternity. I will say it boldly: if the Septuagint translators rightly and properly rendered the Hebrew, which I do not understand (in the first place we read ἐκτεμνέσθω [let him be cut off], in the second ἐξολοθρευθήσεται [he shall be utterly destroyed]), then he is far too bold and plainly wicked who denies that these mean the same as being killed or put to death. If, therefore, you understand by these words "to be regarded as uncircumcised," you think rightly but speak badly, and you do not make your cause any better in any respect. For who would grant this inference: Moses warned that such people would be destroyed by death; therefore he proved Allobrogian excommunication? If you think otherwise, and do so knowingly and deliberately, you act wickedly. I do not wish to answer anything else here.

units.la: Argumentum tuum quartum, sumitur ab immunditia ceremoniali seu legali. Caeterum quia me vides argumentum hoc tam paruifacere, vt penè insanire putem, qui ad illud confugiunt, conaris tu rationes nostras refellere. Quomodo confutes, nondum vidi: & priusquam videam, & ad obiectiones tuas respondeam, causas ordine aliquot referam, cur existimem nullo modo fieri posse, vt aliquis sanæ mentis vel mediocris Theologus, (saltem post admonitionem nostram)hinc Excommunicationem,de qua inter nos controuersemur, comprobari firmaríque credat. Ero fortasse hac in parte longior: attamen oratum volo lectores, vt me excusatum habeant. Quoniam enim tam multi hic impingunt,fusius explicanda haec res visa est.
units.tr: Your fourth argument is drawn from ceremonial or legal uncleanness. But since you see that I think so little of this argument that I almost believe those who take refuge in it are out of their minds, you try to refute our reasons. I have not yet seen how you will refute them. Before I see it, and before I answer your objections, I will set out in order several reasons why I think it impossible for anyone of sound mind or of average theological learning (at least after our admonition) to believe that by this argument the excommunication we are disputing about can be proved or confirmed. I shall perhaps be rather long on this point, but I ask my readers to forgive me. Since so many stumble here, it seemed right to explain this matter at greater length.

units.la: Libri primi finis.
units.tr: The end of the first book.

units.la: Secundus Liber incipit. CAP. I.
units.tr: The Second Book begins. Chapter I.

units.la: De immunditia Legis & morum.
units.tr: On the uncleanness of the Law and of morals.

units.la: Mmunditia duplex reperitur in scripturis. Vna est impuritas Legis, quam externam, corporalem,& Ceremonialem vocare possumus. Altera turpitudo est morum, quam itidem solemus moralem appellare, seu morum viciositatem. Quaeritur ergo nunc,an illa sic figurarit hanc, vt quemadmodum, qui lege immundus erat, ex mandato Dei à sacris & Tabernaculo arcebatur, ita etiam qui graue peccatum commisit, à Sacramentis nostris sit tantisper repellendus, (etiamsi, qui reus est, eis vti velit & cupiat) dum Presbyteris quibusdam iudicetur idoneus, qui ad ea rursus admittatur. Ad hanc quæstionem veluti ad certum scopum, referenda sunt omnia, quae de hac re dicemus. Nos ergo negamus immunditiam Legis hactenus significauisse obscoenitatem morum, vt hinc probari possit, eádem pœna externa plecti vtramque debere: sententiámq; nostram nostrā multis ac validis ex scriptura depromptis argumentis comprobamus. Tam enim multae ac magnae inter has duas deformitates exsistunt differentiae, vt vnius proprietates non possint in alteram sic transferri, vt inde probetur, vnam eandémque pœnam externam vtrique constitutam fuisse.
units.tr: Uncleanness is found in two forms in Scripture. One is the impurity of the Law, which we may call external, bodily and ceremonial. The other is the depravity of morals, which we are likewise accustomed to call moral, or the viciousness of conduct. The question now is whether the former prefigured the latter, so that just as one who was unclean under the Law was excluded from the sacred things and the Tabernacle by God's command, so too one who has committed a grave sin ought to be kept for a time from our Sacraments (even if he, being guilty, wishes and desires to partake of them), until he is judged fit by certain Elders to be admitted to them again. Everything we shall say on this subject should be referred to this question as to a fixed target. We therefore deny that the uncleanness of the Law has hitherto signified the foulness of morals, so that it might be proved that both should be punished by the same external penalty; and we confirm our view with many strong arguments drawn from Scripture. For so many and great differences exist between these two deformities that the properties of the one cannot be transferred to the other in such a way as to prove that one and the same external penalty was appointed for both.

units.la: Primùm quidem accidebat multis impuritas Legis præ- ter & côtra suam voluntatem: vt cum noctu aliquis polluebatur: aut Gonorrhœa corripiebatur: aut vxori condormierat, cui vel menses profluere cœperant, vel muliebris fluxus superuenerat: aut morientibus liberis, parentibus, vxori, fratribus, alijs aderat. Omnia haec tametsi contra voluntātem frequenter nonnullis euenirêt, immundi nihilominus erant, immundus similiter erat, qui rem immundam in Lege prohibitam vel nescienter tetigisset. Cæterum scelerate nullus viuit contra propriam suam voluntatem, sed volentes male agunt, quicunque viciosè agunt. Quocirca manifestū est, non vtrosque eadem pœna externa afficiendos.
units.tr: First, the uncleanness of the Law happened to many beyond and against their will: as when someone was polluted at night, or was seized with gonorrhoea, or had lain with a wife whose menses had begun to flow or whose womb-flux had come upon her, or was present at the dying of children, parents, wife, brothers or others. Although all these things frequently happened to some against their will, they were nonetheless unclean; likewise unclean was one who had touched an unclean thing forbidden in the Law, even unknowingly. But no one lives wickedly against his own will; whoever acts viciously, acts willingly and badly. Hence it is clear that both should not be punished with the same external penalty.

units.la: Secundò constat, Deum nullo in loco purè simpliciterque iussisse Iudæis, vt omnem fugerent immunditiam Legis quouis loco & tempore. Equidem non præcepit eis, vt nullo modo polluerentur: sed pollutis imperauit, vt secundum præsinitionem Legis semper purificarentur: aut si id facere recusarent, occiderentur, Num. 19. Sanè Deus voluit in suo populo esse, qui morientibus adessent, qui funera curarent, qui mortuos sepelirent, qui lustrali aqua pollutos aspergerent ac purgarent: licet omnes illi, qui talia facerent, immundi necessariò redderentur. An eodem modo concessam nobis à Deo facultatem dicemus aliquo tempore & loco scelerate viuendi? Non arbitror: cum omnia facta turpia sub grauissimis pœnis semper & vbique vetuerit.
units.tr: Secondly, it is established that God nowhere simply and plainly commanded the Jews to flee every uncleanness of the Law in every place and time. Indeed he did not order them never to be defiled; but to those who were defiled he commanded that they be purified according to the prescription of the Law, or, if they refused to do so, they were to be killed (Num. 19). Surely God wished that among his people there should be those who would attend the dying, who would care for funerals, who would bury the dead, and who would sprinkle and cleanse the defiled with lustral water, although all who did such things necessarily became unclean. Shall we say that a freedom to live wickedly at some time and place was granted to us by God in the same way? I do not think so, since he has always and everywhere forbidden all wicked deeds under the gravest penalties.

units.la: Tertiò potuit vir optimus & sanctissimus tunc, cum nihil omninò mali & flagitiosi cogitaret aut faceret, Legaliter immundus reddi: vt ex his, quae nunc diximus omnes perspiciunt. At flagitiosus non simul & agit scelerate purus est ac sanctus. Proinde necesse est infinitiès accidisse, vt nullo scelere deformatus, sed inculpatè viuens, immundus hoc modo fieret, atque ad Templum & Sacrificia ire prohiberetur, dum omni turpitudinis genere contaminatus alius, (at secundum Legem mundus) in templum ingrederetur, Diuinóque cultui adesset. Caeterum non mandasse Deum Mosi, vt alios vllos à Templo excluderet, quàm legaliter sordidatos, certo est certius. Quippe neque vnum neque dimidium verbum in omnibus Mosis libris exstat, quo sceleribus inquinati arceri à Templo, ceremonijs, cultúque Dei iubeantur, vt mox pluribus ostendetur. Hoc in loco sufficiat nobis exemplum Adulterae in Templum adductae à Pharisaeis Iohan.8. Ab hac Templum constat minimè fuisse profanatum (alias enim non introduxissent eam Pharisaei,) cum immundus aut Gentilis omninò profanauisset.
units.tr: Thirdly, a most good and most holy man could, at a time when he was thinking or doing nothing at all evil or shameful, be made legally unclean, as everyone sees from what we have just said. But a wicked man is not at the same time acting wickedly and also pure and holy. Therefore it must very often have happened that one living blamelessly, free of any crime, became unclean in this way and was forbidden to go to the Temple and the sacrifices, while another, polluted by every kind of foulness (yet clean according to the Law), entered the temple and took part in divine worship. Moreover, it is more than certain that God did not command Moses to exclude from the Temple any others except those legally defiled. Indeed not one word nor half a word is found in all the books of Moses by which those stained with crimes are ordered to be kept from the Temple, the ceremonies and the worship of God, as will soon be shown at greater length. For the present let the example of the adulteress brought to the Temple by the Pharisees (John 8) suffice for us. It is certain that the Temple was by no means profaned by her (otherwise the Pharisees would not have brought her in), whereas an unclean or Gentile person would have profaned it altogether.

units.la: 4 Hinc aliud discrimen oritur, ab vtriusque poena summtum. Legis enim sordes eiectione è castris puniebantur: Moralis foeditas igne, gladio, laqueo, plagis, seruitute, multa, mutilatione, carcere seu vinculis, castigabatur. Quocirca cum constat dissimilibus poenis vno eodémque tempore affectos fuisse hoc vel illo modo sordidatos, constat illud etiam, quod de principio dictum est, nempe legis maculam non sic significauisse morum viciositatem, vt illius poena huius quoque poena possit existimari. Sanè Moses à ceremonijs & Templo seu Tabernaculo repulit omnes secundum Legem immundos, tametsi nulla sua culpa polluti essent: at solos illos sceleratos, quicunque volentes ac scientes facinus aliquod perpetrasserent, plecti iussit: non negatione Sacrificiorum, sed poenis nuper dictis.
units.tr: 4 From this arises another difference, taken from the penalty of each. For the filth of the Law was punished by expulsion from the camp; moral foulness was chastised by fire, sword, noose, blows, slavery, fine, mutilation, prison or chains. Hence, since it is established that people stained in this or that way were affected at the same time by dissimilar penalties, it also follows what was said at the beginning, namely that the stain of the Law did not so signify the viciousness of morals that its penalty could be thought to be the penalty of the other too. Indeed Moses removed from the ceremonies and from the Temple or Tabernacle all who were unclean according to the Law, although they were defiled without any fault of their own; but he commanded that only those criminals who, willingly and knowingly, had committed some crime be punished, and not by denial of sacrifices but by the penalties just mentioned.

units.la: 5 Etsi enim cum eo, qui inuitus & contra suam voluntatem homicidium, exempli gratia, commisisset, longè mitius ageretur, non tamen eodem poenae genere afficiebatur, quo legaliter immundus affici solebat. Quod si alteram impuritatem ab altera significari voluisset, quomodo nunc aliqui putant, poenas quoque respondere oportuisset.
units.tr: 5 For although one who had committed homicide, for example, unwillingly and against his will was treated much more mildly, he was nonetheless not subjected to the same kind of penalty by which one legally unclean was usually affected. But if the one impurity had been meant to signify the other, as some now think, the penalties too would have had to correspond.

units.la: Differunt sextò, quod facinorosi capite puniebantur, etiamsi paenituisset eos admissi facinoris: sicut è contra qui legaliter immundi fuerant facti, quantumuis volentes tales essent, certis ceremonijs certóque temporis spacio ab immundicia sua vel inuiti liberabantur. Quamobrem vt facinorosis, siue eos facinoris sui paeniteret siue non paeniteret, poena non minuebatur: ita legaliter immundis, siue dolerent propter factum suum, siue non dolerêt, nec poena augebatur, nec purgationis tempus prorogabatur. Deus singulis immunditiæ speciebus certam purificationis formulam, certúmque tempus praescripsit. Quae qui seruauerat, mundus erat, próque mundo habebatur, etsi eum facti sui non paenituisset. Nulli enim constituti fuerunt Iudices, qui in hanc rem inquirerent, quomodò volunt hodiè Seniores quosdam hisce rebus occupari. At animi turpitudo nullo tempore potest definiri: cum alij citò, alij tardè, alij nunquam relipiscant.
units.tr: Sixthly, they differ in that criminals were punished with death even if they repented of the crime committed; whereas, on the contrary, those who had become legally unclean were freed from their uncleanness by certain ceremonies and within a fixed span of time, whether willing or unwilling, however much they wished to be such. So just as the penalty for criminals was not lessened whether or not they regretted their crime, so for the legally unclean neither was the penalty increased nor the time of purification extended, whether they grieved over their deed or not. God prescribed for each kind of uncleanness a fixed form of purification and a fixed time. Whoever kept these was clean and was regarded as clean, even if he did not regret his deed. For no judges were appointed to inquire into this matter, as you now wish certain Elders to be occupied with such things today. But the foulness of the mind can be defined at no time, since some repent quickly, others slowly, and others never.

units.la: 7 In modo etiam purificationis seu emundationis manifestum est discrimen. Quippe turpitudo Legis aqua communi plerunq; eluebatur: sæpè aqua lustrali, de qua Num. 19. legimus, emundabatur: nonnunquam alia ratione tollebatur. At morum viciositas, si in scelus erupisset, sola morte facinorosi expiabatur: si leuius esset peccatum, vel certis sacrificiis, vel multa, vel seruitute, vel plagis aliquot abstergebatur. Quo pacto igitur altera potest alterius figura sic censeri, vt similis poena statuatur vtrique, cum non poenas modo infinitè differentes, verumetiam dispares omninò purgationes Deus praescripserit?
units.tr: 7 The difference is also plain in the manner of purification or cleansing. For the foulness of the Law was generally washed away with water, often it was cleansed with lustral water, of which we read in Num. 19, and sometimes it was removed in another way. But the viciousness of morals, if it had broken out into crime, was expiated by the death of the criminal alone; if the sin was lighter, it was wiped away either by certain sacrifices, or by a fine, or by slavery, or by some blows. How then can one be considered the figure of the other, so that a similar penalty is laid down for both, when God has prescribed not only penalties infinitely different but also purifications utterly dissimilar?

units.la: .. Octauò differunt, quod Legaliter immundus arcebatur à templo quocunque & quacunque de causa immundus esset. Non enim in immunditia discrimen hac in parte erat, sed in tempore. Plerique enim cum occidente Sole aqua abluti mundabantur, Alij septimum expectare diem cogebantur. Nonnullos, vt Leprosos, & Gonorrhoea laborantes finem morbi expectare Lex iubebat. In hoc autem erant similes omnes, quod interim dū immundi essent, à Sacrificijs remouebantur. At non omnes improbos hodie vultis arceri à Sacramentis, sed quosdam solùm. Quare non est verum, quod dicitis, impuritatem Legis significasse turpitudinem morum: sed quosdā duntaxat significauisset corruptos mores. Hos ergo cum ex sacris literis determinare non possitis, liquet hîc quoque non respondere vobis hanc ceremoniam. Si maximè aliquos praefigurasset, non posset hoc tamen de illis intelligi, quos speciatim Lex puniri certis constitutis poenis mandat. Itaque de leuioribus accipiendum esset peccatis: quae ne vos quidem vultis Excommunicatione vindicari. Scriptura docet viciosos ad cultum rectum veramque agnitionem Dei & sui inuitandos esse studiosius, & admonendos diligentius, (interim non debet officium suum negligere Magistratus) quo, tandem mores corrigant, vitámque emendent.
units.tr: Eighthly, they differ in that one legally unclean was excluded from the Temple whatever the cause of his uncleanness. For the difference in uncleanness did not lie in this respect, but in the time. For most, when the sun had set, were made clean by being washed with water; others were compelled to wait for the seventh day. Some, such as lepers and those suffering from gonorrhoea, the Law commanded to await the end of the disease. In this all were alike, that meanwhile, while they were unclean, they were kept away from the sacrifices. But you wish not all the wicked to be kept today from the Sacraments, but only some. Therefore it is not true, as you say, that the uncleanness of the Law signified the foulness of morals; rather it would have signified only certain corrupt morals. Since you cannot determine these from the sacred letters, it is clear that here too this ceremony does not correspond to you. Even if it had prefigured some persons, this could not be understood of those whom the Law specifically orders to be punished with certain fixed penalties. It would therefore have to be understood of lighter sins, which you yourselves do not wish to be avenged by excommunication. Scripture teaches that the vicious are to be invited more earnestly to right worship and to the true knowledge of God and of themselves, and admonished more diligently (meanwhile the magistrate ought not neglect his duty), so that at last they may correct their morals and amend their lives.

units.la: Nonò differunt, quod, qui iuxta Legem immundus erat, etiamsi longo tempore, imò per totam vitam talis permaneret, (vt si vir Gonorrhoea vel Lepra esset affectus: aut si mulier menstruis vel profluuio muliebri laboraret) non tamen pro non Iudaeo, vel non circumcisō, aut pro improbo damnatoue habebatur. Cogebatur nihilominus secundùm ritus patrios viuere, Sabbathum custodire, aliâque talia facere. Quinetiam à Sacramento Expiationis generalis, quae die 10. Mensis Septemb. peragebatur, Leuit. 16. & 23. immundi nulli excludebantur. Etenim Deus per Mosen expresse mandauit, vt sub poena excidijsui omnis anima in populo Iudaico, nulla facta exceptione vel immundorum vel aliorum, illo die, quo Sacerdos in Sanctum-sanctorum ingredicebatur, ad expiandum totius populi peccata, dolorem suum luctu, ieiunio aliisque ceremonijs testificaretur. Ex quo pueri etiam intelligant, non fuisse de immundorum iuxta Legem salute dubitatum, etiamsi in illa impuritate obijssent mortem. Certissimè constat, nullum exstare in sacris literis locum, qui doceat, hosce vel à Deo, vel ab hominibus pro deploratis malisque, siue pro Ethnicis & publicanis habitos fuisse. Poterant enim hi morbi, vt etiam hodie contingit,
units.tr: Ninthly, they differ in this: one who was unclean under the Law, even if he stayed so for a long time, indeed for his whole life (as when a man was afflicted with gonorrhoea or leprosy, or a woman suffered from menstruation or a female flux), was nonetheless not regarded as a non-Jew, an uncircumcised person, or a wicked and condemned man. He was still compelled to live according to the ancestral rites, keep the Sabbath and do other such things. Moreover, the unclean were not excluded from the sacrament of general atonement, which was celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month, Lev. 16 and 23. For God expressly commanded through Moses that, under penalty of being cut off, every soul among the Jewish people, with no exception made for the unclean or anyone else, should on that day, when the priest entered the Holy of Holies to expiate the sins of the whole people, bear witness to their sorrow by mourning, fasting and other ceremonies. From this even boys may understand that there was no doubt about the salvation of the unclean under the Law, even if they died in that impurity. It is most certain that no passage of the sacred writings teaches that these people were held by God or by men to be abandoned and evil, or to be heathens and tax collectors. For these diseases could, as even today happens, fall upon the best people no less than upon criminals.

units.la: gic, git, in optimos quosque non minus, quàm in facinorosos, cadere. Hoc autem quo pacto accommodabimus sceleratis vel excommunicatis? Sanè nullus est excommunicator, qui nō valde metuat, ne damnati sint, qui exclusi moriuntur.
units.tr: But how shall we apply this to the wicked or the excommunicated? Surely there is no excommunicator who does not greatly fear that those who die excluded are damned.

units.la: Magistratus quoque nulla poena afficere illum poterat, qui propter durabilem morbum per omnem vitam immundus manebat. Sed si quis scelerate agere viuerèque pergat, cum non debet Magistratus immunitum sinere.
units.tr: Nor could the magistrate impose any punishment on one who remained unclean for his whole life because of a lasting disease. But if someone persists in living wickedly, the magistrate must not allow him to go unpunished.

units.la: Vndecima differentia est, quod Legalis turpitudo certè solùm tempore, inque certa duntaxat Gente locum habuit. Nam apud solos Iudaeos post Mosen valuit. Morum autem turpitudo semper & vbique turpis fuit, est, erit. Et cum hec fuisset antequam illa ordinaretur, ac maneat postquam illa esse desijt (imò cum non minus tunc fuerit, cum illa vigeret, quàm nunc sit, postquàm illa tot seculis abolita exstinctaque permansit) non video, quomodo hanc illa repraesentare figurareque sic debuerit, vt figurauisse vos contenditis. Vmbrae corporibus cedunt, & figurae desinunt; cum res figuratae esse incipiunt, quoties res externa externam figurat. Nam de internis aliter sentiendum est. Sed neque tunc, cum Legis immunditia observabatur, vicia non erant: neque postquam observari desijt, vicia primùm sunt nota: neque minus etiam nota sunt aut fuerunt vicia ista turpitudine Legis, vt per eam scelera nobis depingenda fuerint. Ex quibus satis liquet, non sic ipsam significauisse vicia, vt argumento inde sumpto Excommunicatio fulciri queat.
units.tr: The eleventh difference is that legal filthiness had its force only for a certain time and among one particular people. For it held sway only among the Jews after Moses. But the filthiness of morals has always and everywhere been filthy, is so now, and will be. And since this existed before that was ordained, and remains after it ceased to be (indeed it was no less filthy then, while that law was in force, than it is now, after that law has been abolished and extinguished for so many centuries), I do not see how that law could represent and figure this in the way you contend it did. Shadows give way to bodies, and figures cease when the things they figure begin to exist; this holds whenever an external thing figures an external thing. For internal things must be judged otherwise. But neither was vice absent when the uncleanness of the Law was observed, nor were vices first known when its observance ceased; nor are those vices any less known, or were they less known, through the filthiness of the Law, so that they had to be depicted to us by it. From these points it is quite clear that the Law did not signify vices in such a way that excommunication could be supported by an argument drawn from it.

units.la: Duodecimum discrimen ex eo nascitur, quod aliquis mundus tangens rem mundam, quae aliorum impuritatem abstergeret ac tolleret, immuudus reddebatur. Equidem qui aquam lustralem, qua plurimos immundos oportebat purgari, te tigerat, eáque alios conspergerat, purgandi gratiâ, immundus erat vsque ad vesperâ, quo tempore aquâ se haud aliter abluere cogebatur, ac si rem quampiam immundam contrectâsset, Num. 19. At quae sceleratum efficiunt animum, ea nequaquam viciositatem curant: nec quae aliorum flagitiis medentur, flagitiosum aliquem reddunt. Proinde hic quoque magna reperietur inter vtramq; dissimilitudo. Sic enim qui à scelere alium liberaret, eo ipso, quo alium sanaret, seipsum scelere inquinaret: quod longè absurdissimum est cogitatu.
units.tr: The twelfth difference arises from this: someone who, being clean, touched a clean thing that was meant to cleanse and remove the impurity of others became unclean himself. Indeed, one who sprinkled the lustral water, with which many unclean persons had to be purified, and sprinkled others with it for the sake of their purification, remained unclean until evening, when he was compelled to wash himself with water just as if he had touched some unclean thing, Num. 19. But things that make a criminal mind do nothing to cure vice, and those that remedy the crimes of others do not make anyone criminal. So here too a great dissimilarity will be found between the two. For someone who freed another from crime would, by the very act of healing another, defile himself with crime, which is the most absurd thing imaginable.

units.la: 13 Addé quod, quo tempore Moses legaliter immundos arcuit à Tabernaculo & Sacrificiis, plurimi mali & flagitiosi fuerunt, ipsemet testé. Proinde consequeretur ipsum eodem tempore eandem rem concessisse ac prohibuisse. Si enim Legis deformitas significauit probrosos homines Sacramentorum negatione coercendos esse, atque eodem tempore tales multos ipse admisit, quod historia demonstrat: consequens est, vt, quod in figura prohibuit, hoc in ipsa re significata permiserit: quod est absurdum dictu pariter & cogitatu.
units.tr: 13. Add that at the time when Moses legally excluded the unclean from the Tabernacle and the sacrifices, many were evil and wicked, as he himself attests. It would follow that at the same time he both conceded and forbade the same thing. For if the deformity of the Law signified that disreputable men must be restrained by exclusion from the sacraments, and at the same time he himself admitted many such men, as history shows, it follows that what he forbade in the figure he permitted in the thing signified. That is absurd to say and to think.

units.la: 14 Taceo quod figurae nullae ponuntur rerum praesentium, sed futurarum. Loquor de rebus externis, quando scilicet signum & signata res externae res sunt, & vtraque æquè nota est. Quod ideo moneo, ne mihi aliquis obijciat circumcisionem, quae praesentis rei imago fuerit. Non enim nescio res internas & spirituales, quas propter imbecillitatem nostram absque externis adminiculis non possimus rectè perspicere, nobis à Deo externis ritibus ac ceremoniis velut simulachris quibusdam adumbrari. At furta & homicidia non minùs incurrunt in oculos nostros, nec minùs nota nobis sunt, denique frequentius nobis occurrunt, quàm contactus excrementi aut cadaueris. Quocirca frustra nobis talia conetur aliquis per aliarum rerum species depingere. Summa est, Deum tunc per legalem immunditiam, ceu per quandam figuram non voluisse docere, quomodo scelera coercenda forent. Hoc enim docuit apertis & explicatis verbis absque omni figura & vmbra, eodem illo tempore, quo secundum Legem pollutos ad purificationem vsque iussit accedi ab aliorum societate.
units.tr: 14. I pass over the point that figures are set for present things, not future ones. I speak of external things, when the sign and the thing signified are both external and equally known. I note this so that no one objects to me circumcision, which might be an image of a present thing. For I am not unaware that inner and spiritual things, which because of our weakness we cannot discern clearly without external aids, are shadowed forth to us by God through external rites and ceremonies, as through certain likenesses. But thefts and murders fall no less under our eyes, nor are they less known to us; indeed they meet us more often than contact with excrement or a corpse. So it is in vain that anyone tries to depict such things to us through the appearances of other things. In sum, God did not wish to teach, through the legal uncleanness as through some figure, how crimes ought to be restrained. For He taught this in plain and explained words, without any figure or shadow, at the very time when, according to the Law, He commanded the defiled to be kept from the company of others until purification.

units.la: Decimoquintò, docet idem, hoc Leprae consideratio. Primum enim certum est, domos, vestes, ligna, lapides, suppellectilem alium; non esse capacem Leprae animi, seu viciositatis morum: at haec omnia Lepra legali infici poterant. Quae ratio etsi in alijs quoque immunditiae speciebus certo modo valet, huic tamen peculiariter competit. Deinde nihil iubentur pro sanatione facere, sed tantum a Deo liberationem exspectare. At sceleratis imperatur, ut vitam corrigant, scelerraque fugiant. Possunt igitur hi se liberare a poena, saltem simulate, si non vere: at illi tale nihil poterant. Tertio praescripsit Deus formam Sacerdotibus secundum quam inter Lepram & Lepram dijudicent, & iuxta quam sanatum aliquem aut non sanatum pronuncient: ipsi pro salute eius nihil facere iubentur. Quae ipsa quoque nullus hominum apte & vere poterit animi leprae, eiusdemque sanationi & dijudicationi aptare. Longe aliter facinorosos a ministris tractari conueniet, si exstinguere lepram istam animorum velint. Postremo qui totus sic erat leprosus, ut vniuersae cutis color vnus idemque esset, non varius, pro mundo habebatur Leuit. 13. Dicemusne ergo illum carere sceleribus, proque sancto tenebimus & innocente, qui sic est vicijs coopertus, ut nihil habeat in se amplius boni & honesti? Caeterum nequis arbitretur aliam esse citati loci sententiam, verba Philonis hac de re ex libro περὶ φιλαρχίας, vbi de virgis Iacobi varicoloribus loquitur, adscribam. [Greek passage transcribed as printed: πάρ' ἓ ἰχ ῖν τοῦ περὶ τῆς λέπρας τεχνῶν γένες δισέρνπτα, τὸν μικρὸν ... ] Dicit autem λευκωθίσα, quoniam Lepra quaedam erat alba instar niuis, ut ex Leuit. cap. 13. Exod. 4. Num. 12. & 2. Reg. 5. apparet.
units.tr: Fifteenth, the consideration of leprosy teaches the same thing. For first, it is certain that houses, garments, wood, stones and other household goods are not capable of the leprosy of the soul, or of moral vice; yet all these could be infected with legal leprosy. Although this reasoning holds in some way for the other kinds of uncleanness too, it applies to this one in particular. Next, they are commanded to do nothing for their healing, but only to await deliverance from God. But the wicked are commanded to correct their lives and flee their crimes. These men can therefore free themselves from punishment, at least in pretence if not in truth; but those others could do nothing of the kind. Third, God prescribed to the priests a form by which they were to distinguish one leprosy from another, and by which they were to pronounce someone healed or not healed; yet they are not commanded to do anything for his health. No man can aptly and truly apply this to the leprosy of the soul, or to its healing and judgment. Criminals should be treated quite differently by the ministers if they wish to extinguish that leprosy of the mind. Lastly, one who was so wholly leprous that the colour of his entire skin was one and the same, not varied, was considered clean, Lev. 13. Shall we then say that he lacks crimes, and hold him holy and innocent, when he is so covered with vices that he has nothing good or honest left in himself? Moreover, lest anyone think the sense of the cited passage is different, I shall add Philo's words on this matter from his book On the Love of Rule, where he speaks of Jacob's variegated rods: [πάρ' ἓ ἰχ ῖν τοῦ περὶ τῆς λέπρας τεχνῶν γένες δισέρνπτα, τὸν μικρὸν ...]. He says leukōthisa [λευκωθίσα], since a certain leprosy was white as snow, as appears from Lev. 13, Exod. 4, Num. 12 and 2 Kings 5.

units.la: Illud insuper propositum nostrum declarat simul ac probat quod non recte cum sceleribus comparetur legis immunditia. Etenim haec macula seu foeditas, qualitas quaedam fuit ac dispositio: at scelera sunt actiones, opera, & fructus quidam eius vicij, quod in hominum animis insitum latet. Proinde non debet haec corporis deformitas & qualitas cum prauis actionibus conferri: Sed cum animi nostri morbo ingenitaque naturae nostrae foeditate & distorsione. Nam vt aliud est immunditia, & aliud actio immundi, quoad immundus est: sic aliud est vitium nobis congenitum, & aliud rursus actio eius seu flagitium. Iccirco qualitatem qualitati, & actiones actionibus comparare conuenit: non autem disputationem vnam operationibus alterius dispositionis. Ergo per immunditiam legis figurata nobis fuit naturæ nostræ corruptio & deformitas, causa videlicet scelerum: non ipsa scelera.
units.tr: This also both declares and proves our point, that the uncleanness of the Law is wrongly compared with crimes. For this stain or foulness was a certain quality and disposition; but crimes are actions, works and certain fruits of that vice which lies hidden, implanted in men's minds. Therefore this bodily deformity and quality should not be compared with wicked actions, but with the disease of our mind and the innate foulness and distortion of our nature. Just as uncleanness is one thing and the action of the unclean man, so far as he is unclean, is another, so the vice innate in us is one thing and its action or shameful deed is another. Hence it is right to compare quality with quality and actions with actions, not one kind of operation with a different kind of disposition. Therefore through the uncleanness of the Law there was figured to us the corruption and deformity of our nature, the cause of crimes, but certainly not the crimes themselves.

units.la: Itasi ceremoniam istam interpretemur, pulchrè consentire omnia reperiemus, quæ de ea scripta inuenimus. Constat terrestrem Hierosolymam terræque promissæ possessionem, speciem quandam fuisse Regni cœlestis. Proinde vt ibi in Tabernaculum immundi nulli, siue aliena siue propria culpa talēs fuissent facti, admittebantur antè purgationem: sic nullus in cœleste Regnum intromittetur, nisi qui animæ naturæque suæ deformitatem aqua lustrali, sanguine videlicet Christi cluerit. Sanctus enim Deus, sanctumque regnum eius: in quo maculatum nullum feret, siue volens siue nolens, sit contaminatus. Quippe vt immunditia legis & volentibus & nolentibus obrepebat, sic naturæ nostræ distorsionem sibi volentes accessuerunt Parentes nostri comestione vetiti pomi, quod poterant non edere: nos autem eandem ab ipsis nolentes ac nescientes accepimus. Sic intellexerunt hanc ceremoniam Iudæi veteres, vt ex Philone perspicimus. Sic D. Ioh. in 21. cap. Apocalyps. exponere voluisse videtur. Sic & Prophetæ nobis eam videntur proposuisse intelligendam, vt ex Esa. cap. 52. & Ioelis 3. apparet. Paulus quoque Apostolus in Epist. ad Hebræos, præsertim cap. 9. huc respexisse videtur. Huc & illud Augustini contra Donatistas scribentis pertinere videtur, vbi non minus scitè quam verè monet, tum prædicta, tum alia scripturæ loca omnia, quæ Ecclesiam dicunt absque immunditia fore, de altero seculo exponenda intelligendaq; esse. Hisce consonat historia Petri, Act. 10. & 11:cap. Cum enim iussus esset immunda animalia edere, atque ille recusaret cusaret, vocem audiuit dicentem, Quod Deus purificauit, tu ne polluas. Hanc visionem cum non intelligeret, à spiritu sancto edoctus est, immunda animalia, quæ edere noluerat, significauisse Gentes, hoc est, fide vera carentes. Ideo Act. 15. cum disceptatio orta fuisset, an & Gentes, quç ad Christum conuerterentur, oporteret circumcidi, & Mosis legem seruare, ait inter alia Petrus. Deus inter nos & ex Gentibus conuersos nihil discreuit, fide purificatis eorum cordibus. Hic minifestè audimus immunditiam legalè denotauisse naturæ nostræ corruptionem seu infidelitatem: & immunda animalia figurauisse homines à Deo alienos fideq; destitutos. Si enim fides purificauit hactenus Gentes, vt inter ipsas & Iudæos nihil Deus discriminis poneret, necessarium omninò est, vt infidelitas & ignoratio Dei, siue naturæ nostræ corruptio, illa esset immunditia, quam legalis illa figurabat. Quam enim labè abstergit à cordibus nostris aliam fides in Christum, vt nos purificet, quàm eam, per quam nascimur filij iræ, quámque ex parentibus nostris nascendo contrahimus? Nullam. Itaque dubitare de hac re porrò non possumus, si modo Spiritussanᴄti interpretationi fidem habere volumus. Ergo sicut legalis pollutio tum aqua lustrali, tum alijs ablutionibus tollebatur, ita immunditia ab ea significata sanguine Christi abluitur: cum vera fiducia apprehendimus beneuolentiam & gratiam Dei in Christo exhibitam.
units.tr: If we interpret this ceremony in this way, we will find that everything written about it agrees well. It is established that earthly Jerusalem and the possession of the promised land were a certain image of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore, just as no unclean person, whether through another's fault or his own, was admitted into the Tabernacle before purification, so no one will be admitted into the heavenly kingdom unless he has washed away the deformity of his soul and nature with lustral water, that is, with the blood of Christ. For God is holy, and holy is his kingdom, and into it he will allow no one stained to enter, whether that person is willing or unwilling to be defiled. Just as the uncleanness of the law crept upon both the willing and the unwilling, so our first parents, who were willing, brought upon themselves the distortion of our nature by eating the forbidden fruit, which they could have refrained from eating; but we received the same distortion from them, unwilling and unknowing. In this way the ancient Jews understood this ceremony, as we see from Philo. In this way St John seems to have wished to expound it in chapter 21 of the Apocalypse. In this way also the Prophets seem to have set it before us to be understood, as appears from Isaiah 52 and Joel 3. The Apostle Paul also, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, especially chapter 9, seems to have had this in view. To this also seems to pertain that statement of Augustine against the Donatists, where he warns, no less wittily than truly, that all the passages of Scripture just mentioned, and others which say that the Church will be without uncleanness, are to be explained and understood of the other age. The story of Peter in Acts 10 and 11 agrees with this. When he was commanded to eat unclean animals and refused, he heard a voice saying, "What God has cleansed, do not you make unclean." Not understanding this vision, he was taught by the Holy Spirit that the unclean animals, which he had refused to eat, signified the Gentiles, that is, those who lacked true faith. So in Acts 15, when a dispute arose whether the Gentiles who were converted to Christ also had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, Peter said, among other things, that God made no distinction between us and the Gentiles who had been converted, their hearts being purified by faith. Here we plainly hear that legal uncleanness denoted the corruption or unbelief of our nature, and that the unclean animals figured men alienated from God and destitute of faith. For if faith has so purified the Gentiles that God makes no distinction between them and the Jews, it must necessarily follow that unbelief and ignorance of God, or the corruption of our nature, is that uncleanness which the law figured. For what other stain does faith in Christ wipe from our hearts, to cleanse us, than that by which we are born children of wrath, and which we contract from our parents by being born? None. Therefore we cannot doubt this any further, if we are willing to trust the interpretation of the Holy Spirit. Thus, just as legal pollution was removed both by lustral water and by other ablutions, so the uncleanness signified by it is washed away by the blood of Christ, when we apprehend with true trust the goodwill and grace of God shown in Christ.

units.la: Qui de præsentis seu visibilis Ecclesiæ statu accipiunt hanc à Templo exclusionem, ij præterquam quod plurima instituto suo nunquam poterunt aptare, manifestam quoque in scripturam inuehunt contradictionem. Quippe contradictoriæ sunt hę orationes. Mares circumcisi omnes, quicunque mundi sunt iuxta legem, Pascha celebrent: &, Qui sceleræ se polluit, etiamsi iuxta legem sit mundus, non celebret Pascha. Hęc enim tantundem significat, atque ista. Non omnis mundus iuxta legem celebret Pascha. Sic contradictoriæ sunt etiam sequentes. Omnis anima Sabbathum seruet: &, scelerè contaminatus Sabbathum non seruet. Item hæ: Omnis anima in die expiationum testificetur luctum: &, Obscœnis præditi moribus non testificentur illo die luctum. Nisi particulares hasce negantes in Sacris literis ostendas à Deo positas, necesse est, vt vel contradictoria in scriptura contineri fateris, vel sententiam tuam falsam esse concedas. Habitus igitur vel dispositio cum alterius habitus vel dispositionis operationibus comparari non possunt.
units.tr: Those who take this exclusion from the Temple as referring to the present or visible state of the Church not only will be unable to fit very many things to their interpretation, but also bring a manifest contradiction into Scripture. For these statements are contradictory: "All circumcised males who are clean according to the law shall celebrate the Passover"; and "He who pollutes himself with crime, even if he is clean according to the law, shall not celebrate the Passover." For the second means exactly the same as this: "Not every one who is clean according to the law shall celebrate the Passover." Likewise the following are contradictory: "Every soul shall keep the Sabbath"; and "one contaminated by crime shall not keep the Sabbath." Likewise these: "Every soul shall testify to mourning on the day of atonement"; and "those endowed with obscene morals shall not testify to mourning on that day." Unless you show these particular negative statements to have been laid down by God in the Sacred Letters, it is necessary either that you admit contradictions are contained in Scripture, or that you concede your opinion is false. Therefore a habit or disposition cannot be compared with the operations of another habit or disposition.

units.la: Sed nec qualitas cum qualitate hac quidem in re conferri potest. Quoniam omnis immunditia legis semper & in omnibus exclusione cohibebatur: licet contra legem nihil facerent immundi, sed ab omni coetu, sicut iuili erant, abstinerent. At nemo propter ingenitam naturæ corruptionem punitur, si scelerati aut vitiosi nihil agat. Quod si velis ab Ecclesia visibilis societate excludi mentem habentes sordidatam, etiamsi scelus nullum admiserint, omnes omnino homines secludi oportebit: quod non modo absurdum est, verumetiam cum hypothesi vestra pugnat. Quod si non dispositiones, sed actiones vtriusque impuritatis conferre inter se malis, tantundem effeceris. Vt enim alias multas differentias omittam, vt quod ingressio in Templum bona est, si mundus sit, qui ingreditur, cum sceleratum factum nullo tempore sit laudabile: & quod actio immundi non potest mala iudicari, si nesciatur ab immundo edita, cum scelus pro scelere omnes agnoscant, etiamsi hominem malum esse prius non sciuissent: (Hic enim ex actione causa, ibi ex causa actionis natura intelligitur) hoc nobis abunde sufficiet, quod actiones immundorum, quoad immundi erant, exclusione longiore non puniebantur, sed morte, Num. 19. Quocirca inde concludendum foret scelerate agentes capitali supplicio afficiendos esse: quod in grauioribus facinoribus equidem debet obseruari. Quocirca non fuit exclusio hæc, qua propter legis immunditiam aliqui prohibebantur venire in cœtus publicos, figura rei cuiuspiam in hoc seculo complendæ, sed imago & simulachrum fuit rei in altera vita perficiendæ.
units.tr: But neither can a quality be compared with a quality in this matter. For all the uncleanness of the law was always and in every case restrained by exclusion, even though the unclean did nothing against the law, but abstained from every assembly, as being unclean. But no one is punished on account of innate corruption of nature if he, though wicked or vicious, does nothing. And if you wish those who have a defiled mind to be excluded from the fellowship of the visible Church, even though they have committed no crime, it will be necessary to exclude absolutely all men: which is not only absurd, but also clashes with your hypothesis. But if you compare not the dispositions but the actions of each impurity with one another, you will have achieved the same result. For, to omit many other differences, such as that entering the Temple is good if the one entering is clean, since a wicked deed is never praiseworthy; and that the action of an unclean person cannot be judged evil if it is not known to have been done by an unclean person, since everyone recognizes a crime as a crime even if they did not previously know the man to be wicked (for here the nature is understood from the action, there the action from the nature of its cause); this will be enough for us: that the actions of the unclean, so far as they were unclean, were not punished by longer exclusion but by death, Num. 19. Hence it would follow that those who commit wicked deeds ought to be subjected to capital punishment, which indeed ought to be observed in the more grievous crimes. Therefore this exclusion, by which some were forbidden to come into public assemblies on account of legal uncleanness, was not the figure of a thing to be fulfilled in this age, but the image and likeness of a thing to be accomplished in the other life.

units.la: Ultimo loco demonstratur idem certissimè ex eo, quod iuxta legem immundus inquinabat cohabitantes, vestes, lectos, scamna, vasa, loca in quibus versabatur. Moribus autem immundus nullum contaminabat à se alium nisi consentientem. Qui immundum secundum legem, vestémque eius contrectabat, aut in domum aliquam, in qua lepra leprosiúe erat, ingrediebatur, is quoque reddebatur immundus: & purificare seu purgare se cogebatur, priusquam cum cæteris in Templum introiret. At qui cum fure vel adultero commorabatur, is non sic foedabatur, ut purificatione legis labem abstergere, hominumque consuetudinem vitare cogeretur. Quippe nullum ex sacris literis proferri testimonium poterit, quo vel patrator sceleris, vel ipsum tangens, vel locus in quo erat, probetur legali forde infectus fuisse. Sceleribus & sceleratis ubique irascitur Deus, nullibi tamen ceremonias institutas legitur, quibus vel ipsi, vel res, homines, loca, ab ipsorum contactu inquinata purgarentur. Quippe supplicio capitis, mutilatione, multa, servitute, cruciatu corporis & plagis emendari sceleratos imperauit. Aliter habet res, si de naturæ nostræ vitiositate loquamur. Etenim generans communicat generato totam hanc naturæ corruptionem, hoc est, talem generat, qualis ipse est, quod ad labem & naturæ depravationem attinet. Secus sit in operationibus. Non enim est necessarium, ut furis aut latronis filii itidem furentur aut latrocinentur, licet naturæ corruptionem necessariò participauerint à parentibus. Edit enim hæc vitiositas varios & diuersos fructus, non eosdem in omnibus.
units.tr: Lastly, the same is most certainly demonstrated by the fact that, according to the law, the unclean person defiled those living with him, and his clothes, beds, benches, vessels, and the places in which he dwelt. But a person unclean in morals defiled no one else except one who consented. Whoever touched a person unclean according to the law, or his clothing, or entered some house in which there was leprosy or the stain of leprosy, was also made unclean, and was compelled to purify or cleanse himself before he entered the Temple with the others. But he who lived with a thief or an adulterer was not so befouled as to be compelled to wipe away the stain by legal purification and to avoid human company. Indeed, no testimony can be brought forward from the Sacred Letters by which either the perpetrator of a crime, or one who touches him, or a place where he was, is shown to have been tainted with legal filth. God is everywhere angry at sins and sinners, yet nowhere do we read that ceremonies were instituted by which either the persons themselves, or things, men, and places polluted by contact with them, were purged. Indeed, he commanded that wicked men be corrected by capital punishment, mutilation, fine, servitude, bodily torment and blows. It is otherwise if we speak of the viciousness of our nature. For the begetter communicates to the begotten this whole corruption of nature; that is, he begets one such as himself, as far as stain and depravation of nature are concerned. It is different with operations. For it is not necessary that the sons of a thief or robber should likewise steal or rob, although they have necessarily shared in the corruption of nature from their parents. For this viciousness produces various and diverse fruits, not the same in all.

units.la: Cæterum quod moribus immundi, si modo legis immunditia non essent contaminati, sua improbitate Templum, Sacrificia, res mundas alias, non sic macularint, ut sanctis & probis pollutæ essent, ac purificari ceremonijs legis opus haberent, non rationibus tantum potest monstrari, sed illustrissimis quoque exemplis declarari. Quanquam: quàm verò pietatis & veritatis amantibus, præter ea, quæ iam dicta sunt, hoc vnum abundè satisfacere possit, quòd nullus scripturæ locus exstat, qui corruptè viuentes, mòdò cæremoniali immunditia carerent, probet sic inquinasse homines & loca vicina, quomodo legis impuritate infecti foedabant, non grauabor tamen exemplis aliquot hanc rem plenius declarare. In veteri Testamento legimus, Num. 5. cap. adulterij suspectam perductam fuisse ad Sacerdotem in conspectum Dei, vt periculum de ipsius castitate fieret per aquas amaras, siue illa nocens esset siue innocens: at non legimus vel eos qui adduxerunt, vel Sacerdotem, vel locum sacrificij, ad quem ducebatur, sic ab ea pollutum fuisse, quomodo ab immundis iuxta legem polluebantur. Nec excusat dubitatio vel mariti vel aliorum: Nam vt maximè patefieret aliquam nocentem esse, non tamen ideo legimus Templum fuisse pollutum. At si quem immundum iuxta legem in Templo fuisse resciuissent etiam postea, mox sanè ex præscripto verbi Dei repurgauissent.
units.tr: That the unclean, by their morals, if indeed they were not contaminated by the uncleanness of the law, did not so defile the Temple, the sacrifices, and other clean things by their wickedness as to be polluted for holy and upright people, and to need purification by the ceremonies of the law, can be shown not only by reasons but also declared by most illustrious examples. Yet for those who love piety and truth, besides what has already been said, this one thing could fully suffice: that there is no passage of Scripture which proves that people living corruptly, if they were free of ceremonial uncleanness, polluted men and neighbouring places in the way that those infected with legal impurity defiled them. Still, I shall not hesitate to declare this matter more fully by some examples. In the Old Testament we read, Num. 5, that a woman suspected of adultery was brought to the priest before the face of God, so that a test of her chastity might be made by the bitter waters, whether she were guilty or innocent. Yet we do not read that either those who brought her, or the priest, or the place of sacrifice to which she was led, were so polluted by her as they were polluted by the unclean according to the law. Nor does the doubt of the husband or of others make any difference: for although it was most plainly made evident that someone was guilty, still we do not read that the Temple was polluted. But if they had discovered that someone legally unclean had been in the Temple even afterwards, they would surely have immediately purified it again according to the prescription of God's word.

units.la: In nouo Testamento simile propemodum exemplum legimus, Iohan. 8. cap. de muliere in adulterio deprehensa. Hanc Pharisæi ad Iesum adduxerunt in Templum, quod certè facturi nunquam fuissent, si per eius præsentiam existimauissent Templi atq; semetipsos pollui. Idem à Christo, quæ vtique pro blasphemo, falso Propheta, seditioso, & vt semel dicam omnia, pro sceleratissimo, Pilato tradebant, non se putarunt inquinari, quod cum eo versarentur: at ex introitu seu contactu Prætorij maculari se non ignorârunt.
units.tr: In the New Testament we read a nearly similar example, John 8, about the woman taken in adultery. The Pharisees brought her to Jesus in the Temple. They would certainly never have done so if they had thought that the Temple and themselves would be defiled by her presence. Likewise, they handed Christ over to Pilate, whom they considered a blasphemer, a false prophet, a seditious man, and, to say everything in one word, most wicked. They did not think they were polluted by associating with him, but they knew they were stained by entering or touching the praetorium.

units.la: Patet idem ex historia Pauli Act. 21. Cum enim hominem esse iudicarent seditiosum & blasphemum, non tamen ab eo putarunt Templi fuisse pollutum: at à Græcis, quos ab ipso introductos non tam vociferabantur quàm mentiebantur, pollutum existimabant. Clarissimè igitur patet, non improbos, sed legaliter immundos, etiamsi moribus essent castissimis, Templum & cohabitantes inquinauisse. Quibus omnibus addere illud etiam potes, quod apud Math. 27. cap. de Iuda legimus his verbis. [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: The same appears from the story of Paul in Acts 21. Since they judged him to be a seditious and blasphemous man, they did not think the Temple was polluted by him. But they did think it was polluted by the Greeks, whom they cried out (and in truth lied) that Paul had brought in. It is therefore quite clear that wicked men were not the ones who polluted the Temple and those who lived in it, but men who were legally unclean, even if their morals were most pure. You may add to all this what we read in Matthew 27 about Judas, in these words: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~8 letters] ἀντιχώρησις. Cum in Templo, inquit, argenteos nummos abiecisset, seceßit. Erat ergo in Templo, vt docent circumstantiæ, cum abiceret. Neque excusat, quod dici potuit ab aliquo, eum non fuisse pro nequam habitum. Nam & Iudas confessus fuerat se innocentem prodidisse: & ipsi eum secti pactum norant: pecuniamque in Thesaurum Templi reponere noluerunt, quia pecunia esset sanguinaria & proditoria. Aperte ergo, ex veteri & novo Testamento, quod propositum erat ostendi: nec tamen Publicanorum meminisse qui vel soli sufficerent nobis ad huius rei probationem.
units.tr: [illegible] He withdrew [ἀντιχώρησις]. When he had thrown down the silver coins in the Temple, he withdrew. So, as the circumstances show, he was in the Temple when he threw them down. Nor is it an objection that someone might say he was not regarded as wicked. For Judas had confessed that he had betrayed innocent blood, and the priests knew the bargain he had made. They refused to put the money into the Temll treasury because it was blood money and the price of betrayal. It is therefore plain, from the Old and New Testaments, what we proposed to show. Nor need we mention the tax collectors, who alone would be enough for us to prove this point.

units.la: Hisce omnib' iam & istud addatur, quod neq; Moses, neq; sancti Iudices, Sacerdotes, Reges, Prophetæ, alij boni & pij a Templo & sacrificijs abstinuerunt, quia multi viciosissimi eadem secum celebrarent. Nec ideo Manna & aqua expetra Christo promanans non fuerunt sancta, quia vnà cum paucis bonis multò plures mali ederunt ac biberunt. Sic & in festo Purificationis siue Expiationis non ideo non expiabantur receptè bonorum & fideliū peccata, quia longè plurimi inter ipsos corruptissimè viuebant. An polluit anceu serpentem sceleribus pollutorum aspectus? Minimè, Progenies illa Viperarum Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum nequaquam foedauit sua nequitia Baptismū Iohannis. Deniq; neq; Iudas maculauit sacrificia coenamq; vltimā Christo alijsq; accumbentib' discipulis, At si legaliter immund' aliquis in Templū fuisset ingressus, nec Prophetæ, nec Sacerdotes, nec alij voluissent vti sacrificijs antequā repurgata fuissent Templū, vasa, homines. Si in coena Domini discubuisset Petr' iuxta legē immundus, certè tota coena sic polluisset, vt alijs celebrare eā tunc non licuisset: quod nequitia Iudæ non potuit perficere, propterea quod Deo sic fuisset visum. Non puto quenquā expectare, vt plurib' aut firmioribus testimonijs vel exemplis probem, quod probandū suscepi: nempe immūditiā morū nō sic homines, vestes, loca, res alias vicinas cōtaminauisse, vt alij nō possent ijs rectè vti, quēadmodū legaliter immūdi talia cōtagione & vicinitate sua inficiebant. Si immūd' in Tèplo fuisset deprehensus, nō licebat alijs sacrificijs ibidē vti ante repurgationē.
units.tr: To all this let this also be added: neither Moses, nor the holy judges, priests, kings, prophets, nor other good and pious people abstained from the Temple and the sacrifices because many very wicked men performed the same rites alongside them. Nor was the manna, or the water flowing from the rock for Christ, any less holy because far more wicked men ate and drank together with the few good ones. Likewise, on the feast of Purification or Atonement, the sins of the good and faithful were not left unatoned because a very great number among them lived most corruptly. Does the sight of the wicked pollute like a serpent with its crimes? By no means. That brood of vipers, the Pharisees and Sadducees, by no means defiled the baptism of John with their wickedness. Finally, Judas did not stain the sacrifices or the last supper with Christ and the other disciples reclining at table. But if a legally unclean man had entered the Temple, neither the prophets, nor the priests, nor anyone else would have wished to use the sacrifices until the Temple, vessels and people had been purified. If Peter, legally unclean, had reclined at the Lord's Supper, the whole supper would certainly have been so polluted that the others could not then lawfully celebrate it. The wickedness of Judas could not bring about that effect, because God had so decided. I do not think anyone expects me to prove what I have undertaken with more or stronger testimonies or examples: namely, that the uncleanness of morals does not defile men, garments, places, or other nearby things in the way that legal uncleanness infected them by contagion and proximity, so that others could not use them rightly. If an unclean man had been caught in the Temple, it was not lawful for others to use the sacrifices there before purification.

units.la: At si malis præditus moribus ingressus fuisset, nulla erat purificatione Templi, vasorum, hominum, aliarum rerum opus: sed bonis omnia manebant sancta & bona. Ex quo satis est manifestum, non sic illos immundos significauisse hos, vt vel tunc vel nunc eadé vtrisq; poena fuerit constituta.
units.tr: But if a man had entered endowed with wicked morals, there was no need for purification of the Temple, vessels, people, or other things. Rather, all things remained holy and good for the good. From this it is clear enough that those uncleannesses did not so signify these, that the same punishment was appointed for both then or now.

units.la: Ex supradictis omnibus hæc necessariò conficiuntur. Primùm, quod præcipuè intendebamus, est, immunditiam legis non ita significauisse aut præfigurauisse scelera, vt in his terris eodem modo eadémque poena coercenda esse concludi possit. Alterum hoc est, improbitatem morum longè fuisse detestabiliorem coram Deo, quam ceremonialem turpitudinem: quantumuis hæc Templum, vasa, homines &c. sic inficeret, vt purgatione ceremoniali opus haberent: illa autem sic neque homines, neque Templum, neque res alias inquinaret. Etenim si comparare pœnas voles, longè graviores illi, quàm huic immunditiei decretæ sunt. Nam scelera graviora cruce, igne, gladio, lapidum iniectione: leviora mulcta, & plagis plectebantur: cum ceremoniali immunditia inquinati plerumq; ad breue aliquod tempus solum à Templi hominumque aditu arcerentur. Quis est ita rudis, vt nesciat maius esse occidi, quàm perdies aliquot à Tépli ingressu remoueri? Proindè si Deus pœnas constituit maiores & acerbiores scelebribus, quàm legis sordibus, detestabiliora quoq; indicauit. Tertium est, perperam alios affirmare legis immunditiam nō vere polluisse castra. Etenim ex infinitis propè locis apparet, Deum tunc ita statuisse ac ordinasse, vt, si pollutus in castris esset, repurgatione indigeret. Qua igitur ratione hoc negabimus, quod Deus tam diserlis explicatisque verbis toties affirmat? Cui maior habenda fides? Deóne an aduersarijs nostris? Si per, non vere, intelligunt, non moraliter, concedo quod dicunt. At ex eo non consequitur, castra per eam non fuisse vere maculata, vt purificari opus haberent per ceremonias à Deo institutas. Cur mortem interminatur ei, quicunque ante purgationem in Sanctuarium venire auderet, Num. 19. si non vere polluebat?
units.tr: From all the above, these things are necessarily concluded. First, which was our chief aim, the legal uncleanness did not so signify or prefigure crimes that it can be concluded that they must be restrained in this world in the same way and with the same punishment. Second, the wickedness of morals is far more detestable before God than ceremonial foulness, although the latter so infects the Temple, vessels, people, and so on, that they need ceremonial purification, whereas the former does not defile men, the Temple, or other things in this way. Indeed, if you wish to compare the penalties, those for crimes were far more severe than those decreed for this legal uncleanness. For graver crimes were punished by the cross, fire, the sword, and stoning; lesser ones by fine and blows; whereas those stained by ceremonial uncleanness were usually kept away for only a short time from access to the Temple and to people. Who is so ignorant as not to know that being killed is worse than being kept away for some days from entering the Temple? Therefore, if God appointed greater and harsher punishments for crimes than for the filth of the law, he also indicated that they are more detestable. Third, others wrongly affirm that legal uncleanness did not truly defile the camp. For in almost countless places it appears that God then so established and ordained that if anyone was unclean in the camp, he needed purification. By what reasoning, then, shall we deny this, which God so often affirms in such plain and explicit words? To whom is greater credit to be given: God, or our opponents? If they mean by "not truly" "not morally," I grant what they say. But it does not follow from this that the camp was not truly stained by such uncleanness, so that it needed to be purified by ceremonies instituted by God. Why does he threaten death to anyone who dared to come into the sanctuary before purification, Num. 19, if he did not truly pollute it?

units.la: Præclarè
units.tr: Clearly.

units.la: Prædarè quoq; ex ijsdem intelligitur, cur immundi secundùm legem eijcerentur ex castris: moribus autem immundi sic non arcerentur. In causa est, quod illi, Deo sic disponente & ordinante, vestes, lectos, loca, in quibus erant, ipsos deniq; homines sic inficiebant, vt purificatione egerent, Num. 19. Aggaei. 2.cap. Quamobrem separatim ab aliis manere iubebantur, donec emundati essent, quod frequentissimè circa vesperam fiebat. Moralis autem neminem inficiebat alium, quàm eum, in quo inerat.
units.tr: Clearly, also, from the same passages it is understood why the legally unclean were cast out of the camp, but those unclean in morals were not so shut out. The reason is that those, by God's arrangement and ordinance, so infected garments, beds, places in which they were, and finally the men themselves, that they needed purification, Num. 19, Hag. 2. For this reason they were ordered to remain apart from the others until they were cleansed, which usually happened towards evening. But moral uncleanness infected no one other than the person in whom it dwelt.

units.la: Proinde non recté concluditur: Deus magis offenditur Sacrificijs impiorum, quam legaliter inquinatorum. Ergo cum hos iusserit abstinere ab externo isto cultu, quantisper emundati non essent, etiam illos arcere iubemur. Quoniam impuris prædití moribus non itá, (sicut legaliter immundi)res aliàs inquinabant, vt earum contactum vsúmq; cæteri fugere cogerētur. Si, cur hi potius, quàm illi, res quaslibet contaminarent, ex me queras, causam me ignorare fatebor, sed Deo interim sic placuisse respondebo: cuius mihi voluntas pro ratione certissima semper fuit, est, erit: alijsq; cunctis esse debet. Hunc duas istas turpitudines sic distinxisse video, vt alteram voluerit inquinare, & velut contagio quodam latè in res vicinas serpere: alteram foedare sic alios noluerit: quantumuis hanc, quam illam, odisset per se magis. Cum ergo quæritur, cur ei, qui semen præter voluntatem noctu emisit, ad sacra adire non licuerit, priusquà mundaretur, scortatori autē & concubinario licuerit? respondeo, quia ille ad se appropinquantes contaminabat, hic Deo & sibi immundus tantum erat: aliósq; non magis inquinabat, quàm si cum vxore legitima cubauisset. Interim pœna erat scortatori alia longè grauior constituta.
units.tr: Therefore it is not rightly concluded: God is more offended by the sacrifices of the impious than by those legally defiled. Therefore, since he has commanded us to abstain from this external worship until they are cleansed, we are also commanded to keep away the others. For those with wicked morals did not defile other things in the way that the legally unclean did, so that others were compelled to shun their contact and use. If you ask me why these rather than those defiled whatever things they touched, I will confess that I do not know the cause, but I will answer that it has so pleased God. His will has always been, is, and will be for me the most certain reason, and it ought to be so for all others. I see that he has distinguished these two kinds of foulness in such a way that he wished one to pollute and, like a kind of contagion, to creep widely into nearby things, and did not wish the other to stain others in this way, although he hated the latter more in itself. Therefore, when it is asked why it was not lawful for one who had emitted semen at night, against his will, to approach sacred things before he was cleansed, but it was lawful for a fornicator and a concubinary man, I answer: because the former contaminated those who came near him, whereas the latter was unclean only before God and himself, and did not defile others any more than if he had lain with a lawful wife. Meanwhile, a far heavier punishment was appointed for the fornicator.

units.la: Discimus hoc quoq; ex prediētis, cum aliquis in scripturis dicitur moribus suis polluisse Templum, Dei cultum, Deum ipsum, seu nomen eius, id sic non esse accipiendum, quasi hæc propterea aliis quoq; immunda essent: sed coràm Deo sic fuisse, iudicandum est. Equidem exemplis Christi, Prophetarum, & Sanctorum omnium sic ostensum hoc fuit paulò supra, vt merito confidam nullum dubitaturum porrò esse. Et quo pacto possit aliquis Dei nomen sic polluere, vt purgatione opus haberet? Significat ergo nomen Dei polluere suis moribus, ita viuere, vt propter nos Deus male audiat. Sic apud Ezech. 20. & 36. pollutum nomen suum dicit Deus apud Gentes, apud quas populus Iudaicus captus detinebatur. Infamabant enim illæ nomen Dei dicentes, Israelitarum Deum non potuisse populum suum seruare. Obiter solum hoc monere volui: nunc ad tua redeo.
units.tr: We learn from what has been said that when in the Scriptures someone is said by his morals to have polluted the Temple, the worship of God, God himself, or his name, this must not be understood as though these things were thereby unclean to others; rather, it must be judged that they were so before God. Indeed, this was shown a little above by the examples of Christ, the prophets, and all the saints, so that I confidently trust no one will doubt it further. And how could anyone pollute the name of God so that it needed purification? Therefore, to pollute the name of God by one's morals means to live in such a way that God is ill spoken of on our account. So in Ezekiel 20 and 36, God says that his name was polluted among the Gentiles, among whom the captive Jewish people were held. For those nations defamed the name of God, saying that the God of the Israelites had not been able to save his people. I wished only to give this note in passing; now I return to your matter.

units.la: Quid legalem vocem immunditiam plenè nunc explicatum habes, spero: Scleratos (iterum dico, & quidem rectè vereq; dico) non fuisse habitos pro immundis talibus, qui Templum & homines vicinos sua præsentia sic inficerent, vt eos repurgari vsitatis ceremonijs oporteret, perspicuè expositi: Hac de causa non fuerunt perinde, vt legali macula infecti, à Sacrificijs temploq; repulsi. Ergo turpes & immundos fuisse dico: at non illo modo, quo, qui cadauer contrectauerat, vel rem aliam talem vetitam. At iniquissima, inquis, Lex Dei fuisset, quod tam seuerè externum contactum puniret, ad scelera verò manifesta velut conniueret. Exhorrui, cum ista tua legi. Pudeat te inconsideratæ istius temeritatis. Video te vel ipsi Deo bellum potius indicturum, quàm à sententia discessurum. At verò tibi cum Deo disputare si libet, experire: mihi non libet. Quæ autem istæc tua est consecutio? Deus non punit scelera Sacramentorum negatione, ergo ad ea veluti conniuet? Supra ostendi longè graviores pœnas hisce constitutas fuisse, quàm sit abstinentia septem dierum à Templo. Rectè dicis carnalibus designari spiritualia: ac proinde carnalem seu corporalem sub lege immunditiam figuram fuisse interioris nostræ deformitatis. Idem nos etiam sentimus & profitemur, vt ex recitatis liquet. Significauit immunditia corporis, animi corruptionē & infidelitatem, vt Apostolus Petrus interpretatur. Exclusio à Templo, exclusionem è Paradyso præteritam, præsentem, & futuram, Purificatio & reditus ad Templum plum, purgationem & reductionem nostram ad Deum per effusum sanguine Christi. Quomodo præsentium rerum & quarum nobis figuræ proponantur dictum est. Apostol. ad Col. 2. nihil habet, quod ad præsente pertineat controuersiam.
units.tr: I hope you now have the legal term "uncleanness" fully explained. I have made it clear that wicked men, I repeat, and I say it rightly and truly, were not regarded as unclean in that sense, that is, as people who by their presence so defiled the Temple and their neighbours that they had to be cleansed by the usual ceremonies. For this reason they were not shut out from the sacrifices and the Temple as those stained with legal defilement were. So I say they were foul and unclean, but not in that way, in which one who had touched a corpse, or some other forbidden thing, was unclean. But, you say, the law of God would be most unjust, since it punished external contact so severely while seemingly winking at manifest crimes. I shudder at your words. Shame on you for this thoughtless rashness. I see you will declare war on God himself rather than depart from your opinion. But if you wish to dispute with God, try it; I do not. But what kind of inference is this of yours? God does not punish crimes by denying the sacraments, therefore he seemingly connives at them? I have shown above that far heavier penalties were laid down for such crimes than abstinence from the Temple for seven days. You are right that carnal things signify spiritual ones, and so the carnal or bodily uncleanness under the law was a figure of our inner deformity. We also think and profess the same, as is clear from what has been quoted. Bodily uncleanness signified corruption of the soul and unbelief, as the Apostle Peter interprets it. Exclusion from the Temple signified our exclusion from Paradise, past, present and future; purification and return to the Temple signified our cleansing and restoration to God through the shed blood of Christ. How figures are set before us of present things and of things to come has been said. The Apostle in Colossians 2 has nothing that bears on the present controversy.

units.la: At cum ab externa impuritate, ais, ad interiorem argumentamur, tanquam ab umbra ad ipsius rei corpus, non obtrudimus ambiguas aut commentitias allegorias. Concedo, si modo externa internis rebus significatis rite aptes. Verum quis tibi dabit intelligens huius negotij, impuritatem sub lege significauisse scelera, fructscilicet nostræ corruptionis, & non ipsam potius depravationem nostram? Deinde, si hoc tibi largiremur, unde quæso probares, eâdem scelera propterea plecti debere pœna, qua legalis turpitudo coercebatur? Loquor de externa Ecclesiæ coercitione. An non manifestè Deus diuersas & discrepantes utriusq; pœnas simul eodemq; tempore posuit? Quæ igitur audacia est, vnius pœnam facere alterius quoq; pœnam, absq; expresso Dei verbo? Baptismum scio & corruptionis nostræ & renovationis Symbolum esse: quia id scriptura me docet. Docetu pariter scripturam legis immunditiam sic poncre symbolum scelerum, vt eadem pœna sint externa punienda.
units.tr: But, you say, when we argue from external uncleanness to inner, as from shadow to the body of the thing itself, we are not foisting on you ambiguous or invented allegories. I grant it, provided you rightly match external things to the inner things they signify. But who will give you, a man who understands this matter, that the uncleanness under the law signified crimes, that is, the fruits of our corruption, and not rather our very depravity itself? Next, even if we granted this, how would you prove that those same crimes ought to be punished by the same penalty by which legal foulness was restrained? I am speaking of external coercion by the Church. Did not God clearly set up different and discordant penalties of each kind at one and the same time? What audacity, then, is it to make the penalty for one the penalty for the other too, without an express word of God? I know that baptism is a sign both of our corruption and of our renewal, because Scripture teaches me so. Show me likewise that Scripture sets legal uncleanness as a sign of crimes, so that the same external penalty must be inflicted for them.

units.la: Quæris num peccatum esse negem, vel cogitare vel facere, vel dicere, quod Deus vetuit? Non nego. An propterea malè dixi, animos illa impuritate non semper fuisse contaminatos? Si impuritas illa simpliciter fuisset peccatum, non permisisset, imò non iussisset Deus aliquos pollui. At iussit aut saltem concessit Sacerdotibus (vt nunc alios taceam) Leuit. 21. & Ezech. 44. contaminare sese in funere matris, patris, fratrum, liberorum. Item iussit mundum aliquem conspergere lustrali aqua immundum: efferre cineres, comburere vaccam, Num. 19. propter quae immundos eos ad vesperâ usq; oportebat fieri. Nihil nunc dicâ de illis, qui inuiti reddebantur impuri. Peccabant, fateor, qui contra Dei mandatū & sine eius permissione immūdi aliquid attingebat. Ex eo tamen non omninò sequitur, ipsa quoq; immunditiâ, quæ peccati actū comitabatur, peccatū fuisse. Aliud est actio contra præceptum Dei exercita, & aliud est macula per hanc actionem contractam: quam Deus figuram deformitatis nostrae esse voluit. Non est necesse, vt figura omnes figurati proprietates contineat. Peccatum certe praecipuè consistit in animi deformitate, quae visibilis non est, sed per suos fructus intelligitur: non in corporis maculis. Si eodem faciens respergitur occisi à se hominis sanguine, signum est sceleris illè sanguinis: at ipse, proprie loquendo, scelus non est. Sed esto, sint istae etiam corporis maculae peccata: de illis saltem affirmari nequit eodem modo peccata fuisse. Etsi illos etiam peccata fuisse poneremus, nullo tamen modo concludere inde posses, eandem sceleribus poenam competere, quae huic labi seu foeditati constituta à Deo fuit.
units.tr: You ask whether I deny that it is a sin to think, or to do, or to say what God has forbidden? I do not deny it. Did I therefore speak wrongly in saying that minds were not always contaminated by that uncleanness? If that uncleanness had simply been sin, God would not have permitted, indeed would not have commanded, some to be defiled. But he commanded, or at least allowed, priests (to say nothing now of others) to defile themselves at the funeral of mother, father, brothers and children: Lev. 21 and Ezek. 44. Likewise he commanded a clean person to sprinkle the unclean with lustral water, and to carry out the ashes and burn the heifer, Num. 19, by reason of which the unclean had to remain so until evening. I will say nothing now of those who were made unclean against their will. I admit that those sinned who, unclean, touched something contrary to God's command and without his permission. Yet it does not wholly follow from this that the uncleanness itself, which accompanied the sinful act, was sin. The act performed against God's command is one thing, and the stain contracted by that act is another, which God willed to be a figure of our deformity. A figure need not contain all the properties of what it figures. Sin certainly consists chiefly in deformity of the soul, which is not visible but is known by its fruits, and not in stains of the body. If someone is sprinkled with the blood of a man he has killed, the blood is a sign of the crime; but properly speaking it is not itself a crime. But grant that these bodily stains are sins too: at least it cannot be affirmed of them in the same way that they were sins. Even if we supposed them to be sins, you could in no way conclude from this that the same penalty is due to crimes as God laid down for this defilement or foulness.

units.la: Cum sic argumentaris, Istiusmodi immundi egebant sacrificijs pro delicto: Ergo rei erat peccati à re proposita plurimùm discedis. Nos enim purificatione eguisse omnes concedimus: non quia ipsamet corporis seu carnis illa macula semper esset peccatum, sed quia naturae nostrae distorsioe, & ab eadem liberationem in memoriam nobis revocaret: quo subinde moneremur purgatione nos per Christi sanguinem egere. Non omnes immundi sacrificio opus habebant: sed sola ablutione aquae plures mundabatur. Et vt omnes sacrificio habuissent opus: non tamen vllo pacto efficihinc posset, Sacramenta peccatoribus interdicenda esse.
