Quomodo namq; sequitur, Immundi per Sacrificium pro delicto redibant in gratiam cum Deo: Ergo qui sceleus admiserunt arcendi sunt à Sacramentis, dum Presbyteri quidam eos censeant idoneos? An non haec ipsa sacrificia quaedam Sacramenta ipsis erant? Hoc magis sequeretur: Multa peccata sine vsurpatione Sacramentorum non expiabantur. Ergo prohiberi non debeant ab vsu eorum, qui eis rectè vticupiunt. Hoc, inquam, rectius concluderetur, quàm quod tu concludere voluisti, si ab his argumentari velimus.
units.tr: When you argue thus, "Such unclean persons needed sacrifices for sin; therefore they were guilty of sin," you depart far from the matter at hand. For we all concede that all needed purification; not because that bodily or fleshly stain was always itself sin, but because it recalled to our minds the distortion of our nature and our need of deliverance from it, so that we would be reminded from time to time that we need cleansing through the blood of Christ. Not all the unclean needed a sacrifice; many were cleansed by washing with water alone. And even if all had needed a sacrifice, it could by no means follow from this that sacraments must be forbidden to sinners. For how does it follow that "the unclean returned into favour with God through a sacrifice for sin; therefore those who have committed crimes must be kept from the sacraments, while some elders judge them fit"? Were not these very sacrifices themselves certain sacraments for them? Rather this would follow: many sins were not expiated without use of the sacraments; therefore those who rightly desire to use them should not be prohibited from their use. This, I say, would be the more correct conclusion, if we are to argue from these things, than the one you wished to draw.

units.la: At excipis hoc loco, Sacrificia pro peccato veluti confesiones quasdam particulares fuisse, quas praecedere alia Sacramenta oporteret. Quoniam saepius à te iam repetitum est, forte etiam postea repetitur, semel tibi respondebo, ne deinceps cogar iterum respondere. Fatemur in omnibus, qui Sacramentis ritè velint vti,saltem externè, requiri peccati admissi agnitionem, poenitentiam, dolorem, & studiū ac desiderium emendandi anteactā vitam. Et quanquam in illis locis, vbi recte instituuntur homines, illeipse actus,nempe desiderium fruendi Coena Dominica cum ceteris pijs & sanctis Dei membris, hoc abundè testatum facere omnibus possit, qui non plus volunt sapere,quàm conuenit,tamen in nostris Ecclesijs, de quib’ ego disputaui,sic est res instituta, vt qui ad Coenam ire cupiût, illustri prius confessione animum suum Ecclesiæ declarent. Nam pridie quam Coena administratur, vocātur vnum in locum qui postridie cogitant accedere, & ad tria capita respondere iubentur: quorum summa hæc est.
units.tr: But at this point you object that sin-offerings were, as it were, certain private confessions, which other sacraments had to precede. Since you have already repeated this often, and perhaps will repeat it again later, I will answer you once, so that I need not be forced to answer again. We grant that in all who wish to use the sacraments rightly, at least outwardly, there is required acknowledgement of the sin committed, repentance, sorrow, and zeal and desire to amend their former life. And although in those places where people are rightly instructed, that very act, namely the desire to enjoy the Lord's Supper with the other godly and holy members of God, can sufficiently show this to all who do not want to be wiser than is fitting, nevertheless in our churches, about which I have been disputing, the arrangement is such that those who desire to come to the Supper must first declare their state of mind to the Church by a clear confession. For on the day before the Supper is administered, those who intend to come the next day are called to one place and ordered to answer three heads, the substance of which is this:

units.la: Primum an in conspectu Dei confiteantur, se peccatores esse,ac mandata Diuina nunquam integrè seruasse: & an eo nomine doleant, gratiamq; Domini nostri Iesu Christi sitiant &c. Deinde vtrum peccata sua propter solam mortem Christi remitti sibi certò credant &c. Demum an ex toto corde cupiant pro his beneficijs Deo grati esse, & omni peccatorum immunditia deposita deinceps seriò decreuerint vitam viuere Christo dignam.
units.tr: First, whether they confess before the sight of God that they are sinners, and have never fully kept the divine commandments; and whether on that account they grieve and thirst for the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Second, whether they firmly believe that their sins are forgiven them for the sake of the death of Christ alone. Last, whether with their whole heart they desire to be grateful to God for these benefits, and, having put off all the uncleanness of sin, have earnestly resolved henceforth to live a life worthy of Christ.

units.la: Cum ad hæc capita sigillatim præsentes omnes (iubentur autem omnes postridie ad Coenam accessuri adesse) respondērunt ita se esse affectos, confidere iubet Minister, peccata remissa ipsis à Deo esse, imbecillitatemq; reliquam non imputatū iri propter effusum pro nobis Christi sanguinem. &c.
units.tr: When all those present, for all were ordered to be present who would approach the Supper the next day, have answered to these heads one by one that they are so disposed, the minister bids them be confident that their sins are forgiven them by God, and that their remaining weakness will not be imputed to them on account of the blood of Christ shed for us, etc.

units.la: Publicas satisfactiones, cum absq; excōmunicatione factas fuisse scribis,tibi aßětior:cum secutas fuisse ais in Ecclesijs Apostolicis,facis pro more tuo:scilicet quod probare debebas,tibi vt probatū sumis. At probaui,respondebis: Age videamus. Sacerdotis & Iudicum munus erat de huiusmoid controuersijs ex lege Domini pronuntiare. An hoc est probare excommunicationem exercuisse illos Sacerdotes? Quod si controuersia aliqua orta fuisset de his & de alijs rebus, aut dubitaretur de aliquo negotio, causæ decisio apud Sacerdotem (vt peritū legis) & Iudicem quærebatur,fateor. Sed hoc quid ad nostram causam facit? Quo in loco, rogo te
units.tr: You write that public satisfactions were made without excommunication, and you say they followed in the Apostolic Churches. You do this as you usually do: you take as proved what you ought to have proved. "But I have proved it," you will reply. Very well, let us see. It was the office of the priests and judges to pronounce on such controversies according to the law of the Lord. Does that prove that those priests exercised excommunication? Granted, if some dispute had arisen about these or other matters, or if some business was in doubt, the decision was sought from the priest, as one skilled in the law, and from the judge. But what has this to do with our cause?

units.la: plurimum, scriptū repertisti, Sacerdotes & Iudices arbitrari & iudicare debuisse, an aliquis resipuisset necne? ac proinde num in templū admitti posset, an non posset? Ex sacrificio potuit Sacerdos in genere suspicari de admisso peccatorum certi scire nihil potuit. Non etiam legimus sacerdotes aliud egisse, quàm iuxta praeceptum Moßis oblata dona sacrificasse. Vnusquisque; ex sua conscientia reum se iudicabat vel non reum: non pendebat ex alieno arbitrio. Neque interdictum erat huic templum: nec definitum tempus, quo sacrificaret. Omnia in peccatoris potestate sic erant, vt à Sacerdotibus coactum neminè legamus. Qui boni erant, vltro adibant: qui mali saepè negligebant: vt ex historia Publicanorum liquet. Adde quod tales non semper erant leguliter immundi. Etenim Leuit. cap. 6. iubet rem ablatam ipso dit obla-tionis reddere. Illa ergo die immundus non erat propter hoc factum, cum ei in templo liceret sacrificium offerre: de qua re paulò supra fusè disputatū est. At hęc quid ad vestri Presbyterij actiones attinent, quod iudicium & potestatem sibi arrogat de cuiusq; cogitationibus censendi?
units.tr: In what passage, I ask you, have you found it written that the priests and judges were bound to judge and decide whether a man had repented or not, and therefore whether he could be admitted to the temple or not? From the sacrifice the priest could suspect in general that sin had been committed, but he could know nothing for certain about the particular sinner. Nor do we read that the priests did anything other than offer the gifts and sacrifices as Moses commanded. Each man judged from his own conscience whether he was guilty or not; it did not depend on another's judgment. Nor was access to the temple forbidden him, nor was a set time fixed within which he had to sacrifice. Everything was in the power of the sinner, so that we do not read of any compulsion being applied by the priests. The good went of their own accord; the wicked often neglected it, as is clear from the story of the tax collectors. Add that such people were not always legally unclean. For Leviticus 6 orders that a thing taken away be restored in the very day of the offering. Therefore on that day the man was not unclean because of this deed, since he was allowed to offer sacrifice in the temple; I have discussed this matter at some length a little above. But what do these things have to do with the actions of your presbytery, which claims for itself the right and power to judge the thoughts of each man?

units.la: Reliquat, vt Esdrę factum consideremus: in quo à teipso non discedis latum pilū. Peccauerant nonnulli alienigenas vxores ducendo. Quod cum Esdras resciuisset, doluit plurimum, iram Dei metuens, nè, qui vix dū liberati fuerant, demùm punirentur. Tandem Sechania consilium & remedium proponente coniurarunt, se nouum cum Deo foedus icturos. Ergo Magistratus edicto publico proposito iussit omnes ex captiuitate reduces intra triduum adesse Hierosolymis sub poena confiscationis bonorū & eiectione ex numerò reductum ex captiuitate. Paruerunt omnes: decretum est, vt, qui vxores illas duxissent, eas vnà cū liberis ex eis natis eijcerent. Quid hic de Sacramentis agitur? An hi, qui profanas vxores duxerant, vel ante vel post ab aliquo iussi sunt abstinere à Templo & Sacrificijs? Post eiectas vxores pro delicto sacrificarunt Arietem, vt iusserat Moses Leuit. 6. Presbyterij, quod de resipiscentia iudicaret, atq; à Sacramentis depelleret, nulla hic mentio. At eiectionis hic fit mentio, inquies. Sic habet.
units.tr: Next, let us consider the deed of Ezra, in which you do not depart a hair's breadth from yourself. Some had sinned by marrying foreign wives. When Ezra learned of it, he grieved greatly, fearing the wrath of God, lest those who had scarcely been set free should at last be punished. At length, when Shechaniah proposed a plan and remedy, they swore together that they would make a new covenant with God. Therefore the magistrate, by a public edict, ordered all who had returned from captivity to be present at Jerusalem within three days, under penalty of confiscation of goods and expulsion from the number of those returned from captivity. All obeyed. It was decreed that those who had married those wives should cast them out together with the children born of them. What is being dealt with here concerning the sacraments? Were those who had married foreign wives ordered by anyone, either before or after, to abstain from the temple and the sacrifices? After the wives were put away, they sacrificed a ram for their offence, as Moses had commanded in Leviticus 6. There is no mention here of a presbytery judging repentance and keeping men from the sacraments. But, you will say, there is mention here of expulsion. So it is.

units.la: At non dicitur prohibendum aliquem fuisse à Templo & Sacrificijs: Neq; hoc etiam scribitur, eijciendos fuisse, qui Gentiles duxerant: sed illos, qui edicto Magistratus non paruissent: ac Hierosolymam venire noluissent. Negari non potest quin fieri potuerit, ut aliquis emaneret, qui nihil peccauerat. Statuerunt novum foedus pangere cum Deo. Merito igitur non habendus fuisset in numero confoederatorum, qui interesse pacto noluisset. An non pure politica fuit haec actio? Sed praestat videre quid tu obijcias.
units.tr: But it is not said that any man was to be kept from the temple and the sacrifices; nor is it written that those who had married Gentile wives were to be cast out. Rather, those were to be cast out who had not obeyed the magistrate's edict and had refused to come to Jerusalem. It cannot be denied that it could have happened that someone turned up who had done no wrong. They had resolved to make a new covenant with God. Therefore he rightly would not have been counted among those in the covenant who had refused to take part in the pact. Was this action not purely political? But it is better to see what you object.

units.la: Ad Sacramenta non pertinere dixi, quia constet magistratum hoc edictum promulgasse. Si verum est, inquis, ut quicquid à Magistratu decernitur, ad sacra non pertineat, quo iure velles sacra civiliaq; omnia penes eandem potestatem esse? Recte dixi hanc rem fuisse civilem, ad Magistratumq; pertinuisse politicum, non autem ad Ecclesiasticum aliquod iudicium, quod scriptura ignorat. Vos certe non permittitis Magistratui, ut suo nomine mandet, quae ad Presbyterij vestri potestatem proprie spectare contenditis. Sane constanter affirmo, ad sacra non pertinere, quicquid Magistratus iure suo praecipit: si sacra à civilibus ita distinguamus, quomodo Pontifex, ac deinde vos discriminatis. At aliter loquendum nobis, qui aliter distinguimus. Politicus Magistratus à Deo accepit totam externam gubernationem rerum tum sacrarum tum civilium. Sed illas iuxta praescriptum verbi Dei ordinare & regere, has ad praefinitionem legum & iuris, quod in loco quolibet valet, gubernare debet: de qua re suo loco fuse agendum erit. In praesente loco, Magistratus hoc edictum propositi: non vestrū Presbyterii. Ergo vel iniuste hoc fecit, quod probare te oportebit: vel politicū fuit: ac proinde ad causam nostrā non pertinet. Ad Esdrā relata causa haec fuit: ut ad peritum legis & partem Magistratus. Hanc enim potestatē à Rege Artaxerxe vnā cum mandato, ut doceret omnes secundum legem Dei sui viuere, ipsemet se accepisse fatetur cap.7. Quis ergo miretur, quod Esdrae dixerunt, surge, ad te pertinet vnā nobiscum? An ex hoc sequitur, non fuisse actionem civilem?
units.tr: I said that this matter did not pertain to the sacraments, because it is clear that the magistrate published this edict. "If it is true," you say, "that whatever is decreed by the magistrate does not pertain to sacred things, by what right would you have all sacred and civil matters under the same power?" I rightly said that this business was civil, pertained to the magistrate as a political matter, and not to some ecclesiastical judgment, which Scripture does not know. You certainly do not allow the magistrate to command in his own name what you strive to claim as properly belonging to the power of your presbytery. I firmly affirm that whatever the magistrate commands by his own right does not pertain to sacred things, if we distinguish sacred from civil things as the Pontiff, and after him you, distinguish them. But we must speak otherwise, since we distinguish otherwise. The political magistrate has received from God the whole external government of things, both sacred and civil. But he must order and rule the former according to the prescription of the word of God, and govern the latter according to the definition of laws and of the right that holds in any place. This matter will have to be treated at length in its own place. In the present place, it was the magistrate who published this edict, not your presbytery. Therefore either he did it unjustly, which you will have to prove, or it was political, and so it does not pertain to our cause. The matter in Ezra's case was referred to him as the expert in the law and as part of the magistracy. For he himself confesses, in chapter 7, that he had received this power from King Artaxerxes, together with the commission to teach all to live according to the law of their God. Who then would be surprised that they said to Ezra, "Arise, the matter belongs to you along with us"? Does it follow from this that the action was not civil?

units.la: Nisi forte Rex Artaxerxes consistorio eum Ecclesiastico præfecit. At hoc tibi erit probandum. Nam potestate dedit constituendi Iudices & præsides, atq; inobedientes morte, exterminatione, bonorum multatione, carcere puniendi: quæ ad vectrum Conciliabulum pertinere negatis.
units.tr: Unless perhaps King Artaxerxes set him over an ecclesiastical consistory. But this you will have to prove. For he gave him power to appoint judges and governors, and to punish the disobedient by death, banishment, fine of goods, or prison. You deny that these things belong to your conventicle.

units.la: Colligis ex publicatione bonorū, Anathemate percutiendos tales fuisse, nec illis licuisse sacros ritus celebrare. Quid Anathematè percuti appelles, nescio. Hoc scio, res quæ Anathema Deo fuissent factę, occidi, cōburi, perdi & disperdi debuisse. Hic cum mortis nulla fiat mentio, vel aliud intelligere te per Anathema oportet, vel falso assuis huic loco tuas imaginationes. Falsum illud etiā est, è Republica Iudæorum siue reducū ex captiuitate exclusos, non fuisse admissos ad Templum sacrosq; ritus: modò circūmcisi essent. Nam qui ex indigenis ad eos accesserant, quos Proselytas vocant, Pascha vnà cum cæteris celebrarunt, cap. 0: cū constet tamen, eos ad hoc consortiū non pertinuisse. Aliud proinde fuit in numero reducum ex captiuitate non censeri: & ab aditu Tẹpli ac sacrificiorū prohiberi. Quare non solum cessante, sed etiam procedente publicatione bonorū admisi fuissent ad sacros ritus, quicunq; circumcisi erant, illisq; vti cupierant. An non hodie multorum bona publicantur, quos excōmunicatos & damnatos nullus existimat? Efdræ factum meritò in dubium à me reuocaretur, si quid eorum fecisset, quæ tu fecisse eum opinaris. Fecisset enim contra legem Domini per Mosen latam: vt in Thesibus demonstrauì. Sanè Moses Deut. 7. vbi hasce nuptias prohibet, non ponit hanc pœnā transgressoribus, vt videlicet à Sacramentis arceantur.
units.tr: You infer from the confiscation of goods that such people were struck with anathema and were not allowed to celebrate the sacred rites. What you call being struck with anathema, I do not know. This I know: things that had been made anathema to God had to be killed, burned, destroyed and utterly destroyed. Since no mention of death is made here, you must either understand something else by anathema, or you falsely attach your own fancies to this passage. It is also false that those excluded from the commonwealth of the Jews, or of those returned from captivity, were not admitted to the temple and the sacred rites, provided they were circumcised. For those of the native people who came to them, whom they call proselytes, celebrated the Passover together with the rest (Ezra 6:21), although it is clear that they did not belong to that fellowship. It was therefore one thing not to be counted among those returned from captivity, and another to be barred from access to the temple and the sacrifices. Hence, even if the confiscation of goods had not ceased, but had gone on, all who were circumcised and wished to use the sacred rites would still have been admitted. Are not the goods of many people confiscated today, whom no one regards as excommunicated and condemned? If I had to revoke Ezra's deed as doubtful, that would be right if he had done any of the things you suppose he did. For he would have acted against the law of the Lord given through Moses, as I showed in my Theses. Indeed Moses, in Deuteronomy 7, where he forbids these marriages, does not attach this penalty to transgressors, namely that they be kept from the sacraments.

units.la: Quæ de facto Iosuæ adfers, iam sunt confutata. Nos enim de solis illis loquimur, vt sæpè monui, qui cupiunt cū Deo reconciliari: at hoc vnū contendimus, non esse à Deo institutum Presbyterium, quod de cordibus hominū dicentiū se pœnitere iudicet, verėne an falsè dicant: atq; sic vel ad Sacramenta admittant, vel ab eisdē remoueant. Immūdi admissi non fuerunt, quia Lex iussit ita fieri. Ostende tu eodē modo scriptū esse de illis, de quib° nos inter nos disputam°. Nisi feceris, frustra litigabis. Ab Ezechia vocatos fuisse ad Paschæ celebrationem etiam non emundatos fateris, cum inficiari non possis. Cum addis, sic vocatos fuisse, ut re & verbis detestarentur idola, quibus serviebant, cœcedo tibi, quod dicis. Et nos idem requirimus in illis, de quibus disputamus. Si idem vos faceretis, quod sub Ezechia factum est, nulla esset inter nos disceptatio de hac re. Vos enim contenti esse non vultis publica priuatãque confessione: sed nescio quibus Presbyteris ad hanc rem delectis unumquemque vultis satisfacere: quale in hac historia nihil legimus factum.
units.tr: The deed of Joshua which you bring forward has now been refuted. For we speak only of those, as I have often warned, who desire to be reconciled with God. But we contend on this one point: that no presbytery has been instituted by God which judges from the hearts of men who say they repent whether they speak truly or falsely, and so either admits them to the sacraments or removes them from the same. The unclean were not admitted because the law commanded it to be done so. Show that it is written in the same way about those whom we are disputing among ourselves. If you do not, you will be contending in vain. You admit that Hezekiah called to the celebration of the Passover even those who were not cleansed, and you cannot deny it. When you add that they were so called that by word and deed they might renounce the idols which they had served, I grant what you say. And we require the same of those about whom we are disputing. If you did the same as was done under Hezekiah, there would be no dispute between us about this matter. For you are not willing to be content with public and private confession, but you wish each man to make satisfaction to I know not what presbyters chosen for this purpose, which we read was nowhere done in this history.

units.la: Argumenta, quæ ex veteri Testamento pro excommunicatione protulisti, inania, euanida, falsa esse, aperte docui. Ostendi interim illud etiam, nihil eorum, quæ contra argumentarum ab immunditia legis desumptum attuli, à te merito iuste reprehendi. Equidem quæ firmitatis aliquid habere visa tibi sunt, libenter præterijsti, nisi fortasse in sequentibus attigisti: quæ autem inflectere aut colore aliquo deformare te posse sperauisti, macularē quidem tentauisti, sed ita tentauisti, ut sperem te insumpsisse in eam rem laboris prorsus pœnitere. Sed meliora vel saltem speciosiora in sequentibus fortasse produces. Proinde quid ex nouo foedere depromperis, age perpendamus.
units.tr: I have clearly shown that the arguments you brought forward from the Old Testament in favour of excommunication are empty, worthless and false. Meanwhile I have also shown that none of the things I set against the argument drawn from the uncleanness of the law deserved to be rightly rebuked by you. Indeed, whatever seemed to you to have some force, you willingly passed over, unless perhaps you touched on it in what follows; as for what you hoped to bend or distort with some colouring, you did indeed try to stain it, but you tried in such a way that I hope you have thoroughly regretted the labour you spent on the task. But perhaps in what follows you will produce better, or at least more showy, material. Accordingly, let us now weigh what you have drawn from the New Covenant.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Confutatio Argumentorum, quæ pro Excommunicatione ex foe- dere nouo petita sunt.
units.tr: Refutation of the arguments drawn from the New Covenant in favour of excommunication.

units.la: Ostquam non illis tantum argumentis, quæ tu infœlicissimè conatus es refellere, sed & aliis insuper demonstrauí excommunicationem hanc, de qua sermo nobis est, non modò non præcipi in sacris literis, verum potius vituperari ac reijci; etiam argumenta, quibus præcipuè niti videtur opinio vestra, confutare volui: quò planius liqueret, causam vos defendere non bonam. Quoniam vero præcipuum fundamentum sententiæ vestræ in verbis Christi apud Matth. 18. Cap. Dic Ecclesiae, colloquere vos anti maduerti, ante omnia declaraui, verba Christi eo in loco posita ad praesentem disputationem nullo modo pertinere. Ad quod probandum isto sum argumento vsus. Scopus Christi est in hoc capite docere, quantum malum sit scandalum illud inprimis, quo infirmus aliquis ita possit offendi, ut religionem deserat. Ideoque dandam esse omnibus nobis operam, ne cuiquam offendiculum praebeamus, quo vel minimus aliquis laedatur. Caeterum quia in priuatis iniurijs persequendis, cum iniuriam mox deferimus ad iudicem; vel aliter vlcisci iludemus, infirmi saepe offenduntur, docet nos Christus, quomodo citra offensionem aliorum componi possint: & per hanc occasionem cohortatur nos ad facilitatem ignoscendi. Quocirca non agitur hoc in loco de grauibus sceleribus, quae nominatim a lege puniuntur, sed de illis peccatis & iniurijs, quae priuatae sunt, quarumque remittendarum potestas penes nos est. Summatim dicam: Christus hic interpretatur legem a Mose Leuit. 19. verf. 17. & 18. propositam, quam Ecclesiasticus etiam 19. cap. fusius explicat: Ad haec ita tu respondes.
units.tr: Having shown that this excommunication, of which we are speaking, is not only not commanded in the Holy Scriptures but is rather condemned and rejected, not only by those arguments which you wretchedly tried to refute but also by others besides, I wished to refute the arguments on which your opinion chiefly seems to rest, so that it might be more plainly clear that you are defending a bad cause. Since I have noticed that the main foundation of your view lies in the words of Christ in Matthew 18, "Tell it to the Church" and "reprove him between you and him alone," I first of all declared that the words of Christ in that place have no bearing on the present dispute. I proved this with the following argument. Christ's purpose in this chapter is to teach how great an evil scandal is, especially that by which a weak person may be so offended that he abandons the religion. Therefore we must all take care not to put a stumbling block before anyone by which even the least of them may be harmed. Moreover, because when we pursue private injuries, if we at once bring the wrong before a judge, or otherwise seek revenge, the weak are often offended, Christ teaches us how such matters may be settled without offending others, and on this occasion he urges us to readiness in forgiving. Hence this passage does not deal with grave crimes, which are punished by name under the law, but with those sins and injuries which are private, and whose forgiveness lies in our power. To put it briefly: Christ here interprets the law set out by Moses in Leviticus 19, verses 17 and 18, which Ecclesiasticus also explains more fully in chapter 19. To this you reply thus:

units.la: Si negemus hic de priuatis duntaxat iniurijs agi, nunquam probaueris. Nam quae ad probandum adfers, pleraque nostro iudicio ita sunt infirma, vt sua sponte concidant. Secundo enerauueris doctrinam de condonandis peccatis. An enim solas leues iniurias tenemur condonare? An condonare est ad testes, ad συνέδριον, ad profanum tribunal pertrahere? Mox hanc disputationem vt superuacaneam rejicis, & vltro concedis, verba illa ad solas priuatas iniurias pertinere, & ob id putas excommunicationi nihil decedere. Indicari enim excommunicatione non illud peccatum, de quo initio mota fuerat controuersia, sed praefractam & procacem contumaciam aduersus Ecclesiam.
units.tr: If we deny that only private injuries are treated here, you will never prove it. For the things you bring forward to prove it are, in our judgment, for the most part so weak that they fall of their own accord. Secondly, you will have weakened the doctrine of forgiving sins. Are we bound to forgive only slight injuries? Or is to forgive the same as to drag someone before witnesses, before the Synedrion, before a secular tribunal? Soon you reject this discussion as superfluous, and you freely concede that those words pertain only to private injuries, and so you think nothing is lost for excommunication. For excommunication is meant to indicate not that sin about which the controversy was first raised, but stubborn and insolent contumacy against the Church.

units.la: Ego mihi persuasi, meis rationibus demonstrasse, Christum in praesente loco praecipue de priuatis iniurijs agere, quo pacto scilicet eas citra offensionem proximi a nobis depellere possimus, vt vereri frustra videar, vt ab aliquo relelrefellantur. Equidem in Thesibus primùm, vt alibi de inde ostendi, eum non de celeribus excommunicationis vindicandis agere, sed quomodo priuatae offensae amicè compoda debeant, vt non habeamus necesse causam continuò ad Iudicem & vera religione alienum adferre. Negas hoc tu, vt negant alij quoque complices tui. At dum neque argumenta nostra diluitis, neque negationem vestram argumentis idoneis confirmatis, absque crimine, puto, eam negligimus. Et quod neutrum perficere potueritis, & iis, quae sequuntur, luce meridiana clarius perspicietur.
units.tr: I was persuaded that by my reasons I had shown that Christ in this passage deals chiefly with private injuries, namely how we may remove them without offending our neighbour; so I seem to fear in vain that anyone will refute it. Indeed, in the Theses first, and as I have shown elsewhere, I showed that he is not dealing with grave crimes to be avenged by excommunication, but with how private offences ought to be settled amicably, so that we need not constantly bring the cause before a judge and something alien to true religion. You deny this, as your other allies also deny it. But while you neither refute our arguments nor confirm your denial by suitable arguments, I think we rightly disregard it, and without blame. That neither of you could accomplish this will be clearer than noonday light from what follows.

units.la: Negotiabi doctrinam de peccatorum condonatione, à nobis cæteruari. Vnde hoc tu probabis? An valet hæc consecutio: Christus hoc loco docet solas priuatas iniurias piè ac sine infirmorum offensione componere: Ergo docet solas priuatas iniurias esse condonandas? Nihilne docuit Christus alibi aliud? aut sola hæc verba eius habemus? Ego certè nec dixi, nec cogitaui vnquam solas leues iniurias esse condonandas. Tenentur enim priuati proximo quæuis peccata condonare. Alia est ratio magistratus, cuius officium est scelerator plectere. At quomodo condones? inquis, si ad synedrium & tandem ad profanum tribunal penetrabis? Hoc nunc facere permittit Christus, cum & priuatim, & cum amicis frustra tentata est reconciliatio, & iniuriosus nihilominus pergit iniurius esse. Cum autem vel obiurgatus vel sponte errorem agnoscit, & condonari sibi iniuriam petit, ignoscendum ei est, quantacunque sit iniuria affecerit. Quorsum verò argumentum hoc adducas (si in controversia de priuata iniuria, habendus est vt Ethnicus & publicanus, qui presbyterium non audierit, multò magis id constituendum est, cum de graui scelere accusatur.) ipse certè non video. Nam si ex hoc concludere velis, quae hic à Christo dicuntur, ad excommunicationis spectare, longissimè erras. Tota causa, vt tumetipse scribis, in recta horum verborum explicatione, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, consistit.
units.tr: I deny that we have distorted the doctrine of the forgiveness of sins. From what will you prove this? Does this inference hold: Christ here teaches that only private injuries are settled piously and without offence to the weak; therefore he teaches that only private injuries are to be forgiven? Did Christ teach nothing else elsewhere, or do we have only these words of his? I certainly neither said nor ever thought that only slight injuries are to be forgiven. For private persons are bound to forgive their neighbour any sins whatever. The case of the magistrate is different, since his office is to punish wrongdoers. But how will you forgive, you say, if you proceed as far as the Synedrion and finally to a secular tribunal? Christ now permits this, when reconciliation has been tried in vain both privately and through friends, and the wrongdoer nonetheless persists in wronging. But when he is rebuked or of his own accord acknowledges his error and asks that the injury be forgiven him, he is to be forgiven, however great the injury he has inflicted. As for why you adduce this argument (if in a controversy about a private injury one is to be treated as a heathen and tax collector who has not heeded the presbytery, much more is this to be decided when a grave crime is alleged), I certainly do not see. For if you wish to conclude from this that what Christ says here pertains to excommunication, you are very much mistaken. The whole case, as you yourself write, rests on the correct explanation of these words: "let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector."

units.la: Inter argumenta, quibus probari Christum hic de ptiuatarum iniuriarum transactione agere, hoc vnum fuit, quod in singulari semper loquitur, dicens: Si peccauerit frater Tuus in Te: corripe eum inter Te & ipsum solum. Item adhibe vnâ Tecum alios. Item Dic Ecclesiae. Item, Sit tibi velut Publicanus & Ethnicus: Non dicit, inquam, Sit Ecclesiae, vel sit toti populo, vel sit aliis quibusdam talis: sed hoc ait, Sit tibi talis. Ex hac interpretatione illud simul perspicì dixi, verba haec, Sit tibi quasi Publicanus & Ethnicus, non hoc significare posse, Sit tibi excommunicatus. Nam qui excommunicatus est, non vni soli talis est: sed omnino omnibus talis est. Ad haec ita tu. Mirabilis sane expositio, vt, Tibi, idem semper valeat, atque tibi soli cùm nihil sit vsitatius, quàm certa hypothesi proposita leges θεσμῶν condere. Exemplo sint omnia Decalogi praecepta. Sed neque ad extremum vsque hanc orationis formam seruauit. Subijcit enim: Quicquid ligaueritis, & quicquid soluueritis. Alij sic respondent: Sub vocula, Tibi, consensus intelligitur totius Ecclesiae. Ratio huius, quae nullo potest eludi sophismate, haec est, quod Ecclesia non fert contraria iudicia. Quis autem non videat contraria esse, si vnus aliquis iubeatur hunc certum hominem pro Ethnico habere, alij autem eundem pro Christiano iubeantur habere? Quod enim vni est dictum, dictum est omnibus.
units.tr: Among the arguments by which it is proved that Christ here treats of settling private injuries, this was the one: that he always speaks in the singular, saying, "If your brother sin against you, reprove him between you and him alone"; likewise, "take with you one or two others"; likewise, "tell it to the Church"; likewise, "let him be to you as a heathen and tax collector." He does not say, I say, "let him be to the Church," or to the whole people, or to certain others; but he says, "let him be such to you." From this interpretation I said it was at once evident that these words, "let him be to you as a heathen and tax collector," cannot mean "let him be excommunicated to you." For one who is excommunicated is not such to one person alone but is altogether such to all. To this you reply thus: "A truly wonderful explanation, that 'to you' should always have the same force as 'to you alone', when nothing is more common than to frame laws on a given supposition [θεσμῶν]. Let all the precepts of the Decalogue be examples. But he did not keep this form of expression to the end, for he adds: 'Whatever you bind, and whatever you loose.' Others answer thus: under the little word 'you' the consent of the whole Church is understood. The reason for this, which no sophistry can evade, is that the Church does not issue contrary judgments. But who does not see that they would be contrary if one man were bidden to hold this particular man as a heathen, and others were bidden to hold the same man as a Christian? For what is said to one is said to all."

units.la: Expositio mea mirabilis non est, nisi mirabile sit, quod verum est: at tua reprehensio, sicut aliae quoque, mirabilissima est. Quo loco dixi ego, Tibi, idem semper significare, ac tibi soli? Si locum ostendere non scies, confictum à te esse inficiari non poteris. Dixi, in praesenti loco vocula, Tibi, non idem significare, ac si dixisset, Sit Ecclesiae, vel toti turbae, vel aliis, qui laesi ab eo non sunt. Significat ergo hoc in loco vox, Tibi, laesum tantum, non autem eos, qui laesi non sunt, vt ex toto orationis contextu patet. Significat interim hoc etiam loco, Tibi, omnes illos, qui dicto modo laedi ponuntur. Extant in sacris literis leges quae privatim magistratui conveniunt, non aliis viris. Extant quae subditis competunt, no magistratibus: quae viris, non mulieribus: quae Domijs non servis: quae parentibus, non filijs: quae divitibus non egenis. Ita etiam hoc praeceptum, non omnibus omnino Christianis, ut praecepta Decalogi; & quae his similia sunt, sed tantum privatim laesis congruit. Non enim dicit Christus, argue quemlibet tibi fratrem occurrentem: sed in te peccantem. Quodcum ad privatos dixerit, non ad magistratus, patet eum de privatis offensis fuisse locutum. Est haec res tam manifesta, ut summus excommunicationis patronus de hac re sic fuerit coactus scribere. Quam particulam aliter (nisi contentiosus esse velis) accipere non potes, quam sub tua conscientia: ita ut non sint plures conscij. Quamobrem, quod deinde dicit, quicquid ligaveritis aut solveritis, de illis tantum accipi debet, qui laesi sunt: non de Ecclesia, ut tu dicis. Non enim dicit Christus haec verba ad Ecclesiam: nec loquitur in tertia persona de Ecclesia: sed ad Discipulos, qui non erant Synedrium sive Ecclesia illa, de qua ibi differebat Christus. Principio dixit, si frater tuus peccaverit in Te, sed per vocylam, Te, intellexit quemlibet; contra quem frater peccaret: non unum aliquem solum ex discipulis. Quod ut nunc liqueat, non dicit, quicquid ligaveris, sed, quicquid ligaveritis: quasi diceret, quicunque offensi estis a fratribus, & hoc modo iniuriosum lucrati fueritis, rata erit haec actio vestra etiam in coelis.
units.tr: My explanation is not wonderful, unless it is wonderful that it is true; but your criticism, like the others, is most wonderful. In what place did I say that "to you" always signifies the same as "to you alone"? If you cannot point to the place, you cannot deny that you have made it up. I said that in this passage the little word "to you" does not mean the same as if he had said "let him be to the Church," or to the whole crowd, or to others who have not been harmed by him. So in this place the word "to you" means only the one who has been harmed, not those who have not been harmed, as is clear from the whole context. Yet in this same place "to you" also signifies all those who are placed in the stated situation of being harmed. There are laws in the Holy Scriptures which belong privately to magistrates and not to other men; there are laws which belong to subjects and not to magistrates; laws which belong to men and not to women; to masters and not to servants; to parents and not to children; to the rich and not to the poor. So too this precept does not suit all Christians absolutely, as the precepts of the Decalogue and similar ones do, but only those who are privately wronged. For Christ does not say, "reprove any brother who meets you," but "who sins against you." That he spoke of private offences is clear, since he spoke to private persons and not to magistrates. This matter is so manifest that the chief champion of excommunication was compelled to write about it in this way. You cannot take this particle otherwise (unless you wish to be contentious) than as "under your own conscience," so that there are not several witnesses. Wherefore what he says next, "whatever you bind or loose," must be understood only of those who have been wronged, not of the Church, as you say. For Christ does not address these words to the Church, nor does he speak of the Church in the third person; he speaks to the disciples, who were not the Synedrion or that Church of which Christ was speaking there. At first he said, "if your brother sin against you," and by the word "you" he meant anyone against whom a brother might sin, not one solitary disciple. So that this may now be clear, he does not say "whatever you bind," but "whatever you (plural) bind": as if he said, whoever of you have been offended by brothers and have thus gained the wrongdoer, your action will be ratified in heaven as well.

units.la: Quae ergo erunt Synedrij partes, inquis, num impune vis Ecclesiae iudicium contemni? Quippe lex, secundum quam tu vis Iudaeos tunc iudicia exercuisse, iubet interfici huiusmodi hominem. Quomodo igitur ad profanum tribunal perrahi haereretur? Egregia vero interrogatio. Distingue tempora, sicut aiunt, & concordem reperies scripturam. Quis nescit illo tempore Iudaeos sub Romanis vixisse, ac Praesidem eorum petentibus omnibus ius dicere solitum fuisse? Civilem potentiam ad se omnem fere pertraxerant, relicta potestate ipsis de rebus sacris iudicandi, & secundum legis ceremonias viuendi: ut ex historia cum profana tum sacra perspicue intelliintelligirilus. Sic Gallio Achaiæ Procõsul Iudæis Paulum accusantibus Act. 18. respondet: Siqua iniuria esset aut maleficium, causam susciperem. Sed cum de lege vestra lis sit, iudex ego esse nolo, ipsi videritis. Proinde impunè poterat, qui volebat iudicium Synedrij contemnere in ciuilibus rebus, id quod ante illud tempus facere nullus citra periculum potuisset. Non dubito, quin hoc bonus nullus fecerit, nisi omninò manifesta ei iniuria fieret à Synedrio. Ataliquos fecisse, vel ex Publicanorum historia constat. Ideo Deus per Mosen hoc solum monet, Leuit. 19. ne mox frater fratri crimen apud Iudicem impingat, sed priuatim potius cum eo in gratiam redeat: (quod in Ecclesiastis cap. 19. pluribus expositum legimus) aliud nihil addit. Tunc enim contemnere nulli Synedrij sententiam licebat. Christus autem addit, illum talem habendum velut Ethnicum & Publicanum: id est, posse talem ad profanum tribunal vocari (qui scilicet suæ Gentis iudicium despiciat) absque offensione cuiusquam: vt qui ipso iam facto declarárit, se prauum & suæ Genti patrum obedientem esse.
units.tr: What then, you ask, will be the powers of the Sanhedrin? Will the judgment of the Church be despised with impunity? For surely the law, according to which you want the Jews to have exercised judgment in those days, commands that such a man be put to death. How, then, could he be dragged before a secular tribunal? That is an excellent question. Distinguish the times, as they say, and you will find the Scripture in agreement. Who does not know that at that time the Jews lived under the Romans, and that their governor was customarily asked by all of them to give judgment? They had drawn almost the whole of civil power to themselves, having left to themselves only the power of judging sacred matters and of living according to the ceremonies of the law; as is clearly understood both from profane and from sacred history. So Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, when the Jews accused Paul, answers in Acts 18: "If there were some wrong or crime, I would take up the case. But since it is a question about your law, I do not want to be the judge; see to it yourselves." Accordingly, anyone who wished to despise the judgment of the Sanhedrin in civil matters could do so with impunity, something no one could have done before that time without danger. I do not doubt that no good man would have done this, unless some plainly manifest injury had been done to him by the Sanhedrin. That some did so is evident even from the history of the publicans. So God, through Moses, gives only this admonition, in Leviticus 19, that a brother should not straightway bring a charge against his brother before a judge, but rather should first be reconciled with him privately (which we read was explained at length in Ecclesiastes 19); he adds nothing else. For at that time it was not lawful for anyone to despise the sentence of the Sanhedrin. But Christ adds that such a person is to be regarded as a heathen and a publican: that is, that such a person may be summoned before a secular tribunal (namely, one who despises the judgment of his own nation) without offence to anyone, since by the very act he has already declared that he is perverse and disobedient to the fathers of his people.

units.la: Ad aliorum obiectionem hoc solùm dicam, tam non ferre sententias contrarias Ecclesiam vel Iudices, cum offenso contrareum permittunt aliquid, ac non offenso non permittunt, quàm non indicant contraria, cùm creditori permittunt debitum abs debitore exigere, alijs non permittunt exigere. Proinde non sequitur, huic concessum est, vt ab hoc pecuniam debitam exiget. Ergo tota ciuitas ab eodem eandem pecuniae summam petere potest. Longè cum venustiùs tum verius ex hoc loco conclusero, excommunicari nullum debere, si propositio vera sit. Sic enim argumentor. Quod vni dictum est, dictum toti est Ecclesiæ. At vni dictum est, vt septuagiès in die culpam deprecanti remittat, Ergo tota Ecclesia deprecanti ignoscere debet, quotiescunque in die sibi ignosci petet. Nulla enim iusta causa proferri poterit, cur tota Ecclesia non debeat facere in hac causa quod singulis eius membris præceptum est. Hoc autem vestris presbyteris non videtur rectum. Etenim non sunt contenti, vt quis deprecetur culpam & fateatur peccatum, sed probare præterea, atque adeo punire volunt, dum ipsis iudicetur satis purgatus.
units.tr: To the objection of others I will say only this: the Church or the judges do not issue contrary sentences when they permit something to the injured party against the offender, and do not permit it to one who is not injured, any more than they indicate contrary things when they permit a creditor to exact a debt from a debtor, and do not permit others to exact it. Therefore it does not follow that, because it is granted to this man, he may exact money owed from this man. Therefore the whole city may seek the same sum of money from the same man. I shall draw a far more elegant and truer conclusion from this passage, that no one ought to be excommunicated, if the proposition is true. For I argue thus: What has been said to one has been said to the whole Church. But it was said to one that he should forgive a brother who asks forgiveness seventy times a day for a fault. Therefore the whole Church ought to forgive the one who asks, as often as he seeks forgiveness on the same day. For no just cause can be put forward why the whole Church should not do in this matter what has been commanded to each of its members. But this does not seem right to your elders. For they are not content that someone should beg pardon for his fault and confess his sin, but they also want him proved, and indeed punished, until it is judged by them that he has been sufficiently purged.

units.la: Assentiris mihi sententiam eorum defendenti, qui per Ecclesiam intelligunt συλλογισμον: at non assentiuntur mihi aut tibi hac in re alij amicitui. Quamobrem validissimis argumentis probabui in postremis Thesibus, per Ecclesiae nomen Christum nihil aliud intellexisse.
units.tr: You agree with me in the opinion of those who defend the view that by the Church is understood a συλλογισμός [a body of persons assembled for judgment]; but neither my friends nor you agree with me in this matter. For this reason I have proved, with very strong arguments, in the final Theses, that Christ understood nothing else by the name of Church.

units.la: Caeterum capitalia penes Synedrium fuisse iudicia, ac gladio animad ducere potuisse Christi tempore in eos, qui contra religionem peccauisent (nam civilium rerum potestas penes Romanos haerebat) sic probabo, ut merito confidam, nullum sanae mentis porro dubitaturum. Probabo, non minus firmiter & aperte, duas iurisdictiones, siue duo iudicia distincta, Ecclesiasticum videlicet ac Politicum, ut hodie ea vos distinguere soletis, in populo Iudaico nullo unquam tempore fuisse. Quae cum praestitero, ad tuas reprehensiones, quotquot falsas esse iudicauero, (nam si veri quid ac boni reperiero, magna cum gratiarum actione suscipiam) aperte & solide respondebo.
units.tr: Moreover, I shall prove, in such a way that I confidently trust no one of sound mind will doubt it further, that in the time of Christ the Sanhedrin held capital judgments, and could put to death with the sword those who sinned against religion (for the power over civil affairs rested with the Romans). I shall prove, no less firmly and openly, that two jurisdictions, or two distinct judgments, namely the Ecclesiastical and the Political, as you are accustomed to distinguish them today, never existed at any time among the Jewish people. When I have done this, I shall answer your criticisms, as many as I shall have judged false, plainly and solidly; (for if I find anything true and good, I will accept it with great thanks).

units.la: Libri secundi finis.
units.tr: End of the second book.

units.la: Liber tertius incipit.
units.tr: The third book begins.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: De munere & distinctione Magistratus.
units.tr: On the office and the distinction of the Magistrate.

units.la: [R]ecta hominum gubernatio omnis vel est visibilis, vel inuisibilis. Hanc internam vocamus, coelestem, diuinam, & spiritualem: illam aeternam, humanam, & corporalem nuncupamus. Porro sicut duplex duntaxat est rectio, sic est necesse, ut duo tantum sint Rectores supremi. Et internae gubernator est Deus: externae Moderator est magistratus vnicus. Absurdum namque est vnius rectionis duos esse sic distinctos rectores, vt alter non fit alterius pars, five vt vnius nomine non omnia administrentur. Quanquam vero visibilis & mundanae proturationis multae sint partes, si res, quas dispensat, spectemus, multiplex tamen ipfa non est. Etenim sicut vnica est mensura, qua res diuerfissimas, vt pannos lineos, laneos, fericeos, argenteos, aureos, mensuramus: & vnum est pondus, quo res omnino discrepantes ponderamus: sic vna est dispensatio rerum omniumque visibilis, tametsi per eam res prorsus dispares, & dissimiles curentur & temperentur. Legum vocamus alias oppidanas, alias rusticanas, alias scholasticas: nec est tamen necessarium, vt tot sint Legislatores: sed vnus idémque ciuibus, rusticis, scholarum rectoribus, leges præscribat. Eodem modo non est alius magistratus, qui res profanas curat, ab eo qui res scholasticas vel sacras disponit. Res quidem inter se differunt, at non differt similiter harum difpensatio & moderatio.
units.tr: Every right government of men is either visible or invisible. We call the one internal, heavenly, divine and spiritual; we call the other eternal, human and bodily. Now, just as there is only a twofold rule, so it is necessary that there be only two supreme rulers. God is the governor of the internal rule, and a single magistrate is the moderator of the external. For it is absurd that there should be two such distinct rulers of one rule, so that neither is a part of the other, or so that not everything is managed under the name of the one. Although the parts of visible and worldly administration are many, if we look at the things it dispenses, it is not in itself manifold. For just as there is one measure by which we measure very diverse things, such as linen, woollen, silk, silver and gold cloths, and one weight by which we weigh things wholly unlike, so there is one administration of all visible things, although through it things entirely unlike and dissimilar are looked after and regulated. We speak of laws for the town, laws for the countryside, and laws for the schools, yet it is not necessary that there be so many lawgivers; rather, one and the same person prescribes laws for citizens, for country folk and for the rectors of schools. In the same way there is not one magistrate who looks after profane affairs and another who arranges scholastic or sacred ones. The things themselves differ among themselves, but the dispensing and governing of them does not differ in the same way.

units.la: Quæ cùm ita habeant, confiteri nos oportet, totius Reipublicae vnicum esse summum gubernatorem, quem vno nomine magistratum vocamus: siue vnus sit numero, qui imperium tenet, siue plures simul Rempublicam regant. Vbi supremus hic in qualibet Republica magistratus, non potest solus curare partes omnes, aliisque partes alias committit regendas; plures tunc magistratus non fiunt, dum superbum nomine & loco alij omnes demandatum sibi munus administrant. Quacunque igitur specie Reipub. (Sunt enim Rerumpubl. species plures) coetus aliquis seu multitudo regatur, semper oportet vnum aliquem magistratum ponere, qui capitis habeat rationem, ad quam omnia referantur. Nam vt monstrosum est corpus biceps, ita monstrosa est Respub. quæcunque sic regitur, vt in ea plures sint magistratus distincti æqué summi. Neque excusat rerum tractandarum dissimilitudo. Iam enim ostensum est gubernationem rerum non variari, subiectarum rerum disponendarum & ordinandarum disparilitate. Sanè tam est hoc omnibus omnium ætatum intelligentibus absurdum visum, vt Pontificij quoque hac potissimum ratione Pontificem suum caput supremum Reipub. declararint, hoc fermè argumento.
units.tr: Since matters stand thus, we must confess that there is one supreme governor of the whole commonwealth, whom we call by the single name of magistrate, whether one person holds the power or several rule the commonwealth together. Where this supreme magistrate in any commonwealth cannot alone look after all parts, and entrusts other parts to others to rule, there are not several magistrates, as long as all the others carry out the duty entrusted to them in the name and place of the one. Therefore, under whatever form of commonwealth (for there are several forms of commonwealth) a body or multitude is governed, it is always necessary to set up some one magistrate who holds the place of the head, to whom everything is referred. For just as a two-headed body is monstrous, so any commonwealth is monstrous if it is so governed that in it there are several magistrates, distinct and equally supreme. Nor does the difference of the matters to be handled excuse it. For it has already been shown that the manner of governing does not vary with the diversity of the things to be arranged and ordered. Indeed this seemed so absurd to all who have understood things in every age that the Papists too, chiefly for this reason, have declared their Pontiff the supreme head of the commonwealth, arguing roughly as follows.

units.la: Deus, aiunt, cum oderit omnem ἀταξίαν, & omnia velit ordine decenti & ἐυχευμένως fieri, duo in vno corpore capita ponere monstrosum putauit. Hinc in ciuitate Christiana non voluit duos esse Magistratus distinctos æquali potestate totam ciuitatem regentes. Quare cum duo sint in Ecclesia gladij, siue potestates, nec ambę possint esse summæ, sed alteram alteri subesse oporteat, & indignior digniori merito subijciatur, subiecta est potestas seu gladius temporalis Ecclesiastico tanquam præstabiliori: vt videlicet absurditas omnis vitetur. Hinc illud dictum originem habuit, Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rodolpho.
units.tr: God, they say, since he hates all disorder [ἀταξίαν] and wills that all things be done in a fitting and orderly [εὐκοσμένως] way, has thought it monstrous to place two heads in one body. Hence in a Christian commonwealth he did not wish there to be two distinct magistrates with equal power governing the whole state. Therefore, since there are two swords, or two powers, in the Church, and both cannot be supreme, but one must be subject to the other, and the less worthy is rightly subjected to the more worthy, the temporal power or sword is made subject to the ecclesiastical as the more excellent, so that every absurdity may be avoided. Hence that saying arose: Peter gave the rock to Peter, and Peter gave the diadem to Rudolph.

units.la: Cæterum quia vnus omnibus vbique rebus præesse, & per se omnia curare nequit, alios ordinat, qui suo nomine res procurent. Ex his alij oppidani, alij Rusticani, alij Scholastici, alij Ædiles, alij præfecti, alij alijs nominibus nuncupantur (nomine vel à rebus, quas curant, vel à personis, quas regunt, vel à locis quibus præsunt, accepto) tametsi vnius & summi Magistratus nomine omnes omnia peragant. Proindè vnus idemque Magistratus, quatenus vel per seipsum, vel per alios res ciuiles tractat, Politicus, quatenus Scholastica disponit ac regit, Scholasticus, quatenus res sacras ordinat & gubernat Ecclesiasticus siue sacer est ac dicitur. Si vel in hac parte, vel in alia quauis aliquid non satis intelligit, consulere peritos debet, quorum consilio administret: vel idoneos homines cuilibet muneri præficere, qui suo nomine rectè singula curare velint ac possint.
units.tr: Moreover, since one person cannot preside over all things everywhere and look after everything himself, he appoints others to attend to affairs in his name. Of these, some are called town officers, some country officers, some school officers, some aediles, some prefects, and they have other names too (the names being taken either from the matters they look after, or from the persons they rule, or from the places over which they preside), although all of them carry out everything in the name of the one and supreme magistrate. Accordingly, one and the same magistrate is political insofar as he handles civil affairs either himself or through others, scholastic insofar as he arranges and rules school affairs, and ecclesiastical or sacred insofar as he orders and governs sacred things. If in this part, or in any other, he does not understand something well enough, he ought to consult experts, by whose counsel he may administer; or else he should set suitable men over each office, who in his name are willing and able to manage each matter rightly.

units.la: Veruntamen vt in rebus profanis curandis ei non licet terminos & fines æquitatis, iusticiæ ac honestatis, hoc est, præscriptionem legum & statutorum Reipub. transcendere: Sic in disponendis & ordinandis rebus sacris, vel ad cultum Diuinum pertinentibus, longè minus ei licet vlla in parte à præscripto verbi Dei discedere: quod tanquam regulam in omnibus debet sequi, ab eoque nusquam vel latum pilum deflectere. Summa est, Magistratum in Christiana Repub. vnicum esse, cui à Deo commissa sit gubernatio externa rerum omnium, quæ vel ad ciuilem, vel ad piam & Christianam vitam pertinent: ius & autoritatem imperandi acius dicendi neque ministris neq; aliis vllis concessum esse. Intelligi hoc debet de ea Repub. dictum, in qua Magistratus & subditi eandem profitentur religionem, eamque veram. In hac, dico, duas distinctas iurisdictiones minimè debere esse. In alia, in qua videlicet Magistratus falsam tuetur sententiam, certo quodam modo tolerabilis videri fortasse possit diuisio rectionum.
units.tr: Yet just as in managing profane affairs he is not allowed to pass beyond the limits and bounds of equity, justice and honesty, that is, beyond the prescriptions of the laws and statutes of the commonwealth, so much less is he allowed, in arranging and ordering sacred things, or those pertaining to the worship of God, to depart in any part from the prescription of the word of God, which he ought to follow as a rule in all things, and never to deviate from it by the breadth of a hair. The sum is this: in a Christian commonwealth there must be one magistrate, to whom God has committed the external government of all things that pertain either to civil life or to a pious and Christian life; and the right and authority of commanding or of speaking has not been granted to ministers or to any others. This must be understood of a commonwealth in which the magistrate and the subjects profess the same religion, and that a true one. In such a commonwealth, I say, there ought by no means to be two distinct jurisdictions. In another, in which the magistrate upholds a false opinion, a division of rule might perhaps seem tolerable in a certain way.

units.la: Vt porrò huius rei veritas magis elucescat, sacris literis, quod diximus, deinceps comprobabimus. Legimus in cap. 4. Deuter. Deum statuta & leges tales suo populo præscripsisse, vt earum sapientiam & iusticiam omnes gentes sint admiraturæ. In hoc sita est, inquit Moses, nostræ apud cæteras nationes sapientiæ & prudentiæ existimatio, vt auditis omnibus hisce institutis fateantur hanc Gentem sapientem esse & prudentem. Etiamsi hoc scriptura non diceret, verum esse nihilominus vel ex eo perspiceretur, quod toties ac tam varie mutata specie Reipub. eædem leges semper seruari potuerunt. Non debet autem alicui mirum videri, quod tam sapienter omnia fuerunt constituta. Cum enim Deo nullus sit sapientior, omnium sapientissimam oportet esse Reipublicæ formam, quam ipse instituit. Quinetiam oportet vnamquamuis tanto esse melius, aptius, sapientius constitutam, quanto ad formam Reipub. à Deo ordinatæ accedit propius: & contra, necessum est, quamlibet tanto esse deteriorem & periculosiorem, quanto ab illa recessit longius. Proinde si, vt constet omnibus, perfecero, Deum in sua Repub. differentes iurisdictiones illas, (Politicam scilicet atque Ecclesiasticam) non instituisse: sed vniuersam gubernationem Reipublicae visibilem, sive circa res civiles & profanas, sive circa res sacras cultumque diuinum versaretur, uni solique Magistratui politico tradidisse: constabit hoc quoque, eandem dispensationem Magistratui Christiano, aliis autem nullis deberi. Nam in novo Testamento nihil de ratione regendi Christus docuit: neque aliquid mutare vel Iudaeos, vel alios iussit. Non hoc dico, Deum voluisse Magistratum sacrificare atque alia huiusmodi, quae Sacerdotibus imperata solis fuerant, facere: sed illud affero, Deum soli Magistratui concredidisse curam & gubernationem tam sacrarum quam prosanarum rerum. Aliud est, facere aliquid, & aliud regere seu facienda ordinare ac disponere. Non enim Magistratus, cum viuendi rationem subditis suis praescribit, & quid ab omnibus ordinibus fieri velit, praecipit, per se omnia facit. Vnus nihilominus omnia agit, ad diuersa officia & causas dissimiles, diuersos & dissimiles adhibens administros.
units.tr: Now, so that the truth of this matter may shine forth more clearly, we shall next prove from the sacred letters what we have said. We read in Deut. 4. that God prescribed to his people statutes and laws of such a kind that all the nations would marvel at their wisdom and justice. In this, says Moses, lies the esteem of our wisdom and prudence among the other nations: that on hearing all these institutions they will confess that this people is wise and prudent. Even if Scripture did not say this, it would nevertheless be plain to see that it is true, from the fact that the same laws could always be kept, although the form of the commonwealth was changed so often and in so many ways. No one ought to find it strange that everything was ordained so wisely. For since no one is wiser than God, the form of commonwealth which he himself instituted must be the wisest of all. Moreover, each commonwealth must be all the better, fitter and wiser established, the more nearly it approaches the form of commonwealth ordained by God; and conversely, any commonwealth must be all the worse and more dangerous, the further it has departed from that form. Therefore, if I shall have shown, so that it is evident to all, that God did not institute in his commonwealth those two different jurisdictions, the political and the ecclesiastical, but committed the whole visible government, whether it was concerned with civil and profane matters or with sacred matters and the worship of God, to one and only one political magistrate, it will also be established that this same administration is owed to the Christian magistrate, and to no others. For in the New Testament Christ taught nothing about the manner of ruling, nor did he order either the Jews or others to change anything. I do not say that God wished the magistrate to sacrifice and do other such things that were commanded to the priests alone; but I maintain that God entrusted the care and government of sacred as well as profane things to the magistrate alone. To do something is one thing, and to rule, or to order and arrange what is to be done, is another. For the magistrate, when he prescribes to his subjects a way of living and commands what he wishes to be done by all orders, does not do everything himself. Nevertheless he alone acts in all things, employing different and dissimilar servants for different offices and matters.

units.la: Consequens modo est, ut probem, Deum non ordinauisse duos Magistratus in Republica Iudaica, sed vni soli ius, facultatem, imperium, autoritatemque credidisse totius visibilis gubernationis: neque potestati ipsius subtraxisse rerum ad cultum Dei pertinentium procurationem. Constat primum, nullum posse in omnibus libris Testamenti veteris verbum ostendi, quo duplex istud imperium, Politicum & Ecclesiasticum approbetur. Nec minus patet illud etiam, Deum Mosi integram formam instituendae Reipublicae tradidisse: illius autem distinctionis nusquam mentionem fecisse. Proinde sequitur, Deum duas hasce iurisdictiones non voluisse distinctas esse, nisi forte aliquid a Mose dicas praetermissum, quod ad substantiam Reipublicae instituendae pertineret, vel eandem mutilam & mancam ipsi a Deo traditam fuisse: quae ambo falsae impieque cogitantur. Quocirca verum est quod asseruimus. Qui contendunt, Deum voluisse duplicem gubernationem in repub. à se instituta, monstrare locum coguntur, in quo mandarit. Quantisper indicare nullum poterunt, nobis non persuadebunt. Constat secundo, nullum huius bipartitæ gubernationis apud Iudæos extare exemplum. Quare aut nullo tempore temperata curataque est eorum respublica secundum institutionem atque voluntatem Dei, aut semper hoc ab omnibus sacris & profanis historicis prætermissum fuit. Quæ cum affirmari à nullo recte vereque posint, patet iterum propositæ causæ veritas. Constat tertio, præcepta & exempla veteris instrumenti omnia docere, unum semper Magistratum non minus sacras, quam profanas res gubernauisse: ut deinceps initio à Mose facto, & clarè demonstrabo.
units.tr: The next thing to prove is that God did not establish two magistracies in the Jewish commonwealth, but entrusted to one alone the right, power, authority and command of all visible government, and did not withdraw from that power the care of things pertaining to the worship of God. First, it is clear that no word can be shown in all the books of the Old Testament that approves this twofold rule, civil and ecclesiastical. Nor is it less evident that God handed Moses the complete form for establishing the commonwealth, and never mentioned that distinction. It follows that God did not want these two jurisdictions to be separate, unless you say that Moses omitted something that belonged to the substance of the commonwealth's establishment, or that the commonwealth was given to him by God incomplete and maimed. Both of these are false and impiously conceived. So what we have asserted is true. Those who maintain that God wanted a double government in the commonwealth he founded are obliged to show the place where he commanded it. Until they can point to none, they will not persuade us. Second, it is clear that there is no example of this twofold government among the Jews. Therefore either their commonwealth was never ordered and governed according to God's institution and will, or this has always been passed over by all sacred and profane historians. Since neither of these can rightly and truly be affirmed by anyone, the truth of the cause we are pleading is again plain. Third, it is clear that the precepts and examples of the Old Testament all teach that one magistrate always governed sacred things no less than profane ones. I will show this clearly from the beginning, starting with Moses.

units.la: Mosen solum velut supremum Magistratum & Reipub. caput rexisse Iudæos, certius est, quam ut ostensione indigeat. Rexit enim in deserto populum ante Sacerdotij institutionem. Quia vero solus perferre laborem non potuit, ex consilio soceri elegit socios, Iudices & præfectos: qui suo nomine disceptantes audirent, causasque iudicarent, ac graviora ad se referrent, Exodi 18. & Deut.
units.tr: That the Jews were ruled by Moses alone, as their supreme magistrate and head of the commonwealth, is more certain than it needs demonstration. For he ruled the people in the wilderness before the institution of the priesthood. But since he alone could not bear the labour, he chose, on the advice of his father-in-law, companions: judges and prefects, who would hear disputes in his name, judge causes, and refer the weightier ones to him (Exod. 18; Deut. 1).

units.la: 1. Quisquis duo loca hæc attentè considerabit, perfacile negotium præsens intelliget. Tantum porrò abest ut distinctum voluerit Deus iudicium de moribus exerceri à Sacerdotibus, ut Mosen iusserit ipsi etiam Aaroni, quem pro Sacerdote suo elegerat, suum præscribere officium. Per Mosen dico, veluti per Magistratum, voluit Deus Aaroni Sacerdotium committere, alijsque omnibus sua officia præfinire, ut intelligeremus, totum visibilem seu externam rerum dispensationem penes Magistratum pium esse. Elegit Deus Aaronem sibi in Sacerdotem, attamen non vocauit eum per se, tametsi antea cum eo locutus fuisset, Exod. 4. & Num. 12. sed per Mosen vocat & inaugurat. Exod. 28. & Leuit. 8. nec eum iubet, cum ei suum munus exponit, peculiare iudicium instituere.
units.tr: 1. Whoever considers these two passages carefully will readily understand the present matter. Far from God wanting judgment on morals to be exercised separately by the priests, he ordered Moses to prescribe the duties even to Aaron, whom he had chosen as his priest. I say through Moses, as through the magistrate, God wished to commit the priesthood to Aaron and to define the duties of all the others, so that we might understand that the whole visible or external dispensation of things rests with the pious magistrate. God chose Aaron as his priest, yet he did not call him directly, although he had spoken with him before (Exod. 4; Num. 12), but calls and installs him through Moses (Exod. 28; Lev. 8). Nor, when he sets out Aaron's office to him, does he order him to establish a separate judgment of his own (Ex. 28; Lev. 8).

units.la: Hinc factum fuit, vt aliqui magno suo malo non crederent, Aaronem a Deo electum, sed a Mose praepositum caeteris. Num. 16. cuius tamen electionem miraculo deinde florentis virgae Aaronis confirmatam viderunt. Sic Aaronem moriturum iubetur idem Moses exuere, & filium eius Eleazarum in Sacerdotio successorem eisdem induturn in defuncti parentis locum subrogare. Num. 20.
units.tr: Hence it happened that some, to their great harm, did not believe that Aaron had been chosen by God, but that Moses had set him over the others (Num. 16). Yet they afterwards saw his election confirmed by the miracle of Aaron's flowering rod. So Moses himself is commanded to strip Aaron of his garments, and to put them on his son Eleazar, to succeed him in the priesthood in place of his dead father (Num. 20).

units.la: Idem postea imperium remisit Iosua, fideliter & obedientiam ei parem promittunt Israelitae. Iosuae 1. Deinde omnibus semper iusit, quid & quomodo facere deberent, sacerdotibus & aliis 3. & 4. capitib. Mox cap. 5. praecipitur ipsi a Deo, non Sacerdotibus, vt circumcidat omnes Israelitas. In summa, Iosua non solum res bellicas & prosanas, verum etiam sacras solus per se & per alios rexit ac temperauit, iuxta praescriptionem legis Dei. Parratio est Iudicum aliorum. Non prohibuit Deus Sacerdotib. veteris Testamenti getere Magistratum; sed iudicarunt Israelem Heli & Samuel ante captiuitatem Babylonicam; post eam semper aut fuerunt participes imperij Sacerdotes, aut soli imperauerunt. Factum hoc est propter figuram Christi, quem non tantum Sacerdotem, verumetiam Regem fore significabatur. Mirabile videtur quod non ex solis prope Leuitis electi sunt Iudices & Magistratus, cum tantae Tribui nulla esset pars terrae assignata. Mirabilius est, quod mulier Israelem aliquando rexit, vt ex Iud. 4. cap. constat. Verum vt-vt haec habeant, hoc constat, ex sacris literis ostendi non posse, duos fuisse sub Iudicib. Magistratus, siue Sacerdotes imperarent, siue alij regnarent. Samuel filios suos constituit per Iudaeam praefectos & Iudices. 1. Sam. 8. at non iniit [?] eos Ecclesiasticum quoddam iudicium a politico distinctum exercere.
units.tr: Afterwards Moses likewise handed authority over to Joshua, and the Israelites promised him faithful and equal obedience (Josh. 1). Then he always commanded all, priests and others, what and how they should do (Chs. 3 and 4). Soon after, in chapter 5, God commands Joshua himself, not the priests, to circumcise all the Israelites. In sum, Joshua alone, both directly and through others, ruled and ordered not only warlike and profane matters but also sacred ones, according to the prescription of God's law. The same is the case with the other judges. God did not forbid the priests of the Old Testament to hold the magistracy; yet Eli and Samuel judged Israel before the Babylonian captivity; after it, the priests either always shared the authority or alone held command. This was done on account of the figure of Christ, who was signified to be not only Priest but also King. It seems remarkable that judges and magistrates were not chosen almost exclusively from the Levites, since so great a tribe had no portion of land assigned to it. It is more remarkable that a woman once ruled Israel, as is clear from Judges 4. But however these things stand, this is certain: it cannot be shown from Holy Scripture that there were two magistracies under the judges, whether the priests governed or other men reigned. Samuel set his sons over Judea as prefects and judges (1 Sam. 8), but he did not undertake to exercise any ecclesiastical judgment distinct from the civil.

units.la: Samuel successerunt Reges, quos manifeste scimus sacra pariter & profana gubernasse. Quippe Dauid conuocauit Principes totius Israelis (inter quos etiam erant Principes familiarum Tribus Leui) non solos Sacerdotes, vt cuhn ipsis de teducenda arca consilium caperet. 2. Sam. 6. & 1. Paralip. 13. Idem Ministros Templi, cantores, ianitores ordinavit: Sacerdotum ac Leuitarum munera distribuit, denique omnia ad cultum Dei pertinentia dispositio, vt in lib. Paralipomenon fœpissimè legimus. Huius ordinationis mentio deinde fit in historia Regum, in 1. Esdrae cap. 3. & 8. Et in lib. Nehemiæ cap. 12. Nõ-tandum est autem, quod non ex proprio consilio, sed ex iussu diuino hæc fecit David, vt ex cap. 29. lib. 2. Paralip. clarissimè liquet. Ibi enim scribitur, eum à Gad & Nathan Prophetis iussum esse sic omnia instituere: qui à Deo non sunt missi ad Sacerdotes, sed ad Regem: ex quo itidem perspicitur, quomodo & à quibus regi Deus velit illa etiam, quae ad cultum suum pertinent. Hanc ob causam præcepit Deus Iosuæ, vt lib. legis die noctuque legeret, quò, secundum præcepta in eo comprehensa cuncta ordinaret. Item electo Regi mandauit lib. Legis manu sua propria transcribere, vt secundum eum Rempub. regeret, nullaque in parte à diuino mandato discederet. Deut. 17.
units.tr: Kings succeeded Samuel, and we know clearly that they governed sacred and profane matters alike. Indeed David called together the princes of all Israel (among whom were also the heads of the families of the tribe of Levi), not only the priests, so that he might take counsel with them about bringing back the ark (2 Sam. 6; 1 Chron. 13). He likewise ordained the ministers of the Temple, the singers and gatekeepers; he distributed the duties of priests and Levites; and in short he arranged everything pertaining to the worship of God, as we read very often in the books of Chronicles. Mention of this ordinance is then made in the history of the Kings, in 1 Esdras chapters 3 and 8, and in the book of Nehemiah chapter 12. It should be noted, however, that David did these things not on his own counsel but by divine command, as is very clear from 2 Chronicles chapter 29. For there it is written that he was commanded by the prophets Gad and Nathan to arrange everything in this way; they were sent by God not to the priests but to the King. From this it is likewise evident how and by whom God wishes even those things that pertain to his worship to be governed. For this reason God commanded Joshua to read the book of the law day and night, so that he might order everything according to the precepts contained in it. Likewise he commanded the chosen king to copy out the book of the law with his own hand, so that he might govern the commonwealth according to it, and depart in no part from the divine command (Deut. 17).

units.la: Eodem modo Salomon fecit: non tantum profanarum rerum curam habuit, verumetiam ad religionem attinentia constituit. Hic iatet cætera quæ cum patre Dauide communia ei fuerunt. Templum Deo ædificauit: idemque ipse, non Sacerdos, dedicauit seu inauguravit 1. Reg. 8. & 2. Paral. cap. 6. Idem summum Sacerdotem Ebiathar à Sacerdotio remouit, & Sadoch ei substituit. 1. Reg. 2. similia deinde fecerunt Reges omnes boni (Mali eadem potestate abusi sunt ad impietatem, quia non ex præscripto Dei egerunt) Asa, Iehosaphat, Ezechias, Ioas, Iosias, vsque ad captiuitatem.
units.tr: Solomon did the same. He not only had charge of profane affairs but also set in order matters pertaining to religion. Here the rest, which he shared with his father David, is plain. He built the Temple to God, and he himself, not a priest, dedicated or inaugurated it (1 Kings 8; 2 Chron. 6). He also removed Abiathar the high priest from the priesthood and put Zadok in his place (1 Kings 2). Afterwards all the good kings did similar things: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Joash, Josiah, down to the captivity. (The wicked used the same power for impiety, because they did not act according to God's prescription.)

units.la: Post captiuitatem Respub. gubernata fuit ab optimatibus, inter quos principem scrè locum tenuerunt Sacerdotes. Durauit ea reipub. forma vsque ad tempus Asamonæorum, teste Iosepho lib. Antiquit. 11. cap. Constituti sunt ipsis initio Magistratus à Persarum Regibus, vt ex lib. Esdræ & Nehemiæ conspicitur: ac permanserunt tributarij Persarum, donec Alexander magnus Hierosolymas peruenit. Sub Macchabæis coepeĸunt in existimatione tanta sanctitatis esse Pharisæi, vt siue de Regibus siue de Pontificib. aliquid mali dicerent, facilè eis fides adhibereĸtur. Quocirca coacti sunt reges ipsis adulari, & participes Imperij sui facere si modo pacatè cupirent regnare; teste Iosepho lib. Antiquit. 13. cap. 23. & 24. & lib. 17. de bello Iudaico cap. 4. Exaĸtis Macchabæis successerunt in imperio Herodes & filius eius Archelaüs. Illo defuncto, & hoc in exilium eiecto, restituta est imperandi potestas Principibus Sacerdotum, Scribis & Pharisæis: illis nimirum, quos historia Euangelica affirmat in Synedrio consedisse. Haec deinde Reipublicæ facies (similis fuit ante Macchabæorum ætatem) duârauit vsque ad excidium, vt Iosephus in lib. Antiquit. Iud. 20. cap. penultimo, his verbis testatur: ὡς ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἀρχαίων ... (intellige Herodis & filij ipsius Archelaij) ἐπίσκοπος μὲν ἦν ἐν πολιτείᾳ· τῶν δὲ ἀποστολῶν τῶν ἐν ἡμέραις Ῥωμαίων ἐν ἐμπορίᾳ.
