Interim tamen parebant Romanis: neque in aliis rebus potestatem seruauerant integram, quàm in rebus ad religionem morésque patrios pertinentibus: quod etiam alibi viuentibus Iudeis permissum fuit, vt ex Iosephi commentariis pluribus locis manifestum fit, maximè verò ex lib. 19. cap. 4. & lib. 4. cap. 12, de qua re aliàs plura diximus ac decimus.
units.tr: After the captivity the commonwealth was governed by the nobles, among whom the priests held almost the first place. This form of commonwealth lasted until the time of the Asmoneans, as Josephus testifies in the eleventh book of the Antiquities. At first magistrates were appointed for them by the kings of the Persians, as can be seen from the books of Ezra and Nehemiah; and they remained tributary to the Persians until Alexander the Great came to Jerusalem. Under the Maccabees the Pharisees began to be held in such esteem for sanctity that, whether they said anything bad about kings or high priests, they were easily believed. Hence the kings were forced to flatter them and to make them sharers of their rule, if they wished to reign in peace (Josephus, Antiquities 13, chs. 23 and 24; and Jewish War 17, ch. 4). After the Maccabees, Herod and his son Archelaus succeeded to the rule. When he died and was banished into exile, the power of ruling was restored to the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees, namely those whom the Gospel history says sat in the Sanhedrin. This form of commonwealth then (it was similar before the time of the Maccabees) lasted until the destruction, as Josephus attests in the last chapter but one of book 20 of the Jewish Antiquities, in these words: [ὡς ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἀρχαίων ... ἐπίσκοπος μὲν ἦν ἐν πολιτείᾳ· τῶν δὲ ἀποστολῶν τῶν ἐν ἡμέραις Ῥωμαίων ἐν ἐμπορίᾳ] (understand: under Herod and his son Archelaus). Meanwhile, however, they obeyed the Romans, and in other matters they did not keep their power whole, except in matters pertaining to religion and ancestral customs. This was also permitted to Jews living elsewhere, as is clear from many passages of Josephus's writings, especially book 19, chapter 4, and book 4, chapter 12, a matter on which we have said more at other times and places.

units.la: Iam verò quod toto hoc tempore Iudicium de moribus nullum fuerit apud eos Ecclesiasticum sed duntaxat politicum, ex consequentibus erit manifestum. Rex Persarum Esdræ imperat. 1. Esdr. 7. vt constituat Iudices & præfectos peritos legis, qui populum recte iudicent ac simul erudiant: & Legi Dei ac Regis non obedientes iubet, non excommunicari, seu poena Ecclesiastica, vt vocatis, puniri, sed morte, carcere, vinculis, plagis, multa, poenis videlicet politicis ... nominatis. Alijs poenis nec affecerunt illi quenquam, nec afficere aliquem potuissent: propterea quod Moses aliter non iubet castigari delinquentes. Iccirco non affecit pœna Ecclesiastica Nehemias falsos Prophetas & proditores cap. 6. neque illos, qui ex vxoribus Azoticis, Asdodithicis, Ammoniticis & Moabiticis liberos genuissent vix semi-Iudaicè loquentes, sacris, ceremonijs & Templo arcuit: sed eos percussit, ⁊ capillos euulsit, iurare coegit ne deinceps vel suas filias illis nuptui darent, vel illorum filias sibi filijsve suis ducerent. Sic & vnum ex filiis Ioiadæ, (Historiæ Manassen vocant,) qui filius erat Eliasibi summi Sacerdotis, generum Sanaballati Horonitæ in exilium egit: non interdixerunt ei Patcr aliísque Sacerdotes vsu sacrificiorum & Templi. Vt semel dicam, tale nihil reperimus: at hunc Nehemiam Sacerdotib. Leuitis, atque alijs cunctis præscripsisse legimus, quid facere & sequi singulos deceret. Post haec temporã in sacris literis nihil reperimus de Reipublicæ gubernatione: Quare ex Macchabæorum & Iofephi inprimis historia peti oportet, quod scire cupimus. Ad Macchabæos quod attinet, nihil aliud inuenimus, quam occisos illos fuisse qui defecerant à Iudæis, lib. 3. Macch. cap. vltimo: & aliquid huc pertinens, cap. 2. Non nescio hunc librum in multis Bibliis desiderari, qui tamen in aliis habetur, & historica fide minimè indignus reputatur. In Iosepho nonnihil reperiet attentus lector, quod nostram sententiam confirmet: quod aliter sententibus patrocinetur, nihil omninò scriptum ab eo notaui. Profectò homini veritatis studioso, & conceptam sententiam pertinaciter contra veritatē defendere nolenti, vel hoc vnicum satisfecerit, quòd Iosephus (Qui Gentis suæ historiam ita scripsit diligenter, vt nimis hæc in re superstitiosus videri possit;) dum etiam res minimas aliquando nimis verbosè persequitur) nullo in loco suorum librorum vnico verbulo meminit Ecclesiastici huius Magistratus, iudiciis de moribus præsidentis, qui à politico fuerit alius, quíque ius habuerit ipsos etiam Reges suos puniendi. Caeterum quis est ita ineptus, qui non intelligat, ad substantiam gubernationis ac Reipub. pertinere talem Magistratum, adeóque nobilissimam maximeque necessariam civitatis partem esse (si quidem pro parte fit habendus) ac proinde absque insigni errore peccatóque negligi ab eo non potuisse? Quocirca talem iurisdictionem inter Iudaeos ipse ignorauit, Idem author scribit, summum Sacerdotem Ioannem aliquando in ipso templo interfecisse Iesum fratrem suum propter contentionem de principatu Sacerdotij lib. antiquit. II. cap.7. at Excommunicatum non scribit. Eodem lib.cap. 8. & ultimo, Item lib.12.cap. 9. Item 13.cap.2. & in hoc libro saepius. Item lib. 18. cap. 5. Item lib. 1. de bello Iud.cap.5. & aliás quoque ostendit, transgressores cum alios, tum eos, qui vel non seruassent sabbathum, vel edissent vetitorum aliquid, coactos fuisse fugere & exulare: nunquam Ecclesiasticae cuiusquam poenae iudicijque meminit. Sic Antiochus, vt lib.12.cap.3. idem refert, iubet illos, qui immundum comedissent, aut in vrbem importassent, aut contra Legis sententiam in Templum ingredi ausi fuissent, multa puniri trium millium drachmarum: Ecclesiasticae poenae nullius commeminit. Cap. vltimo lib. II. Sic scribit: [Greek text] Quisfic desipit, vt putet homines, qui in re tali peccauissent, vt in [Greek] deserta patria & liberis exulare voluisse, siquidé poena ecclesiastica crimen eluere potuissent? Quod si in tali peccato hac poenae locum non habebant, in quo, quaeso te, locum habere potuerunt? Manifestissimè vel hinc apparet, nugas esse, quae de duplici hoc poenarum genere commenti sunt homines.
units.tr: Now that this whole period is covered, it will be clear from what follows that among them there was no ecclesiastical judgment on morals at all, only a civil one. The king of the Persians commands Ezra (1 Esdr. 7) to appoint judges and expert officials of the law who will judge the people rightly and at the same time instruct them. He orders that those who do not obey the Law of God and the king are not to be excommunicated or punished with an ecclesiastical penalty, as they call it, but with death, prison, chains, blows, fines, and the other civil penalties named there. They inflicted no other penalties on anyone, and could not have inflicted any, because Moses does not command any other punishment for offenders. For this reason Nehemiah did not impose an ecclesiastical penalty on the false prophets and traitors (ch. 6), nor did he exclude from the sacred rites, the ceremonies, and the Temple those who had fathered children by wives from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, who scarcely spoke Hebrew. Instead he struck them, pulled out their hair, and made them swear that they would no longer give their daughters in marriage to those peoples or take their daughters for themselves or for their sons. So too, one of the sons of Joiada (the histories call him Manasseh), who was the son of the high priest Eliashib and son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite, he drove into exile; neither the father nor the other priests forbade him the use of the sacrifices and the Temple. To put it briefly, we find nothing of this kind. What we do read is that Nehemiah prescribed to the priests, the Levites, and all the rest what each of them ought to do and follow. After this period the sacred writings contain nothing about the government of the commonwealth. So what we want to know must be sought above all from the history of the Maccabees and of Josephus. As for the Maccabees, we find nothing except that those who had fallen away from the Jews were put to death (3 Macc. last ch.), and something relevant in ch. 2. I am aware that this book is missing from many Bibles, though it is found in others and is not thought unworthy of trust as history. In Josephus the attentive reader will find something that confirms our view; I have noticed nothing written by him that supports the opposing opinion. Surely this one point should be enough for a man who studies the truth and is unwilling to defend obstinately a view he has formed against the truth. Josephus, who wrote the history of his nation so carefully that he may seem overly scrupulous in this matter (since at times he follows even very minor events at excessive length), nowhere in his books mentions a single word about this ecclesiastical magistrate who presided over judgments on morals, separate from the civil one, and who had the right to punish even their own kings. Moreover, who is so foolish as not to understand that such a magistrate belongs to the substance of government and the commonwealth, and is therefore the most noble and most necessary part of the state (if indeed it is to be counted as a part), and that for this reason he could not have been neglected by him without a serious error and sin? For this reason the same author writes that the high priest John once killed his brother Jesus in the Temple itself because of a dispute over the high priesthood (Antiq. 11.7), but he does not write that anyone was excommunicated. In the same book, ch. 8 and the last ch.; likewise book 12 ch. 9; book 13 ch. 2, and often in this book; likewise book 18 ch. 5; likewise book 1 of the Jewish War ch. 5. He shows elsewhere too that transgressors, both others and those who had failed to keep the sabbath or had eaten something forbidden, were compelled to flee and go into exile, and he never mentions any ecclesiastical punishment or judgment of anyone. So Antiochus, as the same author reports (12.3), orders that those who had eaten unclean food, or brought it into the city, or had dared to enter the Temple contrary to the Law, be punished with a fine of three thousand drachmas; he makes no mention of any ecclesiastical penalty. At the end of book 2 he writes thus: [Greek text]. Who is so foolish as to think that men who had sinned in such a matter wanted to be exiled from their country and their children, if they could have wiped out the crime by an ecclesiastical penalty? And if in such a sin this penalty had no place, where, I ask you, could it have had a place? From this alone it is most clearly apparent that the things men have invented about this twofold kind of penalty are nonsense.

units.la: Addam & hoc, quod lib.13.cap.18. Legimus de Hyrcano & Pharisaeis. Cum hos Rex, vt qui eorum esset discipulus, conuiuio excepisset: atque Eleazarus quidam homo turbulentus, Regem dixisset ex matre natu, quae Antiocho
units.tr: I shall add this too, which we read in book 13 ch. 18 about Hyrcanus and the Pharisees. When the king, because he was a disciple of theirs, had entertained them at a banquet, a certain turbulent man named Eleazar said that the king was born of a mother who had been a slave in the time of Antiochus

units.la: Epiphane regnante serua fuissët, ideóque Sacerdotio fungi non posse: idque Rex iniquissimè tulisset (erat enim calumnia) interrogauit caeteros, quid ipsis videretur. Omnibus blasphemum esse respondentibus, rursus interrogauit, qua pœna videretur dignus, Μανῆν ἱματων ἐξ Ἀσεβὴς. ἀ γὰρ ἱδὲκει ἀοιδό-μας, ἵνα ἀναβάντερ ζωῆς: ἀλλα ὅτε ἐ φάτι ἀπὸ τὰς κακίας ἐκ ἀπὸ ἡ ἀχρὰ ἐφι σάι ἐφ ἀλάτωχι φαρισαῖοι. Hoc responsum tam mite ita offendit Regem, vt ipsis defertis ad Sadducaeos transsierit: ex quo deinde maximae calamitates natae sunt. Apparet ex hoc loco, ipsos Ecclesiasticas poenas nullas habuisse, quas peccantibus inflígerent. Quippe sui ordinis hominem, quem mortem non promeruisse iudicarent, non plagis & carcere, sed sacris poenis castigauissent, Regiqué sic magis satisfecissent.
units.tr: Epiphanes, and therefore could not exercise the priesthood. The king took this very unjustly (for it was a slander), and asked the others what they thought. When they all answered that it was blasphemy, he asked again what punishment seemed to them to be deserved. They answered that he deserved stripes and chains, not death, for the thing he had said was said out of anger rather than wickedness, and that the Pharisees were not at fault in this. [Greek: Μανῆν ἱματων ἐξ Ἀσεβὴς. ἀ γὰρ ἱδὲκει ἀοιδό-μας, ἵνα ἀναβάντερ ζωῆς: ἀλλα ὅτε ἐ φάτι ἀπὸ τὰς κακίας ἐκ ἀπὸ ἡ ἀχρὰ ἐφι σάι ἐφ ἀλάτωχι φαρισαῖοι.] This reply was so mild that it offended the king greatly, and he at once deserted the Pharisees and went over to the Sadducees, from which great calamities later arose. It is clear from this passage that they had no ecclesiastical penalties to inflict on sinners. Indeed, if they had judged that a man of their own order did not deserve death, they would have punished him not with blows and prison but with sacred penalties, and in this way would have satisfied the king more.

units.la: Summatim dicam omnia, nullus exstat vel in Iosepho, vel in sacris litteris locus bipartitae illius iurisdictionis, sed vnius fit mentio Magistratus politici, qui profana & sacra direxerit & gubernarit secundum Legis praescriptionem: nec mentio vlla fit aliarum poenarum quàm carceris, plagarum, exilij, mortis, multaesue confiscationis bonorum, & aliarum huius generis corporalium poenarum, cum de poenis delinquentium fit mentio in Bibliis aut Iosephi libris.
units.tr: To sum up everything: there is no place, either in Josephus or in the sacred writings, that mentions that twofold jurisdiction. Instead there is mention of only one civil magistrate, who directed and governed both the profane and the sacred affairs according to the prescription of the Law. Nor is there any mention of any penalties other than imprisonment, blows, exile, death, confiscation of goods, and other penalties of this bodily kind, whenever the punishments of offenders are mentioned in the Bible or in the books of Josephus.

units.la: Ex praedictis omnibus perspicuè patet, in Iudaeorum Repub. quam Deus ipse constituit ac ordinauit, duas hasce iurisdictiones nunquam fuisse, sed vnicum Magistratum res omnes profanas pariter & sacras iuxta Regulam verbi Dei gubernauisse. At verò Deus Rempub. praescripsit populo suo perfectam, numerisque omnibus absolutam, quod ad substantiam attinet: qua neque excogitata sit, neque ǫxcogitari possit alia perfectior, concinnior, aptior. Quis enim cum Deo de sapientia contendat? Qui de praestantia & laude Legum à Deo per Mosen Iudacis tradi tarum plura cupit videre, legat Euseb. 8. lib. de praepar. Euangel. cap. 2. Praeclaram igitur meretur laudem, quae, quoad fieri potelt, proximè ad hanc formam accedit. Quocirca nos confiteri oportet, Deum non mandâsse distincta illa vnius Reipub. in qua eandem cum citibus colit Religionem, Magistratus imperia & iudicia, quae hodie nobis obganniunt quidam. Vnde sequitur, impiè illos facere, qui tali Magistratui partem visibilis potestatis à Deo traditae adimunt, & nescio quibus aliis adscribunt: imò iurisdictionem aliam confingunt, cui ipse quoque Magistratus politicus obnoxius subiectúsque sit. Peccant non minus, cum pium & Christianum Magistratum veluti profanum sacro opponunt: cum vnus ille idémque, quatenus res sacras secundum scripturas gubernat & disponit, sacer, quatenus autem res prosanas secundum Leges curat, Politicus nominetur. Non enim pro rerum dispensatarum varietate variat dispensatio seu gubernatio: vt supra fuit declaratum. Quippe Dij quidam sunt tales Magistratus, & in medio corum Deus habitat, Psalm. 82. Item educatores, altores, curatores, defensores, & nutritii sunt Ecclesiae. Esaiae 49.
units.tr: From all the things said above it is plainly evident that in the commonwealth of the Jews, which God himself established and ordained, these two jurisdictions never existed, but a single magistrate governed all affairs, both profane and sacred alike, according to the rule of the Word of God. Indeed God prescribed to his people a commonwealth that was perfect and complete in all its numbers, so far as its substance is concerned, such that no more perfect, more harmonious, or better-fitted one has been or could be devised. For who can contend with God about wisdom? Whoever wishes to see more about the excellence and praise of the Laws given to the Jews by God through Moses, let him read Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica, book 8, ch. 2. Therefore that form deserves high praise which comes as close to this as possible. Hence we must confess that God did not command that distinct commonwealth in which the same magistrate's commands and judgments, and the same religion, are maintained for citizens, which some now clamour for against us. From this it follows that those act impiously who take from such a magistrate a part of the visible power given by God and ascribe it to I know not what other authorities; indeed they invent another jurisdiction to which the civil magistrate himself is subject. They sin no less when they set the pious Christian magistrate against the sacred, as if he were profane, since that one and the same man, in so far as he governs and arranges sacred matters according to the Scriptures, is called sacred, and in so far as he attends to profane matters according to the laws, is called civil. For the manner of dispensing does not vary with the variety of the things dispensed, as was declared above. Indeed such magistrates are "gods," and God dwells in the midst of them (Ps. 82). Likewise they are the nurses, foster-fathers, guardians, defenders, and nursing fathers of the Church (Isa. 49).

units.la: Profanus igitur est, quisquis profanos eos vocat, magisue profanos existimat sacro illo suo Magistratu: quem Deus nullibi reperitur instituisse vel approbasse. Nam in novo Testamento rationem gubernandi nullam praeficiniit: nec veterem formam mutauit: imò manifestè suis Ministris prohibuit Christus Dominatum; Reges, inquit, Gentium dominantur ipsis. Vos autem non sic. Item palàm dicit se eos mittere ad docendum, quomodo ipse missus fuerit à patre. Certè nullibi legimus Christum iudicia exercuisse de moribus, qualia nobis depingunt quidam: quinimò nec adulteram sua sententia damnare, nec inter fratres arbitrari voluit de bonorum diuisione, tametsi rogaretur: vt doceret nos, se aliud iudicium non agnoscere, quam Magistratus. Hinc Apostolus Paulus Ministros non dixit esse Rectores iudiciorum & Senatus cuiusdam Ecclesiastici, sed dispensatores seu explicatores mysteriorum Dei. Sic & Petrus iubet Ministris ne sic agant curam gregis, ac si dominatum exercerent.
units.tr: Whoever calls the magistrate profane, or thinks him profane in his sacred office, is himself profane, since God is nowhere found to have instituted or approved that office. In the New Testament Christ laid down no plan of government and did not alter the old form. Rather, he expressly forbade his ministers dominion: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you shall not be so." Likewise he openly says that he sends them to teach, just as the Father sent him. We certainly never read that Christ exercised judgments about morals of the kind some depict for us. Indeed he would not condemn the adulteress by his own sentence, nor arbitrate between brothers about dividing goods, though he was asked, so that he might teach us that he acknowledged no judgment other than that of the magistrate. Hence the Apostle Paul did not call ministers the rulers of judgments and of some ecclesiastical senate, but the stewards or expounders of the mysteries of God. So too Peter orders ministers not to exercise the care of the flock as if they were exercising dominion.

units.la: Confirmat hæc omnia doctissimus ætatis nostræ Theologus, Petrus Martyr, in comm. in cap. 8. lib. 1. Samuelis: vbi expresse probat, bicipitem, & ob id monstrosam fore eam Remp. quae Magistratum habet Christianum, si duo sint pari potestate de coercendis moribus iudicia. Tandem disputationem conclusurus ait. Quid ergo, inquies: imperabit Magistratus Ministris & concionatoribus? Respondeo, Verbi Dei & Sacramenta nulli potestati subijciuntur. Ministri autem subijciuntur bifariam, & quod ad mores, & quod ad functionem attinet. Nam si aut perdite viuant, aut officium non faciant, possunt corripi à Magistratu & submoveri. Sed adhuc isti sibi civilem potestatem aliam Ecclesiasticā, aliam profanam: quorum alteram tribuunt Papæ, alteram Magistratui. Sed frustra. Nam quod ad Ecclesiasticam potestatem attinet, satis est civilis Magistratus. Is enim, vt ait Arist. in Polit. curare debet, vt omnes officium faciant, vt Iurisconsulti, vt Medici, vt rustici, vt Pharmacopolæ: inter quos etiam possumus numerare Ministros & concionatores. Quid hic opus est multiplicare capita? Salomon, Dauid Iosias, cum esset Magistratus civiles, tamen putabant Religionem à sua cura non esse alienam. Constantinus, Theodosius, Iustinianus, nihil magis cogitabant, quàm vt veram Dei Ecclesiam constituerent. Hæc Martyr. Similia reperies in expos. it. cap. 19. lib. Iudicū, in loco cōmuni, de Magistratu.
units.tr: The most learned theologian of our age, Peter Martyr, confirms all this in his commentary on 1 Samuel chapter 8, where he expressly proves that a commonwealth which has a Christian magistrate would be two-headed and therefore monstrous if two authorities of equal power had judgment over the restraint of morals. Finally, concluding the discussion, he says: "What then, you will ask? Will the magistrate command the ministers and preachers? I answer: the Word of God and the sacraments are subject to no power. Ministers, however, are subject in two respects, both as to their morals and as to their function. For if they live wickedly or neglect their office, they can be corrected and removed by the magistrate. But these men still distinguish a civil power, one ecclesiastical and another profane, and they assign the one to the Pope and the other to the magistrate. But in vain. For as far as ecclesiastical power is concerned, the civil magistrate is sufficient. For, as Aristotle says in the Politics, he ought to see to it that everyone performs his office: lawyers, doctors, farmers, apothecaries, among whom we may also count ministers and preachers. Why is there any need here to multiply heads? Solomon, David, and Josiah, though they were civil magistrates, nevertheless thought religion was not foreign to their care. Constantine, Theodosius, and Justinian thought of nothing more than establishing the true Church of God." So Martyr. You will find similar things in his exposition of chapter 19 of Judges, under the common topic on the magistrate.

units.la: Non nego interim, hunc ipsum Martyrem Seniorū quoque mentionem facere. At si hos aliam habuisse potestatē in Ecclesia contedas, quàm Presbyteri, de quibus Hieronymus locutus est, habuerunt, contrarium sibi cum facis. Nam apertè castigatione morum in Ministris & concionatoribus penes Magistratum esse supra dixit. Quare vt Consiliarios quosdam Magistratus censuit esse, à quibus doceretur, quid verbo Dei consentancum esset, aut non esset: de qualibus nos Presbyteris in præsentia non disputamus. Scio illud etiam, cum in communi errore cum alijs haesisse, & Seniores & Episcopos arbitratus fuerit potestatē habuisse Principes Excommunicandi Reges & Magistratus. Atà viro pietate, virtute, & prudentia clarissimo, D. Thoma Blarero, Consule Constantiense admonitus, timidius postea de hac re locutus est. Sed tempus est, ut ad tua redeam.
units.tr: Meanwhile I do not deny that this same Martyr also mentions elders. But if you maintain that these had some other power in the Church than the presbyters of whom Jerome spoke had, you contradict yourself. For he said plainly above that the correction of morals in ministers and preachers rests with the magistrate. Hence he judged that the elders were certain counsellors of the magistrate, from whom he would be taught what was or was not consonant with the Word of God. We do not dispute at present about such presbyters. I know also that he was caught in the common error with others, and thought that the elders and bishops had the power of excommunicating kings and magistrates. But, admonished by Thomas Blarer, a man most distinguished for piety, virtue, and prudence, consul of Constance, he spoke more cautiously about this matter afterwards. But it is time I returned to your points.

units.la: Idem nobis indicare voluit Christus, cum dixit, Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo: hoc est, Regnum meum non est politicum, externum, & invisibile. Regnat enim Christus etiam in hoc mundo, sed invisibilis & spiritualis est ipsius gubernatio: quae, ut ipse ait, in veritate consistit & spiritu. Quare cum ex hoc mundo Regnum suum non esse ait, atque interim Regem se esse affirmet, de visibili Regni procuratione loquitur. Ideo Pilato dicebat: Si meum Regnum externum esset & visibile, pugnarent utique Ministri mei pro me ne traderer Iudaeis. Hunc locum mirum est, rabiosum quendam hypocritam ausum esse detorquere ad Excommunicationem: cum multò magis probet, non debere Ministros vllam exercere iurisdictionem externam, quae à gubernatione Magistratus distincta sit.
units.tr: Christ wished to indicate the same thing when he said, "My kingdom is not of this world," that is, my kingdom is not political, external, and visible. For Christ also reigns in this world, but his government is invisible and spiritual, and, as he himself says, it consists in truth and in spirit. Therefore when he says that his kingdom is not of this world, and yet at the same time affirms that he is a king, he is speaking of the visible administration of the kingdom. That is why he said to Pilate: "If my kingdom were external and visible, my ministers would certainly fight for me, so that I should not be delivered to the Jews." It is remarkable that some rabid hypocrite has dared to twist this passage to support excommunication, when it proves far more strongly that ministers ought not to exercise any external jurisdiction distinct from the government of the magistrate.

units.la: Sic cum Caesari ac Deo Christus iubet dare quod utrique debetur, non hoc dicit, Presbyteros quosdam, vel Ministros, vel alios quoslibet pio Magistratui subiectos, debere peculiare constituere iudicium, & distinctam exercere iurisdictionem. Hoc non esset Caesari dare, quod Caesaris est, sed ei adimere, quod Deus ipsi dedit. Probare debebant, qui talib. ineptijs infatuare imperitam multitudinem student, Deum alicubi hoc sibi aut Ecclesiae suae poposcisse, ut in Repub. Christianum habente Magistratum, seorsum Presbyteri & Ministri sinerentur regnare, seu iudicia publica habere de moribus & sceleribus, ipsiusmque etiam suo imperio Magistratum subijcere. Quantisper hoc non fecerint, frustra disputabunt. Nam hoc ipsum quod probare debebant, veluti confessum probatumque inscite sumunt. Nos probauimus Caesaris, hoc est, pij Magistratus totam esse visibilem rerum sacrarum pariter & profanarum gubernationem: ut qui Dei sit Minister, & ipsius nomine ac loco regat,
units.tr: So too, when Christ bids us give to Caesar and to God what is due to each, he does not say that certain presbyters, or ministers, or any others subject to a godly magistrate, ought to set up a separate court and exercise a distinct jurisdiction. That would not be giving Caesar what is Caesar's, but taking away from him what God has given him. Those who strive to befuddle the untutored crowd with such absurdities ought to prove that God has anywhere claimed this for himself or for his Church: that, in a commonwealth that has a Christian magistrate, the presbyters and ministers should be allowed to reign apart, or hold public courts over morals and crimes, and even subject the magistrate himself to their rule. As long as they have not done so, they will argue in vain. For what they ought to prove they take up as if it were conceded and proved, foolishly. We have proved that the administration of both sacred and profane things, the whole visible government, belongs to Caesar, that is, to the godly magistrate, who is God's minister and rules in his name and place.

units.la: Sensus illius loci talis est. Iudæi cùm effent Dei populus, putabant fe nemini seruire debere: ac pugnare quodammodo, Dei populum esse fiue Deo seruire, & hominibus parere: id quod Christi responsum euidentissimè probat. Ipse namque simulationem eorum intelligens, de Deo respondet, licet ipsi dè Deo in sua interrogatione nullam mentionem feciffent. Quippe hoc tantum interrogant Christum, vtrum liceat Cæsari censum soluere: vt, si affirmet, populo inuisum reddât, si neget, Herodis ministris accusent. Respondet ergo eis Christus verbis supra dictis, quasi diceret: Non pugnant inter se Deo seruire & Magistratui, quamdiu vnicuiq; datur quod suum est. Census Magistratus est, quod argumento ab inscriptione & figura nummi ducto probatur. Quare nihil contra Deum facitis, dum Cæsari, quod suum est, reddLtis, modo interim Deo quoque, quod suum est, reddatis.
units.tr: The sense of that passage is this. When the Jews were God's people, they thought they ought to serve no one, and they were in a sense contending that to be the people of God is one thing and to serve God and obey men is another. Christ's answer most clearly refutes this. Understanding their pretence, he replies about God, although they had made no mention of God in their question. For they ask Christ only whether it is lawful to pay the tax to Caesar, so that if he should say yes, they could make him hated by the people, and if he should say no, they could accuse him to Herod's officials. Christ therefore answers them with the words cited above, as if to say: serving God and serving the magistrate are not in conflict, so long as each is given what is his own. The tax belongs to the magistrate, as is proved by the argument drawn from the inscription and image on the coin. Therefore you do nothing against God when you render to Caesar what is his, provided that at the same time you also render to God what is his.

units.la: Adducunt etiam exemplum Regum Sauli 1.Sam.13.& Vzziae.2.Paral.26. contra Dei mandatum officio Sacerdotis fungi volentium; quo significare volunt, quemadmodum hi peccarint, ita etiam pium Magistratum grauiter errare, si res sacras seu Ecclesiasticas curet: id est, si ipsos iuxta & supra se regnare non sinat. Quid ad putidum hoc cauillum dicemus nos? Antequam Deus Aharonem sibi in Sacerdotem elegisset, nihil vetabat eundem esse Sacerdotem & Magistratum, vt exempla Melchisedechi & Mosis ostendunt, Leuit.8. Postea quoque Heli & Samuel vtrumque munus simul administrarunt. Sic & post reditum ex captiuitate Machabaci, tametsi non essent ex Sacerdotali linea Aharonis. Patet igitur his exemplis absurdi nihil sequi, si Magistratus etiam res sacras tractet.
units.tr: They also adduce the examples of King Saul (1 Sam. 13) and Uzziah (2 Chron. 26), who wished to perform the office of priest against God's command. By this they want to signify that, just as these men sinned, so a godly magistrate also errs grievously if he takes charge of sacred or ecclesiastical things, that is, if he does not allow those men to reign beside him and above him. What shall we say to this stinking quibble? Before God chose Aaron to be priest, nothing forbade the same man from being both priest and magistrate, as the examples of Melchizedek and Moses show (Lev. 8). Afterwards too, Eli and Samuel administered both offices at once. So also after the return from captivity the Maccabees did so, although they were not of the priestly line of Aaron. It is clear, then, from these examples that nothing absurd follows if the magistrate also handles sacred things.

units.la: Vt autem rectius intelligatur res, obseruandum est, ideo Deum noluisse cuiuslibet Sacrificijs placari, sed Aharonis solius & ab eo prognatorum, vt Iudæos & nos quoque doceret, solius Christi Sacrificium potuisse itam Dei à nobis tollere. Ergo sicut Iudæos per Aharonitas iussit sibi offerre re Sacrificia mortem Christi significantia, sic etiam vult nos in Christo & per Christum nostra Sacrificia, laudes, invocationes, preces, gratiarum actiones offerre, vt ab eo exaudiamur. Quis nunc nescit Aharonis Sacerdotio sublato, ex æquo nos omnes esse Sacerdotes? Peccavit ergo Rex Saul, quando sacrificare ausus est: & peccavit etiam Rex Vzzias, quando suffire voluit, quae Sacerdotis erant. Sed non peccet perinde Magistratus hodie, qui Ministerio fungeretur, si quidem per negocia utrumque munus praestare posset. An excepit Apostolus Magistratus & potentes, quando in 1.ad Cor.14.dicit, posse omnes nos sigillatim prophetare? Sublata iam sunt sacrificia boum & agnorum, vna cum suffimentis: & reliqua illa tantum sunt sacrificia, quae tunc etiam ab omnibus sibi offerri Deus voluit.
units.tr: But that the matter may be understood more correctly, it must be observed that God did not wish to be propitiated by the sacrifices of anyone at all, but only by those of Aaron and his descendants. This was to teach the Jews, and us too, that the sacrifice of Christ alone could remove the wrath of God from us. Therefore, just as through the Aaronites he commanded the Jews to offer to him sacrifices signifying the death of Christ, so he also wills that we offer our sacrifices, praises, invocations, prayers, and thanksgivings in Christ and through Christ, so that we may be heard by him. Who now does not know that, with the priesthood of Aaron abolished, we are all priests alike? King Saul therefore sinned when he dared to sacrifice, and King Uzziah sinned too when he wished to burn incense, which belonged to the priests. But a magistrate today, who would perform the ministry, would not sin in the same way, provided that by his own labours he could perform both offices. Or did the Apostle except magistrates and the powerful when, in 1 Corinthians 14, he says that all of us can prophesy one by one? The sacrifices of oxen and lambs have now been abolished, together with the incense, and those other sacrifices which God then wished to be offered to him by all are the only ones that remain.

units.la: Iam hoc quoque considerandum est, aliud esse res sacras curare & gubernare, aliud agere. Multas regit res Magistratus, quas ipse per se non facit. Licuit igitur Vzziae disponere, gubernare, ac regere Sacerdotes, ipsorumque officia constituere secundum praescriptum Dei: sacrificare & sufsire non licuit. Equidem Magistratus Sacerdotes ineptos removere, aptiores substituere potest ac debet. Placet hoc Deo si modo id secundum verbi Dei Regulam faciat: vt Salomo fecit 1.Reg.2. Quinimo Persarum Reges recte piéque fecerunt, cum populo ex captivitate reduci Principes siue Duces atque Sacerdotes iuxta praeceptum & voluntatem Dei in sacris expressam libris constituerunt, legitimeque electos confirmarunt. Hoc enim ad eos iuspertinuit, dum Iudaeam suo imperio subiectam & tributariam tenerent. Recte posteriores quoque Reges fecisset, si non ex propria libidine, sed iuxta Regulam à Deo traditam Sacerdotes & Principes Iudaeis subditis suis creauisset. Non peccarunt igitur cum alij, tum Romani, cum Sacerdotes ac Principes ordinarunt aut confirmarunt: sed in hoc peccarunt grauiter, quod Sacerdotium illis crediderunt, qui ab Aharone non descenderant.
units.tr: It must also be considered that it is one thing to take care of and govern sacred matters, and another to perform them. A magistrate governs many things that he does not himself do. So Uzziah was permitted to arrange, govern and direct the priests and to fix their duties according to God's prescription, but he was not permitted to sacrifice or burn incense. Indeed, the magistrate can and should remove unfit priests and put more suitable ones in their place. God is pleased when he does this according to the rule of God's Word, as Solomon did (1 Kings 2). Moreover, the kings of Persia acted rightly and piously when, after the return of the people from captivity, they appointed leaders or princes and priests according to the command and will of God expressed in the sacred books, and confirmed them once lawfully chosen. For this right belonged to them, since they held Judea subject to their rule and tributary. Later kings also would have acted rightly if they had appointed priests and princes for their Jewish subjects, not from their own lust, but according to the rule handed down by God. So both others and the Romans did not sin when they ordained or confirmed priests and princes; but they sinned gravely in this, that they entrusted the priesthood to men who were not descended from Aaron.

units.la: Nec minus recte piéque fecerunt Imperatores Christiani, quod hoc suum ius contra Episcopos, ipsúmque etiam Romanum Antistitem fortiter constantérque aliquot seculis defenderunt.
units.tr: The Christian emperors acted no less rightly and piously in defending this their right, bravely and steadfastly for several centuries, against the bishops and even against the Roman bishop himself.

units.la: Probaui vnicam semper in Repub. Iudaeorum fuisse iurisdictionem, non duas differentes hoc pacto,quo nunc aliqui discriminâdas censent. Supererit igitur,vt alterum quoque probem,scilicet penes Synedrium aetate Christi capitalia iudicia in causis ad religionem proprie pertinentibus fuisse. Et nelongior sim aequo, illa solum producam, quae paucis annis ante natum Christum contigerunt.
units.tr: I have shown that there was always only one jurisdiction in the commonwealth of the Jews, not two distinct ones, as some now think should be distinguished. It remains, therefore, that I also prove the other point, namely that in the age of Christ capital judgments in causes properly pertaining to religion belonged to the Sanhedrin. And lest I be longer than is fair, I shall produce only those cases which occurred a few years before Christ was born.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De potestate Synedrij tempore Romanorum.
units.tr: On the power of the Sanhedrin in the time of the Romans.

units.la: Vm Iudaeam Pompeius occupasset, atque Gabinius deuicto Alexandro Iudaeae statum mutasset, regnare integre coeperunt Pharisaei Hierosolymis. Etenim Dominatum Regium sustulit, atque optimatum gubernationem restituit, tota Iudaea in quinque partes aequalis potestatis fortisfue diuisa: quarum singulae à suo proprio regerentur Synedrio. Aristocratia libenter regebantur, inquit Iosephus, lib.1. belli Iud.cap.6. vnius imperio sublato, Et lib.Antiq.14.cap.10. Cum quinque, ait, Synedria Gabinius instituisset, in quinque partes gentem dispertiuit. His numeratis addit, καὶ ὡς μὲν ἀποπλαγμένοι τῆς δυναστείας ἐν ἀριστοκρατίᾳ ἦσαν. Haec Reipub. facies etsi iterum deinde luxata est, cum Iudaeis Rex datus est à Romanis Herodes ille Magnus (Synedrium magna ex parte iurisdictionem authoritatémque suam sub Hyrcano, cui Principatû Sacerdotij confirmarat Cesar, retinuit: quod vel solius Herodis historia sive iudicium probet:) attamen à morte ipsius filiique eius Archelai mox restituta fuit. Quod quia ex historia Euangelica alio in loco demonstratum à nobis fuit, in praesentia aliquot Iosephi testimonijs confirmasse contenti erimus. Citabo autem non omnia (hoc enim nimis longum foret) sed duo aut tria duntaxat proferam, ex quibus res planissimè demonstrabitur.
units.tr: When Pompey had seized Judaea, and Gabinius, after defeating Alexander, had changed the state of Judaea, the Pharisees began to rule Jerusalem entirely. For he abolished royal rule and restored aristocratic government, dividing the whole of Judaea into five parts of equal power and strength, each to be governed by its own Sanhedrin. Josephus says in Book 1 of the Jewish War, chapter 6, that they were governed as an aristocracy once the rule of one man was removed. And in Book 14 of the Antiquities, chapter 10, he says: "When Gabinius had instituted five Sanhedrins, he divided the nation into five parts." After listing these, he adds: "And, having turned away from dominion, they were in an aristocracy" [καὶ ὡς μὲν ἀποπλαγμένοι τῆς δυναστείας ἐν ἀριστοκρατίᾳ ἦσαν]. Although this form of the commonwealth was afterwards disturbed again, when Herod the Great was given to the Jews as king by the Romans, the Sanhedrin largely kept its jurisdiction and authority, which had been confirmed under Hyrcanus, to whom Caesar had granted the high priesthood. This is proved by the history of Herod alone, or by his judgment. Yet it was soon restored after the death of Herod and of his son Archelaus. Since I have shown this elsewhere from the Gospel history, I will be content for now to confirm it with a few testimonies of Josephus. I will not cite them all, for that would be too long, but will bring forward only two or three, from which the matter will be made perfectly clear.

units.la: Ergo annis à Christi morte plus minus decem cum Claudius Caio Caligulæ in imperio succedissset, tale pro Iudaeis Alexandrinis edictum à Caesare promulgatum fuit. Ex altè repetitis intellexi, Iudaeos, quos Alexandrinos vocant, in Alexandria ab antiquo Alexandrinis cohabitasse, pariqué cum civibus iure à Regibus donatos suisse, quod edicta & rescripta super hac re facta demonstrant. Deinde postquam Alexandria per Augustum nostro subdita est imperio, iura ipsis sua à Præfectis nostris diversis temporibus eò missis conservata esse cognoui: vt nec illo tempore, quo Aquila ibi fuit, in controversiam vocarentur. Et mortuo eorum principe non prohibuit Augustus alios eligere principes, vt qui singulos vellet suis vti moribus, neque cogi eos cuperet, vt patrium cultum transgrederentur. Paulò post, cum, quæ sub Caligula contigerant, perstrinxisset, hæc addit: βίλομαι μηδὲν διὰ τὴν Ταῦν παρ᾽ ἀρροσύνης τῶν Ἰουδαίων τῶν Ἰουδαίων ... Hæc Ioseph. lib. Antiquit. 19. cap.
units.tr: So, about ten years after the death of Christ, when Claudius had succeeded Gaius Caligula in the empire, the following edict was published by Caesar concerning the Alexandrian Jews. I have learned from ancient records that the Jews whom they call Alexandrians had lived in Alexandria from early times alongside the citizens, and had been granted the same rights as citizens by the kings, as edicts and rescripts made on this matter show. Then, after Alexandria was brought under our empire by Augustus, I found that their rights had been preserved by our prefects, who were sent there at various times, so that they were not even called in question at the time when Aquila was there. And when their leader had died, Augustus did not forbid them to choose other leaders, since he wished each people to use its own customs, and did not wish to compel them to abandon their ancestral worship. A little later, after touching on what had happened under Caligula, he adds these words: "I wish that nothing be done through the folly of the Jews..." [βούλομαι μηδὲν διὰ τὴν Ταῦν παρ᾽ ἀρροσύνης τῶν Ἰουδαίων τῶν Ἰουδαίων ...]. These are the words of Josephus, Antiquities, Book 19, chapter [...].

units.la: Cæterum quia in hoc edicto mentio fit ἐθνάρχης seu Principis Iudæorum, operæprecium fuerit declarare, quam ille habuerit potestatem. Igitur Ioseph. lib. 14. Cap. 12. ex Strabone Cappadocè historico (quo maiorem lectori fidem faceret) sic inter alia scribit. Præterquam quod in Aegypto Coloniam habent Iudaei, magna etiam pars vrbis Alexandriæ huic Genti attributa est. καθίκατω καὶ ἐθνάρχης αὐτῶν, ὡς διοικεῖν ... Potestatem, inquit, habent regendi, ius dicendi, causas cognoscendi contractuum, mandata edictaque proponendi instar perfectæ Reipub. Principis. Porrò non solis Alexandrinis Iudaeis concessa fuit haec potestas, sed omnibus in toto Romano orbe habitantibus. Etenim exemplum edicti Claudij Caesaris ris in eodem illo supra citato capite commemorat Iosephus ( Alia plurima Romana. Caesarum, Proconsulum, Senatus,Praefectorum, Decreta, data opera omitto) in quo praecipit omnibus, vt vbique terrarum sinant Iudaeos eifdem viuere ac frui priuilegijs, quae Alexandrinis concessa esse diximus. Qua in re nihil imperat noui Claudius, sed iam ante data confirmat.
units.tr: But since mention is made in this edict of the ethnarch, or prince of the Jews, it will be worth declaring what power he held. Josephus, Antiquities, Book 14, chapter 12, citing the historian Strabo of Cappadocia (to give the reader greater confidence), writes among other things as follows. Besides the fact that the Jews have a colony in Egypt, a large part of the city of Alexandria has also been assigned to this people. "And they have an ethnarch of their own, [καθίκατω καὶ ἐθνάρχης αὐτῶν, ὡς διοικεῖν ...]" that is, to administer. He says they have the power of governing, the right of judging, and of hearing cases of contracts, and of publishing commands and edicts, like the prince of a perfectly constituted commonwealth. Moreover, this power was granted not only to the Alexandrian Jews but to all who lived in the whole Roman world. For Josephus recalls, in the same chapter cited above, an example of an edict of Caesar Claudius (I deliberately omit the many other Roman decrees of emperors, proconsuls, the Senate and prefects), in which he orders everywhere on earth that the Jews be allowed to live by the same customs and enjoy the same privileges that we have said were granted to the Alexandrians. In this matter Claudius commands nothing new, but confirms what had been given before.

units.la: Ex hoc loco illud obiter intelligimus, quomodo Principes Sacerdotum potestatem dare Paulo potuerint Iudaeos extra Iudaeam viuentes Hierosolymam vinctos pertrahendi. Non enim ciuitas vlla facile patitur ab alius vrbis magistratu, cui subiecta non est, cives suos comprehendi, & alio abduci. At Iudaei vbique erant liberi, & quoad ipsorum leges ritusque pertinebant, nemine impediente trahebant. Itaque cum vbique Principes siue {a}ἐθνάρχαι eorum Hierosolymitano parerent magistratui, potuit hoc Paulus perficere.
units.tr: From this passage we understand in passing how the chief priests were able to give Paul authority to drag Jews living outside Judaea back to Jerusalem in chains. For no city easily allows its citizens to be seized and carried off by the magistrate of another city to which it is not subject. But the Jews were free everywhere, and, so far as their laws and rites were concerned, they could be led away without anyone hindering them. Therefore, since their leaders, or ethnarchs, everywhere obeyed the magistrate of Jerusalem, Paul could accomplish this.

units.la: Vix mihi persuadeo, aliquem ita esse vecordem & stupidum, qui Iudaeis in sua patria negatum opinetur a Romanis, quod alibi sub imperio suo viuentibus tam liberaliter concesserunt. Notandum etiam est, quod imperator palam affirmat, Iudaeos haec habuisse a Regibus priuilegia primum (quod historia verum esse perspicue docet) quae omnibus deinde temporibus ipsis conseruata a Romanis suerint. Hoc mirabilius est quod Iosephus lib. 12. cap. 3. scribit, Vespasianum & Titum Alexandrinis eadem consensuasse post Hierosolymae vastationem. Promisit etiam Titus idem in ipso vrbis excidio Hierosolymitanis cum bonam eius partem iam tenerët: sed frustra promisit nolentibus esse saluis. Verum vt omnem dubitandi causam omnibus praecidamus, & omnem effugiendi spem tollamus, concludemus hanc rem Iosephi verbis, quae in libro 20. antiquit. penultimo Cap. scripsit: quibus nihil dici poterit clarius: μετὰ δὲ τέταρ τελευτὴν, ἀρισοκρατία μὲν ἦν ἢ πολιτεία· τὴν δὲ ἀρχαίαν τῆς ἔθνος ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀνάστασιν. Post Herodis & Archelai obitum, inquit, regebatur Respublica Iudaeorum optimātum gubernatione: Principatus autem Gentis Sacerdotibus summis erat concreditus. Quae cum sic habeant, negari non potest, quin Synedrium aetate Christi legitimus fuerit magistratus: ac iure suo gladium tenuerit.
units.tr: I can scarcely persuade myself that anyone is so mad and stupid as to suppose that the Romans denied the Jews this in their own country, when they had granted them such generous privileges wherever they lived under their rule. It must also be noted that the emperor plainly affirms that the Jews first had these privileges from kings (which history clearly shows to be true), and that they were afterwards preserved for them by the Romans in all times. It is even more striking that Josephus, Book 12, chapter 3, writes that Vespasian and Titus confirmed the same privileges to the Alexandrians after the devastation of Jerusalem. Titus also promised the same thing to the Jerusalemites during the very destruction of the city, when he already held a good part of it; but he promised in vain to those who did not wish to be saved. But so that we may cut off every cause of doubt and every hope of escape, we will conclude this matter with the words Josephus wrote in the next-to-last chapter of Book 20 of the Antiquities, words than which nothing could be clearer: "After his death [μετὰ δὲ τὴν τούτου τελευτὴν], the government was an aristocracy [ἀριστοκρατία μὲν ἦν ἡ πολιτεία]; but the supreme priestly office of the nation [τὴν δὲ ἀρχιερατικὴν τοῦ ἔθνους ἀρχὴν] was entrusted to the high priests from the beginning." That is, after the death of Herod and Archelaus, the Jewish commonwealth was governed by an aristocracy, and the leadership of the nation had been entrusted to the chief priests. Since these things stand thus, it cannot be denied that in the time of Christ the Sanhedrin was a lawful magistrate and by its own right held the sword.

units.la: Vtrunque igitur solidè, nisi me animus meus sallit, ostendi: nempe duas distinctas iurisdictiones sive duo distincta iudicia publica de moribus in Republica Iudaeorum nullo tempore fuisse reperta: sed unum magistratum plenam habuisse potestatem iuxta praescriptum Mosis omnem religionem, omnes ceremonias, omnia ad cultum Dei pertinentia vnà cum politicis rebus constituendi, ordinandi, ac regendi. Quod cum affirmo, illud non nego; Magistratum, cuius non vna semper fuit species, quoties de re aliqua dubitaret, peritos & exercitatos in lege in consilium adhibuisse. Deinde illud etiam probaui, Synedrium verum & legitimum magistratum fuisse, & ius gladij retinuisse, quo tempore Christus haec dixit: quanquam non de quibusdam causis, sed de illis solis iudicandi liberam potestatem permisu Romanorum retineret, quae ad religionem seu cultum diuinum moresque patrios, quos peculiares & cum nullis aliis communes habebant, spectabant.
units.tr: Thus, unless my mind deceives me, I have shown both points solidly: namely, that two distinct jurisdictions, or two distinct public courts for morals, were never found at any time in the Jewish commonwealth; but that one magistrate had full power, according to the command of Moses, to establish, order and govern every religion, every ceremony, and everything pertaining to the worship of God, together with political affairs. When I affirm this, I do not deny that the magistrate, which did not always have a single form, called in experienced men skilled in the law as counsellors whenever it doubted some matter. Further, I have also proved that the Sanhedrin was a true and lawful magistrate and retained the right of the sword at the time Christ spoke these words. Yet it kept the free power of judging not in certain cases, but only in those matters which were permitted by the Romans, namely those pertaining to religion or divine worship and ancestral customs, which were peculiar to them and not held in common with any others.

units.la: Dicis ex mea sententia penes Synedrium fuisse spiritualem & ciuilem iurisdictionem. Dixi Gabinij tempore, antequam Romani suos praesides Hierosolymis haberent, Synedrium habuisse potestatem de politicis & sacris rebus pariter iudicandi. At tempore Pilati aliorumque talium Praesidum, pars maxima huius potentiae ad Romanos transijt: ac relicta ipsi est de solis rebus ad religionem attinentibus iudicandi facultas. Haec autem non erat iurisdictio ecclesiastica, vt vos hodie à Politica discernitis: sed Politicae, quam prius totam possederat, pars erat. Nam ius gladij, ceris, plagarum, retinebant, quæ vos ad ecclesiasticam potentiam pertinere negatis. Summa est, Magistratus erat legitimus & politicus quamuis non de omnibus causis, vt prius, sed de certis solum cognoscceret. Satis supérque ostendi, Politicum magistratum non desinere esse quod est, cum è verbo Dei res sacras gubernat, subditisque secundum id viuere cogit. Quæ de particula ✳ obijcis non improbo.
units.tr: You say that, in my opinion, the Sanhedrin had both spiritual and civil jurisdiction. I have said that in the time of Gabinius, before the Romans had their own governors at Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin had the power of judging equally about political and sacred matters. But in the time of Pilate and other such governors, the greater part of this power passed to the Romans, and the power of judging only matters pertaining to religion was left to it. Yet this was not an ecclesiastical jurisdiction, as you today distinguish it from the political; it was a part of the political jurisdiction which it had previously possessed entirely. For they kept the right of the sword, of scourging and of beating, which you deny belongs to ecclesiastical power. In sum, the magistrate was lawful and political, although it did not judge all cases as before, but only certain ones. I have sufficiently and more than sufficiently shown that a political magistrate does not cease to be what it is when it governs sacred matters according to the Word of God and compels its subjects to live accordingly. As for what you object concerning the particle ✳, I do not disapprove of it.

units.la: Reprehendis post hæc triplicem verborum, sit tibi vt Publicanus, explicationem: & ex eo colligis me haesitare. Quod si ita est, vt, qui plures adfert ad rem vnam responsiones, mox etiam haesitet, in perpaucis locis scripti tui certus es. Passim enim in margine notas: Refpub. 1. Refpub. 2. Refpub. 3. Refpub. 4. Potes autem excusari, quod plerumque plures responsiones tuæ nulla sunt responsio. An non in Thesibus diserte ostendi, me tertiam probare, cum dixi: Vera responsio est, quod &c. An non idem tu confiteris, cum me, hanc scribis, vt maximè verbo Dei & illis temporibus congruentem, ampleϲti? An non in primo scripto ostendi postrema maximè consentire cum totis sacris literis, & omnibus circumstantijs? Si ad hæc respicere vales, quam fraternè agas facilè agnoscēs. Sed ad rem ipsam. Primæ & secundæ accusationes non improbarem, si argumentis vtere iustis & bonis. In Thesibus postremis & correctis secundam omisi, quoniam ipsemet probare non potui, postquam expendi primam leuiter attigi quidem, vt quae aliquando fortasse locum potuerit habere: sed ita attigi, vt tertiam mihi probari indicarim. Vtinam vel tu vel alius quispiam errores mihi alios, si modo alicubi erro, quod certè nescio, ita posse tis indicare. Tam non me puderet eos reuocare quàm me non pudet hic fateri, quod verum esse arbitror. Tuæ interim reprehensiones nullius sunt momenti: ex quibus ea tantum attingam, quae propter sequentia sunt vtilia. Valde exaggeras quod dixi Christum agere in 18. Matth. de leuioribus iniuriis. At ego non hoc sentio, de omnino leuibus eum agere. Leuia voco, quae, si conferantur cum sceleribus nominatim à lege punitis, leuia videri possint: quorúmque castigatio ad magistratum non pertineat, si, qui iniuria afficitur, de ea non conqueratur. Ergo fere coincidunt nobis leue & priuatum, sicut graue & publicum: nec negamus inter priuatas iniurias alias alijs esse graviores aut leviores. At detractionem, inquis, speciem ponis. Ego mihi in primo scripto speciem hanc exempli loco notaui: neque video cur tu damnes. An leuicula res est calumnia & obtrectatio quaelibet? Non puto. At non decet fratrem ob eam causam, inquis, per diversa fora trahere: & extra duelli limites fugitantem pellere. Miror te ab affectibus tibi sic eripi, ista ut audeas scribere. Quomodo ego fugitantem extra duelli limites persequor, qui rogatus à me toties ab iniuria tamen desistere non vult? Debeo ignoscere septuagies-septies, si culpam agnoscat ac deprecatur: id est, si poenitere se prositeatur, ut Lucas ait: vel si ἵλαρχος locum apud eum invenierit. Si convinci nolit, & calumniando pergat, non ego sugitantem perttraho per diversa fora: sed cogit ille me facere, quod facere nollem.
units.tr: After this you reproach me for explaining threefold the words "Sit tibi sicut ethnicus et publicanus," and from this you infer that I hesitate. But if it is so, that one who offers several answers to one matter soon also hesitates, you are certain of this in very few places in your writing. For everywhere you note in the margin: Respub. 1, Respub. 2, Respub. 3, Respub. 4. But you may be excused, because for the most part your several answers are no answer at all. Did I not clearly show in the Theses that I approve the third, when I said: "The true answer is that..." etc.? Do you not yourself confess the same, when you write that I have commended this one as most agreeing with the Word of God and with those times? Did I not show in my first writing that the last agrees most with all of Holy Scripture and all the circumstances? If you are able to look back at these things, you will easily recognise how brotherly you are being. But to the matter itself. I would not disapprove of the first and second accusations if you used just and good arguments. In the later and corrected Theses I omitted the second, since I myself could not prove it after weighing it; I touched lightly on the first, as something which might perhaps have some place at some time; but I touched on it in such a way that I indicated the third to be the one I approved. Would that you, or someone else, would point out to me other errors, if indeed I err anywhere, which I certainly do not know; I would be no more ashamed to retract them than I am here to confess what I think is true. Meanwhile your reproofs are of no weight, and I will touch only on those which are useful for what follows. You greatly exaggerate what I said, that Christ in Matthew 18 is speaking of minor injuries. But I do not think he speaks of entirely trivial things. I call minor those things which, if compared with crimes expressly punished by law, might seem slight, and whose punishment does not pertain to the magistrate if the one injured does not complain of them. Therefore private and minor, and public and grave, nearly coincide for us; nor do we deny that among private injuries some are heavier or lighter than others. But you say I put forward the example of slander [detractionem]. I noted this kind in my first writing as an example; nor do I see why you condemn it. Is slander or any kind of detraction so trivial a matter? I do not think so. But you say it is not fitting for a brother to drag another through different courts for this reason, and to drive away one who flees beyond the bounds of the duel. I marvel that you are so carried away by your passions that you dare to write such things. How do I pursue one who flees beyond the bounds of the duel, when he, though asked by me so many times, does not wish to desist from the injury? I ought to forgive seventy times seven, if he acknowledges his fault and begs pardon; that is, if he professes that he repents, as Luke says; or if he finds a place of reconciliation [ἵλαρχος] with him. If he is unwilling to be convicted, and persists in slandering, it is not I who drag him through different courts; he compels me to do what I would not wish to do.

units.la: Mirari te scribis, à me non fuisse animadversum, illud, Sit Tibi, non esse concedentis, sed praecipientis. Ego vero animaduerti eodem modo accipienda esse verba haec, quo alia. Rogo te, si quis gentis suae iudicium despexisset, atque iniuria affectus tolerare maluisset eandem, quàm coram Romanorum praeside litigare, an fecisset male? Non puto. Non enim coactus fuit, qui ab Ethnico vel Publicano laedebatur, mox eos apud suum forum accusare, si ferre maluit iniuriam, quam coràm Romano Iudice ius suum defendere. Cum ergo praefractus ille mihi sit instar Ethnici & Publicani, non minus liberum mihi manet. Deinde cum iubet Christus offensum, si iniuriosus post priuatam admonitionem non desistat, vnum atque alterum assumere, an hoc ita praeceptum putas, ut si offensus post priuatam admonitionem tolerare malit offenforis importunitatem, quàm ali;s causam aperire, id ei non liceat? Accidit foepè, vt offensae inter aliquos nascantur, & alter eorum, qui melior est & prudentior, non velit rem publicari. Is iniuriam inferentem admonebit, vt fe liberet: sed ita, vt fi nihil obtineat, ferre malit quàm vulgare, quod patitur. Vides quam infoeliciter illa quoque refellas, quæ tibi vltrò concedimus?
units.tr: You write that you are surprised I did not notice that "let him be to you" (Matt. 18) is spoken as a command, not as a concession. I did notice it, and I take these words in the same way as the others. I ask you: if someone had despised his people's judgment and, being wronged, had preferred to bear the injury rather than litigate before the Roman governor, would he have done wrong? I do not think so. The man who was harmed by a heathen or a publican was not compelled to accuse him at once before the local court, if he preferred to bear the injury rather than defend his right before a Roman judge. Since that stubborn man stands for me in the place of a heathen and a publican, no less freedom remains to me. Next, when Christ bids the offended man, if the offender does not desist after private admonition, to take one or two others with him, do you think this is commanded in such a way that, if the offended man after private admonition prefers to bear the importunity of the offender rather than disclose the matter to others, he is not allowed to do so? It often happens that quarrels arise between some people, and one of them, who is the better and wiser, does not want the matter made public. He will admonish the one who inflicts the injury, so that he may be rid of him; but only so that, if he gains nothing, he would rather bear the wrong than make public what he suffers. You see how unhappily you refute these points, which we concede to you freely.

units.la: An non admirari omnes facis, cum scribis diuersum hoc loco tradi ab eo, quod mox Petro respondetur? Rationem profers hanc: quia vbi peccatum remittitur feptuagies, neque testes, neque ciuiles magistratus necesse est interpellari. Si Lucam cum Matthaeo voluisses coniungere illud non dixisses, puto. Christus iubet offensum primò omnium tentare, an possit offendentem conuincere peccati, id est eò deducere, vt peccatum agnoscat culpámque deprecetur. Interrogat Petrus quoties hoc facere necesse habeat. Respondet Christus apud Lucam, septies, fi toties dicat fe propter factum suum dolere: apud Matthaeum verò, septuagies-septies. Sensus apud vtrumque est, toties remittendam iniuriam, quoties iniuriam inferens fatebitur fe poenitere, & ab inferenda iniuria vult abstinere. Proinde ad testes non ante veniendum est, quàm fe folum à solo coargui non sinat, vides iterum tibi te debuisse dicere, Frater, an hoc est candidè, pie, simpliciter agere in re tanti momenti?
units.tr: Do you not make everyone marvel when you write that this passage is taught here differently from what is answered to Peter immediately afterwards? You give this reason: that where sin is forgiven seventy times, it is not necessary to call in witnesses or civil magistrates. I think you would not have said that if you had wanted to join Luke with Matthew. Christ bids the offended man, first of all, to try whether he can convict the offender of sin, that is, to bring him to acknowledge the sin and beg pardon. Peter asks how often he must do this. Christ answers, in Luke, seven times, if the offender says each time that he is sorry for what he did; in Matthew, seventy times seven. The sense in both places is that the injury is to be forgiven as often as the one who inflicts it confesses that he repents and wishes to refrain from inflicting it. Therefore one must not go to witnesses until he does not allow himself to be convicted by the one man alone. You see again that you ought to have said to yourself, "Brother": is this acting frankly, piously and simply in a matter of such importance?

units.la: Tertiam expositionem cogi te dicis, vt omnium abfurdiffimam repudiare. Audiamus ergo elegantes tuas rationes, quas adfers. Primum ais, obstant antedictae ratio- nes. Deinde discordarent inter fe Christus & Paulus, quos tu vis idem sentire. Si non huc vsque tuis reprehensioni- bus affuefeuiffem, putarem te ludere in re feria. Si non potuifti veris rationibus refellere, quæ ipsemet non firma fatis esse confiteor, quo pacto inanibus illis ratiunculis veram sententiam delebis? De loco Apostoli tibi id refpõdebo, quod iam ante alijs respondi, ne preciosum tempus frustra male collocam.
units.tr: You say you are forced to reject a third exposition as the most absurd of all. Let us hear, then, the elegant reasons you bring. First, you say the reasons stated above stand in the way. Next, Christ and Paul would disagree with each other, whom you wish to think alike. If I had not by now grown used to your reprehensions, I would think you were joking in a serious matter. If you could not refute with true arguments what I myself confess are not firm enough, how will you destroy the true opinion with those empty little reasonings? About the Apostle's passage I will answer you as I have already answered others, so as not to waste precious time in vain.

units.la: Paulus primum iubet ne omnino litigent: quod nihil est aliud, quàm quod Christus iubet, dandam esse operam, vt vel soli, vel cum amicis aliquot tentemus amicè controuersias componere. Deinde si omninò litigandum sit, prohibet Apostolus coram Gentili Magistratu litigare. Non enim conuenire, vt iusti ab iniustis iudicentur. Ideo ex suo ordine aliquos iubet eligere, qui inter fratres iudicent. Caeterum non permittit hisce delectis Arbitris iudicia de sceleribus & rebus grauioribus, sed minora solum concedit, & de rebus ad victum seu vsum vitae pertinentibus: quae ipse vocat ἐπιτρίμα ἐξουθενημένα, & βιωτικά. Sanè si de illis etiam iussisset iudicare, plurimum de dignitate, potestate, authoritateque magistratus, cui vbique nos parere iubet, detraxisse videri posset. Et hoc quid aliud est, quàm quod Christus dixit, Dic Ecclesiae. Huc vsque pulchrè & apertè respondent omnia.
units.tr: Paul first bids them not to litigate at all, which is nothing other than what Christ bids: that we should take pains to settle disputes amicably, either alone or with some friends. Next, if litigation must be undertaken at all, the Apostle forbids litigating before a heathen magistrate, for it is not fitting that the just be judged by the unjust. Therefore he bids them choose from their own number some who may judge between the brethren. But he does not allow these chosen arbiters to judge about crimes and weightier matters; he grants them only minor cases, and matters pertaining to food or the use of this life, which he calls matters of little account [ἐπιτρίμα ἐξουθενημένα] and matters of this life [βιωτικά]. Certainly, if he had ordered them to judge about those too, he could seem to have greatly detracted from the dignity, power and authority of the magistrate, whom he bids us obey everywhere. And what else is this than what Christ said: "Tell it to the Church"? Up to this point everything answers plainly and openly.

units.la: Sed nihil amplius addit Paulus, inquies, & hoc est, quod nos volumus. Respondeo: tametsi hoc in loco reliqua non ponat Apostolus, quae in Christi verbis contineri ostendi, alibi tamen re ipsa & facto suo declarauit, quid hac de re senserit. Nam cum à sua Gente accusaretur, ac iniuriam sibi fieri cerneret à Iudice, appellauit ad Caesarem. Quo pacto igitur credere vllus homo potest intelligens (quem contendendi libido aliúsue assectus sibi non eripuerit) Paulum offenso non permisisse iniuriam à se depellere auxilio Ethnici Magistratus, siquidem Aduersarius Arbitros audire nollet? Iudicent omnes homines, an quisquam verè putet Apostolum iniuria affectis hoc voluisse aut potuisse negare, quod sibi licere putauit, & facto demonstrauit? Quid si Arbitri isti iniquè iudicauissent, an provocare non licuisset oppresso ad alium Iudicem superiorem?
units.tr: But you will say Paul adds nothing more, and this is what we want. I reply: although the Apostle does not set down the rest in this place, which I have shown to be contained in Christ's words, yet elsewhere he declared by his own deed what he thought about this matter. For when he was accused by his own nation, and saw that an injury was being done to him by the judge, he appealed to Caesar. How, then, can any intelligent man believe (unless lust for contention or some other passion has robbed him of his judgment) that Paul did not allow the offended man to ward off injury with the help of the heathen magistrate, since the adversary refused to hear the arbiters? Let all men judge whether anyone truly thinks the Apostle wished or could deny to the injured what he himself thought lawful and demonstrated by deed. What if those arbiters had judged unjustly? Would it not have been lawful for the oppressed man to appeal to another, superior judge?

units.la: Hoc fi licuit Apostolo, ac nobis licet, quomodo non idem mihi liceat, fi, qui mihi molestus est, Arbitros despiciat, eorúmque sententiae stare nolit, sed ab ea appellet? Non est forte quisquam ita immanis & barbarus, qui tales Iudices contemnat, si non putet iniquè ab ipsis iudicatum: at plurimi sunt, quis-ce causam bonam defendere arbitrantur, ideóque provocant ad superiorem Iudicem. Male fiunt hæc, fateor: attamen fiunt, facta sunt, ac futura videntur: & cum fiunt, non potest oppresso negari, quin se defendat ab illata iniuria. Annon est impius quoque magistratus à Deo præpositus, vt subiectos quoslibet ab iniuria & vi tueatur? Quomodo ergo veteret Apostolus in casu talí, qualis à nobis proponitur, iniuriam patientem quærere sui eam defensionem, quae Deum ipsum habet aucthorem.
units.tr: If this was lawful for the Apostle, and is lawful for us, how is it not equally lawful for me, if he who is troublesome to me despises the arbiters and refuses to abide by their sentence, but appeals from it? Perhaps there is no one so savage and barbarous as to scorn such judges, if he does not think they have judged unjustly; but there are very many who think they defend a good cause, and therefore appeal to a superior judge. These things are done badly, I admit; yet they are done, have been done, and seem likely to be done in future. And when they are done, the oppressed man cannot be denied the right to defend himself against the injury inflicted. Is not the magistrate, too, set over us by God, to protect whatever subjects from injury and violence, even if he is impious? How, then, would the Apostle forbid the injured man, in a case such as we propose, to seek that defence of himself which has God himself as its author?

units.la: Non negauit cuiquam Deus iustam sui defensionem coràm quocunque magistratu: si prius illas rationes reconciliationis, frustra expertus fuisset, quas experiri nos voluit, antequam ad profanum impiúmque magistratum causam nostram deferamus. Habitant nunc sub Turca & Pontifice Romano fideles; Si quis afficiatur ibi à fratre iniuria, nec audire iniuriosus suum coetum vellit, quid aliud potest offensus facere, quam eius implorare Iudicis opem, qui facultatem habet coercendi? At Ecclesia excommunicare, dices fortassè, debet refractarium. Primum hic petitur principium. Quippe de hoc quaestio est, an sit à Deo concessum hoc Ecclesiae. Nos permissum non esse demonstramus: Aduersarij hoc ipso, quod probare eos oportebat sua plerumque probant. Deinde si, qui infert iniuriam, iure se facere, quod facit, dicat, atque ad alium Iudicem prouocet, an negabitur reo ius suum alibi quærere, vt molestia illa liberetur? Certè Apostolus Arbitris & Iudicibus illis plus potestatis non dedit, quàm arbitrandi inter fratres, amiceque componendi dissentientes (quod tu quoque aperte satis confiteris) potestatem vel cogendi.
units.tr: God has not denied anyone a just defence of himself before any magistrate whatever, provided he has first tried in vain those ways of reconciliation which God wished us to try before we bring our cause before a profane and impious magistrate. Now faithful people live under the Turk and the Roman Pontiff. If someone there suffers injury from a brother, and the wrongdoer is unwilling to hear his assembly, what else can the offended man do than implore the help of that judge who has power to restrain? But, you will perhaps say, the Church ought to excommunicate the refractory man. First, here you beg the very point in question, for the question is precisely whether this has been granted by God to the Church. We demonstrate that it has not been permitted; your side, in the very thing it ought to prove, mostly proves its own claim. Next, if the one who inflicts the injury says he does what he does by right and appeals to another judge, will the defendant be denied the right to seek his own right elsewhere, so that he may be freed from that trouble? Certainly the Apostle gave those arbiters and judges no more power than that of judging among brethren and settling disputes amicably (as you too admit openly enough), and not the power of compelling or excommunicating.

units.la: ( gendi nolentes, vel excommunicandi, tunc dedisse credam, cum probatum testimonio scripturæ videro. Quod tum fiet, cum cœlum terra erit: terrâque cœli locum occupabit.
units.tr: (…of compelling the unwilling, or of excommunicating, then I would believe that such power had been given, when I see it proved by the testimony of Scripture. That will happen when heaven is earth and earth takes the place of heaven.)

units.la: Negas deinde Synedrium, ius gladij habuisse, quod satis euidenter probaui. Quæ pro sententia nostra attulimus, amicos tuos opinionem suam mutare coegerunt. Confitentur nunc nobiscum contra te Synedrium legitimum fuisse Magistratum, & ius gladij possedisse. Quę obiicis momenti nullius sunt. Nullum dicis ad Romanorum Tribunal accessurum fuisse. At confutat te vel soli Publicani. Vt hoc ferre de his coactisunt Iudæi, ita & de aliis tulerunt, qui Publicanorum erant similes. An ita aliquando legisti cap. 18. Actorum? Non dabat offendiculum aliis, qui cum iniurioso sic prius expertus fuerat omnia, quomodo Christus docuit. An non Christum tradiderunt Pilato? Qui fieri potuerit, vt impunè Ecclesiam aliquis non audiret, supra expositum fuit.
units.tr: You then deny that the Sanhedrin had the power of the sword, which I have proved quite clearly enough. The arguments I have brought for our view have forced your friends to change their opinion. They now confess with us, against you, that the Sanhedrin was a lawful magistrate and possessed the power of the sword. The objections you raise are of no weight. You say no one would ever come before the Roman tribunal; but even the publicans alone refute you. Just as the Jews bore these things about these men, so they bore them about others who were like publicans. Have you ever read Acts 18 in this way? He did not give offence to others who had first tried everything with the wrongdoer, as Christ taught. Did they not hand Christ over to Pilate? How it could happen that someone should with impunity refuse to hear the Church has been set out above.

units.la: De eiusmodi peccatis dixi: Christum agere, de quibus inter priuatos transigi potest: at de flagitijs priuati transigere non possunt. Item de illis, quę non pudcat reos consiteri coram testibus: at flagitia nullus confitebitur. Has tur coniecturas dicis esse nimium infirmas: quia teneamur etiam grauissimas iniurias priuatis condonare. Quorsum hoc dicis? Ego non de iniurioso loquor, qui semel fecit iniuriam, cuius eum deinde poenitet: sed de eo, qui iniuriosus esse pergit. An non mihi licet hanc à me iniuriam depellere? Cum dicis interpretationem meam locum habere non posse in iniurijs vltrò confessis apud testes, quid dicas, nec ipse, puto, nosti: nec ego intelligo. Qui alteri facit iniuriam, puta tat plerumq; aut simulat se putare, se causam habere, cur faciat, quod facit. Proinde coram testibus etiam fatebitur quod certè non faceret, qui facinus perpetrasset. An coniecturae tibi hæ sunt? Certè ex verbis textus necessariò sic deducuntur, vt quantumcunque coneris, negare tamen non possis. Et quibus ex rebus probabimus genuinum alicuius loci sensum hunc vel illum esse,si non ex verbis hoc modo colligamus? Refelle aliquid horum tu,si potes. Fertiam nihil ad rem facere cum dicis, non improbo.
units.tr: I have said of such sins that Christ is speaking of those which can be settled between private persons, but private persons cannot settle crimes. Likewise, he is speaking of those which the guilty are not ashamed to confess before witnesses, but no one will confess crimes. You say these conjectures are far too weak, because we are bound to forgive even the gravest injuries done to private persons. Why do you say this? I am not speaking of the wrongdoer who committed an injury once and is now sorry for it, but of the one who persists in wronging. Am I not allowed to ward off this injury from myself? When you say that my interpretation cannot hold in injuries freely confessed before witnesses, I think you do not know what you are saying, and I do not understand it either. The one who does an injury to another usually thinks, or pretends to think, that he has a reason for doing what he does. Therefore he will even confess before witnesses what he would certainly not do if he had committed the crime. Are these mere conjectures to you? Certainly these things are necessarily deduced from the words of the text in such a way that, however hard you try, you cannot deny them. And by what means shall we prove that this or that is the genuine sense of any passage, if we do not gather it in this way from the words? Refute any of these points, if you can. I do not object when you say that they have nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: Cap. III. Refutatio interpretationis Bezæ verborum Christi: Die Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Chapter III. Refutation of Beza's interpretation of the words of Christ: "Tell it to the Church."

units.la: Peraui adhuc me in progressu scripti tui firmiora ac meliora inuenturum, sed quo progredior longius tanto sunt omnia imbeciliora & deteriora. Recitas hic nescio quot argumenta, numerumq; in margine notas, quæ non sunt aliud, quàm imaginationes tuæ, alienæ à verbis & mente Christi in hoc loco. Negas Christum in his verbis, de quibus inter nos agimus, docere, quomodo priuatæ iniuriæ citra offensionem siue scandalum proximi componi, transfigi, aut amoueri debeant. At nos hoc itä probauimus in Thesibus primum, deinde etiam supra, vt non habeamus necesse metuere, vt refellas. Et quid opus est verbis in re tam plana? An non Petri interrogatio, deinde parabola subiecta, postea ipsa tractationis conclusio, demum etiam friuolæ & euanidæ tuæ reprehensiones tam d.ferte & tam manifestè hoc probant, vt negari à nullo veritatè quaerente possit? Sed age videamus præclara illa tua argumenta, quibus diuersum ostendere niteris.
units.tr: I have gone on through your writing hoping to find firmer and better things, but the further I go, the weaker and worse everything becomes. Here you set out I know not how many arguments, and mark their number in the margin, but they are nothing other than your own imaginings, foreign to the words and meaning of Christ in this passage.
