You deny that Christ, in these words which we are discussing, teaches how private injuries are to be settled, carried through, or removed without offence or scandal to a neighbour. But we have proved this first in our Theses, and then again above, so that we need not fear you will refute it. And why are words needed in a matter so plain? Do not Peter's question, the parable that follows, the conclusion of the discourse itself, and finally even your own feeble and empty objections prove this so clearly and so plainly that no one who seeks the truth could deny it? But come, let us look at those splendid arguments of yours by which you strive to show the opposite.

units.la: Primum hoc est, Christus hic non agit de priuatis iniurijs transfigendis, sed de offendiculis, quæ quum incidunt, conscientiæ nostræ statum perturbant: quoniam doctrina illa diuersa ab hac est, & à Christo distinctè alibi traditur. Locum non adducis, nisi quod in 5. argumento inducis Christi verba Matth. 5. Si munus tuum detuleris ad altare &c. An hoc est probare apud te? Sic facilè quiduis probaueris. Esto docuerit idem alibi etiam Christus. An propterea hic docere non potuit? Nunquámne docuit aut exposuit Christus bis rem eandem? Non negabis quin praeceperit in hoc capite, vt alij alijs offensas remittant. At quàm sæpè idem hoc docuit ac iussit in alijs locis? cap. 5. Matth. docet nos quid facere debeamus, cum alios offendimus: nos hic autem docet, quomodo offensi ab alijs gerere nos debeamus, ne offendiculo alicui simus.
units.tr: The first is this: Christ here is not dealing with the settling of private injuries, but with stumbling-blocks which, when they occur, disturb the state of our conscience; for that teaching is different from this one and is delivered by Christ elsewhere, distinctly. You bring forward no passage, except that in your fifth argument you cite Christ's words from Matthew 5: "If you bring your gift to the altar," and so on. Is this proof in your eyes? In this way you could prove anything at all. Granted that Christ taught the same thing elsewhere too: could he therefore not teach it here? Did Christ never teach or explain the same matter twice? You will not deny that in this chapter he commanded that they forgive one another's offences. But how often did he teach and command the same thing in other places? In Matthew 5 he teaches us what we ought to do when we have offended others; here, however, he teaches how we ought to conduct ourselves when others have offended us, so that we may not be a stumbling-block to anyone.

units.la: Secundum est. Præcedentia & sequentia declarant, de offendiculis hic agi, quibus Regnum Cœlorum interturbatur: non autem de ratione priuatas iniurias pie à se remouendi. Nego tibi vel antecedere vel consequi aliquid verba haec, Si peccauerit frater tuus in te, quod tuam opinionem declaret atq; confirmet, nostram autem fententiam infirmet. Res plane contrario modo habet, vt omnes eruditi & pij, qui inspicere locum volent, confitebuntur.
units.tr: The second is this: what goes before and what follows shows that here he is speaking of stumbling-blocks by which the Kingdom of Heaven is disturbed, and not of the way to remove private injuries piously from oneself. I deny that these words, "If your brother sins against you," either follow from or lead to anything that would declare and confirm your opinion and weaken ours. The matter stands quite the other way, as all learned and pious people who wish to examine the passage will confess.

units.la: Tertium. Describit loco tertio ordinem, quem seruare deceat, reuocandis in viam fratribus offendiculum alijs præbentibus, quod non fit publicum, sed vni cognitum. Negotibi aliquid horum agere Christum in hoc loco, nisi ex consequente. Monet hoc capite primò & per se, vitanda esse scandula, siue vt nobis caueamus, ne alicui scandalum præbeamus: non autem quomodo eos, qui scandalum nobis præbent, tractemus, vt ex contextu liquet, maximè ex Petri interrogatione, ex Parabola, & ex conclusione. Non dicit Christus, si scandalum prebentem non reduxeritis in viam: sed dicit, si non remiseritis vnusquisq; fratri suo, ex animo delicta eorum, idem vobis continget, quod seruo euenit, qui conservi sui miserri noluit. Quanquam verò tu hanc partem à priore separandam esse dicis, quasi ad eam non pertineat: non tamen credere nos tibi vel possumus vel debemus, nisi prius probaueris: id quod in sempiternum non perficies.
units.tr: The third is this: in the third place he describes the order which ought to be observed in bringing back to the way those brothers who give offence to others, an offence which is not public but known to one person only. I deny that Christ in this passage does anything of this sort, except as a consequence. In this chapter he warns, first and in itself, that stumbling-blocks must be avoided, that is, that we must take care not to give anyone an occasion of offence; but he does not say how we should deal with those who give us offence, as is clear from the context, especially from Peter's question, from the parable, and from the conclusion. Christ does not say, "If you have not brought the one who gives offence back to the way"; he says, "If each of you does not forgive his brother from the heart, his trespasses, the same will happen to you as happened to the servant who would not forgive his fellow servant." Although you say that this part must be separated from the earlier one, as if it did not belong to it, we can neither believe you nor are we obliged to, unless you first prove it; and this you will never do.

units.la: Quartum. Vnicum verbum, lucrefecisti fratrem, confirmat de conscientiæ salute, non autem de damno aliquo ciuiliter farciendo hic agi. Egregia verò ratiocinatio. Rogo te, cum quis fratrem iniuriosum arguit, atq; erroris sui cõuincit, an non eum lucratus est Deo primùm, dum ad peccati fui agnitionem ac poenitentiam perduxit? deinde etiam fibi, dum ex hoste amicum & benevolum reddidit? An potest melior excogitari componendarum iniuriarum ratio? Quomodo igitur tu ex eo, quod fratrem lucratur, concludis, Christum hic non agere de priuatarū offensarum Christiana transactione? An quia conscientia sanatur, iniuriosus esse non definit? Imò amicus mihi fieri ex inimico nequit, priusquam peccatum suum agnouerit odiffeq; coeperit. Ideo dicit Christus ἵνα ἐξ ὤν apud Matth. vt intelligamus cum erroris & iniquitatis conuincendum esse, vt eam agnoscat ac deprecetur non apud nos tantum, sed multò magis apud Deum. Hoc modo fratrem lucrefecisti pariter & soluisti. Si audire te nolit, hoc est, si se conuinci non patiatur & iniustitiam suam necagnoscat, nec deploret, ligatus sic est, vt in coelo etiam ligatus sit. Et hoc est, quod dicere volui, cum dixi, hoc lucrum idem valere quod remissionem, per quam reditur in gratiam: quæ postrema verba tu in tua reprehensione non bene omisisti.
units.tr: The fourth is this: the single phrase, "you have gained your brother," confirms that the matter concerns the salvation of conscience, and not the making good of some civil damage. A remarkable line of reasoning indeed! I ask you: when someone argues with his brother who has done him an injury and convicts him of his error, does he not first gain him for God, while he brings him to the acknowledgement and repentance of his sin, and then gain him for himself, while he makes him from an enemy into a friend and well-wisher? Can a better way of settling injuries be devised? How, then, do you conclude from the fact that he gains his brother that Christ is not here dealing with the Christian settlement of private offences? Is it because the conscience is healed that the wrongdoer stops being a wrongdoer? Indeed, a man cannot become my friend out of an enemy until he has acknowledged his sin and has begun to hate it. That is why Christ says in Matthew [ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου], "you have gained your brother," so that we may understand that he must be convicted of error and injustice, so that he may acknowledge it and beg pardon, not only before us but much more before God. In this way you have both gained your brother and loosed him. If he refuses to hear you, that is, if he will not allow himself to be convicted and neither acknowledges nor laments his injustice, then he is bound in such a way that he is bound also in heaven. This is what I wished to say when I said that this gain amounts to the same thing as forgiveness, through which a man is reconciled; and in your criticism you have not been wise to leave out these last words.

units.la: Quę præterea dicis hic, verba tua sunt, eáq; inania, nullo aut scripturæ testimonio aut ex eadem depromptoargumento confirmata. Quocirca tam possum acdebeo ea facile contemnere, quàm tu facilè ausus es dicere. In sempiternū non probabitis vel tu, vel omnes tui, duo hæc è Synagoga eijci, & velut Ethnicum ac Publicanum estimari, tantùmdem significare, ac Satanæ tradi. Aliud rursus est, Anathema fieri. Aliud quoq; à communi victu arceri. Aliud ab his omnibus est, Excommunicari, siue ex visibili Ecclesiæ societate exturbari, propter causam, de qua inter nos orta est disceptatio. Si speras me omnibus expensis tibi assensurum, speras me asino stupidiorem futurum.
units.tr: As for what else you say here, those are your words, and they are empty, supported by no testimony of Scripture and drawn from no argument of that same kind. Therefore I can and ought to despise them as easily as you have ventured to say them. You and all your followers will never prove that these two things, to be cast out of the synagogue and to be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector, mean the same as being delivered to Satan. It is one thing to be made anathema; it is another to be kept from common food; and it is another again to be excommunicated, that is, thrust out of the visible society of the Church, on account of the matter over which we are at issue. If you hope that I will agree with you in every respect, you hope that I will be more stupid than an ass.

units.la: Quintum argumentum, si rectè conieci, (Oedipus enim non sum) hoc est: Christus iubet non parentem Ecclesiæ iudicio
units.tr: The fifth argument, if I have guessed rightly (for I am no Oedipus), is this: Christ commands that one who does not obey the judgment of the Church be held as a Gentile and a tax collector.

units.la: iudicio haberi velut Ethnicum & Publicanum. At in foro conscientiæ aliquem, vt Ethnicum habere, est ab eius congressu ita abstinere, vt à commercio Ethnici, quibuscum Iudæi nunquam sacra conuiuia habuerunt. Ergo non agit hic de ratione componendi priuatas iniurias citra scandalum, sed de offendiculis ex Ecclesia tollendis. Si voluisses rite concludere, hoc concludere debebas: non esse cum eo sacra conuiuia celebranda, qui iussus sit pro Ethnico haberi.
units.tr: But to hold someone in the forum of conscience as a Gentile is to keep away from his company just as one keeps away from dealings with a Gentile, with whom the Jews never shared sacred meals. Therefore this passage is not about the way of settling private injuries without scandal, but about removing stumbling blocks from the Church. If you had wished to conclude properly, you ought to have concluded this: that one must not celebrate sacred meals with a man who has been ordered to be held as a Gentile.

units.la: Primo loco falsum est, quod tanquam indubitatum ponis, Christum hoc in loco iussisse non audientem Ecclesiam ab omnibus haberi velut Ethnicum. Nulla enim machina nullisq; argumentis vnquam efficies, quicquid tandem tentes, vt hæc verba Christi, Sit tibi, idem significare probes, ac si quis diceret, sit Ecclesiæ toti talis, siue sit à Sacramentis exclusus. Nam de vno, videlicet læso, manifestè loquitur.
units.tr: First, it is false what you lay down as beyond doubt, that in this place Christ commanded that one who does not hear the Church be held by everyone as a Gentile. For by no contrivance and no arguments, however you try, will you ever prove that these words of Christ, "let him be to you," mean the same as if someone said: "let him be such to the whole Church," or "let him be excluded from the sacraments." For he speaks plainly of one person, namely the injured party.

units.la: Secundo falsum est, Christum hic primò & per se agere de foro conscientiæ: cum agat de modo, quo priuatas iniurias à nobis depellere absq; scandalo possimus. Tertio falsum est, velut Ethnicū habere in prædicto loco tantùdē significare, ac pro incircucifo habere cui in templū ingredi nefas esset.
units.tr: Second, it is false that Christ here primarily and in itself treats of the forum of conscience, since he is treating of the manner in which we may drive off private injuries without scandal. Third, it is false that to hold someone as a Gentile in that passage means the same as to hold as unclean one who was forbidden to enter the temple.

units.la: Quando hic iubet Christus Ecclesiam non audientem haberi velut Ethnicum & Publicanum, ab eo qui læsus fuerat, loquitur de re quapiam quæ communis vtriq; esset, Ethnicis & Publicanis. Porrò constat Publicanis circumcisis licuisse in Templum venire, & per consequens Sacrificijs ac ritibus alijs Diuinis interesse. Illud nisi tumetipse nobiscum fatereris, probare conarer. At Ethnico nihil horum licebat. Quare sequitur, Christum hic non loqui de amotione à Sacramentis, aut interdictione Templi.
units.tr: When Christ here commands that the Church that does not listen be held as a Gentile and a tax collector, he speaks by the one who had been wronged, about some matter that would be common to both Gentiles and tax collectors. Moreover, it is established that circumcised tax collectors were allowed to come into the Temple and, consequently, to take part in the sacrifices and the other divine rites. I would try to prove this if you yourself did not confess it with us. But no Gentile was allowed any of these things. Hence it follows that Christ is not speaking here of exclusion from the sacraments or of banishment from the Temple.

units.la: Quinimò ne quis verba Christi, sit tibi velut Ethnicus, in alienum hunc sensum detorqueret, quod factum tamen est, adiecisse videtur nomen Publicani, vt prius illud latius patens, velut coerceret & circumscriberet. Deinde ne quis putaret non audientem Ecclesiam illam habendum similem Ethnico in re qualibet, addidit vtriq; nomini, Ethnici & Publicani, articulum, s, vt se ostenderet loqui de quouis
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone twist the words of Christ, "let him be to you as a Gentile," into this other meaning (which nevertheless has been done), he seems to have added the name tax collector, so that the former word, which has a wider reach, might be restrained and limited by it. Then, lest anyone think that the Church which does not listen is to be regarded as like a Gentile in any respect whatever, he added the article to each name, Gentile and tax collector, so as to show that he speaks of any

units.la: Ethnico, & quovis Publicano, qui in Iudea tunc erat, iniuriáq; Iudeos afficere poterát, Dicit ergo, Sicut tibi velut ille Ethnicus & ille Publicanº, qui scilicet in Iudea sunt, tibiq; iniurij esse possunt. Hoc enim indicare nobis videtur repetitus articulus. Ergo quid erat commune Publicanis Iudaeorū & Ethnicis ibidē agentibus, quod huic aptari causę queat? Nihil certè, nisi hoc, quod neutri facilè respondebat coràm alio magistratu, quàm Romano. De Ethnicis cōstat: de Publicanis vix dubitatur. Quippe cum Romanorum essēt ministri, & quod agebant in detrimentum populi Iudaici facere viderentur, discerpti à Iudaeis fuissent, nisi Rom. potentia eos protexisset. Quod à Pharisęis, Scribis, & Sacerdotibus, qui tū pręerant rebus, nihil potuerint æqui expectare, nullus est qui ambigat; equidem ne quidem colloqui cum eis dignabantur: & Christum atq; Apostolos hoc nomine accusabant, quod eorū consuetudinem non perinde vitarent. Quæ cū sic habeāt, cōstat te perperā hæc verba Christi exponere.
units.tr: Gentile and any tax collector who was then in Judea and could do injury to the Jews. He says, therefore: "Let him be to you as that Gentile and that tax collector, who, namely, are in Judea and can be unjust to you." For the repeated article seems to indicate this to us. So what did the tax collectors have in common with the Gentiles living there among the Jews, that could be applied to this purpose? Certainly nothing, except this: that neither of them could easily answer before any other magistrate than the Roman. That the Gentiles were so is established; that the tax collectors were so is scarcely doubted. Indeed, since they were the servants of the Romans, and seemed to do what was to the detriment of the Jewish people, they would have been torn apart by the Jews, had not Roman power protected them. That they could expect nothing fair from the Pharisees, scribes and priests, who then presided over affairs, no one doubts; indeed they did not even deign to speak with them, and they accused Christ and the apostles on this very ground, that they did not avoid their company in the same way. Since these things stand so, it is clear that you explain these words of Christ wrongly.

units.la: Respondes, ideo Publicanos ad Templū & Sacrificia admissos, quia ex lege non potuerint haberi exsecrabiles hoc nomine, quod redemptores essent Vectigalium: ac proinde Romanorū odio potius, quam ob aliud quicquam infensos eis Iudæos fuisse. Quoniam hęc tua (quæ retrò etiam à te diēta memini) consentanea sunt veritati & sacris literis, ideo libenter admitto. Etenim quod hoc nomine, quod vectigalia redimerent, id est, quod Publicani essent, nulli exsecrabiles esse potuerint, ex 3. & 19. cap. Lucæ clarè patet. Equidem Christus ἀρχιτελώνῃ Zachęo non imperat, ut Publicanus esse desinat. Sic Iohannes ad se venientibus Publicanis non iubet officium deserere, sed hoc tantum mandat, ne vltra constitutum exigant. Sic nec is, qui in Templū ascenderat precatū Luc. 18. nec illi, qui Deū laudarunt ac iustificatunt Luc. 7. leguntur munere suo se abdicauisse, Quocirca dubiū non est, quin simul potuerit aliquis Publicanº esse ac religiosus. Quod porrò iniuste eos oderint Iudaei & ex iā dictis cernitur, & ex alijs præterea colligitur. Quippe certū est multos Publicanos pios & religiosos fuisse. Qui ad Iohannē venerunt, ut baptizarentur, qualesquales antea fuerint, viri boni postea permanserat, vt ex cap.7. & 15. Luc. aperte videmus. De principe eorum Zacheo, dubitandi causa nulla habemus. Ille quoq; cuius mentione facit Luc. 18. cap. ipsiusmet Christi testimonio iustior domum redijt Pharisaeo, qui se neq; rapacè, neq; iniustū, neq; adulterum gloriabatur. Itaq; dubium non est, quin isti, aliiq; tales, non fuerint adeo mali, vt Iudaei merito eos possent odisse. Quamobrem vera est vtraq; pars responsionis tuae: vnde sic ratiocinabor.
units.tr: You reply that tax collectors were admitted to the Temple and the sacrifices for this reason: that by law they could not be regarded as accursed on the ground that they were the farmers of the taxes; and therefore the Jews were hostile to them more from hatred of the Romans than for any other reason. Since I recall that you said these things before, as far back as earlier, and since they agree with the truth and the Holy Scriptures, I gladly admit them. For that no one could be accursed on the ground that they farmed the taxes, that is, because they were tax collectors, is clearly shown by Luke chapters 3 and 19. Indeed, Christ does not order the chief tax collector Zacchaeus to cease being a tax collector. So John, when tax collectors came to him, does not bid them abandon their office, but only commands that they should exact nothing beyond what was fixed. Likewise, neither the man who went up into the Temple to pray (Luke 18), nor those who praised God and were justified (Luke 7), are read to have renounced their calling. Wherefore there is no doubt that a man could be at once a tax collector and a religious man. Moreover, that the Jews hated them unjustly is seen from what has been said already, and is gathered besides from other things. For it is certain that many tax collectors were pious and religious. Those who came to John to be baptized, whatever they had been before, afterwards remained good men, as we clearly see from Luke chapters 7 and 15. Concerning their chief Zacchaeus we have no cause for doubt. That man too, whom Luke mentions in chapter 18, by the testimony of Christ himself went home more justified than the Pharisee, who boasted that he was neither a robber, nor unjust, nor an adulterer. Therefore there is no doubt that these men, and others like them, were not so wicked that the Jews could justly hate them. Thus both parts of your answer are true; from which I shall reason thus.

units.la: Quisquis nullo Diuino iure, nullo Dei mandato ac lege exsecrabilis, nullaq; iusta de causa odio haberi potuit, is nullo vel iure vel praecepto Diuino potuit a Templo & caeremonijs sacris prohiberi.
units.tr: Whoever could not be hated as accursed by any divine right, by any command or law of God, and with no just cause, could not be barred from the Temple and the sacred ceremonies by any right or divine precept.

units.la: Caeterum Publicani ex lege non potuerunt haberi exsecrabiles, nec odij sui aduersus eos iustā causam habuerūt Iudei.
units.tr: But tax collectors could not by law be regarded as accursed, and the Jews had no just cause for their hatred of them.

units.la: Ergo Publicani, quoad tales erant ex lege praeceptoq; Dei nō potuerūt à Templo & cultu diuino submoueri. Propositio certa est ac vera. Assūptio tua est, scripturisq; sanctis cōsona, vt ostendi. In complexione nihil continetur, quod non sit in praemissis expresse positū: nec in forma potest vitii ostendi. Ergo vera conclusione haec posita, sic deinde argumentabor.
units.tr: Therefore tax collectors, as far as they were such, could not by the law and precept of God be removed from the Temple and divine worship. The major premise is certain and true. Your assumption is consonant with the holy Scriptures, as I have shown. Nothing is contained in the conclusion that is not expressly stated in the premises, nor can any fault of form be shown. Therefore, with this conclusion true, I shall argue further thus.

units.la: Publicani ex mandato Dei non potuerunt repelli à Templo cultuq; diuino, vt ex positis à te demonstratum est.
units.tr: Tax collectors, by the command of God, could not be repelled from the Temple and divine worship, as has been demonstrated from what you have laid down.

units.la: At qui Christus dixit Ecclesiam, (de qua tunc loquebatur) non audientem, habendum velut Publicanum.
units.tr: But Christ said that the Church (of which he was then speaking) which does not listen is to be held as a tax collector.

units.la: Ergo pro eo talē haberi voluit, qui iure ac lege nulla diuina posset à Sacramentis à Deo institutis arceri. Quid hinc sequatur vides, opinor, nempe te semel tota causa cecidisse.
units.tr: Therefore he wished that one should be held as such a person as could not by any divine right or law be barred from the sacraments instituted by God. You see, I think, what follows from this: namely that you have fallen once and for all in the whole cause.

units.la: Verū excipies fortasse, nos Christi verba nō rite exponere, eorūq; sensū talem esse dices. Qui Ecclesiā non audit, sit tibi qualis Publicanus nūc est ipsis Pharisēis: hoc est, nō velle Domini, vt eū habeam° sicut Publicanū, sed quales tūc habebātur vulgò à Iudeis Publicani. Putas enim omnes Publicanos bonos & malos à Pharisęis fuisse exclusos: in quo tamē, vt in plerisq; alijs, modū nō tenuerint. Causa libeter dixisses fuisse ἀ'ποσταλαι. Sed cū nō omnes apostatas fuisse videres (ex sacris literis ne vnū quidē deseruisse patriā religionē probabis, nedū plerosq; aut multos) hāc adfers, quia Iudeis fuerint execrabiles: atq; hoc satis esse ad interptationis tuę cōfirmationem,
units.tr: But perhaps you will object that we do not expound the words of Christ correctly, and you will say that their sense is this: "He who does not hear the Church, let him be to you as the tax collector is now to the Pharisees themselves": that is, that the Lord does not will that I hold him as a tax collector, but as tax collectors were then commonly held by the Jews. For you think that all tax collectors, good and bad, were excluded by the Pharisees; yet in this, as in many other things, they did not keep due measure. You would gladly have said that the cause was apostasy [ἀποστασία]. But since you saw that not all tax collectors were apostates (you will not prove from the sacred writings that even one abandoned the religion of his country, much less many or most), you bring forward this: that they were hateful to the Jews; and you say this is enough to confirm your interpretation.

units.la: Quoniam in eiusmodi locutionum genere, inquis, non feper quid iuste, quid moderatè fiat, sed simpliciter interdum, quid fieri soleat attenditur. Ergone satis magna causa fuit exclusionis odium etiam iniustum? Respondes, iure ipsos Iudeis fuisse exsecrabiles, his verbis. Iure tamen Publicanos non superstitiosis soluni (à quibus minimè æquum est, ut Regulam temerè sumamus) sed etiam verè Religiosis suisse abominandos, declarant etiam quærelæ veteres ipsorum Romanorum. Antequam hæc examinemus admonendus es breuiter constantiæ tuæ, quum tam turpiter in vnica pagina tibi contradicas; Supra dicebas, Romanorum odio potius, quam ob aliud quicquam offensos habuisse Iudeos. Nunc dicis iure execrabiles pijs & impijs fuisse. Si propter rapinam & auaritiam iure fuerunt abominandi, ob aliud ipsis fuerunt infensi, quam ob Romanorum odium. Sed ad rem accedo ipsam.
units.tr: "For in this kind of expression," you say, "one does not always look to what is done justly or moderately, but sometimes simply to what is customarily done." Is then hatred, even unjust hatred, a cause large enough for exclusion? You reply that they were rightly hateful to the Jews, in these words: "Yet by right the tax collectors were to be abhorred, not only by the superstitious (from whom it is by no means fair that we should take the rule rashly), but also by those who were truly religious; the old complaints of the Romans themselves also declare this." Before we examine these things, you must be briefly reminded of your consistency, since you so shamefully contradict yourself within a single page. Above you were saying that the Jews were hostile to them from hatred of the Romans rather than for any other cause. Now you say they were rightly hateful to both the pious and the impious. If on account of robbery and greed they were rightly to be abhorred, then the Jews were hostile to them for another reason besides hatred of the Romans. But I come now to the matter itself.

units.la: Demonstrauí huc vsq;, nullum circumcisum iure Diuino potuisse arceri à Templo cultúq; Diuino, propter vitam inhonestam, sed alia ratione voluisse Deum scelera coercere. Ergo si maximè constaret, Pharisæos talequippiam ausos fuisse tentare, contra & præter voluntatem præceptumq; Dei tentauissent. At absurdum fit credere, Christum leges suis ferentem, quas omnibus deinde temporibus abfq; errore vellet obseruari; hoc eos iusisse facere, quod Iudæos iniuste & contra præscriptum verbi Dei facere sciebat. Si voluisset in præsente loco, in quo dicitis eum re maximi momenti instituisse, hoc iubere, quod tu putas, nomine magis proprio fuisset vsus. Etenim Publicanus nullus, quatenus Publicanus esset, iustè aut per se potuit excludi, sed tantum per accidens, hoc est, quatenus esset flagitiosus. Deinde non omnes erant vitiosi, vt oltenfum est. Postremo non soli Publicani ex tua sententia excludebantur, qui excommunicationem & è Synagoga eiectionem pro eadem re ponis. Quis igitur præter te tuiq; similes putet Christum in re tam necessaria Ecclesiæ (quod vos dicitis) tamq; exitiosa (quod res & historiæ probant) instituenda, magis voluisse attendere, quid à perditissimis hypocritis contra praefinitionem Legis diuinae fieret, quàm quid iustè moderatéque ageretur? Regulam nos sumere debere ais non à superstitionibus, sed à Religiosis: & Christum interim vis ab iniusto iniustorum Pharisaeorum facto poenam peccatoribus praescribere. Publicani nulli per se iniusti erant, vt possent iustè excludi, nec omnes erant iniusti, sicut è contra etiam non omnes iniusti ex ordine Publicanorum erant, & nobis tamen vis persuadere, Christum nomine Publicani hoc in loco intellexisse iniustum seu Excommunicatum? Frustra laboras dum firmiora non attuleris.
units.tr: I have shown so far that no circumcised person could by divine law be barred from the Temple and divine worship on account of a dishonourable life; God wished to restrain crimes by some other means. So even if it were certain that the Pharisees had dared to attempt such a thing, they would have attempted it against and beyond God's will and command. But it is absurd to believe that Christ, who was giving laws, would want them observed afterwards in all times without error, and that he would have ordered them to do what he knew the Jews did unjustly and against the prescription of God's word. If he had wished to order, in the present place, where you say he established something of the greatest importance, what you think, he would have used a more proper name. For no tax collector, insofar as he was a tax collector, could justly or in himself be excluded, but only incidentally, that is, insofar as he was wicked. Next, not all were vicious, as has been shown. Finally, according to your opinion, not only tax collectors were excluded, since you equate excommunication with expulsion from the synagogue. Who then, apart from you and your like, would think that Christ, in establishing a matter so necessary for the Church (as you say) and yet so pernicious (as the facts and histories prove), wished rather to attend to what the most abandoned hypocrites did against the prescription of the divine Law than to what was done justly and moderately? You say we ought to take our rule not from the superstitious but from the religious; and meanwhile you want Christ to prescribe a penalty for sinners from the unjust deed of unjust Pharisees. No tax collectors were unjust in themselves, so that they could justly be excluded; nor were all of them unjust, just as, conversely, not all unjust men belonged to the order of tax collectors. Yet you want to persuade us that Christ, by the name of tax collector, meant the unjust or the excommunicated in this place? You labour in vain unless you bring firmer proofs.

units.la: Falsum non minus est, Synedrium aut Pharisaeos Publicanis, quia Publicani essent, aut quia improbè licenterque vixissent, Templo & Sacrificijs interdixisse. Quomodò aut quibus hoc rationibus argumentisq; probabis? Sacrae literae secus docent, vt ex historia Matthaei, Zachaeique colligimus. An reprehensum à Iudaeis aut Pharisaeis aliquando legisti Iohannem Publicanos ad se venientes vnà cum alijs baptizantem? Non nesciebant Iudaei baptismum Iohannis Sacramentum esse poenitentiae, ipso sic docente. Quare si consuetudo tunc fuisset Publicanos ad Sacramenta non admittendi, certè in Iohanne facto hoc vituperassent cum alij, tum Pharisaei, praesertim cum viderent eum neque increpare ipsos, quia Publicani essent, neque hortari vt munus suum deserereent, sed tantum monere, vt non plus exigerent quàm constitutum fuisset. Murmurarunt quidam ex Pharisaeis quod Christus cum Publicanis ederet. At non legimus eos murmurauisse, quod ad Sacramenta & ad Templum venirent. Sanè Pharisaeus, qui Publicanum secum in Templo comprecantem vidit, neque Templum neque se exististimauit contaminari illius praesentia, neque quod huc ingressus fuisset reprehendit, tametsi quid de eo sentiret, non dissimularit. Tantum porrò abest, vt circumcisos à Templo & Sacrificijs Deo offerendis deterrerent Iudaei, vt etiam incircumcisos huc inuitarint: licet his non, vt illis, liceret in atrium interius Templi ingredi.
units.tr: It is no less false that the Sanhedrin or the Pharisees forbade tax collectors the Temple and the sacrifices because they were tax collectors, or because they had lived wickedly and licentiously. How, or by what reasons and arguments, will you prove this? Holy Scripture teaches otherwise, as we gather from the histories of Matthew and Zacchaeus. Have you ever read that John was rebuked by the Jews or the Pharisees for baptizing tax collectors who came to him along with others? The Jews did not fail to know that the baptism of John was a sacrament of repentance, as he himself taught. Therefore, if it had then been the custom not to admit tax collectors to the sacraments, the others would certainly have found fault with this in John's action, and the Pharisees especially, since they saw that he neither rebuked them for being tax collectors nor urged them to abandon their office, but only warned them not to exact more than had been appointed. Some of the Pharisees grumbled that Christ ate with tax collectors. But we do not read that they grumbled that tax collectors came to the sacraments and to the Temple. Indeed the Pharisee who saw the tax collector praying with him in the Temple thought neither the Temple nor himself defiled by his presence, and he did not reproach him for entering, although he did not conceal what he thought of him. So far is it from the case that the Jews deterred the circumcised from the Temple and from offering sacrifices to God, that they even invited the uncircumcised here; although these were not allowed, as the others were, to enter the inner court of the Temple.

units.la: di. Ego sanè persuasus sum, Sacerdotes, Leuitas ,ac Templi Ministros, si maximè ipsis à Deo fuisset mandatum, vt scelere inquinatos arcerent, non fuisse tamen factuℨ. Cum enim ex Sacrificijs ipsi viuerent, proculdubio cupiebant omnes frequentes adesse, quo plus ipsi acciperent. Tanto ergo minus est credibile, ipsos, cum Legem hac de re nullam haberent, tale quippiam in animum induxisse.
units.tr: Indeed I am persuaded that the priests, the Levites and the ministers of the Temple, even if God had commanded them to keep away those defiled by crime, would not have done so. For since they lived from the sacrifices, they undoubtedly wanted everyone to attend in great numbers, so that they themselves would receive more. Therefore it is all the less credible that they, since they had no law on this matter, would have conceived such a thing.

units.la: Falsum denique illud quoque est Christum iubere, vt Ecclesiam, de qua ibi sermo ei fuit, non audientem offensus pro tali reputet, pro qualibus Pharisaei rudisque plebecula Publicanos tenebant. Non enim sic loquitur Christus, sed hoc modo. Si iniurisus Ecclesiam non volet audire, sit tibi eo loco quo Publicanus tibi est, siuè puta sic te cum eo posse agere, quomodo cū Publicano te offendêre ageres. Nō certè dicit Christus, Sit tibi talis qualis Publicanus est Pharisæis, aut alijs quibuslibet: sed simpliciter dicit, Sit tibi qualis Publicanus est, tibi nimirū. Caeterū constat Publicanos à Discipulis, cum quibus tum loquebatur Christus, non habitos fuisse pro exsecrabilibus, aut facinorosis, aut Excommunicatis, cum & Iohanni & Christo eos probari vidissent, frequenter cum eis viuerent, officium illud suum impium non esse scirent, in suo comitatu & ordine Matthaeum secum haberent. Nec aliamen fuit Religiosorum & piorum omnium, quicunque vel suapte natura intelligentes erant, vel Iohanne aut Christo Praeceptoribus vsi fuerant.
units.tr: Finally, it is also false that Christ orders the one who does not hear the Church, of which he was speaking there, to be regarded as an offender, in the way the Pharisees and the common crowd regarded tax collectors. For Christ does not speak in this way, but in this manner: "If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as the tax collector is," or let it be, that is, that you can deal with him as you would deal with a tax collector who had offended you. Certainly Christ does not say, "Let him be to you as the tax collector is to the Pharisees, or to any others," but simply says, "Let him be to you as the tax collector is," that is, to you. Moreover, it is established that the tax collectors were not regarded as detestable, wicked or excommunicated by the disciples with whom Christ was then speaking. For they had seen both John and Christ approve of them, they frequently lived with them, they knew that their office was not impious, and they had Matthew with them in their company and order. Nor was it otherwise with all the religious and pious, whoever were either intelligent by their own nature or had used John or Christ as their teachers.

units.la: Ex praedictis omnibus patet, primum quidem id, cuius causa ista praecipuè diximus, scilicet Publicani nomen in oratione Christi nullo prorsus pacto accipi posse pro Excommunicato aut facinoroso, cum illi, quibuscum loquebatur Christus, Publicanos pro Excommunicatis & nefarijs neutiquam haberent, vt qui non modo scirent hoc, Publicanorum scilicet munus cum Mosaicis legibus non pugnare, verumetiam exploratum tenerent, multos in illo ordine honestos, castos, pios, & Religiosos exsistere. Deinde & illud patet, falsò te scripsisse, Publicanos iure abominandos fuisse non tantum superstitiosis ac prauis, sed etiam bonis & Religiosis. Si causam hi nullam habebant, cur eos abominarentur, (vt tu supra affirmabas) cur vt exsecrabiles odissent ipse non video. Pugnat enim si quid aliud cum pietate hoc maxime, fratrem sine causa odio prosequi.
units.tr: From all that has been said it is clear, first, that the very thing for which we have said these things chiefly, namely that the name tax collector in Christ's saying can by no means be taken to mean the excommunicated or the wicked. For those to whom Christ was speaking did not in any way regard tax collectors as excommunicated or infamous. They not only knew that the office of tax collector did not conflict with the Mosaic laws, but also held it as certain that many in that order were honest, chaste, pious and religious. Next, it is also clear that you have written falsely that tax collectors were rightly to be abominated not only by the superstitious and wicked, but also by the good and religious. If these men had no cause for being abominated (as you asserted above), I do not see why you would hate them as detestable. For if anything at all is opposed to piety, it is this above all: to pursue a brother with hatred without cause.

units.la: Aeque absurdi sint, qui forte putent, Christum per nomen Publicani, non simpliciter Publicanos, sed consceleratos duntaxat voluisse significare. Obstant primum, quae hucusque disputata sunt fere omnia. Deinde quod eodem modo cogeremur dicere, eum non omnes Ethnicos in Iudaea agentes intellexisse, sed impuros, sceleribusque astrictos tantum. Eodem namque modo ait, Sit tibi velut Ethnicus, quo modo dicit, Sit tibi velut Publicanus. Constat autem eum de omnibus Ethnicis locutum. Quare similiter de Publicanis simpliciter locutus existimari debet, quod tu quoque recte iudicas. Praeterea pugnat cum opinione hac, quod Christus nulla omnino exceptione aut mentione bonorum aut malorum vtens, generatim dicit, Sit tibi velut Publicanus: quod certe nunquam fecisset, si hac in parte discrimen aliquod statuere voluisset. Planius opinionis huius falsitas ex eo perspicitur, quod articulum utrique nomini praeposuit Spiritus sanctus. Nam cum Praedicato appositus est articulus, ipsammet natura Praedicati, aut certe emphasim quandam denotat. Non enim idem prorsus significant apud Graecos hae duae Orationes: Petrus est ἀνθρωπος, & Petrus est ὁ ἀνθρωπος. Illa enim Petrum tantum significat hominem esse, haec ipsummet hominem esse innuit. Sic cum dicimus, Voluptatem esse ipsum bonum, τὸ ἀγαθὸν plus dicimus, quam si solummodo bonum dicamus esse. Significat ergo hoc in loco vox ὁ τελώνης, Publicanum, quatenus est Publicanus, ac proinde generaliter sumitur. Si negetur hoc, atque aliam Emphasim contendatur significare, non litigabo hac de re, cum in ipsa causa nihil insit difficultatis: modo illud mihi concedatur, quod negari nulla ratione poterit, Emphasim significare, quae communis esset Ethnicis & Publicanis. At communis alia nulla potest esse ad hanc pertinens causam, in qua ratio docetur priuatas offensiones absque scandalo vitandi, quàm quod neutri alium agnoscebat Magistratū, quàm Romanū.
units.tr: Equally absurd are those who perhaps think that Christ, by the name tax collector, meant not tax collectors simply, but only the wicked among them. First, almost everything argued up to now stands against this. Next, because in the same way we would be forced to say that he did not mean all Gentiles living in Judaea, but only the impure and those bound by crimes. For he says in the same way, "Let him be to you as a Gentile," as he says, "Let him be to you as a tax collector." Moreover, it is established that he spoke of all Gentiles. Therefore he should be thought to have spoken similarly of tax collectors simply, as you also rightly judge. Furthermore, this opinion conflicts with the fact that Christ, using no exception or mention of good or bad at all, says generally, "Let him be to you as a tax collector," which he certainly would never have done if he had wished to make any distinction in this part. The falsity of this opinion is clearer from the fact that the Holy Spirit placed the article before each noun. For when the article is placed before a predicate, it denotes the very nature of the predicate, or certainly a certain emphasis. For among the Greeks these two expressions do not mean exactly the same: "Peter is a man" [ἀνθρωπος] and "Peter is the man" [ὁ ἀνθρωπος]. The former means only that Peter is a man; the latter suggests that he is man himself. So when we say, "Pleasure is the good itself" [τὸ ἀγαθὸν], we say more than if we merely said that it is good. So in this place the word "the tax collector" [ὁ τελώνης] signifies a tax collector insofar as he is a tax collector, and is therefore taken generally. If this is denied, and it is contended that it signifies a different emphasis, I will not dispute the matter, since there is no difficulty in the case itself; provided only that this is granted to me, which cannot be denied on any ground: that the emphasis signifies what would be common to Gentiles and tax collectors. But no other common ground can pertain to this cause, in which the reason taught is to avoid private offences without scandal, than that neither of them recognised any magistrate other than the Roman.

units.la: Ergò immotum nullaque ex parte labefactatū perstat nostrū illud argumentū, quo causa tua tota semel concidit. Nisi enim probes, velut Publicanū haberi, idem significare, quod significat à Sacramentis remoueri, incassū laboraueris. Locū certè aliū in nouo Testamento (in vetere nullū cōtineri per se manifestū est, ac in sequentib' manifestius adhuc fiet) nullum potes indicare, in quo Deus vestrā Excommunicationē instituerit, quam 18. cap. Matthaei, testib' omnibus amicis & praeceptoribus tuis, quos mihi videre audiréue contigit. In hoc autē cap. nihil est quod sententiam tuam probare possit, si nòn probet nomē Publicani. At hoc nihil probare, imò contrarium probare, demonstratum est. Quare integrum permanet nostrum argumentum.
units.tr: Therefore our argument stands unshaken and undamaged on every side, and by it your whole case has once for all collapsed. For unless you prove that being regarded as a tax collector means the same as being removed from the sacraments, you will labour in vain. Certainly you cannot point to any other place in the New Testament (that there is none in the Old is plain in itself, and will become even more plain in what follows) where God instituted your excommunication, apart from Matthew 18, and I have had the chance to see or hear all your friends and teachers as witnesses to that. But in this chapter there is nothing that can support your view, unless the name "tax collector" supports it. That this name proves nothing, indeed proves the contrary, has been demonstrated. So our argument remains intact.

units.la: Nulli Publicano circumciso potuit iure Diuino Templum & ceremoniarum Diuinarum vsurpatio negari: nec vlli negata fuisse (propter causam eam, de qua nos inter nos disputamus) ostendi potest.
units.tr: No circumcised tax collector could, by divine right, be denied the use of the temple and of the divine ceremonies, and it cannot be shown that any such man was denied them (on account of that cause which we are disputing between ourselves).

units.la: At Christus Ecclesiam non audientem iubet haberi ve- lut Publicanum.
units.tr: But Christ orders that the one who does not hear the Church be regarded as a tax collector.

units.la: Ergò iubet pro eo haberi, qui nec possit iure Diuino à Sacramentis à Deo ordinatis depelli, nec depulsus aliquando fuerit. Vestra igitur Excommunicatio nil aliud est, quàm inane figmentū hominū imperare alijs cupientium. Miror vehementer cur refellere tentes, quod dixi, nec Matth. nec Zacchaeū, nec alios Publicanos, (imò nec Christū nec Apostolos, quos in eodē censu cum Publicanis habebant, & peiores existimebant) à Templo & Sacrificijs abactos fuisse, cū sponte fatearis, Publicanos à Pharisæis non fuisse prohibitos ab ingressu Tépli, & orationib' in eo factis. Sed necesse est, vt, qui veritatē impugnat, sibi sæpè fit contrarius. Duobus argumētis hic pugnas, Vnum est, non defuisse voluntatem, sed potestate arcana Dei metúque populi cohibitos suisse. Alterū, Iudæos à Romanis coactos in Téplū passos esse venire: at cum ipsis nunquam sacrificasse. Nisi morem tuum nossem, valdè mirarer adeo friuolas tuas ratiunculas. Quomodo probabis Pharisaeos voluntatem habuisse accendi vel Publicanos vel Christum à Sacramentis, cum nulla huius rei mentio fiat in Scripturis? Hanc fuisse causam, quod videlicet diuinitus ac metu etiam populi cohibiti fuerint, libenter crederem, si scriptura meminisset. Solet enim explicare propositum & consilia Pharisaeorum, & cur, quod cupiebant, non consequerentur, simul exponere: vt cum dicit, eos cogitasse de comprehendendo Christo, at propter metum populi non ausos fuisse. Huius autem rei nullum vestigium inuenitur: cum constet eos apertis vlnis occasionem talem amplexaturos fuisse, si Legis mandatum potuissent praetexere. Ergo omnium hoc esse dicemus, dum non probauerit.
units.tr: Therefore he orders that such a man be regarded as one who cannot by divine right be driven from the sacraments ordained by God, and who has never in fact been driven out. Your excommunication, then, is nothing but an empty invention of men who wish to command others. I am greatly surprised why you try to refute what I said: that neither Matthew, nor Zacchaeus, nor other tax collectors (indeed neither Christ nor the apostles, whom they counted in the same class as tax collectors and considered worse) were cast out from the temple and the sacrifices, since you yourself freely admit that the Pharisees did not forbid tax collectors to enter the temple and pray in it. But whoever attacks the truth is necessarily often at odds with himself. Here you fight with two arguments. One is that the will was not lacking, but they were restrained by the hidden power of God and by fear of the people. The other is that the Jews were compelled by the Romans to allow them to enter the temple, but they never sacrificed with them. Unless I knew your habit, I would be very surprised at such frivolous little arguments of yours. How will you prove that the Pharisees had the will to stir up either the tax collectors or Christ against the sacraments, since there is no mention of this in the Scriptures? I would gladly believe that this was the cause, that they were restrained by divine power and even by fear of the people, if Scripture mentioned it. For it usually explains the purpose and plans of the Pharisees, and why they did not achieve what they wanted, as when it says that they thought of seizing Christ but did not dare because of fear of the people. But no trace of this is found, since it is established that they would eagerly have seized such an opportunity if they could have pretended a command of the Law. Therefore we will say that this is the claim of all, until you have proved it.

units.la: Alterum aequè absurdum est. Ita namque seruarunt Romani Iudaeis suam in Religione libertatem, vt ne quidem signa militaria in vrbem inferrent. Et cum clàm intulisset noctu Pilatus, coactus est iterum tollere. Dicam uno verbo. Nugas adfers. Non coegerunt eos Praesides Romani, vt Romanos intromitterent: ac coegisse me vis credere, vt contra Legem Publicanos paterentur ingredi, quibus magis quam ipsis Romanis infensos fuisse recte affirmas. Quo loco deinde legisti aliquem in Templum admissum esse, & eundem Sacrificijs adesse non potuisse? Si hoc demonstrabis alicui circumcisio negatu; cui illud esset permissum, non iam te nihil omninò dixisse affirmabo.
units.tr: The other argument is equally absurd. For the Romans so preserved the Jews' liberty in religion that they did not even bring military standards into the city. And when Pilate had secretly brought them in at night, he was forced to take them out again. I will say it in one word: you bring trifles. The Roman governors did not compel the Jews to admit Romans. Yet you want me to believe that they compelled them to allow tax collectors to enter against the Law, men whom you rightly assert were more hostile to the Jews than the Romans themselves. In what passage have you then read that someone was admitted to the temple and yet could not be present at the sacrifices? If you demonstrate that circumcision was denied to anyone to whom that was permitted, I will not say that you have said nothing at all.

units.la: Post haec ad verba ligandi & soluendi descendis: in quorum interpretatione duo reprehendis: quod ea cuilibet laeso accommodem: & quod idem significare dicam, ac fratrem admonendo & ad poenitentiam adducendo lucrari, vel inculpabilem reddere. Utrumque tibi displicet. Soluere & ligare, inquis, verba sunt iudicialia: ac proinde soli Publico ministerio attributa reperiuntur: priuato nulli. Deinde non usurpantur in eodem significato, cum modò significant promulgare peccatorum remissionem & retentionem, modò vero iniurias condonare & inexcusabilem quempiam reddere. Illud enim vnius Dei est: istud verò etiam nonstrum. Sed & iniuriam retinere nescio, qui tandem pijs possit accommodari, præsertim in cāusis priuatis. Summa est, verbis Ligandi & Soluendi solennem actionem semper significari affirmas.
units.tr: After this you come down to the words of binding and loosing. In their interpretation you find fault with two things: that I apply them to anyone who has been wronged, and that I say they mean the same as gaining a brother by admonishing him and bringing him to repentance, or making him blameless. Both displease you. "To loose and to bind," you say, "are judicial words, and so they are found assigned only to the public ministry, to no private person. Next, they are not used in the same sense, since sometimes they mean to proclaim the remission and retention of sins, but sometimes to forgive injuries and to make someone inexcusable." For the former belongs to God alone, but the latter to us as well. But I do not know how retaining an injury could fittingly be applied to the pious at all, especially in private cases. In sum, you assert that by the words "binding and loosing" a solemn action is always meant.

units.la: Velim te probatione aliqua docuisse, me perperam verba hæc Christi priuatis omnibus accommodare, qui proximum suum recte ex verbo Dei vel peccati coarguunt, vel in spem erigunt: aut scripturae testimonijs demonstrauisse publico duntaxat Ministerio semper attributi. Tibi certè absque scripturis affirmanti credere non possum. Vis verum tibi dicam? Audacter affirmas & timidè ptobas: adeoque aliud nil fermè vbique agis, quam tibi sumis, quod probare debebas. Hoc certè, quod hic asseris, nullo vnquam tempore probabis. Christus 16. Matth. non ad solum Petrum illa verba dixit, sed in persona eius ad omnes illos, qui cum eo confitentur Christū filium esse Dei viui, & hanc confessionem ad alios docent. An non potest vnusquisque priuatus priuatum arguere & consolari? Sed si docendo huc adduxerit aliquem, vt peccata sua agnoscat, & ex recta fide in Dei benignitate propter meritum Christi acquiescat, an non solutus erit? Si frustra moneat ac doceat, annon maneat, qui sic pertinaciter salutem repudiat, ligatus? Si non saepè priuati ligant ac soluunt, hoc ideo fit, quia vel imperiti sunt, vel negligentes; præsertim vbi Ministrorum adest facultas & copia.
units.tr: I would like you to have taught, by some proof, that I wrongly apply these words of Christ to all private persons who rightly rebuke or encourage their neighbour from the word of God; or to have shown from testimonies of Scripture that they are always assigned only to the public ministry. Certainly I cannot believe you when you affirm this without Scripture. Do you want me to tell you the truth? You affirm boldly and prove timidly, and so almost everywhere you do nothing but assume what you ought to have proved. What you assert here you will never prove at any time. Christ in Matthew 16 did not speak those words to Peter alone, but in his person to all who confess with him that Christ is the Son of the living God, and who teach this confession to others. Can not every private person rebuke and comfort a private person? But if, by teaching, he has brought someone to acknowledge his sins and to rest in God's kindness from true faith, for the sake of Christ's merit, will that person not be loosed? If he admonishes and teaches in vain, will not the one who so stubbornly rejects salvation remain bound? If private persons do not often bind and loose, this is because they are either unskilled or negligent, especially where ministers are at hand and available in numbers.

units.la: Quod si etiam tibi largiremur, Christum eo in loco verba prædicta ad solos Ministros dixisse, quod falsum esse tu quoque non ibis inficias, spero, nihil tamen ex eo præsidij exspectare posses. Etenim solis Ministris hoc licere, alijs Presbyteris nullis, quod tu contendis falsum esse. Deinde nondum probauisses, eadem illa etiam in præsenti loco non pertinere ad omnes priuatos. Equidem præclarè demonstrauì, Christum hic instituere nos, qua ratione iniurias nobis illatas pie à nobis depellere possimus: ex quo consequitur, verba illa ad omnes pertinere, qui à fratribus laeduntur. Interrogatio Petri, tota sequens parabola, Christi conclusio, antecedentia & mediasic probant, vt miror, si quis reperiatur, qui porro negare velit. Non dicit Dominus, Si duo Presbyteri, vel duo Ministri consentient: sed si duo vestrum, hoc est, duo mei discipuli siue Christiani consenserint: quia scilicet hic non de Ministrorum, sed priuatorum omnium officio disserit. Ergo possunt hic duo aut tres quilibet ligare & soluere: non soli Ministri, multo minus soli Presbyteri. Imò ex vno hoc loco propemodum excidERunt Dominatu suo toto Presbyteri tui.
units.tr: But even if we were to grant you that Christ spoke those words in that place to the ministers alone, which you too, I hope, will not deny is false, you could expect no help from it. For that this is permitted to ministers alone, and to no other elders, is what you contend is false. Next, you would not yet have proved that those same words do not pertain to all private persons in the present place. Indeed I have clearly shown that Christ here instructs us by what method we can piously drive away the injuries done to us, from which it follows that the words apply to all who are wronged by brothers. Peter's question, the whole parable that follows, Christ's conclusion, and the preceding and intervening passages prove this so clearly that I wonder whether anyone can be found who would still wish to deny it. The Lord does not say, "If two elders or two ministers agree," but "if two of you," that is, two of my disciples or Christians agree; because clearly he is discussing here the duty not of ministers but of all private persons. Therefore any two or three can bind and loose here, not only ministers, and much less only elders. Indeed, from this one passage alone your elders have nearly lost their whole dominion.

units.la: Non illud solum ex iam dictis liquet, verba illa Christi recte priuatis omnibus, quoties rite ex verbo Dei proximum arguunt aut solantur, accommodatè, verum & illud patet, non solis Ministris tribui. Et quid aliud est fratrem lucrifacere sibi ac Deo? aut quid aliud dicit Christus, cum mox confirmat Patrem suum ratum habiturum in coelis, quae in ipsius nomine duo inter se egerint? Certe ex veteribus & recentioribus plurimi aliter, quàm tu exponunt. Argumentum autem tuum, quia verba sint iudicialia, nihil concludit. Non enim quaecunque iudicialia sunt, soli Ministerio conueniunt, vt nullus ignorat. Imò quia iudicialia & forensia dicis esse, ad Magistratum pertinere asseris: nisi demonstres tempore Christi apud Iudaeos praeter forum Magistratus aliud fuisse forum, in quo publica de puniendis & coercendis improbis iudicia exercerentur. Hoc autem quando, quibus, aut unde sumptis argumentis offendes? Hic ergo, vt alias semper, confisus. Tam verum illud etiam est, quod me ambiguè vti verbis istis asseris. Si argumentum meum attulisses in medium, non erat cur te nunc refutaret. In Thesibus igitur haec sunt verba mea.
units.tr: It is not only clear from what has been said that those words of Christ apply rightly and fittingly to all private persons whenever they correct or comfort their neighbour from the word of God, but it is also plain that they are not assigned to ministers alone. And what else is it to gain a brother for oneself and for God? Or what else does Christ mean when he immediately confirms that his Father will ratify in heaven whatever two of them have agreed upon in his name? Certainly many of the ancient and recent writers explain it otherwise than you do. Your argument, that the words are judicial, proves nothing. For not everything that is judicial belongs only to the ministry, as no one is unaware. Indeed, since you say they are judicial and forensic, you assert that they pertain to the magistrate, unless you show that in Christ's time among the Jews there was, apart from the court of the magistrate, another court in which public judgments about punishing and restraining wicked men were exercised. But when, with what persons, or from what arguments will you bring that proof? Here, then, as always, you are confident. Equally true is what you assert, that I use these words ambiguously. If you had brought my argument into the open, there would have been no reason for you to refute it now. So in my Theses these are my words.

units.la: Cum eadem verba, & modus loquendi idem habeantur Matth. 16. & 18. cap. necesse est, vt si non prorsus idem, simile tamen aliquid dicat Christus. At ligare & soluere Matth. 16. significant Euangelium annunciare, vt, qui ei credit, solutus sit, qui non credit, inexcusabilis redditus sit. Proinde hic etiam non est aliud, quam fratrem orare, vt ab iniuria desistat, indicando gratum hoc esse Deo: quem, si ab incoepto no desistat, propitium habiturus non sit. Cum etiam verba haec, Ligare & soluere, in totis sacris literis, pro eo, quod est, à Sacramentis abiungere, vel ad eadem iterum admittere, nusquam sint posita, miror plurimum, cur in hoc loco id significare putentur. Summa est, nunquam probabitur Ligare idem esse, quod Sacramentorum vsum negare, aut Soluere idem significare, quod eorundem vsum rursus concedere. Si fratrem, qui iniurius tibi est, voluntate atque ira Dei ex verbo eius proposita ab inferenda iniuria deterruetis, lucratúsque sic suetis, soluisti: si non persuaseris, manet ira Dei super eo, quemadmodum super illo manet, vel non manet, qui auditae Euangelij praedicationi non credidit, vel credidit.
units.tr: Since the same words and the same manner of speaking occur in Matthew 16 and Matthew 18, it must be that Christ says something similar, if not exactly the same, in both places. But "to bind and to loose" in Matthew 16 means to announce the Gospel, so that whoever believes it is loosed, and whoever does not believe is left without excuse. Accordingly, here too it means nothing other than urging a brother to stop doing wrong, by showing him that this is pleasing to God, and that if he does not stop what he has begun, God will not be merciful to him. Moreover, since the words "to bind and to loose" are nowhere in all of Holy Scripture used to mean separating someone from the sacraments or readmitting him to them, I am greatly surprised that they are thought to have that sense in this passage. In sum, it will never be proved that "to bind" means the same as to deny the use of the sacraments, or that "to loose" means to restore the use of them again. If you persuade a brother who has wronged you, by setting before him the will and anger of God from His Word, to refrain from doing the wrong, and so gain him, you have loosed him. If you do not persuade him, the anger of God remains upon him, just as it remains, or does not remain, upon the man who has not believed the preaching of the Gospel when he hears it, or who has believed it.

units.la: Ex hisce manifeste perspiciunt omnes, quae hic dicis, falsa esse vniuersa. Nam & priuatis conuenire possunt: & solis Ministris non competunt: nec ambiguè sic vsus sum istis verbis, quia summa sit vtrobique similitudo. Non significant etiam semper solennem actionem, sed priuatam quandoque. Sanè hic aliter exponi non possunt. Quippe vt non potest alius remittere debitum, quam creditor; sic iniuriam remittere nullus potest alius, quam qui passus est. Valde velim te legere, quae in suis locis communibus de triplici remissione eruditissime scripsit vir doctissimus & sanctissimus D. Wolphgangus Musculus. Intelligitur ex praedicatis illud etiam, qui priuato conueniat ligare seu retinere iniuriam: & quo tu candore nobis talia obiecceris, Remisit nihilominus Paulus Iudaeis iniuriam, qua ab ipsis afficiebatur, etiamsi ad Caesarem prouocaret. Hic de alia remittendi ratione sermo est ab ea, qua remittimus in animis nostris.
units.tr: From these points everyone clearly sees that everything you say here is false. For these words can apply to private persons, and they do not belong only to ministers; nor have I used these words ambiguously, since there is the greatest similarity between the two cases. Nor do they always signify a solemn act; sometimes they signify a private one. Certainly they cannot be explained here in any other way. Just as no one but the creditor can remit a debt, so no one can remit an injury except the one who has suffered it. I should very much like you to read what the most learned and most holy Master Wolfgang Musculus wrote most learnedly about the threefold remission in his Loci communes. From what has been said it is also understood that binding or retaining an injury belongs to a private person. And with what candour you object such things to us! Paul nevertheless forgave the Jews the injury by which they were afflicted, even though he appealed to Caesar. Here the discussion concerns a different way of forgiving from the one by which we forgive in our hearts.

units.la: An non boni Ministri cum prædicando Christum incredulos & præfractos ligant, simul etiam iniurias, si qua forte ab ipsis affecti sunt, remittunt? Longissimè differunt, iniuriam in animo remittere alicui, & cauere sibi à futura iniuria ratione ac via licita: de qua hic disserit Dominus. Respondsum simul quoque est sequentibus. Vides enim ligare & soluere hoc modo posse unum & duos, & tres: ac proinde conuenire ea posse & primæ & secundæ admonitioni. Item non agi hic, ut in iudicio (dum adhuc inter priuatos agitur) vbi Iudex aliquis solenniter sedet sententiam dicturus, postquam accusatorem ac reum audiuit.
units.tr: Do not good ministers, when by preaching Christ they bind unbelieving and stubborn men, at the same time also remit any injuries they may have suffered from them? To forgive an injury in one's heart and to guard oneself against a future injury by a lawful method and way are very different things, and it is the latter that the Lord discusses here. At the same time I have answered the following point as well. For you see that to bind and to loose in this way can be done by one, or two, or three, and therefore these things can apply to both the first and the second admonition. Likewise, this is not a matter here as in a court of law (while the case is still being argued between private persons), where a judge sits solemnly to pronounce sentence after hearing the accuser and the accused.

units.la: Non spectant hæc verba ad generalem & quotidianam tantum verbi prædicationem, verum complectuntur etiam applicationem ad singulares personas, fateor: at nego hanc à solis Ministris, multò magis nego à solis Presbyteris illis tuis fieri debere, quos scriptura non nouit: quod pro sexto argumento attulisti.
units.tr: These words do not refer only to the general and daily preaching of the Word, but they also embrace application to particular persons; I grant that. But I deny that this is to be done by ministers alone, and much more I deny that it is to be done by those elders of yours alone, whom Scripture does not know. That is what you brought forward as your sixth argument.

units.la: Septimum argumentum tuum est. Ligare est peccati & immunditiæ laqueis adhuc constrictum pronunciare: denique ex coetu Israelitarum extrudere. Num. 19. Tu, quod sæpè iam dixi, audacissimus es assertor, at timidissimus probator. De ceremoniale immunditia supra egimus: hic tantum monebo, sententiam tuam ex hoc ipso cap. confutari potuisse, si ex ceremonijs argumentari voluissemus. Sanè si eiectio immundi significasset ligationem, etiam purificatio significauisset absolutionem. At purificari immundus à quouis mundo poterat, non à solis Sacerdotibus. Quare solui vnusquisque à priuato quolibet posset. Verum ad rem redeo. Negotibi ligare hoc esse, quod tu dicis, siquidem hoc putes fieri oporteri per Presbyteros tuos solenniter: & neges à priuato & Ministro quolibet posse fieri eo modo, quo dictum iam fuit. Si ostenderis ἐκτεἰβἰἰσεται & ἐξολοθρεύθησεται idem significare ac pro incircumcisio haberi, & à Sacramentis depelli, concedemus tc locum illum non inepte produxisse. Sed haec indè vnde & ex quo authore probabis ? Apage cum istis nugis in re tanti momenti.
units.tr: Your seventh argument is this: "To bind is to declare that a person is still held fast in the snares of sin and uncleanness, and finally to thrust him out of the assembly of Israel" (Num. 19). You are, as I have often said already, a most bold asserter but a most timid prover. We have already dealt with ceremonial uncleanness above; here I will only point out that your opinion could have been refuted from this very chapter, if we had wished to argue from ceremonies. Certainly, if the expulsion of the unclean person signified binding, then the purification of the unclean person would also signify loosing. But an unclean person could be purified by any clean person, not by priests alone. Therefore anyone whatever could loose him in private. But let me return to the point. You claim that binding means what you say, provided you think it ought to be done solemnly by your elders, and you deny that it can be done by a private person or by any minister in the manner just described. If you show that [ἐκτειβισεται] "shall be cut off" and [ἐξολοθρεύθησεται] "shall be utterly destroyed" mean the same as being counted as uncircumcised and driven away from the sacraments, we will grant that you have not brought forward that passage without point. But from where and from which author will you prove this? Away with such trifles in a matter of such great importance!

units.la: Octauum argumentum nititur somnio Iudaei cuiusdam Eliae Leuitae. Ego neque sacris literis, quod vnum disputo, neque probatae fidei historicis te ostensurum esse dico, Exclusionem à Sacramentis cultuque diuino vsurpatam fuisse Iudaeis ex praescripto Mosis aut Prophetarum in talibus de qualibus nos disputamus. Scio Pharisaeos multa perperam nouasse absque Dei mandato: Scio etiam alios post euersam vrbem & dispersionem in omnes orbis terrae partes mirabilia confinxisse: & quibuscunque potuerunt modis suos in obedientia retinere studuisse. His si tu maiorem, quàm verbo Dei, fidem habes, insanire te putabo. An non ineptus es, cum me vis credere, Christum & Apostolum ad ista Iudaeorum posteriorum deliria respexisse? Saltem hoc in mentem tibi venire debebat, quod Paulus in 2. Cor. 3. scribit Iudaeos veteris Testamenti ac Mosis lectionem non intellexisse. In hunc vsque diem, cum Moses legitur, quia cordibus eorum impositum haeret. Adde, quod hic Leuita tuus nostra memoria mortuus primum est, cui tu me potius vis credere, quam septuaginta Interpretibus. Probabilitatis speciem habuisset, si ex Iosepho, qui ex Sacerdotum genere, atque ideo rituum Iudaicorum, qui ante & post Christi aetatem ad excidium vrbis vsque vsurpati fuerunt, scientissimus fuit, aliquid in medium attulisses. Cur non feceris, nota causa est: quia nihil apud eum reperisti, quod non pugnaret cum sententia tua. Cum septuaginta Interpret. conuenit Onkelus interpres Chaldaeus, qui ita Chaldaicè reddit ista, vt ipse in suo Methurgman Elias tuus, vocem, qua is vsus est, Excidium internecionémue significare prodiderit: qua de re nuper, cum eius Leuitae mentio fieret, me amicus meus linguarum peritissimus, & cui de Eliae tui satis constaret, certiorem fecit. An non te pudet repudet harum inceptiarum, in re tanta?
units.tr: Your eighth argument rests on a dream of a certain Jew, Elias the Levite. I say that you will show, neither from Holy Scripture, which is the only thing I am disputing about, nor from historians of approved trustworthiness, that exclusion from the sacraments and from divine worship was practised among the Jews by the prescription of Moses or the Prophets in cases of the kind we are discussing. I know that the Pharisees introduced many things wrongly, without any command of God. I know too that others, after the city was overthrown and the nation was scattered into all parts of the world, invented wonderful things, and tried by whatever means they could to keep their people in obedience. If you put more faith in these things than in the Word of God, I shall think you are mad. Are you not foolish, when you want me to believe that Christ and the Apostle had regard to these later delusions of the Jews? At least this ought to have occurred to you, that Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 3 that the Jews of the Old Testament did not understand the reading of Moses, and that to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts. Add to this that your Levite died in our own memory, first of all. You want me to believe him rather than the Seventy translators! He would have had some appearance of probability if you had brought forward something from Josephus, who came from a priestly family and was therefore most learned in the Jewish rites, which were practised both before and after the time of Christ right up to the destruction of the city. Why you did not do so is well known: because you found nothing in him that did not contradict your opinion. Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast agrees with the Seventy translators; he renders those words in Chaldee in such a way that your Elias himself, in his Methurgeman, has declared that the word which Onkelos used signifies destruction and extermination. My friend, most skilled in languages, and well acquainted with your Elias, informed me of this recently, when mention of that Levite came up. Are you not ashamed of, and do you not reject, these undertakings in a matter of such importance?

units.la: Mirabar, nisi hoc etiam sugillares, quod dixi, Christum formam Disciplinae vestrae mancam proposuisse, si, quod vos vultis, institutum habuerit. Dixi autem hoc, ut eum nihil noui instituisse docerem: quod cum tu quoque sentias, cur hic reprehendas istam meam rationem non video. Attamen videamus quid contra adferas. Multa de Methodis, Definitione, Partitione, &c. dicis: ac nimium tibi indulges. Christus quoties noui aliquid instituit, substantiale nihil omisit: tametsi non per talem Methodum propositurus, ut primum Logicae definiret, deinde partiretur, postmodum causas, consequentia, cognata &c. adferret. Ritum coenae atque Baptismi instituit, & substantiae partem nullam omisit. Idem vos hic factum docere non poteritis, cum eum de priuatis &c. occultis solum peccatis, siue de quotidianis delictis, vt alij vocant, agere confiteamini: Excommunicatio autem non hisce, sed publicis proprie secundum vos infligatur. Si dixi vos verbum arguendi exponere per vocem Excommunicandi, fateor me errasse. At non recordor me dixisse. Dixi quidem, sic non posse exponi, atque ideo ad excommunicationem nihil facere: non autem dixi, quod sciam, vos sic exponere.
units.tr: I would have been surprised, unless you were also sneering at this, that I said Christ had set forth a defective form of your discipline, if He had instituted what you want. I said this, however, to show that He instituted nothing new; and since you too think so, I do not see why you criticise my reasoning here. Nevertheless, let us see what you bring against it. You talk a great deal about methods, definition, division, and so on, and you indulge yourself too much. Whenever Christ instituted something new, He omitted nothing of substance, although He did not propose it by such a method that He first defined, then divided, and afterwards brought forward causes, consequences, related matters, and so on. He instituted the rite of the Supper and of Baptism, and omitted no part of the substance. You will not be able to show that the same was done here, since you admit that He is speaking only of private, hidden sins, or of daily faults, as others call them, whereas excommunication, according to you, is properly inflicted for public sins. If I said that you explain the word "to rebuke" by the word "to excommunicate," I confess I was mistaken. But I do not remember saying so. I did say that it could not be explained in this way, and therefore has nothing to do with excommunication; but I did not, so far as I know, say that you explain it in this way.

units.la: Ex hoc quoque probari posse dixi, Christum verba ligandi & soluendi priuatis tribuere, quia scribatur dixisse, [Greek], iterum dico vobis. Constat autem eum supra nihil de duobus dixisse, nisi cum priuatum a priuato arguendum lucrandumque dixit, hoc ergo nunc repetit. Tu respondes trifariam, pro tuo more. Primum significare hoc aduerbium, aliquando repetitam actionem: At non ostendis hic significare. Syllabas me aucupari stomachose scribis, quod ego vltro fateor, cum ex syllabis & dictiones & orationes conficiantur. Ego absque syllabarum diligente animaduersione nihil possum solidi intelligere. Scio etiam ex vnius syllabae adiectione vel detractione mirabiliter orationis sensum mutari posse. Aucupor ergo syllabas ego, ut genuinam verborum Christi mentem vener, dum tu somnia tua captas, negligens syllabis. Dicis secundo, etiamsi ita sit, ut ad mutuam consensionem haec & superiora spectent, non tamen sequi, ut de priuatis negotijs vel ista vel superiora, vel utraque intelligantur. Vellem te audire cum scripturis loquentem. Iam enim abunde sum edoctus quam facile quiduis affirmes, & nihil probes. Ego non dixi tantum, sed probaui: adeoque sic probaui, ut frustra tu labefactare conatus adhuc fueris.
units.tr: I said too that this can be proved from the fact that Christ is reported to have said, "again [πάλιν] I say to you." Christ said nothing above about two people, except when he spoke of a private person to be rebuked and won over by another private person, so here he repeats that same point. You reply in three ways, as is your habit. First, you say this adverb sometimes signifies a repeated action. But you do not show that it means that here. You write angrily that I am fishing for syllables. I admit this freely, since words and sentences are made up of syllables. Without careful attention to syllables I can understand nothing solidly. I also know that the meaning of a sentence can change remarkably from the addition or removal of a single syllable. So I fish for syllables in order to grasp the true mind of Christ's words, while you chase your own dreams and neglect syllables. Second, you say that even if these words and those above refer to mutual agreement, it does not follow that either or both are to be understood of private matters. I would like to hear you speak from the Scriptures. I have already learned well enough how easily you assert anything and prove nothing. I did not merely say this; I proved it, and proved it so well that your attempts to overturn it have so far been in vain.

units.la: Tertio dicis, confirmationem esse a comparatis hoc modo: Si duorum consentientium preces non sunt irritae, an irritas censebimus Synedrij consentientis preces? Nihil te iuuat hoc etiam effugium. Etenim nisi concedas eum prius sensisse ac dixisse duorum consensum in rem aliquam a Deo petendam ratam haberi, non potuisset dicere, dico iterum. Hoc si concedis, a comparatis valebit argumentum. Nam si non feruetur res eadem in utroque extremo, vana erit comparatio. Qui sic ratiocinatur: Si puer haec intelligit, an non adultos eruditosque intelligere eadem par est? recte colligit, quia pueros etiam ponit intelligere. At si hoc modo argumentaretur: Si puer intelligit, adultum quis neget esse opulentum & bonum? Merito rideretur: quia medium seu rem subiectam mutaret. Cum ergo dicis, Si duorum consensum probat Deus, multo magis Synedrij probabit consensum, nihil concludes, nisi de eadem re vtrobique sic loquaris: Si, quae duo aut tres ligant ac soluunt, Deus rata habet, quomodo irritum ab eo haberi censebimus, si Synedrium liget ac soluat? Saltem hic vides, spero, quomodo tuo tibi gladio iugulum traijcias.
units.tr: Third, you say the confirmation is drawn from parallel cases in this way: "If the prayers of two who agree are not void, shall we judge the prayers of a council in agreement to be void?" This escape does not help you either. Unless you grant that he had first said and taught that the agreement of two in asking something of God is ratified, he could not have said, "again I say." If you grant this, the argument from parallel cases will stand. For if the same thing is not kept at both ends of the comparison, the comparison is empty. Someone who reasons, "If a child understands these things, is it not right that adults and the learned understand the same?" draws a correct conclusion, since he also grants that children understand. But if one argued, "If a child understands, who would deny that an adult is wealthy and good?" he would rightly be laughed at, because the middle term or subject has been changed. So when you say, "If God approves the agreement of two, much more will he approve the agreement of a council," you will conclude nothing unless you speak of the same matter on both sides: "If God ratifies what two or three bind and loose, how shall we judge it void when a council binds and looses?" At least here, I hope, you see how you have run your own throat through with your own sword.

units.la: Postremo conaris respondere ad testimonia Theophylacti & Augustini: quos ego hic non defenderem, si non tua refutatione tu sententiam nostram, vt saepe iam fecifti, egregiè confirmares. Sed præstat primum verba horum authorū, deinde accusationem tuam apponere. Theophylactus compilator Chrysostomi in hunc locum inter alia sic scribit.
