Si tu offensus habes eum, qui te iniuria assecit, sicut Publicanum & Gentilem, erit ille & in cœlo talis. Si autem soluueris eum, hoc est, ignoueris: eritei & in cœlo condonatum. Non enim solum, quæ soluunt sacerdotes, sunt soluta: sed quæcunque & nos iniuria affecti vel ligamus vel soluimus, & ipsa erunt ligata & soluta. Hæc probant, hanc Christi concionem à veteribus quoque de priuatis iniurijs acceptam expositamq; fuisse. Non est dubium, quin idem senserit ac scripserit Chrysostomus, cuius vbiq; scripta hic author in compendium contraxit. Augustinus de verbis Domini super Matthæum sermone 16, hæc habet: Cœpisti habere fratrem tuum tanquam Publicanum, ligas illum in terra: sed vt iustè alliges vide. Nam iniusta vincula disrumpit iustitia. Cum autem correxeris & concordaueris cum fratre tuo, soluisti eum in terra. Cum soluberis in terra, solutus erit in cœlo. Ex his testimonijs satis apparet, ne Veteres quidem non vidisse locum hunc de priuatis agere iniurijs, etsi aliâs non videantur satis appositè exposuisse.
units.tr: Finally, you try to answer the testimonies of Theophylact and Augustine. I would not defend them here, if by your refutation you did not, as you have often done already, admirably confirm our opinion. But it is better first to set out the words of these authors, and then to add your accusation. Theophylact, the compiler of Chrysostom, writes on this passage, among other things, as follows: "If you have a man who has wronged you, as a tax collector and a Gentile, he will be such in heaven also. But if you loose him, that is, forgive him, he will be forgiven in heaven too. For not only what the priests loose is loosed, but whatever we, having been wronged, either bind or loose, these also will be bound and loosed." These words prove that this saying of Christ was also received and expounded by the ancients as concerning private injuries. There is no doubt that Chrysostom thought and wrote the same, since this author has everywhere condensed Chrysostom's writings here. Augustine, in his sermon 16 on the words of the Lord in Matthew, says this: "You have begun to regard your brother as a tax collector; you bind him on earth. But see that you bind him justly. For justice breaks unjust chains. But when you have corrected him and been reconciled with your brother, you have loosed him on earth. When you are loosed on earth, he will be loosed in heaven." From these testimonies it is clear enough that the ancients also saw that this passage concerns private injuries, even if at other times they do not appear to have expounded it very aptly.

units.la: Ad hæc quid tu respondes? Concedimus Augustinum in illo sermone, inquis, ad priuatam reconciliationem trahere istam ligandi & soluendi potestatem: sed præsupposito Ecclesiæ iudicio. Addis hoc etiam: eum in suis concionibus non semper summam rationem habuisse propriæ alicuius loci interpretationis. Alibi autem rectius & magis appositè scripsisse. Ad Theophylactum idem respondes, scilicet Ligare & Soluere priuatos præeunti iudicio Synedrij subscribentes.
units.tr: What do you reply to this? "We grant," you say, "that in that sermon Augustine applies this power of binding and loosing to private reconciliation, but on the presupposition of the judgment of the Church." You add also that in his sermons he did not always take fully into account the proper interpretation of a particular passage, but that he wrote more rightly and more aptly elsewhere. You give the same answer about Theophylact, namely that private persons bind and loose in agreement with the prior judgment of the council.

units.la: Ego non affirmaui Augustinum semper exposuisse verba Christi vno modo. Quoniam ergo aliàs aliter exposuit, patet in vnis sacris literis nobis esse acquiescendum. Ex ipsis verbis & orationis contextu, ex proposito, ex antecedentibus, & consequentibus meam expositionem probaui, & tuam refutaui. Constat autem rectam veramque meam esse, non ob eam causam tantum quia ex ipsis verbis Christi probata est, verumetiam quia neque tu neque alij refellere eam adhuc potuistis. Augustini & Theophylacti verba addidi, non ad probandum, sed ad ostendendum veteres etiam aliquando in veritatem hoc in loco intuitos esse.
units.tr: I did not affirm that Augustine always expounded the words of Christ in one way. Since he expounded them differently at other times, it is clear that we must rest in the Scriptures alone. From the words themselves, from the context of the passage, from its purpose, and from what goes before and after, I have proved my exposition and refuted yours. Moreover, my interpretation is plainly right and true, not only because it has been proved from the very words of Christ, but also because neither you nor others have yet been able to refute it. I added the words of Augustine and Theophylact not to prove it, but to show that the ancients too sometimes looked to the truth in this passage.

units.la: Quod dicis eos concessisse hoc priuatis, suppositio iudicio Synedrij, de tuo affluis. An oblitus es Presbyteros tales nullos fuisse tempore Ambrosij & Augustini? Verumtamen scire ex te velim, quomodo non cogeretur vnusquisque pro soluto ligatoque habere, quem iam ante abs Synedrio, cui nefas sit contradicere, ligatum & solutum nouisse? Loquuntur illi de Ligatione & solutione, quae in prima & secunda admonitione contingere poterat: antequam ad Ecclesiam causa perlata fuisset. Quippe res ipsa nos docet, quod & supra declaraui, potuisse iniuria affectum in prima vel secunda admonitione subsistere: atque iniuriam potius ferre, quam publicare. Poterant igitur secundum hos authores priuati etiam Ligare & Soluere: & poterat nihilominus Ecclesia etiam Ligare & Soluere: si ad eam causa deferretur. Non pugnant haec inter se vllo modo. Quare vides ex horum quoq; sententia falsam esse tuam opinionem: cum priuatis verba haec Christi conuenire negas.
units.tr: As for your claim that they granted this to private persons on the presupposition of the council's judgment, you have made that up out of your own head. Have you forgotten that there were no such elders in the time of Ambrose and Augustine? Yet I would like to know from you how anyone would not be compelled to regard as bound and loosed a man whom he already knew, from the council, which may not be contradicted, to be bound and loosed? Those authors speak of binding and loosing that can happen at the first and second admonition, before the case had been carried to the Church. Indeed, the matter itself teaches us, as I also declared above, that a man who has been wronged can stop at the first or second admonition, and prefer to bear the injury rather than make it public. Therefore, according to these authors, private persons could also bind and loose, and the Church could nonetheless bind and loose too, if the case were brought before it. These things do not conflict in any way. So you see that by their judgment also your opinion is false, when you deny that these words of Christ suit private persons.

units.la: Christum dicis, cum Math. 7. vetet Sanctum dare canibus, & Margaritas obijcere porcis, de Sacramentis potius fuisse locutum, quam de solo simplici verbo. Dominus enim non defitit, inquis, vitam offerre Pharisæis & Sadducæis, quibus nulli alij magis porci fuerunt. Mirarer te hoc adducere, si non solitus esses teipsum oppugnare. An enim vetuit Pharisæis Sacramentorum vsum Christus? Si & Sacramenta concessit, & verbum non negauit, non pro his porcis habuit, de quibus hic loquitur. Nam aliter contra suum mandatum videri posset fecisse. Loquitur Christus de calcantibus Margaritas, & de laniantibus Sanctum offerentes: de quibus Matth. 10. etiam est locutus, cum excusso pedum pulvere deferendos esse tales præcepit. Hi non possunt alij esse, quam doctrinæ hostes & persecutores: quicquid tu tuique similes dicant. Nec aliud tu quodam loco publicè scribis. Verba tua sunt hæc. Pastori danda est opera, vt canes & porcos, id est, manifestos pietatis hostes, distinguat. Quis porrò neget Sacramenta neganda doctrinam pertinaciter repudiantibus & deridentibus? Non dixi ego de solo verbo Christum hic agere: (Nam & Sacramenta comprehendi sub τῶ ὀψιν nomine concedo) sed de verbo præcipuè eum hic agere scripsi: quod frustra tu negas. Qui membra externæ volunt Ecclesiæ videri, illi non calcabunt Sacramenta, nec osserentem laniare tentabunt. Et si quis talis reperiatur, huncego admittendum minimè censeo. Sermo noster de illis est, qui crimen agnoscunt & confitentur: qui emendationem promittunt: qui Sacramentis rectè cum cæteris vti, quantum iudicare nos possumus, desiderant. Hæc si àme dicta legisti, quo animo audes ex me quærere an sceleratum, qui se criminis pœnitere neget, ab eoq; desistere nolle affirmet, admittendum censeam? Si non legisti, qui negligentem te fuisse negabis?
units.tr: You say that when Christ in Matthew 7 forbids giving what is holy to dogs and casting pearls before swine, he was speaking of the sacraments rather than of the simple word alone. The Lord, you say, did not cease to offer life to the Pharisees and Sadducees, for no others were more like swine to them. I would be surprised that you bring this up, if you were not accustomed to attacking yourself. Did Christ forbid the Pharisees the use of the sacraments? If he granted them the sacraments and did not deny them the word, he did not regard them as the swine of whom he speaks here. Otherwise he could seem to have acted against his own command. Christ is speaking of those who trample pearls and tear to pieces those who offer what is holy. He also spoke of these in Matthew 10, when he commanded that such people be left behind with the dust shaken from the feet. These cannot be anything other than enemies and persecutors of the teaching, whatever you and your like may say. Nor do you write otherwise in one place publicly. Your words are these: "Care must be taken by the minister to distinguish dogs and swine, that is, open enemies of piety." Who would deny that the sacraments must be withheld from those who stubbornly reject and mock the doctrine? I did not say that Christ is speaking here of the word alone (for I concede that the sacraments too are included under the general name), but I wrote that he is speaking here chiefly of the word, which you deny in vain. Those who wish to appear to be members of the outward Church will not trample the sacraments, nor will they try to tear to pieces the one who offers them. And if anyone like that is found, I do not at all think he should be admitted. Our discussion concerns those who acknowledge and confess their crime, who promise amendment, and who desire, so far as we can judge, to use the sacraments rightly with the rest. If you have read these things I have said, with what intention do you dare to ask me whether I think a wicked man should be admitted, one who denies that he repents of his crime and affirms that he is unwilling to give it up? If you have not read them, who will deny that you have been careless?

units.la: Miror cur non Apostolum Petrum potius citâris, quam Augustinum, vt porcos esse ostenderes etiam improbè viuentes: sicut alij obiecerunt. Quod hisce respondi, etiam tibi respondeo: non omnes facinorosos eiusdem esse generis, modi, & qualitatis: nec esse necesse, vt Christus in præsenti loco de quibuslibet porcis, vel de ijsdem locutus sit cum Petro. Quinquam ne hoc quidem dicat Apostolus. Hoc dicit, tale quid accidere ijs, qui ab agnita veritate relabuntur ad voluptates morésque huius seculi, quale lotæ sui contingit, quæ mox in luto iterum volutantur. Concedimus tibi libenter, etiam absq; Patrum authoritate seu testimonijs porcos appellari posse etiam Ecclesiæ prius insertos. Concedimus & illud, si tales fiant porci quales sunt, de quibus hic loquitur Christus, neganda ipsis esse verbum & Sacramenta. At non omnes porci tales sunt. Summa est Christus hic loquitur de calcantibus Margaritas & Sanctum repudiantibus, ac praeter haec offerentes discerpere volentibus: nos autem de longè alijs differimus.
units.tr: I wonder why you cite the Apostle Peter rather than Augustine to show that even those who live wickedly are swine, as others have objected. I answer you as I answered them: not all wrongdoers are of the same kind, manner and quality, and it is not necessary that Christ, in the present place, spoke of every kind of swine or of the very same swine he spoke of to Peter. Indeed the Apostle does not even say that. He says that those who fall back from the truth they have acknowledged into the pleasures and manners of this world suffer something like the washed sow, which straightway wallows in the mud again. I gladly grant you that even apart from the authority or testimonies of the Fathers, those who were earlier joined to the Church may be called swine. I also grant that if they become swine such as those Christ speaks of here, the word and the sacraments must be denied them. But not all swine are of that sort. Christ is speaking here of those who trample the pearls and reject the holy thing, and besides, want to tear apart those who offer it. We, however, are discussing people quite different from these.

units.la: Ex dufcrimine verbi & Sacramentorum, quod hic adfers (atque ego probo) alij quidem carpere voluerunt, quod dixi, verbū non esse vilius & indignius Sacramentis, ideoq; cum ab illo facinorosi non absterreantur, ne ab hisquidem eosdem esse repellendos, fi quando intus admoniti vsurpare ea cupiant. Non eadem, aiunt, est verbi & Sacramentorum ratio: quoniam illud infidelibus etiam, haec duntaxat conuertis destinata sunt. Libenter illis do, verbum esse omnibus commune etiam impijs & infidelibus, vt eo tanquam tuba vocentur omnes ad Regni coelestis possessionem, & diuinae beneficentiae agnitionem. Nos non de illis, qui extra Ecclesiam sunt visibilem loquimur, sed de illis folis disserimus, qui baptizati sunt: qui fe Christianos volunt nominari: qui errores peccataque sua agnoscunt: qui cum cæteris Christianis celebrare mortem Domini, fuamq; fidem testatam Ecclesiae facere cupiunt. Hos dicimus admonitos à Ministro, fi accedere velint, Presbyterorum quorundam iudicio non esse arcendos. Hoc illud est, quod in scripturis praeceptum negamus. Hoc est, quod probari nobis volumus: nempe non debere ad Sacramenta illos admitti, qui visibili Ecclesiae inferti, inque ea educati sunt, ac doctrinam eiusdem palàm approbant, & Sacramentis vti cum caeteris defiderant. His nos dicimus tàm non posse Sacramenta negari in externa hac Ecclesiae potestate, quàm non potest eis verbum negari: quod neque dignitate, neque sanctitate, neque vsu cedit Sacramentis.
units.tr: As for the difference between the word and the sacraments, which you bring up here (and which I approve), others have wanted to find fault with what I said: that the word is no less valuable and no less worthy than the sacraments, and therefore, since wrongdoers are not kept from the word, they should not be shut out from the sacraments either, if they are inwardly moved and desire to use them. "The word and the sacraments," they say, "do not stand on the same footing, since the word is destined even for unbelievers, but the sacraments only for the converted." I gladly grant them that the word is common to all, even to the wicked and unbelieving, so that by it, as by a trumpet, all are called to possess the kingdom of heaven and to know the divine goodness. But we are not speaking of those who are outside the visible Church; we are discussing only those who have been baptized, who wish to be called Christians, who acknowledge their errors and sins, and who desire to celebrate the death of the Lord with other Christians and to make their faith known to the Church. We say that if such people, having been admonished by the minister, wish to come forward, they should not be kept back at the judgement of certain elders. This is what we deny is commanded in the Scriptures. This is what we want to prove: namely, that those who have been received into the visible Church, brought up in it, openly approve its doctrine, and desire to use the sacraments with the rest, must not be admitted to the sacraments. To these we say that the sacraments can no more be refused by this external power of the Church than the word can be refused to them; the sacraments yield to the word neither in dignity, nor in holiness, nor in use.

units.la: Quae de Ifmaeli & Efau adfers, ea fi nostro proposito ritè sic accommodabis, vt contrarium eius, quod nos diximus, demonstrent, eris mihi merito, non magnus modo, sed etiam maximus, Apollo. Cum malos bonis res bonas polluere negas; rectè facis: ac nos aduersus te ista non diximus, sed contra illos, qui affirmarunt.
units.tr: If you apply what you bring from Ishmael and Esau to our purpose in such a way that they prove the opposite of what we have said, you will deserve to be called by me not only a great Apollo but the greatest. When you deny that good things are polluted by bad men, you do well; and we did not say those things against you, but against those who asserted the opposite.

units.la: Sunt enim apud nos complures qui dicunt se bona conscientia non posse Sacramentis vti cum alijs quibusdam ipsis multo melioribus: quantum quidem iudicare ego de vtrisq; possum; Cum nos sic argumentatos dicis, Non polluuntur boni a malis in Coena participatione, Ergo malii non sunt a Coena prohibendi, dicis quod nos nullibi diximus. An idem dicit, qui errare affirmat putantes bonos a malis pollui in vsu eorundem Sacramentorum? &, qui malos ideo non arcendos a Coena asserit, vt bonos non contaminent? Contra illos tunc scripsi, qui sic solent ratiocinari: Hic peccator accedit ad mensam Domini: Ergo si ipse etiam accessero, particeps ero peccatorum ipsius: Item, Nolite iugum ducere cum infidelibus. Ergo qui Coenam Domini vsurpat cum malis, iugum ducit cum talibus, & participem se facit scelerum illorum. Item, mali polluunt bonos: Ergo mali sunt arcendi a Sacramentis. Hos dum non recte colligere dico, quod non veram sumant causam, tu me contrarium voluisse concludere opinaris:
units.tr: For there are many among us who say that with a good conscience they cannot use the sacraments with certain others who are far better than themselves (so far as I can judge of either). When you say that we have argued thus: "good men are not polluted by bad men in the participation of the Supper; therefore bad men are not to be kept from the Supper," you say something we nowhere said. Or does the same man say what those affirm who think that good men are polluted by bad in the use of the same sacraments? Or does he who says that bad men are not to be kept away from the Supper say so in order that they may not contaminate the good? I wrote against those who are accustomed to reason in this way: "This sinner comes to the table of the Lord; therefore if I too come, I shall be a partaker of his sins." Likewise: "Do not be yoked with unbelievers; therefore whoever takes the Lord's Supper with the wicked is yoked with them and makes himself a partaker of their crimes." Likewise: "The wicked pollute the good; therefore the wicked are to be kept from the sacraments." Since I say that these men do not draw the right conclusion, and that they do not take up the true cause, you suppose I wanted to conclude the contrary.

units.la: Videamus iam tuum argumentum. Mali sibi-ipsis (non alijs) polluunt Coenam: Ergo ab eius vsu per delectos Presbyteros, lata super hac re publica sententia, arcendi sunt. Vnde probabis hanc consecutionem? imo vero vnde probabis consequentis veritate, etiamsi consecutionem tibi largiremur? Si bona est consecutio tua, necesse est, vt concedas nobis, malos neq; legere neq; audire sacras literas debere nec ferendum, vt Deo agant gratias, vt nomen eius invocent vt orent: vt praestent Eleemosynam: denique vt aliquid eorum faciant, quae alias bona sunt, quoad externa sunt. Quippe omnia haec, & quicquid omnino faciunt, dicunt, cogitant, ipsi sibi polluunt: & apud Deum peccata sunt vniuersa. Quicquid enim non fit ex fide, peccatum est apud Deum: sed non in oculis hominum. Peccata autem adferunt iudicium & damnationem. An tu me feras sic argumentantem? Atqui sic tu argumentaris. Nam propositionem te facere oportet generalem: Vnusquisque est arcendus cendus ab eo, quod sibi polluit: Hæc si falsa sit, mandare tamen adferre oportebit speciale de Sacramentis. Hoc autem vbi scriptum reperisti? Non sunt abstinendi à Sacramentis participare cupientes, sed monendi vt digne, quomodo Christus iusit, participent: sicut nulli interdicendum est precibus, sed instituendi sunt, vt recte ex fide precentur: ne aliter precando peccent. Porro quomodo consequens probabis? Vbi est scriptum de Presbyteris illis cenforibus tuis? Nusquam. Pastores cauere pro viribus debent, ne quis sibi Coenam & res sacras polluat; fateor: At debent illis modis, quos scriptura probat, cauere: non quos ipsi sibi finxerunt. Cum suo munere perfuncti sunt, extra culpam ipsi erunt. Ezech. 3. 3. Sic Apostolus egit in 1. ad Corinth. Cap. 11. Rursus vides iniuste mea à te carpi: iuste autem tua à me refutari.
units.tr: Let us now look at your argument. "The wicked pollute the Supper to themselves (not to others); therefore, by a public sentence pronounced on this matter by chosen elders, they are to be kept from its use." From what will you prove this consequence? Indeed, from what will you prove the truth of the consequent, even if we granted you the consequence? If your inference is sound, you must concede to us that the wicked ought not to read or hear the holy letters, nor should they be allowed to give thanks to God, to call on his name, to pray, to give alms, or finally to do any of those things which are good in themselves so far as their outward nature goes. For all these things, and whatever they do or say or think, they pollute for themselves; and before God all of it is sin. For whatever is not done from faith is sin before God, though not in the eyes of men; and sins bring judgement and damnation. Would you have me argue like that? Yet this is how you argue. For you must make the premise general: "Everyone is to be kept from what he pollutes for himself." If this premise is false, you must still produce a specific command about the sacraments. But where have you found such a command? Those who desire to take part in the sacraments are not to be kept from them, but are to be instructed so that they may take part worthily, as Christ commanded; just as no one is to be forbidden prayer, but is to be taught to pray rightly from faith, lest by praying otherwise they sin. Further, how will you prove the consequence? Where is it written of those censors of yours, the elders? Nowhere. Ministers ought to take care, as far as they can, that no one pollutes the Supper and the holy things for himself; I grant that. But they ought to take care by the methods that Scripture approves, not by those they have invented for themselves. Once they have discharged their office, they will themselves be free of blame (Ezek. 3. 3). So the Apostle acted in 1 Cor. 11. Again you see that my statements are wrongly censured by you, while yours are justly refuted by me.

units.la: Ad historiam Simonis Magi supra respondi. Fuit illa manuum impositio Sacramentum donorum Spiritussancti: non commune Sacramentum erat omnium. Quod tu probabile dicis esse, hoc nos probabile esse tantisper negabimus, dum ex sacris literis probaueris. Quomodo enim sequitur: Petrus negabit Simonem participem esse donorum, quæ argento emere volebat, & quæ non erant omnium Christianorum communia: Ergo si pœnitentiam peccati professus fuisset, ne ad illa quidem Sacramenta fuisset admissus, quæ communia omnibus erant? Aduersarij mei, tui autem socij, contendunt nullum excommunicari posse, præterquam obstinatos & peruicaces, quorumque crimen publicè notum sit. Cæterum Simon (vt facinus eius notum fuerit pluribus) non fuit ante prænomitus: nec pertinax iudicari tunc potuit, quando primum admonitus fuit. Petrus certè non dicit eum pertinaciter egisse, verum graviter peccauisse indicat, & ad pœnitentiâ tunc primum hortatur. Quod si pœnitentiam non acturum vidit, Spiritu Sancto docente cognouit. Adijcis deinde Pauli discessionem à rebellibus Iudæis, iuxta mandatum Christi Matth. 18. vt vbiquc tui maneas similis. Discessit Apostolus à nolentibus. lentibus audire verbum Dei, siue ab illis canibus & porcis, de quibus Matth. 7. Christus praeceperat: nos autem de infertis in Ecclesiam & peccata sua vltro confitentibus, atque emendationem publicè pollicentibus, Sacramentaque appetentibus loquimur. Quid inter hos simile est? Hoc tibi (dicam iterum, postquam toties iam dixi) prorsus tenendum noris: illum admitti ad Sacramenta non debere, qui crimen commiserit quidem, sed palàm fatetur se poenitere, & meliora cogitare, priusquàm Presbyteris quibusdam videatur resipiscentiæ suæ documenta satis magna dedisse.
units.tr: I answered above regarding the history of Simon Magus. That laying on of hands was a sacrament of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; it was not a sacrament common to all. What you say is probable, we shall deny is probable for the present, until you prove it from the holy letters. For how does it follow that: "Peter will deny that Simon shared in the gifts which he wished to buy with money, and which were not common to all Christians; therefore, if he had professed repentance for his sin, he would not even have been admitted to those sacraments which were common to all"? My opponents, and your associates, contend that no one can be excommunicated except the obstinate and the stubborn, and those whose crime is publicly known. But Simon (since his deed was known to many) had not been admonished before; nor could he then be judged obstinate, since he was first admonished at that time. Peter certainly does not say that he acted stubbornly, but he indicates that he had sinned gravely, and at that time for the first time exhorts him to repentance. If he saw that Simon would not repent, he knew it by the teaching of the Holy Spirit. You next add the Apostle Paul's withdrawal from the rebellious Jews, in accordance with the command of Christ in Matt. 18, so that you may remain similar everywhere. The Apostle withdrew from those who were unwilling to hear the word of God, or from those dogs and swine of whom Christ had commanded in Matt. 7. But we are speaking of those who have been received into the Church and who of their own accord confess their sins, who publicly promise amendment, and who desire the sacraments. What is similar between these? Know that this must be held by you, absolutely (I shall say it again, since I have already said it so often): that he is not to be admitted to the sacraments who has indeed committed a crime, but openly confesses that he repents and intends better things, before certain elders are seen to have given sufficiently great evidence of his amendment.

units.la: Cap. IIII. Defensio veræ interpretationis loci 1. ad Corinth.
units.tr: Chapter 4. A defence of the true interpretation of 1 Corinthians 5.

units.la: Cap. 5.
units.tr: Chapter 5.

units.la: Voniam præcipua excommunicationis vestræ fundamenta duo sunt, videlicet Cap. 18. Matth. de quo ante egimus, & exemplum Corinthij, quem Apostolus decreuerat Satanæ tradere, operæprecium erit, vt, quæ de hoc loco dicis, pari diligentia examinemus. Ergo in loci propositi defensione illa primum, (ordinem tuum sequentes) expendemus, quæ contra argumenta nostra adfers. Deinde interpretationem tuam ponderabimus: Velim autem te in reprehendendo potius Theses nostras secutum fuisse, quàm scriptum illud, quod mihi soli magis, quàm alija vllis conscripseram: Sic enim ordo fuisset melior, & argumenta clariora. Sed postquam tibi aliter visum est, sequemur te, quocunque ducis: Lector prudens & diligens cum Thesibus facile conferet.
units.tr: Since the chief foundations of your excommunication are two, namely Matthew 18, which we have already discussed, and the example of the Corinthian whom the Apostle had decided to hand over to Satan, it will be worth our while to examine with equal care what you say about this passage. So, in defending the passage in question, we shall first (following your order) weigh what you bring against our arguments. Then we shall consider your interpretation. I would have wished, however, that in criticising me you had followed my Theses rather than that writing, which I composed for myself alone more than for anyone else. The order would have been better and the arguments clearer. But since you have decided otherwise, we shall follow you wherever you lead. A prudent and diligent reader will easily compare the two with the Theses.

units.la: Argumentum primum tuum ex scripto iam nominato hoc adfers. Apostolus contra & sine mandato Christi nihil fecit: Iam vero ostensum est, Christum neminem, nec Iudam quidem exclusisse. Volui assumptionem ponere hanc. At Christus nec verbo iussit aliquem excludi, nec ipse aliquem exclusit: sed contrarium potius egit, nempe Iudam admisit. Hanc, inquam, assumptionem volui propositioni subtexere: sed in eo scripto neglexi. At in Thesibus factis apertè posui (ut etiam alia completerer) his verbis. Apostolus contra Leges Mosis de Sacramentis, quas Christus non sustulit, nihil unquam vel dixit vel fecit: sed fuit cum caeteris Apostolis patriarum legum observantissimus. Christus autem legem de Paschate celebrando, in cuius locum suam coenam substituit, pro ea parte, qua iubet omnes celebrare, non mutauit, ut abunde supra declaratum fuit. Paulus ergo nec hunc, qui incestum fecerat, nec alium à Coena Domini arcuit. Ad haec debebas respondere tu: & ostendere, Christum mutauisse Legem Mosis pro ea parte: vel aliter fecisse: aut saltem Apostolos facere aliter fecisse. Frustra, crede mihi, latebras istas quaeris. Dicis te de Iuda, imò etiam de hac re tota abunde supra dixisse. Ego verò fateor te nimis multa dixisse: at nihil veri dixisse asserto: iudiciumque huius rei Ecclesiae, eruditisque omnibus permitto.
units.tr: Your first argument is drawn from the writing already named, and it runs thus: the Apostle did nothing against or without Christ's command. Now it has been shown that Christ excluded no one, not even Judas. I wished to put this minor premise, but in that writing I neglected to do so. In the Theses, however, I stated it plainly, with these words: "The Apostle never said or did anything against the laws of Moses concerning the sacraments, which Christ did not abolish; he was, with the other Apostles, most faithful in observing the laws of his fathers. Christ did not change the law about celebrating the Passover, in the part where it orders all to celebrate it, in place of which he put his own supper, as was fully declared above. Therefore Paul kept away neither this incestuous man nor anyone else from the Lord's Supper." To this you ought to have replied, and shown that Christ changed the law of Moses in that part, or acted otherwise, or at least that the Apostles acted otherwise. You seek hiding places in vain, believe me. You say you have dealt with Judas, indeed with this whole matter, at sufficient length above. I for my part grant that you have said far too much, but I maintain that you have said nothing true, and I leave the judgment of this matter to the Church and to all learned men.

units.la: Deinde cum scripsi: Non hoc dixit Apostolus, cur non interdixistis huic vsu Sacramentorum? sed, cur non luxistis? id est, expositore Augustino, cur non luctu & precibus vestris à Deo impetraftis huius hominis sublationem è medio vestri? Respondes tripliciter. Primo, debuisse Augustinum illud, vt tolleretur, ad Corinthios potius quàm ad Deum referre: cum alioqui parata eis fuisset exceptio: luximus quidem, sed Deus eum non sustulit. Secundo, tum demum fuisset precandus Deus aduersus talem, postquam excommunicationem tandem fuissent experti. Tertio non dicit Augustinus lugendum fuisse, vt iste tolleretur, sed vt istud opus tolleretur.
units.tr: Next, when I wrote: "The Apostle does not say, Why did you not forbid this man the use of the sacraments? but, Why did you not mourn? That is, as Augustine explains it, why did you not obtain by your grief and prayers from God the removal of this man from among you?" you reply in three ways. First, Augustine ought to have referred that "that he might be removed" to the Corinthians rather than to God, since otherwise they would have had a ready excuse: "We did mourn, but God did not remove him." Second, God would then have had to be entreated against such a man only after they had at last tried excommunication. Third, Augustine does not say that they ought to have mourned so that this man might be removed, but so that this deed might be removed.

units.la: Quis non videat leuiora esse ista, quam vt argumento satisfaciant? Augustinus ideo Corinthios hoc non tribuit, quia sciebat ipsorum non esse aliquem è medio tollere, vt qui carerent Magistratu: sed petendum hoc à Deo esse. Quod si excepissent, se luxisse, non habuisset causam Apostolus eos accusandi. Cum autem reprehenderet hoc nomine sciebat eos non fecisse: nec voluerunt illi mendacio se excusare, vt tu eos doces. Porrò sciendum hic est, non solum Augustinum hunc luctum sic exponere, verumetiam alios plerosque ex veteribus Graecis. Nam Theophylactus & Oecumenius, qui veterum Graecorum scripta redegerunt in compendia, eodem prorsus modo exponunt. Quando precandus fuerit Deus aduersus istum hominem, indicat Apostolus. Non dicit Paulus, cur non prius tentaftis omnia alia, & tandem Excommunicastis eum? & si ne sic quidem proficeretis, cur non tunc luxistis, vt è medio tolleretur? Nulla talium facta mentione reprehendit, quod non luxerint: vnde patet secundam quoque responsionem euanidam & à mente ac verbis Apostoli alienam esse. Tertio non modo vana est, sed etiam ridicula: praesertim Pauli interrogationem confidérantibus. Non enim queritur Paulus, quod non luxerint vt hoc opus tolleretur, sed de homine, qui scelus perpetrauerat, diserte loquitur. Et cum monui Augustinum quae de luctu. 12. cap. 2. Cor. dicit Apostolus, eodem modo explicare, non erat difficile videre, quae mens eius fuerit. An oblitus es, quae is de hac re scripsit lib.2. Retractationum suarum. Cap.17? Relege igitur, vt negligentiam tuam perspicias & accuses. Lege etiam quę de hac re lib.3. Cap.2. aduersus Epist. Parmen. Item lib. 5. Quaest. 39. in Deuteron. & quam sis infoelix argutator intelliges. Rursus ergo infoeliciter, vt semper adhuc, nos oppugnas. Summatim dicam, probare te oportebit, si aliquid hic contra nos voles adferre, lugere vt aliquis tollatur è medio aliquorum, idem esse, ac eundem illum à Sacramentis arcere per Ministros & Seniores vestros.
units.tr: Who does not see that these points are too trivial to satisfy the argument? Augustine did not assign this to the Corinthians because he knew that it was not for them to remove anyone from their midst, since they lacked a magistrate, but that it was to be sought from God. And if they had replied that they had mourned, the Apostle would have had no ground for accusing them. But since he rebuked them on this account, Augustine knew that they had not done so; nor did they wish to excuse themselves by a lie, as you teach them to do. Moreover, it must be noted here that not only Augustine explains this mourning in this way, but also many other ancient Greek writers. For Theophylact and Oecumenius, who reduced the writings of the ancient Greeks to summaries, explain it in exactly the same way. The Apostle indicates when God is to be entreated against this man. Does not Paul say, Why did you not first try all other means, and at last excommunicate him? And if even so you made no progress, why did you not then mourn so that he might be removed? By making no mention of such things, he rebukes them for not mourning; whence it is plain that your second answer also is empty and alien to the mind and words of the Apostle. Your third answer is not only vain but even ridiculous, especially if one considers Paul's question. For Paul does not complain that they did not mourn so that this deed might be removed, but he speaks plainly about the man who had committed the crime. And when I pointed out that Augustine explains in the same way what the Apostle says in 12. cap. 2. Cor. about mourning, it was not difficult to see what his mind was. Have you forgotten what he wrote on this matter in the second book of his Retractations, chapter 17? Reread it, then, so that you may see and blame your own carelessness. Read also what he says on this matter in book 3, chapter 2, against the letter of Parmenian, and again in book 5, question 39, on Deuteronomy; and you will understand what an unhappy arguer you are. Once again, then, you attack us unhappily, as you always do. In brief, if you wish to bring anything against us here, you will have to prove that to mourn so that someone may be removed from the midst of certain people is the same as keeping that very man from the sacraments by your ministers and elders.

units.la: * Tertio reprehendis quod dixi, miserum illum nihil videri à Corinthijs passum, quàm {ε}ἐπιτιμίας: Etenim cum Paulus eum in 2. Epistola absoluat à tota poena: nec mentionem alius faciat, quam τῆς ἐπιτιμίας à pluribus profectæ: liquet ab eis nihil dum aliud inflictum ei fuisse. Reprondes primum, ἐπιτιμίαν scribi, non ἐπιτιμῶν. Deinde quia hoc te nihil efficere vides, addis Excommunicationem non fieri sine durissima obiurgatione. Tertio, non esse de hoc laborandum, cum iusserit Satanæ tradere, quicquid Corinthij fecerint. Omnibus istis non soluis argumentum, quod probat miserum illum non fuisse exclusum à Sacramentis, sed tantum duriter obiurgatum à Corinthijs. Siue excommunicatio fit cum obiurgatione, siue absque ea, dicit Apostolus huic ἐπιτιμίαν sufficere, alia poena porrò non esse afficiendum: sed hanc ipsam cōuertendam esse in τὴν ἐν ὀλέθρῳ σάρκος. Quid tradere Satanæ sit exponam, cum occasionem tu nobis dabis.
units.tr: Third, you object to my saying that the wretched man seemed to have suffered nothing from the Corinthians beyond "epitimia" [ἐπιτιμίας]. For since Paul in his second Epistle releases him from the whole punishment, and mentions no other than the rebuke [ἐπιτιμίας] given by many, it is clear that nothing else had yet been inflicted on him. You reply, first, that the word is written ἐπιτιμίαν [epitimian], not ἐπιτιμῶν [epitimōn]. Then, because you see that this gets you nothing, you add that excommunication is not carried out without very harsh rebuke. Third, that we should not labour over this, since he ordered that whatever the Corinthians had done should be handed over to Satan. All these points do not refute the argument, which proves that the wretched man was not excluded from the sacraments, but only sharply rebuked by the Corinthians. Whether excommunication is carried out with rebuke or without it, the Apostle says that this rebuke [ἐπιτιμίαν] is enough for him, and that he is not to be punished further by any other penalty; rather, this very rebuke is to be turned into "destruction of the flesh" [τὴν ἐν ὀλέθρῳ σάρκος]. What handing over to Satan is I shall explain when you give us the occasion.

units.la: Reprehendis deinde, quod dixi, miserum illum non videri perseuerasse in scelere: nec ita iussum à Paulo castigari, vt qui adhuc peccaret, sed sicut Magistratus solent scelberatos punire, etiam postquam scelerate egere desierunt. Probaui ex eo, quod bis scribitur à Paulo, eum patrauisse, non autem patrare illud scelus. Respondes, hæc non ad continuationem scortatoris, sed ad ipsum factum referri, quod in suum contubernium nouercam recepisset. Docere hoc Paulum, qui initio capitis non scribat, γυναῖκα ἀσχημονοῦσαν, sed γυναῖκα ἔχειν. Mox ipsum Apostolum amare insectaris, si quidem illum qui iam peccare desijsset, Satanæ voluisset tradi.
units.tr: Next you object to my saying that the wretched man did not seem to have persisted in his crime, nor to have been ordered by Paul to be punished as one who was still sinning, but rather as magistrates are wont to punish criminals even after they have ceased to act criminally. I proved this from the fact that Paul writes twice that he had committed the deed, not that he was committing it. You reply that these words refer not to the continuing of the fornicator, but to the deed itself, that he had taken his stepmother into his household. You say that Paul teaches this, though at the beginning of the chapter he does not write "a woman behaving shamefully" [γυναῖκα ἀσχημονοῦσαν], but "to have a woman" [γυναῖκα ἔχειν]. Soon after, you rail at the Apostle himself, since he wished to hand over to Satan one who had already ceased to sin.

units.la: Parum certè folicitus hic sum, quid quisque credat, tantum dixi videri posse. Tua interim argumenta diuersum non probant. Nam cum Paulus dicit, non nominari hoc scelus inter Gentes, vt aliquis patris vxorem habeat, de eo loquitur, quod inter alios fit, non primò & per se de miseto illo. Exaggeratur crimen miseri ijs verbis : at non ostendiuntur eum tunc etiam apud se habuisse. Quod D. Paulum deinde nescio cuius rei putas accusari posse, si quidem poenitentia affectum nihilominus Satanæ voluerit tradi, in eo nimium sanè tibi indulges. An non Magistratus patrata flagitia plectit, etiamsi poenituerit patratorem facti, & quidem ex mandato Diuino? Cur ergo in tam enormi scelere velis Apostolum iniustè aut crudeliter fecisse, cum propterea quod magistratu careret Ecclesia, ratio alia puniendi non suppeteret? An & Petrum accusabis Ananiam occidentem? Propter hoc factum dicit Scriptura magnum metum totam peruasisse Ecclesiam. Sic apud Mosen frequenter legimus, cum puniri aliquod scelus iubet, ita faciendum, vt cæteris metus incutiatur. Vides cur Spiritussanctus talia per Apostolos egerit? Addidi aliam coniecturam, quod nimirum sic scribar Paulus, ac si ei constitisset de hominis resipiscentia. Sed hæc satis.
units.tr: I am certainly not very anxious about what each man believes; I have only said that it may appear so. Meanwhile your arguments do not prove the contrary. For when Paul says that such a crime is not named among the Gentiles, that someone should have his father's wife, he is speaking of what happens among others, not primarily and directly of that wretched man. The crime of the wretched man is magnified by those words, but it is not shown that he then also had her in his keeping. As for your suggestion that Paul could be accused of I know not what, since he wished the man, though penitent, to be handed over to Satan, you are indulging yourself too much in this. Does not the magistrate punish committed crimes even when the doer has repented, and indeed by divine command? Why then, in so enormous a crime, do you wish the Apostle to have acted unjustly or cruelly, when, because the Church lacked a magistrate, no other way of punishing was available? Or will you also accuse Peter of killing Ananias? Scripture says that great fear came upon the whole Church because of this deed. So too in Moses we often read that when he orders some crime to be punished, it must be done in such a way that fear is struck into the rest. Do you see why the Holy Spirit acted in this way through the Apostles? I have added another conjecture, namely that Paul wrote as if he were certain of the man's repentance. But enough of this.

units.la: Vt ostenderem maius aliquod fuisse Satanæ tradere, quàm à ceremonijs externis amouere, multis adduxi verbis Pauli rationes, (quarum aliquas tu omittis : inuitus scilicet) vt, quòd tanto studio tamque exquisitis verbis se excuset, ac veluti culpam deprecetur 2. & 7. Cap. poster. Epistolæ : quod summa affectí fuissent tristitia Corinthij : quod magna diligentia pro misero intercessissent: quod affirmet Apostolus Corinthios nullo abs se detrimento fuisse affectos : quod dixerit se poenituisse quodammodo : & quæ huius generis alia in Thesibus notaui. His, inquam, non erat opus, si tandem ad resipiscentiam vsque iussisset à Sacramentis repelli. Si perpetuum hoc erat mansurum in Ecclesia : nec in alium finem erat faciendum, quam vt inuitaretur ad poenitentiam, non erat cur tantopere se purgaret : præsertim si Seniores iam ordinauerat &c. Inspiciat Theses qui plenius ista cupit cognoscere. Nunc tua videamus, cum dicas te cogi singula plenè in hoc argumento carpere.
units.tr: To show that handing a man over to Satan was something greater than simply keeping him away from the external ceremonies, I set out Paul's reasons in many words. (You leave some of them out, no doubt unwillingly.) Consider how earnestly and with what careful wording he excuses himself in the second and seventh chapters of the later Epistle, almost as if he were pleading for pardon. He says the Corinthians were overcome with the deepest sorrow, that he had interceded for the wretched man with great diligence, that he assures them they suffered no loss at his hands, that he said he was in some measure sorry, and other things of this kind, which I noted in the Theses. None of this would have been needed if he had ordered the man to be kept from the Sacraments only until he repented. If that exclusion was to remain in the Church for ever, and was to serve no other end than to invite him to repentance, there was no reason for him to clear himself so eagerly, especially since he had already appointed elders, and so on. Let whoever wants to know these matters more fully consult the Theses. Now let us look at your points, since you say you must go through each one in full in this argument.

units.la: Primum dicis, me supra contendisse, Apostolum præcepisse, vt tantum admoneretur. Causas deinde doloris in Corinthijs recitas, sed leues & euanidas ad id, quod vrgeo in argumento. Tertio non se excusare Paulum, ac si peccasset: id quod ego nec dixi nec sensi vnquam. Scio certo certius eum hac in re nulla ex parte peccauisse: cur ergo se perinde ac si peccauisset, purgaret? Quarto nec poenituisse eum, vt qui malè sibi sunt conscij. Concedo non minus hoc quoque, & contra affirmantes, me diuersum probare posse scio. Vltimo nihil horribilius viuentibus proponi posse, ais, (excepta vltimi diei sententia) quàm si quis in Christi nomine pronuncietur ligatus in coelis & in terra.
units.tr: First, you say that I contended above that the Apostle commanded only that the man be admonished. Then you recite the causes of the Corinthians' grief, but they are slight and fade away when set against what I press in the argument. Third, you say Paul did not excuse himself as though he had sinned; I never said or thought this. I know for certain, more certainly than anything, that he was blameless in this matter in every respect. Why then would he clear himself as though he had sinned? Fourth, you say he did not repent, since men who are conscious of having done wrong do not. I grant this no less, and I know I can prove the opposite against those who affirm it. Last, you say that nothing more dreadful can be set before the living (except the sentence of the last day) than to be pronounced bound in heaven and on earth in Christ's name.

units.la: Quæ secundo, tertio, & quarto loco dixisti, satis consutata sunt: nec ad propositum nostrum ascendunt. Quod primo loco mihi tribuis, salsissimum est: nec reperies à me vllo in loco affirmatum. Dixi nihil eum praeter obiurgationem illam multorum perpessum: at non dixi Apostolum hoc tantum iussisse. Hoc modo cum toties mecum agas, & subinde tamen fratrem me appelles, facis certè vt prudentes dubitent, quo me animo ac modo fratrem nomines. Quod postremo dicis, verum esse concedo: at Corinthium illum pronunciatum hoc modo fuisse à Paulo, tunc verum erit, quando quicquid tu dicis, verum erit. Paulus crimen voluit in homine punire: propterea explicatissimè dicit, se statuisse eum tradere ad interitum carnis, quo anima salua maneat. Vides, quàm leuibus ratiunculis veritatem oppugnes?
units.tr: What you said second, third and fourth has been sufficiently refuted and does not bear on our question. What you attribute to me first is utterly absurd, and you will not find it affirmed by me anywhere. I said that he suffered nothing beyond that rebuke from the many, but I did not say that the Apostle commanded only this. By treating me so often in this way, and yet calling me brother from time to time, you certainly make sensible people wonder in what spirit and manner you call me brother. As for your last point, I grant it is true, but that the Corinthian was pronounced in this way by Paul will be true only when whatever you say is true. Paul wished to punish the crime in the man; for this reason he says very explicitly that he had decided to hand him over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved. Do you see how feeble the little arguments are with which you assail the truth?

units.la: Athanasio quoque, Augustino, Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, dixi, maius aliquid visum fuisse tradi Satanæ, quàm à Sacramentis repelli. Hoc quia negare non potes, multum te torques, vt tandem non videaris siluisse. Athanasius, inquis, exceptam fuisse ait animam istius, id est, vitam, sicut in tentatione Iobi factum est. Augustinus tiubanter loquitur. Chrysostomus aperte ad cruciatum corporis refert.
units.tr: I also said, of Athanasius, Augustine, Chrysostom and Theophylact, that handing over to Satan seemed to be something greater than being kept from the Sacraments. Since you cannot deny this, you rack your brains to appear not to have passed over it in silence. Athanasius, you say, states that the soul of that man was spared, that is, his life, just as happened in the temptation of Job. Augustine speaks hesitantly. Chrysostom plainly refers it to bodily torment.

units.la: Quorsum dicas, quicquid hic dicis, ego certe non video. Propositum mihi fuit docere, Patres, quos citaui, affirmauisse aliud quippiam fuisse Satanae tradi, quàm à Sacramentis remoueri. Hoc tu eos scripsisse cum negare nequeas, tamen me reprehendis. At non idem, inquis senserunt hac de re omnes: sed alius corporis cruciatum esse dixit, alius vitam excepit, alius modo hoc, modo aliud quippiam affirmauit, aut titubanter locutus est. Sed quid hoc contra nos facit? Non hoc disputamus, an idem omnes senserint? vel an ita sint interpretati, vt ego exposui? sed hoc quaerimus, an aliud esse putauerint, quàm à Sacramentis depelli, quicquid tandem singuli opinati fuerint esse? Non minus erras, cum scribis, me in vobis oppugnare, quorum authoritate nitar. Nam quatenus eorum testimonijs vtor, rectè me vti ostendi: tu, si potes, diuersum doce.
units.tr: Where you are heading with all this I certainly do not see. My purpose was to show that the Fathers I cited affirmed that being handed over to Satan was something other than being removed from the Sacraments. Since you cannot deny that they wrote this, you nevertheless rebuke me. But, you say, they did not all think alike on this point: one spoke of bodily torment, another excepted life, another affirmed one thing now and another thing then, or spoke hesitantly. But what does this tell against us? We are not disputing whether they all thought the same, or whether they interpreted it as I have set out. We are asking whether, whatever each one happened to think, they believed it to be anything other than being driven from the Sacraments. You are no less mistaken when you write that I am attacking the very authorities on whom I rely. For insofar as I use their testimonies, I have shown that I use them rightly. If you can, prove the opposite.

units.la: Athanasius certè, vt & hoc obiter moneam, non excipit vitam: sed per salutem spiritus intelligit salutem animae, non autem vitam corporalem: quod in ipsius expositione super hunc locum manifeste scriptum legimus. Nec dicit, Apostolum eosdem terminos Diabolo hic praescripsisse, quos Deus ei praefinierat in tentatione Iobi: sed hoc tantum dicit, sicut ibi certum terminum tentationis Diabolo proposuerit Deus, ita Apostolum indicauisse, quatenus eum vellet eidem tradi. Iobus tentabatur solum à Deo: at Corinthius ille plectendus fuisset, si Magistratum habuisset Ecclesia. Iudicium tandem cum permittis Ecclesiae, facis hoc, quod ego vnicè cupio.
units.tr: Athanasius certainly does not, as I may note in passing, except life; he understands by salvation of the spirit the salvation of the soul, not bodily life, as we read plainly written in his own exposition of this passage. Nor does he say that the Apostle here prescribed to the Devil the same limits that God had set for him in the temptation of Job; he says only that, just as God there set a fixed limit to the temptation placed before the Devil, so the Apostle indicated how far he wished the man to be given over to him. Job was tempted by God alone, but that Corinthian would have been punished if the Church had had the magistrate. When at last you grant the judgment to the Church, you do what I wholeheartedly desire.

units.la: Argumentum deinde inuictum, vt rectè dixi à significatione nominis ἀληθὲς, proposui, hoc modo. Perpetua certissimaque haec est regula (quam qui non seruat, potestatem sibi facit omnia pro libidine sua peruertendi) autores exponendi omnes, vt verba in sua propria natiuaque significatione, in qua cum authore nostro alij cuncti vsurpare solent, accipiamus: nisi omnino constet, authorem, quem interpretamur, aliter vsum fuisse: & circumstantiae ac res, de qua sermo est, aliter nos accipere cogant. Caeterum apud omnes Graecos nomen hoc, ἀπώλεια occisionem, mortem, necem, exterminationem, exitium, vt tibi placet, notat: nec aliter. Paulus eo vsus ostendi potest; (semper enim pro morte vel corporis, vel spiritus siue animae, vel vtriusque posuit: pro exstinctione cupiditatum carnis nunquam vsurpauit) nec res nos cogit aliter intelligere. Ergo hic etiam pro morte seu interfectione positum est. Citaui deinde testimonia omnia noui Testamenti, quorum recordari potui, quaeque ab aliis notata animaduerti, in quibus vel nominis huius, vel verbi, vel participij fit mentio, vt sic rem habere demonstrarem. Post haec ita conclusi. Interficere aliud est, quam à Sacramentis arcere. Apostolus hunc decreuerat occidere. Aliud igitur voluit, quam à Sacramentis depellere. Haec expriore illo meo scripto, quod tu magis, quam Theses videris refellere voluisse. Quid ad haec tu?
units.tr: Next I put forward an unanswerable argument, as I rightly said, from the signification of the word [ἀπώλεια], in this form. This is a constant and most certain rule (and whoever does not keep it gives himself licence to twist everything as he pleases): in expounding all authors, we should take words in their proper and native meaning, the meaning in which all others, along with our author, are accustomed to use them, unless it is quite clear that the author whom we are interpreting used them otherwise, and the circumstances and the matter under discussion compel us to understand them otherwise. Now among all Greeks this word [ἀπώλεια] denotes killing, death, slaughter, destruction, perdition, or whatever you like, and nothing else. That Paul used it in this sense can be shown; (for he always used it of death, either of the body, or of the spirit or soul, or of both; he never used it for the extinction of the desires of the flesh); nor does the matter compel us to understand it otherwise. Therefore here too it is used for death or destruction. I then cited all the passages of the New Testament that I could recall, and that I had noticed others mark, in which this noun, or the verb, or the participle is mentioned, to demonstrate that the matter stands thus. After this I concluded as follows. To destroy is something other than to exclude from the Sacraments. The Apostle had decided to destroy this man. Therefore he wished something other than to drive him from the Sacraments. These are the words of my earlier writing, which you seem to have wished to refute more than the Theses. What do you say to this?

units.la: Primum dicis, te malle ἀπώλειαν exitium interpretari, quo videlicet funditus aliquid deleatur & pereat. Deinde omisso eo, inquis, in quo controuersia posita est, id, de quo non ambigitur, in dubium revocas, quod magnum esse in disputando vitium non ignoras. Nos enim nomine carnis declarari arbitramur carnis affectus, quibus perimendis destinata sit etiam excisio ex ecclesia. Haec tua sunt. Quomodo conuerti nomen hoc malis, non laboro: modo id mihi des, quod eripere non potes, occisionem siue mortem significare corporis hoc in loco. Cum enim addit Apostolus τὴν σάρκα, ac deinde adijcit, vt spiritus maneat saluus, hoc est, vt anima salua sit, palam declarat, quatenus eum tradi Satanae velit, nempe vt corporalem vitam adimat: animum non affligat. Recte dicis deinde, magnum esse in disputatore vicium, si quis principium petat. Equidem non ab aliam causam foedum hoc vicium toties in te reprehendo, quam quod turpe esse scio. At hoc tibi fumis, inquies, in praesente loco. Ergo videamus, quid de hac re dixerim.
units.tr: First, you say you would rather interpret [ἀπώλειαν] as ruin, by which something is utterly blotted out and perishes. Then, leaving aside, as you put it, the point on which the controversy turns, you call into doubt what is not in dispute, though you know well that this is a serious fault in debate. For we take the name "flesh" to denote the affections of the flesh, for the destruction of which even excision from the Church is appointed. These are your words. How the word is to be translated I do not trouble about; only grant me what you cannot take away, that here it signifies the killing or death of the body. For when the Apostle adds "the flesh [τὴν σάρκα]" and then adds "that the spirit may be saved", that is, that the soul may be safe, he plainly declares that he wishes the man to be given to Satan so that his bodily life is taken away while his mind is not afflicted. You are right next to say that it is a serious fault in a disputant if someone begs the question. For my part, I rebuke you so often for this shameful fault for no other reason than that I know it is disgraceful. But you will say that this is a fault you charge me with in the present passage. Let us then see what I have said on this matter.

units.la: Dixi nec apud Paulum, nec apud authorem vllum alium
units.tr: I said that neither in Paul nor in any other author is this Greek word found [ἀλεθρος]

units.la: Græcum nomen hoc ἀλεθρος, siue additum ei sit nomen τῆς σαρκὸς siuenõ sit additum, inueniri positum pro exstinctione affectuum carnis: nec causam iustam adferri posse, cur hoc modo potius, quàm proprie positum in praesente loco dicemus. Ostendi Corinthios ita doluisse, vt nullus sanæ mentis posit cogitare, hoc ipsos intellexisse, tradendum esse eum duntaxat ad exstinctionem cupiditatum carnis. Quomodo petiuisset ab Apostolo, vt non traderet Satanæ, hoc est, (vt ex tua expositione consequi oportet) vt non adigeret ad poenitentiam, siue vt non extingueret in eo carnis cupiditates? Quomodo etiam tali petitioni assentiri potuisset Apostolus? imò quomodo scripsisset se condonare ei? An condonando permittebat hoc, vt non deleret seu non castigaret affectus carnis? An extinguere cupiditates aliter non poterat, nisi eijceretur ex Ecclesia? At verbum de eius contumacia nullum legimus post factam admonitionem: imò potius videtur mox poenitentia summa ductus fuisse, vt propè tristitia absorberetur. Propter has & consimiles alias rationes in Thesibus ita hanc rem conclusi. Opponit Apostolus non affectus carnis cogitationi spiritus, sed τὸν ὀλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς, τὴν σωτηρίαν τὸ πνεύματος: id est, mortem corporis animæ saluti: quod & verborum proprietas, & Pauli consuetudo, & verbum σαρκὸς sic probant, vt qui effugium hic quærit, quiduis potius, quàm veritatem, quærere videri possit. Qua fronte igitur tu scribere audes, me omisso eo, quod in controuersia est, id reuocare in dubium, de quo non ambigitur? Si ostenderis τὸν ὀλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς pro cupiditatum carnis exstinctione poni in sacris literis, & argumenta mea confutaueris, iam dicito me falli & fallere alios.
units.tr: that this word [ὄλεθρος], whether or not the phrase "of the flesh" [τῆς σαρκὸς] is added to it, is used to mean the extinction of the desires of the flesh; nor can any just reason be given why we should read it in this way here rather than in its proper sense. I have shown that the Corinthians were so grieved that no one of sound mind could suppose they understood him to be handed over only for the extinction of fleshly desires. How could they have asked the Apostle not to hand him over to Satan, that is (as your explanation requires), not to drive him to repentance, or not to extinguish the desires of the flesh in him? How could the Apostle have assented to such a request? Indeed, how could he have written that he forgave him? Did he permit this by forgiving, so that the desires of the flesh were not destroyed or punished? Or could he not extinguish those desires in any other way than by casting him out of the Church? But we read no word about his obstinacy after the admonition was given; rather, he seems to have been moved at once by such deep repentance that he was nearly swallowed up by sorrow. For these and similar reasons I concluded the matter in the Theses as follows. The Apostle sets against one another not the desires of the flesh and the thought of the spirit, but the destruction of the flesh [τὸν ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς] and the salvation of the spirit [τὴν σωτηρίαν τοῦ πνεύματος], that is, the death of the body against the health of the soul. The proper meaning of the words, Paul's usage, and the word "flesh" itself prove this so clearly that whoever seeks an escape here may seem to be seeking anything rather than the truth. With what face, then, do you dare to write that I, passing over what is in dispute, call into doubt what is not in question? If you show that τὸν ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς is used in the Holy Scriptures for the extinction of the desires of the flesh, and refute my arguments, then you may say that I am mistaken and mislead others.

units.la: Verum si Apostolus, inquis, aperte dixisset, εἰς ὀλεθρον τῶν σαρκῶν τῶν σωμάτων, vt alibi dixit, θαράττῃ τὰς σαρκὰς τῆς σωματος, an mutaretur haec significatio? Respondeo, si Paulus ita dixisset, sciremus ita intelligendum: nunc cum aliter vnà cum Græcis omnibus est locutus, scimus quoque eum sic intelligendum vt loquitur. Quia alibi aliter scripsit, potuisset set etiam hic ita scribere, fi ita voluisset intelligi. Aliud est carnis interitus, & aliud rursus mortificatio affectuum carnis. Tu vocas syllabarum aucupium, quia vides te coargui istis: malles fortase nos ad tua omnia respondere ἀντὶ ἰχϑύος, at facere non possumus. Falsum quoque est, quod adijcis, citata à me testimonia, si vrgere ea velis, docere, ἀλλὰ ϑάνατον secum trahere spiritus perditionem. Mortem spiritus siue animae significare posse dixi: perditionem, vt in nihilum redigatur, nõ potest, quia sic mori homo nullus potest. Nomen τὸ νεκρῶν recté dixi pro occisione affectuũ carnis nullibi poni cum adiectione vocabuli carnis sic absolutè positum, vt hic ἁμαρτίας ponitur: verbum autem ipsemet citaui. Si quæ ex cap.8. ad Rom. citas, ita doceas exponenda esse, vt ei contradicent, quod de hoc nomine diximus, errasse in hoc me libenter profitebor. Quippe quomodocunque res habeat, semper manet firmum & indissolutum, quod probare nos volumus, nomé videlicet, ἀλλὰ ϑάνατον, semper morte, numquá carnis affectuum abscissionem significare. De verbo ἀπεκτείνωμεν tunc respondebimus, cum certi aliquid accusabis. Cum me parum abesse dicis à calumnia, non moueor, dum à fratre proficisci cogito, qui calumniari nescit. Iudicabunt pij & intelligentes omnes, vter nostrūm à calumnia absit longius.
units.tr: But you say: suppose the Apostle had plainly said "for the destruction of the flesh of the body" [εἰς ὄλεθρον τῶν σαρκῶν τοῦ σώματος], as he said elsewhere, "he mortifies the deeds of the body" [θανατοῦτε τὰς πράξεις τοῦ σώματος]; would the meaning then be changed? I answer: if Paul had said it that way, we would know it must be understood that way; but since he has spoken otherwise, in the manner of all the Greeks, we also know he must be understood as he speaks. Because he wrote differently elsewhere, he could also have written here in that way, if he had wanted it understood so. The destruction of the flesh is one thing, and the mortification of the desires of the flesh is another. You call this hunting for syllables, because you see that these things convict you. You would perhaps prefer that we answer all your points "instead of a fish" [ἀντὶ ἰχθύος], but we cannot do that. It is also false, as you add, that the testimonies I cited, if you press them, teach that death [θάνατον] brings the destruction of the spirit along with it. I said that death can mean the death of the spirit or soul; but destruction, in the sense of being reduced to nothing, cannot, because no man can die in that way. I rightly said that the word "dead" [νεκρῶν] is never used absolutely, with the addition of the word "flesh," to mean the killing of the desires of the flesh, in the way that "sin" [ἁμαρτίας] is used here; I myself cited the word. If you show from chapter 8 of Romans that the passages you cite must be explained in a way that contradicts what we have said about this word, I will gladly confess that I have erred in this. For however the matter stands, what we wish to prove remains firm and unshaken: the word "death" [θάνατον] always means death, and never means the cutting off of the desires of the flesh. We will answer the word "let us kill" [ἀπεκτείνωμεν] when you bring forward something definite. When you say I am not far from calumny, I am not troubled, since I think it comes from a brother, who does not know how to calumniate. All devout and intelligent people will judge which of us is further from calumny.

units.la: Quoniam ad id, quod dixi, neque Paulum tantopere se fuisse excusaturum, neque Corinthios ita fuisse doluturos, si ad respiscentiam vsque solummodo iussus fuisset excludi à Sacramentis: ex quo nec ad Ecclesiam nec ad ipsum aliquid mali tanti perueniret, propter quod sic animis angerentur: quoniam, inquam, nihil respondes solidi, ipse quoque præterea. Alia fuit Apostoli ratio, qui inuitus puniebat, ideoq; merito lugebat. Si ad emendationem vsq; tantum voluisset à Sacramentis arcere, aliter fuisset locutus. Quid multis? Poenas infligebat enormiter peccantibus longè grauiores quàm vestra sit exclusio, vt qui potestatem accepisset à Deo non traditâ quibusuis alijs aut ministris aut Senioribus.
units.tr: As for what I said, that Paul would not have made such an effort to excuse himself, nor the Corinthians have grieved so much, if he had been bidden only to exclude the man from the sacraments until repentance, since in that case neither the Church nor the man himself would have suffered so great an evil that they were so troubled in mind, you yourself have nothing solid to answer. The Apostle's position was different: he punished unwillingly, and therefore rightly grieved. If he had wished only to keep the man from the sacraments until amendment, he would have spoken differently. In short, he imposed punishments far heavier than your exclusion on those who sinned grievously, since he had received the power from God, not handed down to any other ministers or elders.

units.la: Non me videre cum dixi, quomodo Satan carnales assectus in nobis extinguat, cũ iubeat Apostolus Spiritu-sanɓo nos delere & compescere carnis fructus, ita tibi peccauisse visus sum, vt calumniam primò, & eo nomine postea expun&to fictionē esse scripseris: quam vt à vobis arceat Dominus, rogas, quid tu scis, quid mihi auditum sit antequam illa scriberem? An ego te spiritusanctii officium dixi ad Satanam transtulisse? Nullo in loco dixi. Quanquam non valdè fortasse peccet, qui hoc de vobis affirmet. Nam dum sic interpretamini verba Pauli ἵνα ὀλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς, vt idem significent, ac si dixisset, ad occisionem cupiditatum carnis, certè videmini ei hoc munus delegare. Qui enim personam alij personae (vt filium praeceptori) ad rem certam, (vt ad castigationem vel institutionem) tradit, is certè videtur permittere tradi rum potestati eius, cui tradit, in eum finem, propter quem tradit. Sed ad rem.
units.tr: I did not see how Satan extinguishes carnal desires in us, when the Apostle bids us destroy and restrain the deeds of the flesh by the Holy Spirit. So I did not think you had made so great a mistake as to write, first, a calumny, and then, on that ground, to say later that it was a fiction. As for your request that the Lord keep it far from you, what do you know of what had been heard by me before I wrote that? Did I say that you had transferred the office of the Holy Spirit to Satan? I said nothing of the kind anywhere. Yet perhaps he who says this of you does not greatly err. For when you interpret Paul's words "for the destruction of the flesh" [εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκὸς] so that they mean the same as if he had said "for the killing of the desires of the flesh," you certainly seem to assign this task to him. For he who hands one person over to another for a particular purpose (as a son to a teacher) to castigate or instruct, certainly seems to allow the one to whom he hands him over to have power over him for the sake of that purpose. But let us return to the matter.

units.la: Citas contra nos Apostolum & deinde Chrysostomum: sed quorsum nescio. Cum enim dicis tradi aliquos ad disciplinam omnis nequitiae magistro, quid aliud dicis, quàm ego dixi? Cur ergo calumniam aut fictionem vocas? Nego tibi, Paulum tradidisse aliquos Satanae ad disciplinam. De Alexandro & Hymenaeo dicit se eos tradidisse, vt iam didicerint non blasphemare. Hos certè non sic excommunicarat, vt Corinthium excommunicare (loquendum mihi est more vestro) decreuerat, cum illi fidem abnegassent. Sic ergo loquitur Apostolus, vt cum dicimus magistratum scelestum aliquem tradidisse carnifici, quo discat non amplius furari, aut latrocinari.
units.tr: You cite against us the Apostle and then Chrysostom, but I do not know to what end. For when you say that some are handed over to the teacher of all wickedness for discipline, what else are you saying than what I said? Why then do you call it calumny or fiction? I deny that Paul handed anyone over to Satan for discipline. He says that he handed over Alexander and Hymenaeus so that they might learn not to blaspheme. He did not excommunicate these men in the way he had decided to excommunicate the Corinthian (I must speak in your manner) when they had renounced the faith. So the Apostle speaks in the way we say that a magistrate has handed some criminal over to the executioner, so that he may learn not to steal or rob any longer.

units.la: Chrysostomi expositionem non accusò vt impiam, sed propriam esse nego: cum nec verbis Apostoli, nec ratione aliqua nitatur. Imò verò cum ait Apostolum non dicere se velle Corinthium tradere Satanae, vt spiritum saluet, sed vt spiritus sit siue maneat saluus, aperte satis perspicitur, eum non tradendum fuisse ad disciplinam. In loco superiore scribitur, ἵνα σωθῇ, vt hic, ἵνα πνεῦμα σωθῇ: vt par sit vtrobique, quod ad hanc rem attinet, ratio. Non tam futilis ergo mea est ratio, quin futilior tua sit accusatio. Si censes Paulum voluisse, inquis, vt iste Corinthi sic interficeretur, vt Ananias ad Petri pedes exanimis cecidit, tu videris, quàm resipiscentiae locum ipsi relinqueret: & quomodo Corinthios excusaturus sit, quod non paterentur. Ad vtrumque hoc supra respondi, & in Thessalonicensibus. Etenim Paulus scelus punire voluit: & de resipiscentia hominis non videtur dubitauisse. Magistratum non iussit Deus sceleratorum poenas differre, dum eum, qui patrauit, poenitebat: poenitentiam suis etiam in ipsa morte concedit Dominus. Apostolus quoque non modo Corinthios pro misero illo deprecantes habuit excusatos, sed maximopere affectum eorum erga miserum illum commendauit, adeo vt & ipse et pepercerit, & illis hortator fuerit, vt benignè eum complecterentur & consolarentur. Tu potius videris, quomodo non sis nimium audax, qui Pauli factum, & Corinthiorum pium afsectum in suspicione aliquâ adducere audes. Multò laudabilior est Corinthiorum pia humanitas & miseratio, quàm parùm Christiana quorundam in censendis proximi cogitationibus seueritas.
units.tr: I do not condemn Chrysostom's exposition as impious, but I deny that it is the proper sense, since it rests neither on the Apostle's words nor on any reasoning. Indeed, when he says that the Apostle does not say he wishes the Corinthian to be handed over to Satan so that the spirit may be saved, but so that the spirit may be or remain safe, it is clear enough that he was not to be handed over for discipline. In the earlier passage it is written "that he may be saved" [ἵνα σωθῇ], as here "that the spirit may be saved" [ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ], so the reasoning is the same on both occasions as far as this matter is concerned. My reasoning is therefore not so trivial that your accusation is not more trivial still. If you think, you say, that Paul wished the man to be so destroyed in Corinth as Ananias fell dead at Peter's feet, you must see how little room for repentance he left him, and how he would excuse the Corinthians for not allowing it. I answered both points above, and also in the Thessalonians passage. For Paul wished to punish the crime, and does not seem to have doubted the man's repentance. God did not order the magistrate to postpone the punishment of criminals while the one who committed the crime repents; the Lord grants repentance even in death itself. Nor did the Apostle merely regard the Corinthians as excusable for praying for that wretched man; he greatly commended their affection towards him, so much so that he himself forgave him, and urged them to embrace and console him kindly. It is rather you who should see how little you are to be called too bold, since you dare to cast suspicion on Paul's deed and the Corinthians' devout affection. The pious humanity and compassion of the Corinthians is far more praiseworthy than the not very Christian severity of some in judging the thoughts of their neighbour.

units.la: Paulus nullo loco dixit, scripsi ego, miserum illû rursus esse ad Sacramenta admittendum, aut in Ecclesiæ societatem iterum recipiendum, sed solam ⟨ἐντολὴν⟩ sufficere ait. Nihil ergo perpessus fuerat aliud. Respondes non referre quid Corinthij fecerint, sed quid Apostolus præceperit, ad quod supra satis respónsum fuit. Quorsum, quæso te, hoc respondes? Nos de Pauli facto loquimur, tu de Corinthijs respodes. Et suprà, cum de Corinthiorum facto ageremus, tu de Pauli præcepto respondebas. Quid facias disputatore tali? Deinde dicis, Apostolum satis exprimere exclusionem factam, cum sufficere dicis, quod cum ipso palàm actu erat. Iaoi ante ad hoc quoq; respósum est, nihil cum eo actum, quàm quod à plurimis fuit obiurgatus. Tu plura cum eo acta videris opinariat ex textu nõ potes probare.
units.tr: Paul nowhere said, "I have written that this man is to be admitted again to the sacraments or received again into the fellowship of the Church," but he says that the command [ἐντολήν] is sufficient. So nothing else had been done to him. You reply that it does not matter what the Corinthians did, but what the Apostle commanded, and an answer to that was given above. Why, I ask you, do you reply this way? We are speaking of Paul's act; you reply about the Corinthians. And above, when we were dealing with the Corinthians' act, you were replying about Paul's command. What kind of disputant are you? Then you say the Apostle sufficiently expressed the exclusion, since you say that what was openly done to him was enough. Already before, an answer was given to this as well: nothing was done to him except that he was rebuked by many. You seem to think more was done to him, but you cannot prove this from the text.

units.la: Si tradere Satanæ idem esset, dixi, quod extra Ecclesiam eijcere, extra quam nõ est salus, non addidisset Apostolus, verba hæc, vt anima seu spiritus saluus maneat. Ex his ego liquere puto, vt nulla præterea adessent argumenta, Apostolum tam non putauisse hunc damnatum iri, si occisus fuisset, quàm non putamus alij nos vel latrones vel alios sceleratos damnari, cum piè in supplicio moriuntur. Respondes primò multa de vestra opinione, quam ego non magnifacio in disputatione tali, in qua testimonia scripturæ quaerimus. Dein-
units.tr: If delivering to Satan were the same as casting out of the Church, outside of which there is no salvation, the Apostle would not have added these words, that the soul or spirit may be saved. From this I think it is clear, even without other arguments, that the Apostle did not think this man would be damned if he had been killed, any more than we think robbers or other criminals are damned when they die piously on the scaffold. You reply first with many things about your own opinion, which I do not value much in such a dispute, where we seek the testimonies of Scripture. Then...

units.la: Deinde negas Apostolum scripsisse, vt saluus maneat: sed vt saluus fiat. Verborum proprietas multò magis meæ quàm tuæ sententiæ suffragatur iudicio eruditorum. Conuertite rectius interpres, vt saluus sit, quod sequentia mox verba, in die Iesu, id est, in die iudicij, clarissimè ostendunt. Quippe non tum primum saluifimus: sed pronunciantur salui, qui iam antè sunt salui. Certè verba hæc aperte satis probant Apostolum de morte corporali fuisse locutum.
units.tr: Then you deny that the Apostle wrote "that his spirit may remain safe," but "that he may be saved." The propriety of the words supports my view much more than yours, in the judgment of learned men. Translators would do better to render it "that he may be saved," as the following words, "in the day of Jesus, that is, in the day of judgment," make very clear. For it is not that they are then first saved; rather, those who were already saved before are pronounced saved. Certainly these words quite plainly prove that the Apostle was speaking of bodily death.

units.la: Si tradere Satanæ idem est, quod à sola Coena arcere, non idem est, ac extra Ecclesiam eijcere, extra quam salus non est. Quoniam Coena non est absolutè necessaria ad salutem. Respondes, non posse aliquem, qui velit participare Coenam, ab ea prohiberi, vbi legitimus sit excommunicationis vsus. Sed addis postea, oportere illum talem desiderium suum ritè testari Ecclesiæ, ne seipsum sallens iudicium sibi cumulet: hoc est, oportere eum Presbyteris placere. An non pugnant hæc, non prohiberi aliquem appetentem: &, iudicium penes alios consistere num recte vereque appetat? Et quis, rogo te, potest legitimus vsus esse vestræ excommunicationis, ab hominibus sine verbo Dei confictae? Abutuntur homines institutis Diuinis: & humano decreto, quod pro lege Diuina tanta animorum contentione nobis obtruditis, legitimè vtemini? An apud solos Allobroges non falluntur homines in iudicando? Item quis hoc scripsit, oportere Sacramenta appetentem desiderium suum Presbyteris ritè, id est, quomodo ipsis videatur esse rectum, testatum facere? Quòd deinde negas, excommunicationem exclusionem esse à sola Coena, sed declaratione dicis exclusionis è Regno coelorum, supra satis superque confutatum fuit, vnà cum aliis, quæ hic allinis.
units.tr: If delivering to Satan is the same as barring from the Supper alone, it is not the same as casting out of the Church, outside of which there is no salvation, since the Supper is not absolutely necessary for salvation. You reply that no one who wishes to take part in the Supper can be kept from it where there is a lawful use of excommunication. But you add afterwards that he must properly declare his desire to the Church, lest, deceiving himself, he heap judgment upon himself; that is, he must please the elders.
