Hoc te probare oportet, aliquos impuros moribus, etiamsi iuxta legem mundi essent, à pascha te & sacrificijs abactos. Nisi tales à Mose exceptos ostendas, à contradictione nunquam eum vindicabis: nisi nostram sententiam, tua deserta, approbes. Moses enim solos immundos iuxta legem, & absentes excipit: caeteris circumcisis omnibus praecipit vt cōcelebrent simul festa. Contorque ac verte te in quotquot figuras velis, argumentum tamen hoc rectè nunquā dissolues. Quocirca necesse est, vt vana sint omnia, quae praeterea de fermento opponis. Praestat tamen ea inspicere.
units.tr: I said that it was absurd, indeed impossible, and by no means to be believed, that God should at the same time openly command something and, at the same time and to the same men, forbid the same thing secretly and under a figure. He commands openly, and repeats the command several times, that all the circumcised, except only those who are legally unclean and absent, should appear before God three times each year with some offering, and celebrate the feasts together. Who then dares to say that God at the same time wished to forbid this same thing under the veil of leaven? Surely he would be commanding contradictory things at once, which is impious to think. To this what do you say? "We grant," you say, "the whole argument: we exclude none but the unclean." You say this. Do you not notice how frankly you are dealing? Our argument concerns the uncleanness of the law; you answer about the impurity of morals. You ought to prove that some who are impure in morals, even though they were clean according to the law, were driven from the Passover and the sacrifices. Unless you show such men excepted by Moses, you will never free him from contradiction; unless you approve our opinion and abandon your own. For Moses excepts only those who are unclean according to the law, and absent; to all the other circumcised he commands that they celebrate the feasts together. Twist and turn yourself into whatever shapes you like, you will never truly dissolve this argument. Therefore it must be that all the things you further object about leaven are vain. Still, it is worth examining them.

units.la: Delaberis deinde ad longam reprehensionem eius, quod dixi, figuras non proponi rerum praesentium. At non erat necesse, si frater esse videriq; cupiebas. Vides enim me dicere de rebus extetnis, vbi signatum est ipso signo frequentius & notius. Internarum rerum non nescio signa nobis à Deo externa proponi, vt imbecillitati nostrae consulat. Sed frustra sic conatis elabi. Docti enim omnes perspiciunt effugium te quaerere. At tecum, inquis, litiges oportet, cum mox dicas Paulum totius vitae sordes cum fermento conferre. Hoc, dixi, Paulum nunquam voluisse aut existimauisse, nempe fermentum in ceremonia Paschatis ita significauisse sordes vitae, vt ex eo posset colligi vestra excommunicatio. Nam tunc, cum vetaret Deus fermenti comestionem sceleribus suas poenas constituit. Ideo dixi Apostolum allusisse ad eum locum hoc aut consimili modo. Sicut Iudaei suum Pascha absque vero fermento celebrarunt, sic nos decet nostrum Pascha absque fermento malitiae aut nequitiae peragere. Fermentum simpliciter sumptum, potest bonum & malum significare, vt ex 13. & 16. Matth. liquet. Quare indicat Paulus, de quo ipse fermento loquatur. Adde, quod potuit corruptionem nostram congenitam significare, & legis immunditia. Nam non edere tantum prohibet Deus fermentum, sed etiam habere in aliquo domus suae loco. Non dicit etiam Apostolus, delinquentes sic esse à Sacramentis arcendos, aut ex Ecclesia exturbandos, vt i fermentum edentibus mortem Deus comminatus est. Hoc certum est, fermentum Iudaeis non significasse scelera sic punienda, vt vos dicitis.
units.tr: You then slip into a long criticism of what I said, that figures are not set forth for present things. But there was no need for this, if you wished to be, or seemed to be, a brother. For you see that I am speaking of external things, where the sign is itself more frequent and better known. I am not unaware that outward signs of inward things are set before us by God, to provide for our weakness. But you try in vain to escape in this way. All learned men, indeed, see that you are seeking an evasion. "But you must dispute with me," you say, "since you soon say that Paul compares the filth of the whole life with leaven." I said that Paul never wished or thought this, namely that in the ceremony of the Passover leaven so signified the filth of life that from it your excommunication could be inferred. For then, when God forbade the eating of leaven, he appointed punishments for wickedness. That is why I said the Apostle alluded to that passage in this or a similar way: just as the Jews celebrated their Passover without true leaven, so it becomes us to celebrate our Passover without the leaven of malice and wickedness. Leaven taken simply can signify both good and evil, as is clear from Matthew 13 and 16. Therefore Paul indicates what leaven he himself is speaking of. Add that it could signify our innate corruption and the uncleanness of the law. For God forbids not only the eating of leaven but also its being kept anywhere in his house. Nor does the Apostle say that offenders are to be excluded from the sacraments in this way, or thrust out of the Church, as God threatened death to those who ate leaven. This is certain: leaven did not signify for the Jews wickedness to be punished in the way you say.

units.la: Ad id, quod dixi, oportere homines occidi, non à Sacramentis arceri, si quidem fermentum edentis poenam velitis transferre ad licenter corruptéq; viuentiu cohercitione, sic
units.tr: As to what I said, that men ought to be killed and not kept from the sacraments, if indeed you wish to transfer the penalty of one who eats leaven to the restraint of those who live licentiously and corruptly, in this way

units.la: legem ficrefpondes. Poenæ iudiciales veteris legis, non sunt hodiè in ecclesiam introducendæ. Item, Paulum non dixisse, occidite, sed tollite è medio. Item, formulam hanc, excindetur animaillaex Israel, non semper significare poenam capitalem, sed interdum idem notare, quod pro incircumciso haberi. Ad primum respondi supra, & hunc quoque duobus verbis, tametsi huc partim pertinet, dicam. Quod Deus magistratus poenis subiecit, nullus eius potestati subtrahere alijsque puniendum committere debet, Matth. 15. etiamsi poenarum modus pro circumstantijs posset esse alius. Apostolum per hæc verba ἐξαιρεῖτε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐκ μέσου ὑμῶν, sicut & per traditionem Satanæ mortem intellexisse abundè supra demonstratum fuit. Nec mandauit tamen Corinthijs, vt miraculum ederent: quod aliqui nobis obijciunt. Hoc enim voluit, vt praesens esset Ecclesia traditioni, quam ipse apud se decreuerat Apostolus: quo videlicet alij magis auocarentur à sceleribus. Quod vltimo loco dicis, hoc constanter totum dico salsissimum esse, & omninò proprietati linguae, vt audio, Hebraicæ, (quam septuaginta te rectius intellexisse arbitror) deinde Græcæ & Latinæ manifestè aduersari in cap. 12. Exodi positum est ἐξολοθρευθήσεται: quod tu exponere potes, vt libet, nos quid significet scimus. Si hoc solum dixisses, hanc formulam non semper ad magistratum pertinere: sed Deum sibi extirpationem eam aliquando reseruare, vt paulò supra rectè scripsisti, facilè tibi assentirer. Sic Deus Corinthios indignè edentes puniuit, & puniet pro sua sancta & iusta voluntate, quos, quando, quomodo vult.
units.tr: You reply that it is the law. The judicial penalties of the old law are not to be introduced into the Church today. Likewise, Paul did not say "kill", but "take away from among you". Likewise, this formula, "that soul shall be cut off from Israel", does not always signify capital punishment, but sometimes means the same as being regarded as uncircumcised. I answered the first point above, and I will say a word on this too, although it partly bears on what is here. That God subjected people to the penalties of the magistrate, no one should withdraw them from the magistrate's power or commit their punishment to others, Matth. 15, even if the mode of punishment could be different according to circumstances. That the Apostle understood death by the words "take out the wicked person from among you" [ἐξαιρεῖτε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐκ μέσου ὑμῶν], as also by "delivering to Satan", has been amply demonstrated above. Nor did he, however, command the Corinthians to work a miracle, as some object to us. For he wanted the Church to be present at the handing over that the Apostle himself had decided upon, so that others might be more strongly deterred from crimes. As for what you say last, that this whole claim is utterly absurd and wholly contrary, as I hear, to the proper character of the Hebrew language (which I think the Seventy understood more correctly), and then to Greek and Latin: in Exodus 12 it is written "shall be exterminated" [ἐξολοθρευθήσεται]. You may explain it as you like; we know what it means. If you had only said that this formula does not always pertain to the magistrate, but that God sometimes reserves that extirpation to himself, as you rightly wrote a little above, I would readily agree with you. Thus God punished the Corinthians who ate unworthily, and he will punish whom, when and how he wills, according to his holy and just will.

units.la: Quartam obiectionem nolo defendere. Sed neque de quinta solicitus sum. Quoniam nec tibi nec mihi prosunt. Frustra igitur de ijs litigemus.
units.tr: I do not wish to defend the fourth objection. But I am not anxious about the fifth either, since neither helps you or me. So we would be quarrelling about them in vain.

units.la: Cum ex scholasticis scripsi, sensum analogicum non esse argumentatiuum, de iis scripsi, qui sic argumentantur: Deus minatur excidium fermentum edentibus durante festo Azymorum. At fermentum significat flagitia: & excidium designat excommunicationem. Ergo flagitiosum excommunicandi à presbyteris quibusdam fictitijs. Quas nobis figuras Spiritussanctus exposuit, & quatenus exposuit, tenemus nos pro certioribus, quàm quicquid excogitaria cunctis potest creaturis certi, veri, firmi, ac non figurati. Nulla est nobis allegoria, quando Spiritussancti habemus expositionem. Allegoricum vocamus, quod expositum non inuenimus, sed accommodare, seruata proportione, studemus ipsi. Hunc sensum dicunt scholastici, & dicimus nos, non esse argumentatiuum. Vbi, quaeso, Paulus dixit, poenam comesti fermenti significare vestram excommunicationem vel interdictionem Sacramentorum? Aut ergo ostende tu locum, in quo Apostolus ceremoniam fermenti sic fuerit interpretatus, aut male dicere define. Quatenus & quomodo exponat Apostolus, iam antè clarè explicatum est.
units.tr: When I wrote, following the schoolmen, that an analogical sense is not argumentative, I wrote this about those who argue thus: God threatens destruction to those who eat leaven during the feast of Unleavened Bread. But leaven signifies crimes, and destruction designates excommunication. Therefore, it is a crime to excommunicate by certain fictitious elders. As to the figures which the Holy Spirit has expounded to us, and so far as he has expounded them, we hold them as more certain than anything that any creature could devise: certain, true, firm, and not figurative. There is no allegory for us when we have the Holy Spirit's exposition. We call allegorical what we do not find expounded, but which we ourselves strive to accommodate, keeping some proportion. The schoolmen say this sense is not argumentative, and we say so too. Where, I ask, did Paul say that the penalty for eating leaven signifies your excommunication or the interdiction of the Sacraments? Either show me the passage in which the Apostle so interpreted the ceremony of leaven, or stop speaking ill. How and in what way the Apostle expounds it has already been clearly explained above.

units.la: Nusquam inueniri dixi nomen, Paschatis, pro Coena Domini positum in nouo Testamento: & quidem verè dixi. At verò tu, vt fraterné reprehendas, hoc saltem dicis, me supra contendisse Coenam Paschati successisse. Quasi verò ex hoc refutetur, quod affirmaui, nomen Paschatis nullibi positum pro Coena Domini. An est necesse, vt quod alteri succedit, illius etiam nomine nominetur, cui successit? Indica tu nobis locum in nouo foedere: & eris magister magnus in Israel. Sed indigna sunt hæc, quæ aut tu scriberes, aut saltem ego refutarem.
units.tr: I said that the name "Passover" is found nowhere in the New Testament used for the Lord's Supper, and indeed I spoke truly. But you, to rebuke me as a brother, at least say this: that I had earlier contended that the Supper succeeded the Passover. As if what I affirmed, that the name Passover is nowhere used for the Lord's Supper, were refuted by this! Is it necessary that what succeeds another thing should also be named by the name of that to which it succeeded? Point out to us a place in the New Covenant, and you will be a great teacher in Israel. But these things are unworthy of being written by you, or at least of being refuted by me.

units.la: Duas dixi à Deo præcipuas recenseri causas, cur absque fermento iussi fuerint Pascha suum edere Iudæi, nempè vt subitæ ac prodigiosæ liberationis è durissima Aegyptiorum seruitute, & primo-genitorum liberationis recordarentur. Haec tu pro tuo more fraterné accusas, & nescio quid de ardore (puto te metiri alios ex tuo ingenio) declamitas. Non potest verè dici, inquis, has præcipuas fuisse causas, quum illa-ipsa liberatio ex Aegypto longè excellentius adumbrarit. Si verus es frater, cur reprehendis tam acerbè, quod confiteri cogeris? Fermenti prohibitio, hæc, quae dixi, primò & præcipuè figurauit, testificante Deo. Quod fi res hæ significatæ aliud deinde excellentius designarint, nihil id contra nos facit: nec nos id vnquam negauimus. Non hoc disputamus, quid liberatio ex Aegypto significarit: sed quid comestio panis absque fermento notarit. Non quid primogenitorum conseruatio portenderit inquirimus: sed quid fermenti vetatio repræsentarit inuestigamus. Ideo dixi, posse etiam seruire futuri Christi agnitioni eiusdemque officii, quia hæc non primò, sed per res significatas indicaret.
units.tr: I said that God especially set forth two causes why the Jews were commanded to eat their Passover without leaven, namely, that they might remember the sudden and miraculous liberation from the hardest slavery of the Egyptians, and the liberation of the firstborn. You, as is your way toward a brother, accuse these things and declaim about I know not what zeal (I suppose you measure others by your own nature). You say it cannot truly be said that these were the chief causes, since that very liberation from Egypt pictured something far more excellently. If you are a true brother, why do you rebuke so bitterly what you are compelled to confess? The prohibition of leaven, these things that I mentioned, first and chiefly figured, God testifying. If those things signified have afterwards designated something else more excellent, that does nothing against us, nor have we ever denied it. We are not disputing what the liberation from Egypt signified, but what eating bread without leaven signified. We are not inquiring what the preservation of the firstborn portended, but we are investigating what the prohibition of leaven represented. So I said that it could also serve for the future recognition of Christ and his office, because it did not indicate this primarily, but through the things signified.

units.la: Acerbius exagitas hæc mea verba, si præter hæc, quæ præterita fuerunt, futuri quoque aliquid significauisse contendatur, falsam doctrinam, aut turpem vitam figurare potuit. At non ita certum exploratumque hoc nobis est, vt sine alio præcepto à figura ad figuratam poenam transferre nobis liceat. Quodnam reperisti in his verbis meis tam graue peccatum? Dixi fermentum præteriti nihil significasse (quod quidem scire nos posse simus) quàm quod scriptura dicit. Ad res futuras quod attinet, ostendi me contendere nolle, sed vrgenti vltrò largiturum esse, potuisse ipsum falsam doctrinam aut turpem vitam denotauisse. Scio Apostolum ad hoc alludere: at tale quid proprie significauisse Iudaeis fermenti illam interdictionem, tu nec probasti, nec probaturus es. Sed vt hanc fugerem disputationem, dixi hoc non esse sic certum nobis, vt liceat poenam comesti fermenti (quam etiam hic falsò concedo fuisse amotionem à Sacramentis) transferre ad flagitiosorum coercitionem à vobis somniatam, nisi verbum accedat, siue præceptum. Nam Apostolus hoc non fecit, nec extat alius scriptor sacer seu Apostolicus qui fecerit: Quocirca recte ac verè dixi, quæ tibi tantopere displicent. Vides mea tolerabilia esse: tuas verò insulsas nugas & odiosissimas cavillationes ferri non posse?
units.tr: You criticise my words more harshly, as if it were contended that, besides those things which have been mentioned, it also signified something future, it could have figured false doctrine or a shameful life. But this is not so certain and clearly established for us that we may transfer the penalty from the figure to the figured without some other precept. What grave sin did you find in these words of mine? I said that leaven signified nothing of the past (which we can indeed know) beyond what Scripture says. As for future things, I showed that I was unwilling to contend, but would freely grant to one pressing that it could have denoted false doctrine or a shameful life. I know the Apostle alludes to this, but you neither proved nor will prove that that prohibition of leaven properly signified such a thing to the Jews. But in order to avoid this dispute, I said that it is not so certain to us that we may transfer the penalty for eating leaven (which I here wrongly concede was also the removal from the Sacraments) to the restraint of wrongdoers which you have dreamed up, unless a word or precept is added. For the Apostle did not do this, nor does any other sacred or apostolic writer exist who did. Wherefore I spoke rightly and truly in the things that so displease you. Do you see that mine are bearable, but that your silly trifles and most odious cavils cannot be endured?

units.la: Quod postremum carpis, hoc est, quod dixi Deum mandasse omnibus manibus vt interessent tribus illis festis: nec excepisse improbos, si modò essent mundi iuxta ceremoniam legis. Respondes pollutos nullos ante purificationem admissos fuisse. Loqueris autem de pollutis secundum legem. gem, cum dicis tales ne ad priuatam quidem mensam admissos fuisse: quod de aliis accipi nequit. At ego hos excipi à Mose iam ante toties inculcaui. Dixi licentius viventes non fuisse repulsos, de quibus solis disputamus. Ad hoc tu pisce magis mutus es. Multo tum rectius & verius, tum prudentius & doctius alij respondent, non fuisse improbos tunc admissos, cum secundum legem Mosis Respub. gubernaretur. Nam Magistratum tales sustulisse ex Dei praecepto & Mosis praescripto: & proinde non suisse Mosi opus exceptione alia. Haec, inquam, etsi nostrae sententiae admodum sunt consentanea, argumentum tamen non soluunt, vt suo loco ostendemus: sed ad veritatem longè accedunt propius quam tua. Scripturae testimonia à te exspectabam: tu vero mihi fabulosos Gentilium Poetas citas. An seruanda nobis omnia putas, quae in suis illi sacris seruarunt? Non arbitror. Ergo ex particularibus colligis: Ethnici improbos abegerunt à suis sacris, Ergo & nos idem decet imitari. Pudeat te sic argumentari: nos non pudet multa non facere, quae ipsi fecerunt: Sed bene factum est, cum ab Ethnicis vestrae opinionis confirmationem petere cogimini.
units.tr: As to what you carp at last, namely, that I said God commanded all men to attend those three feasts, and did not except the wicked, provided they were clean according to the ceremonial law: you reply that no polluted persons were admitted before purification. But you speak of persons polluted according to the law, when you say that such were not even admitted to a private table, which cannot be taken of others. But I have already so often insisted that Moses excepted these. I said that those living more licentiously were not rejected, and these alone are what we are disputing. On this point you are more mute than a fish. Others answer much more rightly and truly, and more prudently and learnedly, that wicked persons were not admitted then, since the commonwealth was governed according to the law of Moses. For the magistrate removed such persons by God's command and Moses' prescription, and therefore Moses had no need of another exception. These things, I say, although they agree very well with our opinion, do not resolve the argument, as we shall show in its place; but they come far closer to the truth than yours. I was expecting testimonies of Scripture from you, but you cite for me the fabulous poets of the Gentiles. Do you think we must keep everything that they kept in their sacred rites? I do not think so. Therefore you infer from particular cases: the heathen drove wicked men away from their sacred rites; therefore we too ought to imitate them. Be ashamed to argue thus. We are not ashamed to leave undone many things which they did. But it is well done that you are compelled to seek confirmation of your opinion from the heathen.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Refutatio argumentorum pro excommun. ex priuato conuictu, & 2. ad Thess. 3. desumptorum.
units.tr: CHAP. VIII. Refutation of the arguments for excommunication drawn from private fellowship at table and from 2 Thess. 3.

units.la: Is explicatis, redis ad argumentum & locum de priuato conuictu, eiusque coniungis alterum 2. ad Thess. 3. cap. sic tandem concludens. Si cum ijs, quos Ecclesia è medio sui sustulit, ne cibum quidem communem capere licet: multo minus in sacris licet cum illis communicare. Falsum est, quod dicis, Apostolum imperare, vt cum illis, qui è medio sublati sunt, cibum non caperent. Quomodo enim cum mortuo capiat aliquis cibum? Deinde vt per illud, tollere è medio, intelligas eiicere ex Ecclesia, rursus falsum est, eum iubere, ne cum talibus cibum capiamus. Etenim nullo in loco prohibet cum Ethnicis cibum capere: imò in eodem capite permittit priuata talium cômercia: atque alibi diserte concedit cum illis cibum capere. Falsa quoque est ratiocinatio haec: Non licet cum fratre vocato cibum capere: Ergo neque in sacris licet cum eo communicare. Quoniam non eadem est rerum sacrarum à Deo instituturum & imperatarum ratio, quae est priuatarum. Id quia supra copiosè declaraui, hoc iam loco, quia hanc rem toties inculcas, & huc me inuitum retrahis, testimonium illius viri adducam, cuius authoritas omni exceptione maior apud te in hac praesertim causa debet esse. Verba eius haec sunt.
units.tr: Having set these matters out, you return to the argument and the point about private table-fellowship, and you join to it the other argument from 2 Thess. chapter 3, concluding at last in this way: If it is not even lawful to take common food with those whom the Church has removed from its midst, much less is it lawful to communicate with them in sacred things. What you say is false, that the Apostle commands them not to take food with those who have been removed from the midst. For how can anyone take food with a dead man? Next, so that you may understand by the phrase "to remove from the midst" the casting out of the Church, it is again false that he orders us not to take food with such people. For in no place does he forbid taking food with Gentiles. Indeed, in the same chapter he permits private dealings with such people, and elsewhere he plainly concedes taking food with them. This reasoning is also false: It is not lawful to take food with a man who is called a brother; therefore neither is it lawful to communicate with him in sacred things. For the rule for sacred things, which God instituted and commanded, is not the same as the rule for private things. Since I have explained this fully above, and since you press this point so often and drag me back to it against my will, I will here adduce the testimony of that man whose authority ought, in this cause especially, to be beyond all exception for you. His words are these.

units.la: Quod autem vetat Paulus cum iis cibum sumere qui vitae sunt dissolutae, id ad priuatam consuetudinem pertinet: non ad publicam communionem. At, dicet aliquis, si homini Christiano non licet cum scelerato versari corporei victus percipiendi causa, multò minus panem Domini cum illo sumere licebit. Respondeo in libertate nostra & facultate positum esse, an familiariter versemur cum sceleratis. Quo fit, vt vnicuique sit ab eo abstinendum. At non est ita in arbitrio nostro positum, an Coenam recipiamus necne. Itaq; diuersa est ratio. Haec ille, & quidem rectè scribit. Etenim sacris literis consentanea sunt. Sanè Apostolus, 2. Thes. 3. monet, vt tales instar fratrum admoneamus. Ergo non vult nos ipsis aliquid eorum negare, quae ad salutem pertinent. Caeterum Sacramenta adminicula esse pietatis & salutis nostrae, nullus, vt ego quidem puto, negat. Proinde non sunt haec neganda petentibus, quomodo priuatum conuiuium negare possumus? Quid multis. Praedicta omnia à tua ratiocinatione sic differunt, vt eam putidam efficiant. Sed videamus nunc quomodo nostra refellas, postquam vidimus quam strenuè tua defendas.
units.tr: "What Paul forbids, however, is taking food with those who live a dissolute life, and that pertains to private custom, not to public communion. But someone will say: if a Christian may not associate with a wicked man for the sake of obtaining bodily food, much less will he be allowed to take the Lord's bread with him. I answer that it lies in our freedom and power whether we associate familiarly with the wicked. It follows that each person must abstain from them. But it is not so within our power whether or not we receive the Supper. Therefore the reasoning is different." These are his words, and he writes rightly indeed. For they agree with the holy Scriptures. Certainly the Apostle, in 2 Thess. 3., advises that we admonish such people as brothers. Therefore he does not want us to deny them anything that pertains to salvation. Moreover, no one, as I at least think, denies that the sacraments are aids to our piety and salvation. Therefore these things are not to be denied to those who ask for them; how then can we deny private table-fellowship? To be brief: all the things mentioned differ from your reasoning in such a way as to make it rotten. But let us now see how you refute our arguments, now that we have seen how vigorously you defend your own.

units.la: Apostoli praeceptum de fugienda priuata familiaritate non oportet sic accipi, vt cum praecepto exemploq; Christi pugnet. At supra ostendi, Deum non labigere peccatores à Sacramentis, sed ad ea potius colligere, ut ad pœnitentiam magis magisq; inuitentur, & facilius iterum erigantur. In hunc enim finem tot ceremoniæ, ac tot Sacramenta instituta fuerunt, ut ad veræ pietatis & sanctitatis amorem ac studium hominès facilius assuescerent, testibus Mose Deuter. 14. & summo quodam excommunicationis patrono. Ad hæc tu sic. Concedimus propositionem: Assumptionem distinguimus. Nam vocabantur ad sacrificia peccatores, sed qui resipiscentiam publicè per sacrificia testarentur. Si præterea nihil requiras, consentimus inter nos. Nam & nos de illis solis disputamus, qui peccatum suum agnoscunt, & meliora promittunt. Hoc oppugnamus (immò iam expugnauimus) quòd dicitis, Deum ordinauisse Presbyteros, qui huius rei sint cognitores & iudices. Dicimus nos, Deum hoc non magis in nouo fœdere præcepisse, quam in veteri præceperit, ut vel Sacerdotes vel alij oblationem pro peccato afferentes examinarent, num verè eos poenituerit, an potius simularent poenitentiam. Vt hic Sacerdotes oblationem recipiebant, neminemque repellebant, pro peccato suo oblationem Deo offerre volentem: sic neque apud nos dicimus Presbyteros esse eligendos, qui ista exigant. Vides, opinor, quam sis vbique miser & infoelix disputator.
units.tr: The precept of the Apostle about avoiding private familiarity must not be understood in such a way that it fights against the precept and example of Christ. But above I showed that God does not drive sinners away from the sacraments, but rather gathers them to them, so that they may be more and more invited to repentance and more easily raised up again. For to this end so many ceremonies and so many sacraments were instituted, that men might more easily become accustomed to love and zeal for true piety and holiness, as Moses witnesses in Deut. 14. and a certain chief patron of excommunication. To these things you reply thus: We grant the proposition; we distinguish the assumption. For sinners were indeed called to the sacrifices, but those who testified publicly through the sacrifices to their repentance. If you require nothing more besides this, we agree with each other. For we too dispute only about those who acknowledge their sin and promise better things. We oppose this (indeed we have already overcome it), that you say God ordained elders who would be the overseers and judges of this matter. We say that God did not command this in the new covenant any more than he commanded it in the old, namely that either priests or others bringing an offering for sin should examine whether they had truly repented or were rather feigning repentance. Just as there the priests received the offering and repelled no one who wished to offer a sacrifice to God for his sin, so neither do we say that elders are to be chosen among us who require such things. You see, I think, how wretched and unhappy a disputant you are everywhere.

units.la: Argumentum aliud fuit tale.
units.tr: Another argument was of this kind.

units.la: Si Apostolus per fugam priuati conuictus intellexisset Sacramentorum negationé, pugnauisset ipsemet secum. Etenim paulò post licentius viuentibus non interdicit, nec interdicere iubet Sacramentorum vsu: sed iudicium Dei proponit. Imò verò scelveratos, inquis, iubet à Massa expurgari: & cum reiectis vetat cibum sumi. Nec tollere è medio aliud significat. Insani enim esset vetare cibum capere cum mortuis. Quorsum ista dicis? Apostolum, dixi ego, post hunc locum, in quo priuatorum commercia præcepit fugere, sceleratis non negare coenam: ac proinde plurimum interesse inter negationem priuatæ sodalitatis ac Coenæ Domini. Si non possit prius esse absq; posteriore, sequitur Apostolum sibi aduersari, qui, quod Cap. 5. aliquibus negauit, deinde Cap. 11. liberè concedit. Tu dicis cum iubere massam expurgari à fermento, id quod verum est, Falsum autem est, quod Corinthijs imperarit illos, quibuscum cibum capere ibi vetat, eodem modo expurgare, quo alterum illum iusserat tolli. Quippe alterum volebat interficere, hos non voluit interfici. Ideo cum his cibum vetat sumere, non cum illo: cum non sit sani hominis vetare cibum capere cum mortuis, vt recte dicis. Sed neq; hoc sani est hominis, affirmare Paulum eandem poenam intelligere per verba; Tollite malum e medio vestri, &c, cum talibus ne cibum quidem capite. Sed & illud sane dictum non est, Apostolum illos quibuscum vetat cibum capere e medio tolli iusisse.
units.tr: If the Apostle had understood the denial of the sacraments by his command to flee private fellowship, he would have contradicted himself. For a little later he neither forbids, nor orders to be forbidden, the use of the sacraments to those living more licentiously, but sets forth God's judgment. But, you say, he orders the wicked to be purged from the lump, and forbids food to be taken with those rejected. Nor does "to take away from the midst" mean anything else. For it would be insane to forbid taking food with the dead. To what end do you say these things? I said, after this passage, in which he commands us to flee private associations with such men, that the Apostle does not deny the Lord's Supper to the wicked; and so there is a great difference between denying private fellowship and denying the Lord's Supper. If the former could not exist without the latter, it would follow that the Apostle contradicts himself, since in chapter 5 he denied something to some people and then in chapter 11 freely concedes it. You say that he commands the lump to be purged of leaven, which is true. But it is false that he ordered the Corinthians to purge out in the same way those with whom he forbids them to take food, as he had ordered the other man to be removed. For he wished the one to be destroyed, and these he did not wish to be destroyed. Therefore he forbids taking food with these, not with that man, since it is not the act of a sane man to forbid taking food with the dead, as you rightly say. But neither is it the act of a sane man to affirm that Paul understood the same penalty by the words "Put away the evil from among you," etc., "with such a one do not even take food." Nor was it certainly said that the Apostle ordered those with whom he forbids taking food to be removed from the midst.

units.la: Posthæc alia quædam adfers, quæ præterire non debeo. Primum affirmas, longè plus esse interdictionem Sacramentorum, quàm priuatæ consuetudinis prohibitionem; quod vt recte dictum probo. At cui minus, inquis, denegatur, qua ratione nobis persuaseris, quod maius est, concedi? Facile persuadebo intelligentibus omnibus, in proposito nostro. Propositio hæc, cui negatur paruum, negatur etiam maius, vera esse potest in donis, non autem in poenis: item in rebus eiusdem generis, non autem diuersis: Item in rebus liberis, non autem in illis, quarum una à Deo præcepta est, altera mandata non est. Hic nullum ex his habet locum.
units.tr: After this you bring forward certain other things, which I must not pass over. First you affirm that the prohibition of the sacraments is far more than the prohibition of private custom, which I grant is rightly said. But, you ask, to one from whom the lesser is denied, by what reasoning have you persuaded us that the greater is granted? I will easily persuade all who understand, in our matter. The proposition that, if the lesser is denied, the greater is also denied, can be true of gifts but not of penalties; likewise of things of the same kind but not of different kinds; likewise of free things but not of those of which one is commanded by God and the other is not commanded. None of these applies here.

units.la: Ad poenas quod attinet manifestum est, quod dico. Etenim cui negatur ciuitas, id est, qui iubetur exulare, ei non negatur mox etiam vita. Qui punitur pecunia, non etiam multatur morte. Paulus imperat bonis, vt malorum societatem deuitent: at non præcipit, vt, quæ Deus omnibus dedit, ipsi aliquibus negent. In summa cui negatur decem aurecorum impunitas, ei non negatur centum aurecorum impunitas, id est, qui decem aureis multatur, non etiam multatur centum. Quod ad res attinet diuersi generis par ratio est. Non enim negatur vita, cui negatur vsus ciuitatis. Non negat medicus vinum, quibus negat aquàm. Non negat Pater filio vestem, cui negat interdum rem viliorem. Hic res diuersissimæ sunt, politicæ ac priuatæ: postea sacræ & publicæ. Denique imperatum est Ecclesiæ membris, vt mortem Domini celebrent Coenæ eius sumptione, at impositum nulli est, vt cum hoc vel illo cibum capiat. Itaque fugere consuetudinem cum aliquo edendi possimus sine transgressione mandati Diuini, at abstinere à Coena Dominica sine praeuaricatione legis non possumus.
units.tr: As far as penalties are concerned, what I say is plain. For to one to whom citizenship is denied, that is, who is ordered into exile, life is not at once also denied. He who is punished with money is not also punished with death. Paul commands the good to avoid the fellowship of the wicked, but he does not prescribe that they deny to some what God has given to all. In sum: to one to whom impunity for ten gold pieces is denied, impunity for a hundred gold pieces is not denied; that is, he who is fined ten gold pieces is not also fined a hundred. The same parity holds for things of different kinds. For life is not denied to one to whom the use of citizenship is denied. A physician does not deny wine to those to whom he denies water. A father does not deny clothing to a son to whom he sometimes denies a cheaper thing. Here the things are most diverse: political and private, and afterwards sacred and public. Finally, it is commanded to the members of the Church that they celebrate the death of the Lord by partaking of his Supper, but it is imposed on no one that he take food with this or that person. Thus we can avoid the custom of eating with someone without transgressing the divine command, but we cannot abstain from the Lord's Supper without violating the law.

units.la: Quo pacto igitur ex negatione illarum inferatur negatio harum? Vides iterum ad quam pauca respicias, cum tua effundis?
units.tr: How, then, is the denial of these things inferred from the denial of those? Do you see again how little you attend to when you pour out your own words?

units.la: Ex particula, putas te aliquid inuenisse. At salleris hic quoque, vt alias semper. Apostolus hic inquit: Praecepi vobis antea in Epistola, & nunc quoque praecipio, non miscerí cum malis, imo nec cibum quidem vos capere cum talibus conuenit. Vetat ergo duo: primum vt non habeant arctam cum talibus consuetudinem, deinde vt ne quidem edant cum eis. Haec tibi vt seruiant, viderint, quicunque vtriusque scripta legent.
units.tr: From a particle you think you have found something. But you are deceived here too, as you always are elsewhere. The Apostle says here: "I wrote to you before in the epistle, and now I also write, not to mix with the wicked; indeed, it is not fitting even to eat with such people." So he forbids two things: first, that they have close familiarity with such people, and second, that they not even eat with them. Whether these words serve you, let those judge who read both writings.

units.la: Non loquitur, inquis, generaliter de malorum consuetudine, vt alibi. Nam excepit illos, qui sunt foris. Concedo hoc totum. Item simul codemque contextu meminit congregatorum in nomine Domini: Hoc vero manifeste falsum est, nisi congregationem hanc aliter exponas. Congregatorum cum absentis sui spiritu memini nit in causa eius, quem tradere Satanae decreuerat. Post de alia re, quanquam affine, loquitur. Scripsi inquit, vobis in Epistola, ne commiscerentur &c. Ergo de re loqui hic incipit, de qua prius cum ipsis egerat, quamquam non satis percepérant. Videntur enim super hac re, vt super alijs etiam plurics interrogasse ac, petiuisse declarationem Apostoli. At de tradendo illo Satanae, cum eo non egerant, vt ex textu ibidem appareret. De longe alio igitur negotio agit. Quo explicato, redit ad priorem causam, scelestum tollit iubens: Hoc igitur dicit, iussi vos consuetudinem prauorum fratrum fugere, non Gentilium, quorum mores iudicabit Dominus: vos autem iudicare vitam ac mores eorum decet, qui fratres nominantur, vt malos lucrifaciatis. Quod de discrimine verborum ἀμέμπτων & ἀμεμπτως adfers, ne dignum quidem est responsione. Accipe vt vis, non mutabis tamen sensum Pauli.
units.tr: You say he is not speaking generally of the custom of the wicked, as he does elsewhere, for he excepts those who are outside. I concede all of this. Likewise, in the same context he also mentions the gathering in the name of the Lord. But this is manifestly false, unless you explain this gathering in some other way. He mentions the gathering in the case of the man whom he had decided to hand over to Satan, with his absent spirit present. Afterwards he speaks of another matter, though a related one: "I wrote to you in the epistle," he says, "that they should not mix together," and so on. So he here begins to speak of the matter about which he had already dealt with them, although they had not fully understood it. For they seem to have asked about this matter, as about many others, and to have sought the Apostle's declaration. But concerning the handing over of that man to Satan, they had not dealt with him at all, as appears from the text itself. He therefore treats of quite a different business. Having explained this, he returns to the earlier cause and removes the wicked man, saying: "Therefore he says this: I ordered you to avoid the custom of wicked brothers, not of the Gentiles, whose manners the Lord will judge; but you ought to judge the life and manners of those who are called brothers, so that you may gain the wicked." As for what you bring up about the difference between the words [ἀμέμπτων] and [ἀμεμπτως], it is not even worth an answer. Take them as you like; you will not change Paul's meaning.

units.la: Vt probarem aliud fuisse apud Iudaeos à priuato conuictu abstinere, quam à Sacramentis prohibere, exemplum Publicanorum adduxi, quibuscum Pharisaei (vt de aliis hic nihil dicam) cibum minimè capiebant, & nihilominus tamen eos ad Templum sacrosque ritus admittebant. Ad haec respondes his verbis. De Publicanis, quibuscum Pharisaei cibum quidem non caperent, conuiuia tamen sacra haberent, alibi diximus. Quid alibi, quaeso te, dixisti? Neutrum negare potes. Nam & conuictum eorum sic vitarunt, vt Christum etiam hoc nomine accusarint. Quod ad Templum & Sacrificia admiserint, ex tota historia sacra constat, maximè ex Cap. 18. Lucae & historia Matthaei. Cum igitur hoc fuerit discrimen apud Iudaeos, quomodo sine scriptura tam confidenter audes affirmare, a priuata sodalitate arcere, idem esse cum eo, quod est a Sacramentis remouere?
units.tr: To prove that among the Jews it was one thing to abstain from private fellowship and another to exclude from the sacraments, I cited the example of the tax collectors, with whom the Pharisees (to say nothing here of others) would not eat at all, and yet they admitted them to the Temple and sacred rites. To this you reply in these words: "About the tax collectors, with whom the Pharisees indeed would not eat but yet held sacred feasts, we have spoken elsewhere." What, I ask you, did you say elsewhere? You can deny neither point. For they so avoided their company that they accused Christ on this very ground. That they admitted them to the Temple and the sacrifices is clear from the whole sacred history, especially from chapter 18 of Luke and the account in Matthew. Since, then, this was the distinction among the Jews, how do you dare to assert so confidently, without any Scripture, that to keep someone away from private fellowship is the same as removing him from the sacraments?

units.la: Attuli ad idem confirmandum hoc argumentum. Si idem vtroque significaretur, & idem vtriusque esset finis, sequeretur, vt contrariorum quoque similis idemque posseт finis esse. Iam negatę priuatae familiaritatis finis est, teste Paulo, vt is, cuius societatem conuictumque fugimus, pudeat. Idem finis etiam est negatae Coenae, vt vos dicitis. Ergo postulat res, vt, sicut conuictus priuatus contrarium poteft facere, nempe vitia altere ac fouere, tum in eo, citi cohabitamus, tum in nobis cohabitantibus, ita etiam Coenae Domini frequens visus vitia possit altere. At hoc est impium vel cogitare. Quocirca non possunt pro eodem sumi ista duo: cum non possit esse affirmationis finis vnus, sicut poteft negationis finis esse vnus, si vobis credamus. Ad hæc multa pro more tuo infoeliciter profers. Cum fine interdicte priuatę consuetudinis, inquis, non debuisti finem institutioni, sed interdictionis Coenę comparare.
units.tr: To confirm the same point I brought forward this argument. If the same thing were signified by both, and the end of both were the same, it would follow that contraries could likewise have a similar and the same end. Now the end of refused private intimacy is, by Paul's testimony, that the one whose company and table we shun should be ashamed. The end of the refused Supper is also the same, as you say. So the matter requires that, just as private fellowship can have the contrary effect, namely nourishing and fostering vices, both in the person with whom we live and in ourselves while we live together, so too the frequent sight of the Lord's Supper could foster vices. But it is impious even to think this. Therefore these two cannot be taken as the same, since the end of an affirmation cannot be one and the same as the end of a negation, if we are to believe you. Besides, you unhappily bring out many things, as is your habit. "With the end of forbidding private custom," you say, "you ought not to have compared the end of the institution, but the end of forbidding the Supper."

units.la: Quo in loco, oro te, sic comparauit, vt tu scribis? An non contuli negationem cum negatione, & affirmationem cum affirmatione? Et quid hæc verba mea, quę tumet-ipse in tuo scripto citasti, significant aliud? Priuatus conuictus, inquam, alit vicia: negatio pudefacit. An etiam, sicut Coenę Domini negationem pudefacere dicitis, eiusdem vsum vitia alere dicetis? Vides quam fraterne agas plerunque? Multa deinde garris sine fructu de collatione horum. Non enim potes negare, quicquid tandem proferas, quin perperam mea sis interpretatus. Addidi hoc etiam, quod tu neglexisti, Apostolum non prohibere malis consuetudinem bonorum, sed bonos monere, vt malos fugiant, vt per eum modum pudefacti se-ipsos agnoscant. At cum Sacramentis interdicitis alicui, non imperatis alijs, vt cum malo non participent Sacramenta, sed dissoluto præcipitis, ne ad ea veniat. Vtrum cohæreant an non cohæreant mortis Domini celebratio, & huius prohibitio, iudicent ex vtrorumque scriptis omnes homines.
units.tr: In what place, I beg you, did I compare it as you write? Did I not compare negation with negation, and affirmation with affirmation? And what do these words of mine, which you yourself cited in your writing, mean otherwise? Private fellowship, I said, feeds vices; refusal shames. Or will you also say that, just as refusal of the Lord's Supper shames, its use feeds vices? See how unbrotherly you often are! Then you chatter at length, to no purpose, about the comparison of these things. For, whatever you bring forward, you cannot deny that you have interpreted my words wrongly. I added also what you neglected: the Apostle does not forbid good men the company of the wicked, but bids good men to flee the wicked, so that the wicked, shamed in this way, may recognise themselves. But when you forbid someone the sacraments, you do not order others not to share the sacraments with a wicked man; you order the dissolute man himself not to come to them. Let all men judge from the writings of both whether the celebration of the Lord's death and this prohibition cohere or not.

units.la: Videor tibi in eo quoq; peccauisse, quod scripsi, impiè prohiberi, qui cupiunt cum alijs mortem Domini in publica ista actione concelebrare. Dura est, inquis, hæc sententia itavniuersaliter enunciata. Quid si enim quispiam, quid cupiat, non satis intelligat? Quid si simulate ipsum agere iusta sit suspicio, vel etiam liqueat? Quid si etiam totius Ecclesię interfit differri ipsius desiderium? Hęc tua sunt. Prima causa ad rem non facit, cum de recte institutis ego me semper disputare protestatus fuerim. Secunda in cerebro tuo nata est. Ego namq; cogor publicè profitenti dolere se propter peccata sua, & constitutum habere apud se deinceps sanctius viuere, fidem habere eum sic sentire tunc, vt dicit. Si non permaneat in proposito bono, meminisse debeo, me quoq; non semper manere. Ipsum cppere, argumentum est alicuius pieratis: quæ non optimi, sed accendi potius excitatique debet. Pendet hæc opinio tua ex opinione & iudicio hominum. Taceo iam, quod Deus non præcepit vel Presbyteris vel alijs tale examen. Tertia est plus quàm futilis. Quomodo enim interfit Ecclesiæ, vt differam hoc facere cum ceteris, quod me iusit Deus facere? Miser es, quocunq; te vertas, disputator. Nunquam tam probè intellexi, quod verissimè dixisse. Aristotelem nunc experior, de defendentibus Thesim: παντα γαρ, inquit, ὑπομνησάτε συμβαίνειν, ὡς ἐλαθὲς ἰχνεύετε ἀρχάς.
units.tr: You think I have also erred in writing that those who desire to celebrate the Lord's death together with others in this public action are forbidden impiously. "This sentence," you say, "is harsh, so universally stated. What if someone does not sufficiently understand what he desires? What if it is a reasonable suspicion, or even clear, that he is acting insincerely? What if it is also in the interest of the whole Church that his desire be deferred?" These are your words. The first point has nothing to do with the matter, since I have always declared that I dispute about things rightly instituted. The second has been born in your brain. For when someone publicly professes that he is sorry for his sins and has resolved to live more holily from now on, I am compelled to believe that he then feels as he says. If he does not persist in the good purpose, I must remember that I too do not always persist. That he desires it is a sign of some piety, which ought not to be restrained but rather stirred up and encouraged. Your opinion depends on the opinion and judgment of men. I say nothing now of the fact that God did not command such an examination either by elders or by others. The third point is more than futile. For how is it in the Church's interest that I should delay doing with the others what God has commanded me to do? You are wretched, disputant, wherever you turn. I never understood better what you said so truly. Now I experience Aristotle's words about those who defend a thesis: for, he says, everything follows, since you trace back the principles without noticing them [παντα γαρ ... ὡς ἐλαθὲς ἰχνεύετε ἀρχάς].

units.la: Cap. IX.
units.tr: Chapter 9.

units.la: Refutatio argumentorum aliorum quorundam pro Excommu- nicatione.
units.tr: A refutation of certain other arguments for excommunication.

units.la: Dfers posthæc argumenta quædam alia pro excómunicatione, quæ nihilò sunt prædicti is firmiora. Quæ breuiter etiam expendemus, vt intelligas te tui vbiq; manere similè. Apostolus, inquis, scribit, si quis nō diligit Dominum Iesū Christū, sit Anathema Maranatha. Ergo vult Presbyteros quosdā sedere & iudicare; quinam verò sint pœnitentes, & qui simulent resipiscentiam: vt scilicet illos ad Cœnam admittant, hos arceant. Si hoc est excommunicare, mille locis fundata est excommunicatio vestra. Diligere Christum est seruare mandata Christi, Ioh. 13. & 15. Quisquis ergo dicet: Qui non seruant mandata Christi sunt exlecrabiles Deo, is excommunicabit hoc modo. Sic excommunicauit Moses, quoties maledictos esse dixit domi, foris, in campo, & vbicunq; sunt, quicunq; non seruant totam Legem: Præclarè tibi conuenit hac in parte cum quodam alio, qui generalis excommunicationis formulam nobis à Mose Deuter. 27. propositam affirmauit. At non de hac excómunicatione loquimur: sed de ea, quam erga lapsos Presbyteri quidam in consessu suo per suffragia lata sententia exercent. Hanc tibi noris probandam, quod videlicet à Paulo sit imperata. Apostolus valdè iniquè accusabatur à Pseudoapostolis, qui eū omninò cōtemptibilem reddere satagebāt. Dicit ergo, Qui non diligit &c. ac si diceret: Deus sit iudex veri diligamus Christum, illumq; perdat, qui eum non verè diligit. Hic genuinus est huius loci sensus.
units.tr: You next bring forward certain other arguments for excommunication, which are no stronger than those already mentioned. We shall weigh these briefly too, so that you may see that you remain everywhere the same. The Apostle, you say, writes: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, Maranatha." Therefore he wants certain elders to sit in judgement and decide who are the true penitents and who only pretend repentance, so that they may admit the one group to the Lord's Supper and keep the other away. If this is excommunication, your excommunication is founded in a thousand places. To love Christ is to keep Christ's commandments (John 13 and 15). So whoever says, "Those who do not keep Christ's commandments are accursed before God," excommunicates in this way. Moses also excommunicated in this way, whenever he declared that those are cursed at home, abroad, in the field and wherever they are, who do not keep the whole Law (Deut. 27). In this respect you agree splendidly with a certain other man who asserted that the formula of general excommunication was set before us by Moses in Deut. 27. But we are not speaking of this kind of excommunication. We are speaking of the one that certain elders exercise against the fallen by a sentence passed by vote in their assembly. You should know that this is to be proved from the fact that Paul commanded it. The Apostle was most unjustly accused by the false apostles, who were trying hard to make him utterly contemptible. So he says, "If anyone does not love," and so on, as if he said: "God be judge: let us truly love Christ, and let him perish who does not truly love him." This is the genuine sense of this passage.

units.la: Tantundem valet, quod ex Epistola ad Galat. adfers: Si quis vobis euangelizauerit præter id quod accepistis, Anathema sit. Ergo excommunicandi iuhr pertinaces sanæ doctrinæ turbatores. Hæc non pugnant cum nostris: qui nō loquuntur de hæreticis falsamq; doctrinam plantantibus. Idem ad locum ex 2. Epist. Iohannis respōsum volo. Interim ne hoc quidē probat hic locus ita excommunicandos esse, vt hic de ista re disputatur. Eadem est ratio [?]gkerius loci ex 5. Cap. ejusdē Epist. Vtinā excindātur, qui nos conturbant. Loquitur enim de falsis Doctoribus. Itē, non dicit, congregate Presbyteros, & eijcite tales extra cœtum vestrum, siue tradite eos Satanæ: sed optat eos à Deo excindi. Sed audiamus Theologiam illam tuam responsionem, quam eidas, qui ex te quærat, cur non ipse exciderit eos. Sic enim respondes.
units.tr: What you bring from the Epistle to the Galatians has exactly the same force: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be anathema." Therefore the obstinate disturbers of sound doctrine are to be excommunicated. These words do not conflict with our position, for we are not speaking of heretics who spread false doctrine. I wish to give the same answer to the passage from the second Epistle of John. Meanwhile, this passage too does not prove that those are to be excommunicated in the way this matter is being disputed here. The same reasoning applies to the passage from chapter 5 of the same Epistle: "Would that those who trouble us were cut off." For it speaks of false teachers. Again, it does not say, "Gather the elders and cast such men out of your assembly, or hand them over to Satan," but it wishes that they be cut off by God. But let us hear that answer of yours which you give to someone who asks you why he himself did not cut them off. For this is how you reply.

units.la: Quamuis Apostolus pro suo iure fortassis id facere potuerit, nunquā tamen id authoritatis sibi vendicauit: vt qui Corinthios nominatim velit congregari, quorū etiā suffragijs, non autē suo ipsius arbitratu, miser ille Satanæ tradatur. Primū dubitare videris, vtrū Apostol pro suo iure id facere potuerit, cum ais id eū fortassis facere potuisse. Deinde non respondes ad obiectionē. Quærit enim idem ille, cur non eodē modo hos exciderit, quomodo Corinthium Satanæ tradere voluit, alios autem tradidit? Falsū quoq; est, Apostolū hanc authoritatē alijs cōmunicasse, & non priuatam sibi seruasse. Omnes eius Epistolæ, omniaq; scripta ipsius te cōsutat: dū ybiq; eam potestatē sibi à Deo traditā indicat, vt in superioribus, clarè ostendimus. Falsum & illud est, eū voluisse suffragijs Corinthiorum miserum illum tradi Satanæ. Dicit enim, ego decreui. Ego, inquit, absens corpore tanquam præsens, [illegible, ~3 letters] iā concluli, cōstituj, decreui, hunc tradere Satanæ. Ergo mentum est alicuius pietatis: quæ non opprimi, sed accendi potius excitarique debet. Pendet hæc opinio tua ex opinione & iudicio hominum. Taceo iam, quod Deus non præcepit vel Presbyteris vel alijs tale examen. Tertia est plus quàm futilis. Quomodo enim interest Ecclesiæ, vt differam hoc facere cum cæteris, quod me iubsit Deus facere? Miser es, quocunq; te vertas, disputator. Nunquam tam probè intellexi, quod verissimè dixisse Aristotelem nunc experior, de defendentibus Thesim: ταῦτα γὰρ, inquit, ὑπομένοντὰ συμβαίνον, ὡς ἀνθρώπων χρῆσις ἀρχάς.
units.tr: Although the Apostle might perhaps have done this by his own right, he never claimed such authority for himself, so that he would wish the Corinthians to be gathered by name, and that wretched man to be handed over to Satan by their votes and not by his own decision. First, you seem to doubt whether the Apostle could have done this by his own right, since you say he perhaps could have done it. Next, you do not answer the objection. For that same man asks why the Apostle did not likewise cut off these men, in the way he wished the Corinthian to be handed over to Satan, but handed the others over. It is also false that the Apostle shared this authority with others and did not keep it private for himself. All his Epistles and all his writings refute you, since everywhere he declares that this power was given to him by God, as we have clearly shown above. It is also false that he wished that wretched man to be handed over to Satan by the votes of the Corinthians. For he says, "I have decided. I, indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged and resolved to hand this man over to Satan." So this is a matter of some piety, which ought not to be suppressed but rather kindled and stirred up. Your opinion depends on the opinion and judgement of men. I say nothing now of the fact that God commanded neither the elders nor others to make such an examination. It is more than futile as a third point. For how does it concern the Church that I should delay doing this with the others, when God has bidden me to do it? You are wretched, disputant, whichever way you turn. I never understood so well what Aristotle said so truly, about those who defend a thesis, and I now experience it: "For," he says, "you are bound to find that everything follows, while you unwittingly track down the principles" [πάντα γὰρ ὑπομνήσατε συμβαίνειν, ὡς ἐλαθὲς ἰχνεύετε ἀρχάς].

units.la: Cap. IX.
units.tr: Cap. IX.

units.la: Refutatio argumentorum aliorum quorundam pro Excommu- nicatione.
units.tr: Refutation of certain other arguments for excommunication.

units.la: Dfers posthæc argumenta quædam alia pro excommunicatione, quæ nihilò sunt prædictis firmiora. Quæ breuiter etiam expendemus, vt intelligas te tui vbiq; manere simile. Apostolus, inquis, scribit, si quis nō diligit Dominum Iesū Christū, sit Anathema Maranatha. Ergo vult Presbyteros quosdā sedere & iudicare, quinam verè sint pœnitentes, & qui simulent resipiscentiam: vt scilicet illos ad Cœnam admittant, hos arceant. Si hoc est excommunicare, mille locis fundata est excommunicatio vestra. Diligere Christum est seruare mandata Christi, Ioh. 13. & 15. Quisquis ergo dicet: Qui non seruant mandata Christi sunt execrabiles Deo, is excommunicabit hoc modo. Sic excommunicauit Moses, quoties maledictos esse dixit domi, foris, in campo & vbicunq; sunt, quicunq; non seruant totam Legem. Præclarè tibi conuenit hac in parte cum quodam alio, qui generalis excommunicationis formulam nobis à Mose Deuter. 27. propositam affirmauit. At non de hac excommunicatione loquimur: sed de ea, quam erga lapsos Presbyteri quidam in consessu suo per suffragia lata sententia exercent. Hanc tibi noris probandam, quod videlicet à Paulo sit imperata. Apostolus valdè iniquè accusabatur à Pseudoapostolis, qui eū omninò cōtemptibilem reddere satagebāt. Dicit ergo, Qui non diligit &c. acsi diceret: Deus sit iudex veri diligamus Christum, illumq; perdat, qui eum non verè diligit. Hic genuinus est huius loci sensus.
units.tr: You next bring forward certain other arguments for excommunication, which are in no way firmer than the ones above. We shall weigh these briefly too, so that you understand you remain everywhere like yourself. The Apostle, you say, writes: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema maranatha." Therefore he wants certain elders to sit in judgement and decide who are truly penitent and who only feign repentance, so that they may admit the former to the Lord's Supper and keep the latter away. If this is excommunication, your excommunication is founded in a thousand places. To love Christ is to keep Christ's commandments (John 13 and 15). Whoever therefore says, "Those who do not keep Christ's commandments are detestable to God," will be excommunicating in this way. In this way Moses excommunicated, as often as he said that those were cursed who do not keep the whole Law, at home, abroad, in the field, and wherever they are. In this part you agree very well with a certain other man, who asserted that the formula of general excommunication was set before us by Moses (Deut. 27). But we are not speaking of this excommunication. We are speaking of that which certain elders exercise against the fallen, by a sentence passed by votes in their assembly. You should know that this is to be proved as having been commanded by Paul. The Apostle was most unjustly accused by the false apostles, who strove to make him wholly contemptible. He therefore says, "If anyone does not love..." and so on, as if he were saying: "Let God be the judge whether we truly love Christ, and let him perish who does not truly love him." This is the genuine sense of the passage.

units.la: Tantundē valet, quod ex Epistola ad Galat. adfers: Si quis vobis euangelizauerit præter id quod acceptistis, Anathema sit. Ergo excōmunicandi iuris pertinaces sanæ doctrinæ turbatores. Hæc non pugnant cum nostris: qui nō loquimur de hæreticis falsamq; doctrinam plantantibus. Idem ad locum ex 2. Epist. Iohannis respōnsum volo. Interim ne hos quidē probat hic locus ita excommunicasdos esse, vt hic de ista re disputatur. Eadem est ratio alterius loci ex 5. Cap. ciusdē Epist. Vtinā excindātur, qui nos conturbant. Loquitur enim de falsis Doctoribus. Itē, non dicit, congregate Presbyteros, & eijcite tales extra coetum vestrum, siue tradite eos Satanæ: sed optat eos à Deo excindi. Sed audiamus Theologicam illam tuam responsionem, quam ei das, qui ex te quætat, cur non ipse exciderit eos. Sic enim respondes.
units.tr: What you bring from the Epistle to the Galatians has just as little force: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be anathema" (Gal. 1). Therefore the right of excommunication belongs to the stubborn disturbers of sound doctrine. These words do not conflict with our position, for we are not speaking of heretics who plant false doctrine. I want the same answer given to the passage from the second Epistle of John. Meanwhile this passage does not even prove that such people are to be excommunicated in the way that is being disputed here. The same holds for another passage, from the fifth chapter of the same Epistle: "Would that those who trouble us were cut off" (Gal. 5). For he speaks of false teachers. Again, he does not say, "Gather the elders, and cast such men out of your assembly, or deliver them to Satan," but he wishes that they be cut off by God. But let us hear that theological answer of yours, which you give to the one who asks you why he himself did not cut them off. For this is how you reply:

units.la: Quamuis Apostolus pro suo iure fortassis id facere potuerit, nunquā tamen id authoritatis sibi vendicauit: vt qui Corinthios nominatim velit congregari, quorū etiā suffragijs, non autē suo ipsius arbitratu, miser ille Satanæ tradatur. Prior mihi dubitare videris, vtrū Apostol' pro suo iure id facere potuerit, cum ais id eū fortassis facere potuisse. Deinde non respondes ad obiectionē. Quæritenim idem ille, cur non eodē modo hos excideri, quomodo Corinthium Satanæ tradere voluit, alios autem tradidit? Falsū quoq; est, Apostolū hanc authoritatē alijs cōmunicasse, & non priuatam sibi seruasse. Omnes eius Epistolæ, omniaq; scripta ipsius te cōfutant: dū vbiq; eam potestatē sibi à Deo traditā indicat, vt in superioribus, clarē ostendimus. Falsum & illud est, eū voluisse suffragijs Corinthiorum miserum illum tradi Satanæ. Dicit enim, ego decreui. Ego, inquit, absens corpore tanquam præsens, iā conclusi, cōstitui, decreui, hunc tradere Satanæ.
units.tr: "Although the Apostle might perhaps have been able to do this by his own right, he never claimed such authority for himself, so as to wish that the Corinthians be gathered by name, and that by their votes, and not at his own discretion, that wretched man be delivered to Satan." You seem to me to doubt first whether the Apostle could have done this by his own right, since you say he perhaps could have done it. Then you do not answer the objection. For the same questioner asks why he did not likewise have these men cut off, in the way he wished the Corinthian to be delivered to Satan, and yet delivered others. It is also false that the Apostle shared this authority with others and did not keep it private to himself. All his Epistles and all his writings refute you, since everywhere he declares that this power was committed to him by God, as we clearly showed above. It is also false that he wished that wretched man to be delivered to Satan by the votes of the Corinthians. For he says, "I have decided." "I," he says, "absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged and determined and decided to deliver this man to Satan" (1 Cor. 5).

units.la: Ergo non expectabat suffragia Corinthiorum. Quid ergo voluit? Voluit congregata Ecclesia tota, (non tantum Presbyteris quibusdam) & ipsius Spiritu cum virtute Christi sibi concessa hunc Satanæ dedere: vt metum & terrorem incuteret omnibus, ac poenas sceleris commissi ille lueret. Cur ergo non idem Galatis iussit? Respondeo quia Deo non est visum. Apostoli enim non potuerunt vti & quoties vellent edere miracula: nec potuerunt quosuis omni loco & tempore vel affligere vel occidere: sed quando Deo visum fuit vtile, necessarium & salutare.
units.tr: Therefore he did not wait for the votes of the Corinthians. What then did he wish? He wished the whole gathered Church (not merely certain elders), with the power of Christ and his Spirit granted to him, to deliver this man to Satan, so that he might strike fear and terror into all, and that man might pay the penalty for the crime he had committed. Why then did he not order the same for the Galatians? I answer: because it did not seem good to God. For the apostles could not work miracles whenever they wished, nor could they afflict or kill whomever they pleased in every place and at every time. Rather, they did so when it seemed useful, necessary and salutary to God.

units.la: Ergo non respondes ad obiectionem meam de Galatis. Quippe eadem est quæstio, quod ad nostrum attinet propositum, siue quæratur cur eos non exciderit, siue cur non à Sacramentis arceri iusserit. Quinimò tanto magis hæc vrget, quàm illa quæstio, quod facultatem affligendi Deus solis Apostolis, & quibus præterea aliis voluit paucis, concesfit, hanc autem rem tu contendis ab Apostolo omnibus Ecclesijs fuisse imperatam. Qua igitur ratione, quod in omnibus Ecclesijs semper & vbiq; voluit obseruari, ipse neque hic, neq; alibi fecit, aliosue facere iussit? Hic certè Pseudoapostolos optat à Deo excindi, ipse excommunicari non iubet.
units.tr: So you do not answer my objection about the Galatians. Indeed, as far as our purpose is concerned, the question is the same whether one asks why he did not cut them off, or why he did not order them to be kept from the sacraments. Moreover, this question presses harder than the other one, since God granted the power of afflicting only to the apostles and to a few others whom he wished, whereas you maintain that this matter was commanded by the Apostle to all the Churches. By what reasoning, then, did he himself neither here nor elsewhere do, nor order others to do, what he wished to be observed always and everywhere in all the Churches? Here at least he wishes the false apostles to be cut off by God; he does not order that he himself be excommunicated.

units.la: Iubet Apostolus Rom. 16. vt declinemus seu vitemus dissensiones & scandala suscitantes contra doctrinam veram: ex quo tu excommunicationem cupis concludere: sed frustra laboras. Dictum enim hoc est ad omnes & singulos: (quemadmodum illud etiam, quod ex Iohanne sequitur) non ad quosdam Presbyteros. Cauere etiam nobis omnino debemus omnes & singuli à falsis Doctoribus. At vix hoc fieri posse arbitraris, si non præcepta talia omnia ad veltram excommunicandi facultatem referantur. Rationem adfers duplicem: Vna est, quod non sit cuiusuis animadvertere hæreses. Altera, quod priuato cuiusqi arbitrio hunc vel illum defugiendum relinquere, nihil aliud sit, quam schismatibus & offendiculis fauuam aperire. Respondeo nullo praeterea op° esse Presbyterio tali, quale vos fingitis, sed bonis & diligentibus Ministris: qui & auditores suos recte ac diligenter instituant, & a quibus cauendum sit prudenter doceant. Quod offendiculis hoc modo ianuam aperiri putas, tuum est somnium cui nos credere non conuenit: dum aliter Deo visum fuisse cerniimus.
units.tr: The Apostle bids us in Romans 16 to avoid or shun those who cause divisions and offences against the true doctrine. From this you wish to conclude excommunication, but you labour in vain. For this is said to all and to each, as is also what follows in John, and not to certain elders. We must all and each of us altogether beware of false teachers. You think this can hardly be done unless all such precepts are referred to your power of excommunication. You bring two reasons: first, that it is not for everyone to discern heresies; second, that to leave it to each person's private judgement to avoid this or that man is nothing other than to open the door to schisms and stumbling-blocks. I answer that no such eldership as you imagine is needed, but good and diligent ministers, who both properly and carefully instruct their hearers and prudently teach whom they must beware of. As for your view that the door is thus opened to stumbling-blocks, that is your dream, and we ought not to trust it, since we see that God has willed otherwise.

units.la: Iohannes in secunda epistola sua non iubet Presbyteros quosdam in hunc finem ordinatos, licentius viuentes a Sacramentis arcere: sed iubet omnibus & singulis Christianis, vt Christi doctrinam non adferentem, sed huius loco falsam & haereticam spargere volentem, hospicio non recipiant. Hoc contra nos non facit: qui idem semper faciendum omnibus verae pietatis amatoribus iudicauimus.
units.tr: In his second Epistle John does not order certain elders appointed for this purpose to keep from the sacraments those who live too licentiously. Rather, he orders all and each of the Christians not to receive into their house one who brings not the doctrine of Christ but who wishes to spread a false and heretical doctrine in its place. This does not support you against us, for we have always judged that the same should be done by all lovers of true piety.

units.la: Iudas quoque in sua Epistola, nil aliud vult, quam vt operam demus, quo omnes saluos faciamus, quomodo scilicet vnumquemque possumus. Itaque alios monet clementia & humanitate, alios seueritate acrique obiurgatione seruandos: sic videlicet, vt carnalia eorum facta dictaque odio habeamus: de Sacramentis eorumque interdictione, aut Presbyterorum vestrorum potestate & poenis, ne somniauit quidem aliquid Iudas, cum epistolam illam scriberet.
units.tr: Jude too, in his Epistle, wishes nothing other than that we take pains to save all, in whatever way each of us can. Thus he advises some to be saved by mercy and kindness, and others by severity and sharp rebuke: namely, so that we hate their carnal deeds and words. As for the sacraments and their prohibition, or the power and penalties of your elders, Jude did not so much as dream of anything of the kind when he wrote that Epistle.

units.la: Ex omnibus istis luce meridiana clarius est, vestram Excommunicationem neque exemplo niti, neque verbo alio quo firmari in sacris literis inuento: sed merum & purum esse hominum figmentum. De Excommunicatione loquor, vt de principio monui, non Diuina, sed humana: quam videlicet quidam ad hoc delecti Presbyteri exercent erga lapsos, at peccatum & naturae suae corruptionem agnoscentes, confitentes, deplorantes: quantumuis saepe relabantur. Sunt enim tales, non intemperantes, sed incontinentes, vt loquuntur Philosophi: nec destituuntur omni sensu pietatis, tametsi crebro ab affectibus suis victi succumbant cupiditatibus carnis. Verum de hac re aliàs saepe monui: nunc iam superesset considerandum, quibus Presbyterium suum defendas rationibus & scripturis.
units.tr: From all these things it is clearer than midday light that your excommunication rests neither on example nor on any word found in Holy Scripture that might confirm it, but is the pure and simple invention of men. I am speaking of excommunication, as I warned at the beginning, not divine but human: the kind which certain elders chosen for this purpose exercise against the fallen, who nevertheless acknowledge, confess and lament their sin and the corruption of their nature, however often they relapse. For such people are not intemperate, but incontinent, as the philosophers say; nor are they wholly lacking in a sense of piety, even though they often succumb, overcome by the desires of the flesh. But I have often warned about this matter elsewhere. It now remains to consider with what reasons and Scriptures you defend your eldership.

units.la: Libri tertij finis.
units.tr: End of the third book.

units.la: Liber quartus incipit.
units.tr: The fourth book begins.

units.la: CAP. I. De Presbyterio.
units.tr: CHAP. I. Of the Presbytery.

units.la: VOd supra feci in principio huius de Excommunicatione decertationis nunc quoque faciendum mihi duco: vt quale Presbyterium oppugnem, recte intelligatur. Non nego Presbyterium tale, quale apud Iudaeos tempore Christi fuit Hierosolymis: quod frequenter <bl>ἀρχισυνάγωγοι</bl> Euangelistae, & <bl>συνέδριον</bl>, & nunquàm <bl>γερουσία</bl> & <bl>συναγωγὴ</bl> vocare solent. Hoc supra indissolubilibus rationibus legitimum fuisse Magistratum Iudaeorum, & ius gladij possedisse, ostendi: ac deinceps etiam, opportunitate data, iterum ostendam. Non nego etiam Presbyterium, quale in 1. ad Corinth. 6. describitur, vbi Ecclesia Magistratu pio destituitur. Non nego Presbyterium, (Si quis ita velit appellare,) doctorum scilicet hominum Collegium, qui in literis sacris exercitati sint, & de causis Religionis interrogati respondere possint: De quali Presbyterio videtur Ambrosius loqui, cum in vetusta Ecclesia Seniores fuisse dicit, sine quorum consilio nihil fieret. Hoc solum nego & oppugno Presbyterium, nempe Consessum & Senatum quorundam ex Ecclesiae corpore collectum, qui Senatus in hunc finem constitutus sit, vt Excommunicationis, de qua hucusque disputauimus, negocium tractet seu gubernet: ac sententiam ferat, an, qui se poenitere dicunt, ex animo loquantur: & vtrum à Sacramentis arcendi, vel non arcendi videantur. Dicam planius: oppugno tantum Iudicium de moribus, quod hodie Ecclesiasticum nominant, distinctum à Iudicio politici Magistratus. Nempe duas iurisdictiones siue duo discriminata de moribus Iudicia publica & externa nego in vna Repub, esse oportere, cui pius Magistratus à Deo praepositus est. Iam ergo quid contra nos adferas videamus.
units.tr: What I did at the beginning of this dispute about excommunication, I think I must do again here, so that it may be rightly understood what kind of presbytery I am attacking. I do not deny that there was a presbytery such as existed among the Jews at Jerusalem in Christ's time, which the Evangelists often call the archisynagogues [ἀρχισυνάγωγοι] and the council [συνέδριον], and which they never call the senate of elders [γερουσία] or the synagogue [συναγωγὴ]. I have shown above, by unshakeable arguments, that this was the lawful magistracy of the Jews and possessed the right of the sword, and I will show it again later when the opportunity arises. I also do not deny the presbytery described in 1 Corinthians 6, where the Church is deprived of a godly magistrate. I do not deny a presbytery (if anyone wishes to call it that), namely a college of learned men who are practised in the sacred letters and can answer when questioned about matters of religion. It seems that Ambrose speaks of this kind of presbytery when he says that in the ancient Church there were elders, without whose counsel nothing was done. This alone I deny and attack: a presbytery, that is, a council and senate drawn from some part of the body of the Church, set up for this purpose, that it should handle and manage the business of excommunication, of which we have disputed so far, and pass judgement on whether those who say they repent speak from the heart, and whether they seem to be kept from the sacraments or not. To speak more plainly, I attack only that judgement on morals, which people today call ecclesiastical, as distinct from the judgement of the civil magistrate. Indeed I deny that there ought to be two jurisdictions, or two separate public and external courts of judgement concerning morals, in the one commonwealth over which a godly magistrate has been set by God. Let us now see what you bring against us.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Defensio argumentorum contra Presbyterium Excommunicato- rum.
units.tr: A Defence of the Arguments against the Presbytery of Excommunicators.

units.la: IRo argumento nostro primo adfers hoc, quod nos ad probandum protulimus, Apostolum nullos Excommunicauisse, nec alijs tale quid imperasse. Si voluisset Apostolus aliquos per Seniores Excommunicari, proculdubio ordinauisset tales apud Corinthios, vbi minora correxit. At nihil tale praecipit: sed hoc mandat, vt vnusquisque seipsum probet, non autem vt alij alios examinent. Noluit ergo quenquam per vestrum illud Presbyterium Excommunicari. Ad haec tu sic respondes: Corinthi talem aliquem coetum institutum fuisse ambigi non potest. Inquit enim Apostolus, Congregatis vobis in nomine Domini. Et quod conuenire illiusmodi debeant ad dijudicanda talia ex his verbis patet, (quibus eosdem illos compellat, quos iuc ferat vetus fermentum expurgare.) Nonne de iis, qui intus sunt, vos iudicatis? Porrò sui-ipsius explorationem nihil obstare Presbyterij examini & inquisitioni, sic colligimus. Fuerunt harum causarum Iudices constituti, vt ex Apostolo colligimus: Ergo inquisitores: nisi forte velis absque causae cognitione iudicauisse.
units.tr: To our first argument, which we put forward to prove that the Apostle excommunicated no one and ordered no one else to do so, you bring this reply. If the Apostle had wanted some to be excommunicated by the elders, he would surely have set up such a body among the Corinthians, since there he corrected lesser faults. But he orders nothing of the kind. He commands that each one should test himself, not that they should examine one another. So he did not want anyone to be excommunicated by your presbytery. To this you respond: that some such assembly was set up at Corinth cannot be doubted, for the Apostle says, "When you are gathered together in the name of the Lord." And that such men ought to meet to judge such cases is clear from these words, in which he addresses those same people whom he bids to purge out the old leaven. "Do you not judge those who are within?" Moreover, we gather that examining and inquiring by the presbytery is not ruled out by self-examination. The judges of these cases, as we gather from the Apostle, were appointed; therefore they were inquirers, unless you wish to say they gave judgment without hearing the case.
