units.la: Respondes audacter, Paulum Corinthi instituisse illos vestros Seniores. Ergo ante hoc tempus instituerat. Hoc autem quis non videt falsum esse? Quippe accusauisset solos Presbyteros, non totam Ecclesiam. Sed nullo verbo Seniores reprehendit, quasi officium non fecerint, negligentesque inspectatores fuerint. Non accusat etiam, quod ad Sacramenta incestuosum admiserint. Nulla Seniorum illorum, nulla Excommunicationis, nulla
units.tr: You boldly answer that Paul set up your elders at Corinth. Then he had set them up before this time. But who does not see that this is false? For he would have accused only the presbyters, not the whole Church. Yet he does not rebuke the elders in a single word, as if they had failed in their duty and been negligent overseers. Nor does he accuse them of admitting the incestuous man to the sacraments. There is no mention of any such elders, no excommunication,

units.la: Sacramentorum interdictionis ; nulla praecedentis Iudicij, nulla electionis officijque Presbyterorum, nulla vllius rei fit mentio huc spectantis : sed totam Ecclesiam obiurgat, quod non luxerit, vt è medio ille tolleretur. Rogo te, an non ad Seniores vestros pertinere dicitis, vt rixas, simultates, controuersias ac lites inter fratres natas amicè & piè dirimant & componant? At tales in Ecclesia Corinth. aliquos ordinatos fuisse negat Apostolus. Ex quo certè consequitur, nullos fuisse Presbyteros à Paulo institutos ante scriptam hanc epistolam. Liberè incunctanterque dico, mihi videri desipere omnes, quicunque hoc in loco talem consessum institutum contendere audent. Etenim toti Ecclesiae ex aequo mandat, quicquid hic mandat : Seniores ne nominat quidem. Discedis etiam à Praeceptoris tui placitis, qui palam scribit, quod & verum est, Paulum hunc non à delecto numero, sed à toto coetu voluisse Excommunicari, vt vos loqui soletis. Adde quod non iubet eos consulere & per suffragia sententias ferre, vtrum ille tradendus videretur Satanae, an non videretur. Tertiò non iubet eos tradere alium quempiam Satanae : sed sibi eam potestatem reseruat. Quartò non iubet ipsos nefarium illum tradere Satanae : sed iubet vt suam sententiam in congregatione Ecclesiae promulgent.
units.tr: no prohibition from the sacraments, no prior judgment, no election or office of presbyters, no mention of anything bearing on this. Instead he rebukes the whole Church for not having seen to it that the man was removed from their midst. I ask you: do you not say that it belongs to your elders to settle and compose, kindly and piously, the quarrels, rivalries, disputes and lawsuits that arise among brethren? Yet the Apostle denies that any such men had been appointed in the Church at Corinth. From this it certainly follows that no presbyters had been appointed by Paul before this letter was written. I say freely and without hesitation that all those who dare to contend in this passage that such a council was instituted seem to me to be out of their minds. For what he commands here, he commands to the whole Church alike; he does not even name elders. You also depart from the opinions of your own teacher, who plainly writes, and rightly, that Paul wished this man to be excommunicated not by a select number but by the whole assembly, as you yourselves are wont to say. Add that he does not bid them consult and pass sentence by votes whether that man ought to be handed over to Satan or not. Thirdly, he does not order them to hand anyone else over to Satan, but reserves that power to himself. Fourthly, he does not order them to deliver that wicked man to Satan, but orders them to declare their sentence in the assembly of the Church.

units.la: Si vnquam probabilem rationem adduxeris, qua ostendas verba haec, Ego decreui hunc hominem vobis & spiritu meo cum virtute Christi congregatis Satanae tradere, idem significare, quod haec aut similia denotant : Eligite ex vestro coetu Presbyteros, qui sint morum Censores: & quos indignos putabunt Sacramentorum participatione, ab eisdem arceant : Si, inquam, probabilis illa idem notare, quod haec nobis indicant, paratus sum quiduis pati. Ergo cum neque antea instituerit Presbyterium vestrum neque nunc tale quid praeceperit, neque postea doceri possit instituisse, qui non te pudet affirmare, eum in his verbis aliquid huiusmodi praecepisse? At de ijsdem dicit, ais, Nonne de ijs, qui intus sunt, iudicatis? Concedo de eisdem loqui, cum de tota loquatur Ecclesia: sed nego eum de tali iudicio loqui. Iusserat Apostolus facinorosos vitare: quod cum ipsi de Ethnicis etiam intellexissent, sine quorum commercio viuere tunc non poterant, respondet eis Apostolus, se non intelligere Ethnicos, sed nominatos fratres. Addit illos habituros Iudicem Deum: ipsos autem suos fratres iudicare debere digni sint an indigni, quibuscum ipsi familiariter viuerent. Summa est, loquitur de omnibus & singulis Ecclesiae membris, non de Presbyteris: & de iudicio quo singuli singulorum vitam iudicant, non de publico aliquo iudicio Presbyterij.
units.tr: If you ever bring a plausible reason to show that these words, "I have decided to deliver this man to Satan, when you are gathered together with my spirit and the power of Christ," mean the same as the following: choose from your assembly presbyters who are to be censors of morals, and let them keep away from the sacraments those whom they judge unworthy to share them, if, I say, that plausible reason indicates the same as these words do for us, I am ready to suffer anything. Since, then, he neither set up your presbytery earlier nor commanded anything of the kind now, and it cannot be shown that he set it up afterwards, why are you not ashamed to assert that in these words he commanded something of this sort? But you say he speaks of the same people: "Do you not judge those who are within?" I grant that he speaks of the same people, since he speaks of the whole Church; but I deny that he speaks of such a judgment. The Apostle had ordered them to avoid wicked men. When they understood this even of the heathen, without whose company they could not then live, the Apostle answers that he did not mean the heathen, but those called brethren. He adds that those outside will have God as judge, but that they themselves ought to judge their brethren, whether they are worthy or unworthy of those with whom they live on familiar terms. In short, he speaks of all and each of the members of the Church, not of the presbyters; and of the judgment by which individuals judge the lives of individuals, not of some public judgment of a presbytery.

units.la: Concedo adultum, si baptizandus esset, examinandum prius fuisse, an doctrinam intelligeret, eidemque ex animo assentiret. Concedo etiam nunc vtile esse dum infantes adhuc baptizamur, vt adolescétia non prius admittatur ad coenam, quàm cognitum sit mysteria haec ab ipsis rectè percipi. At nego vel propter hoc vel propter illud Deum iussisse Presbyterium vestrum instituere. Quod cum ipse videaris affirmare, dum non in omnes dicis inquirere oportere Presbyterium, sed in eos duntaxat, qui vt rei delati sunt flagiciosę vitae, pluribus docere iam non volo. Hoc te probare decebat, Deum alicubi praecepisse, ne qui ex ijs, qui flagicium admiserunt, ad perceptionem Sacramentorum admittantur, priusquam à certis Presbyteris ad hanc rem delectis idonei iudicati sunt. Dum hoc non probabis, causam tuam infelicissimè ages. Nam Paulus ad Thessal. separate vos ab hominibus inordinatè viuentibus, eosque non obiurgate, vt hostes, sed admonete, vt fratres.
units.tr: I grant that if an adult were to be baptized, he should first be examined as to whether he understood the doctrine and agreed to it from the heart. I grant too that it is useful even now, while infants are still being baptized, that a young person is not admitted to the Lord's Supper until it is known that he rightly grasps these mysteries. But I deny that God commanded your presbytery to be set up for either this purpose or that. You seem yourself to affirm this, since you say that the presbytery ought to inquire not into everyone, but only into those who have been accused of a scandalous life. I do not wish to teach more on this point now. You ought to have proved that God has somewhere commanded that those who have committed a scandal should not be admitted to receiving the sacraments until they have been judged fit by certain presbyters chosen for this task. Unless you prove this, you will plead your cause most unhappily. For Paul to the Thessalonians says: separate yourselves from those who live disorderly, and rebuke them not as enemies but admonish them as brethren.

units.la: Argumentum secundum facis ex ijs, quae de Israeliticae politiae statu dixi: quod argumentum non debilitabit solum Presbyterium vestrum, sicut antecedens, verumetiam prorsus cuertet. Est autem tale. Rempublicam instituere in hoc mundo aeque prudenter nullus potest, atque Deus suo populo instituit: quod & per se notum est, & à Deo ipso affirmatum Deuter. 4. Quocirca optimè sapientissimeque constituta est ea Respub. quaecunque ad Regulam Diuinae proxime accesserit, quantum cuiusque circumstantiae patiuntur. At in Repub. Iudaeorum duae discriminatae iurisdictiones, siue duo distincta iudicia de moribus publica nunquam fuerunt: sed uni Magistratui politico totum hoc tributum est. Ergo ne nunc quidem necessarium est, ut in Repub. Christiana separatae sint iurisdictiones siue separata iudicia publica de moribus, eo videlicet modo, quo vel Pontifex primum, vel deinde etiam vos Ecclesiastica iudicia morum a politicis distinguitis. Tu vero quid ad haec? Nugas pro more tuo promis.
units.tr: You make a second argument from what I said about the state of the Israelite commonwealth. This argument will not only weaken your presbytery, as the previous one did, but will utterly overthrow it. It runs thus. No one can set up a commonwealth in this world as wisely as God set one up for his people; this is both self-evident and affirmed by God himself in Deuteronomy 4. Therefore that commonwealth is best and most wisely constituted which comes nearest to the divine rule, as far as the circumstances of each place allow. But in the commonwealth of the Jews, two separate jurisdictions, or two distinct public courts for morals, never existed; rather, the whole of this task was assigned to the one civil magistrate. Therefore it is not necessary even now that, in a Christian commonwealth, there should be separate jurisdictions or separate public courts for morals, in that way in which either the Pontiffs at first, or afterwards you also, distinguish ecclesiastical courts of morals from civil ones. But what do you say to this? You offer trifles, as is your custom.

units.la: Dicis Mosen, Iosuam, Dauidem, Salomonem, alios nihil eorum egisse, quae ad Aharonem spectabant. Proinde distincta fuisse munera Sacerdotum a Regia & ciuili potestate. Ego dixi, antequam Deus sibi elegisset Aharonem & filios eius in Sacerdotes, non fuisse sic distincta haec munera, quin in eundem utrumque caderet. Certe Moses, ut caeteros mittam, Aharonis munera obijt Leuit. 8. At post hoc tempus non licuit vlli amplius; Propterea merito castigati sunt Saul & Vzias. Sed quorsum haec? Ego de Iudicijs publicis in quibus aliquis accusatur & damnatur ut sceleris, & pro delicti gravitate punitur, quaero: quod ipse quoque dissimulare non es ausus. Ergo quid hic dicas notemus.
units.tr: You say that Moses, Joshua, David, Solomon and others did none of those things which pertained to Aaron, and that therefore the priestly offices were distinct from the royal and civil power. I said that before God chose Aaron and his sons as priests, these offices were not so distinct that both did not fall on the same man. Certainly Moses, to pass over the others, performed Aaron's duties (Lev. 8). But after this time it was no longer permitted to anyone; therefore Saul and Uzziah were rightly punished. But to what purpose are these things? I am asking about public courts in which someone is accused and condemned of a crime and is punished according to the gravity of the offence, a matter which you yourself have not dared to dissemble. Let us therefore note what you say here.

units.la: Moses, inquis, Soceri sui consilio scorsum iudicia ciuilia constituit, Exod. 18. alibi autem, quae propria iudicia Sacerdotum erant, describit. Duplicem hunc ordinem Iehosaphat etiam obseruauit, oppidatim Iudices politicos seorsum constituens: Hierosolymis vero ex Leuitis, Sacerdotibus, & capitibus patrum aliquos collocauit ad iudicium & causam Domini. Hoc dicimus illud esse Synedrion Ecclesiasticum ab alijs ciuilibus distinctum: ad cuius exemplar Apostoli postea Collegium instituerunt. Haec tu.
units.tr: "Moses," you say, "by the counsel of his father-in-law set up civil courts apart (Exod. 18), and elsewhere he describes the courts that were properly those of the priests. Jehoshaphat also observed this double order, setting up civil judges separately in the towns, but at Jerusalem he placed some of the Levites, priests and heads of the fathers' houses for judgment and the cause of the Lord." We say that this was the ecclesiastical Sanhedrin, distinct from the other civil courts, after whose pattern the Apostles later instituted their college. Thus far you.

units.la: Principio locum a te peto, in quo Moses peculiare Sacerdotum iudicium de moribus & sceleribus iudicandis & puniendis constituerit. Scio multis in locis Aharoni praescribi quid facere ipsum aliosque Sacerdotes & Leuitas Dominus voluerit: At mandatam ei distinctam iurisdictionem, id est, potestatem fuisse datam puniendi improbos per Iudicium siue Synedrium Ecclesiasticum, nullus in sempiternum nedum Beza demonstrabit. Quàm frigidum est, quod Iosaphat hoc discrimen ponere dicis? Primum dicitur in textu.2.par.Iip.19. pium hunc Regem in omnibus oppidis munitis constituisse Iudices, eosque admonuisse officij sui: vt se Domino indicare meminissent. Deinde scribitur idem quoque Hierosolymis fecisse. Tertiò ex quibus constituerit illos Iudices exponitur, nempè ex Leuitis, Sacerdotibus & familiarum Principibus. Quartò additur, ad quam rem delecti constitutique sint, videlicet ad Iudicium Domini & ad causam. Addit mox, eos iudicare & cognoscere debere praeterea OMNEM causam, quae venerit ad eos de fratribus suis, qui habitant in vrbibus Regni Iosaphat, inter sanguinem & sanguinem, inter Legem & Praeceptum, statuta & iudicia &c. Tandem concludens ait: summus Sacerdos Amazias omnibus causis Domini: Zebadias autem Dux Iudae cunctis negocijs Regiis praesidebunt.
units.tr: At the outset I ask you to name a passage in which Moses established a special judgment of the priests for judging and punishing morals and crimes. I know that in many places the Lord prescribes to Aaron and the other priests and Levites what he wished them to do. But that Aaron was given a separate jurisdiction, that is, the power to punish wicked men through a judgment or Sanhedrin of the Church, no one, Beza included, will ever demonstrate. How feeble is your claim that Jehoshaphat draws this distinction! First, the text of 2 Par. 19 says that this pious king appointed judges in all the fortified towns and reminded them of their duty, that they should remember to judge for the Lord. Then it is written that he did the same at Jerusalem. Third, it is explained from whom he appointed those judges: namely, from the Levites, the priests and the heads of families. Fourth, it is added for what purpose they were chosen and appointed: namely, for the judgment of the Lord and for the cause. Immediately he adds that they must judge and hear ALL the cases that come before them concerning their brothers who live in the cities of Jehoshaphat's kingdom, between blood and blood, between law and command, statutes and judgments, and so on. Finally, concluding, he says: Amariah the chief priest shall preside over all the causes of the Lord, and Zebadiah the leader of Judah over all the king's affairs.

units.la: Quis non videat hoc in loco Synedrium Hierosolymitanum esse Magistratum Politicum? Etenim Senatus, in quo causae omnes, capitales & ciuiles diiudicantur, quique punire iubet plagis, multa, seruitute, gladio, igne &c. Politicus est. Nam si vera vos hucusque scripsistis & dixistis, (quod etiam post versus non ita multos in hoc scripto repetis) nec debet nec potest Synedrium vestrum inter sanguinem & sanguinem; inter Legem & Praeceptum, inter Statuta & Iudicia iudicare: id est, non potest, vt hic Senatus facere iubetur, de qualibet causa cognoscere. Qui caput. 17. Deuter. cum hoc loco conferet, de partenulla dubitabit.
units.tr: Who does not see that in this passage the Sanhedrin of Jerusalem is a political magistracy? For a senate in which all cases, capital and civil, are judged, and which orders punishment by blows, fines, servitude, the sword, fire and so on, is political. For if what you have written and said so far is true (and you repeat it, not many verses later, in this writing), your Sanhedrin neither ought nor is able to judge between blood and blood, between law and command, between statutes and judgments: that is, it cannot, as this senate is ordered to do here, take cognizance of every kind of cause. Anyone who compares this passage with Deuteronomy 17 will have little doubt on the matter.

units.la: Duo tamen monere minus exercitatos in sacris literis volo. Primum est, causam Domini hoc in loco, & vbicunq; de iudiciis sermo habetur, non religiosam duntaxat significare, verumetiam alias in iudicio propositas, praesertim vero viduarum & pupillorum, adeoque oppressorum causas, quorum se Deus passim promittit vindicem fore: de qua re paulo post copiosius agemus. Alterum est, Leuitas & Sacerdotes non minus fuisse lectos in consortium Iudicum, quàm alios quoslibet: quod cum tu quoque recte scripseris in opere quodam tuo, non habeo necesse pluribus probare. Nota sunt, quae de vrbibus refugij, in quibus soli Leuitae Magistratum gerebant, biblia tradunt. Opus erat hominibus in Lege Dei exercitatis, vt secundum praescriptum Dei recte iudicaretur: quomodo hodie Sapientes Magistratus Iurisconsultos Iudiciis suis praeficiunt. Verum hoc interest inter nostros & Iudaeorum Iureperitos: quod nostri suas Leges seorsum descriptas habent à sacris literis: Iudaei autem omnes suas Leges, ad cultum Dei, ad ceremonias, ad politiam, ad Iudicia spectantes, omnes, inquam, in iisdem libris interspersas habebant. Quamobrem necesse erat Sacerdotes, quibus munus docendi impositum praecipuè fuerat, prae caeteris statuta & iudicia Dei nouisse. Deinde Leuitas, quibus peculiariter commissa erat cura Templi, quíque Sacerdotibus adesse alias cogebantur. Ex his fere Praefecti creabantur Regionum, vt ex 1. Paral. 26. cap. clarè perspicimus. Hanc ob rem Sacerdotes & Leuitae cum aliis familiarum Principibus legebantur.
units.tr: Yet I want to warn those who are less practised in the sacred letters of two things. The first is that the cause of the Lord in this passage, and wherever judgments are spoken of, means not merely a religious cause but also other causes brought before the court, especially those of widows and orphans, and thus of the oppressed, whose avenger God everywhere promises to be. We shall deal with this matter more fully a little later. The second is that Levites and priests were chosen no less than any others to sit as judges. You yourself have rightly written this in a certain work of yours, so I need not prove it at length. The things the Bible relates about the cities of refuge, in which only Levites held the magistracy, are well known. Men trained in the law of God were needed so that judgment might be rightly given according to God's prescription, just as today the wise set lawyers over their courts. But there is this difference between our jurists and the Jewish experts in law: our laws are written down separately from Holy Scripture, whereas the Jews had all their laws, those concerning the worship of God, the ceremonies, the polity and the judgments, I say all of them, scattered through the same books. Therefore it was necessary that the priests, to whom the office of teaching had been especially entrusted, should above all others know the statutes and judgments of God. Next came the Levites, to whom the care of the Temple had been particularly committed, and who were otherwise required to attend the priests. From these were usually drawn the prefects of the regions, as we see clearly from 1 Par. 26. For this reason the priests and Levites were chosen along with the other heads of families.

units.la: Constat ego, sanctum hunc Regem non instituisse hoc in loco Presbyterium seu iudicium Ecclesiasticum, sed Synedrium ordinauisse summum illud, ad quod ex tota Iudaea omnes causae deferebantur, quae in priusquam oppidorum Iudiciis explicari nequiuerant: quemadmodum Deus praeceperat Deuter. 17: Si quid latuerit te in Iudicio, inquit Moses, inter sanguinem & sanguinem, inter causam & causam, inter plagam & plagam, in rixarum rebus intra portas tuas, tunc surges & ascendes ad locum, quem elegerit Deus tuus: & venies ad Sacerdotes, Leuitas, & Iudicem, qui tunc erit. Haec iisdem ipsdem propemodum verbis repetiuit Scriptor lib. Paralip. in historia praesente. Dicit enim primo Regem constituisse ludices ex Sacerdotibus, Leuitis, & Principibus familiarum: ad quos Moses iubet ascendere. Dicit eosdem debere O M N E S causas, quae ex omnibus vrbibus ad ipsos deferantur, cognoscere & iudicare. Exponit mox quas causas intelligat, dicens, inter sanguinem & sanguinem, inter Legem & Praeceptum, statuta & Iudicia. Haec Moses ita expressit: inter sanguinem & sanguinem, causam & causam, plagam & plagam, &c. Quae cum ita sint clara, aperta, certa, vt negari a nullo possint, miror equidem qui tu ausus fueris ad tuum Presbyterium detorquere.
units.tr: I maintain that this holy king did not establish in this passage a presbytery or ecclesiastical judgment, but ordained that supreme court to which all causes from the whole of Judea were referred, which could not be settled in the courts of the towns. This is just as God had commanded in Deuteronomy 17: "If anything shall be hidden from you in judgment," says Moses, "between blood and blood, between cause and cause, between plague and plague, in matters of strife within your gates, then you shall rise up and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose, and you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and the judge who shall then be." The writer of the Book of Chronicles, in the historical passage, repeated these almost in the same words. For he says first that the king appointed judges from the priests, the Levites and the heads of families, to whom Moses bids them go up. He says that these same men must hear and judge ALL the causes that are referred to them from all the towns. He then explains which causes he means, saying: between blood and blood, between law and command, statutes and judgments. Moses expressed this thus: between blood and blood, cause and cause, plague and plague, etc. Since these things are so clear, open and certain that no one can deny them, I am indeed amazed at how you have dared to twist them to suit your presbytery.

units.la: Quod deinceps multis verbis exponis, Magistratum curam habere ἐπιστατοῦντα, ac operam dare debere, vt ossicium suum singuli faciant, Ministeriumque rite ex verbo Dei constituatur & defendatur, recte quidem a te dicitur: at causam tuam non reddit meliorem. Oportet enim te ostendere, Presbyterij vestri iurisdictionem partem esse Ministerij. Quod nisi probaueritis, frustra litigabitis. Sed velim ex te audire, quomodo Magistratus suturus sit ἐπιστατοῦντες simul & subiectus imperio Presbyterorum? Etenim potestati ἐπιστατοῦσαι subiectae sunt caeterae facultates, quibus ipsa imperat. Vestri autem Presbyteri Magistratum suum in ordinem redigunt, & parere nolentem iudicio publico condemnant, poenaq; afficiunt. Architectonicus ergo erit, sicut fuit sub Pontificibus Romanis: hoc est, minister vester & exsecutor.
units.tr: What you then explain at length, that the magistrate should have the care of the ἐπιστατοῦντα [overseeing], and should take pains that each one performs his office, and that the ministry is rightly constituted and defended according to the Word of God, you say rightly enough; but it does not make your cause any better. For you must show that the jurisdiction of your presbytery is a part of the ministry. Unless you prove this, you will be contending in vain. But I should like to hear from you how the magistrate is to be at once ἐπιστατοῦντες [overseer] and subject to the rule of the presbyters. For all other powers are subject to the power that presides, and it commands them. Yet your presbyters reduce the magistrate to their order, and condemn him, if he refuses to obey, by public judgment, and inflict punishment on him. So he will be an architectonic [governing] power, just as he was under the Roman pontiffs: that is, your minister and executor.

units.la: Quod addis, non licere Magistratui, re ita postulante, docere & Sacramenta administrare (si modo per negotia possit vtrique muneri sufficere) id verum non est. Nusquam enim Deus vetuit. In veteri Testamento si licuit vni vtrunque munus administrare, cur non & nunc liceat? Nota est historia Heli & Samuelis. Non moror, quod mox dicis, Mosen suis Tribunal ab Aaronico distinxisse: (Aaroni nullam iurisdictionem nullumue Tribunal concedit scriptura scorsum) cum nusquam prohibuerit Sacerdotibus in Tribunali politico sedere siue Magistratum gerere. Imò in Samuele probauit, cum dicat Deus,non Samuelem,sed se contemptum,quando pro eo & filijs eius Regem sibi constituì petiuerunt 1. Sam. 8. Post reditum ex captiuitate voluit Deus Sacerdotes etiam iudicare populum, vt in 44. cap. Ezech. legimus. At verò cum Magistratus nostri hodie praestare per se ipsos vtrumq; non possint, debent per alios Ministerium curare.
units.tr: As for your addition, that it is not lawful for the magistrate, when the situation demands it, to teach and administer the sacraments (if only his business allows him to suffice for both duties), this is not true. For God has nowhere forbidden it. If in the Old Testament it was lawful for one man to perform both offices, why should it not be lawful now? The story of Eli and Samuel is well known. I do not dwell on what you say next, that Moses distinguished his own tribunal from the Aaronic one (Scripture nowhere grants Aaron a separate jurisdiction or tribunal), since it nowhere forbids priests to sit in a political tribunal or to hold the magistracy. Indeed, it proved this in the case of Samuel, when God says that it was not Samuel but himself who was despised, when they asked for a king to be set over them in place of him and his sons (1 Sam. 8). After the return from captivity God willed that the priests also should judge the people, as we read in Ezekiel 44. But since our magistrates today cannot themselves perform both offices, they must see to the ministry through others.

units.la: Sed nec illud verum est, quod hoc loco praeterea dicis, cuius sit docere & Sacramenta dispensare, eius quoque necessario esse de doctrinae & Sacramentorum contemptoribus ex verbo Dei cognoscere & dijudicare: hoc, inquam, salsissimum est, si eousq; extendas hanc dijudicationem, vt potestatem comprehendere putes puniendi vel à Sacramentis abigendi participare cupientes. Hoc est, quod toties petimus vt probetis: vos autem praeter fas & æquum tanquam probatum subinde vobis sumitis. Adde, quod argumentum tuum, si tam esset verum, quam est falsum, hoc solum probaret, solos Ministros verbi potestatem hanc obtinere. Vbi igitur Presbyterium vestrum manebit? Vultis enim alios quoque vnà cum Ministris in hoc Collegio Iudices esse: quomodo praeter Sacerdotes à Iosaphat concedis familiarum Principes allectos cum Leuitis. Puto equidem te, cum ista scriberes, parum fuisse memorem eorum, quae in praefatione in nouum Testamentum ad principes Galliae scripsisti. Quomodo cū ista tum illa cōsonare ostendes? Quae ad verba ligandi & soluendi attinent, supra fusè & solidè sunt explanata. Nunc tuae rationes expendendae veniunt,
units.tr: Nor is it true what you add in this passage, that whoever has the duty of teaching and dispensing the sacraments must necessarily also have the duty of recognizing and judging, from the Word of God, the despisers of doctrine and of the sacraments. This, I say, is most absurd, if you extend this judging so far that you think it includes the power of punishing those who desire to share in the sacraments, or of driving them away. This is precisely what we have so often asked you to prove, and you keep presuming it as proved, contrary to right and justice. Add to this that your argument, even if it were as true as it is false, would prove only this: that the power in question belongs to the ministers of the Word alone. Where, then, will your presbytery remain? For you want others also to be judges in this college along with the ministers, just as you concede that the heads of families were chosen with the Levites in addition to the priests by Jehoshaphat. I suppose that when you wrote these things you were rather forgetful of what you wrote in the preface to the New Testament addressed to the princes of France. How will you show that both this and that agree? As for the matters concerning the words of binding and loosing, they have been explained at length and solidly above. Now it is time to weigh your arguments.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Confutatio argumentorum, quibus Presbyterium suum quidam afferiput ant.
units.tr: Refutation of the arguments with which certain men support their presbytery.

units.la: Ofes, inquis, tam manifestè duplicem illam administrationem discernit, vt penè incredibile sit quenquam, qui hoc non videat, inueniri posse, Deinde hoc probaturus adducis testimonium ex cap. 10. Leuit. vbi scriptum est, Aaronem cum suis filijs debere discernere inter sanctum & profanum, inter mundũ & immundum: & præterea docere Israelitas præcepta mandataque Dei. Quænam hæc est, obsecro te, consecutio: Deus iussit Sacerdotes docere populum distinguere munda ab immundis, atque insuper docere legem Dei: Ergo iusssit constitui Collegium Senatorum, qui distinctam exerceant iurisdictionem de moribus à potestate politici Magistratus? Argumentum tale est, quale prius illud fuit. Deus iussit verbi sui Ministros populum docere & Sacramenta dispensare: Ergo iussit Presbyterium eligi, quod corruptis præditos moribus à Sacramentis per solenne iudicium abstirreat: nec ante ad eadem rursum admittat, quam dignos & idoneos censuerit. Cum iubet eos discernere inter mundum & immundum, hoc iubet, vt populum doceant ex lege, quæ sint munda & immunda: quæ sacra sint & quæ profana: non instituit Iudicium publicum siue Senatum aliquem Presbyterorum, qui iudicia de moribus publicè exerceat. Verum esse, quod dico, manifestissimis verbis probat Ezech. cap. 44. vbi officium & munus Sacerdotum ex Mose repetit.
units.tr: You show, you say, that this double administration is distinguished so clearly that it is almost incredible that anyone who does not see it can be found. Then, to prove this, you cite a passage from Leviticus chapter 10, where it is written that Aaron with his sons must distinguish between holy and profane, between clean and unclean, and moreover teach the Israelites the precepts and commandments of God. What sort of inference is this, I beg you? God commanded the priests to teach the people to distinguish clean things from unclean, and in addition to teach the law of God. Therefore he commanded that a college of senators be set up, who should exercise a separate jurisdiction over morals, apart from the power of the civil magistrate? The argument is of the same kind as the earlier one. God commanded the ministers of his Word to teach the people and dispense the sacraments. Therefore he commanded that an elder board be chosen, which by solemn judgment should exclude from the sacraments those endowed with corrupt morals, and should not readmit them to the same until it judged them worthy and fit. When he commands them to distinguish between clean and unclean, he commands them to teach the people from the law what is clean and unclean, what is holy and what is profane; he does not institute a public court or any senate of elders that would exercise public judgment over morals. That what I say is true, Ezekiel chapter 44 proves in the plainest words, where he repeats the office and duty of the priests from Moses.

units.la: Plurimum equidem miratus sum, cum te apud Mosen testimonia seu institutione vestri Presbyterij quærere vidi. Nam tui fermè omnes Synedriũ de quo Christ' locutus sit, post captiuitatè Babylonicā incepisse demũ aiunt: alij tunc natũ asserunt, cum Iudæis à Romanis erept' fuit gladius. Quod.n. gladium ante habuerit, nunquã illis in mentẽ venit negare. Penes Dauidem, Salomonẽ & antea apud Mosen & Iosuam non dubitant affirmare omnẽ potestatẽ coercendorũ vicioru fuisse. Probant sententiã suã Augustini testimonio in 39. quæst. super Deut, affirmantis hoc agere nunc in Ecclesia excomunicationẽ, quod tunc agebat interfectio. Simile quippiã in lib. de fide & operib. cap. 2. affirmat. Hinc alij præceptũ peculiare in veteri Testamento de Excõm. nullum exstate concedũt: sed hoc in illo de prauis interficiendis cõtineri affirmât. Tu ergo, vt video longè oculatior fuisti hisce omnib'. Valde sunt multa, quæ hic reprehendi possent. Primo quidem præter vnum te nullus (puto) est, qui scribat Mosen Leuit. 10. & Deuter. 17. de eisdem personis & eisdem rebus eodémque officio locutum fuisse. Etenim in priore loco de solis Sacerdotibus loquitur: & quod eorum ossicium sit, qui Sacerdotio funguntur, declarat. In posteriore loco de Iudicibus loquitur: & quod horum munus sit exponit. Tu autem affirmas Mosen hoc loco longius progredi, & Sacerdotum iurisdictionem, de qua Leuit. 10. egerit, pluribus exponere. Atque omnia συνεδρικὰ esse dicis: cum sola haec ad Ecclesiasticum Synedrium pertinuisse contendas. Quæ quam sint falsa, nullus eruditus non videt.
units.tr: I was greatly surprised when I saw you seeking the testimony and institution of your presbytery in Moses. For almost all your people say that the Sanhedrin of which Christ spoke only began after the Babylonian captivity; others say it arose when the sword was taken from the Jews by the Romans. As for having the sword before that, no one ever thought to deny it. They do not hesitate to affirm that under David, Solomon, and earlier under Moses and Joshua, all power of restraining vices was lodged in the magistrate. They support their opinion by the testimony of Augustine in his Questions on Deuteronomy, question 39, where he affirms that what excommunication does now in the Church, killing used to do then. He affirms something similar in his book On Faith and Works, chapter 2. Hence others concede that there is no special precept in the Old Testament about excommunication, but maintain that it is contained in the command to put wicked men to death. You, then, as I see, were far more keen-sighted than all of these. There are very many things here that could be criticised. First, apart from yourself I think there is no one who writes that Moses in Leviticus 10 and Deuteronomy 17 spoke of the same persons, the same matters, and the same office. For in the former passage he speaks only of the priests and declares what the office of those who discharge the priesthood is. In the latter he speaks of judges and sets out what their duty is. But you affirm that Moses in this place goes further, and explains at greater length the jurisdiction of the priests, of which he treated in Leviticus 10. And you say that all these things are synedrial [συνεδρικά], when you contend that these alone pertained to an ecclesiastical synedrion. How false these claims are, no learned man fails to see.

units.la: Secundo dicis, mentionem fieri Deuter. 17. sanguinis, causæ, plagarum, rixarum, &c. non quod de facto, sed quod de iure controuerso ex tabulis sacris responderit Synedrium: Iudicem vero, id est, supremum gubernatorem cum suo Synedrio (Huius enim Synedriū facis diuersum à Synedrio Sacerdotum) de facto sic iudicasse, quomodo de iure ab illo fuerit responsum. Ego contra dico, siue de facto siue de iure responderit, sententias Capitales dixisse, & de controuersijs omnibus sic pronunciasse, vt à sententia appellare nulli licuerit. Vos autem negatis in Conciliabulo vestro lites eiuscemodi decidendas esse: cum sint merè ac purè politicæ, sicut hodie politica distinguitis ab Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: Second, you say that Deuteronomy 17 mentions blood, cause, plagues, quarrels, and so on, not because the synedrion actually decided these, but because it answered from the sacred tablets on the law in dispute; while the judge, that is the supreme governor, with his own synedrion (for you make this synedrion different from the synedrion of the priests), judged the matter in fact as it had been answered by the other in law. I contend on the contrary that, whether they answered in fact or in law, they pronounced capital sentences and gave judgment on all controversies in such a way that no one was permitted to appeal from the sentence. But you deny that disputes of this kind are to be settled in your conventicle, since they are purely and simply political, just as today you distinguish political matters from ecclesiastical ones.

units.la: Tertiò dicis, ab Ecclesiastico hoc Synedrio licuisse ad iudicis Synedrium prouocare: quod non minus falsum esse textus docet. Etenim Moses aperte ait, interficiendum esse illum, qui vel Sacerdotis sententiæ vel Iudicis assentire nolet. Non ergo liberum facit ab illo ad hunc prouocare.
units.tr: Third, you say that from this ecclesiastical synedrion it was permitted to appeal to the judge's synedrion; but the text shows this to be no less false. For Moses plainly says that he must be put to death who refuses to assent either to the sentence of the priest or to that of the judge. Therefore he does not make it free to appeal from the one to the other.

units.la: Quartò cum dicis, Sacerdotem primo de iure respondisse, Iudicem postea pronunciasse, vt à neutro appellare liceret, prioribus contradicis: & Iudicem Synedrij illius carnificem ac ministrum facis: quod fere solum aliqui expetere videntur. Quid enim aliud est, cum quæritur, vtrum hic homo poenam mortis meruerit an non meruerit, si quis meruisse respondeat, quam capitis damnare? An hoc politicum non est, quia gladium nullus Iudicum sua manu stringit? At sententia sua stringere alios iubet. Quod si politicum hoc non est, nulla nunc in Imperio politica iudicia habemus, exceptis admodum paucis.
units.tr: Fourth, when you say that the priest first gave the answer in law and the judge afterwards pronounced sentence, so that it was lawful to appeal from neither, you contradict what went before, and you make the judge of that synedrion the executioner and minister of the other, which only a few people seem to desire. For what else is it, when the question is whether this man has deserved the penalty of death or not, and someone answers that he has deserved it, than to condemn him to the axe? Is this not political because no judge draws the sword with his own hand? Yet by his sentence he orders others to draw it. And if this is not political, we have no political courts at all in the Empire today, except for a very few.

units.la: Quinto, falsum est duo Synedria distincta vel à Mose 17. Deuter. vel à Iosaphato 2. Paralipom. 19. describi: quod etsi ex textu patere cuiuis poterit, non grauabor tamen declarare. Primum igitur hoc, ut confessum pono, (Tu enim dicis idem) sanctum hunc Regem nihil instituisse huc pertinens, nisi quod Deus per Mosen instituit imperavit. Constituit ergo Iudices in omnium urbium portis, sicuti Moses Deuter. 16. praecepit. Hoc facto, constituit etiam summum illud Synedrium, ad quod provocare iniuriam sibi fieri existimantibus fas erat: cuiusque sententiam Iudices alij in causis obscuris sciscitari cogebantur, ut ex 17. cap. Deuter. liquet. Ergo sive hoc Iudicium concedatur eodem modo ius dixisse Hierosolymitanis, quomodo per oppida alia Iudices inhabitatoribus eorum ius dixerunt, sive de appellationum causis duntaxat cognouisse, sive utrunque exercuisse (Quod Graeca versio, & Ioseph. lib. 9. Antiquit. cap. 1. ipsa denique res testificantur) nostra nihil hic refert. Quoniam nihilominus manet Senatus vere politicus. Etenim quaecunque in singulis oppidis natae fuissent lites, rixae, & controversiae, si ab eius loci Magistratu non potuissent explicari, Hierosolymitano Synedrio decidendae proponebantur. Posteriores Iudaei ad summum hunc Senatum relatum scribunt, de Rege creando, de bello inferendo, de Pontifice inaugurando, de Reipub. vectigalibus ordinandis, de Templi sumptibus decernendis, de rebus Tribuum iudicandis, de censura Pseudoprophetarum, Magorum, &c. Quomodo igitur non fuit politicum iudicium, in quo causae omnes, sive ad cultum Dei & ceremonias, sive ad politiam & res civiles, sive ad sanguinem & capitales poenas attinerent, explicabantur, & quid faciendum foret decernebatur & edicebatur? Equidem quod de capitalibus etiam differentijs & causis sententiam ferre debuerit, vel ex eo solo perspiciatur, quod cum de condemnandis Idololatris à Iudicibus locutus fuisset Moses, statim addit. Si quid te latuerit. &c.
units.tr: Fifth, it is false that two distinct synedria are described either by Moses in Deuteronomy 17 or by Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 19. Although this can be plain to anyone from the text, I will not hesitate to explain. First, then, I lay this down as granted (for you say the same): this holy king instituted nothing relevant here, except what God commanded through Moses. He therefore appointed judges at the gates of all the cities, just as Moses commanded in Deuteronomy 16. Having done this, he also set up that supreme synedrion, to which those who thought themselves wronged were permitted to appeal, and whose sentence the other judges were compelled to seek in obscure cases, as is clear from Deuteronomy 17. So whether it is granted that this court gave judgment to the Jerusalemites in the same way as the other judges gave judgment to the inhabitants in their towns, or that it only heard appeals, or that it exercised both functions (as the Greek version, Josephus, Antiquities book 9 chapter 1, and the very nature of the matter attest), this makes no difference to our case. For nonetheless the senate remains truly political. Indeed, whatever quarrels, brawls, and controversies arose in the individual towns, if they could not be settled by the magistrate of that place, they were put before the Jerusalem synedrion to be decided. The later Jews write that to this supreme senate were referred the appointment of a king, the waging of war, the inauguration of the high priest, the ordering of the revenues of the commonwealth, the decreeing of the costs of the temple, the judging of matters concerning the tribes, the censure of false prophets, magicians, and so on. How then was it not a political court, in which all causes, whether they concerned the worship of God and the ceremonies, or the polity and civil affairs, or blood and capital penalties, were explained, and what was to be done was decreed and ordered? Indeed, that it was bound to pronounce sentence even in capital cases may be seen from this alone: when Moses had spoken of the judges condemning idolaters, he immediately adds, "If anything be hidden from you," and so on.

units.la: Secundum, quod velut confessum omnibus pono, illud est, Mosea nulla alia publica Iudicia constituisse de moribus, quam quorum facit mentionem Exod. 18. Numeri 11. Deuter. 1. & 16. & 17. Cæterum constat omnibus, (nec tu negas, vt arbitror) Iudices illos, de quibus Exod. 18. Deuter. 1. & 16. scriptum est, verè & merè politicos fuisse. Si ergo Ecclesiasticum aliquod iudicium publicum de vitiorum siue scelerum coercitione instituit; necessarium est, vt vel in cap. 11. Num. vel in 17. cap. Deuter. instituisse putetur. At in vtroque loco politica instituit Iudicia. Proinde Ecclesiasticum nullum instituit, quod μυμέλιαῖς, vt tu loqueris, de vitijs iudicaret: ac solennibus poenis, depulsione scilicet à Sacramentis, eadem coerceret. Equidem septuaginta illi viri, qui 11. Num. electi fuerunt, quosque spiritu Mosis & Prophetiç Deus impertiuit, attributi sunt Mosi, vt socij essent laborum eius: & in Repub. administranda siue populo regendo Mosen, non Aaronem, adiuuarent. Conquestus enim fuerat Moses, quod solus gubernationi non sufficeret. Ideo dicit Deus, se eosdem illos spiritu Mosis donauisse, vt sustinerent vnà cum ipso onus rectionis: nec Moses deinceps solus cogeretur pondus illud portare. Hęc ita sunt expressis verbis in textu posita, vt de ijs ambigere nullus omninò homo sanus possit. Sed nec de eo dubitari potest, an Mosis gubernatio politica fuerit. Quocirca non potest ex hoc loco asseri sacrum illud vestrum Presbyterium.
units.tr: Second, which I lay down as granted by all, is that Moses appointed no other public courts for morals than those he mentions in Exodus 18, Numbers 11, and Deuteronomy 1, 16, and 17. Moreover, it is agreed by all (nor do you deny it, as I think) that those judges of whom Exodus 18, Deuteronomy 1, and Deuteronomy 16 speak were truly and purely political. If then he instituted some ecclesiastical public court for the restraint of vices or crimes, it must be supposed that he instituted it either in Numbers 11 or in Deuteronomy 17. But in both places he instituted political courts. Therefore he instituted no ecclesiastical court which, as you put it, would judge vices by "dispensing" [μυμέλιαῖς] and restrain them by solemn penalties, namely exclusion from the sacraments. Indeed, those seventy men who were chosen in Numbers 11, and to whom God imparted the spirit of Moses and prophecy, were assigned to Moses so that they might be partners in his labours, and help Moses, not Aaron, in administering the commonwealth and ruling the people. For Moses had complained that he alone was not sufficient for government. So God says that He had given those same men the spirit of Moses, so that they might bear the burden of ruling together with him, and that Moses should no longer be forced to carry that weight alone. These things are set down in the text in such express words that no sane man can possibly doubt them. Nor can it be doubted whether the government of Moses was political. Wherefore your sacred presbytery cannot be asserted from this passage.

units.la: Iam quod nec in 17. Deuteron. tale Presbyterium ordinarit Moses, ex supra dictis constare omnibus hominibus poterit. Etenim Iudicium, ad quod velut ad supremum confessum ab inferioribus & politicis iudicijs fit appellatio, non potest non esse politicum. Item, Iudicium quod sententiam fert de capite & sanguine, quodque lites & rixas quaslibet per sententiam supremam, à qua nulli appellare liceat, decidit, politicum est iudicium. Item, Iudicium in quo sedet princeps Reipublicæ, ac suo nomine cum cæteris Iudicibus dicit sententiam, de capite, de fortunis, de seruitute, de multa, de plagis, denique de antedictis omnibus, politicum est iudicium. Quid multa dicam? Impossibile est, vt negetur hoc Iudicium, quod 17.Deuter, institutum ponitur, politicum fuisse. Puto ex septuaginta illis, quos 11. Num. Deus iussit eligi, constituisse supremum hoc Synedrium, quod vnà cum Principe sic ferret imperij onus & labores, vt hi cum Mose ferre iussi sunt. Confirmat suspicionem meam, quod & 18. Exodi, & 1. Deuter. Moses manifestè sibi reseruauit causarum difficiliorum & obscurarum dijudicationem: quas post electionem septuaginta horum virorum, quos Deus eisdem donis eodemq; spiritu, prout ei visum fuit, ornauerat, vnà cum ipsis explanauit. Hi postea Principibus ac Regibus assedisse videntur, vt causas graues ex verbo Dei exponerent.
units.tr: Now, that Moses did not appoint such a presbytery in Deuteronomy 17 can be clear to all men from what has been said above. For a court to which appeal is made from the lower and civil courts, as to a supreme assembly, cannot but be civil. Likewise, a court which pronounces sentence on life and blood, and which settles all disputes and quarrels by a supreme sentence from which no one may appeal, is a civil court. Likewise, a court in which the prince of the commonwealth sits and, in his own name together with the other judges, pronounces sentence on life, property, slavery, fines, beatings, and, in short, all the matters mentioned, is a civil court. Why say more? It is impossible to deny that the court which Deuteronomy 17 sets up was civil. I suppose that from those seventy whom God ordered to be chosen in Numbers 11 he established this supreme Sanhedrin, which would bear the burden of government and its labours together with the prince, just as they were commanded to bear them with Moses. My suspicion is confirmed by the fact that in Exodus 18 and Deuteronomy 1 Moses plainly reserved to himself the decision of the more difficult and obscure cases; and after the choice of these seventy men, whom God had adorned with the same gifts and the same spirit as he saw fit, he explained them together with them. These men afterwards seem to have sat beside princes and kings, to expound weighty cases from the word of God.

units.la: Sed hoc vt-vt habeat, illud iam constat, Iosaphatum non instituisse Hierosolymis duo distincta de moribus iudicia, videlicet Ecclesiasticum & politicum: sed vnicum ordinauisse ex præcepto Dei ac Moßis 17.Deuter. Synedrium: quod de causis omnibus siue ad Religionem cultumque Dei spectarent, siue ad politicam vitam pertinerent, sententiam ferret, à qua nulli appellare fas esset. Cumque dicit toti Synedrio: Admonebitisque eos, & non delinquent contra Dominum, nec veniet ira super vos & fratres vestros: hoc intelligit, scilicet ipsos debere de iure dubitantes admonere quid sit æquum, iustum & legi Dei consentaneum, vel iniquum, iniustum & cum lege Diuina pugnans. Sic enim inquit, vitabitis iram Dei, dum recte eos docebitis iudicare, ne fontes dimittant & innocentes puniant: quæ res iram Dei prouocat.
units.tr: But however that may be, this is now established: Jehoshaphat did not set up at Jerusalem two distinct courts for morals, namely an ecclesiastical and a civil one; he appointed a single Sanhedrin by the command of God and of Moses in Deuteronomy 17, which should pronounce sentence in all causes, whether they concerned the religion and worship of God or pertained to civil life, and from which it was not lawful to appeal. And when it says to the whole Sanhedrin: "And you shall admonish them, and they shall not sin against the Lord, nor shall wrath come upon you and upon your brethren," he means that they ought to instruct those who are in doubt about the law what is equitable, just, and consonant with the law of God, and what is unjust, iniquitous, and contrary to the divine law. For he says: you will avoid the wrath of God, while you teach them rightly to judge, lest they pervert the sources and punish the innocent, which thing provokes the wrath of God.

units.la: Sed excipis, Moses dicitiuxta Legem, quam docuerint te, & & iuxta iudicium, quod dixerint tibi. Item, Iosaphat, ait, Summum Sacerdotem in causis omnibus Domini, Zebadiam autem in negocijs Regijs Principes fuisse. Ergo diftinʇta fuerunt Synedria. Tantundem hæc probant, ac superiora omnia. Quo pacto probabis, non fuisse totius Synedrij, quod ab vtroq; (Mosè scilicet ac Iosaphato) coniunctim describitur? Videlicet legem docere, hoc est, docere, quid iuxta prefinitionem legis rectum & iustum sit, vel iniustum: quid mandatum aut prohibitum: quid faciendum omittendum esset. Moses certè non tribuit hoc separatim quibusdam, sicut nec Iosaphat, sed coniunctim toti Iudicio: tametsi Sacerdotes non inficior peritiores fuisse, ac rectius sæpè iudicare potuisse. Etenim iudicando etiam docere legis sententiam iussit Moses, sicut ipse seipsum fecisse scribit. Exod. 18. his verbis: Iudico inter virum & socium suum, notaque facio statuta Dei & Legis eius.
units.tr: But you object that Moses says: "according to the law which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you." Likewise, Jehoshaphat, you say, placed the high priest over all the causes of the Lord, and Zebadiah over the king's affairs. Therefore the Sanhedrins were distinct. These things prove no more than all the foregoing. By what means will you prove that this was not one body of the whole Sanhedrin, which is described jointly by both (namely Moses and Jehoshaphat)? That is, to teach the law: to teach what is right and just according to the prescription of the law, or unjust; what is commanded or forbidden; what ought to be done or left undone. Moses certainly did not assign this separately to certain persons, nor did Jehoshaphat, but jointly to the whole court; although I do not deny that the priests were more skilled and could often judge more correctly. For Moses also ordered that, in judging, they should teach the sense of the law, just as he himself writes that he did, in Exodus 18, in these words: "I judge between a man and his neighbour, and I make known the statutes of God and his law."

units.la: Qua etiam ratione ostendes non fuisse totius Synedrij simul & indiuulsè sententias ferre? Moses dicit, indicabunt tibi sententiam: facies quod indicauerint: obseruabis quæ docuerint: iuxta legem quam docuerint: & iuxta sententiam, quam tulerint: non discedes ab eo quod pronunciauerint. Omnia, inquam, coniunctim ponit: nunquam diuidit. Quod autem dicitur, si quis contumaciter recusct obedire summo Sacerdoti aut iudici, propter diuersa tempora dictum fuit. Quippe Principes siue Iudices non semper fuerunt ijdem: sed sæpè soli Sacerdotes gubernarunt. Qua eadem ratione quoque non dicit, ascende Hierosolymam, sed in vrbem, quam sibi Deus elegerit. Quippe non in vna semper vrbe arca fuit ante captam Hierosolymam. Eodem modo loquitur Deut. 19. cum de teste falso loquitur. Et stabunt, inquit, coram Iehouah, id est, coram Sacerdotibus & Iudicibus, qui tempore illo futuri sunt. Quis hic arbitretur distincta iudicia proponi, & non potius vnicum? Sed huic aliquando Sacerdos, vt Heli & Samuel, absque Iudice: aliquando cum Iudicibus præsedit. Sic cum summus Sacerdos dicitur in negotijs Dei præesse, Zebadius autem in rebus Regijs, non facit distincta Synedria, sed vtrumq; eidem Synedrio præfuturum dicit: ita tamen, vt aliter Dei causas, aliter Regis negotia præcipuè curet.
units.tr: By what reasoning will you also show that the whole Sanhedrin did not pronounce sentences together and undivided? Moses says: "They shall tell you the sentence; you shall do what they have pointed out; you shall observe what they teach, according to the law which they teach, and according to the sentence which they have pronounced; you shall not turn aside from what they declare." He sets all these things together, I say; he never separates them. As for what is said, that if anyone stubbornly refuses to obey the high priest or the judge, this was said because of differing times. For the princes or judges were not always the same, but often the priests alone governed. By the same reasoning he does not say "go up to Jerusalem," but "to the city which God shall choose," for the ark was not always in one city before Jerusalem was taken. In the same way he speaks in Deuteronomy 19 when he speaks of a false witness: "and they shall stand before Jehovah," that is, before the priests and judges who shall be in that time. Who here would think that distinct courts are proposed, and not rather one? But sometimes the priest, as Eli and Samuel, presided without a judge; sometimes he presided with judges. So when the high priest is said to preside over the affairs of God, and Zebadiah over the affairs of the king, he does not make distinct Sanhedrins, but says that each would preside over the same Sanhedrin; yet in such a way that the one takes especial care of God's causes, the other of the king's business.

units.la: Quicquid verò per negotia Domini, ac Regis intelligendum contendatur, semper hoc permanet firmum, Iudicia non fuisse à Iosaphato duo distincta instituta, sed vnicum: cui iussit præesse simul Sacerdotem & Zebadian. Etenim ad lectos Iudices simul omnes dicit Rex: Super vos erit summus Sacerdos in omni causa Domini, & Zebadias, in omni negotio Regio. Non hic distinguit, vt dicat vni parti ipsorum præficiendum Sacerdotem, parti alteri Zebadiam: sed omnibus vtrumque. Vnde Iosephus, qui harum rerum minimè fuit ignarus, cum & Sacerdos, & Legum atque cõsuetudinum Iudaicarum(vt ipse de seipso testatur in fine librorum de antiquitate) scientissimus fuerit, in lib. Antiquit. 9. Cap. 1. eos nominat ἱεράρχας, cum sic scribit. ἐρχοῦντες δ' αὐτῶν ἀπολείπειν Ἀμασίας τὴν ἱερὰν ... Sanè ἱεράρχας eos non vocasset, si diuersis Senatibus scorsum præpositos fuisse singulos putasset. Intelligitur idem ex eo quoque quod dicit, & præfecti coràm vobis erunt Leuitæ. Certè Ministros facit Leuitas vtriusque ex æquo. Pari igitur potestate præsidebant in eodem iudicio: licet alteri causæ Dei, alteri negotia Regia diligentius commendata fuissent. Quanquam non peccet forte, qui Senatores hos per officia distributos dicat, vt alij magis hæc, alij illa negotia tractarint. Sed communi tamen nomine omnes suum officium administrauisse, ac politici Magistratus partes fuisse, certissimum est.
units.tr: However the affairs of the Lord and the King are to be understood, this always remains firm: Jehoshaphat did not establish two distinct courts, but one, over which he ordered the priest and Zebadiah to preside together. For the king says to all the judges at once: "Over you shall be the high priest in every cause of the Lord, and Zebadiah in every royal matter." Here he does not distinguish, so as to say that the priest should be placed over one part of them and Zebadiah over the other; but he sets both over all. Hence Josephus, who was by no means ignorant of these matters, since he was both a priest and most learned in the laws and customs of the Jews (as he testifies of himself at the end of his books on antiquity), in book 9 of the Antiquities, chapter 1, calls them hierarchs, when he writes thus: "...". Certainly he would not have called them hierarchs if he had thought that each was set over separate senates. The same is understood from what he also says: "and the Levites shall be your officers before you." Certainly he makes the Levites ministers of both equally. They therefore presided with equal power in the same court, although the causes of God were entrusted with more care to one, and the royal affairs to the other. Yet perhaps he would not be wrong who says these senators were distributed by offices, so that some handled these matters more, others those. But that all administered their office under a common name, and that these were parts of the civil magistracy, is most certain.

units.la: Porrò fuisse Leuitas veluti Ministros Magistratus tum ex Cap. 26. lib. 1. Paralip. tum ex Iosephi historia, tum etiam ex 5. Cap. Act. perspicipoteft. Lucas in Actis vocat horum principem, quem etiam Synedrio & cõsilijs interfuisse colligimus, ἐρμηνευτὴς τῶν ἱερῶν. Constat autè ex Mose & historia Regum Leuitis curam siue custodiam Templi demandatam fuisse. Quæ idcirco dico, vt, quantum erres, intelligatur, cum hic sentire videris, Leuitas per singula oppida collocatos fuisse praeter alios Iudices, ut ibi etiam peculiare Iudicium Ecclesiasticum exercerent. At huius rei Scriptura nec vnica quidem syllaba commeminit, sed tantum Iudices causarum omnium per oppida ordinatos dicit: ut per Mosen Deus praeceperat. Nec sacrorum iudicum mentionem facit, nec quas causas tractare debuissent vel hic vel alibi exponit: sed, ut ante dixi, Leuitas tam dicit esse coram Zebadia, quam coram Sacerdote.
units.tr: Moreover, that the Levites were as ministers of the magistracy can be seen both from chapter 26 of 1 Chronicles, and from the history of Josephus, and also from Acts 5. Luke in Acts calls the chief of these hermeneutes of the sacred things, whom we also gather to have been present at the Sanhedrin and the councils. It is established from Moses and from the history of the Kings that the care or guard of the Temple was entrusted to the Levites. I say this so that you may understand how far you err, since here you seem to think that the Levites were placed in individual towns besides the other judges, so that they might there also exercise a peculiar ecclesiastical court. But Scripture does not make mention of this thing even by a single syllable; it only says that judges of all causes were appointed in the towns, as God had commanded through Moses. Nor does it make mention of judges of sacred things, nor does it set forth here or elsewhere what causes they ought to have handled; but, as I said before, it says the Levites were before Zebadiah as much as before the priest.

units.la: Verum enimuero quid verbis opus est amplius? Rex Iosaphatus hac in re a scripto Dei ac Mosis discedere nec potuit, nec debuit, nec voluit. Quare cum declaratum sit, duas distinctas istas iurisdictiones a Deo non esse mandatas: & a Mose nullo in loco institutas, per se patet, Iosaphatum tale nihil cogitasse. Ideo non anxie hic nobis quaerendum videtur, quid per negotia Domini & Regis sit intelligendum. Per negotia Dei idem hoc intellexit, quod supra dixit, Non homini iudicabitis, sed Ichouae, qui erit vobiscum in iudicio. Non dissentiunt ab his, quae Rabini annotarunt, qui iudicium causarum capitalium afferunt vocatum fuisse iudicium animarum. Scriptura omnia iudicia frequentissime vocat Iudicia Dei. In 1. Cap. Deut. de politicis Iudicibus haec legimus. Non timebitis vobis a quoquam: quia Iudicium Dei est. Sic Exod. 18. Moses socero interroganti cur totos dies ibi sederet, respondet. Quia venit ad me populus ad quaerendum Deum, hoc est, ad quaerendum Iudicium. Hac de causa toties vocantur Iudices in Scriptura Dij, ut ex Cap. 22. Exod. & Psal. 82. liquet. Significat ergo hic causa Dei, causam quamlibet in Lege Dei expressam, & Iudicibus ad dijudicandum propositam. Regis autem negotium eas notat causas, quae ad Regem proprie pertinebant.
units.tr: But indeed, why need we more words? King Jehoshaphat could not, ought not, and would not depart from the writing of God and of Moses in this matter. Wherefore, since it has been shown that these two distinct jurisdictions were not commanded by God, nor instituted in any place by Moses, it is plain in itself that Jehoshaphat thought nothing of the kind. Therefore it does not seem necessary for us to inquire anxiously here what is to be understood by the affairs of the Lord and of the King. By the affairs of God he understood the same thing that he said above: "You shall not judge for man, but for Jehovah, who will be with you in judgment." They do not disagree with those things which the rabbis have noted, who say that judgment in capital causes was called the judgment of souls. Scripture very frequently calls all judgments the judgments of God. In chapter 1 of Deuteronomy we read of civil judges these words: "You shall not fear any man, for the judgment is God's." So in Exodus 18 Moses, when his father-in-law asked why he sat there all day, answers: "Because the people come to me to seek God," that is, to seek judgment. For this reason judges are so often called gods in Scripture, as is clear from Exodus 22 and Psalm 82. So the affair of God here signifies any cause expressed in the law of God and proposed to the judges for decision. The affair of the king, however, marks those causes which properly belonged to the king.

units.la: Quae quales essent, paulo supra ex Rabinis diximus. Si per illas libet res ad cultum Dei spectantes, per haec res ciuiles accipere, non pugnabo. Etenim Sacerdotem imprimis decebat operam dare, ne in fide & ceremonijs, error admitteretur. Pertinebat hoc ad Regem non minus (ut ex 17. Deut. ynusquisq; videre potest) sed peculiariter tamen Sacerdoti hoc mādatur:quem verisimile est Regibus omni tempore diligētiorem fuisse in lectione ac meditatione Legis. Vt hic non excluditur Zebadias,ita non remouetur à negotijs Regis Amasias: sed commune fuit vtrobiq; munus.
units.tr: What these were like, we said a little earlier, drawing on the rabbis. If it pleases someone to take the matters that pertain to the worship of God by those, and to take these as civil matters, I will not quarrel. For it was above all fitting for the priest to take care that no error be admitted in faith and in ceremonies. This charge pertained no less to the king (as anyone can see from Deut. 17), but it was entrusted especially to the priest; and it is likely that the kings were always more diligent than others in reading and meditating on the Law. Just as Zebadiah is not excluded here, so Amariah is not removed from the king's business; but the office was common to both.

units.la: Si magis placet per causas Dei accipere causas appellationum per Regis negotia iudicia alia, ne hic quidem tecum litigabo. Rectè hic praeficitur Sacerdos, cum in Lege sit exercitatus magis, & causæ tales obscurae sunt ac difficiles iudicatu. Si Sacerdotem in Dei nomine, Zebadiam autem Regis praesedisse affirmetur,non refragabor: etsi prius dictas expositiones(maximè verò primam) veriores putem. Ad huius loci intellectionem conferet plurimum inspectio 26. Cap. lib. 1. Paralip. vbi scribitur Hasbias cum fratribus Regioni vltra Iordanum versus occidentem praefuisse in omni opere Domini & Ministerio Regis. Item Iediam constituit Dauid praefectum Rubenitis,Gaditis,& dimidiæ Tribui Manasis in omni re Dei & Regis. Eadem propè verba sunt, quæ postea repetuntur in historia Iosaphati: & tribuitur manifestè vtraq; potestas eisdem: non mandatur diuersis. Quare hic etiam vni Iudicio imperatur vtrumq;, licet alteri hæc, alteri illa magis negotia commendentur. Conducet fortasse nonnihil & loci alterius illius ex 19. Deuter. consideratio: Et stabunt duo illi, quibus lis est, coràm Iehoua, id est,coràm Sacerdotibus & Iudicibus, qui erunt tempore illo. Nunc tempus est, vt videamus quomodo probes Iudaicum Synedrium ciuilem iurisdictionem non habuisse.
units.tr: If it is more pleasing to take the causes of God as the appeals in cases of religion, and the other judgments as the king's business, I will not contest this point with you either. It is right that the priest is set over these here, since he was more practised in the Law, and such causes are obscure and difficult to judge. If it is asserted that the priest presided in the name of God, and Zebadiah for the king, I will not object, although I think the explanations given earlier (especially the first) are truer. For understanding this passage, a close look at chapter 26 of 1 Chronicles will contribute greatly, where it is written that Hashabiah with his brothers, a thousand men, presided over the district beyond the Jordan to the west, in all the work of the Lord and the service of the king. Likewise David appointed Jehiel as prefect over the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in all matters of God and the king. These are almost the same words that are afterwards repeated in the history of Jehoshaphat, and both powers are clearly assigned to the same men; they are not committed to different persons. Therefore here too both are enjoined on one court, although these duties are more commended to one and those to the other. Perhaps the consideration of that other passage, from Deut. 19, will also help somewhat: "And those two men, between whom there is a dispute, shall stand before the LORD," that is, before the priests and the judges who will be in that time. Now it is time that we see how you prove that the Jewish Sanhedrin did not have civil jurisdiction.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Vtrum Synedrium politicus fuerit Magistratus.
units.tr: Whether the Synedrium was a political magistrate.

units.la: Vm Sacerdos, inquis, Ieremiam Prophetam reum ageret blasphemiæ, nō sedit inter Iudices Sacerdos,Ierem.26:sed egit accusatorē apud Regios Magistratus. Ergo Synedrium tempore Christi caruit coercitione ciuili. Non animaduertis quàm lubrica sint, que; quæcunq; ex theca tua promis? Concedo tibi Synedrium tuum caruisse iurisdictione ciuili: quoniam est figmentum, & in populo Iudaico nunquam fuit, nisi forte aliquis somniauerit tale quidpiam. Sed ad tua propius. An suisset æquum, vt Sacerdos simul accusator esset ac Iudex? An non in quolibet Iudicio accusatores, etiamsi alias ex numero sint Iudicum, è Consessu aliorum exire coguntur dum suam agunt causam? Inepta ergo est tua isthæc argumentatio. His adde illud etiam, quod Ieremiæ tempore regnabat Hierosolymis Rex, penes quem, vt in Monarchia fieri solet, omnis potestas erat: Christi tempore regebantur ea specie Reipub. quam Aristocratia Græcè Iosephus nominat. Quid quæso, potest te in disputando infœlicius esse?
units.tr: When the high priest, you say, prosecuted the prophet Jeremiah for blasphemy, the priest did not sit among the judges but acted as accuser before the royal magistrates (Ierem. 26.). Therefore the Synedrium in Christ's time lacked civil coercion. Do you not see how slippery and how unreliable whatever you bring out of your own storehouse is? I grant you that your Synedrium lacked civil jurisdiction, since it is a fiction and never existed among the Jewish people, unless perhaps someone has dreamed up something of the sort. But let us come closer to your own case. Would it have been fair for the priest to be accuser and judge at the same time? In any trial, are not accusers, even if they are otherwise among the number of the judges, required to leave the bench of the others while they plead their own cause? Your argument is therefore pointless. Add to this that in Jeremiah's time a king reigned at Jerusalem, in whose hands, as usually happens under a monarchy, all power lay. In Christ's time the commonwealth was governed in the form that Josephus calls in Greek aristocracy. What, I ask, could be more unfortunate for you in this dispute?

units.la: Quæris etiam, vnde Caiaphæ & eius Collegarum potestas in Christum fuerit? Hoc à me supra fusè & firmiter est declaratum: in præsentia breuiter respondebo à Deo primum fuisse. Deinde à Persarum Regibus, atq; aliis illis, qui Iudæam sibi subiecerant. Demum etiam à Romanis permittentibus. Quod Deus post reditum ex captiuitate non voluerit Rempub. per Regem aut monarcham gubernari, declarat Ezechiel. Cap. 44. de Sacerdotibus loquens: Et in controuersia ipsi stabunt ad iudicandum: iuxta iudicia mea iudicabunt eam. De Persarum Regibus ac Romanis declarant Esdras, Nehemias, ac Iosephus. Sed quid disputo tecum? Tu ipse scribis vos non negare, quin habuerint præhensionem & coercitionem in illis, quæ ad ipsorum ritus spectabant. An tibi praehensio & coercitio pars nulla videntur ciuilis iurisdictionis? Sed, inquis, non licuit hoc ipsis ex verbo Dei: sed fuerunt reliquiæ confusionis, quæ sub Macchabæis coepit. Hoc vnde probabis? Sarè Christum & Apostolos nihil tale reperies in Sacerdotibus reprehendisse. Quinetiam ex verbo Dei contrarium probaui: quod non minus clarè ex historia Iosephi cernitur. Quid dicam amplius? Nihil habes, quo te sustentes.
units.tr: You ask also whence the power of Caiaphas and his colleagues over Christ came. I have set this out above at length and firmly, so for the present I will answer briefly. It came first from God; then from the kings of Persia and the other rulers who had subjected Judea to themselves; and finally from the Romans, by their permission. That God did not wish the commonwealth to be governed by a king or monarch after the return from captivity, Ezekiel declares in chapter 44, speaking of the priests: "And they shall stand in controversy to judge; according to my judgments they shall judge it." Esdras, Nehemiah and Josephus declare the matter concerning the kings of Persia and the Romans. But why do I dispute with you? You yourself write that you do not deny that they had apprehension and coercion over those matters which concerned their rites. Does apprehension and coercion seem to you no part of civil jurisdiction? But, you say, this was not permitted them by the word of God; rather they were remnants of the confusion that began under the Maccabees. How will you prove this? Surely you will find that Christ and the Apostles never rebuked the priests for any such thing. Indeed I have proved the contrary from the word of God, which is seen no less clearly from the history of Josephus. What more can I say? You have nothing to lean on.

units.la: Quàm infœliciter Synedrium per id tempóris, quo Christus
units.tr: How unhappily you deny that the Sanhedrin, at the time in which Christ

units.la: docuit, ciuilem iurisdictionem habuisse neges, vidimus: nunc quomodo rationes nostras refellas, quibus iudicia capitalia penes illud fuisse demonstrauimus, inspiciendum. Romani, inquis, nulli Regioni in Prouinciam redactę gladij potestatem permiserunt. Ego hoc dico ipsa falsitate salsius esse, si de illis rebus intelligi etiam velis, quae ad Religionem seu ἀνδρογύνων, patriosue ritus spectabant. Et vt nunc de aliis nihil dicam, de Iudæa sic probaui, vt mirer an aliquis sanæ mentis porro sit negaturus post auditas nostras probationes. Cur ergo Christum, inquis, ab ipsis prehensum, vinctum, blasphemiæ accusatum, damnatum, non occiderunt, nisi quia ius gladij non habuerunt? Respondeo tibi, multas causas concurrere, & sibi inuicem succedere. Prima est, quod sic Deo visum fuerat, vt Gentilibus traderetur. Matth. 20. Propior est, quod propter festi propinquitatem non poterant occidere: nec tamen viuere eum diutius volebant. Ob eandem hanc causam non introierunt in Prætorium, Iohan. 18. Huc accedit, quod intelligebant se hoc pacto facilius iram populi euitaturos. Ideo scribit Lucas, eos quæsiuisse, hoc est, captasse occasionem occidendi. Et Iudam ait quæsiuisse rationem, qua sine turba eum traderet, Luc. 22. Sic enim ratiocinabantur. Si nos eum occidemus iuxta legem blasphemi Leuit. 24. lapidibus à populo erit obruendus: in quo concursu populus facilè mouebit turbas. Si Romanus Præses fecerit, nullus se opponere audebit. His adde, si iubet, quod eum cupiebant crucifigi (Sic enim mori eum oportebat) quod clamoribus suis apud Pilatum abundè probant: Lex autem blasphemum lapidibus necare iubebat. Postrema est, quod apud Pilatum eum accusarunt præcipuè, quod populum aduersus Caesarem concitaret, quod tributum dare prohiberet, seque Regem faceret. Quæ cum falsa comperisset Pilatus, & damnare ob id nollet, veriti ne eum absolueret, addunt blasphemum esse, & secundum eam legem ei moriendum esse. Cum nec sic quidem proficerent, sed multò magis nutare Pilatum cernerent, hoc obijciunt, eum Cæsaris amicum non fore, si eum, qui contra Cæsarem se Regem faceret, impunitum dimitteret. Quare cum propter hanc causam, propter quam præcipuè accusarant, ipsi punire neminem possint, recte dicunt, sibi nullum occidere licere. Propter blasphemiam occidere potuissent, ideoque Pilato dicunt Legem se habere, secundum quam moriendum ei esset. Cum à Pilato, qui ob eam causam damnare eum nollet, iuberentur secundum eam legem necare, propter dictas causas noluerunt. Etenim Prophetias impleri oportuit, ipsis etiam nescientibus? Habes causas, ut hic nec Chrysostomi nec Augustini defensionem frustra suscipiam.
units.tr: taught, had civil jurisdiction, we have seen. Now we must examine how you refute our arguments, by which we showed that capital judgments belonged to it. The Romans, you say, granted the power of the sword to no region reduced into a province. I say that this is more false than salt, even if you wish it understood of those matters which concerned religion [ἀνδρογύνων] or the ancestral rites. And, to say nothing for now of other places, I have proved the case for Judea in such a way that I wonder whether anyone of sound mind would still deny it after hearing our proofs. Why then, you ask, if they had seized Christ, bound him, accused him of blasphemy and condemned him, did they not kill him, unless because they did not have the right of the sword? I answer that many causes concurred and followed one another. The first is that it had so seemed good to God, that he should be handed over to the Gentiles (Matth. 20). The second is that, because of the nearness of the festival, they could not kill him, and yet they did not want him to live any longer. For this same reason they did not enter the Praetorium (John 18). To this is added that they understood that in this way they would more easily escape the anger of the people. So Luke writes that they sought, that is, watched for an opportunity to kill him (Luke 22); and he says that Judas sought a way to hand him over without a crowd. For they reasoned thus: "If we kill him ourselves according to the law on blasphemers (Lev. 24), he must be stoned by the people, and in such a gathering the people will easily stir up tumults. If the Roman governor does it, no one will dare to oppose." Add to this that, if he ordered it, they wanted him crucified (for in this way he had to die), as their shouts before Pilate amply prove; but the law ordered a blasphemer to be put to death by stoning. The last cause is that before Pilate they accused him chiefly of stirring up the people against Caesar, of forbidding the payment of tribute, and of making himself king. When Pilate found these charges false and was unwilling to condemn him on that account, fearing that he would acquit him, they added that he was a blasphemer and must die according to that law. When even so they made no headway, but saw Pilate wavering all the more, they threw in this: that he would not be a friend of Caesar if he let go unpunished one who made himself king against Caesar. Therefore, since they could punish no one for the very cause for which they had chiefly accused him, they rightly say that it was not lawful for them to kill anyone. They could have killed him on account of blasphemy, and so they tell Pilate that they have a law by which he ought to die. When Pilate, who for that cause was unwilling to condemn him, bade them put him to death according to that law, they refused, for the reasons stated. For was it not necessary that the prophecies be fulfilled, even though they did not know it? You have the causes; so I shall not vainly take up the defence of Chrysostom or of Augustine here.

units.la: Ad id, quod dixi, Pilatum permittere, ut secundum legem suam ipsimet eum condemnarent, ideoque fateri Pilatum, ipsis licuisse patriarum legum transgressores capite plectere: Respondes, negando Pilatum illis capitale iudicium concessisse. Ratio tua est, quod Iudæi recupidè arrepturi fuissent hanc occasionem, cum nihil magis exoptassent. Item per sarcasmum dixisse Pilatum, tollite eum vos & crucifigite eum. Haec est egregia tua ad argumentum nostrum responsio. Nego tibi Pilatum non concessisse ipsis capitale Iudicium, quod ex permissu Cæsaris habebant, cum dixit, Accipite eum vos, & secundum Legem vestram iudicate eum. Item cum dixit: Tollite eum vos, & crucifigite eum. Non fuit sarcasmus hac in parte: sed quum capitale crimen in eo non invenirent, atque ideo secundum Leges Romanorum interficere non posset, iussit ut secundum suas Leges ipsi eum occiderent.
units.tr: To what I said, that Pilate allowed them to condemn him themselves according to their own law, and therefore that Pilate confessed that they were allowed to punish transgressors of their ancestral laws with death, you reply by denying that Pilate granted them capital judgment. Your reason is that the Jews would have seized this opportunity eagerly, since they desired nothing more; and likewise that Pilate said, in mockery, "Take him yourselves and crucify him."
