This is your fine answer to our argument. I deny to you that Pilate did not grant them capital judgment, which they held by Caesar's permission, when he said, "Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law." Likewise when he said, "Take him yourselves and crucify him." There was no mockery in this part; but since they could find no capital crime in him, and therefore could not put him to death according to Roman laws, he ordered them to kill him according to their own laws.

units.la: At, inquis, cupidissimè hanc occasionem arripuisse. Imò verò habebant iam potestatem: sed quoniam Deus volebat Christum à Gentibus necari, factum quoque est, ut non ante caperetur, quàm instaret iam, imò incepisset parasceuë Paschatis. Hanc ipsemet Christus causam esse dixit, Matth. 26. quod eum in Templo docentem non coeperint. Praeterea iniecerat Deus ipsis metum populi. Matth. 26. Mar. 14. quae res secerunt, vt cum viuum ferre amplius non possent mortemque differri longius nollent, à Pilato contenderint, vt eum de cruce suspensum necaret. Certè si debuisseт à populo lapidibus obrui, vt Stephano postea accidit, blasphemique occidi solebant, vix absque tumultu futurum praeuidebant.
units.tr: But, you say, they seized this opportunity most eagerly. Indeed, they already had the power; but since God willed that Christ be killed by the Gentiles, it also came about that he was not seized before the feast was already at hand, indeed had already begun on the Paraskeve of the Passover. Christ himself said that this was the reason, that they did not seize him while he was teaching in the Temple (Matt. 26.). Moreover, God had put fear of the people into them (Matt. 26.; Mark 14.). These things brought it about that, since they could no longer bear him alive and did not want his death delayed any longer, they pressed Pilate to have him put to death by hanging on the cross. Certainly, if he had had to be stoned by the people, as happened later to Stephen, and blasphemers were customarily put to death in that way, they foresaw that it would hardly happen without a tumult.

units.la: Stephano exemplum produxi, vt in causis ad Religionem attinentibus capitalia iudicia penes Synedrium esse monstrarem. Hunc etenim captum & coràm iudicio accusatum (sed falsò) libera responsione eius exasperati extra vrbem lapidari iusserunt. Et, quod Lex iubet, testes primos lapides in damnatum iacere, factum hoc fuisse ex eo dixi apparere, quod scribitur, testes depositue vestes suas ad pedes Sauli Actor. 7. &22. Ex his conclusi Stephanum non sic per tumultum occisum, quomodo qui à vulgo interficitur, quod interficiendi ius non habet. Per tumultum complura hic sunt facta, & quidem iniuste, fateor: attamen historia docet, eos habuisse potestatem prehendendi, iudicandi, condemnandi, & demum occidendi. At, inquis, cum nondum peroratsset, ac priusquam eum condemnassent ex vrbe eiectum lapidarunt. Concedo de condemnatione nos nihil legere: at secundum suam opinionem manifestum erat ipsius crimen, scilicet blasphemiæ, cum se diceret, Iesum videre à Dextris Dei. Quod de eiectione dicis, indignum est responsione. Quis enim non videat falsum esse hanc propositionem: Quicunque iusu & permisu Iudicum eijcitur ex loco aliquo & exciditur, is per tumultum occiditur ab ijs,qui ius interficiendi nullum habent? Cum aperte falsa haec sit enunciatio generalis, quomodo tu subiectione singularis concludere te credis?
units.tr: I brought forward the example of Stephen to show that in cases pertaining to religion, capital judgments lay with the Synedrium. For when he was seized and accused before the court (but falsely), they, exasperated by his free reply, ordered him to be stoned outside the city. And I said that it appears from this that, as the Law commands, the witnesses cast the first stones at the condemned man, because it is written that the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of Saul (Acts 7 and 22). From these facts I concluded that Stephen was not killed in such a tumult as one who is killed by the common crowd, which has no right to kill. Many things were done here by tumult, and indeed unjustly, I admit; yet the history shows that they had the power to seize, to judge, to condemn and finally to kill. But, you say, they stoned him, and cast him out of the city, before he had finished speaking, and before they condemned him. I grant that we read nothing about a condemnation; but according to their own opinion his crime was plain, namely blasphemy, since he said that he saw Jesus at the right hand of God. What you say about the casting out is unworthy of an answer. For who does not see that this proposition is false: whoever is cast out and expelled from some place by the order and permission of judges is killed in a tumult by those who have no right to kill? Since this general statement is plainly false, how do you believe you can draw a conclusion about a particular case from it?

units.la: Conaris & illud eludere, quod de Apostolo Paulo legimus, eum accepta potestate à Principibus Sacerdotum ad Synagogas, viros & foeminas in carcerem coniecisse, atque suo etiam suffragio occidisse, Actor. 26. Quem locum miraris à me non prolatum. At non mirareris, si Theses correctas vidisses: & cogitasses me non sperauisse Theologos inuentum iri adeo audaces, qui negare eiusmodi vellent. Si potuerunt dare facultatem Apostolo pios etiam alibi viuentes, (vt Damasci) comprehendedi, in carcerem coniciendi, Hierosolymam pertrahendi, suffragioque suo interficiendi, certè habuerunt ipsi quoq; eandem. Sanè Apostolus ingenuè coràm Præsidibus Romanorum fatetur se ista fecisse, ac potestatem faciendi à Sacerdotibus & Senioribus accepisse, Actor. 22. & 26. nec reprehensos vel Pontifices vel Paulum hanc ob rem legimus, quasi aliquid contra Romanorum voluntatem ac iussa egerint. Puto te Cap. 5. Act. non satis attentè legisse, cum ista reprehenderes. Etenim solum nobis sufficere posset. Capiunt ibi Apostolos palàm, & quidem per publicos Ministros, per Templi [Greek] & suos [Greek] : collocant in custodia publica: conuocant totum Concilium: iubent dicere sententias: deliberant de interficiendis, [Greek] : & à Gamaliele aliter persuasi, cædi eos imperant. Quid quasi amplius petis? Si non habuissent potestatem tollendi, Gamaliel dicturus certè videtur fuisse, non debere eos hoc facere, ne irritarent Romanos. At neq; alij neq; ipse tale aliquid dixisse legitur: tantum cauere monet, ne tàdem [Greek] reperiantur. Quæ cum nobis omnia sacræ literæ præscribant, quomodo nō te pudet negare, capitalia iudicia penes Synedrium illum fuisse? Sed age videamus quid respondeas.
units.tr: You also try to get round what we read about the Apostle Paul: that, having received authority from the chief priests, he cast men and women into prison for the synagogues and even added his vote to have them put to death (Acts 26). You are surprised that I did not cite this passage. You would not be surprised if you had seen the corrected theses, and had considered that I did not expect to find theologians so bold as to want to deny such things. If they could give the Apostle authority to seize, imprison, drag to Jerusalem, and put to death by his vote even pious people living elsewhere (as at Damascus), then they certainly had the same authority themselves. Indeed the Apostle openly confesses before the Roman governors that he did these things and that he had received the power to do them from the priests and elders (Acts 22 and 26). We read that neither the high priests nor Paul were rebuked for this, as if they had acted against the will and commands of the Romans. I think you did not read Acts chapter 5 carefully enough when you objected to these things. That chapter alone should be enough for us. There the apostles are seized openly, and indeed by public officers, in the Temple and in their own houses. They are placed in public custody, the whole Council is summoned, the members are told to give their opinions, they deliberate about putting them to death, and, persuaded otherwise by Gamaliel, they order them to be beaten. What more do you ask? If they had not had the power to put people to death, Gamaliel would surely have been expected to say that they ought not to do this, lest they provoke the Romans. But neither he nor anyone else is recorded as saying anything of the kind. He only warns them to take care lest they be found fighting against God. Since Holy Scripture prescribes all these things to us, how is it that you are not ashamed to deny that the capital judgments lay with that Sanhedrin? But come, let us see what you answer.

units.la: Coercitionem modicâ & præhensionem, inquis, causa religionis habuisse non negamus. Sed hæc licentia orta est ex cōfusione vtriusq; iurisdictionis: quas Christus postea separauit. Si verum est, quod dicis, pessimè contendunt alij tui socij in præsente causa, non posse vllum excommunicari à Ministris & adiunctis ipsorum, nisi accedat consensus Magistratus. Hi ergo coniungunt iterum, quæ Christus te iudice separauit. At multò te hic sentiunt rectius. Vbi, rogo te, distinxit externam gubernationem in Ecclesiasticam & ciuilem, eo modo scilicet quo vos distindistinguitis? Aut quo in loco tribuit presbyterio ius publica de moribus iudicia habendi à Sacramentis arcendi? ac magistratus, quibus parere debebant, sibi subijciendi? Excipies fortasse, te id supra probauisse, cum cap. 18. Matth. tractares. At verò sic probasti, vt me atque omnes intelligentes adeoque temetipsum necesse sit tui misereri. Ego autem veris & indisolubilibus argumentis & testimonijs tum sacrae tum prophanae historiae demonstraui, Synedrium Iudaicum ius & potestatem habuisse de capite iudicandi, adeoque verum fuisse magistratum: idque ex voluntate atque ordinatione Diuina. Legito Ezech. Esdram, Nehemiam, Iosephum, si adhuc dubitas. Vides ergo Paulum, cum se suffragium atque sententiam de morte & capite Christianorum à se captorum dixisse profitetur, non hoc solum voluisse dicere, se assensum fuisse, sed hoc quod verba ipsa vere sonant. Frustra igitur producis ex historia, quae Iudaei, vel tunc vel aliquot post seculis per impotentiam egerunt.
units.tr: You say that we do not deny that they had the power to restrain and arrest people for reasons of religion, in a small way. But this licence, you say, arose from the confusion of the two jurisdictions, which Christ afterwards separated. If what you say is true, then your other allies in the present cause argue very badly, when they say that no one can be excommunicated by the ministers and their associates unless the consent of the magistrate is added. Thus they join together again what Christ, according to you, separated. But they judge far more rightly than you do here. Tell me, where did Christ distinguish external government into ecclesiastical and civil in the way you distinguish it? Or in what place did he grant to the eldership the right to hold public judgments on morals, to bar people from the sacraments, and to subject to itself the magistrates whom they ought to obey? You will perhaps object that you proved this above, when you treated Matthew chapter 18. But you proved it in such a way that it is necessary for me and for all intelligent readers, and for yourself, to pity you. I, however, have demonstrated by true and indissoluble arguments and testimonies, both of sacred and of profane history, that the Jewish Sanhedrin had the right and power to judge concerning capital matters, and so was a true magistrate, and that this was by the will and ordinance of God. Read Ezekiel, Ezra, Nehemiah and Josephus, if you still doubt. You see, then, that when Paul professes that he gave his vote and judgment for the death and capital punishment of the Christians he had seized, he did not wish to say only that he had consented, but meant exactly what the words truly say. It is therefore in vain that you bring forward from history things which the Jews did at that time, or some centuries afterwards, through lack of power.

units.la: Verum si poterat, inquis, à Synedrio damnari capitis, quid erat necesse concipi votum de eo interficiendo in via? Respondeo ob id factum, quod in sua potestate eum non amplius haberent. Votum ergo illud conceperunt mali nebulones, vt gratificarentur Senioribus illis, quos videbant vnicè cupere Pauli mortem. Sciebant ijdem Romanos non temerè occisuros quenquam propter religionis causas, si in sua potestate haberent. Lysias quoque non de Religione quaerit, sed num Aegyptius ille sit, interrogat, qui seditionem excitaret. Deinde cum propter excitatam inter Iudaeos dissensionem periclitari eum videret ne discerperetur, rapi iusit è medio illorum. Quod cum vidissent Iudaei, facile intellexerunt, non sibi datum iri potestatem eum occidendi, praesertim cum ad sui defensionem absque vinculis productum conspicati suissent. Et cum Paulus ait. 23. Actorum, Tu sedes iudicans me secundum Legem, an non agnoscit eum Iudicem? Et paulò post, cum diceret: Nesciebam quod esset Pontifex, scriptum est enim, Principi populi tui non maledices, an non pro Principe agnouit Pontificem? Cur ergo accusant coram. Felice, & non potius sibi dedi postulant? Causa ex historia nota est, & ex epistola Lysiæ: quia nolebat occidi hominem Romanum, in quo crimen mortis aut etiam carceris nullum repericbatur. Paulus quoque negabat se contra legem aliquid fecisse: & rem ita habere probabat, Act. 24. & 25. Miror ergo cur putidas hasce interrogatiunculas nobis obijcias. Ego ex te hic multò iustius quaero, cur non verba Tertulli oratoris cap. 24. notaueris? aut si notauisti, cur dissimulaueris. Hunc Paulum, inquit, à nobis comprehensum voluimus secundum legem nostram condemnare: nisi Lysias superuenisset, magnaque vi eum è manibus nostris eripuisset. Audis hic conquerentes, quod Lysias per vim, nullo iure, ipsis eum eripuerit? ac proinde in causa fuerit, quò minus eum potuerint secundum legem suam condemnare? Patet ex his & petiuisse Iudæos eum sibi dedi, quod etiam à Festo petiuisse videntur: at non erat in more Romanorum positum, vt Romanum hominem, quem in sua tenerét potestate, facilè alijs traderent.
units.tr: But, you say, if they could be condemned to death by the Sanhedrin, why was it necessary to form a plot to kill him on the way? I answer that this was done because they no longer had him in their power. Those wicked scoundrels therefore made that vow in order to please those elders, whom they saw were desiring only Paul's death. The same men knew that the Romans would not lightly kill anyone for reasons of religion, if they had them in their power. Lysias too does not inquire about religion, but asks whether that Egyptian is the man who stirred up sedition. Then, when he saw that Paul was in danger of being torn apart because of the dissension stirred up among the Jews, he ordered him to be snatched from their midst. When the Jews saw this, they readily understood that the power of killing him would not be given to them, especially since they had seen him brought forward, without chains, for his defence. And when Paul says (Acts 23), "You sit judging me according to the Law," does he not acknowledge that man as judge? And a little after, when he says, "I did not know that he was the high priest, for it is written, You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people," did he not acknowledge the high priest as a ruler? Why then do they bring their accusation before Felix, and not rather ask that he be handed over to them? The reason is known from the history and from the letter of Lysias: because he did not want a Roman citizen, in whom no crime deserving death or even imprisonment was found, to be killed. Paul too denied that he had done anything against the law, and proved that the matter stood so (Acts 24 and 25). I am surprised, then, why you throw these foolish little questions at us. I rightly ask you in turn: why did you not note the words of the orator Tertullus (Acts 24)? Or if you did note them, why did you pass them over in silence? "We wished," he says, "to condemn this Paul, seized by us, according to our law; but Lysias came upon us and with great force snatched him from our hands." Do you hear here the complaint that Lysias, by violence and without any right, tore him from them, and that therefore he was the cause why they could not condemn him according to their law? From these things it is plain that the Jews asked for him to be handed over to them, as they also seem to have asked of Festus. But it was not the custom of the Romans easily to hand over a Roman citizen whom they held in their own power to others.

units.la: Quod de Festo obijcis interrogante num Hierosolymis vellet apud se iudicari, miror quomodo obijcias, cum apertè in textu dicatur, Festum voluisse hac in re Iudaeis gratificari. Ergo falsò dixit, apud me, cum Iudaeis vellet concedere: quod & Paulus intellexit, cum sic respondit. Sto ad Caesaris tribunal, vbi me oportet iudicari: Iudaeos iniuria nulla affeci. Quod si non hoc cogitasse Festum contendas, id saltem meminerat Apostolus, in quanto periculo fuisset antea Hierosolymis. Sed interpretare hæc vt libet, semper hoc constabit nihilominus, eos potestatem habuisse de capite iudicandi in causa religionis ac rituum suorum. Probaui hæc omnia fusius in superioribus: quæ hic repetere non est opus.
units.tr: As to what you object concerning Festus, who asked whether Paul wished to be judged before him at Jerusalem, I am surprised how you can object this, since the text plainly says that Festus wished to gratify the Jews in this matter. So he did not say falsely "before me," when he wished to grant something to the Jews. Paul also understood this when he answered thus: "I stand before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews." But if you insist that Festus did not have this in mind, at least the Apostle remembered how great a danger he had been in previously at Jerusalem. But interpret these things as you please, it will always nonetheless be established that they had the power to judge capital cases in matters of religion and of their own rites. I have proved all these things more fully above, and there is no need to repeat them here.

units.la: Quæ de Gallione Præfecto Corinthiorum, & de Ephesiis hic commemoras, ad rem praesentem nec tibi vsui esse possunt nec mihi. At illud, cuius causa ego protuli, pulcherrimè declarant: nempe non potuisse Synedrium Iudaicum in causis iniuriarum, & ad religionem non spectantibus parere nolentes cogere: quod idem tu supra de Corinthiis quoque recte affirmabas. Ergo permittit Christus iniuria affecto, si quidem iniuriosus nolit desinere iniurius esse, postquam ab Ecclesia admonitus fuit, sic cum aduersario agere, atque si cum Ethnico vel cum Publicano lis ei esset: qui coram alio magistratu conueniri tunc non poterant, quam Romano. Sic dum male confutae laceraeque vestis tuae partem vnam infeliciter sarcire studes, aliam imprudenter laceras.
units.tr: What you mention here about Gallio, the governor of the Corinthians, and about the Ephesians, can be of use neither to you nor to me for the present matter. But that for the sake of which I brought these examples they make most clearly plain: namely, that the Jewish Sanhedrin could not compel, in cases of injury and in matters not concerning religion, those who refused to obey. You yourself rightly affirmed this above about the Corinthians as well. Therefore Christ permits the person who has been wronged, if indeed the wrongdoer will not cease to do wrong after being admonished by the Church, to deal with his adversary as if the dispute were with a heathen or a tax-collector; and those men could not then be sued before any other magistrate than the Roman. So, while you unhappily try to patch one part of your garment, which has been badly refuted and torn, you imprudently tear another.

units.la: Synedrium Ecclesiasticum apud Iudaeos nullum suisse, sic, puto, declarauimus, vt omnes homines intelligentes infelices tuos conatus miseraturi sint. Argumentum vnicum ex Iosaphati historia perperam expositu protulisti, quod salsissimum esse ostendi: simulque mea contra vestrum Presbyterium firmissima permanere demonstrauî. Iam ergo quomodo probes Iudaico Synedrio successisse Presbyterium noui Testamenti videamus. Quanquam ridiculum est velle videre, an hoc illi succedere debuerit, cum indissolubiliter monstratum sit, illud nunquam fuisse vel à Deo institutum, vel à Iudaeis vsurpatum: attamen ne queratur nos aliquid omisisse, agè haec etiam percurramus.
units.tr: I think we have shown that there was no ecclesiastical Sanhedrin among the Jews, in such a way that all intelligent people will pity your unhappy efforts. You have produced one argument, from the history of Jehoshaphat, wrongly expounded, which I have shown to be utterly absurd; at the same time I have demonstrated that my position against your eldership stands firmly. Let us now see how you prove that the eldership of the New Testament succeeded the Jewish Sanhedrin. Although it is ridiculous to want to see whether it ought to have succeeded that body, since it has been indissolubly shown that it was never either instituted by God or taken up by the Jews, nevertheless, so that no one may complain that we have left something out, let us also go through these matters.

units.la: CAP. V. Confutatio argumentorum pro Presbyterio, ex novo Testamen- to conquisitorum.
units.tr: CAP. V. Refutation of the arguments for the presbytery, sought out from the New Testament.

units.la: Primo loco sic ratiocinaris. Necessaria fuit initio nascentis Ecclesiae cognitio de doctrina, de offendiculis: In summa opus fuit, vt aliqui Iudices conuenirent ad eligendos ministros, ad constituenda Diaconorum & viduarum Collegia. Ergo Presbyterium excommunicantium successit Synedrio Iudaeorum. Respondeo cognitionem fuisse necessariam: sed tuum modum fuisse necessarium, nego. Etenim scriptura nô neglexisset nobis eum exponere, si necessarius fuisset. Quę nobis tradidit, eum ego solum necessarium esse iudico. Docuit ea nos quid, quomodo, per quos, agendum sit cum falsis Doctoribus imputæ vitæ hominibus: at non docuit vestrum Presbyterium instituere, multò minus docuit peccatores poenitentes tantisperà Sacramentis arcere, dum vestris Presbyteris digni censeantur. Et quo pacto sequitur, oportet aliquos esse Iudices in Ecclesia, qui de his rebus cognoscant, ministros eligant, Diaconorum & Viduarũ Collegia curent: Ergo presbyterium excōmunicantium succesfsit in locum Synedrij Iudaici? Hoc perinde est, ac si quis concludat, hoc esse animal, & proinde canem esse: cum possit equus esse aut asis, aut aliud quodpiam. Legimus Apostolos dedisse ministros Ecclesijs: & eosdem non totis Ecclesijs: sed earum ministris præcipisse, vt eis prospicerent cap. 1. ad Titum: at non legimus excommunicantium Presbyterorum Collegium hoc facere debuisse.
units.tr: In the first place you reason thus. At the beginning of the nascent Church, knowledge of doctrine and of stumbling-blocks was necessary; in short, there was need for some judges to meet in order to choose ministers and to set up the colleges of deacons and widows. Therefore the presbytery of excommunicators succeeded the Synedrion of the Jews. I answer that the knowledge was necessary, but that your manner of it was necessary, I deny. For Scripture would not have neglected to set this out for us, if it were necessary. What it has handed down to us, I judge alone to be necessary. It has taught us what, how and through whom we must deal with false teachers and men of impure life; but it has not taught us to set up your presbytery, much less taught that penitent sinners are to be kept from the sacraments for so long as they are not judged worthy by your elders. And how does it follow that: there must be some judges in the Church who examine these matters, choose ministers, and take care of the colleges of deacons and widows; therefore the presbytery of excommunicators succeeded in the place of the Jewish Synedrion? This is just as if someone concluded: this is an animal, and therefore it is a dog, when it could be a horse, or an ass, or something else. We read that the Apostles gave ministers to the churches, and not to whole churches, but charged the ministers of them to look after them, Titus chapter 1; but we do not read that a college of excommunicating elders was bound to do this.

units.la: Quid post tempora Apostolorum sit factum, non valdè laboro in huius litis explicatione: quam solis scripturæ testimonijs dirimi oportet. Hoc interim ex te velim audire, vbi gentium hoc tuum presbyterium fuerit? Equidem in Orientis Ecclesijs non fuisse, clarissimè docet historia Ecclesiastica: quæ hanc potestatem non tribuit presbyterorum aut aliorum consessui, sed Episcopis. His enim solis dictum fuisse putarunt Veteres, quicquid ligaueritis &c. Et sanè 18. Matth. (de altero loco nemo ambigit) tametsi Ecclesiæ mentio facta fuisset, non ad hanc, sed ad Apostolos verba hæc locutus est Christus. Si consideràre voles quæ historiae de presbytero poenitentiario vocato tradunt, omninò tibi displicebis. Si quod tale vnquam in Ecclesijs exstitit Presbyterium, in sola Africa fuit: in aliarum orbis regionum nulla. Quare nec veteris Ecclesiae exemplis te defendere poteris: de quibus tamen parum soliciti nunc sumus. Hoc enim solum quærimus, quod scriptura iubeat. Ad ministrorum electionem quod attinet, etiam tunc, cum excommunicatores in Ecclesia esent, non ab his, sed ab Ecclesia post Episcopos electos fuisse eos nouimus.
units.tr: What happened after the times of the Apostles I do not labour over much in the explanation of this dispute, which must be settled by the testimonies of Scripture alone. Meanwhile I should like to hear from you where in the nations this presbytery of yours was. Indeed, that it was not in the churches of the East, ecclesiastical history clearly teaches; it does not attribute this power to elders or to any other assembly, but to bishops. For the Ancients thought that the words "whatever you shall bind" were spoken to these alone. And indeed Matthew 18 (no one doubts about the other passage): although mention of the Church was made there, Christ spoke these words not to the Church but to the Apostles. If you wish to consider what the histories relate about the so-called penitentiary presbyter, you will be utterly displeased with yourself. If any such presbytery ever existed in the churches, it was in Africa alone; in no other region of the world. Wherefore you cannot defend yourself even by examples from the ancient Church; yet we are now not much concerned about these. For we seek only this: what Scripture commands. As for the election of ministers, even at that time, when there were excommunicators in the Church, we know that they were chosen not by these, but by the Church after the bishops had been chosen.

units.la: Quan-
units.tr: Quan-

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De Presbyterorum electione, ex quibus iudicium constare debeat, & quando institutum fuerit.
units.tr: On the election of elders: from whom the judgment ought to consist, and when it was instituted.

units.la: Vanquam vero de nominibus nô valdè sum anxius, cum de re constet, tamen obseruandum est, magnum esse discrimen inter iudices, qui, an aliquos ad ministerium sit aptus, & quomodo pauperibus atque Viduis sit subueniendum, iudicant: & illos Censores, qui in confesso publico cum authoritate & coactione sententias dicunt de repellendis vel admittendis ad Sacramenta: quique verò poenitentes à simulatoribus dignoscere posse putantur. Ergo nullo in loco dixi, Ecclesiam sceleratos debere interficere, cum magistratu caret. Hoc autem dixi, licere Ecclesiae comprecari Deum, vt qui enorme aliquod scelus perpetrauit, puniatur, quomodo ipsi videatur. An non semper in publicis precibus hoc solet Ecclesia facere, scilicet orare Deum, vt hostes Euangelij vel conuertat, vel perdat? Cur non idem contra immaniter facinorosos facere possit? Certè Apostolus Corinthios non reprehendit, quod non interfecerint incestuosum; sed quod non rogarint Deum, vt eum è medio sui tolleret. De cæteris, quæ hic præterea scribis, soepè iam est dictum.
units.tr: Although I am not very anxious about names, since we agree on the thing itself, it must still be observed that there is a great difference between those judges who decide whether someone is fit for the ministry or how the poor and widows are to be helped, and those censors who, in public confession, pronounce sentences of exclusion or admission to the sacraments with authority and compulsion, and who are thought able to tell true penitents from pretenders. So I nowhere said that the Church ought to put the wicked to death, since it lacks the magistrate's sword. What I did say is that the Church may pray God to punish whoever has committed some monstrous crime, in whatever way God sees fit. Does the Church not always do this in its public prayers, praying God either to convert or to destroy the enemies of the gospel? Why, then, could it not do the same against men notoriously guilty of wicked deeds? Certainly the Apostle does not rebuke the Corinthians for failing to kill the incestuous man, but for failing to pray God to take him out of their midst. As for the rest of what you write here, I have already said it many times.

units.la: Secundo loco probare conaris, Presbyteros excommunicatores à Paulo non fuisse tunc institutos, cum in 1. Cor. 6. aliquos litibus <bl>σιφι</bl> præfecit: quod libenter tibi concedo: quia verum est, & à me firmius probatum, quàm hoc in loco tu probes.
units.tr: Second, you try to prove that the elders who excommunicate were not instituted by Paul at the time when, in 1 Cor. 6, he set certain men over the lawsuits. I gladly grant you this, because it is true, and I have proved it more firmly than you prove the opposite here.

units.la: Tertiò, ne Diaconos quidem ad hoc eligi affirmas, vt vestri Presbyterij munus gerant: quod & ego sentio ac dico.
units.tr: Third, you assert that deacons too are not chosen for this purpose, namely to perform the office of your eldership. I also think and say the same.

units.la: Quartò contendis non solis ministris hanc demandatam esse prouinciam, tametsi ad hos præcipuè spectet veram doctrinam tueri, offendiculis priuatis & publicis mederi, arguere, monere, increpare, adeoque ligare & soluere. Concedo hæc quoque omnia, nisi quod nec solis ministris nec vnà cum aliis data est authoritas excommunicandi. Quomodo soluant ac ligent ministri & alij, supra exposui. Quinam igitur iudicio sijo sunt ministris adiungendi? Pastores, inquis, seu Prophetæ, & peculiariter nominati Doctores. Sed quomodo hoc probas? Respondes, te sequentibus argumentis probaturum: quæ priusquam consideremus, argumentum quoddam meum me defendere oportet: quod hoc loco tu protua consuetudine immeritò equidem sugillas. Est autem tale.
units.tr: Fourth, you contend that this charge has been committed not to the ministers alone, although it chiefly belongs to them to guard true doctrine, to remedy private and public offences, to rebuke, admonish, reprove, and so to bind and loose. I grant all of these things too, except that authority to excommunicate has been given neither to the ministers alone nor together with others. How ministers and others bind and loose I have set out above. Who, then, in your judgment, are to be joined to the ministers? "Pastors," you say, "or prophets, and especially named teachers." But how do you prove this? You reply that you will prove it by the following arguments. Before we consider them, I must defend one of my own arguments, which you, by your usual practice, unjustly carp at. It is this.

units.la: In nouo Testamento, quoties nomen Presbyteri pro munere seu officio sacro, non pro ætate, ponitur, nusquam positum inuenimus pro alijs, quàm pro ministrantibus verbo. Ergo falsum est, Apostolos præter verbi ministros alios quosdam Presbyteros eligi mandasse, quorum aliud esset munus. Excipio interim hic, vt alias semper, Arbitros litium apud Corinthios ordinatos: si quis fortasse velit hos Presbyteros nominare. Hoc argumentum tu sic refelli putauisti. Non magis efficax, inquis, est hoc argumentum, quàm si pariter concludas, nullos fuisse alios Presbyteros, quàm Apostolos, quoniam & isti interdum Presbyteri dicuntur. Mirificus es disputator. Non sic argumentatus sum: ministri aliquando vocantur presbyteri. Ergo præter ministros nulli alij sunt presbyteri. Sed ad tua. Negare non potes, quin presbyteri vocentur in scriptura alij quidam præter Apostolos: & nihilominus affirmare audes, simile tuum esse argumentum meo. Ego sic dico: vbicunque presbyteri fit mentio, semper significat eum, qui verbum tractat. Ergo præter hos nullus reperitur presbyter in nouo Testamento. Si tuum vis simile esse, sic erit formandum. Vbicunque nomen presbyteri ponitur in nouo Testamento, semper significat Apostolum. Ergo præter Apostolos nulli nominantur presbyteri in nouo foedere. An non vides Antecedens tuum manifeste falsum: meum autem perspicuè verum esse? Apage cum istis refutationibus. Si voles, quod post Apostolorum tempora Ecclesiae fecerint, obseruare, intelliges nunquam Veteres nomen presbyteri aliter vsurpasse. Quippe historia Ecclesiastica presbyteros præter ministros verbi nullos nouit. Sed nec Africani Iudices, de quibus loquuntur, presbyteros vocarunt: nisi re vera tales, hoc est, verbi ministri simul essent. Figmentum igitur hoc vestrum vobis relinquimus.
units.tr: In the New Testament, whenever the name "elder" is used of a sacred office or function, not of age, we find it nowhere used of anyone but those who minister the Word. Therefore it is false that the Apostles commanded any other elders to be chosen besides the ministers of the Word, elders with a different function. Meanwhile I here except, as I always do, the judges of lawsuits appointed among the Corinthians, if anyone perhaps wishes to call them elders. You thought this argument could be refuted thus: "This argument," you say, "is no more effective than if you concluded in the same way that there were no elders except the Apostles, since they too are sometimes called elders. You are a wonderful debater." I did not argue like that. My argument is: ministers are sometimes called elders; therefore, besides the ministers there are no other elders. But let us come to yours. You cannot deny that other men besides the Apostles are called elders in Scripture, and yet you dare to affirm that your argument is similar to mine. I put it like this: wherever mention is made of elders, it always signifies the one who handles the Word; therefore no elder is found in the New Testament besides these. If you wish your argument to be similar, it must be formed thus: wherever the name "elder" is placed in the New Testament, it always signifies an Apostle; therefore no one besides the Apostles is named an elder in the New Testament. Do you not see that your antecedent is manifestly false, and mine plainly true? Away with such refutations! If you will observe what the Church did after the time of the Apostles, you will understand that the ancients never used the name "elder" otherwise. Indeed, ecclesiastical history knows no elders apart from the ministers of the Word. Nor did the African judges, of whom they speak, call them elders, unless in fact they were such, that is, at the same time ministers of the Word. We therefore leave this fiction of yours to yourselves.

units.la: Primum argumentum tuum hoc est. Ad Synedrium Iudaeorum legebantur præter Leuitas & Sacerdotes aliarum Tribuum præcipuae authoritatis viri. Ergo præter ministros continet presbyterium Prophetas & Doctores. Mirandum est, si non aduertisti, quàm hic sis miser. Primum enim negasti supra ad Prophetas testamenti veteris pertinuisse hanc potestatem, sed fuisse eam Sacerdotum duntaxat ex institutione Mosis. Proinde locum te monstrare conuenit, qui Prophetis noui foederis tribuat hanc facultatem, quam prioribus Deus negauerat. Deinde nullos hodie habemus Prophetas, præter scripturarum interpretes, id est, publicos Ministros & doctores. Tertio si adiungendi sunt Ministris Doctores, ne solis illis vribus instirui poterit presbyterium vestrum, in quibus scholæ publicæ sunt. Nam alibi vix reperies Doctores seu docentes Theologiam publicè præter ministros. Quid igitur vrbibus atque regionibus alijs fiet? Quarto pugnant hæc expresse cum eo, quod supra dixisti, scilicet de cötemptoribus verbi Dei & Sacramentorum cognoscere, ad illos necessariò pertinere, quorum sit Sacramenta & verbum dispensare. Nam Doctores non administrant Sacramenta, quicunque non sunt etiam ministri. Quinto non satis conueniunt cum ijs quae ad Galliæ principes in quadam præfatione scribis, vbi Magistratus quoque participes facis huius dignitatis. Sexto, aduersatur his tuis verbis, quae in Epistolis tuis post hoc scriptum exaratis leguntur. Presbyterium partim ex pastoribus partim ex Presbyteris proprie sic appellatis, quos Paulus gubernationes vocat, compositum est. Septimo non habemus etiam pastores alios quam ministros & Magistratus.
units.tr: Your first argument is this: to the Jewish Sanhedrin there were summoned, besides the Levites and priests, men of chief authority from the other tribes; therefore the eldership contains, besides the ministers, prophets and teachers. It is remarkable, if you did not notice how wretched you are here. For first, you denied above that this power belonged to the prophets of the Old Testament, asserting that it belonged to the priests alone by the institution of Moses. Therefore it is fitting that you show a passage which grants this faculty to the prophets of the New Covenant, a faculty which God had denied to the former. Second, today we have no prophets except the interpreters of Scripture, that is, public ministers and teachers. Third, if teachers are to be joined to the ministers, your eldership cannot be set up from those alone in whose places there are public schools. For you will scarcely find teachers, or those who teach theology publicly, anywhere else apart from the ministers. What then will happen to other cities and regions? Fourth, these things clearly conflict with what you said above, namely that the knowledge of those who despise the Word of God and the sacraments belongs necessarily to those whose task it is to dispense the sacraments and the Word. For teachers do not administer the sacraments unless they are also ministers. Fifth, they do not agree well with what you write in a certain preface to the princes of Gaul, where you make the magistrates also sharers in this dignity. Sixth, your words are contrary to what is read in your letters written after this. The eldership is composed partly of pastors and partly of elders properly so called, whom Paul calls "governments." Seventh, we have no pastors other than the ministers and the magistrates.

units.la: Iam ad argumentum tuum venio. Nec antecedens, nec consequens, nec consecutio vera est. Etenim apud Iudaeos Synedrium sacrum tale nullum fuisse demonstrauimus, quale nobis Presbyterium vos fingitis. Deinde quomodo tibi constas? Supra volebas Synedrium hoc Iudaeorum à Mose institutum & mandatum fuisse Leuit. 10. vbi Aharoni & filijs eius mandat, vt populum doceant legem intelligere, & munda ab immundis discernere: quae verba soli Aharoni & filijs ac successoribus eius dixit: nec in se continent praeceptum de erigendo Iudicio publico de moribus. Hic autem vis etiam Leuitas, & praeter hos Principes aliarum Tribuum seu familiarum coniungi: quod etiam supra in historia Iosaphati simili errore dixisti. Consequens falsum censebunt omnes homines, nisi testimonium ex sacris literis producas. Consequentiam etiam pueri intelligent falsam esse.
units.tr: Now I come to your argument. Neither the antecedent, nor the consequent, nor the inference is true. For we have shown that among the Jews there was no sacred Sanhedrin of the kind you imagine for us as an eldership. Next, how do you hold to your own position? Above you wanted this Jewish Sanhedrin to have been instituted and commanded by Moses in Leviticus 10, where he commands Aaron and his sons to teach the people to understand the law and to distinguish the clean from the unclean. But these words he spoke only to Aaron and his sons and successors; they do not contain a command to set up a public court concerning morals. Here, however, you want the Levites, and besides them the princes of the other tribes or families, to be joined in as well, which you also did above in the story of Jehoshaphat with a similar error. Everyone will judge the consequence false unless you produce testimony from the sacred writings. Even boys will understand that the inference is false.

units.la: Alterum est tale. Si non ex toto corpore aliqui delecti sedeant, vix illis conueniet nomen vniuersale Ecclesiae. Ergo Prophetas & Doctores ibi sedere cum ministris oportet. Vt antecedens verum sit, quis vel consecutionem tibi largiatur, vel consequens admittat. Falsum est consequens: nec ex Antecedente vllo pacto sequitur. Puto obliuum te esse, quod supra dixisti, Ecclesiae nomen in Christi verbis significare Synedrium, non turbam totam. Quid ergo vetat, quo minus aliquot ministri sufficiant, cum apud veteres soli Episcopi repraesentarint hac in parte Ecclesiam?
units.tr: The second argument is this: if some chosen men do not sit from the whole body, the name of the universal Church will hardly fit them; therefore prophets and teachers must sit there with the ministers. For the antecedent to be true, who would either grant you the inference or admit the consequent? The consequent is false, and in no way does it follow from any antecedent. I suppose you have forgotten what you said above, that the name "Church" in the words of Christ signifies the Sanhedrin, not the whole crowd. What, then, prevents a few ministers from being enough, since among the ancients the bishops alone represented the Church in this respect?

units.la: Tertium, hoc velut fraeno cohercetur Pastorum & populi potestas. Ergo Deus iussit Prophetas & Doctores cum ministris distinctam iurisdictionem ab ea, quae magistratui debetur, de vicijs cohercendis exercere. Puto nunc tandem omnes risuros, cum ego summe cogor miserari vicem fortunamque tuam. Non vides falsa esse vniuersa? Alij contendunt hanc potestatem Ecclesiae seu populi esse: tu hac ipsa populi potestatem quasi fraeno vis coherceri.
units.tr: Third, the power of the ministers and of the people is restrained, as it were, by a bridle. Therefore God commanded that prophets and teachers, with the ministers, exercise over the restraining of vices a jurisdiction distinct from that which is owed to the magistrate. I suppose everyone will now at last laugh, since I am forced to pity your plight and your fortune in the highest degree. Do you not see that all these things are false? Others contend that this power belongs to the Church or to the people; you wish this very power of the people to be restrained, as it were, by a bridle.

units.la: Quartum & quintum tale est. Apostolus in Epist. ad Romanos, & in 1. ad Corinth, 12. meminit τὼν χαρισμάτων ἢ τὼν ἰδιῶν manifestè à cæteris donis distinguens. Ergo ad Ministros allegi oportet ad Presbyterium excómunicantium Prophetas & Doctores. Responsio eadem est, quæ supra. Nam consecutio impossibilis est probatu. Quoniam ut in præsentia cætera sileam, quibus testimonijs probabis, Paulū per gubernationes intellexisse tale Presbyterium, de quali vos loquimini? Potius cœlum terra erit, quam istud ex sacris literis tu sis demonstraturus. Valde namq; multa sunt genera Gubernatorum. (Miror cur non etiam τὸς ἀνθρώπους addduxeris. Etenim nulla maior est ἀνάγκης sub cœlo facultate Excómunicandi: quæ omnes potestates orbis Christiani terruit) Sed nec verius est consequens. Qui namque probabis Prophetas & Doctores significatos fuisse per χαρίσματα & ἰδιοφίλους? Imò verò quomodo te ipsū à contradictione vindicabis? Supra dixisti prouinciam hanc à Deo per Mosen solis Sacerdotibus impositam fuisse: quando Levit. 10. eos iusit munda ab immundis distinguere, ac populum legem voluntatem Dei docere. Postmodum etiam Leuitas & Patriarchas addidisti veteribus. In novo fœdere negas solis Ministris concessum esse ius hoc Presbyterij seu excómunicandi: sed cooptandos esse præterea Prophetas & Doctores. Deinde his etiā adiungis τὰς ἰδιοφίλους apud Paulum & τὰς χαρισμάτων, velut alios à Ministris, Prophetis, Pastoribus, & Doctorib². Quod si Prophetæ & Doctores docent, non fuerunt addendi velut diuersi à Ministris & docentibus: nisi forte ob hanc causam distinguas, quod non administrant Sacramenta. At hoc quomodo verum defendes, τὰς χαρισμάτων alios esse à Ministris? An non Apostolus Ministros vocat χαρισμάτων in 1. ad Tim. 5. & 1. ad Thess. 5. cap. Postremò an in Presbyterio Allobrogico soli Prophetæ & Doctores cum Ministris sedeant, (Audio non ita esse) affirmare non possum: alibi non observari certo scio. Fideli opus est memoria falsâ defendentibus. Nam vt vera vbique consonant, sic falsa passim discordant.
units.tr: The fourth and fifth arguments are of the same kind. The Apostle, in the Epistle to the Romans and in 1 Corinthians 12, mentions the gifts [τῶν χαρισμάτων] and the (...) [τῶν ἰδιοφίλους], clearly distinguishing them from the other gifts. Therefore, you must say, the Prophets and Teachers ought to be chosen along with the Ministers to the eldership that excommunicates. My answer is the same as before, for the inference cannot be proved. Leaving aside for now the other points, by what testimonies will you prove that Paul by "governments" meant such an eldership as you speak of? Heaven will sooner become earth than you will demonstrate this from the sacred letters. There are indeed many kinds of governors. (I am surprised you did not also bring in [τοὺς ἀνθρώπους]. For no power under heaven is greater than the power of excommunicating, a power which has terrified all the powers of the Christian world.) But the consequence is not more true either. For how will you prove that the Prophets and Teachers are meant by "gifts" and [ἰδιοφίλους]? Indeed, how will you rescue yourself from contradiction? Above you said that this charge was laid by God through Moses on the Priests alone, since in Leviticus 10 he commanded them to distinguish the clean from the unclean and to teach the people the law and the will of God. Afterwards you also added the Levites and the Patriarchs to the Old Testament. In the New Testament you deny that the right of this eldership or of excommunicating belongs to the Ministers alone, but say that Prophets and Teachers must also be co-opted. Then you add to these also [τὰς ἰδιοφίλους] in Paul and [τὰς χαρισμάτων], as if they were different from Ministers, Prophets, Pastors and Teachers. But if the Prophets and Teachers teach, they ought not to have been added as different from the Ministers and teachers, unless perhaps you distinguish them on this ground, that they do not administer the Sacraments. But how will you defend the truth of this, that the gifts [τὰς χαρισμάτων] are other than the Ministers? Does not the Apostle call Ministers "gifts" [χαρισμάτων] in 1 Timothy 5 and 1 Thessalonians 5? Finally, whether in the Allobrogian eldership only the Prophets and Teachers sit with the Ministers (I hear this is not so), I cannot affirm; I know for certain it is not observed elsewhere. Those who defend falsehood need a faithful memory. For as truths everywhere agree, so falsehoods everywhere disagree.

units.la: Vltimum argumentū (nisi deinceps alia inveniam: quæ non sint in margine annotata) hoc est. Paulus in 1. ad Tim. 5. scribit, Presbyteros, qui bene praesunt, duplici honore dignos esse, maximè verò τὴν διπλῆν τιμὴν ... Ergo ad Presbyterium nostrum iussit Deus cum Ministris allegi Prophetas & Doctores. Haec enim tua fuit Propositio, cuius nobis probationem pollicebatur. Proinde optima fide tua argumenta recitasti: quod ideo moneo, ne quis, cum parum venusta & appositá videbit, arbitretur me non rectè repetiuisse. Antequam respondeam ad argumentum, illud obiter tantum monebo, te supra dixisse, inter eos non posse numerari, qui docent: hic autem Paulus ex tua sententia ipsos numerat non tantum inter eos, qui diligenter docent, sed & inter eos, qui pulchrè & bene praesunt siue gubernant. Nam in doctrina & verbo sedulò laborantes, dicit, bene praesse. Iam ad rem.
units.tr: The last argument (unless I find others later which are not noted in the margin) is this. Paul, in 1 Timothy 5, writes that elders who rule well are worthy of double honour, and above all [τὴν διπλῆν τιμὴν] ... Therefore God commanded that Prophets and Teachers be chosen along with the Ministers to our eldership. For this was your proposition, the proof of which you promised us. Accordingly, in good faith you recited your arguments, and I warn of this so that no one, seeing them as rather inelegant and ill-fitting, may think I have not quoted them correctly. Before I answer the argument, I will only note in passing that you said above that those who teach cannot be counted among those who rule; yet here Paul, on your view, counts among those who rule well not only those who teach diligently, but also those who govern well or rule. For he says that those who labour diligently in doctrine and the word rule well. Now to the matter.

units.la: Hoc argumentum in Thesibus refutaui, dicens, κοπιᾷν, consignificare diligentiam & laborem adeoque defatigationem: unde Graeci κόπος appellant affectum quem Latini lassitudinem nominant. Hinc Chrysostomus non κοπιῶντας vocat delicatos aut remissos, qui contra gelu & spinas iugum non sustinent. Ad id tu respondes: non negare te emphasin hic esse in verbo κοπιᾷν minimè negligendam: at si mea expositio valeat, frustra addita haec esse, ... Absurdum enim hanc esse orationem. Omnibus verbum Dei docentibus benè cupio, praesertim verò diligenter verbum Dei docentibus. Loquendum sic esse potius: omnibus verbum Dei docentibus benè cupio, ijs praesertim qui diligenter docent.
units.tr: I refuted this argument in my Theses, saying that [κοπιᾷν] signifies diligence and labour, and so also weariness; hence the Greeks call [κόπος] the condition which the Latins call lassitude. Hence Chrysostom does not call those who labour [κοπιῶντας] the soft or the slack, who do not endure the yoke against frost and thorns. To this you reply that you do not deny that emphasis is to be placed on the word [κοπιᾷν], by no means to be neglected here, but that if my exposition holds, these words are added in vain ... For, you say, the sentence would be absurd: "I wish well to all who teach the word of God, especially to those who teach the word of God diligently." It should rather be put thus: "I wish well to all who teach the word of God, especially to those who teach diligently."

units.la: Primò quidem non proposui ego exemplum orationis tale, qualem tuum est. Haec namque mea sunt. Pastoribus omnibus benè volo, ijs praesertim, qui summa fide, industria, labore, oves suae fidei creditas pascunt. Omnes studiosos amo, praesertim verò dies & noctes studijs suis inuigilantes. Non prorsus eadem verba sunt, Pastor, & pascere: item studiosus, & studere. Itaque non est talis verborum ταυτολογία qualem tu proponis; Sic Apostolus diuersa ponit, κάλως προεστῶτες, & κοπιῶντας ἐν λόγῳ ... Vides iam, non meam expositionem, sed tuam accusationem, vanam & inanem esse? Quod si etiam quis hoc modo loquitur: omnibus qui verbum Dei recte sincere que docent, bene et apte ijs praefertur, qui id magna sedulitate docent, an absurde locutus videbitur? Non puto. Sic enim loqui solemus omnes aliquando. Hoc tantum discrimen est, quod vocidae, verbum Dei, non repetuntur; sed pro ijs ponitur pronomen: Idi Quia recte docere omnes Ministri possunt; & inter hos nihilominus alij alijs in munere suo diligentiores esse possunt, ideo dicit Apostolus omnes tales duplici honorario dignos esse: illos praesertim, qui in suo officio docendi & exhortandi sunt magis seduli, immo ad defatigationem usque laboriosi. Docui pluribus ex scriptura locis, non posse nec debere alitet locum hunc exponi: praecipue vero id probare clare is, qui in 1. ad Thess. 5. habetur, Rogamus autem vos fratres [illegible, ~12 letters] &c. Qui non videt hunc locum exponere illum, sive quia num esse alterius interpretem, is plusquam exctus est.
units.tr: In the first place, I did not put forward an example of such a sentence as yours. For mine are these: "I wish well to all pastors, especially to those who with the greatest faith, industry and labour feed the sheep entrusted to their faith. I love all students, especially those who watch over their studies day and night." The words are not altogether the same: pastor and to feed, likewise student and to study. So it is not the kind of tautology you propose. Thus the Apostle sets out different things: "those who rule well" [καλῶς προεστῶτες] and "those who labour in the word" [κοπιῶντας ἐν λόγῳ]. Do you now see that not my exposition but your accusation is vain and empty? But if someone speaks in this way: "to all who teach the word of God rightly and sincerely, he is well and fittingly preferred who teaches it with great diligence," will he seem to have spoken absurdly? I do not think so. For we all sometimes speak like this. The only difference is that the noun, "the word of God," is not repeated, but a pronoun is put in its place. Because all Ministers can teach rightly, yet among these some can nevertheless be more diligent than others in their office, the Apostle therefore says that all such men are worthy of double honour, but especially those who are more zealous in their office of teaching and exhorting, indeed labouring even to weariness. I have shown from many places of Scripture that this passage cannot be explained otherwise, and especially that 1 Thessalonians 5 clearly proves this, where it is written: "But we beseech you, brethren [illegible, about twelve letters], etc." Whoever does not see that this passage explains that one, or that the one is the interpreter of the other, is more than blind.

units.la: Quem habes (quaeso te) tuae expositionis authorem apud Veteres? Nullum. Quoniam duplex hoc Presbyterorum genus ignorarunt; sed ingenue confitentur omnes Presbyteros esse Sacerdotes: Legito Athanasium, Chrysostomum, Theophylactum, Oecumenium, Ambrosium. Etsi enim hic Seniorum facit mentionem, attamen & de longe alijs intellexit, & Paulum de ijs hic loqui non dicit. Ipse namque in lib. de dignitate Sacerdotali asserit omnes Presbyteros esse Sacerdotes: An non satis indicat Apostolus, se de eiusdem ordinis hominibus loqui, cum idem & aequale omnibus praemium tribuit? Ineptit qui putat ipsum voluisse eodem praemio honorari Vestros Presbyteros, sipio Ministros iudicavit dignos. Quaeso vero quisquam hodie idem y trisque stipendium decernat. Denique ipsum quoque testimonium de bonoris tribuit, quod alibi quoq; Ministris verbi accommodat, nopnihil sententia declarat. Taceo iam, quod plerique omnes recentiores, vestris exceptis, duplicem hunc Presbyterorum ordinem reijciunt, quod nuper admodum Witten-
units.tr: What author of your exposition (I ask you) do you have among the Ancients? None. For they were unaware of this twofold kind of elders; rather they all frankly confess that elders are priests. Read Athanasius, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Ambrose. For although here he makes mention of the elders, nevertheless he understood it of quite different men, and does not say that Paul is speaking here of them. For in his book on the priestly dignity he asserts that all elders are priests. Does not the Apostle sufficiently indicate that he is speaking of men of the same order, when he assigns the same and equal reward to all? He is foolish who thinks he meant that your elders, whom he judged worthy of the same honour as the Ministers of the word, should be honoured with that reward. Indeed who today would decree the same stipend for both? Finally, the testimony itself, which he elsewhere also applies to the Ministers of the word, somewhat declares its sense. I say nothing yet of the fact that almost all the more recent writers, except your own, reject this twofold order of elders, as the Theologians of Württemberg recently bore splendid witness against the Jesuits.

units.la: Wirtenbergenses Theologi contra Iesuitas praeclarè testati sunt, Sic vides tertium causae vestrae fundamentum te prorsus perdidisse, ac proinde spe omni excidisse.
units.tr: So you see that you have utterly lost the third foundation of your cause, and consequently have fallen from every hope.

units.la: Sex argumenta tua, quibus probare volebas, ad Presbyterium vestrum praeter verbi Ministros allegendos esse Prophetas & Doctores peculiariter vocatos, in fumum abierunt, & nusquam comparent amplius, à veritatis lumine dissipata.
units.tr: Your six arguments, by which you wished to prove that Prophets and specially called Teachers ought to be chosen for your eldership besides the Ministers of the word, have gone up in smoke, and nowhere appear any more, scattered by the light of truth.

units.la: Quare de aliis tibi cogitandum noris.
units.tr: Therefore you may know that you must think of other things.

units.la: Ab his tuis argumentis transfis ad reprehensionem eius, quod dixi, nō debere duos Magistratus seu duas iurisdictiones in vna Repub. poni, quae coactionem ambae habeant. Esse enim Excommunicationem velut exilium quoddam. Cum ergo primū hic quaeris, an biceps fuerit populus Israeliticus praecipuè sub Rege Iosaphato, cum vnus Regis, alter Dei negotijs distinctè praeessent: respondeo tibi non suisse bicipitem. Addo etiam distincta de moribus Iudicij neque alijs neque tunc in illo populo fuisse: vt satis supra declarauì. At iudicia, inquis, de mundis & immundis ostendimus apud Synedrium fuisse. Quo loco ostendistī? Leuit. 10. Ezech. 44. demonstratur Sacerdotibus hoc iudicium esse commissum. At Iudicium de moribus cum eorundem coercitione Sacerdotibus permissum esse in aeternum non docebis, Dico sic, vt haberent Iudicium hoc distinctum à politico iudicio. Nam Sacerdotes etiam fuisse Iudices & Praefectos, munerâque obiuisse Politica omnia, & per se solos, & cum alijs, & sub Regibus, sic est notum, & à nobis ita demonstratum, vt qui deinceps negare audeat, merito iudicetur simulare, vt lenissimè dicam.
units.tr: From these arguments of yours I pass to your rebuke of what I said: that two magistrates or two jurisdictions, each having coercive power, should not be set up in one commonwealth. For excommunication is, as it were, a kind of exile. Therefore, when you first ask here whether the people of Israel was two-headed, especially under King Jehoshaphat, when one had charge of the king's affairs and the other of God's affairs separately, I answer you that it was not two-headed. I add also that there was no separate jurisdiction over morals either among that people or at that time, as I have sufficiently declared above. But, you say, we have shown that judgments concerning clean and unclean were held before the Sanhedrin. Where did you show this? Leviticus 10 and Ezekiel 44 show that this judgment was committed to the Priests. But you will not prove that the judgment concerning morals, with its coercion, was permitted to the Priests for ever. I say this: they had this judgment distinct from the political judgment. For that the Priests also were judges and prefects, and discharged all political duties, both by themselves alone, and with others, and under kings, is so well known and has been so demonstrated by us, that whoever dares deny it afterwards deserves to be judged as pretending, to put it most gently.

units.la: Adfers etiam exemplū Vziae Regis suffire volentis, & Sacerdotis prohibentis. Verū quorsum haec Deus aperte vetuerat omnib^9 praeterquā Aaronitis sacrificare & suffire alias; talia agere: caulam exposui iam ante. Iussit etiā Deus Sacerdotibus, vt legem alios docerent, & quid quisque facere deberet, indicarent omnibus. Rectè ergo dixit Azarias: Non est tuum suffire Ichouae: Sed Sacerdotum filiorum Aaronis, &c.
units.tr: You also adduce the example of King Uzziah, who wanted to burn incense, and the priest who forbade him. But why? God had clearly forbidden everyone except the sons of Aaron to sacrifice and burn incense, and to do such things otherwise. I explained the reason for this earlier. God also commanded the priests to teach the law to others and to tell everyone what each ought to do. So Azariah rightly said: "It is not yours to burn incense to Jehovah, but the sons of Aaron the priests, etc."

units.la: Ostende tu nobis eodem modo à Deo institutum vestrum Presbyterium, vt ordinatum legimus Aaronis Sacerdotiū: Deinde commonstra sic esse ei imperatum distinctum iudiciū à Iudicio Magistratus de moribus coercendis instituere, vt nos munus suffiendi imperatum ostendere possumus. Horum si nihil potes, quid nobis ista obijcis?
units.tr: Show us that your eldership was instituted by God in the same way as we read that the priesthood of Aaron was ordained. Then demonstrate that it was likewise commanded to establish a judgment distinct from the magistrate's judgment for correcting morals, just as we can show that the duty of burning incense was commanded. If you can do none of these, why do you throw these things at us?

units.la: Dauidem, dixi ego, nec per Prophetam Nathan, nec per Sacerdotes, aut alium quemlibet iussit Deus excommunicari. Respondes, Prophetam non habuisse ius hoc. Recte: sed nec ius habuit puniendi: tamen denunciauit ei sententiam Domini: denunciaturus etiam excommunicationem erat, si iussus fuisset. Quod si aliud non est, quam promulgatio Excommunicationis in coelo factæ, qui magis conueniebat alijs, quam Prophetis? Certè Prophetæ sæpius talia denunciarunt iudicia, quam vlli alij. Nugaris igitur, Iccirco rectius alij respondent, ideo non Excommunicari debuisse, quia resipuerit. At de Manasse alijsque talibus quid dicent? Item quomodo excusabitis Prophetas, quod nullo in loco Sacerdotes hoc nomine accusarunt, quod videlicet promiscuè omnes ad Sacrificia admiserint, nullum repulerint, aut repelli iusserint mundum iuxta Legem?
units.tr: I said that God commanded David to be excommunicated neither through the prophet Nathan, nor through the priests, nor through anyone else. You reply that the prophet did not have this right. Quite so, but neither did he have the right to punish; yet he announced to David the sentence of the Lord, and he would have announced excommunication too, had he been commanded to do so. But if excommunication is nothing other than the publication of a sentence made in heaven, who was better suited to it than the prophets? Certainly the prophets announced such judgments more often than anyone else. So you are trifling. Others answer more rightly that he ought not to have been excommunicated because he repented. But what will they say about Manasseh and others like him? Likewise, how will you excuse the prophets, who in no place accused the priests of this offence, namely that they admitted everyone indiscriminately to the sacrifices, rejected no one, and never ordered that the unclean, according to the Law, be turned away?

units.la: Ex Psalm. 51. ais, liquet manifestè, eum à Sacrificijs abstinuisse, vt immundis præscriptum erat vsquedum expiaretur. Hoc quia supra, vt aperte falsum neglexi, confutandum hic erit, cum sit à te, vt verum, repetitum. Quis tibi dixit, Dauidem toto illo tempore, quo in adulterio vixit, (quod ex historia colligimus prope annum durauisse) nunquam in Tabernaculum fuisse ingressum? nunquam sacrificasse, aliaque Sacramenta celebrauisse? An interea negocia nulla expedijt? An in mensa cum suis non edit? An pro Tribunali ius nulli dixit? An denique tum non regnauit, sed velut immundus solus sedit? Si affirmabis absque scripturis, vt te facere oportet, nemo tibi credet: præsertim cum ex scriptura coniecturæ diuersum indicantes desumi posint. Si factum fuisse occultum contendas, rursus absque scriptura loquêris: quæ indicia & argumenta nobis præbet diuersum affirmandi. Nam quod 2. Samuel. 12, dicitur: Tu fecisti clàm, ego coràm toto faciam Israele, de eo dicitur, quod Abfalon palàm fecit, 2. Samuelis 16. (vbi palàm cum concubinis patris sui rem habuit) ac non studuit celare, vt Dauid. Hic enim tegere suum factum reuocatione mariti Uriæ voluit.
units.tr: You say from Psalm 51 that it is clearly evident that David abstained from sacrifices, as was prescribed for the unclean until they were cleansed. Since I already set this aside above as manifestly false, it must be refuted here, since you repeat it as if it were true. Who told you that David, during the whole time he lived in adultery (which we gather from the history lasted nearly a year), never entered the Tabernacle, never offered sacrifice, and never celebrated the other sacraments? Did he transact no business in the meantime? Did he not eat at table with his people? Did he not administer justice from the tribunal? Or finally, did he not then reign, but sit alone like one unclean? If you affirm this without Scripture, as you must, no one will believe you, especially since conjectures pointing the other way can be drawn from Scripture. If you contend that the deed was hidden, again you speak without Scripture, which gives us indications and arguments for affirming the contrary. For what is said in 2. Samuel 12, "You did it secretly, but I will do it before all Israel," refers to the fact that Absalom did it openly, 2. Samuel 16 (where he had relations with his father's concubines in public), and did not strive to conceal it as David did. For here David wished to cover his deed by recalling Uriah, the husband.

units.la: An non post denunciationem Prophetæ scribitur ægrotauisse puerum, Dauidemq; statim à morte eius, ingressum fuisse Templum vt oraret? Certè qui in Templum oratum ingredi poterat, idem etiam sacrificatum introire poterat. His iam illud adde, quod non dicit Dauid in Psal. 51. se non audere sacrificare: sed dicit, Libera me Domine de sanguinibus, vt lingua mea prædicet laudes tuas. Quoniam si sacrificijs delectaueris, dedissem vtiq; : sed magis corde pœnitente oblectaris. Manifestè ostendit licuisse sibi Sacrificium offerre Domino, séque facere paratum fuisse, nisi sciuisset Deum magis delectari corde contrito, quam holocaustis. Confutat ergo Dauid, non probat ,tuam opinionem. Postea orat, vt Hierosolymæ muri perficiantur, (Qui tum nondum perfecti fuerunt, neque suos hostes tum integrè deuicerat, vt Uriæ historia declarat.) quo possint omnes tuò cultum à Mose institutum solenniter celebrare. Mirificum disputatorem esse oportet, qui serió se putet ex his conficere posse, Dauidem instar immundorum secundum Legem à Templo & ceremonijs abstinuisse. Probauì etiam supra, improbos non prohibitione Templi, sed poenis alijs coercitos fuisse: Hi enim non polluebant Templum & res alias, sicut immundi Legis. Quæ præterea hic allinis, ad rem nihil faciunt, aut falsa sunt.
units.tr: Is it not written that after the prophet's denunciation the boy fell ill, and that David, immediately after his death, went into the Temple to pray? Surely one who could enter the Temple to pray could also enter it to sacrifice. Add to this that David, in Psalm 51, does not say that he dared not sacrifice; he says, "Deliver me, O Lord, from blood, that my tongue may proclaim your praises. For if you had delighted in sacrifices, I would surely have given them; but you take pleasure rather in a repentant heart." He clearly shows that it was lawful for him to offer sacrifice to the Lord, and that he would have done so, had he not known that God delights more in a contrite heart than in whole burnt offerings. So David refutes your opinion; he does not prove it. Afterwards he prays that the walls of Jerusalem may be completed (they were not yet finished at that time, nor had he then wholly defeated his enemies, as the history of Uriah declares), so that all may solemnly celebrate the worship instituted by Moses. He must be a marvellous disputant who seriously thinks he can conclude from these things that David, like the unclean according to the Law, abstained from the Temple and the ceremonies. I have also shown above that the wicked were restrained not by exclusion from the Temple but by other penalties, for they did not defile the Temple or other things as the unclean of the Law did. The other things he adds here either have no bearing on the matter or are false.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Vtrum penes Presbyterium fuerit potestas Excommunicandi.
units.tr: Whether the power of excommunication belonged to the Presbytery.

units.la: V probaturus Presbyterium illud tuum potestatem habere excommunicandi, ad argumenta quædam mea prius respondes: deinde ad rem accedis. Quâquam non erat necesse, vt ad hæc refellenda descendere, cum ostenderim planissimè, hoc Presbyterium à Deo nunquā institutum esse,ac proinde potestatem hanc accipere non potuisse,attamen vt facilius tuam infelicitatem in defendendo falso dogmate perdiscas, agè hunc quoq; labore deuoremus. Argumentū meū hoc fuit. Apostolus Paulus cum de castigationib' loquitur,vt traditione Satanę, & similib', sibi eam soli tribuit:alijs nullis cōmendat: Ideo passim,scribit se duriter delinquentes tractaturū:in virga & authoritate venturū: cum potestate à Deo sibi tradita aćturū:cum luctu rediturū: se ait tradidisse Satanę: se decreuisse Corinthiū tradere: sibi iubet non obedientes indicari, non alijs vllis: verbo nullo in omnibus suis Epistolis huiusmodi castigationes alijs mandat. Ad hæc tu vide ne pro more tuo respondeas.
units.tr: You undertake to prove that your Presbytery has the power of excommunication, but first you answer some of my arguments and only then come to the matter itself. Yet there was no need to descend to refuting these, since I have shown very plainly that this Presbytery was never instituted by God, and so could not have received this power. Still, so that you may more easily learn how unhappy you are in defending a false doctrine, let us take on this labour as well. My argument was this. When the Apostle Paul speaks of punishments, such as delivery to Satan and the like, he assigns this power to himself alone and commends it to no others. So throughout his letters he writes that he will deal sternly with those who offend, that he will come with the rod and with authority, that he will act with the power given him by God, that he will come back in sorrow, that he has delivered someone to Satan, that he has decided to deliver the Corinthian, and that he orders the disobedient to be named to him and to no one else. In all his Epistles he never entrusts such punishments to anyone else. Be careful, then, that you do not answer in your usual way.

units.la: Nos verò quęrimus, inquis, an nō mortuis Apostolis illa potestas seu virga fuerit æquè necessaria ? Deinde ad quos fuerit translata ? Tu videris quid sis ex historia responsurus. Ideo autem non meminit Collegij huius, quoniam illi ipsi præcipuè minatur, vt quod non fungeretur officio suo.Respondeo, nobis multa videri necessaria, quæ Deo talia non sunt visa. Etenim si hęc potentia visa ei fuisset necessaria, Ecclesiæ tradidisset.At traditam nullo in loco legimus. Potuit interim Deus extra ordinem potestatem dare Apostolis improbos puniendi, sicut aliorum miraculorum virtutem dedit,quib',quatenus,quando,vbi,quomodo, voluit.Initio data est Apostolis, vt doćtrina, quæ videbatur noua, confirmaretur. Deus nouit melius nobis, quid vtile sit ac necessarium. Ergo respondeo tibi apertè,potestatem tradendi Satanę, quę Paulo fuit data, necessariam sic non fuisse Ecclesiæ, vt esset ordinaria potestas. Nam si talis exstitisset, commendata alicubi Ecclesię fuisset . Etenim necessariorum nihil omisit scriptura. Et causa cur non meminerit Collegij Presbyterorum hęc est, quod tale nec instituerat nec instituere cogitabat : id quod ex præcedentibus satis patet. Supra ex hoc loco volebas nos colligere Presbyterij vestri institutionem, hic non meminisse eius Apostolum rectè asseris: quæ quomodo sis conciliaturus, videris ipse. Quam belle in huius loci expositione vobis constetis, alibi obiter indicaui: quemadmodum de historia quoque multa iam ante diximus: quam si tuae opinioni patrocinari ostenderis, virum te esse dicemus.
units.tr: But, you say, we ask whether that power or rod was not equally necessary after the Apostles died, and to whom it was then transferred. You will have to see what you can answer from history. He does not mention this college because he threatens chiefly those who fail in their duty. I answer that many things seem necessary to us which did not seem so to God. For if this power had seemed necessary to him, he would have handed it on to the Church. Yet we read nowhere that it was handed on. God could in the meantime give the Apostles, outside the ordinary course, the power of punishing the wicked, just as he gave them the power of other miracles, to whom, as far as, when, where and how he willed. It was given to the Apostles at the beginning so that the teaching, which then seemed new, might be confirmed. God knows better than we what is useful and necessary. So I tell you plainly: the power of delivering to Satan that was given to Paul was not so necessary to the Church that it should be an ordinary power. For if it had been, it would have been commended somewhere to the Church, since Scripture omits nothing that is necessary. And the reason why he makes no mention of a college of Presbyters is that he neither instituted such a thing nor intended to, as is clear enough from what has gone before. Earlier you wanted us to infer the institution of your Presbytery from this passage, and now you rightly say that the Apostle does not mention it here. How you will reconcile these, you must see for yourself. I have elsewhere briefly shown how consistently you hold to your views on this passage, and I have already said much about the history too. If you show that it supports your opinion, we will call you a man.

units.la: Cum ergo quaeris, cur etiam caeteros iubeat in nomine Domini congregari? Respondeo, Apostolum haec verba, in nomine Domini non referre ad congregationem, sed dicere: Ego decreui patratorem huius sceleris in nomine Domini tradere Satanae collectis vobis & spiritu meo, cum virtute Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quod si deinde etiam potuissent Corinthij & spiritus Pauli eodem modo affecti cum virtute Christi colligi, potuissent plures alios ita tradere, quomodo hunc tradituri fuerant, si non ignouisset ei Apostolus. Caeterum non sic habuerunt Pauli spiritum secum postea: quod quidem constare nobis possit ex sacris literis. Quoniam nullo in loco eos sic iussit colligi: nec spiritus sui hoc modo affecti praesentiam promisit. Ideo autem voluit eos esse praesentes, vt abterrerentur caeteri a sceleribus, quod in facto Petri aduersus Ananiam, & Pauli contra Magum vsuuenit. Metuebat enim ne hoc scelus impunitum manens instar fermenti caeteros contaminaret. Quocirca non iussit Presbyteros solos, sed totam Ecclesiam colligi cum suo spiritu. Quam longissime differunt haec duae orationes: Decreui vobis & meo spiritu cum virtute Christi collectis hunc in nomine Domini Satanae tradere: & statui hunc hominem vestro consensu & suffragio Satanae tradere. Multo longius recedit haec a veritate: Volo vos Satanae vel hunc vel alios tradere.
units.tr: When you ask, then, why he also orders the others to be gathered in the name of the Lord, I answer that the Apostle does not refer the words "in the name of the Lord" to the gathering. He says: "I have decided to deliver the perpetrator of this crime to Satan in the name of the Lord, when you are gathered together and my spirit is with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ." If the Corinthians, and the spirit of Paul, were then also gathered together in the same disposition with the power of Christ, they could have delivered many others in the same way as they were going to deliver this man, had the Apostle not pardoned him. But afterwards they did not have the spirit of Paul with them in this way, as we can know from the sacred letters. For he nowhere ordered them to be gathered in this manner, nor did he promise the presence of his spirit in such a case. He wanted them to be present so that the others might be frightened away from sins, as happened in Peter's dealing with Ananias and in Paul's against the magician. For he feared that this crime, if left unpunished, would like leaven contaminate the rest. Therefore he did not order only the Presbyters to be gathered, but the whole Church, with his spirit. These two statements differ very far from each other: "I have decided, when you are gathered with me and my spirit, with the power of Christ, to deliver this man in the name of the Lord to Satan," and "I have resolved to deliver this man to Satan by your consent and vote." Your statement departs even further from the truth: "I want you to deliver either this man or others to Satan."

units.la: Cur ergo illos obiurgat, quod non pridie fecissent? Respondeo, non obiurgat, quod non tradiderint Satanae hoc modo, quo ipse tradere in animo habebat: sed quod non comprecati Deum fuissent, vt enormę hoc scelus puniret. Si hoc secissent, siue Deus exaudisset eos, siue non exaudisset, fuissent ipsi suo munere perfuncti. Saltem constitisset omnibus, sibi turpe scelus illud ex animo displicuisse.
units.tr: Why, then, does he rebuke them for not having done it the day before? I answer that he does not rebuke them for not delivering the man to Satan in the way he himself intended to deliver him, but for not having called upon God to punish so enormous a crime. Had they done so, then whether God heard them or not, they would themselves have discharged their duty. At the least it would have been clear to everyone that they were heartily displeased by that shameful crime.

units.la: Cur ergo de flagiciosis a cōuictu priuato arcendis agens, & quidem occulta Dei iudicia a manifestis distinguens, diserte scriberet, An non de ijs,qui intus sunt iudicatis? Cur eos iubet vitari? Cur σημεῖα praeciperet? Haec tua sunt. Nescio quae nobis occulta Dei iudicia hic narres. Apostolus loquitur de apertis iudicijs membrorum Ecclesiae. Nec aliud dicit, quàm si dixisset hoc vel simili modo: Cum vos dixi fugere debere Scortatores, Adulteros &c. intelligo eos, qui inter vos sunt, & fratres nominantur. Horum debetis vitam & mores obseruare, & quos impuros esse cognouistis vitare, ne vos quoque inficiamini: ipsi autem pudefiant & in viam redeant. Hoc est iudicium de quo ibi loquitur Apostolus: nempe fuga priuatae sodalitatis testificari, illum talem nomine suo indignè viuere. Sic iudicare suos iubet, non exteros, cum suo iudicio hic nihil profecisset, sed derisi magis fuissent. Iubet autem per Epistolam indicari tales (Quanquam aperte falsum est, σημεῖα καὶ ὑποτάξεις non etiam significare hoc, nempe per epistolam indicare, tamen permitto tibi, vt quod velis, significare arbitreris. Esto enim, significet semper cum infamia indicare, aut atro colore notare: Quid tuae ex hoc opinioni accedit, vel nostrae sententiae decedit?) vt eos obiurget atque castiget prout Deum velle cognorit. Et quia indicare per Epistolam iubet, manifeste patet, non concessisse ipsum Ecclesiae potestatem eo modo aliquos castigandi.
units.tr: Why, then, when he is speaking of those to be shut out of private fellowship because of scandalous conduct, and is plainly distinguishing hidden judgements of God from manifest ones, does he write explicitly, "Do you not judge those who are within?" Why does he order them to be avoided? Why would he prescribe signs? These are your own inventions. I do not know what hidden judgements of God you are describing here. The Apostle is speaking of the open judgements upon the members of the Church.
