He says nothing other than if he had said, in this or a similar way: "When I told you that you ought to flee from fornicators, adulterers, etc., I mean those who are among you and are called brothers. You must observe their life and manners, and avoid those whom you know to be impure, lest you too be infected; but let them be ashamed and return to the right path." This is the judgement of which the Apostle speaks there: namely, to bear witness by withdrawing from private fellowship that such a man lives unworthily of his name. He orders his own people to judge in this way, not outsiders, since outsiders would have accomplished nothing by their judgement, but would rather have been mocked. He orders such men to be indicated by letter. (Although it is plainly false that σημεῖα καὶ ὑποτάξεις does not also mean this, namely to indicate by letter, nevertheless I grant you that you may take it to mean whatever you wish. Suppose it always means to indicate with infamy, or to mark with a black colour: what does this add to your opinion, or take from our view?) so that they may rebuke and chastise them as they recognise God wills. And because he orders them to be indicated by letter, it is clearly evident that he did not grant the Church itself the power to punish anyone in that way.

units.la: Posthaec concludis rem perinde ac si praeclarè tuam causam egisses. At non vendes posthaec vel nobis, vel alijs, sumos tuos. Didicimus per Dei gratiam non pendere ab hominibus, sed verbum Dei consulere. Presbyterium vestrum ostendi scripturis sacris ignotum esse, ac fuisse semper. Dicis quidem tu, Presbyteros fuisse, qui augustiorem functionem in Ecclesia haberent, & Ecclesiasticis iudiciis cum Ministris praesiderent: at nos probationis exspectatione seu desiderio fines, vt video, contabescere ac mori. Iniuriam facis Apostolo maximam, cum eum Excommunicatores vestros, quos ignorauit, scribis alicubi Presbyteros appellauisse. Non nescio, Apostolum Presbyterij mentionem facere in 1. ad Timoth. 4. cap. at vestrum Presbyterium eum intellexisse, ne tu quidem, puto, dixeris: qui affirmare quiduis soles, vt Dominatum illum tueasimilar affirmare quiduis soles, vt Dominatum illum tueáris.
units.tr: After this you conclude the matter as though you had argued your case brilliantly. But you will not sell us or anyone else your smoke after this. By God's grace we have learned not to depend on men but to consult the Word of God. I have shown that your Presbytery is unknown to the holy Scriptures and has always been so. You indeed say that there were Presbyters who held a more august office in the Church and presided with the ministers over ecclesiastical judgements; but we, as I see, are wasting away and dying with waiting and longing for proof. You do the Apostle the greatest injustice when you write that he somewhere called your excommunicators, whom he did not know, Presbyters. I am not unaware that the Apostle mentions the Presbytery in 1 Timothy chapter 4. But I think you yourself would not say that your Presbytery understood him to mean it, since you are accustomed to affirm anything at all in order to defend that domination.

units.la: Libri quarti finis.
units.tr: End of the fourth book.

units.la: Liber quintus incipit.
units.tr: Here begins the fifth book.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: De vsu Excommunicationis.
units.tr: On the use of excommunication.

units.la: VIlum posse ex sacris literis vsum in Ecclesia ostendi eius rei, quae falsò Ecclesiae obtruditur, vt præceptum Diuinum, cum à Deo imperata nunquam fuerit, omnes, credo, sani intelligunt. Facilè ego dixero, quantum mali pepererit. Vniuersam Religionē ferè sola, aut certè præcipuè foedissimè conspurcauit, & tantum non euertit. Quot hominum millia æternùm perdiderit, nouit Dominus: ex historia constare posse arbitror, in Imperio Germanico propter Excommunicationem supra quinquies centena hominum millia diuersis temporibus trucidata fuisse. Ingenue profiteor, me persuasum esse, si quidem exstet hodie Deus ille fortitudinum Danielis, aliud esse non posse, quàm Excommunicationem. Haec enim verè fortis Deus fuit, qui omnes Reges & Principes, omne robur, omnes conscientias, ipsam etiam sacrosanctam scripturam Pont. Romani pedibus subiecit. At nos, inquies, aliter instituimus: Pontificum factum non probamus. Audio quidem hoc dici: sed contrarium video & experior. Permulta alia in Pontificibus rectè reprehendimus: at eadem deinde fecimus ac facimus: postquam nobis paulum confirmati videmur. Nolo exempla dissipatarum Ecclesiarum, iniquorum iudiciorum, & aliarum confusionum atque malorum, quæ ætate nostra ex hac vel sola vel præcipuè orta sunt, commemorare: quia sunt odiosa. Hoc autem dicam, non debere nos, vt præceptum Diuinum, Ecclesijs obtrudere, quod Deus non praecepit.
units.tr: I believe all sensible people understand that no use of excommunication can be shown from the Holy Scriptures, and that it is falsely foisted on the Church as a divine precept, since God never commanded it. I could easily say how much harm it has caused. It has almost alone, or at least chiefly, most foully defiled the whole of religion and has come close to overthrowing it. The Lord knows how many thousands of people it has damned forever. I think it can be established from history that, because of excommunication, more than five hundred thousand people have been slaughtered at various times in the German Empire. I freely confess that I am persuaded, if that God of fortitude of Daniel exists today, he can be none other than excommunication. For this has truly been a strong god, one that has placed under the feet of the Roman Pontiff all kings and princes, all power, all consciences, and even Holy Scripture itself. But, you will say, we have done things differently: we do not approve of the Pontiffs' conduct. I do hear this said, but I see and experience the opposite. We rightly criticise many things in the Pontiffs, yet afterwards we do the same things that they did and still do, as soon as we seem to have grown a little more secure. I do not wish to recall the examples of ruined churches, unjust judgements and other disorders and evils that in our own age have arisen from this one thing alone or chiefly, because they are odious. But I will say this: we ought not to impose on the churches, as a divine precept, what God has not commanded.

units.la: Quod dicis eam conseruare Ecclesias, & sanare hominum conscientias, falsum esse liquet ex dictis. Si per hanc voluisset Deus Ecclesias conseruari, non omisisset eius fundationem. Nisi forte Deus hoc non vidit vtile fore suae Ecclesiae: quod Excommunicatores isti tam salutare esse experti sunt. Si quid perdidit Ecclesias, Excommunicatio perdidit. Sanandae sunt hominum conscientiae vulneratae, non Excommunicatione, quae meros parit Hypocritas (animalia Deo inuisa supra omnia:) sed illis remedijs, quae sapientissimus Deus noster nobis praescripsit. Iactas tu in praefatione & alias etiam experientiam huius rei, forte quia soli Allobroges sapiunt. Vidi ego permultos Viperas manibus sine incommodo, sed cum lucro tractantes. At non ideo non erant illae venenatae, quia earum virus industria sua isti caucbant. Non vituperο, vt Magistratus in quouis loco eligat viros aliquot prudentes & pios, atque his etiam adiungat Ministros verbi aequiores & prudentiores, qui in vitam moresque hominum inquirant loco Magistratus, licenter viuentes ad se vocet, pro delicti ratione increpent & obiurget, adeoq; cum res postulare videbitur, ad Magistratu factum deferat. Nō hoc improbo, si fiat, sed summe laudo. Et prodest ex Senatu ordini huic aliquos interesse, vt fideliter narrare omnia possint, cum opus est. Hoc primum accuso, quod Ecclesia sibi sumit ius & potestatem eligendi. Deinde quod nō Magistratus nomine, sed contra aut praeter eius voluntate atq; mandatu tales eliguntur. Tertio, quod ipsum quoque Magistratum sibi subijciunt. Imprimis vero impium esse dico, dixi, & dicā tatisper, dum rectius ex verbo Dei edoctus fuero, quod Presbyterium hoc (si ficlibet nominare) sibi arrogat ius homines Sacramentis rite cupientes vti ab eis arcendi, & ea facere prohibendi, quae Deus facere iussit.
units.tr: That the Ban preserves the Churches and heals men's consciences is plainly false, as is clear from what has been said. If God had wanted the Churches preserved by it, he would not have left out its foundation. Unless perhaps God did not see that it would be useful to his Church, which these excommunicators have found to be so salutary. If the Ban has destroyed anything, it has destroyed the Churches. Wounded consciences must be healed, not by excommunication, which produces nothing but hypocrites (creatures most hateful to God), but by those remedies which our most wise God has prescribed to us. In your preface and elsewhere you boast of experience of this matter, perhaps because only the Allobroges are wise. I have seen many men handle vipers with their hands without harm, but with profit. Yet those vipers were not any less poisonous because these men guarded against their venom by their own skill. I do not find fault with the magistrate choosing in any place some prudent and godly men, and joining with them some more mild and prudent ministers of the Word, who inquire into people's lives and conduct in the magistrate's place, call to account those who live licentiously, rebuke and reprove them according to the nature of the offence, and, when the matter seems to require it, report the deed to the magistrate. I do not disapprove of this if it is done, but I highly commend it. And it is useful for some men from the Senate to take part in this body, so that they can report everything faithfully when need arises. This is my first accusation: that the Church claims for itself the right and power of choosing. Second, that such men are chosen not in the name of the magistrate, but against or apart from his will and commission. Third, that they also subject the magistrate himself to themselves. Above all, I say, I have said, and will go on saying, until I am taught more correctly from God's Word, that it is impious for this eldership (call it what you like) to claim for itself the right of keeping from the sacraments men who desire rightly to use them, and of forbidding them to do what God has commanded.

units.la: Falsu & illud est, ne quid dicā gravius, non sufficere Magistratus gladium cohercendis malis. Qui Psa.101. legit, atq; historias sanctorū Regū, qui populū sibi subiectū Deo seruire coegerūt, & abominationes omnes sustulerunt, adeoq;
units.tr: It is also false, not to say anything harsher, that the sword of the magistrate is not enough to restrain evils. Whoever reads Psalm 101, and the histories of the holy kings who compelled the people subject to them to serve God, and removed all abominations, and [...] [killed those who did not seek God], will, if he considers carefully, not think that these things are asserted by you with much piety, to say nothing yet of Moses.

units.la: Deum non quaerentes interfecerunt, attentè consideravit, vt iam Mosen taceam, parum piè haec à te affirmari cogitabit. Sed rari sunt tales Magistratus. Nouit haec omnia Dominus antequam nos moneamus. Nostrum est ab eo precibus nostris flagitare tales: non autem aliam formam fingere, cuius deinde ipsum authorem & fabricatorem faciamus. Sed Pontifex quoque sedebat, inquis, de ijs ipsis τυμπανιστὴς iudicans, quae τοπιτιωὺ fuerant dijudicata. Si de moribus eum iudicauisse asseris seorsum à Iudicibus politicis, quomodo scilicet vestrū Presbyterium nunc sedet in suo conciliabulo iudicans, falsū fuit, est, erit, quod dicis. Probatione opus nulla est. Inspiciat vnusquisque locos, quos pro te citas, ex 4. & 5. & 6. Leuit. & infinitum discrimen esse perspiciet. Sanè videtur ideo Deus leges de puniendis delinquentibus non tradidisse seorsum, vt nunc apud nos fit, ne nobis imaginaremur distinctas iurisdictiones externas. Sed de his supra egimus. Hortaris tu Principes vt instituant: at boni & pij Ministri omnes, vt ab ea sibi caueant, monebunt cunctos Magistratus Christianos.
units.tr: But such magistrates are rare. The Lord knew all these things before we admonish him. It is our task to beg such men of him by our prayers, not to devise some other form, whose author and maker we then make him. But, you say, the high priest also sat, judging about these very matters [τυμπανιστὴς], which had been decided [τοπιτιωὺ]. If you assert that he judged concerning morals apart from the civil judges, then whatever you say, that your eldership now sits in its own conventicle judging, was, is, and will be false. No proof is needed. Let each man look at the passages you cite from Leviticus 4, 5 and 6, and he will see an infinite difference. Surely God seems to have not given laws on punishing offenders separately, as now happens among us, so that we might not imagine distinct external jurisdictions. But we have treated these matters above. You urge the princes to establish such a thing; but all good and godly ministers will warn every Christian magistrate to beware of it.

units.la: Quam sit praeposterum subditos habere & exercere iurisdictionem externam, in qua publicè per sententias in cōfesfu damnent suos Magistratus infliǵta poena, nullus est intelligens, qui non videat. In sacris literis nullum exemplum reperitur. Quocirca summè miror ego, quod Dauidis exemplum adducere te non pudet, cum à Propheta iusu Dei solus à solo obiurgatus fuerit. Vbi Presbyterij sententiis damnatus, aut damnari iusus est? Aut quis vnquam dubitauit, an Ministris liceat improbè agentes Magistratus, ex verbo Dei obiurgare, arguere, reprehendere, increpare, adeoque soluere & ligare? Dico autem ex verbo Dei, ne de vestris ligaturis me loqui opineris. Expressius exemplum in Vzzia Rege & Azaria Sacerdote cum nos habere dicis, pro tuo more loqueris. Sacerdos hunc obiurgauit rectè ex verbo Dei, cum contra manifestum eius mandatum in sacrario suffire vellet. Iussit eum ex loco exire, in quo Sacerdotibus solis licebat Sacrificare & suffire. Deinde cum lepra in fronte apparuisset, coactus est iuxta Legem vitare Templum. At vbi scriptum est hunc sententiis Presbyterij damnatum? Nulla vel Iudicis vel Iudicum hic mentio: sed tantum scribitur octoginta robustis Sacerdotibus stipatum Azariam Sacerdotem.
units.tr: How absurd it is for subjects to have and exercise external jurisdiction, by which in public assembly, through sentences, they condemn their magistrates to a punishment inflicted, is clear to anyone who understands and does not see it. No example of this is found in Holy Scripture. Therefore I greatly wonder that you are not ashamed to adduce the example of David, when by God's command he was rebuked by a prophet alone, by one alone. Where was he condemned, or ordered to be condemned, by the sentences of a presbytery? Or who has ever doubted whether ministers may, from the Word of God, rebuke, argue against, reprove, censure, and so loose and bind magistrates who act wickedly? I say from the Word of God, lest you think I am speaking of your bindings. You say that we have a more explicit example in King Uzziah and the priest Azariah; you speak in your usual manner. The priest rightly rebuked him from the Word of God, when he wished to burn incense in the sanctuary against God's manifest command. He ordered him to leave the place where only priests were allowed to sacrifice and burn incense. Then, when leprosy appeared on his forehead, he was compelled by the Law to avoid the Temple. But where is it written that he was condemned by the sentences of a presbytery? No mention is made here of a judge or judges; it is only written that Azariah the priest was accompanied by eighty strong priests.

units.la: Et qui tandem magis rectiusque cum Apostolo Iudicentur τὴν κυριότητα αὐτῶν, ἢ τὰν δεξιὰν ἐλεγχθῆναι, quàm Excommunicatores? Certè nulli suos Magistratus despiciunt, maioreque contumelia afficiunt. Sed non Excommunicatur Magistratus, respondent ad hoc argumentum aliqui, quatenus magistratus est, sed scelera solum ipsius reprehenduntur: ac debent alioqui omnes etiam Excommunicato Magistratui obedientiam. Haec illi. Ego vero Magistratui subditos ne maledicere quidem affero debere Leuit. 22. multò minus poenis afficere. Neque interim hoc sentio, non esse eos ex verbo Dei increpandos, monendos, docendos & vrgendos: sed non esse eos potestati & iurisdictioni subditorum visibili subijciendos. Et putida est responsio, non Excommunicari Magistratum, quoad Magistratus est. Nam qui hoc sibi licere existimat, Catabaptista est. Quod si responsio valet, poterit vnusquisque suam nequitiam excusare ac dicere, se non Magistratum, quia talis est, vlcisci, sed iniuriosum vel Tyrannum persequi. Si excipias, Scripturam hoc vetare: illud non minus prohibere respondebo: id quod me abundè demonstrauisse puto. Dicitis quidem Magistratui exclusò nihilominus obedientiam deberi. Sed quis credat me illi parère velle, cui ego vitae totius modum cum potestate & coactione praescribere me posse arbitror? Facilè est obedientiam praestare ei, qui contra voluntatem tuam facere nihil audit. Sanè Magistratus, quem sibi subiecit Presbyterium, nihil aliud est, quàm seruus Presbyterij: dum pro eius arbitratu cogitur in quoslibet molliter, duriter, cruciatu corporis, exilio, vinculis, morte &c. animaduertere.
units.tr: And who should be judged more rightly and more properly, in the words of the Apostle, [τὴν κυριότητα αὐτῶν] or [ἢ τὰν δεξιὰν ἐλεγχθῆναι], than the excommunicators? Certainly they despise their magistrates more than anyone and treat them with greater contumely. But some respond to this argument that the magistrate is not excommunicated as magistrate, but only his crimes are rebuked; and that otherwise all must owe obedience even to an excommunicated magistrate. So they say. But I assert that subjects ought not even to curse a magistrate (Leviticus 22), much less to inflict punishments on him. Yet I do not hold that he should not be rebuked, admonished, taught and urged from the Word of God; only that he should not be subjected to the visible power and jurisdiction of subjects. And the answer that the magistrate is not excommunicated in so far as he is magistrate is rotten. For whoever thinks he may do this is an Anabaptist. And if this answer holds, anyone will be able to excuse his wickedness and say that he is not avenging the magistrate because he is a magistrate, but pursuing an unjust person or a tyrant. If you object that Scripture forbids this, I will reply that it forbids the other thing no less; I think I have amply demonstrated this. You say indeed that obedience is still owed to a magistrate who has been excluded. But who would believe that I am willing to obey him, when I think I can prescribe to him the manner of his whole life with power and compulsion? It is easy to render obedience to one who hears nothing against your will. Truly, the magistrate whom the presbytery has subjected to itself is nothing other than the servant of the presbytery, since at its pleasure he is forced to punish anyone, mildly or harshly, by bodily torture, exile, chains, death, and so on.

units.la: Tacebo nunc, quòd alij Excommunicationis Patroni retinus contenduut, nullum omninò Excommunicandum absque consensu Magistratus. Satis porrò constat, nullum consensurum in sui Excommunicationem. Nec Theodosius nec alius vllus volens Excommunicatus fuit, teste historia. At boni, excipiat aliquis, volent. Ego autem ne dicentibus quidem credam, si quidem Excommunicationem putent esse poenam talem, qualem vos eam esse dicitis: vel saltem tale existimeut esse testimonium. Aliud est dicere, omnes extra periculum, & aliud, cum vides periculum praesens. At cupiunt resipiscere. Si ita est, possunt non Excommunicati resipiscere. Non puto vos satisfactiones veterum reducere velle. Ergo ne hic quidem veritati consentanea, aut aliorum opinioni consentientia dicis. Nec plus veritatis aut iudicij in eo est, quod dicis, Magistratum non sanare conscientias dum punit. Etenim pius Magistratus puniendo non minus sanat, imò multò magis, quam vos Excomunicando. Quippe Deus multos ad se per tribulationes & afflictiones vocavit, qui secundis rebus omnia neglexerunt. Vt vt hoc habeat, Deo non debemus videri velle sapientiores. Nouit ipse qua ratione ac via vnumquemlibet ad se pertrahere debeat.
units.tr: I will now pass over the point that other defenders of excommunication contend that no one at all may be excommunicated without the consent of the magistrate. It is quite certain that no one will consent to his own excommunication. Nor did Theodosius, or anyone else, willingly submit to excommunication, as history attests. But someone will object that good men would consent. I, however, would not believe even those who say so, if they think excommunication is a punishment of the kind you say it is, or at least regard it as a testimony of that kind. It is one thing to say that all are safe from danger, and another to see the danger present. But they desire to repent. If so, they can repent without being excommunicated. I do not suppose you wish to bring back the satisfactions of the ancients. So here again you say nothing consistent with the truth, or in agreement with the opinion of others. Nor is there any more truth or judgement in your claim that the magistrate does not heal consciences when he punishes. For a godly magistrate, by punishing, heals no less, indeed far more, than you do by excommunicating. God has called many to himself through tribulations and afflictions, who had neglected everything in prosperity. Whatever the case, we ought not to seem to want to be wiser than God. He himself knows by what reason and way he ought to draw each one to himself.

units.la: Si Azariae exemplum secutus fuisset Ambrosius, recte fecisset. Fecit enim ille, quod Deus facere in Lege sua iusserat: hic autem fecit, quod Deus vetuit facere. Etenim arcuit eum à Templo, à Sacramentis, à verbi auditione. Quo, quaeso te, iure aut cuius mandato ausus est hoc tentare? Ipse tu non semel affirmas, non debere quenquam excludi à verbi praedicatione, si praesertim audire cupiat. Qua ratione ergo factum illud defendis? Factum hoc ipsius vt tyrannicum meritò exaggerandum, damnandum, & exsecrandum censeo. Quoniam tumet inficiari, vt maximè velis, non possis, cum contra Dei praeceptum Imperatorem poenitentem, culpam deprecantem, verbum Dei audire cupientem prohibuisse à templi aditu, precibus & verbi auditione tot mensium spacio. An sic velles tecum agere Deum? Quid multis est opus? Hoc facto suo, quod vt iustù defendi à nemine veritatis studiofo poterit, non tantum initium fecit Tyrannidi Romanae, verumetiam fundamentum posuit. Imitatus praeclarè fuit ille, qui etiam collum pedibus calcare prostrati Imperatoris est ausus.
units.tr: Ambrose would have done rightly if he had followed the example of Azariah. For Azariah did what God had commanded in his Law; but Ambrose did what God forbade. For he kept the emperor from the Temple, from the sacraments, and from hearing the Word. By what right, I ask you, or by whose command, did he dare to attempt this? You yourself affirm more than once that no one ought to be shut out from the preaching of the Word, especially if he desires to hear it. On what ground, then, do you defend that deed? I judge that deed of his, as tyrannical, to be rightly magnified, condemned and execrated. For though you wish very much to deny it, you cannot, since against God's precept he forbade the penitent emperor, who was begging pardon for his fault and desired to hear the Word of God, access to the church, prayer and the hearing of the Word for so many months. Would you wish God to deal with you in that way? Why need there be more? By this deed, which no one who studies the truth can rightly defend, he not only made a beginning of Roman tyranny, but also laid its foundation. He imitated admirably the man who dared to tread on the neck of the prostrate emperor.

units.la: Cur non ex epistolis eius potius, inquis, hausisti historiam, quam ex impuris lacunis? Cur me vis ex ipso Ambrosio historiam recitare, quam is numquam, quod scimus, integram scripsit? Certè non reperies apud eum causam irae Theodosij expressam: & recte quidem omittunt in sua causa Rhetores, quae nocere ipsis possunt. Didicerat in praefectura Mediolanensi imperare: nec dum dedidicerat factus Episcopus: Non enim subito mutantur mores, cum radices egerunt in nobis. Ego Ambrosium credo non negaturum, si vixisset, causam irae habuisse Theodosium, quam referunt Nicephorus aliique historici ab odio Ambrosij & causa eius alienissimi.
units.tr: Why, you say, did you not draw the history from his letters rather than from these impure pools? Why do you want me to recite from Ambrose himself a history which, as far as we know, he never wrote in full? Certainly you will not find in him a clear statement of the cause of Theodosius' anger; and rhetoricians rightly leave out in their own case what could harm them. He had learned to rule while prefect of Milan, and he had not yet unlearned it when he became bishop. For manners are not changed suddenly, once their roots have grown in us. I believe Ambrose, had he lived, would not deny that Theodosius had a cause for anger, which Nicephorus and other historians report, historians who were very far from Ambrose's hatred and from his cause.

units.la: Habes ad scriptum tuum plenam & solidam responsionem, qua Thesium mearum veritas ita declaratur & defenditur, ut merito sperem, imo persuasissimum habeam, nullum ex omnibus pijs, si modo, quae contra disputavi, recte intellexerit, eam posthac sententiam de illa vestra Excommunicatione probaturum. Quod ut facere vnusquisque rectius pariter ac utrius possit, illa quoq; argumenta, quae ab alijs obiecta partim, legi in scriptis eorum de hac controversia, partim aliàs cognovi, examinare breviter constitui. Sic enim apparebit, nihil Dominatus huius defensoribus praesidij opifq; relictum esse.
units.tr: You have a full and solid reply to your writing, by which the truth of my theses is so set forth and defended that I may rightly hope, indeed I am thoroughly persuaded, that none of all the godly, if only he has rightly understood what I have argued against you, will henceforth approve that opinion of yours about that excommunication of yours. So that each man may do this the more rightly, and that both sides may be able to do so equally, I have decided briefly to examine those arguments also which others have put forward, some of which I have read in their writings on this controversy, and some of which I have otherwise come to know. For thus it will appear that nothing has been left to the defenders of this domination as protection or aid.

units.la: CAP. II. Confutatio aliorum quorundam argumentorum, quae pro Excom- municatione ab aliis excogitata sunt.
units.tr: CHAP. II. Refutation of certain other arguments, which have been devised by others in favour of excommunication.

units.la: Deferunt isti pro Excommunicatione ex veteri testamento locos complures, ex cap. Esaiae 1. 52. 66. Ierem. 6. & 7. Ezech. 23. 33. Psal. 50. & similes alios. Sed facilis est responsio. Quod ad rem ipsam attinet, non damnat Deus Sacrificia, sed abusum. Putabant enim Iudaei, se praeclare satisfecisse Dei voluntati, si externa sacrificia obtulissent, quomodocunq; animis affecti essent: cum longè aliud Deus ab ipsis postularet. Itaque non absolutè reücit Deus cultum impiorum à se institutum, sed hactenus solum, quatenus eo non sic vtebantur, vt ipse iusserat. Vt enim qui indecorè edenti modestiam commendat, comestionem turpem vituperat, non simpliciter abstinentiam à cibo imperat: ita Deus quoque non omninò ritus à se ordinatos aspernatur, sed abusum eorum damnat. Sic etiam Christus Matth. 6. non voluit Ieiunia, orationes & pecuniae seu opum iustam collectionem prohibere, sed abusum voluit tollere. Nam vt caetera mittam, quis neget licere nobis opes liberis nostris honestè citraque proximi detrimentum colligere, vt ex 2.Cor.12.cap. liquet? Addam, quod à viro excellenter pio & docto, linguaeque Hebraicae non imperito didici, morem esse Hebraeorum, vt, quum duo proponunt recta & iusta, quorum alterum probent, alterum negent, comparatio solum inter ea facta intelligatur. Sic cum Osee. 6. dicitur, Misericordiam volo, non Sacrificium, sensus est, magis misericordia delector. Ita Prouerb. 8. dicitur: Accipite castigationem meam, non argentum. Eodem modo Christus prohibet colligere thesauros, & sollicitum esse pro victu: non quia omnem de his rebus nos velit curam abiicere, sed quoniam vult nos maiore studio coelestia conseetari.
units.tr: Those men cite for excommunication several passages from the Old Testament: from Isaiah chapters 1, 52 and 66, Jeremiah 6 and 7, Ezekiel 23 and 33, Psalm 50, and other similar ones. But the answer is easy. As far as the matter itself is concerned, God does not condemn sacrifices, but the abuse of them. For the Jews thought they had fully satisfied the will of God if they offered external sacrifices, however their minds were disposed; whereas God demanded something quite different from them. Therefore God does not absolutely reject the worship of the wicked which he himself instituted, but only so far as they did not use it in the way he had commanded. For just as one who commends modesty to a man who eats indecorously condemns the disgraceful eating, and does not simply command abstinence from food, so God also does not altogether spurn the rites he ordained, but condemns their abuse. So also Christ in Matthew 6 did not wish to forbid fasting, prayers and the lawful gathering of wealth or goods, but wished to remove the abuse. For, to pass over other things, who would deny that we may lawfully gather wealth for our children, honestly and without harm to our neighbour, as is clear from 2 Corinthians 12? I will add what I learned from a man excellently godly and learned, and not unskilled in the Hebrew tongue: that it is the custom of the Hebrews, when they set forth two things right and just, of which they approve one and deny the other, that only a comparison between them is understood. So when it is said in Hosea 6, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice," the sense is, "I take more delight in mercy." Thus Proverbs 8 says, "Receive my instruction, not silver." In the same way Christ forbids us to gather treasures and to be anxious for food; not because he wishes us to cast off all care for these things, but because he wishes us to pursue heavenly things with greater zeal.

units.la: Iam ad argumentum venio, quod tale fuerit. Deus execratur Sacrificia impiorum. Ergo eligendi Presbyteri, qui malis prohibeant sacrificare. Si bona est consecutio probabo ex eisdem locis, non licere alicui malo praestare eleemosynam: quiescere die Sabbathi: inuocare Deum: agere ei gratias: & quae huiusmodi sunt alia. Constat enim Deum in eisdem locis offendere omnia haec sibi displicere in impiis. Quocirca si non valet, Deus auersatur impiorum orationes: Ergo Presbyteri sunt eligendi, qui nullum sinant inuocare Deum, gratias ei agere, Sabbatho quiescere, eleemosynam praestare, nisi quos dignos esse iudicauerint: Si non valet, inquam, proximè dicta ratiocinatio, ne illa quidem valere poterit. Etenim eodem modo omnia haec in eisdem locis prohibentur mala. At si quis tunc, cum prophetae talia concionarentur, in die Sabbathi ausus fuisset opus facere, certe ipsorum etiam Prophetarum suffragio necatus fuisset. Quare longe aliter haec intellexerunt, quam Aduersarij mei intelligere se simulent.
units.tr: Now I come to the argument, which was of this kind: God abhors the sacrifices of the wicked. Therefore elders are to be chosen who will forbid the wicked to sacrifice. If the inference is sound, I will prove from the same passages that it is not lawful for anyone to give alms to a wicked man, to rest on the Sabbath day, to call upon God, to give thanks to him, and other things of this kind. For it is plain that God in the same passages is offended, and that all these things displease him in the wicked. Wherefore, if it does not hold, that God turns away from the prayers of the wicked, then elders are to be chosen who will allow no one to call upon God, to give thanks to him, to rest on the Sabbath, or to give alms, except those whom they have judged worthy. If the reasoning just stated does not hold, I say, then neither can that reasoning hold. For in the same way all these things are forbidden as evil in the same passages. But if anyone had then dared, while the prophets were preaching such things, to do work on the Sabbath day, he would certainly have been put to death even by the vote of the prophets themselves. Therefore these passages were understood in a very different way from what my opponents pretend to understand them.

units.la: Vrgent nihilominus locum Ezech. 23. cap. in quo Deus queritur, tam fuisse eos impudentes, vt, quo die filios suos Idolis mactauisent (horrendum dictu) auderent etiam in templum ingredi, quasi re bene gesta, cum Moses 31. Num. in castra ante septimam diem nollet intromittere, qui hostes suos occidisset, idque iussu Domini. Frustra vero vrgent, propterea quod hanc rem supra fuse exposuimus. Etenim si profanatio fuit legalis siue ceremonialis, ad nos non pertinet. Si moralis, supra iam ostensum est, aliam huic poenam constitutam fuisse. Adde, quod Propheta hic nullos accusat presbyteros aut Seniores, quod tales non arcuerint, sed cum probis omnibus ad eadem Sacramenta admiserint. Si praeceptum huis rei aliquod habuisset, saltem vestigium aliquod in reprehensione Dei appareret. Locus in 33. cap. hoc tantum habet: Cum te iubeo, inquit Deus, impio dicere, eum moriturum, nisi emendet vitam, nec ei indicaueris, morietur ipse quidem, at tu non impune feres: Sin autem ei dixeris, nec ille tamen fiat melior, peribit ille quidem, verum tu extra culpam eris. Non loquitur hic Deus de excommunicatione, sed de reprehensione peccatorum, quae Ministris commendata est.
units.tr: Nevertheless they press the passage of Ezekiel chapter 23, in which God complains that they were so shameless that on the very day on which they had slaughtered their sons to idols (horrible to say) they dared also to enter the temple, as if the deed were well done; whereas Moses in Numbers 31 would not admit into the camp before the seventh day the man who had killed his enemies, and that by the Lord's command. But they press it in vain, since we have set forth this matter at length above. For if the profanation was legal or ceremonial, it does not concern us. If it was moral, it has already been shown above that a different punishment was appointed for it. Add that the prophet here accuses no elders or seniors of not having kept such people away, but of having admitted them, along with all the godly, to the same sacraments. If he had had some precept for this matter, at least some trace of it would appear in God's rebuke. The passage in chapter 33 has only this: "When I bid you say to the wicked man that he will die unless he amends his life, and you do not warn him, he will indeed die, but you will not go unpunished; but if you warn him, and yet he does not become better, he will indeed perish, but you will be free from blame," says God. God is not speaking here of excommunication, but of the reproof of sins, which has been committed to ministers.

units.la: Argumentantur praeterea ex 23. cap. Deuter. Deus vetuit sibi offerri mercedem meretricis & precium canis: multo minus voluit ad Sacrificia admitti meretricem. Respondeo, multis modis non valere argumentum. Primum non sequitur consequens ex antecedente. Non enim scortum poenitentiam prae se ferens Deus voluit arceri a Templo, quia pecuniam turpiter acquisitam offerri sibi vetuit. Deinde voti nomine duntaxat offerri sibi prohibet tale precium : quod aliis omnibus Sacrificijs aptari fortasse non potest. Nam Deus animal, cui vel defit aliquid vel superfit, offerri sibi voti nomine prohibet: pro spontaneo sacrificio tale offerri non prohibet Leuit. 22. Quod si non sequitur, Deus non vult hoc voti nomine, ergo nullo alio modo vult sibi offerri: quomodo sequetur, ergo ipsum offerentem repudiat? Item Leuit. 2. in oblatione ignita prohibet mel offerri: at non in cunctis alijs oblationibus. Non potuit meretrix de suo patrimonio, aut honestè acquisitis offerre? Certè nullibi scriptum hoc inuenimus. An ex se natum primogenitum Deo non potuit offerre ac circumcidere? An quia mutilum animal Deo offerre in plerisque oblationibus non licebat, mutilum quoque hominem Deus abominabatur sic, vt in Templum venire non posset? Alia est hominum, & alia rerum Deo offerendarum ratio. Non probat Deus Zizaniam in tritico: attamen externos ministros ante messem non vult euellere.
units.tr: They also argue from Deut. 23: God forbade the wage of a harlot and the price of a dog to be offered to him, so much less did he will that a harlot be admitted to the sacrifices. I answer that the argument fails in many ways. First, the consequent does not follow from the antecedent. God did not wish a prostitute who showed signs of repentance to be kept out of the Temple merely because he forbade money dishonestly gained to be offered to him. Second, he forbids such a price to be offered only in the name of a vow, and this perhaps cannot be applied to all other sacrifices. God forbids an animal that is either lacking something or has something superfluous to be offered to him in the name of a vow, but he does not forbid such an animal to be offered as a voluntary sacrifice (Lev. 22). If it does not follow that God does not want it in the name of a vow, therefore he wants it offered in no other way, how will it follow that he rejects the one offering it? Likewise, in Lev. 2 he forbids honey to be offered in the burnt offering, but not in all the other offerings. Could the harlot not have offered from her own patrimony, or from goods honestly acquired? We certainly find nowhere written that she could not. Could she not offer and circumcise a firstborn son born of herself to God? Or, because it was not permitted to offer a maimed animal to God in most offerings, did God so abhor a maimed man that he could not come into the Temple? The reason for men and the reason for things offered to God are different. God does not approve of tares among the wheat, yet he does not wish the outward ministers to be uprooted before the harvest.

units.la: An etiam illum, qui canis precium posside bat, exclusum dicent? Multa detestatur in nobis Deus, nec tamen nos mox abijcit, aut abijci ab alijs præcipit. Imperauit scorti mercedem canisque præcium sibi non offerri, vt turpe lucrum se detestari ostenderet: ex quo non poterit concludi, Presbyteros quosdam eligendos, qui ipsas etiam personas à rectè faciendo absterreant. Pharisaei Iudae precium in aerarium sacrum reponere noluerunt, ipsum è templo non eiecerunt: quod sanè facturi fuerant, vt erant magni externarum ceremoniarum obseruatores, si legibus imperatum sciuissent.
units.tr: Will they also say that the man who possessed the price of a dog was excluded? God detests many things in us, yet he does not cast us off at once, nor order others to cast us off. He commanded that the wage of a harlot and the price of a dog not be offered to him, to show that he detests base gain. From this it cannot be concluded that certain elders should be chosen who would frighten the very persons away from doing right. The Pharisees did not want to put Judas's price into the sacred treasury, but they did not cast him out of the Temple. They certainly would have done so, being great observers of outward ceremonies, if they had known that the law commanded it.

units.la: Quidam praeterea ex 27. cap. Deuter. generalis excommunicationis formulam mutuatur hoc modo: Sicut in hoc loco iusit Deus Leuitas malè malis, & bene bonis precari cum assensu populi: Sic & nos malos generatim excludimus, dicentes, excludimus adulteros, fures, idololatras. Primum nullius meminit Moses vel hic, vel 11. Deuter. vbi eiusdem rei fit mentio, exclusionis à Sacramentis & Sacrificijs. Deinde sacrificare & conuiuari prius omnes coram Domino oportuit: quod nō erat aliud quàm sacramēto vti. Nec multò antè, quàm hoc fecisset, quod hic iubet Moses, circumcisi à Iosua omnes fuerant, ac Pascha simul omnes cōcelebrauerant. Tantum igitur abest, vt imprecatio illa fuerit excōmunicatio, vt manifestissimè contrarium ex hoc ipso loco probetur. Postremò nō debuit hoc sæpius fieri, sed semel tantum, post ingressum in terrā promissam: quod Iosuae 8. peractum legimus: postea nunquam amplius. Non enim vbique erant montes Gerizim & Ebal. Semel igitur tantum generalis illa excommunicatio facienda fuerit. Quod si nunc quoque voluint Aduersarij ministros hoc duntaxat modo excommunicare, vt malis iram & iudicium Dei, bonis eiusdem clementiam declarent quomodo hic factum fuit, nulla erit inter nos lis amplius.
units.tr: Some also borrow from Deut. 27 a formula of general excommunication in this way: just as God commanded the Levites in this place to curse the wicked and bless the good, with the assent of the people, so we too exclude the wicked in general, saying: we exclude adulterers, thieves, idolaters. First, Moses mentions nothing of this kind, either here or in Deut. 11, where the same matter is mentioned, namely exclusion from the sacraments and sacrifices. Second, all had first to sacrifice and feast before the Lord, which was nothing other than partaking of the sacrament. Nor long before Moses commanded what he commands here, all had been circumcised by Joshua and had together celebrated the Passover. So far is that imprecation from being excommunication, that the contrary is most clearly proved from this very place. Third, it ought not to have been done often, but only once, after entry into the promised land. We read that this was done in Joshua 8, and afterwards never again, for Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal were not everywhere. Therefore that general curse was to be pronounced only once. But if now too our adversaries wish to excommunicate ministers only in this way, so as to declare the wrath and judgment of God to the wicked and his clemency to the good, as was done here, there will be no further dispute between us.

units.la: Ethnici, dicunt praeterea, non admittebantur in Templum. At facinorosus est Ethnicus. De his enim scribitur Ezech. 16. Patres vestri sunt Amorrhæi. Item, si transgressor fueris legis, circumcisio tua versa est in præputium, Rom. 2. Item, infidele est deterior 1. Timoth. 5. Ergo arcebantur scelerati à Templo & Diuinis ritibus. Miror quod illud Pharisæorum tacuerunt, Samaritanus es. Si Dei iudicium spectabimus, non inficiabimur, quin impij fratres deteriore sint loco & conditione infidelibus. At si extemam Ecclesiæ faciem intuebimur, multa reperiemus in improbis, quæ non competunt Paganis & Turcis. Quod quia est notum, nolo in hoc hærere diutius: præsertim verò cum supra demonstratum sit circumcisis malis etiam licuisse in templum ingredi, cum Gentili non liceret, qualisqualis esset moribus. Falsissima igitur est argumenti Assumptio, cum de externa & visibili Ecclesia loquimur. Nunquam enim circumcisus fuerit incircumcisus: nec baptizatus vnquam fuerit non baptizatus, (externè scilicet) is præsertim, de quo nobis sermo est.
units.tr: The Gentiles, they further say, were not admitted into the Temple. But a wicked person is a Gentile. For of such people it is written in Ezek. 16: "Your fathers were Amorites." Likewise, "if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision" (Rom. 2). Likewise, "an unbeliever is worse" (1 Tim. 5). Therefore the criminals were kept from the Temple and from the divine rites. I wonder that they have kept silent about that saying of the Pharisees, "You are a Samaritan." If we look to the judgment of God, we will not deny that impious brothers are in a worse place and condition than unbelievers. But if we look to the outward face of the Church, we will find many things in the wicked that do not belong to pagans and Turks. Since this is well known, I do not wish to dwell on it longer, especially since it has been shown above that even the circumcised wicked were allowed to enter the Temple, whereas a Gentile was not allowed to, whatever his morals. The assumption of the argument is therefore utterly false when we speak of the external and visible Church. For a circumcised man is never uncircumcised, nor is a baptized man ever unbaptized (outwardly, of course), especially the one of whom we are speaking.

units.la: Proferunt hoc etiam: Deus iubet Sabbathū sanctificare. Ergo viciosi à sacramētis arcebantur. Quot erit opus fulcris & & substructionibus, vt super hoc fundamento turris illa: Babel, Excommunicatio scilicet, firmetur? Sabbathum est sanctificandum. Sabbathum est quoddam Sacramentum. Ergo Sacramenta (concludamus nunc, si libet vniuersè): sunt sanctificanda. At verò licenter viuentes contaminant, non sanctificant. Tali aut neganda. Ergò dissoluté viuentibus neganda sunt Sacramenta. Non possunt autem improbi arceri, nisi à delectis ad eam rem presbyteris. Hi sunt igitur eligendi, vt hoc munus gerant. Nisi modo aliquo tali forment argumenta, quomodo propositum conclusuri sint, equidem non video. Errores ingentes nolo reprehendere, quoniam an sic forment ignoro. Hoc solum respondebo: Si quid ex praecepto Decalogi confici posset, hoc efficeretur, turpiter viuentibus non esse concedendum, vt in Sabbatho quiescant à laboribus, atque orationi, nominis Diuini inuocationi, verbi Dei auditioni, lectioni, meditationi vacent. Nam si ita inquinant Sacramenta, vt ad ea admitti nequeant, non poterant tales, ad iam dicta, quibus Sabbathum sanctificabatur, admitti. Deus autem ob has ipsas causas iubet seruari ab omnibus bonis & malis, atque non seruantem mandat interfici, mandato hoc soepè repetito. Exemplum extat Num. 15. de eo, qui ligna collegerat. An potest aliquid talibus absurdius cogitari argumentis? Poena capitis erat posita non seruantibus Sabbathum: tantum abest, vt alicui interdiceret eius obseruatio. Haec sunt, quae ex veteri foedere probata adhuc cognoui pro excommunicatione ab aduersarijs: quorum videlicet supra non sit mentio facta. Nunc eadem breuitate percurremus, quae ex nouo Testamento producunt. Ex cap. 5. Mat. sic arguunt. Christus iubet munus oblaturum priùs reconciliari fratri, relicto ad altare munere. Ergo non vult nos vti Sacramentis priusquam fratri sumus reconciliati. Non puto accurata hic opus esse responsione. Quippe nec inuocare Deum, nec erratorum veniã ab eo petere debemus, nisi priùs remiserimus omnibus, qui iniurij nobis fuerint. Marci. 11. Quis me sic ferat ratiocinantem? Deo munus quod offers integrè non placet, si iniurius fratri fuisti, nec eum placauisti. Ergo vult eligi presbyteros, qui tibi oratione & inuocatione Dei interdicant. Etenim munera nostra, quæ nunc feré offerimus Deo sacrificia sunt laudis & gratiarum actionis. Si hæc absurda est, inutilis & illa est. Nam non minus hoc, quàm illud, mandatum nobis est. In summa, vt, quæ agimus, Deo placeant, animum oportet abomni prauia cogitatione vacuum pitrumque esse. Non disserit ibi Christus de externa Ecclesiæ gubernatione, sed de Christiani hominis perfectione: vt cum ad hunc perfectionis gradum nos pertingere non posse perspeximus, de nobis desperemus, & in vna Dei miseticordia propter meritum Christi acquiescendum nobis intelligamus. Alioqui si nihil Deus probaret, quod ab hac perfectione recessit, nihil omninò facere nobis liceret boni & recti: & essemus omnes excommunicandi. Ideo non dicit, si presbyteri te iubebunt relinquere munus, relinquito: sed si apud te ipsum fueris recordatus. Non loquitur ergo de prohibitione, qua alij nobis vetant cultum à Deo institutum, sed de eo, quod noster nobis animus dictat. Citius ex hoc loco Missam Pontificiam probaueris, quàm excommunicationem.
units.tr: They also put forward this: God commands the Sabbath to be sanctified; therefore the vicious were kept from the sacraments. How many props and underpinnings will be needed to make that tower of Babel, namely excommunication, stand firm on this foundation? The Sabbath is to be sanctified. The Sabbath is a certain sacrament. Therefore the sacraments (let us now conclude in general, if you like) are to be sanctified. But those who live licentiously defile them rather than sanctify them. Therefore they are to be refused, or denied to such people. Therefore the sacraments are to be denied to those living dissolutely. But the wicked cannot be kept away except by elders chosen for that purpose. These, therefore, are to be chosen to carry out this office. Unless they frame their arguments in some such way, I indeed do not see how they will reach their proposition. I do not wish to censure their huge errors, since I do not know whether this is how they frame them. I will answer only this: if anything could be inferred from the precept of the Decalogue, this would follow: that those living shamefully should not be allowed to rest from their labours on the Sabbath, and to be free for prayer, invocation of the name of God, hearing, reading and meditating on the Word of God. For if they so defile the sacraments that they cannot be admitted to them, such people could not be admitted to those aforementioned things by which the Sabbath was sanctified. But God, for these very reasons, commands it to be kept by all, good and bad, and commands that the one not keeping it be put to death, a command often repeated. An example is in Num. 15, concerning the man who gathered sticks. Can anything more absurd be thought up than such arguments? The penalty of death was set for those who did not keep the Sabbath; so far is it from forbidding its observance to anyone. These are the arguments which, from the Old Covenant, I have so far learned are put forward by the adversaries for excommunication, and of which, as is plain, no mention was made above. Now, with the same brevity, we will run through what they produce from the New Testament. From Matth. 5 they argue thus: Christ commands the one offering a gift to be first reconciled to his brother, leaving the gift at the altar. Therefore he does not want us to use the sacraments before we have been reconciled to our brother. I do not think an exact reply is needed here. Indeed, neither should we invoke God nor ask him for pardon of our errors unless we have first forgiven all who have wronged us (Mark 11). Who could put up with such reasoning? The gift you offer to God is not pleasing if you have wronged your brother and not appeased him. Therefore he wants elders to be chosen who will forbid you prayer and the invocation of God. For our gifts, which we now offer to God, are sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving. If this is absurd, then that is useless too, for no less is this commanded us than that. In sum, so that what we do may please God, the mind must be free of every depraved thought. Christ is not discussing there the external government of the Church, but the perfection of the Christian man, so that when we see that we cannot attain this degree of perfection, we may despair of ourselves and understand that we must rest in the sole mercy of God on account of the merit of Christ. Otherwise, if God approved nothing that has departed from this perfection, it would be altogether unlawful for us to do anything good and right, and we would all be excommunicated. So he does not say, "If the elders bid you give up the office, give it up," but "If you have recalled it to your own mind." Therefore he does not speak of the prohibition by which others forbid us the worship instituted by God, but of what our own mind dictates to us. You would sooner prove the Papists' Mass from this place than excommunication.

units.la: Qui rectè inter Ecclesiæ gubernationem internam & externam distinguit, facilè se ex plerisque obiectionibus explicat. Internae solus Deus beneficentissimus præest: nec tantum sapienter, iustè & benignè ad salutem suorum omnia administrat, sed etiam cogitationes solus rectè citraque errorem iudicat. Ipsi lex posita non est, sed sibimet ipse lex est, vt qui errare nescit. Longè aliter in externa rectione res habet, in qua falli infinitè omnes possumus. Quamobrem facere hic nihil debemus, quàm quod mandatum expressè nobis legimus. In hoc locum habet illud Christi, qui non est aduersarius nobis, hic nobiscum est Marci. 9. Et vt semel omnia dicam, in hac ita tenendum est, Quod Deus facere iussit, ab eo reuocari aut retrahi nullus ab hominibus debet: si modo externè sic fiat, vt praecepit Deus. Nam boni sunt externi actus omnes, quoad nos, quicunque iuxta praefinitionem verbi divini fiunt, licet Deo, qui agentis animum intuetur & iudicat, non ex omni parte probentur. Multi hodie, ut olim Pharisæi, & Pauli tempore alij, verbum Dei docent vel quaestus, vel ambitionis, vel contentionis causa: quos tamen, dum veritatem docent, tam nullus prohibere debet, quam non prohibuit Christus Pharisæis Matth. 23. vel æmulis suis Apost. Paulus. Philip. 1. Gaudebat Apostolus, quod Christus annunciaretur, tametsi non ignoraret, parum sincerè ab ipsis fieri, quod faciebant. Sic nullus vituperandus est, si in aduersis opem Divinam imploret; si Deo gratias agat: si nomen eius laudet ac praedicet; si Eleemosynas praestet, egenosque re, opera, consilio subleuet; in concionibus frequens adsit; aliaque à Deo imperata faciat, quocunque animo talia faciat. Animum enim iudicabit Deus: nos externa haec damnare non conuenit.
units.tr: Whoever rightly distinguishes the internal from the external government of the Church easily answers most objections. Only God, most beneficent, presides over the internal government. He not only administers all things for the salvation of his people wisely, justly and kindly, but he alone also judges thoughts rightly and without error. No law has been laid down for him, but he is a law to himself, since he cannot err. In external government the situation is quite different, and all of us can err endlessly. Therefore here we ought to do nothing except what we read has been expressly commanded to us. To this applies the saying of Christ in Mark 9: "He who is not against us is on our side." And to say it all in a word: in this matter it must be held that no one among men ought to recall or withdraw what God has commanded to be done, provided it is done externally in the way God has prescribed. For all external acts are good as far as we are concerned, whatever is done according to the rule of the divine word, even though they may not be approved in every respect by God, who looks at and judges the mind of the agent. Many today, as the Pharisees once did and others did in Paul's time, teach the word of God for the sake of gain, ambition or contention. Yet while they teach the truth, no one ought to forbid them, any more than Christ forbade the Pharisees in Matthew 23, or the Apostle Paul his rivals in Philippians 1. The Apostle rejoiced that Christ was proclaimed, although he did not doubt that what they did was done with little sincerity. So no one is to be blamed if he implores the divine help in adversity, gives thanks to God, praises and proclaims his name, gives alms and relieves the needy with goods, work and counsel, is regularly present at sermons, and does the other things God has commanded, whatever his intention in doing them. For God will judge the mind; it is not for us to condemn these external things.

units.la: Homines illa, sohtm possunt recte laudare & vituperare, quae diiudicare possunt. Idcirco cum actiones internas seu cogitationes intelligere, & sine errore iudicare nulli possunt, nullæ his poenæ à legibus constitutæ sunt. Solus Deus vt sine errore eas iudicat, ita eadem quoque punit. Exteriorum porrò actuum alij sunt boni, alij autem vitiosi. Illis laus & premium, hisce vituperatio & poena debetur. Boni sunt, quoscunque Deus exerceri iussit: mali autem, quicunque cum lege praeceptoque Dei pugnant. Et horum alij sunt leuiores, & ferè nominantur peccata: aliij grauiores, & frequenter scelera vocantur. Vtrosque vult Deus à magistratu coherceri, imprimis autem scelera. Quanquam verò actus prohibiti ex consensu & dissensu voluntatis magis minusue reddantur viciosi, nunquam tamen fiunt laudabiles. Homicidium, exempli gratia, inuitum non eadem poena punitur quidem, qua voluntarium punitur, attamen non efficiuntur ob id laudabile & bonum. Par ratio est bonorum actuum. Etsi namque non eadem meretetur laudem, idemque praemium, qui vel inuitus vel insciens aliquid boni egit, & qui idem hoc volens ac prudens fecit, nunquam tamen ille, ac si vitiosi aliquid patrauisset, reprehendi poterit.
units.tr: Men can rightly praise and blame only those things which they are able to discern. Therefore, since no one can understand internal acts or thoughts and judge them without error, no penalties for them have been established by laws. God alone, who judges them without error, also punishes them. Among external acts, some are good and others evil. Praise and reward are due to the former, blame and punishment to the latter. Those are good which God has commanded to be performed; those are evil which conflict with the law and command of God. Of these evil acts, some are lighter and are commonly called sins, while others are graver and are often called crimes. God wills that both be restrained by the magistrate, but above all crimes. Although prohibited acts are made more or less wicked according to the consent or dissent of the will, they never become praiseworthy. For example, homicide committed unwillingly is not punished with the same penalty as that committed willingly, yet on that account it does not become praiseworthy or good. The same reasoning holds for good acts. For although he who does something good unwillingly or unknowingly does not deserve the same praise and reward as he who does the same thing willingly and knowingly, yet the former can never be blamed as if he had committed an evil act.

units.la: Ergo si non possunt mala, quae praeter voluntatem euenerunt, commendari, nec bona, quae ab inuito malo que animo profecta sunt, damnari, quomodo, quaeso, licebit alicui vetare, quod eum Deus iusisit facere, ac facere ipse cupit? Aliter legimus sanctos Reges atque alios magistratus egisse. Coegerunt enim subditos, vt ritus a Deo institutos, externe saltem, obseruarent, aliterque facientes interemerunt. Nam vt alios locos nunc omittam, sic scriptum inuenimus. 2. Paralip. 15. Et quisquis non quaesierit Iehouam Deum Israelis, interficiatur a paruo vsque ad magnum, & a viro vsque ad mulierem. Patet igitur quantum a scopo aberrent, qui peccata Sacramentorum interdictione volunt plectere. Nam praeterquam quod rem a Deo omnibus praeceptam, &, quatenus sub iudicium nostrum cadit, id est, quatenus externa est, bonam prohibent, etiam falcem in alienam mittunt messem. Quoniam scelerum castigatio, quatenus externi actus sunt viciosi, ad magistratum pertinet: quoad autem a depravata voluntate promanant, soli Deo subijciuntur recte cognoscenda & punienda. Peius adhuc faciunt, cum, quae Deus facere iusisit, prohibent, quia videlicet externa actio bona, quod ad nos attinet, latens videatur vicium habere coniunctum.
units.tr: Therefore, if evil things that happen against the will cannot be commended, nor good things that proceed from an unwilling or evil mind be condemned, then how, I ask, will anyone be permitted to forbid what God has commanded to be done and himself desires to be done? We read that holy kings and other magistrates acted otherwise. For they compelled their subjects to observe, at least externally, the rites instituted by God, and they put to death those who acted otherwise. For, to omit other passages for now, we find it written thus in 2 Chronicles 15: "And whoever would not seek the LORD God of Israel should be put to death, from small to great, and from man to woman." It is therefore clear how far from the mark they are who wish to punish sins by forbidding the sacraments. For apart from the fact that they forbid a thing commanded by God to all, and good so far as it falls under our judgement, that is, so far as it is external, they also put the sickle into another's harvest. For the punishment of crimes, insofar as the external acts are wicked, belongs to the magistrate; but insofar as they proceed from a corrupt will, they are subject to God alone, to be rightly known and punished by him. They do even worse when they forbid what God has commanded to be done, because a good external act, so far as it concerns us, seems to conceal some vice attached to it.

units.la: Obijciunt etiam ex Iohanne de Synagoga aliquid: Ecclesia & Synagoga, inquiunt, significant idem. Ergo ab hac pelli, est ex illa eijci. Hoc autem est ab vsu rerum sacrarum arceri. Respondeo, nomen Ecclesiae siue congregationis interdum significare totam concionem: aliquando particularem coeuntum. Nonnunquam senatum totius congregationis. Quod posterioribus etiam locum seu aedificium denotet nullus nescit. Eodem fere modo nome Synagogae plura significat. Quippe & pro tota congregatione populi ponitur apud septuaginta Interpretes. Sumitur quoq; pro particulari concione, vt Matth. 6. & alias soepius. Item pro Senatu, vt Deut. 35. Iosuæ 20. plal. 82. Sic Matth. 10. & Mar. 13. positum videtur. Idem enim in his locis videntur significare duo hæc nomina συνέδριον & συναγωγὴ. Probatur idem ex eo, quod in Synagogis nocentes virgis aut plagis caedebantur. At in 25. Deuter. iubetur plagis dignus coram Iudice prosterni & caedi. Erant ergo ibi iudicia. Nectandum in his locis obiter illud etiam fuerit, quod addunturἡγεμόνες & βασιλεῖς: quod Lucas quoque cap. 21. fecit, cum antea 12. cap. τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας pro eisdem posuisset. Nam conijcimus ex his, sic intelligendum per συνέδριον & συναγωγὴν in his locis magistratum Iudaeorum, quomodo per τὰς ἀρχὰς, per τὰς ἐξουσίας, per τὰς ἡγεμονίας καὶ βασιλεῖς intelligimus magistratus Gentilium. Hic enim vnus, vel vnius nomine plures sedebant: ibi plures simul iudicabant. Frequenter notat ædificium: vt cum Iesus in Synagogam scribitur ingressus, ibique docuisse. Tales erant in singulis vrbibus Iudæ: & extra Iudæam vbi, cunque Iudæi multi habitarent. Fuerunt quoque in aliquibus vrbibus plures vna, vt ex sacris libris colligimus.
units.tr: They also raise an objection from John about the synagogue: the Church and the synagogue, they say, signify the same thing; therefore to be driven out of the one is to be cast out of the other, and this is to be shut off from the use of holy things. I answer: the name Church or congregation sometimes signifies the whole assembly, sometimes a particular gathering of those who meet, and sometimes the senate of the whole congregation. That it also denotes the place or building no one is ignorant of. In almost the same way the name synagogue signifies several things. Indeed it is used for the whole congregation of the people by the Seventy. It is also taken for a particular assembly, as in Matthew 6 and very often elsewhere. Likewise it means the senate, as in Deuteronomy 35, Joshua 20 and Psalm 82. So Matthew 10 and Mark 13 seem to be put in this sense. For in these passages the two words συνέδριον [council] and συναγωγὴν [synagogue] seem to signify the same thing. The same is proved from the fact that in the synagogues those who were guilty were beaten with rods or stripes. But in Deuteronomy 25 it is commanded that the one deserving stripes be laid down before the judge and beaten. There were therefore judgements there. In these passages it should also be noted in passing that the words ἡγεμόνες [rulers] and βασιλεῖς [kings] are added, which Luke also did in chapter 21, although earlier in chapter 12 he had used τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας [the principalities and the powers] for the same things. For we conjecture from this that συνέδριον and συναγωγὴν are to be understood in these passages as the magistracy of the Jews, just as by τὰς ἀρχὰς [the principalities], τὰς ἐξουσίας [the powers], and τὰς ἡγεμονίας καὶ βασιλεῖς [the governments and kings] we understand the magistrates of the Gentiles. For the one senate, or one man in the name of several, sat there, whereas here several sat together and judged. It often denotes the building, as when it is written that Jesus entered the synagogue and taught there. Such synagogues existed in each town of Judea, and outside Judea wherever many Jews lived. There were also several in some towns, as we gather from the sacred books.

units.la: Ergo cùm idem significare dicuntur Ecclesia & Synagoga, videndum est, in quo significato sumatur vtrunque. Hoc enim non obseruato, necesse est rem confundi & obscurari: nec verum esse poterit, eandem vtriusque rationem esse. Nam si Ecclesia ponatur pro concione vel societate fidelium: Synagoga autem sumatur vel pro ædificio, vel pro senatu, vel pro vtroque, non poterit eadem esse vtriusque conditio. Planius intelligit hoc, quisquis duo hæc apud se considerabit: nempe apud Iudæos potuisse aliquem ex particulari Synagoga eijci, ex vniuersali seu ex toto populo non potuisse eijci. Non potuit enim ex instituto Dei per Mosen circūcisus, aut ex Gente Iudæa natus, eijci ad Gentiles, seu in exilium ex tota Iudæa exturbari. Interfici improbos iusit Deus: non iusit extrudi ex populo suo, aut cogere vt se dicerent non esse Iudæos. Imò si qui Iudaismum siue coactè siue sponte abnegassent, hos ipsos vbicunq; deprehendere potuerunt, occiderunt. Sic enim in AEgypto fecisse legimus in 3. lib. Macchabæorum. Ideo non arcebatur à Templo, qui ex Synagoga aliqua eiectus fuerat, vt mox apertius declarabo. Alterum quod considerandum diximus, hoc est, Magnum fuisse discrimen inter gubernationem externæ Ecclesiæ Iudæorum & nostræ. Nam non est Ecclesia nunc vni loco alligata, vt tunc erat: sed par est ratio & potestas æqualis cuiusq; particularis & totius Ecclesiæ. Secus habebat res in Ecclesia Iudaica: quæ sic erat vni loco astricta, vt, quod alibi fieret, non rectè fieret, in rebus & ceremonijs plurimis.
units.tr: Therefore, when Church and synagogue are said to mean the same thing, we must consider in which sense each is taken. If this is not observed, the matter is bound to be confused and obscured, and it cannot be true that both have the same condition. For if Church is taken for an assembly or fellowship of the faithful, while synagogue is taken either for a building, or for a senate, or for both, then the condition of the two cannot be the same. Anyone who considers these two things will understand this more clearly: among the Jews, someone could be cast out of a particular synagogue, but could not be cast out of the universal body, that is, the whole people. For a man circumcised by God's institution through Moses, or born of the Jewish nation, could not be driven out to the Gentiles, or exiled from all of Judea. God commanded that the wicked be put to death; He did not command that they be thrust out from his people, or forced to say that they were not Jews. Indeed, if any had renounced Judaism, whether under compulsion or of their own will, they were put to death wherever they could be found. For we read that this was done in Egypt, in the third book of Maccabees. Therefore the one who had been cast out of some synagogue was not thereby barred from the Temple, as I will soon declare more plainly. The second point we said must be considered is this: there was a great difference between the external government of the Jewish Church and ours. For the Church is not now tied to one place, as it was then; rather, the principle and power of each particular Church and of the whole Church are equal. Things were otherwise in the Jewish Church, which was so bound to one place that many things in rites and ceremonies that were done elsewhere were not done rightly.

units.la: Quis non incipiat videre nunc, aliud fuisse ἀποσυνάγωγον fieri apud Iudæos, quàm excommunicari apud nostros? Etenim excommunicatus à particulari Ecclesia, putatur ex tota & Vniuersali Ecclesia eiectus. Eadem enim est forma regendi, & similis potestas totius & particularis Ecclesiæ. At hoc apud Iudæos non erat. Nam Sacrificia (& Sacramenta, excepta circumcisione, expiatione &c ) tantum Hierosolymis celebrari poterant: in particularibus Ecclesijs seu Synagogis celebrari non poterant. Quomodo igitur Sacramenta negauissent, quibus ipsimet carebant? Si negandi aliquid ius habebant, hoc negare poterant, quod in eorum potestate erat. In Synagogis legebatur singulis Sabbathis Moses. Ab huius auditione prohiberi nullus poterat, qui audire cuperet. Nam fuisset hoc factum contra præceptum Mosis. Vnde etiam videntur Ethnicos admisisse in Synagogas, vt ex 13. & 14. præterea ex 12. & 18. Cap. Actor. colligimus. At hisce in Templum introire fas non erat. Ergo cum iussisset Moses omnes mundos ascendere Hierosolymam sacrificatum, non potuit vlla Synagoga hoc vetare. Aliud ergo fuit ἀποσυνάγωγον facere, quàm Templo, Ceremonijs & Sacrificijs à Deo præceptis alicui interdicere.
units.tr: Who does not now begin to see that being made put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον] among the Jews was something other than being excommunicated among us? For a man excommunicated from a particular Church is thought to be cast out of the whole and universal Church. The form of governing is the same, and the power of the whole Church and of a particular Church is alike. But this was not so among the Jews. For sacrifices, and the sacraments (except circumcision, expiation and so on), could be celebrated only at Jerusalem; they could not be celebrated in the particular congregations or synagogues. How, then, could they have denied sacraments which they themselves did not have? If they had any right of refusal, they could refuse only what was in their power. In the synagogues Moses was read every Sabbath, and no one who wished to hear him could be barred from hearing him, for that would have been done against the command of Moses. Hence it seems they admitted Gentiles into the synagogues, as we gather from Acts 13 and 14, and also from Acts 12 and 18. But these people were not permitted to enter the Temple. Therefore, since Moses had commanded all men who were clean to go up to Jerusalem to sacrifice, no synagogue could forbid this. So to be made put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον] was one thing, and to forbid someone the Temple, the ceremonies and the sacrifices commanded by God was another.

units.la: Qui exempla huius rei petit, Christum & Apostolos sibi proponat. Christum Ioh. 8. Samaritanum vocant. Nazaretani non solum extra Synagogam & vrbem expulerunt, verum etiam de montis supercilio præcipitare voluerunt. Et quis dubitat Christum ἀποσυνάγωγον factum à Iudæis, qui decreuerant ἀποσυνάγωγους facere confitentes Iesum esse Christum? An propterea ei vel Templo vel Ceremonijs interdixerunt? Si prætextu Legis hoc potuissent facere Pharisæi, cupidissimè occasionem hanc tàm speciosam arripuissent. At non reperimus in sacris literis vllum verbum, ex quo nobis vel suspicandi detur occasio, tale quid eos cogitauisse: aut tale quid ei ab vllo homine obiectum exprobratumq; fuisse. Quis vnquam ei dixit, In Templum introire tibi non licet, cum sis ἀποσυνάγωγος factus? Frustra excipis, arcano Dei consilio seruatum, quoniam sæpe legimus quid in animo habuerint facere Iudæi, etsi perficere non potuerint. Huius autem rei nullum omninò vestigium extat. Proinde figmentum esse meritissimò dicimus, quod sic obijcitur.
units.tr: Let whoever seeks examples of this matter take Christ and the Apostles as his model. In John 8 they call Christ a Samaritan. The Nazarenes not only drove him out of the synagogue and the city, but even wanted to hurl him from the brow of the mountain. And who doubts that Christ was made put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον] by the Jews, who had decreed that those confessing Jesus to be the Christ should be made put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγους]? Did they, on that account, forbid him either the Temple or the ceremonies? If the Pharisees could have done this under the pretext of the Law, they would most eagerly have seized so plausible an opportunity. But we find nothing in the sacred writings from which we may even suspect that they had any such thing in mind, or that any man ever objected such a thing to him and reproached him with it. Who ever said to him, "It is not lawful for you to enter the Temple, since you have been made put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγος]"? In vain do you object that it was kept back by the secret counsel of God, since we often read what the Jews intended to do, even when they could not carry it out. But of this matter there is no trace at all. Therefore we rightly say that the claim, as it is put forward, is a fiction.

units.la: Ad Apostolos quod attinet, ex 4. & 5. Cap. Act. liquet, quod dicimus, Cum enim ex summa Synagoga, cæsi prius, exturbati fuissent, mox in Templo docuerunt, Sacramentisq; pro more suo vsi sunt, vt ex 21. Act. apparet: nec legimus eos hoc nomine ab vllo homine accusatos aut reprehensos. Ex quot Synagogis eiectus fuit Paulus? Legat qui vult, Acta, & 2. ad Cor. Cap. 11. Quis huic cum Hierosolymam redijsset, inquit, Templum sacrificaturus pro se & pro alijs ingressus fuisset, idq; suadentibus Apostolis faceret, obiecit, quod non licuerit ei ritibus & ceremonis sacris vti? Hoc accusarunt, eum docere Legem non esse seruandam: item eum profanauisse Templum, non ingressu suo, sed Gentilium introductione: quod mentitum erat. Paulus certè cum in Iudicio se excusat, apertè dicit, se contra Legem nihil fecisse. Proinde non faciebat contra Legem, qui ἀποσυνάγωγος factus in Templum introibat & Sacrificijs iuxta Mosis præscripta vtebatur. Quomodo ergo non falsum est ἀποσυνάγωγον γίγνεσθαι idem fuisse, atque illud est, quod hodie vocant excommunicari?
units.tr: As far as the Apostles are concerned, Acts 4 and 5 make clear what we say. For when they had first been beaten and thrown out of the great synagogue, they soon taught in the Temple and used the sacraments in their customary way, as appears from Acts 21; nor do we read that they were accused or rebuked by any man on this account. By how many synagogues was Paul cast out? Let whoever wishes read the Acts, and 2 Corinthians 11. When he had returned to Jerusalem and entered the Temple to offer sacrifice for himself and for others, as the Apostles advised him to do, someone objected that he was not permitted to use the sacred rites and ceremonies. They accused him of teaching that the Law was not to be kept, and also of profaning the Temple, not by his own entry but by the introduction of Gentiles; and this was a lie. Certainly when Paul defends himself before the court, he plainly says that he had done nothing against the Law. Therefore he who had been made put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγος] and entered the Temple and used the sacrifices according to the prescriptions of Moses was not acting against the Law. How, then, is it not false that to become put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον γίγνεσθαι] was the same thing as what they today call being excommunicated?

units.la: Patet igitur facilius esse dicere, quid non fuerit ἀπροσήλυτος[?] fieri, quàm ostendere quid fuerit. Quod non fuerit hoc, quod Aduersarij dicunt, planissimè demonstratum est. Quid fuerit, difficile hic dictu est, vt diuersum non possit affirmari. Etsi verò nobis sufficit indicasse, non id esse, quod nostris hominibus est excommunicari, attamen non pigebit aliquid hac de re amplius proponere. Ergò videtur ignominia quædam fuisse, ac si quis hodie infamia aliqua notaretur. Ioh. 12. Videtur etiam particularis fuisse relegatio, vt si quis ex vrbe aliqua solummodo relegaretur: vt cum Luc. 4. relegatus est à Nazaretanis. Videtur quoque negatio fuisse iuris ciuitatis Iudaeorum: vt nimirum ἀπροσήλυτος fa-ctus, non amplius haberetur pro vero Iudæo, sed velut Proselyta. Quippe hi non recensebantur inter Iudaeos, tametsi à Templo & ceremoniis propterea non arcerentur.
units.tr: It is therefore plain that it is easier to say what it was not to be made a non-proselyte [ἀπροσήλυτος fieri] than to show what it was. That it was not what our adversaries say has been most clearly demonstrated. What it was is hard to say here, since no different account can be affirmed with confidence. Yet although it is enough for us to have indicated that it was not what excommunication is among our people, nevertheless I will not hesitate to propose something more on this matter. It seems, then, that it was a kind of disgrace, as if someone were branded today with some infamy (John 12). It also seems to have been a partial banishment, as when someone was relegated from one city only, as when Christ was banished by the Nazarenes (Luke 4). It seems also to have been a denial of the civil rights of the Jews, so that one who had been made a non-proselyte was no longer regarded as a true Jew, but as a kind of proselyte. For such persons were not counted among the Jews, although they were not on that account kept from the Temple and the ceremonies.

units.la: Equidem Proselytas, qui inter Iudæos habitarunt, constat semper à veris Iudæis distinctos fuisse, tempore Mosis, Prophetarum, & ipsiusmet Christi: tametsi eisdem cum Iudæis vterentur Sacramentis, atque in idem ingrederentur Templum. Proinde fuit vel idem, vel simile quidpiam cum eo, quod apud Esdram Cap. 10. legimus, ex societate reducum ex captiuitate delere. Consentit hoc cum eo, quod in 23. Deuter. legimus, de recipiendis in Ecclesiam, hoc est, in nomen, Gentem, & Genus Iudæorum. Valde namque absurdum foret cogitare, Deum nolle compressum, exsectum, spurium, Ammonitam, Moabitam in regnum suum recipere: qui non est acceptor personarum, sed omnes inuocantes se recipit. Non igitur noluit Deus hosce circumcidi, & in Templum atque ad Sacramenta admitti: sed noluit pro veris Iudaeis eos haberi. Aegyptios autem & Idumæos vult post tertiam generationem recipi: quod certè intelligendum est de illis, qui patrem, auum, abauumq; habuerunt circumcisos.
units.tr: Indeed it is established that the proselytes who dwelt among the Jews were always distinguished from the true Jews, in the time of Moses, of the Prophets, and of Christ himself, although they used the same sacraments as the Jews and entered the same Temple. Therefore it was either the same as, or something similar to, what we read in Ezra 10, the removal of those from fellowship with the returnees from captivity. This agrees with what we read in Deuteronomy 23 about the receiving into the Church, that is, into the name, nation and race of the Jews. For it would be very absurd to think that God was unwilling to receive into his kingdom the crushed, the mutilated, the bastard, the Ammonite, the Moabite, since he is no respecter of persons but receives all who call upon him. Therefore God did not wish these people to be circumcised and admitted to the Temple and to the sacraments, but he did not wish them to be regarded as true Jews. He wills, however, that Egyptians and Edomites be received after the third generation (Deut. 23), which must certainly be understood of those whose father, grandfather and great-grandfather had been circumcised.

units.la: Alias enim nec post millesimam generationem recipiendus aliquis fuisset. Ergo qui tales erant, Inquilini, Peregrini, Proselytæ, vocabantur, pro veris Iudæis non reputabantur, nec ad Synagogam proprie pertinebant, quantumuis interim Sacramentis communibus cum Iudæis vterentur.
units.tr: For otherwise no one would be received even after the thousandth generation. Therefore those who were of this sort were called sojourners, strangers and proselytes; they were not reckoned as true Jews, nor did they properly belong to the synagogue, although in the meantime they used the common sacraments with the Jews.
