units.la: Sed vt paulo ante dixi, quicquid tandem exi\u00adstimetur suisse ἀποσυνάγωγον fieri, constat ex prædictis omnibus, non idem fuisse cum eo, quod hodie vocant excommunicari. Nec videtur prorsus prætereundum esse, quod scriptura non vtitur alijs verbis, quàm ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν, & ἀποσυνάγωγὸν γίγνεσθαι: quæ sanè verba mitius aliquid significare videntur, quàm condemnare, eijcere, perdere, pro deplorato habere, excommunicare. Vltimò illud etiam addam, Pharisæos contra Mosis Deique præcepta exclusisse à Sacramentis circumcisos, siquidem eo, quod ἀποσυνάγωγος aliquos fecerunt, à Sacramentis exclusisse (quod falsum esse demonstraui) pertinaciter affirmentur. Nobis autem non malorum exempla, sed Dei mandata sequenda sunt. Exposui hanc rem pluribus, quod mirificè quidam sibi in hoc argumento placent: & quia à Beza non est tractatum, tametsi pem nobis eius rei fecisset.
units.tr: But, as I said a little earlier, whatever at last is judged to have been to be put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον fieri], it is clear from all the foregoing that it was not the same as what they today call excommunication. Nor does it seem that we should pass over the fact that Scripture uses no other words than to make put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγον ποιεῖν] and to become put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγὸν γίγνεσθαι]; these words certainly seem to signify something milder than to condemn, cast out, destroy, hold as lost, or excommunicate. Lastly I will add this also: the Pharisees are pertinaciously asserted to have excluded the circumcised from the sacraments, contrary to the precepts of Moses and of God, since by making some put out of the synagogue [ἀποσυνάγωγος] they excluded them from the sacraments (which I have shown to be false). But for us it is not the examples of evil men that must be followed, but the commands of God. I have set out this matter at some length, because certain men take wondrous pleasure in this argument; and because it has not been treated by Beza, although he had given us hope of it.

units.la: Libri quinti finis.
units.tr: End of the fifth book.

units.la: Liber
units.tr: Book

units.la: Liber Sextus incipit,
units.tr: Here begins Book Six,

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: Confutatio duorum Libellorum Latinorum pro Excommuni- catione.
units.tr: A Refutation of Two Latin Booklets in Favour of Excommunication.

units.la: DVm superiora scriberem, commodùm oblata mihi sunt tria de excommunicatione scripta: duo Latina, & Germanicum unum: quę illustriss. Principi aduersus me à primarijs suis Theologis oblata fuerunt. Ad Latina non est necesse, vt aliquid præcipuè dicam. Alterum enim planè puerile est, & hoc præcipuè argumento nititur. In diuersis societatibus diuersam oportet disciplinam & diuersas esse pœnas. Ergo in societate Christiana oportet esse interdictionem Sacramentorum & excommunicationem. Ratiocinatio est talis: Animal est, Ergo Gallus. Cur non vel Asinus, vel Hircus, vel aliud quidpiam? Item, Christus cum remittendi dedit potestatem, etiam ligandi dedit. Non inficiamur. Sed ita dicimus dedisse verbo ligandi facultatem, quomodo dedit remittendi potestatem. Rursus est argumentatio à Genere ad speciem affirmando. Tale etiam est tertium, Ecclesia est communio, Ergo etiam communionis priuatio. Simile & illud est, Qui credentes admittunt in communionem, etiam contumaces eijciunt. Quomodo admittendi potentiam à Deo acceperunt, sic etiam eijciendi facultatem habere libenter concedo. Nemo, puto, ægrè feret, quod talibus argumentatoribus pluribus non respondeo.
units.tr: While I was writing the above, three writings on excommunication happened to be brought to me: two in Latin and one in German. They were presented against me to the most illustrious Prince by his leading theologians. I need not say anything particular about the Latin ones. One of them is plainly childish and rests mainly on this argument: different societies need different discipline and different penalties, so in the Christian society there must be the withholding of the sacraments and excommunication. The reasoning runs: "It is an animal, therefore a cock." Why not an ass, or a goat, or something else? Again, when Christ gave the power of loosing, he also gave the power of binding. I do not deny it. But I say that he gave the power of binding in the same way that he gave the power of loosing. Again, the argument is from genus to species, affirmed. The third is of the same kind: the Church is a communion, therefore also the deprivation of communion. Similar is the claim that those who admit believers to communion also cast out the stubborn. I readily grant that just as they received from God the power of admitting, so they also have the power of casting out. I think no one will be upset that I do not answer many such arguers.

units.la: Alterum iactantiæ plus habet, veritatis non amplius. Si enim aliquid habet veri, ad rem non pertinet: quod breuiter etiam indicabo. Primum exponit vsum Presbyterij in Ecclesia, quæ mihi merito licet contemnere, cum scripturas nullas proferat. Hoc tamen reprehensione dignissimum est, quod Ministros neminem habere asserit, à quibus ex officio corrigantur. Nam Deus hoc Magistratui mandauit. Nec excipiuntur Ministri, cum scribitur, omnem animam subiectam debere esse potestati. Verum bene habet, quod seipsos produnt. Quæram ego, quis Presbyteros peccantes corriget? Respondebit, opinor, Ministrorum hoc esse. Sic muli mutuum scabent, dum alteri alteris dicent, tu parcito vnguibus, parcam ego dentibus. Contendit idem, Magistratum subijci Presbyterio, & nihilominus in excommunicatione ait necessarium esse consensum Magistratus. Si subiectus est Iudicio Presbyterij, ab eoque poterit excommunicari Magistratus, cogetur consentire, velit, nolit. Quid istis opus est laruis? Locū, quo probet, citat ex 1. Cor. Cap. 5. Quis non videat quid agatur hic? Sed de ista re supra satis.
units.tr: The other has more boasting than truth. If it has anything true in it, it does not bear on the matter, as I will briefly point out. First, it sets out the function of the eldership in the Church, which I may rightly despise, since it cites no Scripture for it. Yet this is most worthy of reproof: it asserts that the ministers have no one above them by whom they may be corrected in their office. For God has committed this to the magistrate. Nor are the ministers exempted when it is written that every soul must be subject to the powers. Still, it does well to betray themselves. I ask: who will correct erring elders? They will reply, I suppose, that this is the business of the ministers. So mules scratch one another, while each says to the other: you spare your claws and I will spare my teeth. The same author contends that the magistrate is subject to the eldership, and yet in excommunication he says the consent of the magistrate is necessary. If the magistrate is subject to the judgement of the eldership, and can be excommunicated by it, he will be forced to consent whether he wills it or not. What need is there of such masks? To prove his point he cites 1 Cor. 5. Who does not see what is going on here? But I have said enough on this matter above.

units.la: Argumentatur idem à comparatis hoc modo, Immundi legaliter arcebantur. Multò igitur magis arcendi sunt immundi moribus. Contendit hic author, solos contumaces excommunicandos. Quod si est ita, quomodo valebit argumentum ab immundis? Etenim cum primū aliquis immundus fuisset redditus, siue volens siue nolens talis esset factus, statim erat ad purificationem usq; exclusus. Si ergo valet hoc: Corpore immundus excludebatur, Ergo moribus impurus multò magis est excludendus. Si, inquam, hoc valet, etiam illud valebit: Corpore immundus etiamsi non esset in hac re contumax, excludebatur. Ergo multò magis moribus immundus secludendus fuerit, licet minimè sit in scelere pertinax. Igitur si verum esset, quod verum nunquam fuit, est, erit, Christum Matth. 18. voluisse illum excommunicari, qui iudicium Ecclesiæ despexisset, hoc est, contumacem, non posset argumentum ab immundis non contumacibus desumi. Consequens etiam est, vt Apostolus malè iusserit Corinthium illū excommunicari, vt quem ab Ecclesia constet non fuisse isto modo admonitū, quomodo admonēdos aiunt: & proinde neq; contumax videtur fuisse. Praeterea, Petrum aiunt excommunicasse Ananiam & Saphiram, ac Simonem Magum: qui certè non fuerunt solenniter praemoniti, sed statim castigati. Adde, quod crimen Ananiae & Saphirae occultum fuit prorsus. Sed & de Simone Mago nō videtur constitisse Petro, num esset contumax futurus, vt ex textu colligimus. Item citant ex Augustin. quaest. 39. super Deuter. Excommunicationem subijsse in locum interfectionis. At interficiebātur olim, (sicut & hodie Magistratus faciunt) qui crimen patrauerant, tametsi eos scelcris poenituisset. Postremo probat factum Ambrosij, qui Theodosiū tot mensibus non passus est in Templum venire, tametsi factum suum doleret, minimeque contumax esset.
units.tr: The same author argues from comparison in this way: "The unclean were legally kept out; therefore the morally unclean must all the more be kept out." This author contends that only the stubborn are to be excommunicated. If that is so, how will the argument from the unclean hold? For as soon as anyone had become unclean, whether he willed it or not, he was at once shut out until purification. If it is valid to say, "one unclean in body was excluded, therefore one impure in morals must much more be excluded," then the following will also be valid: "one unclean in body was excluded even if he was not stubborn in this matter; therefore one unclean in morals must much more be shut out, even if he is not obstinate in sin at all." So if it were true, which it never was, is, or will be, that Christ in Matthew 18 wished that one should be excommunicated who had despised the judgement of the Church, that is, the stubborn, then the argument from the unclean, who were not stubborn, could not be drawn. It also follows that the Apostle wrongly ordered that Corinthian to be excommunicated, since it is clear he had not been admonished in that way, as they say must be done, and therefore does not seem to have been stubborn. Besides, they say Peter excommunicated Ananias and Sapphira, and Simon Magus. Yet these were certainly not formally warned beforehand, but were punished at once. Add that the sin of Ananias and Sapphira was entirely secret. And as for Simon Magus, it does not seem to have been clear to Peter whether he would be stubborn in future, as we gather from the text. They also cite Augustine, Quaestiones 39 on Deuteronomy, that excommunication took the place of killing. But in former times those who had committed crimes were put to death (as the magistrates do today), even though they repented of their wrong. Lastly, he defends the deed of Ambrose, who did not allow Theodosius to come into the church for so many months, although Theodosius grieved for his deed and was not in the least stubborn.

units.la: Hoc etiā nomine peccat argumentū ab immundorū cōparatione, quod his non negabatur salus: quod non habebātur pro improbis, sceleratis, ac damnatis: quod admittebātur ad Sacramentorū quorundam celebrationē, scilicet Sabbathi & expiationis cōmunis, quę quotannis semel fiebat & praecipuū erat mortis ac meriti Christi simulachrū, sicut Paul. ad Hebreos dilucidè ostendit. Cogebātur enim haec Sacramenta etiā immundi obseruare, (etsi ad Templū non possent venire) lustu, ieiunio, precibus, cessatione-que ab operibus: quēadmodū alios quoq; ritus nihilominus obseruare tenebantur. Non ergo reputabatur immūdus, etiāsi talis morereturpro nō Iudaeo vel non circumcisso, vel pro deplorato. At excommunicati, quādiu tales sunt, inter condēnatos censentur.
units.tr: This argument from the comparison with the unclean also errs in another respect: salvation was not denied to them; they were not regarded as wicked, criminal, or damned; and they were admitted to the celebration of certain sacraments, namely the Sabbath and the common atonement, which was held once a year and was the chief image of the death and merit of Christ, as Paul clearly shows to the Hebrews. For the unclean were compelled to observe these sacraments as well (although they could not come to the Temple), by mourning, fasting, prayers, and abstaining from work, just as they were bound to observe the other rites too. So the unclean man was not regarded as an unbeliever or uncircumcised, nor as one given up for lost, even if he died in that state. But excommunicated people, as long as they are such, are counted among the condemned.

units.la: Peccat tertio, cum rectè se concludere putat: Qui noctu praeter voluntatē polluebatur, excludebatur ea die è Templo. Ergo multo magis exclludendus est, qui cum scorto se volēs commisceuit. Etenim non valet cōparatio inter duo peccata, quorū vtriq; sua propria constituta est poena: sed cū vtrumq; vna eadēq; poena punitur. Tūc, inquā, vel leuius sic punitur, magis ergo grauius sic est puniendū. Idcirco talis est collectio authoris. Homicidiū qui praeter voluntatem cōmiserat, ad vrbē refugij conferre se cogebatur. Ergo multo magis illō confugere debet, qui aliquem sciens ac prudens interfecit.
units.tr: He errs a third time when he thinks he concludes rightly: "One who was polluted at night against his will was excluded from the Temple that day; therefore one who knowingly consorted with a harlot must much more be excluded." For the comparison between two sins does not hold when each has its own fixed penalty, but when both are punished by one and the same penalty. If the lighter offence is punished in this way, then the heavier must be punished in this way too. Yet the author's inference is of this kind: "One who had committed homicide without intent had to flee to a city of refuge; therefore one who knowingly and deliberately killed someone must much more flee to it."

units.la: Item, Hic aliquid insciens fregit vel contaminauit, vel aliquem pulsauit, vel aliud quidpiam fecit, atque reprehensionem meruit: Ergo si idem sciens aut volens fecerit vel is, vel alius, magis obiurgandus fuerit. Nimis pauca summuntur in conclusione, praesertim si certa & peculiaris poena definita sit vtrisque. Potest hoc intelligi clarius in diuersis vitijs, vt si sic colligat aliquis: Ebriosus multatur aliquot aureis, multo igitur magis latrocinia exercens sic multandus est. Sed de Legis immunditia supra fuse egi.
units.tr: Again: "Here one who has unknowingly broken or defiled something, or struck someone, or done something else, has deserved reproof; therefore if the same person, or another, does it knowingly or willingly, he should be reproved all the more." The conclusion takes too little into account, especially if a certain and particular penalty is fixed for both. This can be seen more clearly in different vices: if someone should infer, "A drunkard is fined a few gold coins; therefore one who practises robbery must be fined in the same way, and much more." But I have already dealt at length with the uncleanness of the Law above.

units.la: Adfert posthaec argumenta, quibus probat, ad Sacramenta non esse admittendos vel haereticos vel pertinaciter in sceleribus perseueraturos: in quo a nobis non dissentit. Nos enim neutros admittendos contendimus. Quae praeter haec adfert, non sunt digna, quibus confutandis tempus perdamus, cum ex supradictis responsio pateat. Leuia sunt: rem propositam non concludunt: & morbo communi laborant, externae societatis iudicium a Iudicio Diuino non distinguunt. Preterea habent Apostolum in illis ipsis 2. Capitibus 10. scilicet ac 11. Cor. ex quibus deprompta sunt, apertum aduersarium, vt in Thesibus primum, deinde in superiore confutatione planum fecimus. Vidimus & expendimus cum haec tum alia talia, antequam de hac re scriberemus Theses nostras. Presbyterium vbi in sacris literis contineatur, non docet: in quo prope totius disputationis cardo versatur.
units.tr: He then offers arguments by which he proves that heretics, or those who will persist obstinately in sins, are not to be admitted to the sacraments. In this he does not disagree with us, for we contend that neither kind should be admitted. The other arguments he brings are not worth the time it would take to refute them, since the answer is clear from what has been said. They are trivial, they do not prove the point at issue, and they suffer from the common disease of failing to distinguish the judgement of an outward society from the judgement of God. Moreover, they have the Apostle as an open adversary in the very chapters from which they are drawn, namely 1 Corinthians 10 and 11, as we showed first in the Theses and then plainly in the earlier refutation. Before we wrote our Theses on this matter, we looked at and weighed both these and other such arguments. He does not teach where the eldership is contained in the sacred letters, and on that point nearly the whole hinge of the dispute turns.

units.la: Vt autem clarius intelligatur, quam frigide ad nostra respondeat, ex tribus, quae refellere voluit, duo breuiter attingam. Iudae namque praesentiam in Coena vltima frustra coner anxie defendere, cum nec ex defensione commodum, nec ex negligentione incommodum ad nos redeat.
units.tr: So that it may be clearer how coldly he answers our points, I will briefly touch on two of the three he wished to refute. I shall not anxiously try to defend in vain the presence of Judas at the Last Supper, since neither the defence brings any advantage nor neglect of it any harm to us.

units.la: Quanquam si maxime constaret omnibus, quod ambiguum & inexplicatum adhuc est, Iudam nouae Coenae non interfuisse, non tamen excusaret eiusdem praesentiam in celebratione veteris Coenae, quod isti adferunt, scilicet crimina ipsius occulta fuisse. Nam si potuit Petrus Ananiam & Saphiram, quorum factum erat occultissimum hominibus, Excommunicare (Aiunt enim hos à Petro tunc fuisse Excommunicatos.) cur non potuisset aut debuisset Christus Iudam semouere ab agni esu? Sed ista omnia libenter praetereo, vt quae causam nostram vix eminus attingant.
units.tr: Even if it were agreed by all what is still doubtful and unresolved, that Judas was not present at the new Supper, that would not excuse his presence at the celebration of the old Supper, which they bring up, namely that his crimes were secret. For if Peter could excommunicate Ananias and Sapphira, whose deed was most hidden from men (for they say these two were then excommunicated by Peter), why could Christ not have removed Judas from eating the lamb, or why ought he not to have done so? But I gladly pass over all these points, since they barely touch our cause even from a distance.

units.la: Apostolus, inquam ego, iussit vnumquemque seipsum probare: non imperauit Presbyteris quibusdam alios probare. Respondet iste author, cum de secretis conscientiae loqui. Deinde, inquit, sequitur hinc, maximè arcendos esse aliquos, cum iubeat examinare se vnumquemque priusquam adeat. Falsum est, Apostolum de solis secretis loqui peccatis. Manifeste namque loquitur de rixas mouentibus, de sectas excitantibus, de contemptoribus fratrum pauperum, de inebriantibus se in loco coenae, de vescentibus Idolothytis, (quod peccatum sane grauissimum erat, à Mose prius, deinde etiam à concilio Apostolorum vetitum) & huiusmodi aliis. Hos iubet se explorare, ne sibi iudicium edant non distinguendo coenam Domini à coenis aliis. Ad alterum supra copiose respondi. Non sequitur hinc arcendos lapsos: sed dandam esse omnibus operam, vt digne vsurpent mysteria Dei. Permittit iudicium nostris conscientijs, non praeficit eis vestrum Presbyterium, de quo nunquam sominiauit Apostolus.
units.tr: The Apostle, I say, ordered each one to examine himself; he did not command certain elders to examine others. This author answers as though I were speaking only of the secrets of conscience. Then, he says, it follows that some must be kept away above all, since he orders each one to examine himself before he approaches. That is false. The Apostle is not speaking only of secret sins. He clearly speaks of those who stir up quarrels, who create factions, who despise the poor brothers, who get drunk at the place of the meal, who eat things sacrificed to idols (a sin very grave indeed, forbidden first by Moses and then also by the council of the Apostles), and others of that kind. He orders these men to test themselves, so that they do not bring judgment upon themselves by failing to distinguish the Lord's Supper from other meals. I have already answered the other point at length. It does not follow from this that the fallen are to be kept away; rather, every effort must be made that all partake of the mysteries of God worthily. He leaves the judgment to our consciences; he does not set your presbytery over them, and the Apostle never mentions any such thing.

units.la: Dixi etiam Sacramenta expetentes hoc ipso testari poenitentiam anteactae vitae & desiderium emendationis. Nam in Ecclesijs nostris, qui ad coenam accessuri sunt, se peccauisse, gratia Dei egere, inque ipsius misericordia propter Christi mortem acquiescere palàm confitentur, emendationemque promittunt. Etiam Hypocritae, inquit iste author, accedunt, quos tamen non poenitet. Item Esa. 1. dicere potuissent, nos sacrificando testamur, manus nos sanguine plenas non habere. Vtrùm simulatè aliquis agat an verè, iudicat Deus: nostrum est de omnibus bene sperare, cum nesciamus quo momento Deus corda emollire incipiat. Ad Esaiae cap. 1. supra respondimus. Si illi dixissent Prophetae, peccauimus,
units.tr: I have also said that those who seek the sacraments thereby bear witness to repentance for their past life and to a desire for amendment. For in our churches, those who are about to come to the Lord's Supper openly confess that they have sinned, that they need the grace of God, and that they rest in his mercy through the death of Christ, and they promise amendment. "Hypocrites also come," says this author, "and yet they are not sorry." Likewise, in Esa. 1. they could have said, by offering sacrifices we testify that we do not have hands full of blood. Whether someone acts feignedly or truly, God judges. It is our part to hope well of everyone, since we do not know at what moment God begins to soften hearts. I have already answered the objection from Isaiah chapter 1 above.

units.la: Y & & madent sanguine manus nostrae: at poenitet nos & porrò alij eximus: comprecare nobiscum Deum, vt nostri misereatur: an amplius aliquid petiuissét? Quid facturus fuerit, exemplum Iohannis Baptistae praeclarè nos docet.
units.tr: If they had said to the prophet, "We have sinned, and our hands are wet with blood, but we repent, and others will follow us: pray with us to God that he may have mercy on us," would they have asked for anything more? What he would have done is clearly taught by the example of John the Baptist.

units.la: Putat idem author nos plurimum errare, cum asserimus Christum 18. cap. Matth. nomine Ecclesiae Synedrium intellexisse: vt qui contendat, per vocabulum Ecclesiae, totum coetum seu concionem seu congregationem significari. Quod adeo firmum putat, vt non vereatur hac in parte Calvinum, Viretum, Bezam, vniuersam Ecclesiam Genevensem erroris hac in re insimulare: credo, vt nos oppugnet, quod tamen nulla ratione iusta facit. Ad me quod attinet, constanter aio, rectam & veram etiam esse illorum interpretationem, Dic Ecclesiae, id est, Dic Synedrio. Ab hac sententia cur aliqui eorum, qui publicè priuatimque defenderunt, nunc resiliant, causa quaeri potest, nisi si ea est, quod vident, nos ita probasse Synedrium Iudaeorum legitimum fuisse Magistratum, vt negare porrò non ausint. Interim lectorem moneo, me non habere necesse addere, quae illi, addunt quaeque inepte dici author noster iudicet: scilicet Christum ijsdem verbis iussisse futuras Ecclesias ad analogiam Iudaicae Presbyterium seu Consistorium instituere, cui offensus dicat. Ego enim verba haec, Dic Ecclesiae, idem significare affero, quod ista significant, Dic Magistratui tuo, si non est impiae religionis defensor. Hunc esse genuinum Christi verborum sensum, non illum, quem author iste adfert, nunc iam probabo.
units.tr: This same author thinks that we are greatly mistaken when we assert that Christ, in Matth. 18., by the name of the Church understood the Synedrium, as if someone were to contend that by the word Church is meant the whole assembly, or the sermon, or the congregation. He thinks this so firm that he does not hesitate to charge Calvin, Viret, Beza and the whole Church of Geneva with error in this matter, and I believe he does so in order to attack us, though he does it without any just reason. As for me, I steadfastly maintain that their interpretation is right and true as well: "Tell it to the Church," that is, "tell it to the Synedrium." Why some of those who have defended this publicly and privately now draw back from this view may be asked, unless the reason is that they see we have proved the Synedrium of the Jews to have been a lawful magistracy, so that they no longer dare to deny it. Meanwhile I warn the reader that I do not need to add what they add, and what our author judges to be foolishly said: namely, that Christ by these same words ordered the future churches to set up an elders' board or consistory on the analogy of the Jewish Presbyterium, at which he takes offence. For I affirm that these words, "Tell it to the Church," mean the same as these, "Tell it to your magistrate, if he is not a defender of an impious religion." That this is the genuine sense of Christ's words, and not the one this author brings forward, I will now prove.

units.la: Suppono ergo primum id, quod ab omnibus concedi existimo, Christum Ecclesiae praecepisse dicere, quae in Iudaea tunc esset, quámque discipuli esse scirent, hoc est, Discipulos intellexisse, cuinam Ecclesiae Dominus mandaret dicere. Etenim si de Ecclesia fuisset locutus, quae nullibi inueniretur, & cuius constitutio nondum esset exposita, nec ad sui temporis locique consuetudinem sermonem suum accommodasset, à nullo fuisset intellectus
units.tr: I assume first, then, what I believe is conceded by all: that Christ bade them tell the Church that then existed in Judea, and that the disciples knew which it was; that is, the disciples understood to which Church the Lord was commanding them to speak. For if he had spoken of a Church that is found nowhere, whose constitution had not yet been set out, and if he had not adapted his speech to the custom of his own time and place, he would have been understood by no one.

units.la: catchword: tus
units.tr: catchword: tus

units.la: ſtus. At vero Discipulos Christi verba intellexisse, cum ex aliis circumstantibus, tum ex eo maxime perspicimus, quod, cum alias saepe scribantur quaedam non satis perceperint, hic neque mirati aliquid sunt, nec dubitarunt, nec declarationem petierunt. Hoc solum admiratur Petrus, quod toties iuberetur fratri culpam deprecanti ignoscere: ex quo conijcimus caetera eum recte intellexisse. Ac de Iudaeorum Ecclesia Discipulos accepisse verba Magistri, docet Petri interrogatio. Cum enim quaerit, quoties fratri in se peccanti teneatur ignoscere, ostendit se de Iudaeis verba Domini accepisse: ut qui Gentilem nullum reputaret fratrem. Nam de spirituali Gentilium fraternitate nihil intellexerunt Apostoli ante resurrectionem Domini. Adde, quod ab ipsomet Christo iussi fuerant Gentiles & Samaritanos cavere, atque ad solas perditas oves domus Israelis quaerendas proficisci, Matth. 10. Et quod de eadem Ecclesia Christus fuerit locutus, verba haec, sit tibi velut Ethnicus & Publicanus, abunde ostendunt. Quippe Iudaeis Ethnicos opponit, eisque Publicanos coniungit: quod iurati essent Romanorum Ministri contra suam Gentem: ac proinde sub sola Romanorum protectione instar Ethnicorum tuti viverent. Equidem odio eos ita prosequebantur Iudaei, ut, si Romanorum potentia non protexisset, discerpturi ac dilaniaturi vivos viderentur. Molestissime seruitutem iugumque Romanorum, imprimis autem tributi exactionem ferebant: ut vel ex unica interrogatione, qua, utrum Caesari tributum soluere liceat, quaerunt, liquere posset, si alia omnia ignoraremus.
units.tr: tus. But in fact the disciples understood the Lord's words, as we perceive both from the other surrounding circumstances and above all from this: although in other places they often did not sufficiently grasp certain things that were written, here they neither marvelled at anything, nor doubted, nor asked for an explanation. Peter alone marvels that he is so often commanded to forgive a brother who asks pardon for his fault; from this we conjecture that he understood the rest correctly. And that the disciples took the words of their Master to refer to the Church of the Jews is shown by Peter's question. For when he asks how often he is bound to forgive a brother who sins against him, he shows that he took the Lord's words of Jews, since he regarded no Gentile as a brother. For the Apostles understood nothing of the spiritual brotherhood of the Gentiles before the Lord's resurrection. Add that Christ himself had ordered them to beware of Gentiles and Samaritans and to go only to seek the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 10). And that Christ spoke of this same Church is amply shown by the words, "let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector." Indeed, he sets Gentiles over against Jews and joins tax collectors to them, because they were sworn servants of the Roman officials against their own nation, and so lived safely under the sole protection of the Romans, like Gentiles. Indeed the Jews so hated them that, had the power of the Romans not protected them, they would have seemed ready to tear them to pieces and rend them alive. The Jews bore the servitude and yoke of the Romans very resentfully, and above all the exaction of tribute; this could be clear from the single question by which they ask whether it is lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, even if we knew nothing else.

units.la: Suppono secundo, nomina, quibus apud Hebraeos significatur Ecclesia, bifariam vsurpata fuisse. Etenim significant aliquando concionem seu multitudinem vel totius populi vel vnius urbis aut loci: aliquando autem huius turbae Senatum, Praefectos, Magistratum, aut quocunque modo libet appellare: praesertim quando non vnus aliquis, sed plures simul præessent. Scio Ecclesiam interdum etiam poni pro collectione, quae in vna domo est: sed haec ad institutum nostrum non pertinet. Christus enim hic de Ecclesia vel vrbis vel pagi alicuius loquitur. Ac quod totam nomina illa coniicionem plerumque designent, extra controuersiam pono. Quod autem pro Senatu & Magistratu nonnunquam sumantur, manifestum est ex cap.35. Num. vbi quater, &20. Iosuae, vbi bis, & Psal.82. vbi semel reperimus. Septuaginta interpretes nomen, quod in proximè dictis locis Magistratum seu Iudices significat, & alijs in locis propè omnibus, in quibus totam multitudinem denotat, fere expresserunt nomine τῆς συναγωγῆς. (Obiter tantum hic monebo, idem nomen hoc, quod in modo citatis locis Magistratum significat, in exemplari Syriaco legi cap.18.Matth. vbi Græcè scriptum est ἐκκλησία.) Est hic loquendi modus nobis admodum familiaris & vsitatus. Dicimus enim Imperium fecisse, dixisse, decreuisse, quod Imperator cum Imperij ordinibus fecit aut decreuit. Dicimus hanc vel illam Ecclesiam sic vel sic sentire, cum, qui in ea præcipui sunt, sic sentiunt. Dicimus indicauisse aut conquestos esse aut offerre seu declarare Reipublicae, quod eius Senatui indicauimus. Dicimus nos à Repub. absolutos, iudicatos, offensos, donatos, quoties à Senatu aliquid tale tulimus. His ita declaratis, propositum sic argumentor.
units.tr: I suppose, second, that the names by which the Church is signified among the Hebrews were used in two ways. For they sometimes signify an assembly or multitude, either of the whole people or of one city or place; but sometimes they signify the senate of that crowd, its prefects, its magistrate, or whatever name one likes to give it, especially when not one man but several preside together. I know that the Church is sometimes also taken for a gathering that is in one house, but this does not pertain to our purpose. For Christ here speaks of the Church of some city or village. That those names for the most part designate an assembly I lay down beyond controversy. That they are sometimes taken for the Senate and the magistrate is clear from Numbers 35, where we find it four times, from Joshua 20, where twice, and from Psalm 82, where once. The Seventy translators rendered the word, which in the passages just cited means magistrates or judges, and in almost all the other places where it denotes the whole multitude, nearly always by the word "of the synagogue" [τῆς συναγωγῆς]. (I will only note in passing that this same word, which in the passages just cited means magistrates, is read in the Syriac copy at Matthew 18, where the Greek has "church" [ἐκκλησία].) This mode of speaking is very familiar and customary with us. For we say that the Empire has done, said, or decreed what the Emperor with the orders of the Empire has done or decreed. We say that this or that Church thinks thus or so, when those who are foremost in it think thus. We say that we have reported to the Commonwealth, or complained to it, or offered or declared, what we have reported to its Senate. We say that we have been acquitted, judged, offended, or favoured by the Commonwealth whenever the Senate has passed some such thing. With these things thus declared, I argue my point as follows.

units.la: Christus vel intellexit Ecclesiae nomine totam multitudinem Hierosolymae, veleiusdem Presidesue Principes ac Magistratus: hoc est, vel accepit in primo significato, vel in secundo. (Nam præter notiones hasce duas nulla est alia, quae nostrae causae aptari possit.) Caeterum non potuit multitudinem intelligere. Nam pugnat hoc expresse cum Lege & statutis Dei per Mosen promulgatis: contra quae Christum nihil aut fecisse aut iussisse, omnino certum est. Equidem tantum abest; vt in externa Reipub. gubernatione Iudaeorum aliquid mutarit aut reprehenderit, vt prorsus nullum nobis nouum praeceptum de exercendis iudicijs reliquerit. Consulit Apostolus Corinthijs, vt Arbitros ex suo corpore eligarit, ne coram profano Magistratu de rebus minimis litigare cernerentur: at longius hoc valere non voluit, quàm dum subiecti Magistratu ageret Ecclesia. Quod si igitur in ratione gubernandi apud Ethnicos nihil praecepit mutari, quomodo censeri possit aliquid nouare voluisse in administratione ab ipsomet Deo Patre suo imperata? Iussit porrò Deus omnes controuersias & lites, quae inter priuatos amicè componi non possent, coram delectis iudicibus explicari. Sanè à tempore Mosis vsque ad excidium vrbis constantissimè hoc seruatum est, vt publica Iudicia, non à populo, sed à Magistratibus exercerentur. Constat igitur iam Christum intellexisse per Ecclesiam, non turbam, sed Synedrium.
units.tr: Christ either understood by the name Church the whole multitude of Jerusalem, or its presidents, princes and magistrates; that is, he took the word either in the first sense or in the second. (For apart from these two notions there is no other that can be fitted to our case.) But he could not have meant the multitude. For this expressly conflicts with the Law and the statutes of God promulgated through Moses, against which it is entirely certain that Christ did nothing and commanded nothing. Indeed, he was so far from changing or censuring anything in the external government of the Jewish commonwealth that he left us no new precept at all about the exercise of judgments. The Apostle advises the Corinthians to choose arbiters from their own body, so that they should not be seen litigating over trifling matters before a profane magistrate; but he did not wish this to hold for longer than while the Church acted under the magistrate's authority. If, then, in the manner of governing among the Gentiles he ordered nothing to be changed, how can it be thought that he wished to introduce something new in an administration commanded by God the Father himself? Moreover, God ordered that all controversies and suits which could not be settled amicably between private persons be argued before chosen judges. Indeed, from the time of Moses down to the destruction of the city this was most constantly observed, so that public judgments were exercised not by the people but by the magistrates. It is therefore now established that by the Church Christ understood not the crowd but the Synedrium.

units.la: Confirmat iam dicta, pariterque propositum probat, quod Discipuli, quos patriarum legum ad obitum vsque obseruantissimos fuisse ex Act. perspicimus, nihil contradicunt: qui non videntur tacituri fuisse, si contra Mosis instituta receptumque morem aliquid imperari sibi arbitrati fuissent. Quod Christi mentem perceperint, ex eo liquet, quod de re alia nulla vel dubitasse vel interrogasse eos videmus, quàm de crebra iniuriarum remissione. Deinde, quod de alia Ecclesiae gubernatione, quam visitata & sua, intelligere non potuerunt. Quomodo enim de Ecclesia post Christi mortem fundanda & ordinanda intellexissent, qui nec moriturum nec reuicturum Christum credebant? Ne tum quidem persuadere ipsis Dominus potuit, cum Hierosolymam ascendens apertissimis eis verbis praedixeret, Luc. 18, & alibi. Quinimò post resurrectionem quoque ignoraverunt, quale Christi Regnum esset futurum, quod prorsus mundanum & Iudaico simile expectabant, adeoque hoc ipsum restituendum putabant, priusquam Spiritu-sancto coelitus induerentur. Quocirca non de alia Ecclesia verba Christi acceperunt, quàm de Senatu siue Synedrio, quod nomine aliàs Ecclesiam quoque significante nominari non nesciebant. Acceperunt autem recte cum nullus in totis sacris scripturis apex inueniatur, qui non recte eos hoc loco Christi sententiam percipisse indicet.
units.tr: He now confirms what has been said and proves the point at hand. The disciples, whom we see from the Acts to have kept their ancestral laws most scrupulously until their deaths, raise no objection. They would hardly have kept silent if they had thought that something was being commanded against the institutions of Moses and the custom they had received. That they grasped Christ's meaning is clear from the fact that we see them doubting or asking about no matter except the frequent forgiveness of wrongs. Secondly, they could not have understood it as referring to any other government of the Church than the one they knew and had seen. For how could they have understood anything about a Church to be founded and ordered after Christ's death, when they believed that Christ would neither die nor rise again? The Lord could not even persuade them of this when, going up to Jerusalem, he foretold it to them in the plainest words (Luke 18), and elsewhere. Indeed, even after the resurrection they did not know what sort of kingdom Christ's would be. They expected it to be wholly worldly and like the Jewish kingdom, and so they thought this very thing had to be restored before they were clothed with the Holy Spirit from heaven. Therefore they did not take Christ's words as referring to any other Church than the Senate or Synedrium, which they knew was also sometimes called by the name of the Church. They took them rightly, since no point in all of Holy Scripture can be found that does not show that they rightly understood Christ's meaning in this place.

units.la: Probat illud etiam, quod Christus iussit Ecclesiae dicere, quae potestatem haberet iniuriosum ad se vocandi, testes examinandi, causam cognoscendi, sententiamque dicendi. Etenim iubeturob eum finem is, qui iniuriam patitur, post primam admonitionem duobus aut tribus sibi adiunctis animum iniuriosi pertentare, vt, si nihil proficiat, coràm Ecclesia causam suam idoneè probare testibus possit. Testes autem coràm iudicibus examinantur, vt de controuersia pronunciari iustè possit. Certè oportet tales esse, qui testes audiunt, vt imperare possint. Alioqui enim aut venire, aut testimonium dicere facile recusauerint. Caeterum non habuisse populum, vel turbam, vel aliàs, vel Christi aetate authoritatem vocandi, audiendi & examinandi testes per se, vel mandandi aliis quibusdam, nullus est, qui nesciat. Rursus igitur patet, eum non turbae, sed Synedrio siue Magistratui iussisse indicare, qui ex praescripto Mosis hanc potestatem solus obtinebat.
units.tr: What Christ commanded also proves this: that the Church should be told, that is, the body with the power to summon the wrongdoer, examine witnesses, hear the case and pronounce sentence. For the one who suffers the wrong is ordered, after the first admonition, to take two or three others with him and press the wrongdoer, so that if nothing is gained, he may be able to prove his case properly before the Church by means of witnesses. Witnesses, however, are examined before judges, so that a just judgement can be pronounced on the dispute. Certainly those who hear the witnesses must be of such a kind that they can give orders, for otherwise they would easily refuse to come or to give testimony. Moreover, no one who knows anything can deny that the people, or the crowd, or anyone else in Christ's day, had no authority to summon, hear and examine witnesses by themselves, or to commission others to do so. Again, then, it is plain that he did not order the matter to be declared to the crowd, but to the Synedrium or magistrate, who alone held this power according to the rule of Moses.

units.la: Praeterea iussit Ecclesiae dicere Christus, cui tum dicere offensus posset. Sed turbae seu concioni indicare qui potuisset? Non poterat connocare populum: quia neque Magistratus tulisset, neque illa paruisset. Quis non videt in contrarias partes mox scindendam multitudinem, vbi nullis legibus cohercita liberè agit? Iterum ergo sequitur, ipsum iussisse dicere Iudaicae Ecclesiae Praesidibus & Rectoribus. Si excipias, aliquos à multitudine ad hanc rem deligendos fuisse, frustra excipias. Primum, quia impossibile est docere, populum potestatem habuisse tales iudices eligendi, aut tales post Mosen habuisse. Si Christum dedisse ius hoc in praesente loco dicas, rursus nihil dixeris. Nam non potest hoc ex verbis doceri verum esse. Deinde contra Mosis legem hoc fuisset praeceptum. Tertiò, quid Pharisaeos ad hoc dicturos fuisse censes? Certe omnes occasiones observabant, vt eum contra Legem docere aut facere deprehenderent. Si verò de eo potuissent affirmare, eum Leges Mosis contuellere: populo dignitatem & ius gubernandi contra Magistratum, cui Deus per Mosen hoc imperium tribuisset, asserere: contra Magistratum subditos armare: si, inquam, verè potuissent haec dicere, an non seditionis reum peregisset?
units.tr: Besides, Christ told them to tell the Church, but whom could he have told at that time who could take offence? Could he have summoned the people? No, because neither would the magistrate have allowed it nor would the crowd have obeyed. Who does not see that the multitude, when it acts free of any legal restraint, is soon split into opposing parties? Therefore it follows again that he ordered them to speak to the presidents and rulers of the Jewish Church. If you should make an exception, that some were to be chosen from the multitude for this business, your exception is useless. First, because it is impossible to show that the people had the power to elect such judges, or had such a power after Moses. If you say that Christ gave this right in the present passage, you will have said nothing, for this cannot be proved to be true from the words. Secondly, such an order would have been against the law of Moses. Thirdly, what do you think the Pharisees would have said to this? They were certainly watching for every chance to catch him teaching or doing something against the Law. If they could truly have claimed that he was overturning the laws of Moses, that he was asserting the dignity and right of the people to govern against the magistrate, to whom God had granted this authority through Moses, and that he was arming subjects against the magistrate, could they not truly have said these things, and would he not then have been made out a defendant in sedition?

units.la: Age verò concedamus haec de Christianorum Ecclesia sola dicta esse (quod falsum esse prorsus certum est.) Demonstare nihilominus oportet, Deum alicubi mandasse huic Ecclesiae, vt ex suo corpore certos aliquos ad hoc munus eligat, licet Magistratum Rectoremque pium nata a Deo fuerit. At hoc quibus testimonijs demonstrabitur? An dicent, Dic Ecclesiae, idem significare, quod significat, Constitue aliquos, qui nomine Ecclesiae talia administrent? At verò probanda erit haec interpretatio scripturae testimonijs. Haec autem vbi inuenient? Deinde quod in alijs isti reprehendunt, hoc ipsum faciunt. Nisi enim concedant Christum in hac dicendi formula, & loci in quo versabatur, & temporis illius consuetudinis, quae tunc vigebat, & auditorum captus rationem habuisse, impossibile est, vt his verbis adiuuentur. Oportet ergo vt confiteantur, Christum iussisse Senioribus dicere, qui tunc erant, vt secundum analogiam nunc intelligamus dicendum illis, qui nunc sunt. Cum esset docturus Deo sacrificia nostra non placere, si odium aleremus aduersus fratrem, iubet munus ad altare relinquere, & fratri prius reconciliari: non quod nesciret sacrificandi morem illum mox habiturum finem suum: sed quod per analogiam intelligere nos vellet, quid à nobis postulet Deus, quando exaudire eum nostras preces cupimus. Ergo ipsimet testantibus iusit Synedrio dicere. Tunc enim Ecclesia nulla erat, post turbam, cui possent homines conqueri, & causas suas testibus productis probate. Postremò nunquam demonstrare nobis poterunt, quòsnam eligi ex Ecclesiae corpore oporteat: de qua re hodie ingens inter Excommunicatores est controuersia.
units.tr: But let us grant that these things were said for the Church of Christians alone (which is entirely certain to be false). Nevertheless, it must be shown that God has somewhere commanded this Church to choose certain persons from its own body for this office, even though the Church was born with a pious magistrate and ruler. But by what testimonies will this be shown? Will they say that "tell the Church" means the same as "appoint some who may manage such things in the name of the Church"? But this interpretation will have to be proved by testimonies of Scripture. Where will they find these? Besides, they do here what they find fault with in others. For unless they concede that Christ, in this form of speech, took account of the place where he was, of the custom of that time which then prevailed, and of the capacity of his hearers, it is impossible for them to be helped by these words. They must therefore confess that Christ ordered them to speak to the elders who then were, so that by analogy we now understand that it is to be said to those who now are. When he was about to teach that God does not like our sacrifices if we harbour hatred against a brother, he bids us leave the gift at the altar and first be reconciled to our brother. He did not do this because he did not know that the custom of sacrificing would soon come to an end, but because he wished us to understand by analogy what God asks of us when we desire him to hear our prayers. So, by their own admission, he ordered them to speak to the Synedrium. For at that time there was no Church, only the crowd, to which men could complain and prove their causes by producing witnesses. Finally, they will never be able to show us which persons ought to be chosen from the body of the Church, a question on which today there is a huge controversy among the excommunicators.

units.la: Sed donemus hoc etiam in praesentia, & quaeramus illud potius, vtrum delectis illis concedant potestatem admonendi, obiurgandi, & Excommunicandi, an non concedant? Si facultatem habent Excommunicandi, ipsi sunt Ecclesia, cui Christus iussit, dicere. Proinde verum est, quod dixi, causas tales non debere toti Ecclesiae proponi dijudicandas, sed solis ab Ecclesia delectis: quibus Iudaeorum Synedrium respondebat. Si Excommunicandi facultatem non permittunt, saltem authoritatem audiendi testes, examinandi, admonendi & obiurgandi non negabunt. Etenim non poterit istis negari, quod testibus ante hos conceditur, & post hos Ecclesiae: praesertim cum testes examinare eos oporteat, vt rem excussam, explicatam, difficultatibusque omnibus liberatam Ecclesiae proponant expendendam & iudicandam. Concedit eis hoc author hic noster his verbis. Quod si fratres priuatis horum admonitionibus non resipiscant, ad extremum officium fuerit totius Presbyterij, nomine Ecclesiae significati, tales accersere, & coram toto Presbyterorum coetu obiurgare, corrigere, monere. Notandum hic est obiter, quod dicit, ad extremum: & quod Ecclesiae nomine ait significari Presbyterium: quae aperte cum ante dictis pugnant. Constat autem id, quod dixi, hoce potestatem habere monendi, obiurgandi, corrigendi. Quo posito, quatuor fuerint gradus, non tres solum, vt in Christi verbis cernimus. Primum enim priuatim arguendus erit iniuriam faciens: deinde cum duobus aut tribus alijs admonendus: tertio à delectis Presbyteris audiendus & obiurgandus: quarto, si horum dehortationem despiciat Ecclesiae accusandus: ac demum, si ne hanc quidem audiat, velut Ethnicus & Publicanus erit habendus. Etenim pro eiusmodi haberi nequit, nisi qui Ecclesiae obiurgationem spreuit: non autem, si Presbyteros illos despexerit: nisi Presbyteri sint illa Ecclesia.
units.tr: But let us grant this for the moment as well, and ask instead whether they concede to those chosen the power to admonish, rebuke and excommunicate, or not. If they have the power to excommunicate, they themselves are the Church to which Christ told them to speak. Therefore what I said is true: such cases ought not to be submitted to the whole Church for judgement, but only to those chosen by the Church, and the Jewish Synedrium corresponded to these. If they do not grant the power of excommunicating, they will at least not deny the authority to hear witnesses, to examine, admonish and rebuke. For it cannot be denied to them what is granted to witnesses before them and to the Church after them, especially since they must examine the witnesses so that they may lay the matter, thoroughly investigated, explained and freed of all difficulties, before the Church for weighing and judging. Our author here concedes this to them in these words: "But if the brethren do not repent after private admonitions from these, it will be the last duty of the whole eldership, signified by the name of the Church, to summon such persons and to rebuke, correct and admonish them before the whole assembly of elders." It must be noted here in passing that he says "the last duty," and that he says the eldership is signified by the name of the Church. These statements clearly conflict with what he said before. It is agreed, however, that what I have said is true: the eldership has the power to admonish, rebuke and correct. Granting this, there would be four stages, not only three, as we see in Christ's words. For first the wrongdoer must be rebuked in private; then he must be admonished with two or three others; thirdly he must be heard and rebuked by the chosen elders; fourthly, if he scorns their dissuasion, he must be accused before the Church; and finally, if he does not listen even to this, he must be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. For he cannot be regarded as such unless he has scorned the rebuke of the Church, and not if he has scorned those elders, unless those elders are that Church.

units.la: Non praetereundum est hoc loco, quod ex Aduersarijs
units.tr: It should not be passed over at this point that some of our opponents

units.la: aliqui dicunt, Magistratum tales eligere debere saltem ab initio, etiamsi Ecclesia nec petat, nec iubeat, nec consentiat. Quomodo, rogo te, poterunt isti vice Ecclesiae sedere, qui nolente ea sedent & iudicant? & non ab ea, sed iniuria ea electi sunt? Si verum est, Christum nomine Ecclesiae intellexisse totam multitudinem, falsum est, Magistratui hoc permitti, ut nolente Ecclesia hos ei Presbyteros imponat. Quanquam enim Magistratus praecipuum est Ecclesiae membrum, tamen ipsimet interpretibus non iusit Christus membro primario & principi indicare, sed Ecclesiae toti: in qua non facit alios alijs potentiores, quod ad hanc rem attinet. Nam si principali membro iussisset indicare, aut facultatem dedisset illum Senatum eligendi, Magistratui dedisset, hoc est, Synedrio: quod isti negant. Quare si tota Ecclesia potestatem hanc accepit, non habet eam Magistratus, nisi populus ei unanimi & expresso consensu concesserit, aut ipse sibi vsurpauerit. Neque excusat, quod semel tantum hoc ei volunt licere. Nam si Deus non dedit, nullo potest iure vel semel vel scepius sibi vendicare. Si autem semel iure potest, semper potest: nisi expressum Dei verbum demonstretur, quod semel duntaxat permitti mandet. His rationum pugnis & contradictionibus necessario se inuoluunt isti falsa sua interpretatione.
units.tr: say that the magistrate ought to choose such elders, at least at the beginning, even if the Church neither asks, nor commands, nor consents. How, I ask you, can those men sit in place of the Church who sit and judge against its will, and who were chosen not by it but wrongly? If it is true that by the name of the Church Christ meant the whole multitude, then it is false that the magistrate is allowed to impose such elders on it against the Church's will. For although the magistrate is the principal member of the Church, Christ did not order them to tell the primary and chief member, but the whole Church, in which, so far as this matter is concerned, he does not make some more powerful than others. For if he had ordered the chief member to be told, or had given the power of choosing that Senate, he would have given it to the magistrate, that is, to the Synedrium, which they deny. Therefore, if the whole Church has received this power, the magistrate does not have it, unless the people have granted it to him by unanimous and express consent, or he has seized it for himself. Nor does it help that they want this to be permitted to him only once. For if God has not given it, no one can claim it by any right, once or more often. And if he can rightly claim it once, he can always claim it, unless a express word of God is shown ordering that it be permitted only once. By these battles of argument and contradictions, these men are necessarily entangled in their false interpretation.

units.la: Restat alia difficultas. Constat ex supradictis & ipsorum pariter concessione, multitudinem nihil posse ordine decenter iudicare, nisi eligat, qui causas quaslibet audiant, examinent, explicent, iudicent, ac tandem Ecclesiae perspicue proponant. Ergo ut ista apte peragantur, & confusio caueatur, Presbyteros eligendos esse clamant, qui ius habeant excommunicandi. Nos vero unde hoc efficiant nondum videmus. Esto enim potestatem hanc habeat propter iam dictam causam coetus Magistratu carens: An propterea consequetur hoc turbae in illo quoque coetu concessum esse, qui pium sortitus est Magistratum? Minime gentium. Inscite namque ratiocinantur a genere ad speciem affirmando, qui sic colligunt. Vt ordine peragantur cuncta & & confusio vitetur, eligendi aliqui sunt, qui res regant: Ergo tales quidam ex plebe eligendi sunt. Cur enim hi potius, quàm alij fuerint eligendi? An quoniam animal est, quod mouetur, mox canis est, & non homo aut aliud quodpiam? Ordine in Ecclesia sicut in rebus aliis vniuersis opus est, fateor. At vbi ordinem nobis praescripsit Deus, ordinem alium quaerere non habemus necesse. Hic autem praescripsit. Frustra igitur laboramus, vt alio res ordine meliore administremus.
units.tr: There remains another difficulty. It follows from what has been said above, and from their own concession as well, that a multitude cannot judge anything properly in an orderly way unless it chooses men who will hear the causes, examine them, explain them, decide them, and finally lay them plainly before the Church. So, in order that these things may be carried out fittingly and confusion be avoided, they cry out that elders must be chosen who have the right of excommunicating. But we do not yet see how they make this follow. Granted that the assembly without a magistrate has this power for the reason already mentioned: will it follow that the same right has been granted to the crowd in that assembly which has a godly magistrate? By no means. For they reason foolishly, inferring from the genus to the species by affirming, when they conclude as follows: so that everything may be done in order and confusion avoided, some men must be chosen to govern affairs; therefore certain such men must be chosen from the common people. For why should these rather than others be chosen? Is it because a thing that moves is an animal, and so straightaway a dog, and not a man or something else altogether? I admit that in the Church, as in all other things, there is need of order. But where God has prescribed the order for us, we have no need to seek another order. And he has prescribed it here. It is therefore in vain that we labour to administer the matter by some other, better order.

units.la: Certum est, Deum Magistratui externae gubernationis imperium & ius omne credidisse: nec res politicas tantum, sed etiam sacras ita ipsius potentiae subiecisse, vt has ex praescripto verbi Dei, illas iuxta scriptas leges & aequitatem administret. Quod cum sit in veteri Testamento à Deo mandatum, à pijs omnibus Iudicibus & Regibus vsurpatum, & in nouo non reperiatur mutatum: merito dicimus Ecclesiam, quae Magistratum habet pium, non posse ex voluntate Dei nouum sibi eligere Senatum, qui publica exerceat iudicia. Sanè si exstaret aliqua permissio aut concessio talem Senatum eligendi, non posset haec longius extendi, quàm ad Ecclesias Magistratu carentes: ad alias illas non posset, quaecunque aliàs potestate Magistratus suos eligendi carent. Non enim armauit Deus vspiam subditos contra suos Magistratus: nec praecepit partem eis gubernationis adimere, aliisque imponere, qui ipsum quoque Magistratum in ordinem redigant, suoq; Dominatui externo subijciant. Itaque vt maximè sit verum, Ecclesiam pro tota concione positam fuisse à Christo, sequetur nihilominus Magistratui, vbi is pius est, indicandum fore. Nam multitudini dici non potest. Ergo eligendi aliqui in eius locum. At in nouo Testamento nulli tales iubentur eligi, multò minus definit scriptura, qui sint eligendi. Quare si ordo est seruandus, optimus erit diuinus ordo. Hic autem est, vt Magistratus iudicijs de moribus praesit.
units.tr: It is certain that God entrusted to the magistrate the power of external government and all right of it; and he subjected to the magistrate's authority not only civil affairs but also sacred ones, so that the magistrate administers the latter according to the prescription of the Word of God and the former according to written laws and equity. Since this was commanded by God in the Old Testament, was practised by all godly judges and kings, and is not found changed in the New, we rightly say that a Church which has a godly magistrate cannot, by the will of God, choose for itself a new senate to exercise public judgments. Certainly, if there were any permission or grant of choosing such a senate, it could not be extended further than to churches lacking a magistrate; it could not reach those other churches which, lacking any power of choosing their own magistrates, are in that position. For God has nowhere armed subjects against their magistrates, nor commanded that part of the government be taken from them and imposed on others, who would bring the magistrate himself into order and subject him to their external lordship. And so, even if it is entirely true that the Church was established by Christ for the whole assembly, it will nevertheless follow that, where the magistrate is godly, the matter must be referred to him. For it cannot be said to the multitude. Therefore some must be chosen in its place. But in the New Testament no such men are commanded to be chosen, and much less does Scripture define who are to be chosen. Wherefore, if order is to be kept, the best order will be the divine order. This, however, is that the magistrate presides over judgments concerning morals.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Refutatio alius libelli pro Excommunicatione.
units.tr: A refutation of another book in favour of excommunication.

units.la: Onsequens nunc est, vt de Germanico scripto aliquid insuper dicam. In hoc plus est, arbitratu meo, ingenij, doctrinae, iudicij, industriae, probabilitatis & veritatis, quam in alijs omnibus, quae mihi videre adhuc contigit. Idem quoque acerbius & asperius est alijs. Etenim non Vrsinis solummodo unguibus, quibus immeritos dilaniet, sed etiam Viperinis dentibus, quibus cor ad viuum vsque pungat, armatum est. Verum multo me delectat magis venusta tractatio, & ad veritatem accessio, quàm offendat asperitas disputationis. Quam ob rem omnibus illis, quae in nos dicit, omissis, de ipsa re agemus. In toto fermè scripto contendit nos velle, ad coenam admittendos omnes, modò se nominent Christianos, illos etiam, qui à sceleribus suis discedere nec velint, nec cogitent, sed in eisdem se perseuerare velle palàm profiteantur. Quinetiam vtgere nos, vt haec doctrina populo inculcetur. Ad hanc accusationem respondeo, summam nobis iniuriam fieri. Semper enim ita de hac re disputauimus, vt Ecclesiae nostrae consuetudinem obseruandam censeremus. Deinde semper adiecimus, nos de solis illis loqui, qui doctrinam rectè intelligunt, eandemque probant & amplectuntur, & denique Sacramentis rectè vti desiderant cum ceteris. Rectè intelligo, quod ad externa attinet, de quibus solis iudicat Ecclesia: cum animus vni Deo rectè notus sit. Haec cum vbique inculcemus, immeritò insimulamur alterius sententiae. An enim potest is doctrinam Christianam intelligere, probare, amplecti, qui se in sceleribus proluere statuit instar porci in coeno seuolutantis? An potest talis desiderio teneri Sacramentis ritè cum ceteris Ecclesiae membris eodémque modo, saltem externè, vtendi? Qui statuit malus esse non prodibit in Ecclesiae faciem, vt se pœnitere prioris vitæ testetur, ac meliorem promittat.
units.tr: Next, I must say something more about the German writing. In my judgment it has more talent, learning, judgment, diligence, plausibility and truth than any other I have so far come across. It is also harsher and sharper than the others. It is armed not only with bear's claws, with which it tears to pieces those who do not deserve it, but also with viper's teeth, with which it pierces the heart to the quick. Still, I take much more pleasure in its elegant treatment and its approach to the truth than I am offended by the harshness of its dispute. So I will pass over everything it says against us and deal with the matter itself. Nearly the whole writing argues that we want everyone admitted to the Lord's Supper, provided only that they call themselves Christians, including those who neither wish nor intend to turn from their wickedness, but openly profess that they want to persist in it. He even urges us to have this teaching impressed upon the people. I reply to this accusation that we are being done a great wrong. For we have always argued this matter in such a way that we have judged the custom of our Church should be observed. Then we have always added that we speak only of those who rightly understand the teaching, approve and embrace it, and finally desire to use the sacraments rightly along with the others. I say "rightly understand" with regard to outward things, which alone the Church judges, since the heart is known rightly to God alone. Although we insist on this everywhere, we are wrongly accused of holding a different opinion. For can anyone understand, approve and embrace Christian doctrine who has resolved to wallow in sins like a pig rolling in mud? Can such a person long to use the sacraments rightly, along with the other members of the Church, and in the same manner, at least outwardly? Someone who has decided to remain wicked will not come forward before the face of the Church to testify that he repents of his former life and promises something better.

units.la: Semel dicam: hoc nec dixi nec cogitaui vnquam. Illud autem scripsi & cogitaui, si quis veniat ac se pœnitere profiteatur, correctionemque morum promittat, hunc, si cum cæteris de Ecclesia rectè cupiat particeps fieri Sacramentorum, repelli à Presbyteris quibusdam non debere. Idem hoc cum apertis verbis hic Scriptor testetur, nulla est, nullaque fuit inter nos hac in parte dissensio.
units.tr: I will say it once: I neither said nor ever thought this. But I did write and think this: if someone comes and professes repentance and promises amendment of life, such a person, if he wishes to become a rightful sharer with the others in the sacraments of the Church, should not be repelled by certain elders. This same writer testifies to this in plain words. There is, and there has been, no disagreement among us on this point.

units.la: Sic enim scribit: Vbi populus rectè docetur rectèque admonetur, pauci inuenientur, qui fidem & pœnitentiam non profiteantur, quantumuis multi ex his sint Hypocritæ: præsertim si intelligant non liberum sibi fore, vt se Christianos vocitent ac contra Christi instituta in contemptum Dei pertinaciter viuant. Quod si obijciat aliquis, nullum ita forè impudentem, qui admonitus non polliceatur emendationem & resipiscentiam: ac proinde excommunicationè minimè opus fore: huic respondendum est, vehementer de hoc lætandum, & nulla vtique tunc excommunicatione opus fore. Hæc ille.
units.tr: For he writes thus: "Where the people are rightly taught and rightly admonished, few will be found who do not profess faith and repentance, however many of them may be hypocrites, especially if they understand that it will not be lawful for them to call themselves Christians and to live stubbornly against the institutions of Christ in contempt of God. But if anyone objects that there is no one so shameless who, when admonished, does not promise amendment and repentance, and that therefore there will be no need of excommunication at all, the answer must be that we should rejoice greatly at this, and that then there will indeed be no need of any excommunication." So he says.

units.la: Itaque in vno ex præcipuis disputationis nostræ capitibus pulchrè inter nos conuenit. Non enim concedet author scripti, opinor, vt Sacramenta illis negentur, quicunque ea petunt, & cupiunt rectè cum Ecclesia vsurpare, nec excommunicati adhuc sunt, siue quos ipse iudicat non esse Excommunicandos. Etenim palàm scribit, Sacramentorum negationem testimonium duntaxat esse excommunicationis. Quocirca cum testimonium alicuius rei, vt eruditionis, nulli demus, aut dare debeamus, nisi cui ipsa competit res siue eruditio; ne Sacramenta quidem negare poterunt illi, qui rem, cuius hæc nego testimonium est, scilicet excommunicationem non habet. Aliarum pœnarum similis est ratio. Non enim testimonio notari debet exilij, nisi qui declaratus est exul. Ex his manifestè patet, non dissimulare nos in hac parte.
units.tr: Thus, on one of the principal points of our dispute, we agree well. For I suppose the author of the writing will not concede that the sacraments should be denied to those who ask for them and desire to share them rightly with the Church, and who are not yet excommunicated, or whom he himself judges should not be excommunicated. Indeed he plainly writes that the denial of the sacraments is only a testimony of excommunication. Accordingly, since we give a testimony of some matter, such as learning, to no one unless that person actually possesses the matter, or the learning, to which the testimony refers, so those who do not have excommunication, the thing to which the denial of the sacraments is the testimony, cannot be denied the sacraments. The reasoning is similar for other punishments. For no one should be marked with the testimony of banishment unless he has been declared an exile. From this it is clear that we are not dissembling on this point.

units.la: Alterum caput est de Magistratu & Presbyteris, (siue de duplici iurisdictione in vna Republica) in quo leuiter dissentire videmur. Quippe nos dicimus, Deû nullibi imperauisse Ecclesijs sub pio Magistratu agentibus, Presbyteros eligere, qui distinctam iurisdictionem exerceant à iurisdictione Magistratus: siue qui publica iudicia de moribus habeant cum coactione & poenis, quibus ipsos etiam Magistratus suos in ordinem redigant. Quippe à Deo soli Magistratui omnem externam Reipub. gubernationem commendatam esse affirmamus: quam tamen ad praescriptum & Regulam verbi Dei administrare teneatur. In hoc capite, si non omninò sentit nobiscum, non tamen prorsus diuersum sentit. Enim in parte nulla scripti sui affirmat, Presbyteros tales ex mandato Dei necessariò eligendos (Qui videlicet iudicent, num ij, qui se poenitere peccatorum suorum asseuerant, seriò id asserant, an simulatè & fictè dicant.) Etenim duobus in locis liberum videtur Ecclesiæ relinquere: in tertiò Magistratui hoc ius tribuit. Primus locus sic habet. Nullus ne pertinax quidem excommunicari debet vel à Ministris, vel ab ijs, qui forte ipsis adiungantur, contra voluntatem & sine consensu totius Ecclesiæ aut maximæ partis eiusdem. Alter verò ita habet. Proinde vt etiam aliqui melioris & necessarij ad executionem ordinis causa ad hoc Iudicium destinentur, &c. Tertius hic est. Oportet insuper contumaces authoritate publica ex mandato & ordinatione Magistratus per consistorium Ecclesiasticum, aut per alios, quos ad hoc munus deligere volet, ad poenitentiam sedulò reuocari. Duobus praeterea locis alijs dicit, nihil referre, siue ijdem, siue diuersi vtramque iurisdictionem exerceant, dummodo vtraque exerceatur. Proinde necessum est, vt vel Ministris verbi gladiuni insuper concedat, (quod eum velle non arbitror) vel Magistratui tribuat potestatem Excommunicandi. Aliter enim non poterit vtrumque munus ab vnis eisdemque administrari. Confitetur ergo author, hanc iurisdictionem non esse partem tertiam Ministerij, vt alij contendunt. Item ex eisdem testimonijs, in
units.tr: The second head concerns the magistrate and the elders (or the twofold jurisdiction in one commonwealth), on which we seem to differ slightly. We say that God has nowhere commanded Churches living under a godly magistrate to choose elders who would exercise a jurisdiction distinct from that of the magistrate, that is, who would hold public judgments about morals with coercion and penalties, by which they could even bring the magistrates themselves into line. Indeed, we affirm that God has committed all outward government of the commonwealth to the magistrate alone, which he is nonetheless bound to administer according to the rule and pattern of the Word of God. On this head, if he does not agree with us entirely, he does not think altogether differently. For in no part of his writing does he affirm that such elders must necessarily be chosen by command of God (who would judge whether those who assert that they repent of their sins are asserting this in earnest, or are speaking falsely and feignedly). Indeed, in two places he seems to leave the matter free to the Church; in a third he grants this right to the magistrate. The first place reads: "No one, even if obstinate, should be excommunicated either by the ministers or by those who may be joined with them, against the will and without the consent of the whole Church or its greater part." The other reads: "Therefore, that some of better quality and necessary for carrying out the order may also be appointed to this judgment," and so on. The third is this: "The contumacious must further be called earnestly to repentance by public authority, by the command and ordinance of the magistrate, through the consistory of the Church, or through others whom he wishes to choose for this office." Moreover, in two other places he says it makes no difference whether the same or different persons exercise the two jurisdictions, provided both are exercised. Therefore it is necessary that either he grant the ministers of the Word the sword as well (which I do not think he wishes), or he grant the magistrate the power of excommunicating. Otherwise, the two offices cannot be administered by the same persons. The author therefore confesses that this jurisdiction is not a third part of the ministry, as others contend. Likewise, from the same testimonies, in

units.la: quibus solis Presbyterij videtur mentionem facere voluisse, minifestè perspicitur, eum non putare, Deum imperauisse horum electionem expresso mandato, sed ordinis solum causa probare. De ordine supra satis dictum est: nunc sufficiat monuisse, nihil posse verius dici, quàm Presbyterium illud à totis sacris literis ignorari, nullóue in loco imperatum esse. De magistratus autem officio longissimè discedithic author ab aliorum prope omnium opinione. Quippe contendunt omnes fere alij, ipsum quoque Magistratum Presbyterij iudicio subijci: consensum eius non requirunt, dum Excommunicari eum à Presbyterio posse confidenter affirmant. Sed quia nostram sententiam euidentibus ex scriptura & Iosepho rationibus ac testimonijs supra demonstrauimus, non est necesse, vt hoc iam loco pluribus eadem repetamus.
units.tr: which alone he seems to have wished to mention elders, it is most clearly seen that he does not think God commanded the choosing of these by an express command, but approves them only for the sake of order. I have said enough about order above; it is enough now to remind that nothing more true can be said than that the eldership is unknown throughout all the holy letters and was commanded in no place. But from the duty of the magistrate this author departs very far from the opinion of almost all others. For almost all the others contend that the magistrate himself is also subject to the judgment of the eldership; they do not require his consent, since they confidently affirm that he can be excommunicated by the eldership. But since we have demonstrated our opinion above by evident arguments and testimonies from Scripture and from Josephus, there is no need now to repeat the same at length in this place.

units.la: Quòd si de his inter vos consentitis, interroget fortasse aliquis quid ergo est, de quo controuersamini? Respondeo, in paucis, & ad rei substantiam non valdè pertinentibus: nempe in particularibus quibusdam vel sententijs vel loquendi formulis, & quorundam scripturæ locorum interpretatione. Dico ingenuè, si tam prope ad veritatem accessissent alij, me contra neminem disputaturum fuisse. Nunc quia in campum hunc descendimus, explicanda nonnulla sunt, quæ aliàs omitti facilè potuissent. Primum dicit, quæstionem iam non esse amplius, qui sint ad Sacramenta admittendi, sed qui sint pro visibilis Ecclesiæ membris habendi. Puto se hac ratione, vt arbitror, definitionem nostram infirmare.
units.tr: But if you agree with them on these matters, someone may perhaps ask: what then is the point on which you are disputing? I answer briefly, and on points that do not bear much on the substance of the matter: namely, on certain particular opinions or forms of speech, and on the interpretation of some passages of Scripture. I say frankly that if the others had come so near to the truth, I would not have disputed against anyone. But since we have entered this field, some things must be explained which could otherwise easily have been omitted. First, he says that the question is no longer who are to be admitted to the sacraments, but who are to be regarded as members of the visible Church. I think that by this method, as I believe, he weakens our definition.

units.la: Sed non est ita. Nam visibilem societatem ab inuisibili seiunximus: & de illa sola nos loqui monuimus. Cum ergo in hac societate omnes illos contineri putemus, qui præterquam quod eandem fidem profitentur, eandémque doctrinam nobiscum approbant, laudant, amplectuntur, ijsdem quoque Sacramentis ritè cum Ecclesia participant, aperte patet, pro excluso ex hac externa communione nullum haberi posse, nisi qui vel omnibus
units.tr: But that is not so. For we have separated the visible society from the invisible, and we have warned that we speak only of the former. Since we think that all those are contained in this society who, besides professing the same faith, also approve, praise and embrace the same doctrine with us, and who rightly take part with the Church in the same Sacraments, it is plainly clear that no one can be regarded as excluded from this external communion unless he is deprived either of all the aforesaid things, or of some of them, or of one of them.

units.la: prædictis, vel aliquibus, vel vno priuatur. At duo priora eripi nec debent nec possunt. Consequens igitur est, vt pro eiecto ex visibili Ecclesia is tantum habeatur, cui Sacramentis interdicitur. Nam & mali, fratres nostri sunt propter communia Sacramenta: vt Catholici Donatistis recte responderunt apud Augustin. in Collatione 3. dici.
units.tr: But the first two cannot be taken away, nor ought they to be. It follows, therefore, that only the one from whom the Sacraments are withheld is regarded as cast out of the visible Church. For even the wicked are our brothers because of the common Sacraments, as the Catholics rightly answered the Donatists in Augustine, in the third day of the Collation.

units.la: At negatio Sacramentorum, inquis, est solummodo appendix & testimonium Excommunicationis: quæ est ipsum-met iudicium Dei in verbo eius expressum, & Ecclesiæ contra impœnitentes ad promulgandum commissum. Respondeo, nos de excommunicatione agere, non Diuina, sed humana seu externa: itemque de ea, qua quis à Presbyteris quibusdam ex visibili coetu seclusus intelligitur ac videtur, siue spiritualis Christi Ecclesiæ membrum sit, siue non sit. Caeterum vehementer scire velim, quo in loco scriptum sit, Excommunicatos à Deo in sanctis Scripturis, debere à certis Presbyteris arceri à Sacramentis ab ipso institutis? Ebriosos, Hypocritas &c. (nisi resipiscant) excommunicauit Deus. Vbinam autem tales circumcisos aut baptizatos iussit à Sacramentis, præsertim si pœnitentiam vitæ anteactæ præ se ferant, repelli? Quocirca nugas & fabulas nobis obtrudunt, qui putidis eiusmodi Sophismatis illudere nobis studeant. Ad Ecclesiam visibilem quod attinet, pro excluso nullus habetur, qui Sacramentis nobiscum vtitur recte, quantumcunque ex verbo Dei dicatur propter vitia sua à Deo exclusus. Aliud enim est à Deo excludi, & aliud ex visibili coetu piorum eijci. Quomodo autem & per quos promulgatio sententiæ Dei fieri debeat, supra declaratum fuit, vbi de hac re multum egimus.
units.tr: But you say that the denial of the Sacraments is only an appendix and a testimony of excommunication, which is itself God's judgment expressed in his Word, and which has been committed to the Church to be proclaimed against the impenitent. I answer that we are treating of excommunication not divine but human or external, and of that by which someone is understood and seen to be shut out from the visible assembly by certain elders, whether or not he is a spiritual member of Christ's Church. Moreover, I would very much like to know in what place in Holy Scripture it is written that those excommunicated by God must be kept from the Sacraments instituted by him by certain elders. God has excommunicated drunkards, hypocrites and so on (unless they repent).
