But where has he ordered that such men, circumcised or baptized, be repelled from the Sacraments, especially if they show repentance for their former life? Therefore those who strive to mock us with such rotten sophisms are foisting trifles and fables upon us. As far as the visible Church is concerned, no one is regarded as excluded who rightly uses the Sacraments with us, however much it may be said from God's Word that he has been excluded by God on account of his vices. For it is one thing to be excluded by God, and another to be cast out of the visible assembly of the godly. Moreover, how and through whom the sentence of God ought to be proclaimed was set out above, where we dealt at length with this matter.

units.la: Sed pugnat cum voluntate Dei, vt per verbum alicui remissio peccatorum negetur, & eadem per Sacramenta confirmetur. Non inficior. Cui verbum Dei absolutè negat remissionem, ei certè Sacramenta non sunt concedenda. Caeterum verbum Dei pœnitentiam profitentibus non negat peccati remissionem. Quare ne Sacramenta quidem talibus negari poterant. Postulat Deus in vsu Sacramentorum fidem à nobis & resipiscentiam: nec recte his vtitur, qui absque his vtitur, fateor. At ex hoc non sequitur, Deum velle Presbyteros eligi, qui fidem & poenitentiam profitentem tantisper à Sacramentis abstinere cogant, dum ipsis videatur verè resipuisse. Fateor illud etiam, Sacramenta Ecclesiæ esse instituta, non aliis. Sed Ecclesiam oportet cogitare visibilem seu externam & internam: verbum externum & internum: Ministrum externum & internum: in Sacramentis quoque esse res externas & internas. Secundo scire oportet, quæ vnius systoechias sunt, non cohærere necessariò & semper cum rebus alterius systoechias. Posunt enim externa sine internis esse, quod sæpissimè fit: & hæc nonnunquam etiam sine illis. Iccirco non sequitur, ad illum non pertinere Sacramenta, qui non est in societate Ecclesiæ interioris: modò membrum sit exterioris Ecclesiæ. Sed quemadmodum exterioris tantum societatis communionis, ita res tantum externas ab externo Ministro suscipit: interna dona non percipit, propterea quod instrumento suscipiendi seu ore animæ caret.
units.tr: But, they say, it is contrary to the will of God that remission of sins be denied to someone by the Word and yet confirmed to him by the Sacraments. I do not deny it. To one to whom the Word of God absolutely denies remission, surely the Sacraments are not to be given. But the Word of God does not deny remission of sins to those who profess repentance. Therefore the Sacraments too could not be denied to such people. God requires faith and repentance from us in the use of the Sacraments, and I grant that he uses them wrongly who uses them without these. But it does not follow from this that God wills elders to be chosen who compel a man professing faith and repentance to abstain from the Sacraments for as long as it seems to them that he has truly repented. I also grant this, that the Sacraments were instituted for the Church, not for others. But we must consider the Church as visible or external and internal; the Word as external and internal; the minister as external and internal; and in the Sacraments there are likewise external and internal things. Secondly, we must know that things belonging to one order (systoechia) do not necessarily and always cohere with things of another. For external things can exist without internal ones, which happens very often, and sometimes these too exist without those. Therefore it does not follow that the Sacraments do not pertain to one who is not in the fellowship of the inner Church, provided he is a member of the outer Church. But just as he receives only the external fellowship and communion, so he receives only external things from the external minister; he does not receive the inner gifts, because he lacks the instrument of receiving them, that is, the mouth of the soul.

units.la: Post hæc ad id, quod ex Mose adduxi, respondere conatur. Moses, dixi, nullos iusit à Sacramentis arceri circumcisos, præter legaliter immundos: cæteris autem si ea negligerent excidium interminatus est. Ergo non habet excommunicatio præceptum apud Mosen. Deus, respondet is, in Testamento veteri mandati cuiuslibet pertinacem violatorem interfici iussit, Num. 15. Deut. 17. vt ne profanarentur abeis Sacramenta. Item, Admirabile est, quod Deū præcepisse affirmant, manifestos Dei contemptores ad Sacramenta esse admittendos: cum in omni suo populo talem nullum ferri voluerit: & prophetæ omnes contra hanc Sacramentorum deformationem concionentur. Sed nec aduersatur quicquam magis huic opinioni, quam quod Deus cū pertinacia aduersus mandatū aliquod (cuius violatio alias non esset capitalis) peccantē, excindi ex populo suo mandat.
units.tr: After this he tries to answer what I have brought forward from Moses. Moses, I said, ordered no one to be kept from the Sacraments if circumcised, except those legally unclean; but he threatened destruction to the rest if they neglected them. Therefore excommunication has no precept in Moses. God, he replies, commanded in the Old Testament that the stubborn violator of any command be put to death, Num. 15, Deut. 17, so that the Sacraments might not be profaned by them. Again: it is remarkable that they assert God commanded manifest despisers of God to be admitted to the Sacraments, when he wished no such person to be tolerated in any of his people; and all the prophets preach against this deformation of the Sacraments. But nothing is more opposed to this opinion than that God commands one who sins stubbornly against some command (whose violation would otherwise not be a capital offence) to be cut off from his people.

units.la: Nullo igitur pacto sequitur, Deus aperte impios occidi iubet, Ergo voluit eos eijci ex suo populo. Contrarium huius palam & firmiter coeluditur: quod apostatarū exemplū declarat, ipsismet Aduersarijs testantibus. Quocirca non fuit opus peculiari mandato de depulsione à Sacramentis: cū in illo de corporali poena afficiendis comprehensi inclusumue contineretur. Quid porro egerit ac dixerit Deus, cū tales ex negligentia non sunt occisi, sed ad cultum Diuinū nihilominus sunt admissi, in citatis Prophetarū locis perspicitur. Illud etiam non sequitur, omnes in falsa doctrina prauisq; moribus pertinaces, qui aliter non comeruerint morte, nunc esse occidendos: sed nouū hoc est dogma. Et vt ita esset, morerētur tamen impoenitentes, non vt Christiani, sed vt excōmunicati & praecisi à corpore Christi. Itaq; de hacre lōgè rectius scripsit Augustinus, dicens: Hoc enim nunc agit excōmunicatio in Ecclesia, quod tunc agebat interfectio. Hęc iste: quibus addi potest eiusdem August. testimonium ex 2. Cap. lib. de fide & operibus: vbi asserit factum Mosis & Pinehæ in transgressores gladijs animaduertentium praefigurauisse malorum in Ecclesia coercitionem, quando visibilis in ea gladius cessaturus esset.
units.tr: Therefore in no way does it follow that, because God orders openly impious men to be killed, he therefore wished them to be cast out of his people. The contrary of this is plainly and firmly concluded, as the example of the apostates shows, the Adversaries themselves bearing witness. Wherefore there was no need of a special command for removal from the Sacraments, since it was contained and included in that command concerning the infliction of bodily punishment. What God did and said when such men were not put to death through negligence, but were nevertheless admitted to the divine worship, is clear from the passages of the prophets cited. Nor does it follow that all those obstinate in false doctrine and wicked morals, who have not otherwise deserved death, are now to be killed; but this is a new dogma. And even if it were so, the impenitent would die not as Christians but as excommunicated and cut off from the body of Christ. Therefore Augustine wrote far more correctly about this heresy, saying: "For what excommunication now does in the Church, slaughter did then." So far he; to which can be added the testimony of the same Augustine from the second chapter of the book On Faith and Works, where he asserts that the deed of Moses and Phinehas, who punished transgressors with the sword, prefigured the restraint of evil men in the Church, when the visible sword in it would cease.

units.la: Ad haec respondendum iam est. Pertinaces mandatorum Dei violatores occidi iussisse Mosen, fateor: & cum Deū mutauisse consilium nullibi legamus, eosdem nunc etiam absq; peccato interfici posse puto. At non hoc in quæstione erat, sed illud, An scilicet Deus praeceperit scelere inquinatos, si quidem à Magistratu iuxta decretū Dei non puniantur, vel à Sacerdotibus, vel à Presbyterio illo cōmentitio, à Sacramentis remoueri? Hoc illud est, cuius probationem postulauimus: & nunc etiam postulamus. At probatum est, inquies. Expendamus igitur argumenta. Primum hoc est, Deus pertinaciter contra mādatum, cuius transgressio alias non esset morte mulctanda, peccates, iussit necari, vt non deformaret Sacramēta. Ergo voluit eos arceri à Sacramētis per delectos ab Ecclesia Presbyteros. Secundū, Deus manifestos suorum mandatorum contemptores non voluit in suo populo ferri, vt non possent Sacramêta polluere. Ergo si Magistratus eos non occideret, iussit eosdê Moses à delectis quibusdam aliis ab aditu Templi & ceremoniarum sacrarum vsu prohiberi. Tertium, Omnes Prophetæ accusant abusum istum Sacramentorum. Ergo Moses non recte vsurpantibus iussit eorum vsu interdici à delectis ex toto coetu ad eã rem Presbyteris.
units.tr: To these things a reply must now be made. I grant that Moses ordered stubborn violators of God's commands to be killed; and since we read nowhere that God changed his counsel, I think the same may now also be killed without sin. But that was not the question at issue. The question was rather whether God commanded men polluted with crime, if indeed they are not punished by the magistrate according to God's decree, to be removed from the Sacraments either by the priests or by that fictitious eldership. This is the point whose proof we demanded, and we demand it still. "But it has been proved," you will say. Let us then weigh the arguments. The first is this: God ordered stubborn sinners against a command whose transgression would not otherwise be punishable by death to be killed, so that they might not defile the Sacraments. Therefore he wished them to be kept from the Sacraments by elders chosen by the Church. Second: God did not wish manifest despisers of his commands to be tolerated among his people, so that they could not pollute the Sacraments. Therefore, if the magistrate did not kill them, Moses ordered them to be barred from the entrance of the Temple and from the use of the sacred ceremonies by certain chosen men. Third: all the prophets accuse this abuse of the Sacraments. Therefore Moses ordered that those who use them wrongly be forbidden their use by elders chosen from the whole assembly for this purpose.

units.la: Respondeo ad primum, salsissimum esse, quod dicitur, ideo Deum vel pertinaces vel aliter malos poena capitis afficere iussisse, vt ne profanatent Sacramenta. Vehementer velim locum Scripturæ citatum, qui sic esse demonstret. Alias causas nobis refert: huius nullo in loco meminit. Non ideo iusi sunt occidi, vt Sacramenta non polluerent: sed quia occidebantur, polluere ea non poterant. In 15. Cap. Num. non adducitur Sacramentorum pollutio pro causa: sed quia talis Iehouam probro afficiat, verbum eius spernat, & præcepta irrita faciat. In Deut. eædem ferè causæ adferuntur, cum lex scribitur. Qui Sacerdoti aut Iudici restiterit, è medio vestri tollatur, vt populus tot audiat & timeat: nec porro superbè, seu pertinaciter agat. Quæ hic mentio pollutionis Sacramentorum? An eadem prædicta valent, ac si scriptum esset, Occidite talem, ne ad Pascha vel Sacrificia admissus ea polluat? Non puto. Ergo manebit argumentum nostrum, quantisper non fuerit Antecedens probatum. Et si possibile foret, vt probaretur, non tamen sequeretur ex eo consequens: quod per se est merum purum q; figmentum.
units.tr: To the first I answer that it is most absurd to say that God ordered stubborn or otherwise wicked men to be punished with death so that they would not profane the Sacraments. I would very much like the passage of Scripture cited to show that this is so. It gives other reasons for it, and in no place does it mention this one. They were not ordered to be killed so that they would not pollute the Sacraments; rather, because they were killed, they could not pollute them. In Num. 15 the pollution of the Sacraments is not adduced as the cause; rather, because such a man reproaches Jehovah, despises his word and makes his precepts void. In Deuteronomy almost the same causes are given, when the law is written: whoever resists the priest or the judge is to be taken from among you, so that the people may hear and fear, and not act further proudly or stubbornly. What mention of pollution of the Sacraments is here? Do the aforesaid things have the same force as if it were written, "Kill such a man, lest he, admitted to the Passover or the sacrifices, pollute them"? I do not think so. Therefore our argument will stand, so long as the antecedent has not been proved. And even if it could be proved, the consequence would not follow from it; for in itself it is a pure and simple fiction.

units.la: In secundo asperè loquitur, vt nobis inuidiam conflet. At nihil tale nos diximus. Hoc affirmamus, Moses in suo præcepto non excipit licenter viuentes, modò sint circumcisi & secundum legem mundi. Ergo non iusit aliquem Iudæu arceti. Cum tantum circumcisos & legaliter mundos admitti præcipit, clarè hoc indicat, se eos intelligere, qui Iudaicam religionem patriosq; ritus probarent & obseruarent, saltem externè. Nam eo fuerũt ingenio Iudei, vt Mosis decreta oppugnantem, aut manifestè Deum despicientem, vnguibus potius dilaniaturi fuerint, quam eum ferrent: cuius rei illustre exstat exemplum (Præter ea, quæ apud Iosephum, Efdram,& Nehemiam legimus)in lib.3. Machabæorum. Qui in aliis rebus peccarent, & contra Deū, Mosen, Templum, Patriam Religionem apertè nihil dicerent aut facerent, facilè tollerabantur, quoties Magistratus non rectè officium faceret. Nullum in toto veteri Testamento verbum reperitur,quo demonstrari queat, vllum vnquam circumcisum & Mosaicos ritus obseruare volentem ab eorundem obseruatione prohibitum fuisse à Sacerdotibus, qui propter cōmissum scelus aliquod à magistratu non fuisset punitus.Nihil enim tale eos iusserat Moses facere, si Magistratus negligens esset. Quare non est cur nobis affingant asperos istos sermones, aut obiciant Apostatas atq; alios tales. De illis ergo agamus, qui pro Iudæis habebantur,& ritus Mosaicos obseruabant, atque mandata Diuina minimè contemnere videre volebant, tametsi non sic viuerent, vt ea præscribebant.
units.tr: In the second point he speaks harshly, so as to stir up hatred against us. But we have said nothing of the kind. We affirm this: Moses, in his precept, does not exclude those who live licentiously, provided they are circumcised and ritually clean according to the law. Therefore he did not order that any Jew be shut out. Since he commands that only the circumcised and legally clean be admitted, he clearly indicates that he means those who approve and observe the Jewish religion and its ancestral rites, at least outwardly. For the Jews were so disposed that they would sooner have torn to pieces with their nails anyone who opposed the decrees of Moses or openly despised God than have endured him. A notable example of this is found in the third book of Maccabees, besides what we read in Josephus, Ezra and Nehemiah. Those who sinned in other matters, but who said or did nothing openly against God, Moses, the Temple or the national religion, were easily tolerated, whenever the magistrate failed to do his duty. Nowhere in the whole of the Old Testament can one find a word by which it could be shown that any circumcised man who wished to observe the Mosaic rites was ever forbidden their observance by the priests, on account of some crime he had committed, when the magistrate had not punished him. For Moses had given no such order to be carried out in case the magistrate was negligent. Therefore there is no reason for them to attribute these harsh words to us, or to bring up apostates and others of that sort against us. Let us then deal with those who were regarded as Jews and observed the Mosaic rites, and who wished to appear to despise the divine commands in no way, even though they did not live as those commands prescribed.

units.la: Cum dicimus Mosen hominem Iudæum, si peccatum morte dignum admisisset,occidi quidem mandasse, at à Sacramentis repelli; si non puniretur, (Quod sæpè futurum non nesciebat)non mandasse:cum,inquam,hoc dicimus,respondent isti,ob hanc causam iussos esse tales occidi,ne Sacramenta pollùerent.Hoc ego consideremus. An non occidendus erat, quisquis adulterium vel homicidium, vel crimen aliud,cui capitis poena constituta fuerat,admisisset, etiamsi eum deinde factì sui ex animo pœnituisset? Non potest negari. Cæterum vos conceditis Sacramenta nequaquam pollui à verè pœnitentibus, & de emendatione serió cogitantibus. Ergo ob aliam causam occiditur, qui sic affectus est. Igitur si ex occisione eorum, quibus poena capitis à Deo imposita est, probetur, tales à Sacramentis arcendos, concedi & illud oportebit, nullum ad Sacramenta admittendum esse,qui crimen morte dignum patrauit: siue admissi sceleris eum pœnituerit, siue non poenituerit. (Etenim tales occidebantur tunc mandato Diuino, & occidedi etiam nunc sunt, siue doleant factum suum, siue non doleant.) At istud est inconueniens. Ergo ne prius quidé rectè affirmatur.
units.tr: When we say that Moses commanded that a Jew who had committed a sin worthy of death should indeed be put to death, but should be cut off from the sacraments only if he were not punished (which he well knew would often happen), and had not commanded that, our opponents reply that such men were ordered to be put to death for this reason: so that they would not defile the sacraments. Let us consider this. Was not the man who had committed adultery, or murder, or another crime for which the penalty of death had been appointed, to be put to death, even if he afterwards repented of his deed from the heart? It cannot be denied. But you grant that the sacraments are by no means defiled by those who truly repent and seriously consider amendment. Therefore a man so disposed is put to death for some other reason. So if from the putting to death of those on whom God imposed the penalty of death it is proved that such men must be shut out from the sacraments, then it must also be conceded that no one who has committed a crime worthy of death should be admitted to the sacraments, whether or not he repents of the crime he committed. (For such men were then put to death by divine command, and they are still put to death today, whether they grieve for their deed or not.) But this is absurd. Therefore the first point is not rightly affirmed either.

units.la: Secundo, non potuit hac via profanatio Sacramentorum præcaueri. Etenim facinora hæc sœpè sunt occulta. Item sœpè puniri nequeunt, vt, homicium Ioabi, quod Dauid punire non est ausus 2. Sam. 3. Sœpè ob alias causas negligentur, quemadmodum eundem cernimus incestum filii, accædem, quàm Absalon fecit, impunita reliquisse. An hos in Templum non venisse & Sacramentis vsos non fuisse censebimus? Aliorum malorum tanta fuit turba, vt Psal. 14. affirmet ne vnum quidem repertum fuisse bonum. Ergo nihilominus erat opus exceptione, vt videlicet tales, siquidem à Magistratu non punirentur, à Sacramentorum participatione submouerentur. At hanc exceptionem Deus Mosen non iussit addere: tametsi præclarè nosset, quomodo quouis tempore Magistratus ossicium essent facturi. Ex quo rursus efficitur, Deum nihil tale mandauisse.
units.tr: Secondly, the profaning of the sacraments could not be prevented in this way. For such crimes are often hidden. Again, they often cannot be punished, as with the murder by Joab, which David did not dare to punish (2 Sam. 3). Often they are neglected for other reasons, just as we see that the incest of Absalom's son with his father's concubines, which Absalon committed, was left unpunished. Shall we suppose that these men did not come into the Temple and did not use the sacraments? The multitude of other evils was so great that Psalm 14 asserts that not even one good man was found. Therefore there was nonetheless need of an exception, namely that such men, if they were not punished by the magistrate, should be removed from participation in the sacraments. But God did not order Moses to add this exception, although he knew very well how magistrates would act at any time. From this again it follows that God commanded nothing of the kind.

units.la: Tertio contendunt Aduersarij, quosdam esse excommunicandos, qui capitis poenam non meruerunt: vt si quis propter leuem iniuriam admonitus priuatim & publicè quiescere tamen nolit, quia vel sit ita obstinati ingenij, vel quia se iustè facere putet, quod facit: is, inquam, propter pertinaciam excommunicandus, at non interficiendus fuerit. Quod si ergo contendatur, Deum voluisse tales (vt qui secundum ipsos non comprehendantur in numero interficiendorum) à Sacramentis abigi, monstrandus est locus, in quo mandatum hoc continetur. At monstrari in veteri Testamento non potest. Manet ergo firmum, quod diximus, Deum sceleratos occidi mandasse, à Sacramentis arceri non iussisse: modò non essent legis iminundiția contaminati. Certè qui aliter sentit, non potest à contradictione Mosen vindicare. Nam contradictoriæ sunt orationes: Omnis mundus secundum legem celebret Pascha: &; Aliquis mundus secundum legem (nempe qui licenter vixit, at legaliter mundus est) non celebret Pascha.
units.tr: Thirdly, our opponents contend that some should be excommunicated who have not deserved the penalty of death: for example, if someone, having been admonished privately and publicly, refuses nonetheless to be quiet about a slight injury, either because he is of such an obstinate disposition, or because he thinks he is right in what he does. Such a man, I say, should be excommunicated on account of his obstinacy, but not put to death. If, then, it is maintained that God wished such men (who, according to them, are not included among those to be put to death) to be driven away from the sacraments, the passage in which this command is contained must be pointed out. But it cannot be pointed out in the Old Testament. Therefore what we have said stands firm: God commanded that the wicked be put to death, but did not order that they be kept from the sacraments, provided they were not contaminated by legal uncleanness. Certainly whoever thinks otherwise cannot clear Moses of contradiction. For these statements are contradictory: "Every man who is clean according to the law shall keep the Passover," and "Some man who is clean according to the law (namely one who has lived licentiously, but is legally clean) shall not keep the Passover."

units.la: Ad tertium respondimus supra: ideo hic paucis nos expediemus. Prophetæ reprehenderunt abusum & dehonestationem Sacramentorum: at nulli circumcisio interdixerunt vsu eorum. Sacrificia impiorum Deo non esse gratiora, quam si vetita animalia ipsi offerentur testati sunt: at nullo in loco docuerunt debuisse tales à Sacerdotibus repelli. Accusant Sacerdotes quod præuaricentur, & populum non recte instituant: sed non accusarunt hoc nomine vnquam & vsquâ, quod indecorè viuentes ad Sacrificia & Templum admiserint. Loquor de mundis iuxta legem. Inuchuntur in Magistratus, & negligentiam eorum in puniendis sceleribus damnant, adeoq; studium in fouendis exsecrantur: interim non iubent Sacerdotibus, vt publica exerceant suaquædam de moribus iudicia, criminisq; conuictos iubeant à Sacramentis abstinere. Denique dicunt semper hęc turpia & mala esse coram Domino: in oculis Domini: in conspectu Dei: non autem in facie Ecclesiæ. Nos autem non quid Deus iudicet hic quærimus: sed quid in hac re præceperit in Ecclesia externa facere, inuestigamus. His nunc addamus, quod ante diximus etiam, si ex his locis probare aliquis conetur, eligendos qui turpitudine morum inquinatos à Sacramentis arceant, concedendum & illud fore, eligendos qui malis interdicant oratione, lectione, Eleemosynarum distributione. &c.
units.tr: To the third point we replied above, so here we shall dispose of it briefly. The prophets rebuked the abuse and dishonouring of the sacraments, but none of them forbade the circumcised the use of them. They testified that the sacrifices of the impious were no more pleasing to God than if animals forbidden by the law were offered to him, but in no place did they teach that such men ought to be turned away from the sacrifices by the priests. They accuse the priests of prevaricating and of not instructing the people correctly, but they never accused them, on this ground, of admitting to the sacrifices and the Temple those who lived dishonourably. I am speaking of men who are clean according to the law. They inveigh against the magistrates and condemn their negligence in punishing crimes, and they denounce their zeal in cherishing them; yet they do not order the priests to exercise any public judgments of their own on morals, nor do they command that those convicted of crimes abstain from the sacraments. Finally, they always say that these shameful and evil things are before the Lord, in the eyes of the Lord, in the sight of God, but not in the face of the Church. We, however, are not inquiring here what God judges, but what he has commanded to be done in the external Church in this matter. To this we now add what we have also said before: if anyone tries to prove from these passages that elders should be chosen who keep from the sacraments those defiled by the shamefulness of their morals, it must also be conceded that elders should be chosen who forbid evil men by prayer, by reading, by the distribution of alms, and so on.

units.la: Patet ex prædictis, manifeste sequi, quod author sequi negat. Deus flagitiosos interfici iussit: & si forte non interficerentur, non iussit eos ab vsu ceremoniarum à se in Ecclesia sua institutarum abstterreri. Ergo non voluit aliquem propter huiusmodi causam à recto vsu ceremoniarum repelli à quibusdam alijs, qui non essent in Magistratus loco & munere. Hoc, inquam, recte, vere, necessarioq; sequitur, non contrarium, vt is existimat, quicquid de manifestis Idololatris & Apostatis nos scribere affirmet. Hi enim si non interficiantur, à Magistratu, non à fidelis illis Presbyteris sunt coercendi. Verum de his in præsentia non disputamus, sed de illis differimus, qui doctrinam amplectuntur veram, quoíque dolor & pœnitentia peccatorum suorum tangit, etiamsi foepe in hac pugna succumbant.
units.tr: It is plain from what has been said that what the author denies follows manifestly. God commanded that the wicked be put to death, and if perhaps they were not put to death, he did not command that they be debarred from the use of the ceremonies which he had instituted in his Church. Therefore he did not wish anyone to be kept from the right use of the ceremonies on this kind of ground by certain others who were not in the place and office of the magistrate. This, I say, follows rightly, truly and necessarily, and not the contrary, as he supposes, whatever he may assert we write about manifest idolaters and apostates. For if such men are not put to death, they are to be restrained by the magistrate, not by the faithful elders. But we are not disputing about these men at present; we are discussing those who embrace the true doctrine, and whom sorrow and repentance for their sins touch, even if they often succumb in this struggle.

units.la: Cum deinde addit, Non fuisse opus mandato peculiari de submouendis flagitiosos à Sacramentorum vsurpatione, quia hoc in illo de interficiendis talibus, velut pars in toto, aut angustius in patentiore contineretur, manifeste secum pugnat. Quoniam supra dixit, Iudaicum Synedrium aetate Christi vtramque iurisdictionem tenuisse: & fuisse necessarium, vt vtraque ex Mosis decreto administraretur: & ob id putat, Iudices ex Sacerdotibus fere ac Leuitis constitisse. Quod si ergo vtramque iurisdictionem habuit & exercuit, etiam excommunicauit absque gladio. At hoc fecit vel sine mandato Mosis, vel cum mandato. Si absque mandato fecit, vere nos diximus, mandatum à Deo per Mosen nullum fuisse propositum hac de re. Si mandatum habuerunt, falsum est, in illo de interficiendo sic fuisse comprehensum, vt eorum non esset opus ponere. Hoc enim modo solo gladio & morte excommunicabant. At positum est, eos absque gladio, vt hodie solent quidam, excommunicasse. (Sialiter intelligunt Synedrium vtramque iurisdictionem habuisse, nempe absque hac excommunicatione, ad argumentum nostrum non respondent: ac plane ridiculi sunt (Ergo expressum habuerunt mandatum sine interfectione excommunicandi: quod non potuit in illo de interficiendo contineri. Pugnant ergo quae supra dixit cum praesentibus.
units.tr: When he then adds that there was no need for a special command about removing the wicked from the use of the sacraments, because this would be contained in the command about putting such men to death, as a part within a whole, or a narrower thing within a wider, he clearly contradicts himself. For he said above that the Jewish Sanhedrin in the time of Christ held both jurisdictions, and that it was necessary that both be administered according to the decree of Moses; and for this reason he thinks that the judges were made up mostly of priests and Levites. If, then, they had and exercised both jurisdictions, they also excommunicated without the sword. But they did this either without a command of Moses or with one. If they did it without a command, then we spoke truly: no command was laid down by God through Moses on this matter. If they had a command, it is false that it was so included in the command about putting to death that there was no need to set it down. For in this way they excommunicated only by the sword and by death. But it has been stated that they excommunicated without the sword, as some do today. (If they understand that the Sanhedrin had both jurisdictions, namely apart from this excommunication, they do not answer our argument, and they are plainly ridiculous.) Therefore they had an express command for excommunication without killing, which could not have been contained in the command about putting to death. So what he said above is at odds with what he says now.

units.la: Supra etiam obtendimus, fieri non potuisse, vt excommunicationis huius praeceptu contineretur in illo de interfectione. Sequeretur enim, omnes illos excommunicandos, qui crimen admisissent, etiamsi minime pertinaces essent: quod nostEr author cum alijs quibusdam expresse negat. Item, solos illos excommunicandos, & omnes illos, quos Moses iusserat occidi. Item, cessante gladio cessaret excommunicatio. Si negetur, ostendere mandatum oportet. Si exstat eorum falsum est in illo comprehensum sic fuisse, vt peculiari nullo res egeret praecepto. Nam Magistratu officium non faciente, non potuerunt vlli alij excommunicare, cum mandatum non exstaret. Ideo Prophetas neminem hoc nomine reprereprehendisse ostendimus. Ex omnibus perspicuè patet, si Deus voluisset excommunicationem in Ecclesia regnare, peculiari eam mandato fuisse institutendam. At non fecit, testibus etiam Aduersarijs. Ergo exerceri eam noluit ab aliis quàm quibus gladium commendauit.
units.tr: We have also argued above that the command of excommunication cannot be contained in the command about killing. For it would follow that all those who had committed a crime would have to be excommunicated, even if they were not at all obstinate; our author, with some others, expressly denies this. Likewise it would follow that only those would be excommunicated, and all those whom Moses had ordered to be killed. Again, when the sword ceased, excommunication would cease too. If this is denied, the command must be shown. If it exists, it is false that it was so included in the other command that no special precept was needed. For when the magistrate was not performing his office, no others could excommunicate, since there was no command for it. So we have shown that the prophets never rebuked anyone on this ground. From all this it is perfectly clear that, if God had wished excommunication to reign in the Church, he would have instituted it by a special command. But he did not do so, as even our opponents admit. Therefore he did not wish it to be exercised by anyone other than those to whom he entrusted the sword.

units.la: Vidimus quantum valeat ista ratiocinatio. Deus turpiter viuentes iussit occidi. Ergo voluit eos à Sacramentis arceri, quia interdictio Sacramentorum contineatur in mandato de interficiendis improbis. Nunc quæ deinceps sequi\-tur, perpendeda sunt, Non satis intelligo, quo hæc dicantur: Illud etiam nō sequitur, omnes pertinaciter malos, si aliter non peccarint capitaliter, morte multandos esse. Est hoc nouū dogma. Et vt ita sit, moriuntur nihilominus, qui absq; pœnitentia supplicium capitis adeunt, non vt Christiani, sed vt membra à corpore Christi præcisa. Primum quidem, non disputaui ego, vtrū, qui à Mose iubentur interfici, hodie quoq; sint omnes capite plectendi. Hoc dixi, quod negari à nemine potest, illos omnes, quos aduersarij asseuerantèr affirmant excōmuni\candos, apud Mosen iuberi non excōmunicari, sed interficiis ac proinde excōmunicationem eam, de qua inter nos litigamus, à Deo non fuisse mandatam Iudeorum Ecclesiæ. Hoc illis erat refutandum, non quærendum, an idem omnes nunc quoq; morte sint multandi? Deus vult scelera coherceri, ac pœnas constituit sceleratis, vt earum metu cæteri à malè agendo deterreantur. Hanc suam voluntatem vult explieri, etiamsi non omninò & præcisè eisdem poenis in quo\uis loco & tempore præceperit vti.
units.tr: We have seen how weak this reasoning is. God ordered those who lived wickedly to be killed; therefore he wished them to be shut out from the sacraments, because the exclusion from the sacraments is supposed to be contained in the command to kill the wicked. Now the consequences that follow must be weighed. I do not sufficiently understand what these people mean. Nor does it follow that all who are obstinately wicked, if they have not otherwise sinned capitally, must be punished with death. That is a new doctrine. And even granting it, those who go to the capital punishment without repentance die nonetheless, not as Christians but as members cut off from the body of Christ. First, I did not argue whether those whom Moses commanded to be killed must all still be punished with death today. What I said is something no one can deny: that all those whom our opponents confidently assert ought to be excommunicated are, according to Moses, commanded not to be excommunicated but to be killed; and therefore God did not command that excommunication, about which we are disputing, for the Church of the Jews. This was what they had to refute, not to ask whether all of them must now also be punished with death. God wishes crimes to be restrained, and he appoints punishments for criminals so that others may be deterred from doing evil by fear of them. He wishes this his will to be carried out, even if he did not command that exactly these same punishments be used in every place and time.

units.la: Ceterum ex antegressis & concessis ab authore, eadem illa sequi, nisi isto modo, quo dixi, exponamus, haud est difficile monstratu. Probauitis ex 15. Num. & 17. Deut. cum contumacia peccantes, licet aliàs peccatum non sit capitale, occidendos esse. Præterea scripsit, nihil magis nostram sententiam refellere, quam quod Deus pertinaciter peccantes omnes voluerit interfici. Ex his certè sequitur, aut Deum in nouo Testamento aliud imperasse, aut sententiam mutasse, aut concedendum est, quod diximus à Magistratu gistratu gladium tenente eosdem nunc etiam castigandos: licet alijs pœnis eos ad obedientiam reuocare seu cogere nunc possit: vt ego quidem arbitror. Equidem si ita præceptum de repellendis sceleratis à Sacramētis, in edicto de tollendis ex hac vita improbis continetur, vt peculiari mādato nullo egeat, necessum est, vt, quicunque excommunicandi sunt, occidendi etiam sint. Si id neges, consequetur peculiari de his mandato opus esse: nec completi hoc totum illud, sed partem quandam solum. Si autem asseueres, efficitur quod dictum est, nempe cum peruicacia peccantes, tamen si peccatum non mereatur capitis pœnam, capite plectendos esse.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not hard to show that the same consequences follow from what has gone before and what the author has conceded, unless we explain it in the way I have said. You have proved from Numbers 15 and Deuteronomy 17 that those who sin with obstinacy must be killed, even though the sin is otherwise not capital. Besides, he wrote that nothing refutes our view more than that God wished all those who sinned obstinately to be killed. From these things it certainly follows either that God commanded something else in the New Testament, or that he changed his mind, or else we must concede what we have said: that those who now hold the sword of the magistrate should also punish the same people, though they may now compel or recall them to obedience by other penalties, as I for my part think. Indeed, if the precept about removing the wicked from the sacraments is contained in the edict about removing the wicked from this life, so that it needs no special command, then necessarily all who are to be excommunicated are also to be killed. If you deny this, it will follow that a special command about them is needed, and that the whole of that command has not been fulfilled, but only a part of it. If, on the other hand, you assert it, what we said follows: that those who sin with obstinacy must be punished with death, even if the sin does not deserve the penalty of death.

units.la: Augustinum, scribit, prudentius de hac re locutum, cum in locum interfectionis successisse scribit excommunicationem. Magna profecto prudentia est absque scriptuqris loqui scilicet. Quo loco iussit Deus excommunicationem hanc, vice interfectionis in Ecclesiam inducere? Nullum de hac re verbum in omnibus sacris libris reperitur. Et vt maximè largiamur eis, quod hic dicit Augustinus, quid hoc ipsis proderit? Cogentur nihilominus concedere consequentia omnia:
units.tr: He writes that Augustine spoke more wisely on this matter, when he wrote that excommunication succeeded in place of killing. Indeed, it is great wisdom to speak without Scripture, clearly! In what passage did God order that this excommunication be introduced into the Church in place of killing? No word about this matter is found in all the sacred books. And even if we grant them everything that Augustine says here, what will this profit them? They will nonetheless be forced to concede all the following consequences:

units.la: 1 Primum, in Ecclesia Iudaica nunquam fuisse excommunicationem. Successit enim interfectioni: quę ad excidium vsq; vrbis penes eam remansit, saltem ex parte.
units.tr: 1. First, that there was never any excommunication in the Jewish Church. For it succeeded killing, which, at least in part, remained with that Church until the destruction of the city.

units.la: 2 Deinde omnes, qui capitale crimen patrarunt, excommunicandi fuerint. Tales enim omnes interficiendi erant, siue pœniteret eos facti siue non pœniteret.
units.tr: 2. Next, that all who committed a capital crime would have had to be excommunicated. For all such persons were to be killed, whether or not they repented of the deed.

units.la: 3 Præterea soli illi excommunicari poterant, qui pœnam mortis apud Iudæos meruerant.
units.tr: 3. Furthermore, only those could be excommunicated who had deserved the penalty of death among the Jews.

units.la: 4 Item falsum erit, quod asserunt, solos contumaces excludendos. Nam qui capitale crimen patrarat, occidebatur, licet minimè pertinax esset.
units.tr: 4. Likewise, what they assert will be false, that only the obstinate are to be shut out. For whoever had committed a capital crime was put to death, even if he was in no way obstinate.

units.la: 5 Postremò non habebit ea locū in nostris Ecclesijs, quibus Deus largitus est piū Magistratū, siue gladiū. Quippe cedit Vicarius, cum is, cuius vicè suppleuerat, per seipsū officium suum facit. Fieri hoc tanto magis oportet, quia interfectio est ordinatio Diuina: Excommunicatio non est. Idcirco disceptatio haec tota iudicari otiosa & superuacanea poterit.
units.tr: 5. Lastly, this will have no place in our Churches, to which God has granted a godly magistrate with the sword. For the vicar gives way when the one whose place he had filled performs his office himself. This must all the more be so, because killing is a divine ordinance, whereas excommunication is not. Hence this whole dispute may be judged idle and superfluous.

units.la: Sed aliter videtur Aduersario, qui excommunicatione opus esse censet, tametsi magistratus probe suo fungatur munere: propterea quod huius & Ecclesiae officia distincta sint, & magistratus externam solum modestiam quaerat, animae salutem negligat. At pugnat secum. Quoniam paulo supra dixit, praeceptum excommunicationis contineri in mandato de interficiendis improbis: nec peculiari ob eam rem iussu opus fuisse. Quomodo ergo iam nihilominus opus esse affirmat, etsi magistratum sedulo puniat nocentes? Formam Reipub. cuius inter se partes aptius cohaerent, sapientiusque dispositae sint, excogitare nullus poterit ea, quam Deus ipse fundauit, constituit, ordinauit. In hac non fuit necessarium peculiare de excommunicandis flagitiosis mandatum, propterea quod capitis supplicio punirentur. Igitur ne nunc quidem fuerit necessarium, dum vitia, quae apud Iudaeos capitalia erant, prope omnia sunt capitalia, aut certe alijs grauibus poenis coherceantur. Item, si vicem gerit interfectionis, vbi ea non est in Ecclesia, quomodo locum habebit vna cum interfectione?
units.tr: But our opponent, who thinks excommunication necessary even though the magistrate performs his duty well, sees the matter differently, on the ground that the offices of the magistrate and of the Church are distinct, and that the magistrate seeks only outward decency and neglects the salvation of the soul. But he contradicts himself. For a little above he said that the precept of excommunication is contained in the command about killing the wicked, and that for this reason no special command was needed. How, then, does he now affirm that it is nonetheless necessary, even though the magistrate diligently punishes offenders? No one could devise a form of commonwealth whose parts cohere more fittingly and are arranged more wisely than the one God himself founded, established and ordained. In this form there was no need for a special command about excommunicating the wicked, because they were punished with capital punishment. So it is not necessary even now, since the vices which were capital among the Jews are almost all capital still, or are at least restrained by other severe penalties. Likewise, if excommunication takes the place of killing, where killing is not in the Church, how will it have a place alongside killing?

units.la: Adde quod non animaduertunt isti, se tacitè Deum accusare, qui improbos à magistratu puniri iusserit, excommunicari non iusserit. An solam externam modestiam & non simul salutem populi sui quaesiuit Deus, cum praeceptum excommunicationis seorsum nullum proposuit, sed in praecepto de interficiendis facinorosis comprehendit? An forte postea eum huius consilij sui poenituit; & quae coniunctim à magistratu administrari tunc voluit, postea discreuit, partémque alijs quibusdam à magistratu commendauit? Sacrae literae hoc nullo in loco referunt. Quippe sigillatim scelera recensent, quae capitis supplicio coherceri debent, excommunicationis eius, de qua disputamus, nunquam & nusquam meminerunt. Ergo pius magistratus officio suo fungens solam externam modestiam in Repub. plantabat, subditorum & peccantium salutem non procurabat? Mira certè res sit, si Deus per magistratum apud Iudæos non solum externam modestiam, verumetiam salutem suorum quæsierit: per nostros autem magistratus prius solum efficiat, alterum per presbyterium ab eo nullibi institutum procuret.
units.tr: Add to this that these men do not notice that they are tacitly accusing God, who ordered the wicked to be punished by the magistrate but did not order them to be excommunicated. Did God seek only outward decency for his people, and not at the same time their salvation, when he set forth no separate precept of excommunication but included it in the precept about killing the criminals? Or perhaps he later repented of this plan of his, and what he then wished to be administered together by the magistrate, he afterwards separated, committing a part of it to others and not to the magistrate? The sacred letters record this nowhere. Indeed, they list individually the crimes that must be restrained by capital punishment, and nowhere at all do they mention that excommunication about which we dispute. Therefore did the godly magistrate, performing his duty, plant only outward decency in the commonwealth and not procure the salvation of his subjects and of the sinners? It would be a strange thing indeed if God among the Jews sought through the magistrate not only outward decency but also the salvation of his people, while among us the magistrate would bring about only the first, and the second would be procured through the eldership, which God has nowhere instituted.

units.la: Quæret hic fortasse aliquis, quid tunc faciendum sit, cum magistratus in suo munere negligens est, ac scelera non ea severitate punit, qua oportet? Respondeo, id esse faciendum quod in sacrosancto verbo suo nos docuit. Non docuit autem hanc excommunicationem: quare non est haec pro mandato Divino Ecclesiae obtrudenda. Quid docuit autem? Quoties Reges non fecerunt officium, misit Prophetas, qui eos increparent, ad diligentiam cohortarentur & ad obedientiam Dei tum Magistratus, tum Sacerdotes, tum subditos aliios quovismodo impellerent, exhortationibus, obtestationibus, minis, denique bonorum promissione malorumque denunciatione. Tales conciones Prophetarum non legimus habitas sub piis Regibus, Davide, Salomone & aliis: sed sub impiis & officium suum negligentibus. Non legimus etiam, eos tunc vel excommunicasse aliquos, vel excommunicati ab aliis iussisse: sicut nullo in loco eos reprehendisse invenimus vel Sacerdotes vel alios, velut hac in parte negligentes. Idem igitur Ministri nostri imitari debent, & caetera Deo committere: eumque cum piis cunctis comprecari, ut pro sua miserecordia rebus afflictis opem ferat, quomodo ipse novit esse salutare atque utile.
units.tr: Perhaps someone will ask here what must then be done, when the magistrate is negligent in his office and does not punish crimes with the severity that is fitting. I answer that what must be done is what he has taught us in his holy Word. Yet he has not taught this excommunication; therefore it is not to be forced upon the Church as a divine command. What, then, has he taught? Whenever kings did not do their duty, he sent prophets who rebuked them, urged them to diligence and to obedience to God, and by exhortations, entreaties, threats, and finally by promises of good and warnings of evil, moved the magistrates, the priests and the other subjects in whatever way they could. We do not read that such sermons of the prophets were delivered under the godly kings, David, Solomon and others, but under the impious kings who neglected their office. Nor do we read that the prophets then either excommunicated anyone, or ordered others to excommunicate; just as we nowhere find them rebuking priests or others as negligent in this respect. Therefore our ministers ought to imitate the same, and commit the rest to God, and pray with all the godly that he, in his mercy, may bring help to afflicted affairs in the way he himself knows to be salutary and useful.

units.la: Etsi enim nos iudicamus remedium huius mali praesentissimum & saluberrimum esse posse excommunicationem: non tamen ita iudicavit Deus, cuius statutis addere nos nil debemus. Ipse namque homine longe sapientior non omisisset, si quidem utilem suae Ecclesiae cognovisset. Praevidit is ac praedixit saepe suo populo, quales essent habituri magistratus: at nunquam iussit, ut cum non facerent ipsi officium, subditi iudicia peculiaria de censendis moribus improimprobisque cohærcendis poenarum inflictione instituerent, quibus ipsi præsiderent. Vidit prorsus omnipotens & sapientissimus Deus Ecclesiæ multò perniciosiorem sore abusum excommunicationis, quàm abusum imperij magistratus. Docuerunt hoc nos superiores ætates. Docet idem ratio, vt nostras experientias taceam. Nam si presbyteri illi in re aliqua non recté sentiant, de qua non magnoperè solicitus sit magistratus, nunquam quiescent, priusquam totam Ecclesiam secum sentire coëgerint: quod & antea factum, & nunc etiam fieri videmus.
units.tr: Even if we judge that excommunication may be the most immediate and most wholesome remedy for this evil, God has not judged so, and we ought not add anything to his decrees. He is far wiser than man, and he would not have left it out if he had known it to be useful for his Church. He foresaw and often foretold to his people what kind of magistrates they would have, yet he never commanded that, when the magistrates failed in their duty, the subjects should set up their own courts for censuring morals and restraining the wicked by the infliction of penalties, with themselves presiding over them. Almighty and most wise God certainly saw that the abuse of excommunication would be far more harmful to the Church than the abuse of magisterial power. Earlier ages have taught us this, and reason teaches the same, not to mention our own experience. For if those elders disagree on some matter that does not greatly concern the magistrate, they will never rest until they have forced the whole Church to think as they do. We have seen this done before, and we see it happening now.

units.la: Quod præterea dicit author à magistratu castigatos non fore meliores, aut non morituros Christianos, mihi non probatur. Primum, quia Dei mandatum est, vt, qui aliquid morte dignum patrauit, moriatur, nulloque modo absoluatur: siue doleat propter factum siue non doleat. Deinde, quia apud Christianos summa diligentia tales simul erudiuntur ex verbo Dei: multò, inquam, diligentius instituuntur, quàm vlli alij. Tertio, quia ex rebus mundanis & externis nihil est sub hoc coelo, quod magis nos ad agnitionem & inuocationem Dei perducat, modò recta institutio accedat, quàm afflictio, crux, & aduersarum rerum sensus. Qui tunc, cum moriendum sibi videt, non desiderat cum Deo redire in gratiam, is nullis excommunicationibus huc pertrahetur. Omnium ætatem & locorum exempla nos doceant, in mortis discrimine plurimos ad Deum seriò confugisse, qui nullis antea exhortationibus mouebantur. Non frustra sub cruce detinet suos Dominus.
units.tr: Moreover, the author says that Christians who are punished by the magistrate will not become better, or will not die as Christians. This does not seem right to me. First, because it is God's command that whoever has committed a crime worthy of death should die, and he may in no way be absolved, whether he grieves over the deed or not. Second, because among Christians such people are instructed with the greatest care from the Word of God; they are, I say, taught far more diligently than anyone else. Third, because nothing under this heaven leads us more to the knowledge and invocation of God, provided right instruction is added, than affliction, the cross and the feeling of adversity. The person who, when he sees that he must die, does not wish to be restored to favour with God, will not be drawn back by any excommunication. The examples of every age and place teach us that very many, in the peril of death, have seriously turned to God, though they had been moved by no exhortations before. The Lord does not keep his people under the cross for nothing.

units.la: Atnon omnes, inquiés, resipiscunt in supplicio. Sed nec omnes in Domino moriuntur, qui domi suæ pácatè ex morbo decedunt. Nec omnes excommunicati corriguntur, imò plurimi efficiuntur magni hypocritæ: & sub ea specie multo plus nocent, quàm alij indissimulanter mali. Nullum est sub hoc sole animal, quod Deo & coelitibus cunctis magis inuisum sit, Hypocritâ. Verum vt-ut ista habeant, non decet nos inquirere in statuta Dei, sed eius voluntati obedire, nec supra ipsum sapere velle. Definiuit in suo verbo sceleribus omnibus suas poenas: definitæ etiam sunt in legibus Cæsarum, & iure, quo nos hodie utimur. Pius magistratus sic res temperabit, vt à voluntate & regula verbi Diuini minimum abscedat, atque ad eius gloriam & iusum omnia dirigat.
units.tr: "But not all," he says, "repent under punishment." Yet neither do all die in the Lord who pass away peacefully from illness in their own homes. Nor are all excommunicated people corrected; indeed very many become great hypocrites, and under that appearance do far more harm than those who are openly wicked. There is no creature under this sun more hateful to God and to all the heavenly beings than the hypocrite. However these matters stand, we ought not to pry into the decrees of God, but obey his will, and not wish to be wiser than he is. He has set in his Word a penalty for all crimes; they are also fixed in the laws of the Caesars and in the law we use today. A godly magistrate will so manage affairs that he departs as little as possible from the will and rule of the Word of God, and directs everything to his glory and justice.

units.la: Reprehendit praeterea, quod dixi, Iohannem omnes admisisse ad baptismum, qui cuperent baptizari: Pharisæos, Publicanos: nec omnes tamen fuisse verè bonos & pios, sed multos extitisse improbos. Dicit confessos fuisse peccata sua, scio. Nam si quis non fateretur peccatum, qui poterat is baptizari baptismo poenitentiæ: Non enim poenitere nos debet sanctæ & incorruptæ vitæ, puto. Hoc volebam: Iohannem publica peccati confessione contentum fuisse; non postulauisse nescio quam satisfactionem: nec arrogauisse sibi facultatem inter verè & simulatè confitentes dijudicandi. Si imitari tuos voluissent presbyteros, non tam cito ac facile admisisset Pharisæos nonnullos, quos pro Hypocritis vt viperarum progenie habebat, vt ex verbis eius patet. Sed cum in hac parte non discrepet authoris huius sententia à nostra, magis miror, cur hæc carpere voluerit.
units.tr: He further finds fault with what I said, that John admitted to baptism all who wished to be baptized, Pharisees and tax collectors, and that not all of them were truly good and godly, but many turned out to be wicked. He says they confessed their sins; I know it. For if anyone did not confess his sin, how could he be baptized with the baptism of repentance? I suppose we ought not to repent of a holy and blameless life. My point was this: John was content with public confession of sin; he did not demand some kind of satisfaction, nor did he claim for himself the power of distinguishing between those who confessed truly and those who confessed in pretence. If your elders had wished to imitate him, he would not so quickly and readily have admitted some Pharisees, whom he called hypocrites and a brood of vipers, as is clear from his words. But since the author's opinion does not differ from ours on this point, I am more surprised why he wished to pick at it.

units.la: Contra id, quod dixi, non arcendos à sacramentis qui recte eis vti cupiant cum Ecclesia, obijcit cap. 66. Esaiæ & Salom. Prouerb. 15. de qua re satis est dictum supra. Miror, quod inter Dei & visibilis Ecclesiæ iudicium isti homines non distinguant, cum plus differant, quam coelum à terris distat. Non dicimus nos, Sacramenta Christum & Belial vnire debere: sed hoc contendimus, non debere ea disiungere à visibili societate, quos Deus ista via separari noluerit. Faciunt praeterea nobis iniuriam (imò vera calumnia est) cum dicunt, nos omnes sine vllo examine velle admitti, qualesquales sint ac esse velint. Quippe sic volumus vnumquemque admitti, quomodo Ecclesiæ nostræ consuetudo & regula iubet. Dixi quoque, fieri posse, vt repente aliquis mutetur, qui ante fuerit non bonus, vt exemplum habemus Publicani Luc. 18. item Zachaei, item mulieris peccatricis Luc. 7. Dixi autem, vt ostenderem, non semper malos permanere, qui semper ante mali fuerint: benéque sperandum de eo, qui se poenitere affirmet. Haec cur accusect, non video. Non secretum Dei consilium, sed peccatoris confessionem spectare debet Ecclesia;
units.tr: Against what I said, that those who desire to use the sacraments rightly together with the Church should not be kept away from them, he objects Isaiah chapter 66 and Solomon, Proverbs 15. Enough has been said about this matter above. I wonder that these men do not distinguish between the judgement of God and the judgement of the visible Church, since they differ more than heaven is distant from earth. We do not say that Christ and Belial ought to be joined in the sacraments; but we contend that those whom God has not wished to be separated in this way should not be cut off from the visible fellowship. Moreover, they do us an injustice (indeed it is a true calumny) when they say that we want everyone to be admitted without any examination, whatever sort of people they are and whatever they wish to be. Certainly we want each person admitted in the manner that the custom and rule of our Church prescribes. I also said that it may happen that someone who was previously not good is suddenly changed; we have the example of the tax collector, Luke 18, likewise of Zacchaeus, and likewise of the sinful woman, Luke 7. I said this to show that those who have always been wicked do not always remain so, and that one should hope well of a person who declares that he repents. Why he finds fault with this I do not see. The Church ought to look not to the secret counsel of God but to the confession of the sinner.

units.la: Accusat etiam nos inconstantiae, & Theses sibi ipsis repugnare scribit, quia Haereticorum & Apostatarum excommunicationem admittant. Vtinam vero ipsi non magis secum & cum veritate ipsa pugnarent. Equidem in Thesibus ab initio monui, me de sola illa excommunicatione agere, qua aliqui doctrinam intelligentes, probantes, amplexantes & sacramentis recte vti cupientes, quod ad externum vsum attinet, ab eisdem propter anteactae vitae turpitudine a quibusdam presbyteris repelluntur; quia scilicet non videtur eis serio dolere, qui lapsus fuit, ac sibi dolere id profitetur. Sane vt Idololatra & Apostatam negamus membrum esse Ecclesiae Christi, sic etiam nequitiam suam defendentem negamus inter membra Ecclesiae censendum esse. Et quemadmodum illos ex Christiano coetu iudicamus exterminandos, sic hos quoque putamus in eo coetu non esse ferendos. Verum neque de his, neque de illis quaerunt nostrae Theses: sed disputatur in eis de solis doctrinam amplexantibus, & sacramentis rite cum ecclesia vti cupientibus, hoc est, poenitentiam eodem modo, quo alij, profitentibus. Quare non pugnant mea Theses, dum, quod praeter hoc est, non oppugnant. An eodem modo sua ipsi defendere possint a contradictionibus, iudicium sit penes lectores. Malim eos vbique sibi & inter se in veritate constare.
units.tr: He also accuses us of inconstancy, and writes that our Theses contradict themselves, because they admit the excommunication of heretics and apostates. Would that they themselves did not fight more against themselves and against truth itself! In the Theses, from the beginning, I did indeed warn that I am dealing only with that excommunication by which certain persons who understand, approve, embrace the doctrine and wish to use the sacraments rightly, so far as external use is concerned, are repelled from them by certain elders on account of the disgrace of their former life; for it seems to them that the one who has fallen does not seriously grieve, though he professes that he does. Certainly, just as we deny that an idolater and apostate is a member of the Church of Christ, so too we deny that someone who defends his wickedness should be counted among the members of the Church. And just as we judge that those must be cut off from the Christian assembly, so we think that these too are not to be tolerated in that assembly. But our Theses ask nothing about these or those; they dispute only about those who embrace the doctrine and wish to use the sacraments duly with the Church, that is, who profess repentance in the same way as others. Therefore my Theses do not contradict themselves, since they do not attack what lies outside this. Whether they can defend their own statements against contradictions in the same way is left to the judgement of the readers. I would rather they were consistent with themselves and with one another everywhere in the truth.

units.la: Laus Deo. Heidelbergae Prid. Natiuitatis Domini, MDLXIX.
units.tr: Praise be to God. Heidelberg, the day before the Nativity of the Lord, 1569.

units.la: QVAEDAM EX EPISTO- LIS SVMMORVM THEOLOGO- RVM AD ERASTVM EXARATIS AD hanc rem maximè congruentia, fideli- ter desumpta.
units.tr: Certain passages from the letters of leading theologians written to Erastus, most pertinent to this matter, faithfully extracted.

units.la: Clariss. viro D. Thomae Erasto doctori Medico, Domino meo honorando, fratri & amico intimo, Heidelbergam, S. D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Mr. Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, my honoured lord, brother and closest friend, at Heidelberg, greetings.

units.la: PEro vltimas meas, Domine obseruande, & frater charissime, redditas esse tibi: quibus, inter alia, reuocauimus, per te aliquot studiosos nostros Erasmum Kauffman, Stephanum Aberli, & Ioannem Heinrichum Locherum. Quòd si literae meae tibi nondum sunt redditae, valdè oro vt eos moneas festinent, & reditum non protrahant, sed rectâ domum veniant. Gratissimum mihi foret officium, si Ioannes Iacobus Frisius apud vos esset, aut in vicinia, id ipsum ei significares, vt & ipse domum rectà redeat. Sunt causse iustissimae, & necessariae, ob quas reuocantur. A postremis verò meis ad te datis, mox accepi Theses tuas, insuper & Tractationem de Excommunicatione. Legi, & auidè quidem. Dedi legenda D. Vuolphio, Lauatero, Hallero, Zuinglio, & imprimis Gualthero, & Simlero, &c. Placent illa nobis. Neque enim existimamus negotium coenæ Dominicæ implicandum huic negotio. Diu cum Anabaptistis nostris contendimus hac de re, & ostendimus Ecclesiam veram posse esse, & dici Ecclesiam, quae excommunicatione hac careat. Rursus tamen contendimus disciplinam esse debere in Ecclesia, ac satis esse, si ea administretur à magistratu. Interim nunquam damnauimus Ecclesiam Geneuensem, quæ suam habet disciplinam. Nos si talem inducere vellemus in nostras Ecclefias, perderemus certò has citius, quàm seruaremus. Vide quid in Confesione nostra hac de re scripserimus. Sentimus nos praeterea vobiscum, non facere ad aedificationem Ecclesiarum Palatinatus, neque ère vel bono fore Principis, si talis instituatur disciplina, id est, Excommunicatio, qualem nonnulli volunt: quos optaremus diligentius apud se expendere illud Apostoli: Data est mihi potestas ad aedificationem, non destructionem &c. Multa sanè sunt hic, maximè exulceratissimo hoc tempore consideranda. Breuiter, tecum, mi Domine, & frater, sentimus. Multum haec causa nos exercuit.
units.tr: I trust my last letters have been delivered to you, honoured Sir and dearest brother, in which, among other things, I recalled through you some of our students: Erasmus Kauffman, Stephen Aberli and John Henry Locher. But if my letters have not yet reached you, I earnestly beg you to warn them to hurry and not delay their return, but to come straight home. It would be a most welcome service if John James Frisius were with you or nearby, and you would tell him the same, so that he too may return home directly. The reasons for recalling them are most just and necessary. Soon after my last letters to you, I received your Theses and also your Treatise on Excommunication. I have read them, and eagerly. I have given them to be read by Wolphius, Lavater, Haller, Zwingli, and especially Gualter and Simler, and others. They please us. For we do not think the matter of the Lord's Supper should be entangled in this business. For a long time we have contended with our Anabaptists over this question, and have shown that the true Church can be, and be called, a Church that lacks this excommunication. Yet again we maintain that discipline ought to exist in the Church, and that it is enough if it is administered by the magistrate. Meanwhile we have never condemned the Church of Geneva, which has its own discipline. If we wished to introduce such a discipline into our churches, we would certainly ruin them sooner than preserve them. See what we have written in our Confession on this matter. Furthermore, we agree with you that it does not serve the building up of the churches of the Palatinate, nor is it for the good of the Prince, if such discipline is set up, namely excommunication of the kind some want. We would wish them to weigh more carefully that saying of the Apostle: "The power was given to me for building up, not for destruction," and so on. There are certainly many things here to be considered, especially at this most inflamed time. In short, my Lord and brother, we agree with you. This question has greatly exercised us.

units.la: Vt ad priorem causam redeam, prudentissimus & pijssimus Princeps Elector, pro religioso suo animo, curabit, vt scelerati puniantur, & disciplina fit moderata in populo suo: atque vt excommunicationem instituat talem, qualem quidem volunt, videt haud dubiè non admodum facere ad incrementum & conseruationem Ecclesiae. Dominus benedicat illi, & seruet ipsum.
units.tr: To return to the former matter: the most prudent and most pious Elector, out of his religious spirit, will take care that the wicked are punished and that discipline among his people is moderated. As for his setting up excommunication of the kind some wish, he clearly sees that it does not greatly contribute to the growth and preservation of the Church. May the Lord bless him and keep him.

units.la: Sed si nos id obtinere possemus, vt magistratus peccata serio puniret, & scandala auferret, abundè nobis satisfactum esset. Non cupimus noua iudicia, neque maiore fungi potestate, & miseros homines exagitare, & ex abalienatis, longe magis abalienatos reddere, &, sicuti aliquando accidisse vidimus: inferiores gradus concendere, superiores verò intactos relinquere, &c. Aeternum vale. Tigurì 17. Octobris. 1568.
units.tr: But if we could bring it about that the magistrate seriously punished sins and removed scandals, we would be fully satisfied. We do not desire new courts, nor to exercise greater power and harass wretched men, and make the estranged far more estranged; nor, as we have sometimes seen happen, to climb to the lower steps while leaving the higher ones untouched, and so on. Farewell forever. Zurich, 17 October 1568.

units.la: Bullingerus Senior Tuus.
units.tr: Bullinger the Elder, your own.

units.la: Clarissimo viro D. Thomae Erasto Doctori Me- dico, Domino meo honorando, & fratri longè charissimo Heidelbergam, S. D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, my honoured lord and most dear brother, at Heidelberg. Greetings.

units.la: Binas à te, Domine honorande, & frater charissime, literas accepi, priores scriptas mense Septembri: posteriores. 9. Octobr. Prioribus interrogabas, quando primum homines coeperint propter delicta sola vitae excommunicari?
units.tr: I have received two letters from you, honoured lord and dearest brother: the first written in September, the second on 9 October. In the first you ask when men first began to be excommunicated for the sole fault of their life.

units.la: Ego vero hic nihil certi possum tibi respondere. Satis vetustum hoc esse video. Quia cum Ecclesia careret magistratu, cito consilia iniit, quomodo sceleratos coherceret. Nec tum illis aliud visum est commodius remedium, quàm excommunicationis. Et ne quid hic apud te intimum, & optimum meum amicum, & fratrem dilectissimum dissimulem: Gualtherus, Vuolphius, & ego scripsimus literas ad illustrissimum Principem Palat. Electt, satis longas, in quibus eius Celsitudini exponimus: Audire nos, propter excommunicationem, quam alij inductam, alia eiectam velint, exoriri odia, & dissidia inter doctos, atque ministros. Orare itaque si quid huius fit, ipsius authoritate interpositâ, dissidentes componat, & ne in apertum certamen erumpere sinat malum hoc: cum hoc tempore aliâs satis afflicta sit Ecclesia. Exponimus item eius Celsit. Quanta super hac re sustinuerimus contra Anabaptistas, certamina: quibus nunquam concedere voluimus, ut disciplinam, & coenam commiscerent. Coenam esse publicam & laetam gratiarum actionem, & non poenam. Disciplinam verò comprehendere monitionem, & correptionem, adeoque poenam. Cohercerí debere scelera & sceleratos per magistratum Christianum. Proinde obsecrare nos, ne nova iudicia erigat in Ecclesia: sed cuiet potius, ut coena sit libera omnibus peccata sua agnoscentibus, & veniam à Christo petentibus &c. Multet vero & coherceat petulantes, & offendentes Ecclesiam alia ratione commoda. Testamur, quod res est, inscijs partibus, & secretò nos ad illustriss. Principem illa scribere. Interim tamen scripti tui De excommunicatione facimus mentionem: id quod à studiosis nostris huc ad nos reuertentibus acceperimus: indeque occasionem acceperimus scribendi ad ipsum. Probamus autem scriptum tuum tanquam salutare, & Ecclesijs vtile, veritatique consentaneum &c. Haec te nescire nolumus, ut si huius aliquid audieris, scias quid sit. Quanquam arbitramur illustriss. Principem admonitionem nostram sibi se- li reseruaturum, qua duntaxat dissidia manifesta in Ecclefia prævenire voluimus. Dominus benedicat nostro consilio, & labori. Nemo est alioqui, cui hoc nostrum communicauerimus cónsilium. Et præstat hoc, quod plurima sint irritabilia valdè ingenia, & quæ cum semel odisse coeperunt, nunquam in gratiam reduci possunt. Dominus medeatur talibus & conseruet Ecclesias in pace, & auertat scandala, præcidátque aduersarijs sua gaudia, quæ capiunt ex nostris disensionibus. Noua memoratu digna non habemus hic vlla. A te expecto quid habeas. Studiosi nostri omnium vestrûm benevolentiam prædicant. Proinde maximas tibi, omnibúsque vobis ago gratias. Quod si pestis ingruerit, tu nostris fis bonus consultor. Si schola non migrauerit in alium saniorem locum, tum illis da salutaria cõsilia, si forte locum mutent, & ascendant Argentoratum, aut ad alia tutiora loca, in quibus tamen non negligantur, sed in literis progrediantur. Apparent etiam in vrbe nostra aliqua pestis initia. Dominus faciat, quod bonum est in oculis suis. Vale æternum: Dominus benedicat tibi, & seruet te. Tiguri 29. Octob. 1568.
units.tr: Here I can give you no certain answer. I see that this is quite an old practice. When the Church lacked a magistrate, it quickly devised ways to restrain wicked people, and at that time no remedy seemed more suitable to them than excommunication. And so that I may conceal nothing from you, my most intimate and best friend and most beloved brother: Gualtherus, Wolphius and I have written a fairly long letter to the most illustrious Prince, the Elector Palatine, in which we set out to his Highness that we hear that, on account of excommunication, one party wants it introduced and another wants it removed, and that hatred and discord are arising among the learned and the ministers as a result. We therefore beg that, by his authority, he settle the disputants, if anything of this kind is happening, and that he not allow this evil to break out into open conflict, since the Church is already sufficiently troubled at this time. We also set out to his Highness how much we have endured in struggles against the Anabaptists over this matter; we have never been willing to concede that they should mix discipline and the Supper. The Supper is a public and joyful thanksgiving, not a punishment; but discipline comprises admonition and correction, and so also punishment. Crimes and criminals ought to be restrained by a Christian magistrate. Accordingly we beg him not to set up new courts of judgment in the Church, but rather to see to it that the Supper is open to all who acknowledge their sins and seek pardon from Christ, etc. Let him, however, fine and restrain the wanton and those who give offence to the Church by other suitable means. We testify, as is the case, that we are not taking sides and that we wrote those things to the most illustrious Prince in secret. Meanwhile, however, we make mention of your writing on excommunication, which we learned from our students returning here to us, and from which we took the occasion to write to him. We approve your writing as wholesome, useful to the Churches, and consonant with the truth, etc. We do not wish you to be ignorant of these things, so that if you hear anything of this, you will know what it is about. Although we think the most illustrious Prince will keep our admonition to himself alone, which we wished chiefly to forestall the open discords in the Church. May the Lord bless our counsel and our labour. Otherwise there is no one to whom we have communicated this our counsel. And it is worth noting that very many minds are extremely irritable, and once they have begun to hate, they can never be brought back into favour. May the Lord heal such people, preserve the Churches in peace, avert scandals, and cut off from our adversaries the joy they take in our disagreements. We have no new matters worth mentioning here. I look to you to tell me what you have. Our students commend the goodwill of all of you; therefore I give you and all of you the greatest thanks. If plague should break out, be a good adviser to us. If the school does not move to some healthier place, then give them wholesome counsel, in case they perhaps change their location and go up to Strasbourg or to other safer places, where they will not be neglected but will make progress in their studies. Some beginnings of plague are also appearing in our city. May the Lord do what is good in his eyes. Farewell forever; may the Lord bless you and keep you. Zurich, 29 October 1568.

units.la: Bullingerus Senior tuissimus.
units.tr: Your most devoted Bullinger the Elder.

units.la: Clariss. viro D. Thomae Erasto Doctori Medico, Domino meo honorando & fratri charissimo Heidelberg. S. D.
units.tr: To the distinguished man, Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, my honoured lord and dearest brother, at Heidelberg. Greetings.

units.la: ACcepi literas tuas, honorande Domine, & frater charissime, quas scribebas die Purificationis, mittebásque per Albinum nostrum. Ea exhilararunt me, & contristarunt vehementer. Multa mecum Zuleg. contulit de infelice illa excommunicatione. Ego illi respondi pluribus. Intellexi illum omnino ex ijs esse vnum, & quidem non postremum, qui illam cuperet inductam. Tandem hoc consilij dedi: si vestri disidFent, conuocentur, qui disident, & amicè inter se conferant, valeatque in collatione veritas. Sit libera coena Domini, gratulatio, & non supplicium, sit in Ecclesia disciplina, sed quam administret bonus Magistratus. Tuâ responsionem, cuius in literis meminisi expecto, cupidè. Zuleg.nihil dixi de literis nostris ad Principem. Si nouit, pulchrè dissimulauit.
units.tr: I have received your letter, honoured lord and dearest brother, which you wrote on the day of the Purification and sent through our Albinus. It cheered me and grieved me greatly. Zuleg. discussed much with me about that unhappy excommunication, and I answered him at length. I understood that he is entirely one of those, and indeed no small one, who desired it to be introduced. At last I gave this counsel: if your people disagree, let those who disagree be called together and let them confer amicably with one another, and let the truth prevail in the discussion. Let the Lord's Supper be free, a thanksgiving and not a punishment. Let there be church discipline, but let it be administered by a good magistrate. I eagerly await your reply, of which you made mention in your letter. I said nothing to Zuleg. about our letter to the Prince. If he knows of it, he has cleverly kept quiet.

units.la: Non dissimulaui me vidisse Theses tuas, easque mihi non displicere, vt ne reliquis quidem. Scripsi praeterea ad Bezam nostrum, admonens ne quid contra te in hac caufla vulget. Si velit, priuatis literis conferat: ac spero ipsum ea quae pacis sunt, quaesiturum. Zanchus ad generum meum scribit, se nolle huic negotio immiscéri: Vuillingus constanter videtur meliores sequi partes. Annitimini omnes, vt quantum fieri potest, pax in Ecclesia seruetur, & capita, de quibus est concertatio, placidè excutiantur. Vale. Saluta D. Thomanum in Cancellaria, & excusa me, quod nihil scripserim ei. Accepi quas ille ad me misit Calend. Februarij. Saluta fratres & amicos, imprimis Ioannem Miscouium, & Casparem Malinium meos illos Polonos. Tigurii 20. Febr. 1569.
units.tr: I do not deny that I have seen your theses, and I do not dislike them, nor do I dislike the rest. I have also written to our Beza, advising him not to publish anything against you in this cause. If he wishes, let him confer with you by private letter, and I hope he will seek the things that belong to peace. Zanchius writes to my son-in-law that he is unwilling to be involved in this business. Vuillingus seems steadfastly to be taking the better side. Strive, all of you, that as far as possible peace be kept in the Church, and that the points over which there is contention be examined calmly. Farewell. Greet Dr. Thomas in the Chancery, and excuse me for not having written to him. I received the letter he sent me on the Kalends of February. Greet the brothers and friends, especially John Miscovius and Caspar Malinius, my Poles. Zurich, 20 February 1569.

units.la: Tuifsimus Bullingerus.
units.tr: Your most devoted Bullinger.

units.la: Clariff. viro D. Thomae Erafto Doctori Medico, Heidelbergae agenti, Domino meo honorando & fratri chariff. S. D.
units.tr: To the distinguished man Mr. Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, living at Heidelberg, my honoured lord and dear brother. Greetings.

units.la: HAcipsa hora exoptatissimas tuas literas vna cum responsione ad Argumenta excommunicatorum, accepi, libenter hanc lecturus exhibiturúsq; eandem aliis quoque symmystis, & fratribus. Quid nobis de ea videatur, breuii, si quidem tabellionem commodum assequuti fuerimus, datis ad te literis exponemus. Nunc verò tot mihi sunt negotia, vt vix breuissimum tempus alimento concedere possim; Spero breui plus otij me habiturum. A discessu Zulegeri scriptis ad Bezam literis, hortabar ne finteret animum suum exacerbari contra te, vt, quod nonnulli sperent, publicum scriptum edat in tuas Theses, quibus & alia quaedam adieci &c. Ad ea secunda Martij his mihi verbis respondit: Miror quis illum sparserit rumorem, me aliquid edítuediturum in Erastum, ac eius Theses. Eas mihi displicere neque apud te, neque apud illum dissimulaui. Addidi etiam ad illum scribere me missurum confutationem, sed priuatim & amicè scriptam. Sic enim ab eo dissentio, vt valdè probem in eo eximia Dei Dona. Et eum spero, re tota expensa, multa saltem in sua sententia mutaturum: vtpote veritatis amantem.
