Vtinam verò, quicquid hoc rei est, cum solis amicis contentus fuisset communicare. Quam responsionem omnino sequi decreueram, & multò etiam magis tuis acceptis literis, seruare decreui. Quod eum quoque idem deinceps facturum mihi polliceor. Ipsius libellum contra Astrologiam diuinatricem, curaui his diebus hic excudendum &c. Hæc ille ad me. Proinde te etiam atque etiam hortor, ne quicquid est huius contentionis in publicum extrudatur, si vlla ratione per aduersarios fieri potest. Nemo credit, quantum gaudium inde conciperent hostes nostri communes. Vale & commenda me bonis & amicis nostris.
units.tr: I received your most welcome letter, together with your reply to the arguments of the excommunicators, at this very hour. I shall read it gladly and will show it to our other colleagues and brothers too. What we think of it I will set out in a letter to you shortly, if we manage to find a convenient carrier. For the present I have so much business that I can scarcely spare the briefest time for my food; I hope to have more leisure before long. After leaving Zurich I wrote to Beza, urging him not to let his mind be inflamed against you, so that (as some hope) he would not publish a written attack on your Theses, to which I have also added some other matters. In reply to that letter, on the second of March, he answered me in these words: "I am surprised that anyone has spread the rumour that I am going to publish something against Erastus and his Theses. I have made no secret, either to you or to him, that I dislike them. I also added that I would write to him a refutation, but a private and friendly one. For I dissent from him so far, and yet I greatly approve in him the outstanding gifts of God. And I hope that, when the whole matter has been weighed, he will at least change many things in his opinion, since he loves the truth. Would that, whatever this affair is, he had been content to share it only with his friends. I had firmly decided to follow that course of reply, and, all the more after receiving your letter, I have decided to keep to it. I promise that he too will do the same from now on. I have recently arranged for his little book against divining astrology to be printed here." So he wrote to me. Accordingly I urge you again and again not to let anything of this controversy be thrust into the public eye, if it can in any way be prevented through our opponents. No one believes how much joy our common enemies would take from it. Farewell, and commend me to our good and friendly colleagues.

units.la: Tuissimus Bullingerus Senior.
units.tr: Your most devoted Bullinger the Elder.

units.la: Ornatiss. viro D. Petro Datheno in Palatinatû Concionatori aulico, Domino meo honorando & fratri dilecto. S. D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Master Peter Dathenus, court preacher in the Palatinate, my honoured lord and beloved brother. Greetings.

units.la: VLtimis illis tuis ad me datis literis, Petre Dathene, frater in Domino dilecte, quereris quod approbarim Theses D. Erasti, contra Disciplinam Ecclesiasticam scriptas, quas tu non tantum impias esse dicis, sed insuper etiam viam sternere ad atheismum. Vnde me hortaris & obsecras, vt data aliqua occasione, publicè tester, me nouas illas Theses improbare. Quod nisi faciam, futurum vt videar dissentire non tantum à doctâ illa vetustate, sed etiam à Zuinglio & Oecolampadio aliisque, adeoque & cum memetipso pugnare. Qua re nominis mei celebritatem, non tam obscualia ratione cohercendos esse, & in viam reducendos arbitramur, qui existimamus & credimus coenam dominicam à Domino esse institutam, non vt sit ventilabrum aut cribrum, quo cribrentur aut dispergantur ab inuicem homines, sed synaxim, id est, coagmentationem, societatem, communionē & coniunctionem, ad colligendos congregandosque homines peccatores, eos putamus, qui peccatorum suorum mole depressi, peccata sua agnoscunt, hæc sibi remissa per mortem Christi credunt, ideo iam ad coenam Domini accedunt, gratias acturi &c. Hæc sane non debet tibi, mi frater, noua videri opinio, nuper à nobis inuenta: tum in superiore Germania, inter ecclesias reformatas, Tigurina, quæ semper sic sensit, facilè fuerit & sit omnium prima, vt quæ anno 1500, plantari coepit.
units.tr: In your last letter to me, Peter Dathenus, beloved brother in the Lord, you complain that I approved the Theses of Master Erastus, written against church discipline, which you say are not only impious but also pave the way to atheism. On this basis you urge and beg me to declare publicly, on some suitable occasion, that I disapprove of those new Theses. If I do not, you say, I will seem to dissent not only from that learned antiquity but also from Zwingli, Oecolampadius and others, and so to contradict myself. Indeed, we think that people who are not so much to be restrained by violence as to be brought back to the right way should be considered: those who believe and maintain that the Lord's Supper was instituted by the Lord not as a winnowing fan or sieve, by which men are sifted and scattered from one another, but as a synaxis, that is, a joining together, a fellowship, communion and union, for gathering and assembling sinful men. We hold that they are the ones who, weighed down by the burden of their sins, acknowledge their sins, believe that these are forgiven them through the death of Christ, and therefore now come to the Lord's Supper to give thanks, and so on. Indeed, my brother, this opinion should not seem new to you, as if it had only lately been discovered by us. It was held in upper Germany among the reformed churches, and the Tigurine church, which has always thought this way, was easily the first of all, having begun to be planted in the year 1500.

units.la: Ergo dum clarissimus vir D. Eraftus, diuersum ab his, quoad summam totius causæ huius, quantum ego quidem in Thesibus eius videre potui, non sentiat, nec nullam in Ecclesia disciplinam esse velit, sed magistratui Christiano suum ius vendicet, atque ita viam oligarchiae ecclesiasticæ (quæ alicubi suppullulare queat) dissidijs in Ecclesia suppeditanti, intercludere, studio pacis & concordiæ, fatagat, scelera interim non impune grassari, sed legitime coherceri postulet, ac sacram coenam, sanctè non prophane, iuxta canonem Apostolicum, Probet autem seipsum homo, & sic de pane hic edat, & calice bibat, celebrati, & ab ea nō temere arceri homines peccatores cupiat, neque admonitionem ecclesiasticam, aut alia ad emendationem Ecclesiæ vtilia & necessaria disoluat & abijciat, non video quomodo atheismo, vt ais, viam sternat, maxime cum nullum fidei articulum, tota illa sua disputatione, vel in dubium vocare, vel conuellere euertereque cogitet. Quod loca aliquot scripturae, vt Math. 18. & 1. Corinth. 5. aliter interpretatur, quam alijs nonnullis videatur, id quidem non ignoras, Petre frater, ipsum commune habere cum alijs scriptoribus, cum veteribus tum neotericis, quibus tamen eam ob diuersitatem, nemo vnquam atheismum impegit.
units.tr: Therefore, although the most distinguished Master Erastus, so far as I could see in his Theses, does not hold a view different from ours on the main point of this whole question, and does not wish that there be no discipline in the Church, but claims its right for the Christian magistrate, and strives in the interest of peace and concord to close off the way to an ecclesiastical oligarchy (which might spring up somewhere) that would feed divisions in the Church; and although he demands that crimes, meanwhile, not run riot with impunity but be lawfully restrained; and that the holy supper be approached holily, not profanely, according to the apostolic canon, "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of this bread and drink of this cup" (1 Cor. 11); and although he wishes that sinful men not be rashly kept away from it, and does not dissolve or cast aside ecclesiastical admonition or other things useful and necessary for the amendment of the Church: I do not see how he paves the way to atheism, as you say, especially since in that whole disputation he intends neither to call in doubt nor to overthrow and destroy any article of faith. As for the fact that he interprets some passages of Scripture, such as Matt. 18 and 1 Cor. 5, differently from some others, you, my brother Peter, are not unaware that in this he shares a common position with other writers, both ancient and recent, and yet no one has ever charged them with atheism on account of this difference.

units.la: Modestiam ergo in te, mi frater Dathene, requiro, ne forte, non sine causa, eam nobis inijcias cogitationem, si quando potestatem consequamini in Ecclesia excommunicandi, sore vt omnes, quotquot per omnia vestra nō approbarint, atheismi sitis condemnaturi, ac expulsuri ad ipsos vsque religionis nostrae hostes truculentissimos. Quæres quem finem tandem consequutura sit, & quam graues inde turbæ & omnium ordinum conuulsiones sint exorituræ, res & tempus ipsum docebunt. Si meliora consequantur libenter vanus fuero vates, interim puto solicitudinem illam meam, non esse impiam, & de nihilo conceptam.
units.tr: I therefore ask you, my brother Dathenus, to show moderation, lest perhaps, and not without cause, you bring upon us this thought: that if you ever gain the power to excommunicate in the Church, all who do not approve everything you say will be condemned as atheists by you and driven out to the most savage enemies of our religion itself. You will ask what end this will finally have, and what severe disturbances and upheavals of every order will arise from it. The matter and time itself will teach us. If better things follow, I shall gladly have been a false prophet. Meanwhile I think that my anxiety is not impious and is not conceived out of nothing.

units.la: Nisi vero Theses D. Erasti improbauero, existimas tu me mihi ipsi repugnaturum, hoc est, scriptis meis contradicturum. Cæterum si mecum repetiuero omnia, quæ hac de causa in libris meis editis, scripsi, non video me vel tantillū à mea discedere sententia, quā ab initio mei ministerij, per annos circiter 48. tenui, ac vltimò in Confess. nostra exposui.
units.tr: Unless, indeed, I disapprove of the Theses of Master Erastus, you think I will be opposing myself, that is, contradicting my own writings. But if I go over again with myself everything I wrote on this matter in my published books, I do not see that I have departed in the slightest from the opinion I have held since the beginning of my ministry, for about forty-eight years, and which I finally set out in our Confession.

units.la: Etenim vt huius aliquid repetam in 1. ad Corinth. cap. 5. principio demonstro cōtra Anabaptistas (cum quibus hac de re perpetua sunt nobis certamina) excōmunicationem non esse exercendam à toto Ecclesiæ cœtu, sed à delectis ad hoc hominibus. Deinde ostendo excommunicationem quidem apud veteres fuisse exclulsionem à cōmunione Sacramentorum. Adijcio tamen supplicium esse temporale & disciplinam externam, ad medendū institutam. Tradere sathanæ nihil aliud esse, quam in aduersitatem conijcere. Ad interitum carnis, significare ad mortificandum externū hominem adeoque ipsum scelus designatum. Item esse Ethnicum & Publicanum significare, esse haberiqué inter facinorosos, quibus nihil neque officij neque synceri committas: vt nos solemus mæchos, ἐντρεπόμενα deprehensos, honore, honore & trabea exutos, publicè dedecorare. Adodo Paulum in 2. ad Cor. 2. cap. vsum ἐπιτιμίᾳ, pro ἐπιμία, id est, mulcta: & posteriore hoc loco Apostolum exposuisse, quid in priore intellexerit per traditionem sathanæ.
units.tr: For, to recall something of this, first in my commentary on 1 Corinthians 5, I argue against the Anabaptists (with whom we have constant disputes on this matter) that excommunication is not to be exercised by the whole body of the Church but by men chosen for this purpose. Then I show that excommunication among the ancients was indeed exclusion from communion in the sacraments. I add, however, that it is a temporal punishment and an external discipline instituted for healing. To deliver to Satan means nothing other than to cast into adversity. "For the destruction of the flesh" signifies mortifying the outward man, and so the very crime intended. Likewise, to be a heathen and a tax collector means to be regarded and treated among wrongdoers, with whom you have no duty or sincere fellowship; just as we are accustomed to publicly disgrace adulterers caught in the act [ἐντρεπόμενα], stripping them of honour and of the robe. I also adduce Paul in 2 Corinthians 2, who used the penalty [ἐπιτιμίᾳ] for [ἐπιμία], that is, a fine; and in this later passage the Apostle explained what he had understood in the earlier by the delivering to Satan.

units.la: Concludo & hortor omnes, curent, vt salutare hoc pharmacum,è coetu sanctorum,Pontificis auaritia eliminatum, reducatur:hoc est,vt scelera offendentia plectantur.Et sub finem capitis,subijcio S.Augustini,de visu disciplinae, sententiam, ex tertio libro contra Epistolam Parmeniani, vehementem quidem illam, non tam contra Donatistas, quam contra Anabaptistas,& Anabaptistas nostro saeculo similes.
units.tr: I conclude and exhort everyone to take care that this wholesome remedy, cast out of the assembly of the saints by the greed of the Pope, be brought back; that is, that offensive crimes be punished. And at the end of the chapter I add the opinion of St Augustine on the sight of discipline, from the third book against the Letter of Parmenianus, a vehement passage indeed, aimed not so much at the Donatists as at the Anabaptists, and at men in our own age like the Anabaptists.

units.la: In 2. ad Thessalonicen. cap. 3. abstentionis memini. Nam habemus abstentionem seu exclusionem, qua à tribuum societate, & publicorum pascuorum visu-fructu excludimus contumaces & omnes admonitiones contemnentes. Interim no dissimulo eundem locum etiam aliter posse interpretari. Ab his omnibus, quoad summam rei, nihil dissidet, quod scripsi in Comment.meis ad 18. cap.Matth. Sub finem enim inter alia dico, Finis consilij Domini est, (in negotio disciplinae) vt corrigantur scelerati in Ecclesia, & auferantur scandala. Proinde si illi corrigi possunt & haec auferri, alio modo, pro temporis loci personarumque ratione prudenter,sancte & utiliter ordinato, nihil prohibet. &c. Et mox, videant qui hodie cupiunt ecclesiasticam disciplinam reductam, ne nimium seueri sint,& imprudenti zelo suo, & ipsam Domini coenam omnibus reddant inuisam, & Euangelij cursum plus impediant, quàm promoueant. Adde, ne dum certos aliquot excommunicare perguntnon modo hos non sanent, verumetiam totam communionem,maximo cum bonorum detrimento & luctu, dissoluat.
units.tr: In 2 Thessalonians 3 I recalled abstention. For we have an abstention or exclusion, by which we shut out from the fellowship of the tribes, and from the public use of the pastures, the obstinate and all who scorn admonitions. Meanwhile I do not conceal that this same passage can also be interpreted otherwise. On the substance of the matter, nothing I wrote in my Commentaries on Matthew 18 differs from all these. Near the end I say, among other things, that the purpose of the Lord's counsel (in the matter of discipline) is that wicked men in the Church be corrected and offences removed. Therefore, if they can be corrected and these removed by another way, prudently, holily and usefully ordered according to the circumstances of time, place and persons, nothing forbids it, and so on. And soon after: let those who today desire that ecclesiastical discipline be restored take care not to be too severe, and by their imprudent zeal not make the Lord's Supper itself hateful to everyone, and hinder the course of the gospel more than they advance it. Add that, while they go on excommunicating certain individuals, they not only do not heal these but even dissolve the whole communion, with the greatest loss and grief to good men.

units.la: Ab his nihil variant quae 10. Sermone Decadis. 5.exposui. Eas audio, vt hoc obiter quoque referam,paulo ante typis Heydelbergae excusas, & admodum laudatas,nunc vero prohiberi, ne vel legantur vel distrahantur. Quod si verum est,non video quomodo illi,qui hoc faciunt,factum hoc suum excusare, & leuitatis Papisticaeque tyrannidis crimen à se propulsare possint. An enim non oportuerat prius admoneri authorem, amicum praesertim & fratrem, & si qua re peccarat, indicare, eiusque responsionem audire ? Verum haec sunt nostra illa tempora, in quibus refrixit charitas, abundauit iniquitas.
units.tr: Nothing I set out in the tenth sermon of the fifth decade differs from these. I hear, to mention this in passing too, that they were printed not long ago at Heidelberg and highly praised, but now they are forbidden to be read or sold. If this is true, I do not see how those who do this can excuse their deed, or ward off from themselves the charge of levity and Papistical tyranny. Was it not right first to admonish the author, especially a friend and brother, and, if he had erred in any way, to point it out, and to hear his reply? But these are our times, in which love has grown cold and iniquity has abounded.

units.la: Aa 4 Libro
units.tr: Aa 4. Book

units.la: Postremis duobus capitibus, ita perspicue, opinor, hac de causa dissero, vt si quibus videar in prioribus aliquid dixisse obscurius, in hisce posterioribus lucidissimè me loquutum esse, fateri cogantur.
units.tr: In the last two chapters, I argue on this matter, I think, so clearly that if some should find that I have said something rather obscurely in the earlier ones, they will be compelled to admit that I have spoken most lucidly in these latter.

units.la: Quod si qui mea scripta mihi malicioè peruertere instituerint, & antilogias contexere, quod & in contumeliam maiorum nostrorum ab aduersarijs factum scimus, perrexerint: pergam & ego mea rectè interpretari. Interpretatio enim ei competit, qui id, de quo controuertitur, edidit. Hæc quidè copiosius quam ipse ab initio me facturum existimaueram, exposui, quo tibi fratri meo commonstrem, me, si quis mea rectius expendat, mecum non pugnare.
units.tr: But if some have begun to pervert my writings maliciously and to weave counter-arguments against them, as we know was done by our adversaries also to the discredit of our forebears, and persist in it, I too shall go on interpreting my own words correctly. For interpretation belongs to the one who published what is in dispute. I have set this out more fully than I had myself originally intended, so that I might show you, my brother, that if anyone weighs my writings more accurately, he will find that I am not contradicting myself.

units.la: Quæ tu verò refers de celebritate & obscuritate nominis mei, nihil prorsus moror. Scit, qui corda novit Dominus, quid laboribus illis meis quæsiuerim. Non meam vnquam illis quæsiui gloriam, sed Dei ac Christi eius ecclesiæque & ministrorum eius profectum. Vnde certissimè scio, viros bonos, qui in Belgio alijsque locis, meis vsi sunt scriptis, & vtuntur adhuc forte, & propter ea me amarunt, suasque preces pro me effuderunt ad Dominum, ideo hoc fecisse, & facere adhuc, quod viderunt scriptis illis meis, me recta adducere ad vnicum mundi saluatorem Iesum Christum, in quo fideles plenissimè omnia inueniunt, quæ veræ salutis sunt, cui & charitate & vitæ innocentia seruiendū esse docui: præterea qua potui euidentia, & Antichristum, & hunc mundum oppugnaui, erroresque plurimos detexi.
units.tr: As for what you say about the fame and obscurity of my name, I pay it no attention at all. The Lord, who knows hearts, knows what I sought in those labours of mine. I never sought my own glory in them, but the progress of God, of Christ, of his Church and of his ministers. So I know most certainly that good men, who in Belgium and elsewhere have used my writings, and perhaps still use them, and have therefore loved me and poured out their prayers to the Lord for me, have done so because they saw that my writings lead people straight to the one Saviour of the world, Jesus Christ, in whom the faithful find most fully everything that belongs to true salvation; that I taught that he must be served with love and innocence of life; and that, as clearly as I could, I have attacked both Antichrist and this world and exposed very many errors.

units.la: Hi si intellexerint, in his constanter me adhuc progredi, neque in his vel iota immutare aut retractare (id quod si necesse sit, improbitasque aduersariorum compulerit facilè demonstrauero) licet non probem, quæ nonnulli de excommunicatione disputant, & vel nolentibus obtrudere volunt, tamen talem me proculdubio non iudicabūt esse, qualem me nonnulli esse, præter meum meritum, deferunt. Quod si vero vnam hanc ob causam illi me oderint meaq; spreuerint, susq; déque fero. Satis mihi fuerit, si meos labores approbauerit Dominus. Ei enim probari summum mihi est gaudiū, improbari mundo nulla prorsus solicitudo.
units.tr: If they understand that I still advance constantly in these things, and do not change or retract the least part of them (which, if it should become necessary, and if the wickedness of my opponents compels it, I shall easily demonstrate), then although I do not approve what some dispute about excommunication, and wish to force even on unwilling people, they will surely not judge me to be the kind of man that some, beyond my deserts, report me to be. But if for this one reason they hate me and despise my labours, I bear it lightly. It will be enough for me if the Lord approves my labours. To be approved by him is my greatest joy; to be disapproved by the world causes me no anxiety at all.

units.la: Quantum vero attinet ad doctam, vt ais, vetustatem, non male cum illa mihi congruit. Scio enim illam suis fecisse temporibus, quod potuit, & ad Ecclesiæ sui temporis conseruationem facere putauit. Scio item vetustatem illam sanctam, in vsu eucharistiæ multa obseruasse & eam ad multa attraxisse, quæ hodie nec in vsu sunt, neque probare possumus, licet interim cum ipsa non male congruamus. Quomodo temporibus Apostolorum Corinthij coenam celebrarent, nemo nescit. Et quamuis Paulus eum modum reprehenderit atqi abrogarit, nihilominus tamen vetustas illa, Agaparum vsum in coetus factos induxit, qui hodie non vsurpatur, nec per omnia & in omnibus probari potest. Tertullianus de Monogamia & Cyprianus ostendunt mulierculas eucharistiæ reliquias in suas afferuasse cistas. Hesychius in Leuiticum commemorat reliquias eucharistiæ esse à prisci s ad templa combustas. Nicephorus Ecclesiast. hist. lib. 17. Cap. 25. testatur eucharistiæ reliquias Constantinopoli à pueris è ludo vocatis esse consumptas. Hieronymus attestatur coniuges in nuptijs suis, in suas edes deferri eucharistiam voluisse. Eusebius Eccles. hist. lib. 5. Cap. 24. ex Irenæo commemorat, Romæ fuisse morem, vt ex alijs Ecclesijs aduentantibus Episcopis, pastor Romanus mittere solitus sit eucharistiam, pacis vnitatisq; fidei symbolum. Satyrus Ambrolij frater (vt ipse Ambrosius refert in Oratione habita in funere fratris) agens in naui vel mari, eucharistiam vel collo suspensam circumportauit. Cypriani, Augustini & Caroli magni Francorum regis seculo, data est infantibus eucharistia, & ea de re nostro seculo disputauit doctiss. & nobilissimus vir D. Ioan. à Lasco. Iam etiam sumpta est antiquitus eucharistia ad contestationem innocentiæ & purgationè criminis obiecti. Baptizati sunt præterea mortui antiquitus, & impositā est eis eucharistia in os. Quod tamen abrogatum constat Conc. Carthaginen. 3. canone 6. De viatico alijsq; similibus nihil dicam nunc.
units.tr: As for learned antiquity, as you call it, it does not agree badly with me. For I know that it did in its own times what it could, and thought it was doing so for the preservation of the Church of its time. I know too that that holy antiquity observed many things in the use of the Eucharist and drew many practices into it which are today neither in use nor can we approve, although meanwhile we do not agree badly with it. How the Corinthians celebrated the Supper in apostolic times, no one is unaware. And although Paul rebuked and abrogated that practice, nevertheless that antiquity introduced the custom of agapes in the assemblies, which is not practised today and cannot be approved in every respect and in all things. Tertullian in his book On Monogamy and Cyprian show that little women carried remnants of the Eucharist away in their chests. Hesychius, on Leviticus, records that remnants of the Eucharist were burned by the ancients in the temples. Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, book 17, chapter 25, testifies that remnants of the Eucharist at Constantinople were consumed by boys called in from school. Jerome attests that spouses wished the Eucharist to be brought into their own homes at their weddings. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 24, records from Irenaeus that it was the custom at Rome for the Roman minister to send the Eucharist, a symbol of peace, unity and faith, to bishops arriving from other churches. Satyrus, brother of Ambrose (as Ambrose himself reports in the oration delivered at his brother's funeral), when travelling by ship or at sea, carried the Eucharist about hung round his neck. In the age of Cyprian, Augustine and Charlemagne, king of the Franks, the Eucharist was given to infants, and in our own age the most learned and noble man, Mr John à Lasco, disputed about this matter. Also, the Eucharist was anciently taken as a testimony of innocence and to clear a crime laid against someone. Moreover, the dead were anciently baptized, and the Eucharist was placed in their mouths. Yet it is established that this was abrogated, Council of Carthage 3, canon 6. About viaticum and other similar things I will say nothing now.

units.la: Hæc, inquam, omnia vsurpata sunt à doctā illa & sancta vetustate, vt mirum non sit, si eadem disciplinę Ecclesiasticę immiscuerint eandem eucharistiam. De qua interim in scriptis Apostolicis nullũ habemus disertum & expressum mandatum: sicut & de illis omnibus,quæ apud veteres obseruata audiuimus, nullum Dei mandatum habemus. Vnde non irreligiose illis hodie caremus, licet veteribus fuerint in vsu. Neq; vero idcirco male nobis cum doƈta vetustate conuenit. Quid quod apud eosdem veteres legimus,super poenitentes constitutos Presbyteros iudices (id quod propter Nouatianos circa Cypriani tempora,anno circiter Domini 250. coepisse apparet) ad quorum iudicia & iussum, ad communionem fideles vel accessere, vel suspensi in coetu sacro non communicarunt? Atq; ritum hunc apud plerasq; Ecclesias Christi vsurpatum, magna religione, abrogarunt alij viri sanƈti in Ecclesia,reducentes libertatem veterem,vt quilibet iuxta canonem Apostolicum,suę reliƈtus conscientiæ, ad cœnam accederet, dicente videlicet Apostolo, Probet autem seipsum homo &c. Neq; Episcopi pauci vel obscuri, aut pauce Ecclesiæ hunc ritum sunt sequutæ. Extant huius rei aperta testimonia in Ecclesiastica historia, apud Socratem lib. 5. Cap. 19. & apud Sozomenum lib. 7. Cap. 16. Illa ergo cum ita habeant, eaq; ipsa quæ iam vltimo commemoraui apud doƈtam vetustatē sint vsurpata, nec paucis in locis aut obscuris in Ecclesijs, quę hodie in nostris vsurpatur & nos profitemur, sine causa & in vanum mihi obijcitur doƈta vetustas.
units.tr: All these things, I say, were practised by that learned and holy antiquity, so it is no wonder if it mingled the same Eucharist into church discipline. Meanwhile we have no clear and express command about it in the apostolic writings, just as we have no command of God about all those things which we hear were observed among the ancients. Hence we do not lack them today out of irreligion, although they were in use among the ancients. Nor, for this reason, does learned antiquity agree badly with us. What of the fact that in the same ancient writers we read that elders were appointed as judges over penitents (which seems to have begun because of the Novatians, around the time of Cyprian, about the year of the Lord 250), and that by their judgments and command the faithful either came to communion or, when suspended, did not communicate in the sacred assembly? This custom, practised in many churches of Christ, other holy men in the Church abrogated with great piety, restoring the old liberty, so that each person, according to the apostolic canon, left to his own conscience, might come to the Supper, the Apostle saying, "But let a man examine himself," and so on. Nor did a few obscure bishops or a few small churches follow this rite. Clear testimonies to this exist in ecclesiastical history: in Socrates, book 5, chapter 19, and in Sozomen, book 7, chapter 16. Since these things stand so, and since the very practices I have just mentioned were used by learned antiquity, and not in a few obscure churches, while the practices we use and profess today are the same, learned antiquity is objected to me without cause and in vain.

units.la: Quantum vero attinet ad clariss. virum D.Huldr. Zuinglium B. M.primum harum Ecclesiarum Heluetiearum restauratorem, nihil ille nobis reliquit in hac Ecclesia exercendum,quod non hodie num vsq; in diē fideliter custodiamus. Neq; enim vnquam nouandis permutandisq; aut alternandis rebus in Ecclesia studuimus, scientes quanta inde mala exoriantur in populo, quäta deniq; schismata & offendicula inde exstant,& quantam inde ansà conuiciandi sibi ar ripiant aducrsrij. Nunquā vero Zuinglius disciplinæ Ecclesiastic æ misceri voluit cœnā mysticam. Nunquam voluit cœnam Domini gratulatoriā & lętam redemptionis cōmemoratioamoratione verterent, in triste supplicium peccatorum, eorum inquam, qui peccata agnoscentes, ad Christum festinant, quem credunt tradito corpore & sanguine suo fuso, ipsis peccatorum remissionem impetrauisse, & credentes hoc, inuitare ad hoc conuiuium sacrum & mysticum. Addebat, apertum esse satis, quales ipse Dominus primae suae coenae, quae haud dubie omnium fuerit absolutiss. adhibuerit conuiuas. Neque decere vt nos Dei filio, qui solus corda filiorum hominum perspecta habet, acutiores nobis sumamus oculos, aut nobis-ipsis in coena sumamus iudicium, quod ille nobis neq; praecepto neque exemplo dedit. Attigit huius causae aliquid in amica sua ad Lutherum exegesi, Tomo operum eius 2. Fol. 359. 6.
units.tr: As for the most illustrious man, Mr Huldrych Zwingli, of blessed memory, the first restorer of these Helvetic churches, he left us nothing in this Church to be carried out that we do not faithfully keep to this very day. For we have never striven to innovate, to change or alternate things in the Church, knowing what evils arise from this among the people, what schisms and stumbling-blocks result, and what occasion of reviling the adversaries they seize. Zwingli never wished the mystical supper to be mixed with church discipline. He never wished to turn the Lord's Supper, a joyful and cheerful commemoration of redemption, into a sad punishment of sinners, I mean those who, acknowledging their sins, hasten to Christ, whom they believe to have obtained for them the forgiveness of sins by his body given and blood shed, and who, believing this, are invited to this sacred and mystical feast. He added that it was clear enough what guests the Lord himself admitted to his first supper, which was undoubtedly the most perfect of all. Nor is it fitting for us, who have the Son of God alone, who has the hearts of the sons of men perfectly known, to take sharper eyes than his, or to take judgment upon ourselves at the Supper, which he gave us neither by precept nor by example. He touched on something of this matter in his friendly exposition to Luther, in volume 2 of Luther's works, folio 359, at the sixth point.

units.la: Praeterea disputatum est in urbe Bernensi cum Anabaptista Pistore Meyero, Aprilis 19. anno 1531. viuente adhuc Zuinglio. Cumque vehementer Anabaptistae, vt hodie quoque excommunicationem vrgerent, sine qua nulla posset dici & esse vera Ecclesia, rogaretur a Berchtoldo Hallero, qui primus Euangelium amplis. reipub. Bernens. annunciauit, & quid contentiosissimis & turbulentis. hominibus hac in causa respondere posset, respondit Zuinglius, quod & Berchtold Anabaptistae reddidit, id quod in Actis folio d.2.b.sic refertur, Die Apostel sind vnder der heilichen oberkeit gestin, welche die lasier nit gestrafft, so ein Christ schuldig sol. Da mit nun auch die kirch ein straff der lasteren hette, hat sy die warnung vnd ussschliessen an die hand genommen, dan mit dem Schwert, das inen nit beuolhen, konnend sy nit straffen. Das ist die ursach der bann, by inen gesin. Nachdem aber die Christenlich oberkeit die laster selbs straft, wirt der Bann nit me von nothen sin. Rursus disputatu est cum Anabaptistis Zofinge municipio vel oppido Bernatum in Argonia, mense Iulio, anno 1532. ac inter alia in Actis sol. 68. & 10. haec leguntur: Es mag ein andere straaff vnd züchtigung in der kirchen gottes gebruchet werden. Dan für ein heiden vnd publicanen halten. Denn Christus nicht anders reell, Dan D die lasser gestraafft werdind. Sso ist sie nit vnbillich, so man glich iezt ouch ein andere straaff benampset, also so man es Der o-berkeit befilcht ge.
units.tr: Moreover, a disputation was held in the city of Bern with the Anabaptist Pistor Meyer, on 19 April 1531, while Zwingli was still alive. When the Anabaptists vehemently urged excommunication, as they do today also, saying that without it no church could be called or be true, Berchtold Haller, who first proclaimed the Gospel to the most illustrious commonwealth of Bern, was asked how he could answer these most contentious and turbulent men on this point. Zwingli replied, and Berchtold passed this on to the Anabaptists, as is recorded in the Acts on folio d.2.b, thus: "The apostles were under the holy magistracy, which did not punish the vices a Christian ought to be punished for. So that the Church too might have a punishment for vices, it took up warning and exclusion, for it could not punish with the sword, which was not entrusted to it. That is the reason for the ban among them. But since the Christian magistracy itself punishes vices, the ban will no longer be necessary." Again, a disputation was held with the Anabaptists at Zofingen, a town of Bern in Argovia, in July 1532, and among other things in the Acts, folios 68 and 10, these words are read: "Another penalty and correction may be used in God's church, namely to hold him as a heathen and a publican. For Christ spoke of nothing else than that vices should be punished. So it is not unreasonable, if now also another penalty is named, that this be entrusted to the magistracy."

units.la: Neq; variat ab his tantillum D. Musculus, egregium Christi organum, & celebris Ecclesiæ Dei doctor, Bernensis Ecclesiæ minister & professor Theologus. Quid enim scripserit de Disciplina Ecclesiastica, in locis illis suis communibus, sub Titulo, de Ministris verbi Dei folio 57. nemini est obscurum. Ex his autem omnibus clarèt, me hac in causa nihil sentire, vel à Zuinglio vel ab Ecclesijs vel doctoribus Helueticarum Ecclesiarum, qui nunc viuunt & iam inde vixerunt, in Ecclesiarum gubernatione, ab annis 50. diuersum &c.
units.tr: Nor does the outstanding instrument of Christ and celebrated teacher of the Church of God, Master Musculus, minister of the Bernese Church and professor of theology, differ from these in the slightest. No one can be unaware of what he wrote about church discipline in his Loci communes, under the title "On the ministers of the Word of God," folio 57. From all of this it is clear that in this matter I hold no view different from Zwingli, the churches of Helvetia, and the teachers of the Helvetic churches who now live and have lived since then, in the government of the churches, for some fifty years.

units.la: Quamuis vero incomparabilis vir D. Ioan. Oecolamp. minister Basiliensis Ecclesiæ, in ea Ecclesia excommunicare coeperit magis, quam opus coeptum absoluerit, nunquam tamen alijs per Heluetiam Ecclesijs (licet in publicis Heluetiorum fidelium comitijs frequentibus Aromniæ in Argouia celebratis, attentasset) persuadere potuit, vt excommunicationem ex coena Domini excludentem, recipere vellent. Et quanquam Zuinglius suis rationibus, quibus hodie adhuc vtimur, niteretur, easq; Oecolamp. suo exponeret, ac diceret vereri se ne ædificium hoc Oecolampadij diuturnum & stabile foret &c. deniq; hortaretur illum ne nimis rigide ageret, & mysticam coenam plerisq; redderet ingratam adeoq; difficilem & onerosam &c. nunquam tamen regessit illi ea, quæ nunc impingüntur nobis, nunquam ille dixit Zuinglium impium esse & atheismum fouere, quinimo nihilominus cōcordes inter se vixere, & mutua in pace ædificarunt, sibi à Domino creditas Ecclesias, non discissi inter sese, mutuis sese laceraruunt vulneribus, quo nunc pröh dolor, res inclinatę videntur.
units.tr: Although the incomparable Master Johannes Oecolampadius, minister of the Basel church, began to excommunicate more in that church than he completed the work he had begun, he could never persuade the other churches of Helvetia to accept an excommunication that excludes from the Lord's Supper, though he attempted it at the public and well-attended assembly of the faithful of Helvetia held at Aarau in Aargau. And although Zwingli relied on his own reasons, which we still use today, and set them out to Oecolampadius, saying that he feared this edifice of Oecolampadius would not be lasting and stable, and finally urged him not to act too rigidly and not to make the mystical supper unpleasant, difficult and burdensome to most people, he never returned to him the charges that are now hurled at us. He never said that Zwingli was impious and fostered atheism. On the contrary, they nevertheless lived in harmony with one another and built up in mutual peace the churches entrusted to them by the Lord. They were not divided from each other, nor did they tear each other with mutual wounds, as things now, alas, seem to be tending.

units.la: Accedit hisillud quoq; quod Basileæ anno 1536. mense Februario, in Comitia publica vocati, coiere præcipui omnes Helueticarum Ecclesiarum ministri, qui cum præsentibus bus etiam beatę memoriæ D. Capitone & Bucero Argentoratensis Ecclesiæ ministris, & Legatis Neocomensis Ecclesiæ &c. inter se diu & multum, & diligenter de omnibus Christianæ fidei dogmatibus,etiam de excommunicatione contulissent, in hanc tandem sententiam conspirauerte omnes, quæ & nostra Confess. vltima, cuius & antea meminimus, est exposita.
units.tr: To this may be added the following. At Basel in February 1536, the leading ministers of all the Helvetic churches were called to a public assembly and came together. Along with those present, the late Master Capito and Bucer, ministers of the Strasbourg church, and envoys of the Neuchâtel church, they conferred at length and carefully with one another on all the doctrines of the Christian faith, including excommunication. At last they all agreed on the opinion that was set out in our Confession, the last one, which we have also mentioned before.

units.la: Quid quod nulla vnquam fuit concertatio de excommunicatione inter nostram Tigurinam & Geneuensem Ecclesiam nobis prædilectam. De qua mirorte scripsisse. Neq; putes nos ita esse dementes vt hic omnia ad rigorem illum Geneuensis Ecclesiæ exigere & reuocare velimus &c. Etenim cum ante annos aliquot turbæ essent in illa exortæ Ecclesia graues: & nos ea de re requisiti, occasionem habuissemus nostra obtrudendi aut commendandi saltem, attamen sequuti sumus, vt par erat,pacis consilia. Itaq; neq; illorum inchoatam disciplinam voluimus impedire, rigidam aut lentam nuncupare, neq; occasionem aduersarijs offerre sæuius tumultuandi. Nam vt in alienas Ecclesias nullum nobis sumimus imperium, ita sanè si qui in suis Ecclesijs, quorum ratio illis rectius quàm nobis perspecta est, aliquos citra turbam & querelas, à coena, per disciplinam suam, splendido cum fructu,excludunt,id iudicio Ecclesiæ ipsorumq; fidei permittimus. Interim vero nos, plurimas ob causas,neq; coenam Domini gratulatoriam, disciplinę Ecclesiasticæ immiscemus, neq; dissimulamus rogati palàm profiteri (si modo nullum præsens periculum iam aliquos exerceat) melius videri nobis, talem exclusionem omittere, quam exercere, si videlicet periculū sit conturbationis schismatisq;, atq; adeo eam plus Ecclesiæ obfuturam quam profuturam.
units.tr: Moreover, there has never been any dispute about excommunication between our Zurich church and the Geneva church, which is very dear to us. I am amazed that someone has written about this matter. Do not think that we are so mad as to wish to force and recall everything here to the strictness of that Geneva church. For when some years ago serious disturbances arose in that church, and we were asked about the matter and had the opportunity to press or at least recommend our own view, we nevertheless followed, as was fitting, the counsels of peace. Thus we neither wished to hinder their discipline, which had been begun, nor to call it harsh or lax, nor to offer our opponents an occasion for more violent uproar. For just as we claim no authority over other churches, so, if some in their own churches, whose reasons are better known to them than to us, exclude certain people from the Lord's Supper through their discipline, without disturbance or complaint, with splendid fruit, we leave that to the judgement of their church and of their faith. Meanwhile, for many reasons, we do not mix the Lord's Supper, which is a thanksgiving, with church discipline. And when asked, we do not hide our view, which we openly profess: if there is no present danger already troubling anyone, it seems better to us to omit such an exclusion than to practise it, if there is clearly a risk of confusion and schism, and so such exclusion would do more harm to the Church than good.

units.la: Hæc vsque huc exposui tibi,Petre frater, copiosius quam ab initio me facturum putaueram, vt intelligeres me non ob paucas nec iniustas ob causas,nolle in arenam descendere cum D. Erasto, quem præterea noui iam ab annis aliquot,fideliter & permultum laborasse in propagando Euangelio, præsertim apud vos in Palatinatu, adeo vt si fideles eius labores non præcessissent, tibi alijsq; exulibus vix tale patuisset hospitium, quali nunc frueris, vnà cum alijs multis. Beneficia eius tum in peregrinos, tum domesticos collocata, eruditio item eius eximia & singularis, deniq; vera eius & syncera pietas, ob quæ à bonis laudatur omnib°, aliud sanè ei destinarat premium, quam nunc ipsi repêditur à nonnullis. Aut si in hoc negotio videbatur errare tam turpiter, quare non protinus ab initio collatum est amicè cum ipso? Quin audio hoc ipsum multoties ab ipso frustra esse postulatum.
units.tr: I have set this out to you so far, brother Peter, more fully than I had thought I would at the start, so that you may understand that I am unwilling to enter the arena against Master Erastus, not for a few or unjust reasons. Moreover, I have known for some years that he has laboured faithfully and very much in spreading the Gospel, especially among you in the Palatinate, so that if his faithful labours had not gone before, such a hospitality as you now enjoy, together with many others, would hardly have been open to you and other exiles. His benefits, bestowed both on strangers and on his own people, his outstanding and singular learning, and finally his true and sincere piety, for which he is praised by all good men, had surely prepared for him a different reward from the one that some now repay him with. Or if he seemed to err so shamefully in this business, why was it not discussed with him in a friendly way from the beginning? Indeed, I hear that he himself has often asked this in vain.

units.la: Aperta est autem area sponte, homini peregrino, cui ne cum suis quidem bene convenire potuit, vt is intempestiua sua de excommunicatione disputatione, Eridis pomum vobis relinqueret. Aut cur maluerunt nonnulli apud vos, aliena etiam auxilia ex alijs petere Ecclesijs, quam sine alieno auxilio, vt concordes vtrinq; manerent Ecclesiæ, cum ipsomet conferre Erafto, qui ad omnia æqua, vt audio, recipienda, se semper obtulit? Videte ne vestra illa imprudentia aperueritis fores nunquam terminandis litibus, ac inter se commiseritis viros in Ecclesia opt. doctiss. atq; præstantiss., quos magis oportuerat, si qua visa oboriri nubecula dissensionis, dispellere & in concordiam redigere, quam ad arma & prælia concitare. Beati pacifici, inquit Dominus, quoniam filij Dei nuncupabuntur. Non tantum, mihi crede, vtilitatis vestra illa exclusione conferetis Christi Ecclesiæ, quantum mali dedistis, si noua & acerba inter doctos & pios viros, ob hanc causam exoriantur certamina. Ita sanè luctus grauis pios & pacificos in Ecclesia viros torquebit, & tripudiandi insultandiq; nobis dabitur communibus aduersarijs occasio. Apostolus semper & in omnibus, ea quæ ad ædificationem & pacem faciunt, sectari vult ab omnibus, qui etiam palam fatetur, potestatem sibi datam esse ad ædificandum, non destruendum. Dominum Deum nostrum pacis & concordiæ amatorem, ex animo oro, vt omnibus sopitis dissensionibus, in vnitate sancta & charitate ritatem fyncera nos coniungat, & in pace conseruet. Vale Tiguri 1. Iunij. Anno 1570.
units.tr: But the field has been opened of its own accord, by a foreigner who could not even get along well with his own people, so that by his untimely dispute about excommunication he left you the apple of discord. Or why did some among you prefer to seek foreign help from other churches, rather than, without foreign help, remaining at peace on both sides, by conferring with Erastus himself, who, as I hear, has always offered himself to accept everything that is fair? Take care that by your imprudence you have not opened a door through which quarrels will never be settled, and that you have not set against one another men in the Church who are most excellent, most learned and most eminent, men whom it would have been better, if some small cloud of dissension had appeared, to disperse and bring back to harmony, rather than to stir up to arms and battle. "Blessed are the peacemakers," says the Lord, "for they shall be called the sons of God." Believe me, by that exclusion you will bring no more benefit to the Church of Christ than the harm you have done, if new and bitter contests arise between learned and pious men for this cause. Thus a grievous mourning will surely torment the pious and peaceable men of the Church, and our common adversaries will be given an occasion to exult and mock. The Apostle always and in all things wishes that those things which build up and make for peace be pursued by all, and he openly confesses that the power given to him is for building up, not for destroying. I earnestly pray to the Lord our God, the lover of peace and concord, that, with all dissensions quieted, he may join us in holy unity and sincere charity, and keep us in peace. Farewell. Zurich, 1 June, in the year 1570.

units.la: Bullingerus tuus.
units.tr: Your Bullinger.

units.la: Clariss. viro D. Thomæ Erafto Doctori Medico, Domino meo honorando, & fratri charissimo Hei- delberg. S. D.
units.tr: To the distinguished man, Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, my honoured lord and most dear brother, Heidelberg. Greetings.

units.la: LEpusculus noster omnia tua mihi, Domine colende, & frater charissime, tradidit. Pro quibus omnibus maximas ago gratias. Legimus responsionem tuam posteriorem, neque displicuit cuiquam nostrum. Omnes probarunt. Et ego libentius eam legi, quàm priorem, id est, proximè Thesibus adiunctam. Non quòd aliquid in ipsa displiceret: sed quòd videatur implexior, & difficilis intellectu. Id quod aduersariorum tribuo confusaneis argumentis. Postremo hæc expeditior, & facilior esse videtur. Existorum scriptis vix me expedio. Displicet autem omnibus, & dolet vehementissime; quòd isti hanc moventtragœdiam, & ad arma, præter omnem necessitatem conclamant. Scripsimus Principi literas, & quidem soli. Quòd si ipse eis illas communicat, vt eos nobiscum committat, dolet nobis eò recidisse res. Non libenter cum vllis, nedum cum Symmystis, committimur, & concertationum pertæsi, non libenter pugnamus. Ego imprimis, qui iam senex, & propè valetudinarius; certaminibus minus sum idoneus. Continuis propè calculi doloribus distringor, ac puto me hoc anno excreuisse supra ducentos. Existimo me per annos ministerij mei quadraginta septem propè militasse abundè. Dominum itaque oro, vt pacem mihi concedat, aut si omnino in pugnam me extrudere statuit, ampliores concedat vires, quàm nunc me habere experiar. Vigor enim animi, & vis memoriæ plurimùm me destituunt quotidie. Quia tamen hæc res
units.tr: Our little pamphlet has delivered to me all your writings, honoured lord and most dear brother, and for all of them I give the greatest thanks. We have read your second reply, and it has displeased none of us; all of us approve it. I read it more willingly than the earlier one, that is, the one recently attached to the Theses. Not that anything in it displeased me, but it seems more involved and harder to follow. I put this down to the confused arguments of your opponents. In the end this one seems more straightforward and easier. I can hardly extricate myself from their writings. Everyone is displeased and most deeply grieved that these men are stirring up this tragedy and crying out to arms beyond all necessity. We have written to the Prince, and to him alone. If he himself passes the letters on to them, so that he may set them against us, we regret that things have come to this. We are not willing to contend with anyone, much less with the fellow-initiates, and, weary of disputes, we do not fight gladly. I especially, who am now old and nearly an invalid, am less fit for battles. I am almost continually beset by pains of the stone, and I think I have passed more than two hundred stones this year. I reckon that in the forty-seven years of my ministry I have served enough. I therefore pray the Lord to grant me peace, or, if he has decided to thrust me altogether into the fight, to grant me greater strength than I find I have now. For vigour of mind and power of memory desert me more every day. Since, however, this matter

units.la: videtur spectare ad conturbationem Ecclesiarum permitiosissimam, scribimus iam iterum Principi illustrissimo, & aliquanto copiosius, exponentes illi pericula varia,& grauissima : quæ oritura timemus ex hac excommunicationis institutione. Hortamur item, quàm possumus grauissimè (tres Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ pastores, Gualterius, Vuolphius, & ego)ne quid temere nouent, & ministros inter se committant &c. Non possum singula commemorare. Quæ scribimus, neque exemplum nostræ Epistolæ tibi mittere, ne forte Princeps indignè ferret alijs quoque esse communi- cata, quæ nos-ipsi soli nostro sigillo obsignata mittimus, si quando intelligeret, nos eius exemplum ad te quoq; misisse. Preterea vix ipsum exemplum Principi destinatum potui commodè describere. Ergo cum vnum modo superesset exemplum, quod ipse quoque scripsi,non potuimus illud amandare, & ipso carere. Necdum planè conualui ex morbo, qui mę diu, & multum, grauissimeq; exercuit. Proinde boni consule, quod exemplum, vel copiam, quam vocant, ad te non mitto. Hoc autem crede, summam fidem, & diligentiam esse adhibitam pro nostris viribus, ne quid omitteretur, quod ad hanc causam maximè pertinere videtur. Quod reliquum est,oremus Dominum,vt apud Principem illustriss. efficiat, quod Ecclesiæ Dei sit salutare. Ad quod vnicè respeximus. Id tamen significandum tibi putauimus, initium nos fecisse à gratulatione. Gratulamur enim Principi de noua nupta, & optamus, vt illa exprimat moribus Hefteram &c,si forte Epistola nostra in manus veniat Principissę, inueniat, quod moueat,& iuuet. Sed & vnicè in hoc intendimus vt ipse constituat disciplinam legitimam, quę melius possit constitui, si coena non misceatur, sed libera permittatur, vt sit communio,coniunctio, & læta gratulatio, consolatioue hominum fidelium peccatorum, non autem excommunio, non separatio, & tristis querela; denique dirum supplicium, & poena &c. Dabit fortassis Dominus aliàs,vt commodè tibi mittamus exemplum.Aut habes, haud dubiè in aula, inter Principis optimos,& intimos,qui tibi nostram possint cõmonstrare Epistolā. Hæc dum scribo,en adferuntur literæ à fratre nostro Beza, qui sub finem Epistolæ addit:Respondi Thesibus Erafti,& misi Heidelbergam:mittam etiam exemplum ad vos, ac spero,id neq; tibi neq; fratribus di'spliciturum.Illico ergo rescripsi, id est, hodie prima Augusti,& significo illi, nos expectare, & libenter lećturos,quæ miserit. Interim quomodo affećti simus erga hanc causam, non dissimulamus: hortantes illum,ne oleum addat camino.Eos qui ipsum instigent subinde ad pugnam, non tales esse,quales ipse existimat.Nec dissimulamus,nos scripsisse Principi,eumq; adhortatum,vt diligenter, & prudenter,quid hic inceptet,& quo hæc res tandē recidere possit,secũ expendat.&c. Et multa huius generis alia illi exposui.Quę fortassis illi non probabuntur per omnia.Nos pacē Ecclesiarum, & iustũ earum incrementum quærimus, & optamus,illúmq; ad studium tale adhortamur, ne, & multos offendat,& nos-met-ipsos risui exponamus omnibus nostris aduersarijs &c.Habebis ergo,Erafte frater,quod agas.Hortor autē te,mi Domine,& frater,vt & synceræ veritatis rationem habeas, & sanćtissimæ pacis, coherceásq; affećtus,si quos ille tibi mouit,& si respondere volueris,respõdeas perspicuè,breuiter,& dispositione illustri ad rē,præterita persona aduersariorum omniū, quantum quidē hoc fieri poterit. Modestia seper,& ab omnib⁹ probata est,& probatur adhuc. Dominus suam gratiã tibi,& nobis omnibus concedat.Scis alioqui Bezã esse fratrem nostrum,& virum eruditissimum, & de Ecclesia Dei bene meritũ. Ergo sicubi videatur vehementior,amore potius,& cõmoda,claráq; necnon cuidenti responsione lucrandus,quàm odio & conuiciis persequendus,sæuiúsq; excipiendus erit,omniáq; huc collimanda,vt si fieri potest,in pace, sicuti Dei filios decet, coalescamus,& non sinamus semina discordiæ,& inuidiæ in corda nostra spargere Sathanã. Verum sat scio, hæc te aliàs sedulò faćturum,pro tua pietate insigni.Certè me hæc causa ita torquet, & vrit,vt nunquam desinam patrem orare cœlestē, vt nostri misertus, affećtus coherceat, certaminą; sedet, pacemque concedens › concedes, nos in sancta concordia vniat, atq; conseruet. Nunc vale, Domine honorande, amice integerrime, & frater in Domino charissime. Dominus benedicat tibi. Plura scripsi, quam fere vires admiserint, & ego me ab initio scripturum putauerim. Tuas expecto ad nundinas. Si vixero, rursus ad te scribam, volente Domino. Tiguri 1. Augusti 1569.
units.tr: seems to threaten the most destructive disturbance of the Churches, we are writing again, and at greater length, to the most illustrious Prince, setting out for him the various and very grave dangers that we fear will arise from this institution of excommunication. We also urge, as earnestly as we can (the three ministers of the Zurich Church, Gualter, Wolf, and I), that they do not rashly introduce anything new, and do not set ministers against one another, and so on. I cannot recount each point. We are not sending you a copy of our letter, lest perhaps the Prince took it ill that what we sent to him alone, sealed with our own seal, had been communicated to others, should he ever learn that we had also sent a copy to you. Moreover, I could scarcely make a convenient copy of the version intended for the Prince. Therefore, since only one copy was left, which I myself wrote, we could not send it away and be without it. Nor have I yet fully recovered from the illness that has long and sorely plagued me. Accordingly, please take it in good part that I am not sending you the copy, or the transcript, as they call it. But believe this: the greatest faithfulness and diligence have been applied, as far as our powers allow, so that nothing that seems most pertinent to this cause has been left out. As for the rest, let us pray the Lord that he may bring about, with the most illustrious Prince, what is salutary for the Church of God, to which alone we have looked. Yet we thought it should be made known to you that we began with congratulation. For we congratulate the Prince on his new bride, and we hope that she will take on the manners of Esther, and so on, if perhaps our letter comes into the hands of the Princess and finds something that moves and helps her. But we aim solely at this: that he himself should establish a lawful discipline, which could be better established if the Supper is not mixed up with it, but is freely permitted, so that there may be communion, fellowship and joyful thanksgiving, and the consolation of faithful sinners, and not excommunication, not separation and sorrowful complaint, in short a dreadful punishment and penalty, and so on. Perhaps the Lord will grant at another time that we may conveniently send you a copy. Or you surely have, at court, among the Prince's best and most intimate, someone who can show you our letter. As I write this, see, letters arrive from our brother Beza, who adds at the end of his letter: "I have replied to the Theses of Erastus and sent them to Heidelberg. I will also send a copy to you, and I hope this will displease neither you nor the brethren." I therefore wrote back at once, that is, today, the first of August, and told him that we are waiting for, and will gladly read, what he has sent. Meanwhile we do not conceal how we are affected toward this cause, urging him not to add oil to the fire, and saying that those who keep urging him to fight are not such as he supposes. Nor do we conceal that we have written to the Prince and urged him to weigh carefully and prudently what is being undertaken here, and where this matter may finally lead, and so on. I have set out many other things of this kind for him, which perhaps will not be approved by him in every respect. We seek and wish for the peace of the Churches and their just growth, and we urge him to such zeal, lest he both offend many and expose ourselves to ridicule before all our adversaries, and so on. You will have, therefore, brother Erastus, something to act upon. I urge you, my lord and brother, to keep both sincere truth and most holy peace in view, and to restrain whatever feelings he has stirred in you. If you wish to reply, reply clearly and briefly, with a clear arrangement fitted to the matter, leaving aside the persons of all the adversaries, as far as this can be done. Modesty has always been approved by all, and is approved still. May the Lord grant his grace to you and to us all. You know, besides, that Beza is our brother and a most learned man, who has deserved well of the Church of God. Therefore, wherever he seems more vehement, he is to be won over by love, by courtesy and by a clear and plain reply, rather than pursued with hatred and reproaches and met more fiercely; and everything must be aimed at this, that, if it can be done, we may be united in peace, as befits the sons of God, and not allow Satan to sow seeds of discord and envy in our hearts. Truly I know well that you will often do these things on other occasions, given your remarkable piety. Certainly this cause so torments and burns me that I shall never cease to pray the heavenly Father that, taking pity on us, he may restrain feelings and quarrels, and, granting peace, may unite and preserve us in holy concord. Now farewell, honoured lord, most upright friend, and brother most dear in the Lord. May the Lord bless you. I have written more than my strength nearly allowed, and I had thought at the start that I would write less. I await yours at the fair. If I live, I will write to you again, the Lord willing. Zurich, 1 August 1569.

units.la: Tuus Bullingerus.
units.tr: Yours, Bullinger.

units.la: Exemplum Epistolae Bullingeri ad Bezam, ab eo- dem Bullingero missum ad Erastum.
units.tr: Copy of a Letter from Bullinger to Beza, Sent by the Same Bullinger to Erastus

units.la: D. Theod. Bezae, Henricus Bullingerus. S. D.
units.tr: To Dr. Theodore Beza, Henry Bullinger. Greetings.

units.la: LEgam libenter, quae respondisti ad Theses Erasti nostri. Nollem ego illa publicari. Spero te priuato scripto ista agere. Nam vehementer doleo, vt, quod ex animo sentio, dicam liberè, & te non celem, Coenam Domini, quae alioqui plus nimium diutinis disputationibus est conquassata, & populo parum grata facta, in nouam rursus rapi controuersiam: & quae instituta est à Domino ad congregandam Ecclesiam, ad communionem, societatemq;, & consolationem, deniq; ad gratulationem, & gratiarum actionem fidelium, nunc propter disciplinam fundandā trahi ad dispergendam Ecclesiā, excommunione, vt sic dicam, ad separatione, inquam, & tristeq; supplicii, deniq; ad querelas, & contentionem fidelium.
units.tr: I would gladly read the reply you have made to the Theses of our Erastus, though I would rather it were not published. I hope you are handling these matters in a private writing. For I am greatly distressed, and I will speak freely and not conceal from you what I truly feel: the Lord's Supper, which has already been shaken by overlong disputations and made rather unwelcome to the people, is being dragged back into a new controversy. It was instituted by the Lord to gather the Church, for communion, fellowship and consolation, and finally for the joy and thanksgiving of the faithful. Now, for the sake of founding church discipline, it is being turned to scattering the Church, to excommunication (so to speak), that is, to separation, and to the sad punishment of sinners, and finally to complaints and strife among the faithful.

units.la: Mea quidem sententia, potest in Ecclesia iusta constitui disciplina, vt interim Coena Domini libera maneat omnibus illis, qui se iuxta Pauli doctrinam probarunt, neq; conuertatur in poenam &c. Et quidem magna cum solicitudine audimus quosdam Heidelbergae, quos tu forte meliores, & prudentiores esse putas, quam sint, importunissimè excommunicationem illam suam disciplinarem vrgere, ac Principem optimum impellere, vt eam inuitis omnibus obtrudat. Rursus nobiles, ignobiles, & plebeios hoc indignissimè ferre, vt periculum sit, ne ea res in tumultū aliquem, cum aliisquì omnia sint exulceratissima, desinat. Atq; vtinam falsò hec hæc metuam. Non sine causa murmurant, quod omnia fere administret Princeps per Niderlanderos, siue Belgas, homines peregrinos, suis illis penitus præteritis.
units.tr: In my own judgement, a sound discipline can be established in the Church while the Lord's Supper remains free for all those who have proved themselves according to the teaching of Paul, and is not turned into a punishment, and so on. Indeed, we hear with great anxiety that certain people at Heidelberg, whom you perhaps think better and wiser than they are, are most importunately pressing that disciplinary excommunication of theirs and urging the excellent Prince to force it upon everyone against their will. Meanwhile the nobles, the commoners and the common people take this very badly, so that there is a danger that the matter will end in some tumult, since all things are already most sore. And would that I were wrong to fear this! Not without cause they murmur that the Prince administers almost everything through the Netherlanders, or Belgians, foreigners, with his own people entirely passed over.

units.la: Proinde te oro, atq; obsecro, vt prudenter in hac causa omnia expendas,& agas,neq; oleum camino addas,ne dum isti, qui subinde te instigant,& purgatissimam Ecclesiam(ne quid hic aliud suspicer) volunt instituere, breui nullam habeant, doleantq; se imprudenter egisse,in periculum nihilominus adductis bonis omnibus, vnà cum optimo Principe, maximo item cum infirmorum scandalo, & hostium nostrorum tripudio insolentissimo.
units.tr: Therefore I beg and entreat you to weigh and handle everything prudently in this affair, and not to add oil to the fire. Otherwise those who keep urging you on, and wish to set up a most pure Church (I will not suspect anything else here), will soon have no Church at all, and will regret having acted unwisely, since all good people will nevertheless be brought into danger along with the excellent Prince, and also to the great scandal of the weak and to the most insolent triumph of our enemies.

units.la: Præterito itaq; mense scripsimus ad illustriss. Principem, hortantes ipsum, vt res suas hac in causa piè, prudenterq; instituat,neue in Ecclesia disisidijs, contentionibusq; nouis,& perniciosissimis occasionem vllam præbeat,quin potius iusta instituta disciplina, & Cœna Domini in libero, & gratulatorio vsu relicta, pacem Ecclesiarum,Ministrorumq; promoueat, atq; conseruet. Video enim nunc maximè, si vnquam aliàs, nobis opus esse moderatione sancta, & concordia firma, præcisis omnibus disisidiorum,& contentionum occasionibus. Dominus Iesus dirigat nos spiritu suo sancto. Vale Tiguri, 1. Augusti, Anno nostræ salutis 1569.
units.tr: Last month, therefore, we wrote to the most illustrious Prince, urging him to conduct his affairs in this matter piously and prudently, and not to give any occasion for new and most pernicious divisions and disputes in the Church. Rather, let him, with proper discipline established and the Lord's Supper left in free and joyful use, promote and preserve the peace of the Churches and of the ministers. For I see now most of all, if ever before, that we need holy moderation and firm concord, with every occasion of division and contention cut off. May the Lord Jesus guide us by his Holy Spirit. Farewell. Zurich, 1 August, in the year of our salvation 1569.

units.la: Clariss. viro D. Thomæ Erasto Doctori Medico peritiss. Heidelbergæ agenti, Domino meo colendo, & fratri charissimo
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Dr. Thomas Erastus, a most skilled doctor of medicine practising at Heidelberg, my honoured lord and most dear brother

units.la: S. D.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: Spero vltimas meas esse redditas tibi, missas per Iacobum Lepusculum. Oro autem mihi digneris significare, quid factum sit cum literis nostris ad Principem Illustriss. scriptis, & quomodo res Ecclesiasticæ habeant apud vos. Concepi mœrorem maximum ex disisidio illo infelici vestro, ac peiora subinde metuo. Dominum autem oro, vt omnibus pacatis, sanctam in Ecclesia pacem conseruet. Sunt & alia plurima, quæ me contristant vehementer. Quibus accedit corporis etiam afflicta valetudo. Subinde enim alijs, atque alijs fatigor. Nunc capitis, & dentium dolor me affligit, sed & calculus vrit, & curæ me conficiunt, vt iam non commemorem reliquias morbi, quo hac æstate graviter laboraui, me sentire adhuc. Interim agnosco, Domino ita placere, & ipsum me hoc modo exercere, qui electis suis omnia in bonum conuertit. Hunc ora pro me Dominum. Beza nondum misit, quam promisit responsionem ad Theses tuas. Expectamus tamen eas. Respondit autem ad meam adhortationem, qua cohortatus sum ad pacis studium, & ne oleum camino addat, neue illos audiat, qui ipsum ad pugnam incitant, quos vereor, non tam bonos esse, quàm ipse fortassis arbitratur. Amicissimè mihi respondit, & interalia: Noli dubitare, inquit, de meo animo pacis cupido &c. Dominum ego ex animo oro, vt vtrumq; in vera charitate, & pace coniungat, coniunctosq; in vnitate conseruet. Non puto me scripturum per Froschouerum nostrum, discedentem Francofordiam. Vix has scribo. Oro ergo, vt boni consulas hæc. Nam ineptum rebus me fieri indies magis magisq; sentio. Sed anni ætatis meæ & corpus exhaustum hæc adferunt, & forte adferent magis impedita. Dominus faciat mecum, quod bonū est in oculis suis. Cuius bonæ voluntati me prorsus subijcio, cupiens, si velit, dissolui, & esse cū Christo. Benè vale, Domin° benedicat tibi, & seruet te. Tiguri. 23. Augusti 1569. Saluta fratres, & amicos nostros. Omnes nostri te quoq; saluere iubet in Domino.
units.tr: I hope my last letters have been delivered to you, sent through James Lepusculus. I beg you to let me know what has happened to our letter written to the most illustrious Prince, and how ecclesiastical affairs stand among you. I have conceived the greatest sorrow over that unhappy dispute of yours, and from time to time I fear worse. I pray the Lord that, with everything calmed, he may preserve holy peace in the Church. There are also many other things that trouble me greatly, and to these is added the affliction of my bodily health. For I am worn out now by one ailment and then another. Now the pain of my head and teeth afflicts me, and the stone burns me, and cares wear me down, not to mention the remnants of the illness with which I laboured severely this summer, which I still feel. Meanwhile I acknowledge that this pleases the Lord, and that he exercises me in this way, he who turns all things to good for his elect. Pray the Lord for me in this. Beza has not yet sent the reply he promised to your Theses. Still we await it. He did, however, reply to my exhortation, in which I urged him to pursue peace, and not to add oil to the fire, nor to listen to those who incite him to battle, whom I fear are not as good as he perhaps supposes. He answered me most friendly, and among other things said: "Do not doubt," he writes, "my desire for peace," and so on. I pray from my heart that the Lord may join both of you in true charity and peace, and preserve those joined in unity. I do not think I shall write again through our Froschauer, who is leaving for Frankfurt. I am scarcely writing these lines. So I beg you to take these things in good part. For I feel more and more each day that I am becoming unfit for affairs. But the years of my life and my worn-out body bring this, and perhaps will bring it more seriously. May the Lord do with me what is good in his eyes. I submit wholly to his good will, desiring, if he wishes, to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Farewell well; may the Lord bless you and keep you. Zurich, 23 August 1569. Greet our brothers and friends. All of ours bid you also greet in the Lord.

units.la: Tuus Bullingerus.
units.tr: Yours, Bullinger.

units.la: Clariss. viro D. Thomæ Erasto Doctori Medico, Heidelbergæ agenti, Domino meo honoran- do & fratri charissimo S. D.
units.tr: To the distinguished man, Dr. Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, practising at Heidelberg, my honoured lord and dearest brother: greetings.

units.la: BInas à tua humanitate literas accepi. Priores quidem datas in Roetelen 19. Septembris. Posteriores autem Heidelbergæ 10. Octobris. Ac initio Dominum oro, vt ipse nuptijs illis Sororis vxoris tuæ benedicat, tibiq; & tuis fœlices, & faustas esse velit. Vtinam verò placuisset tibi, quando Basileam vsq; venisti, ad nos vsq; penetrare. Sed id propter negotia tua tibi fuisset forte incommodum. Proinde gratias Deo ago, quod saltem per literas possumus colloqui coram, si hic non datur.
units.tr: I have received your letters, kindly sent. The earlier one was dated at Rötteln on 19 September, and the later one at Heidelberg on 10 October. At the outset I pray the Lord to bless those marriage rites of your wife's sister, and to grant that they be happy and fortunate for you and yours. I wish indeed that it had pleased you, when you came as far as Basel, to make your way on to us. But perhaps that would have been inconvenient for you because of your business. So I thank God that we can at least speak with each other by letter, since we cannot do so face to face.

units.la: In prioribus illis tuis promittis te formulam iuramenti Ministris Ecclesiarum nuper à Principe Illustrissimo præscriptam, elegantem, & bonam missurum. Sed per obliuionem forte factum est, dum posteriores literas submitteres, illam non adiecceris. Nisi ergo tibi graue sit, oro vt posthac mittas. Cupio enim videre.
units.tr: In your earlier letters you promised to send me the form of oath that the most illustrious Prince recently prescribed for the ministers of the Churches, a fine and good one. But perhaps through forgetfulness, when you sent the later letter, you did not add it. So, unless it is a trouble to you, I beg you to send it hereafter. For I wish to see it.

units.la: Posterioribus, vt & prioribus, multa commemoras de infelici certamine excommunicatorio. Id quod me mirum in modum affligit. Metuo enim certamen hoc non tam Principi illustriss. quàm omnibus aliis Ecclesijs maximum daturum malum. Vnde cum nihil aliud possim, Dominum oro, vt ipse odiosas has altercationes, benignè componat, ne incendium hoc latius serpens pacificas Ecclesias quoq; inflammet atq; consumat.
units.tr: In your later letters, as in the earlier ones, you tell me much about the unhappy controversy over excommunication. This greatly distresses me. For I fear that this dispute will do the greatest harm not only to the most illustrious Prince but also to all the other Churches. Since I can do nothing else, I pray the Lord that he himself will kindly settle these hateful quarrels, lest this fire, spreading more widely, also inflame and consume the peaceful Churches.

units.la: Petis hac in re à me duo: principio, vt tibi descriptam epistolam, quam vltimo ad illustriss. Principem hac de causa misimus, submittam. Ego verò, qui in omnibus, hac etiam in re, si fieri posset, tibi inseruire sum paratisimus, hoc tamen, quod petis facere non possum. Etenim scis Principem Illustriss. nos ab initio primæ Epistolæ attestatos sanctè, insciis partibus vtrisq; hæc scribere, & quidem soli. Postea tamen submisimus exemplum eius Epistolæ descriptum tibi. Quod multis vicibus descriptum, & ad varia loca transmissum intelligimus. Vnde fides, & authoritas nostra merito apud Principem laborat. Id quod merito nobis dolet. Ac sententius Principis Illustriss. animum à nobis ab eo tempore alienatum. Non enim ad priores respondit, sed & ad posteriores vltimò missas nihil rescripsit, ac ne quidem nunciauit. Condonabis ergo nobis si aliquandiu adhuc, feruente contentione mittere illas ad te diftulerimus. At hoc tibi persuasum habebis nihil aliud nos illi scripsisse, quàm quod breui summa literis ad Francofordienses nundinas missis ad te, exposuimus.
units.tr: In this matter you ask two things of me. First, that I send you a copy of the letter which we last sent to the most illustrious Prince on this business. I would gladly serve you in all things, this included, if it were possible; but what you ask I cannot do. For you know that from the beginning of the first letter we solemnly declared, in both parties' ignorance, that we wrote these things alone and to him alone. Afterwards, however, we did send you a copy of that letter. We learn that it has been copied many times and sent to various places. Hence our faith and authority, rightly so, are under strain with the Prince, which truly grieves us. And since that time the Prince's mind has been estranged from us. For he has not answered our earlier letters, and he has not even replied to our latest one, nor has he given any notice of receiving it. So you will forgive us if, while the controversy is burning so fiercely, we have put off sending those letters to you for some time. But you may be assured that we wrote to him nothing other than what we set out, in brief summary, in the letter sent to you for the Frankfurt fair.

units.la: Deinde petiuisti tibi quoque transmitti exemplum refponsionis Bezanæ, transcriptum. Cæterùm in veritate tibi affirmo, huius ne tantum vidisse. Promisit quidem ab initio transmissurum ad nos exemplum. Eius autem rei, cùm inde ab eo quinas, vt minimum dixerim, literas acceperim, ne verbo quidem meminerit. Neque nos illum promissionis vel admonuimus, vel admodum vrsimus. Proinde nihil mittere possumus. Nam, nobis crede, nihil ab illo hactenus accepimus. Improbatur autem nobis vehementer, quod scriptum ad te missum, tibi non redditur. Cuius culpam sustinent maiorem, qui tibi non reddunt. Qui verò illi sint, nescimus. Totam enim causam hanc ignoramus. Nunc verò scripsi ego veteri meo amico, & fratri D. Zanchio Vrsino, quem semper expertus sum hominem esse mafuetum, & modestum. Adhortatus sum, vt amicè hac de re tecum conferat. Nec dissimulaui, quæ hic mea sit sententia. Dominum oro, vt infœlix hoc certamen, ipse sua gratia dirimat, atque componat. Video enim hoc Ecclesiæ noxium valde futurum. Vnde te adhortor, & oro, vt hic te, quantum salua veritate fieri potest, amica collatione cum Vrsino nostro committi suas. Dominus det suam gratiam &c. Optimè vale, frater, & Domine honorande, & dilecte, & rescribe per primum quemque tabellionem. Tuas enim desidero. Saluta fratres omnes. Tiguri 5. Nouembris 1569. Nostri legati à Comitijs Badensibus nondum rediere. Salutant te fratres omnes.
units.tr: Next, you asked that a copy of Beza's reply also be sent to you. But in truth I assure you that I have not even seen it. He did promise at the beginning to send us a copy. Yet, although I have received, to put it mildly, five letters from him since then, he has not so much as mentioned the matter. Nor have we reminded him of the promise, or pressed him very hard. Therefore we cannot send anything. For, believe us, we have so far received nothing from him. We strongly disapprove, however, that a writing sent to you is not returned to us. Those who do not return it bear the greater blame for this. Who they are we do not know, for we are ignorant of the whole affair. But I have now written to my old friend and brother, Dr. Zanchius Ursinus, whom I have always found to be a gentle and modest man. I have urged him to confer with you about this matter in a friendly way. Nor have I concealed what my own opinion here is. I pray the Lord that he himself, by his grace, will end and settle this unhappy dispute. For I see that it will be very harmful to the Church. Hence I urge and beg you to entrust yourself to our Ursinus here for a friendly conference, as far as this can be done without sacrificing the truth. May the Lord give his grace, etc. Farewell, brother, honoured and beloved lord, and write back by the first messenger who comes. For I long for your letters. Greet all the brothers. Zurich, 5 November 1569. Our envoys have not yet returned from the Diet at Baden. All the brothers greet you.

units.la: Tigurus Bullingerus.
units.tr: Bullinger of Zurich.

units.la: Appendix epist. Bullingeri.
units.tr: Appendix to Bullinger's letter.

units.la: PRomiserat Dominus Beza se missurum ad nos confutationem Thesium D. Erasti, rogans vt diligenter legeremus. mus'. Sed qui factum sit, nescio, quod toto illo anno nihil misit. Anno demum 1570. misit, simul missa est ad nos,& D. Erasti responsio ad D. Bezae confutationem, scripta. Proinde utrumque scriptum legimus, & inter se contulimus. Quid vero nobis videatur, scripsit ad D. Bezam tam suo, quam meo nomine D. Gualtherius. Eodem enim illo tempore aegrotabam. Rogabam ergo, ut scriberet tam suo, quam meo nomine.
units.tr: Dr. Beza had promised that he would send us a refutation of Dr. Erastus's Theses, asking us to read it carefully. But how it came about I do not know, for he sent nothing during that whole year. Only in 1570 did he send it, and at the same time there was sent to us Dr. Erastus's written reply to Dr. Beza's refutation. So we read both writings and compared them with each other. What we think of them Dr. Gwalther has written to Dr. Beza, in his own name as well as mine, for at that time I was ill. I therefore asked him to write in his own name as well as mine.

units.la: D. Theodoro Bezae.
units.tr: To Dr. Theodore Beza.
