units.la: Dilutius fortasis quam par fuit tuum de excommunicatione scriptum apud me detinui, sed condonabis mihi charissime & observande in Christo frater hanc moram, cuius causas multas adducere possem, nisi & tua humanitas mihi perspecta esset, & tu ipse scires, quam multa praeter expectationem negotia, incidant ijs qui in Ecclesiae ministerio constituti sunt, quae illos non sinunt, prosuo arbitrio atque instituto agere. Accessit his quod eodem fere tempore, quo librum tuum accepimus, suam quoque ad illum responsionem misit D. Erastus, quam quia tum tuis omnia conferre oporteret, non ita breui tempore lectio utriusque absolui potuit. Et quia tam haec mihi cognitu necessaria videtur in tanta sententiarum varietate utrumque scriptum aui de legi, rationes quę utrinque afferuntur expendi, & de re ipsa pro mei ingenij modulo non indiligenter cogitaui, quod & alij quidam ex nostris fecerunt, imprimis autem pater & affinis meus, reuerendus D. Bullingerus & Simlerus gener, nec puto te indigne laturum, si quid sentiam, libere & breuiter exponam. Video te mi frater multa erudite, multa bene & pie dicere, de quibus non multa nobis est controuersia. Rursus autem de ijs quae praecipua sunt huius causae capita D. Erastus ita disputat ut tuam de illis sententiam rationibus & argumentis meo iudicio minime contemnendis confutet. Sunt ea:
units.tr: Perhaps I have kept your writing on excommunication with me for longer than was proper, and I have been too thorough with it. Dear brother, whom I honour in Christ, please forgive this delay. I could give many reasons for it, if your kindness were not already known to me and you did not yourself know how many unexpected affairs come upon those who hold office in the ministry of the Church, affairs that do not allow them to act according to their own judgement and plan. Moreover, about the time we received your book, Dr. Erastus also sent his reply to it. Since I had to compare everything in your work with it, I could not finish reading both in a short time. And because, given such a variety of opinions, it seemed to me necessary to know the matter, I read both writings carefully, weighed the arguments put forward on each side, and thought about the question itself with what modest ability I have. Some others among us did the same, especially my father and kinsman, the reverend Dr. Bullinger, and Simler, my son-in-law. I do not think you will take it amiss if I set out freely and briefly what I think. I see, my brother, that you have said many things learnedly and many things well and piously, and that on these we have little quarrel. But on the principal heads of this cause, Dr. Erastus argues in such a way that he refutes your opinion on them with arguments and reasons which, in my judgement, are by no means to be despised. They are these:

units.la: 1 Primum, an Coena Domini, quam is communionis symbolum & lętam atq; publicam gratiarum actionem, pro præstito nobis redemptionis beneficio esse voluit, excómunicationi seruire debeat, adeoq; in vsum aliū conuerti, quam qui nobis à Christo monstratus & ab Apostolis traditus est.
units.tr: 1. First, whether the Lord's Supper, which he wished to be a symbol of communion and a joyful and public thanksgiving for the benefit of redemption bestowed on us, ought to serve excommunication, and so be turned to a use other than that which Christ showed us and the Apostles handed down.

units.la: 2 Deinde, an ab eius vsu arceri debeant ad certum tempus qui pœnitentiam profitentur, & cum Ecclesia mortem Domini annunciare cupiunt.
units.tr: 2. Next, whether those who profess repentance and desire to proclaim the Lord's death with the Church ought to be kept from its use for a set time.

units.la: 3 Deniq; an ad mensam Domini accessuro non sufficiat si seipsum probauerit, & fidem in seipso inuenerit viuam cum serię contritionis atq; pœnitentię spiritu coniunctam.
units.tr: 3. Lastly, whether it is not enough for one who is about to come to the Lord's table to examine himself and find in himself a living faith joined with the spirit of true contrition and repentance.

units.la: 4 Postremo, an vbi Magistratus est Christianus Presbyterium instituí debeat, cui publica morum disciplina, & quos illi meruisse putarint, à sacris communibus arcendi potestas committatur. Hęc inquam nobis præcipua videntur quę in hac causa controuertuntur. Nec enim nobis aliqua (vt puto) liseft de alienis à fide, de Christianæ Religionis hostibus & pœnitere nescijs, quorum incurabilis contumacia omnibus plus satis perspecta est.
units.tr: 4. Finally, where the magistrate is Christian, whether an eldership should be established, to which the public discipline of morals is committed, and the power to keep from the holy communion those whom they judge to have deserved it. These, I say, seem to us the principal points in dispute in this cause. For, as I think, we are not permitted to say anything about those who are alien to the faith, enemies of the Christian religion, and ignorant of repentance, whose incurable obstinacy is already seen by everyone well enough.

units.la: De primo autem multi non temere dubitant, quando vident quam periculosum omnibus sæculis fuerit Dei institutis bono etiam zelo abuti. Nec ego videre possum, cur conscientiarum carnificina ex eo fieri debeat, quod vt fidei confirmandæ & recreandis afflictorum conscientijs seruiat à Domino institutum est. Et feres nos opinor patienter, si hic abs te dissentiamus. Etenim in lege olim eos qui peccarant non à Tabernaculo & sacris communibus excluios, sed potius iussos fuisse legimus vt pro delicti ratione sacrificium facerent. Et cum obległalem immunditiem, quæ in corpore hærebat à sacrorum vsu arcerentur, neminem tamen propter delictum aliquod reiectum fuisse constat. Scio quidem aliquos vestrum examinis cuiusdam meminisse, quo eorū qui peccauerant poenitentia probata fuerit, priusquam victimas offerrent. At nos in causa controuersa non libenter aliquid admittimus quod coniecturis solis, non autem expressis sacris scripturis testimonijs nititur. Prophetas quidem legimus grauiter eos corripuisse, qui indignè sacris communicabant: at censores constitutos fuisse ab illis, qui sacrificaturos singulos vel publicè vel priuatim probarent, & prout ipsis videretur vel admitterent, vel reijcerent, nusquam me legisse memini.
units.tr: Many people, not without reason, doubt the first point, when they see how dangerous it has always been to abuse God's institutions, even with a good zeal. Nor can I see why the torture of consciences should arise from that which the Lord instituted to confirm faith and to comfort the consciences of the afflicted. And I think you will bear with us patiently if we disagree with you here. For we read that in the law of old those who had sinned were not shut out from the Tabernacle and the holy communion, but rather were commanded to offer a sacrifice according to the nature of their offence. And although those who were troubled by legal uncleanness clinging to the body were kept from the use of the sacred things, it is nevertheless certain that no one was rejected on account of some offence. I know that some of you recall a certain examination by which the repentance of those who had sinned was tested before they offered their victims. But in a disputed cause we are not willing to admit anything that rests on conjectures alone and not on plain testimonies of Holy Scripture. We indeed read that the prophets sharply rebuked those who took part in the sacred things unworthily; but I do not recall ever reading that censors were appointed by them, who would approve each person offering sacrifice, either publicly or privately, and who would admit or reject him as they thought fit.

units.la: In secundo capite maior adhuc difficultas sese offert. Nam vt constet aliquem excludi debere, non videmus tamen, eundem, si poenitentiam profiteatur, diutius debere suspendi, quo minus Ecclesiae sacramentis communicet. Cum enim Coena Domini publicfit gratiarum actio, & adfidei confessione pertineat, durum nobis videtur alicui obstare, ne quod per se bonum, sanctum & praecipnum est Christiani hominis officium faciat. Nitimini vos loco qui Matth. 18. habetur, de quo multa dici poterant, quae nunc breuitatis causa omittimus: sed vt demus illic excommunicationem eiusmodi praecipi, eadem tamen eius loci authoritate non poterit longius extendi, quam donec qui exclusus est, se poenitere fateatur, & culpam deprecans cum Ecclesia reconciliari cupiat. Nam qui dixit, sit tibi tanquam Publicanus & Ethnicus, idem fratri peccatori septuagies septies remittere iubet. Quo praecepto Ecclesiam quoque astringi, non opinor negabitis: siquidem illic de excommunicatione agi pergetis contendere. Cur enim Ecclesia quae solis Christianis constat, rigidior sit in vindicandis iniurijs quam singulos esse deceat? Aut qua ratione illa adhuc alienum ducet à familia Domini, quem ipse paterfamilias in gratiam recepit? Velimus nos exemplum adduci, quo probetur, Deum peccatores ad se conuersos & veniam petentes non absque omni mora recipere. Annon publice in patrem, in fratrem primogenitum, in totam domum, denique in ipsos coelos peccauerat filius ille prodigus? Atqui non scandalum domi forisque dederat? Reuerso tamen & scelus confitenti mox ignoscit pater, dignitati pristinae illum restituit, annulo reconciliationis restitutum ornat, & propter illum magtari vult, vitulum illum saginatum, vt conuiuium paret, quo tota domus simul cum illo gaudeat? Cur ergo nos diutius arceamus eos à læto illo & salutari epulo Ecclesiæ, qui eandem cum illo confesionem ædunt? Cur satisfactiones præterea novas exigemus? At periculum est inquis ne qui penitentiam simulent. Fateor. Num vero periculum hoc cuitabimus, si totos annos à communione arceantur? Hypocritam certe impium nulla temporis mora emendabit. Nec est quod nos falli metuamus, dum Dei patris mansuetudinem imitamur. Hypocritae suo periculo nos fallent, sibi ipsis iudicium edent & bibent, nos extra culpam erimus. Te autem rogo, mi frater, an non ipsi quoque falli possumus, & eum zelo inconsulto à Coena excludere quem verè commersum ipse Christus iam suo corpore & sanguine pascere dignatur? Quam vero indignum hoc fuerit, ei tristitiam nouam parere, quem Dei filius in se gaudere vult? Qua ratione rigorem cum excusabimus, si eum rei ciamus quem Dominus noster vlnis expansis complectitur? Hic certè periculum est ne serui illius nequam socij deprehendamur, qui heri in se clementiam expertus, conseruum suum durius tractarit. Et cum constet Ioannem absque curiosiori examine ad baptismum admisisse omnes qui se poenitere dicebant, Apostolos item mox baptizauisse eos, qui fidem in Christum profitebantur, non videmus cur à Coena repelli debeant, qui fidem eandem nobiscum profesi sunt: peccato autem aliquo Ecclesiam offenderunt, cum qua nunc in gratiam redire cupiunt.
units.tr: In the second head a greater difficulty presents itself. For although it is established that someone ought to be excluded, we do not see that the same person, if he professes repentance, ought to be kept back for long from taking part in the sacraments of the Church. For since the Lord's Supper is a public thanksgiving and belongs to the confession of faith, it seems hard to us to hinder anyone from doing what is in itself a good, holy and especially important duty of a Christian. You rely on the passage in Matthew 18, about which much could be said, but which for the sake of brevity we now omit. But even if we grant that excommunication of this kind is commanded there, nevertheless by the same authority of that passage it cannot be extended longer than until the one who has been shut out confesses that he repents, and, deploring his fault, desires to be reconciled with the Church. For he who said, "Let him be to you as a publican and a heathen," also bids you forgive a sinning brother seventy times seven. I do not think you will deny that this precept binds the Church as well, since you will insist that the passage there treats of excommunication. For why should the Church, which consists only of Christians, be more rigorous in avenging wrongs than individuals ought to be? Or by what reasoning will it still count as a stranger to the household of the Lord one whom the Father of the household himself has received back into favour? Let us have an example brought forward to prove that God does not receive sinners who turn to him and ask pardon without any delay. Did not that prodigal son sin openly against his father, against his elder brother, against the whole household, and finally against heaven itself? Yet did he not give scandal at home and abroad? When he returned and confessed his wickedness, the father at once forgave him, restored him to his former dignity, adorned him with the ring of reconciliation, and wished the fatted calf to be killed for him, so that a feast might be prepared in which the whole household might rejoice together with him. Why then should we keep for longer from that joyful and saving banquet of the Church those who make the same confession as he did? Why, moreover, shall we demand new satisfactions? But, you say, there is a danger that some may feign repentance. I grant it. But will we avoid this danger if they are kept from communion for whole years? Certainly no period of time will reform an impious hypocrite. Nor have we reason to fear being deceived while we imitate the gentleness of God the Father. Hypocrites will deceive us at their own peril; they will eat and drink judgement to themselves, and we shall be free of blame. But I ask you, my brother, whether we ourselves may not also be deceived, and by a rash zeal exclude from the Supper one whom Christ himself has truly received, and deigns already to feed with his body and blood? How unworthy it would be to bring fresh sorrow upon one in whom the Son of God wishes to rejoice! On what ground shall we excuse harshness if we reject one whom our Lord embraces with outstretched arms? Here, surely, there is danger that we are found to be like that wicked servant's fellow servants, who, having himself received mercy the day before, treated his fellow servant more harshly. And since it is established that John admitted to baptism, without a more careful examination, all who said they repented, and that the Apostles soon afterwards baptized those who professed faith in Christ, we do not see why those should be repelled from the Supper who have professed the same faith as we do, but have offended the Church by some sin, and now desire to return into favour with it.

units.la: Ista certè quae infinitis exemplis tam veteris quam noui Testamenti probari poterant, nos mouent, vt priuatum illud examen quo quisque seipsum probet, secundum Pauli praeceptum, sufficere putemus ijs, qui ad Domini mensam voluint accedere. Nam si quid praeterea voluisset fieri Apostolus, magna erat illud praecipiendi occasio, cum ex professo de legitimo Coenæ vsu disseresset apud eos, qui innumeris erroribus atque vitijs polluti ipsam quoque horribili vsu prophanarant. Sed vidit prudubiò, quam periculosum sit aliorum conscientias rimari mari velle, quando nihil facilius est, quàm seuerius in alios animaduertendo sanctitatis maioris existimationem venari: & sæpè tentationum lineis metiuntur per importunos illos censores, qui consolatione potius subleuari & confirmari debebant. Ideo in hac ipsa causa grauiter monebat videndum esse ne à Sathana occupemur, cuius machinationes nemo Christianus ignorat.
units.tr: These things, which could be proved by countless examples from both the Old and the New Testament, move us to think that the private examination by which each one tests himself, according to Paul's precept, is sufficient for those who wish to come to the Lord's table. For if the Apostle had wished anything more to be done, there was a great opportunity to command it, since he was discussing the lawful use of the Supper expressly with those who, polluted by countless errors and vices, had profaned it with a dreadful use. But he surely saw how dangerous it is to want to search out the consciences of others, since nothing is easier than to hunt for a reputation for greater holiness by punishing others more severely; and such men, by their troublesome censures, often measure out the lines of temptations, when they ought rather to be relieved and strengthened by comfort. Therefore, in this very matter, he gravely warned that we must take care not to be overcome by Satan, whose schemes no Christian is ignorant of.

units.la: Quæ de presbyterio in Ecclesijs constituendo scribis facilè admittimus illic vbi Magistratus non est Christianus. Nam oportet esse aliquos quorum authoritate in officio contineantur, qui ad peccandum procliuiores sunt, ne Religio exterorum ludibrijs exponatur. Sub Christianis autem principibus cura ista ijs commodius & tutius committi videtur, qui ad Reipub. gubernacula sedent: & nescio quam tutè noui Magistratus possint creari, quia multa sequuntur incommoda, quæ nunc recensere longum foret. Hoc tamen dissimulare non possum in Palatinatu nulla prius scandala tam atrocia incidisse, quam ea sint quæ Seniorum illic constitutorum culpa acciderunt. Et quis obsecro eos posthac feret correptores, qui sceleratissimum hominem Siculum Sodomitam, & eundem pestilentiss. calumniatorem impune elabi passi sunt, ne ad iudices legitimos traheretur? Putarunt enim lentius procedendum esse vt ipsi eius causæ cognitores esse possent. Hac ratione profecto illos mihi excusauit homo Italus tibi probe notus & vir bonus cum exemplum illud ei obiicerem. Quid vero est Magistratus partes sibi vendicare, si hoc non est? Est equidem insatiabilis hominum ambitio, & rari inveniuntur qui potestate sibi data non insolentiores fiant. Et si veteres historias euoluamus maxima & nocentissima Ecclesiæ scandala ex Episcopis & reliquis ministris enata fuisse patebit. Quod ipsum nunc in Germania quoque fieri videmus inter Lutheranos superintendentes, qui tumia potestate armati nihil non licere sibi putant. Quid vero de ijs qui Heydelbergae hanc causam agunt sperare possimus satis. nos vna hæc audacia admonet, qua suæ sententiæ subscribere nolen-
units.tr: You write that it is easy for us to accept the setting up of an eldership in the churches where the magistrate is not a Christian. For there must be some men by whose authority those who are more prone to sin are kept in their duty, lest the religion of outsiders be exposed to mockery. Under Christian princes, however, that charge seems to be entrusted more suitably and safely to those who sit at the helm of the commonwealth, and I do not know how safely new magistrates could be created, since many inconveniences would follow, and to list them now would take too long. I cannot, however, pass over this: in the Palatinate no scandals were ever so atrocious beforehand as those which occurred through the fault of the elders appointed there. And who, I ask you, will henceforth tolerate such censors, who allowed that most wicked man, the Sicilian sodomite and at the same time a most pestilent slanderer, to slip away unpunished, so that he would not be dragged before lawful judges? For they thought it should proceed more slowly, so that they themselves might be the examiners of his case. The Italian man, well known to you and an honest man, certainly excused them on this ground when I put that example to him. But what is it to claim for oneself the functions of the magistrate, if this is not? Human ambition is indeed insatiable, and few are found who do not become more arrogant when given power. And if we unroll the older histories, it will be plain that the greatest and most harmful scandals of the Church have arisen from bishops and other ministers. We see the same thing happening now in Germany too, among the Lutheran superintendents, who, armed with such power, think nothing is not permitted to them. As for what we may hope from those who are pleading this cause at Heidelberg, we have enough: this one boldness warns us, by which they accuse of atheism those who refuse to subscribe to their opinion, and indeed men in whose faith, teaching and morals no good man has ever found any fault. If, therefore, we fear that they may be able to establish a new tyranny in the churches on these principles, who will say that we fear this without cause? As for what I have written elsewhere, we do not stand in the way of those who think they can usefully employ that form of discipline, so that they may enjoy their own opinion. This at least we advise: let them not try to put on, or rather to force upon, everyone's feet the same shoe, nor, over a matter still disputed, and for which the same formula cannot be laid down everywhere, tear the churches apart from one another, and by weaving new contentions, offer a joyful spectacle to their common enemies.

units.la: volentes atheismi accusant, & eos quidem viros in quorum fide, doctrina, moribus nemo bonus aliquid vnquam desideravit. Quod si ergo nouam in Ecclesijs tyrannidem his principijs stabilire posse metuimus, quis nos absque causa id timere dicet? Quod autem alias scripsi non obstamus nos, quo minus suo sensu fruantur, qui illa disciplinae forma se vtiliter vti posse videnť. Hoc saltem monemus, ne eundem calceum omnium pedibus induere, vel potius obtrudere conentur, neue ob rem adhuc controuersam, & cuius eadem formula vbique constitui non potest, Ecclesias abs se inuicem diuellant, & nouas concertationes texendo, laetum communibus hostibus spectaculum praebeant.
units.tr: Those who refuse to subscribe to this opinion of theirs, they accuse of atheism, and yet these are men in whose faith, teaching and morals no good person has ever found anything to fault. If, then, we fear that a new tyranny may be established in the Churches on these principles, who will say that we fear this without cause? As for what I have written elsewhere, we do not stand in the way of those who think they can use that form of discipline to good effect, so that they may enjoy their own opinion. We advise only this: that they should not try to fit the same shoe to everyone's feet, or rather force it upon them, and that they should not, over a matter still in dispute, and for which one and the same formula cannot be laid down everywhere, tear the Churches apart from one another. By weaving new quarrels they would give joy to their common enemies, who would have a splendid spectacle.

units.la: Bene mi obseruande frater facturos nos putaucro, si causam hanc totam silentio posthac premamus, ne in publicam ostentationem erumpat, qua de re cum nuper D. Bullingerum ad te scripsisse scilicet ego prolixior esse nolo. Nihil fraterna charitate atque concordia Ecclesijs vtilius & salutarius accidere potest. Eam nos vobiscum colemus, quoad vitam Deus dederit, & de nobis omnibus idem vobis pollicemur. Si quid liberius abs me scriptum videbitur, tuae humanitatis illud acceptum feres, qua fretus sic mihi agendum putaui. Dolet nobis vehementer vrbem vestram pestis flagello indies magis ingrauescenti affligi, & prae aliis triste nobis fuit auditu, optimum & clarissimum fratrem D. Remundum periclitari, aut etiam ad Dominum iam nunc commigrauisse. Illum quidem si iam hac vita defunctus est vere beatum viuere, & ministerij sui, in quo fidelissimus fuit, praemia percipere scimus, at Ecclesiam membro vtili & necessario orbatam esse non possumus non dolere. &c. Deus pater misericordiae & consolationis vobis omnibus adsit, Ecclesiae & scholae nostrae misereatur, tequeimprimis mi humanissime Beza & frater obseruande seruet ad sui nominis gloriam, & studijs tuis benedicat: Amen. Tig.uri 3. Augusti 1570.
units.tr: My dear and esteemed brother, you will think we shall do well if from now on we keep this whole cause buried in silence, so that it does not break out into public display. About this matter, since Bullinger has recently written to you, I do not wish to be more lengthy. Nothing can be more useful or more wholesome for the Churches than fraternal charity and concord. We shall cultivate this with you for as long as God grants us life, and we promise you the same on behalf of all of us. If anything I have written seems too free, you will put it down to your kindness, on which I relied when I thought I ought to proceed in this way. We grieve greatly that your city is afflicted by the scourge of plague, which grows more severe every day, and it was especially sad for us to hear that our best and most distinguished brother, Master Remundus, is in danger, or even that he has already now departed to the Lord. Indeed, if he has already finished this life, we know he lives truly blessed and receives the rewards of his ministry, in which he was most faithful; yet we cannot but grieve that the Church has been deprived of so useful and necessary a member. &c. May God the Father of mercies and consolation be with you all, have mercy on the Church and our school, and preserve you, above all, my most kind Beza and esteemed brother, to the glory of his name, and bless your studies: Amen. Zurich, 3 August 1570.

units.la: Rod. Gualtherus.
units.tr: Rod. Gualtherus.

units.la: D.Carolo Ionuillæo Geneuensi Rodolphus Gual- therus Tigurinus. S.
units.tr: To Charles Ionuillæus of Geneva, Rudolf Gualther of Zurich. Greetings.

units.la: SEmper te amauì humanissime & doctissime Ionuillæe, & quidē magno tuo merito:nunc autem te dignum video quem magis amem & colam, qui de ijs quæ de me ad vos perlata sunt,me tam amice admonendū esse putaris.Qui illi sint qui hinc ad vos profecti ista narrarent, aut fortasis adhuc nobiscum agentes isthuc perscripserunt, nescio, hoc autem non sine dolore iam annis aliquot experti sumus, plerosq; fore qui Geneua ad nos veniunt, de disciplina quidem splendidè disserere, vix vero vllam vel scholasticam vel domesticam disciplinam, qualis apud nos habetur,ferre posse aut velle. Interim ijdem nos accusant, qui disciplinam omnem ex Ecclesia sublatam velimus: & non sine calumnia nos contra disciplinam pugnare dicunt:quando non omnia probamus, quæ ipsi de excommunicatione aut potius de exclusione à coena Domini mystica sentiunt. Quod ad me attinet illos vehementer falli satis arguit, quod Homil. in Lucam 193. disciplinam Ecclesiæ necessariam esse affirmo. Quod si eam abs me in concionibus publicis oppugnari dicunt impudentior est eorum calumnia, quam vt aliquam confutationem mereatur. Nec enim puto aliquem apud vos vel etiam in tota Helvetia tam hostilii in me animo esse, vt tale quid de me cogitare possit, cum multis æquo seuerior & vehementior in corripiendis corruptis hominum moribus atque deliciis esse videar. Quae autem contra excommunicationem dico aut scribo ad Anabaptistas maxime pertinent, sicut in eiusdem operis Homilia 160. est videre. Quia enim isti sub illius prætextu multis fucum faciunt, non possumus non nostros monere, ne ipsorum præstigijs sese seduci patiantur. Quod si de excommunicatione dicendum sit, nunquam ea nobis prorsus aut in genere damnata est: quin & legibus nostris ea præcipitur,qua à tribuum societate & publicorum pascuorum vsu-fructu excluduntur, qui contemptis admonitionibus tam publicis quam priuatis, aliter viuunt quam homines Christianos deceat. Vt vero aliqui à coetibus sacris aut à coena Domini arceantur, id in nostris Ecclesijs nunquam receptum fuit: vt nec in multis alijs, quas tamen ob neglectam fidei & doctrinae puritatem, aut ob introductam morum licentiam, nemo hucusque merito potuit accusare. Nec enim à quoquam hactenus idoneis & firmis argumentis demonstratum fuisse vidimus, exclusionis aut separationis symbolum ex ea fieri debere, qua Ecclesia colligi & eius vnitas conseruari atque foueri debet, quo nomine illam veteres συνάξιν dixerunt. Miror igitur mi charissime Ionuillæ, qua ratione dicas me istis Ecclesiæ temporibus calamitosissimis nouum quoddam & inauditū velut paradoxon inuehere praeter omnium expectationem. Cur enim nouum & inauditum dicatur, quod in nostra Ecclesia iam inde ab initio per annos 50 receptum fuit? Zuinglius certe beatæ memoriæ, primus Religionis apud Heluetios instaurator eadem diserte scripsit in amica ad Lutherum Exegesi, quæ hodie nos docemus & sentimus. Idem etsi cum D. Oecolampadio amicitia & amore syncerissimo coniunctus esset, nunquam tamen voluit Exclusionem à coena in Ecclesiam Tigurinam introducere, cum ille aliquameius formulam, bono zelo Basileæ instituret, quæ nec ipso adhuc viuente plenè exerceri, nec postea diutius retineri potuit, quod prudentissimi quique viderent, satius esse Christianis magistratibus suam authoritatem confirmare, qua improbi & contumaces, admonitionum diuinarum contemptores facilius simul & tutius coercentur, quam cum publici motus periculo presbyterium quoddam nouum aut senatum Ecclesiasticum instituere, qui fortassis nos multo post alio opus haberet, cuius imperio inde enascens tyrannis frenaretur. Quid vero D. Bullingerus, præceptor & pater meus vnicè obseruandus, de hac caussa sentiat, eius aduersus Anabaptistas liber abunde testatur, & ea imprimis quae habentur cap. 9. lib. 6. &c. De Musculo quid dicere attinet, qui dum Ecclesiæ Germaniæ superioris magis quam nunc florerent, Augustæ magna cum laude, & nō minori postea Bernæ docuit? Is vt passim admonet ministros de colligendo potius quam excludendo sollicitos esse debere: ita in priorem ad Corinth. hoc negotium sic tractat, vt non obscurum sit eum à nostra sententia minimè esse alienum. Posset his adijcere Constantiensis Ecclesiae exemplum, quæ illic docente Ambrosio Blaurero, Consulatum vero gerente Thoma fratre eius, socero meo colendo, disciplinam exercuit seuerissimam in omnes qui dissolutius vixerunt: sed idem exclusionem à Coena sacra admiscendam esse nunquam putauit. Possunt ista opinor sufficere aduersus eos, qui me dogma vel potius paradoxon nouum & inauditum inuehere calumniantur. Adde tamen me nihil vnquam vel docuisse in hac causa, vel scripsisse, quod à communi fratrum, qui in nostris Ecclesijs docent sententia dissentiat. De causa ipsa nunc prolixius disputare nolo. Si qui autem Exclusionem à sacris mysterijs in sua Ecclesia cum fructu exercere posse putant, fruantur illi suo sensu: Et libertatem hanc nemini nos inuidemus. Nos equidem cum ante annos aliquot vester Senatus ad nostrum de hac re retulisset, non nostros modo verumetiam Bernenses, Scaphusianos, & Basilienses fratres monuimus, ne alicuius consilij vestris authores essent, quo inchoatæ tunc apud vos disciplinæ formula atque morum reformatio posset impediri. Noluimus enim in alienas Ecclesias nobis aliquod ius aut imperium vendicare. Recte igitur scribis nos omnes qui Ecclesiae Tigurinae gubernacula tenemus, concordiae & pacis Ecclesiasticae studiosos fuisse semper: nec facile ad certamina prosilire. Istud certe studium nos monet ne temere aliquibus alicuius innouationis authores simus, nec libenter in messem aliorum falcem mittimus, quod sciamus innouationes plerunque cum rixis & contentionibus esse coniunctas. Quae autem nuper in Luca meo scripsi, non contentionis ergo (à cuius libidine haetenus alienisialienissimus fui) scripsi, sed pacis Ecclesiasticæ conservandæ causa, quam ego iam pluribus annis perturbatam fuisse vidi ab illis qui excommunicationem violenter obtrudendo, aliorum labore collectas & instauratas Ecclesias sua importunitate disperserunt. Certè quanta mala Anabaptistae nostro sæculo dederint, longum esset commemorare. Optas tu vt priusquam via contentionibus aperiatur, cum doctis & amicis conferam. Non aperui ego viam contentionibus, vbi autem & per quos ea aperta sit, satis iam omnes norunt. Quod si quis me petulantius aggrediatur, mēque ad scribendum cogat, faxo vt omnes me modestiae studere, nec quicquam absque Ecclesiæ nostrae & amplissimi Senatus authoritate atque consensu facere intelligant. Contulerunt nostra ætate sæpius de hac causa viri doctrina & pietate eximij, & in eo semper consenserunt, disciplinam in Ecclesia necessariam esse (quod ipsi quoque adhuc fatemur, imò vrgemus & vrgebimus, quoad vitam Dominus dederit) eius vero rationem atque formulam cuilibet Ecclesiæ liberam relinqui debere, vt ea vtatur quæ Ecclesiam ædificet, non concutiat aut euertat. Nunquam item dissimulauimus Coenam Dominicam illis vbi Magistratus est Christianus maiori cum periculo quam emolumento cum hac causa misceri. Cogitare me iubes, quam multa & grauia incommoda sequantur si excommunicatio ab Ecclesia tollatur neque eius vsus retineatur. At ego non minus diligenter & mature cogitandum puto, quanta animorum distractio, & quam horribilis rerum perturbatio oritura sit, si qui apud ipsos receptum disciplinae modum absque omni discrimine omnibus alijs Ecclesijs etiam nolentibus & reluctantibus volunt obtrudere. Nobis certe sufficere videtur si disciplina instituatur quam magistratus legitimus exerceat. Etiamsi nulla fiat per certos homines à coetibus sacris, ab auditione verbi & Coenæ myst icæ vsu exclusio. Hæc liberius scribo, mi frater, quia non tam mea quam Ecclesiarum nostrarum causa hic agitur: & non ignoro qui præcipui sint huius fabulæ actores, cuius vtinam catastrophe sit læta, & quæ ad Ecclesiae communis ædificationem faciat. Te autem ni frater obseruande rogo, vt ista boni consulas, & de nobis omnibus tibi persuadeas, nos nihil minus cogitare, quam vt vestrae aut aliis Ecclesiis turbas demus: & puto vestros homines non ignorare, quo studio & animi candore Ecclesiam vestram simus complexi hactenus: quam in posterum quoque amare & complecti non desinemus. Salutem tibi dicit D. Bullingerus. Tu quaeso ex me salutes D. Bezam, Budaeum, Heßnaltum, & reliquos amicos & fratres mihi in Domino plurimum obseruandos. Vale Tiguri pridie Calend. Maij, Anno Filij Dei in carne manifestati. 1570.
units.tr: I have always loved you, most kind and learned Ionuillæus, and rightly so, given your great merit. Now, however, I see you as even more deserving of my affection and esteem, since you have thought fit to warn me so kindly about what has been reported to you concerning me. I do not know who those were who went from here to you to tell these things, or who perhaps, while still dealing with us, wrote them up there. But for some years now we have found by experience, not without grief, that many who come to us from Geneva speak splendidly about discipline, yet can scarcely bear or wish for any discipline at all, whether in school or at home, of the kind that prevails among us. Meanwhile these same people accuse us of wanting to remove all discipline from the Church, and they say, not without slander, that we fight against discipline, since we do not approve everything they think about excommunication, or rather about exclusion from the Lord's mystical Supper. As far as I am concerned, the fact that I affirm, in my Homily on Luke 193, that church discipline is necessary is quite enough to prove how greatly they are mistaken. If they say that I attack it in my public sermons, their calumny is too shameless to deserve any refutation. For I do not think there is anyone among you, or even in all of Switzerland, so hostile to me that he could think any such thing of me, since I seem to many to be more severe and vehement in rebuking the corrupt morals and pleasures of men. What I say or write against excommunication, however, applies chiefly to the Anabaptists, as can be seen in Homily 160 of the same work. For since they use excommunication as a pretext to deceive many, we cannot but warn our own people not to let themselves be led astray by their tricks. But if the matter of excommunication must be discussed, it has never at all been condemned by us, either as a whole or in general. Indeed, our own laws even prescribe it, by which those are excluded from the fellowship of the tribes and from the use of the common pastures who, despising admonitions both public and private, live otherwise than Christians ought to live. But that some should be kept from sacred assemblies or from the Lord's Supper has never been accepted in our Churches, just as it has not been in many others, which yet no one has so far been able to rightly accuse of neglecting the purity of faith and doctrine, or of introducing licence in morals. For we have never seen it demonstrated by anyone, with sound and firm arguments, that a token of exclusion or separation must come out of that by which the Church is gathered and its unity preserved and cherished, which the ancients called synaxis [συνάξις]. I am therefore amazed, my dearest Ionuillæus, by what reasoning you say that in these most calamitous times of the Church I bring in some new and unheard-of paradox, contrary to everyone's expectation. For why is it called new and unheard-of, when it has been received in our Church from the very beginning, for fifty years? Zwingli, of blessed memory, the first restorer of religion among the Helvetii, certainly wrote the same things plainly in his friendly Exegesis addressed to Luther, which we teach and hold today. Although he was joined in friendship and most sincere love with Dr. Oecolampadius, he never wished to introduce exclusion from the Supper into the Zurich Church, when Oecolampadius, with good zeal, was establishing a certain formula at Basel. That formula could not be fully carried out even while he was still alive, nor could it be maintained for long afterwards, as all the most prudent saw. It is better for Christian magistrates to confirm their own authority, by which the wicked and stubborn, the despisers of divine admonitions, are restrained more easily and more safely, than to set up some new eldership or ecclesiastical senate, with the risk of public disturbance, which perhaps we would need much later, and by whose rule the tyranny that arose from it would be checked. As for what Dr. Bullinger, my teacher and father, whom alone I must hold in highest regard, thinks of this matter, his book against the Anabaptists bears ample witness, especially what is found in chapter 9 of book 6, etc. What need is there to speak of Musculus, who taught with great praise at Augsburg, while the Churches of Upper Germany flourished more than they do now, and afterwards with no less praise at Bern? As he often admonishes, ministers ought to be concerned with gathering rather than excluding. So too in his commentary on the first Epistle to the Corinthians he treats this business in such a way that it is not unclear that he is by no means alien to our opinion. I could add to these the example of the Church of Constance, which, while Ambrosius Blaurer taught there, and his brother Thomas, whom I must honour as my father-in-law, was consul, practised the most severe discipline against all who lived too loosely. Yet that same Church never thought that exclusion from the holy Supper should be added. These things, I think, may suffice against those who slander me by saying that I bring in a new and unheard-of doctrine, or rather paradox. Add to this that in this matter I have never either taught or written anything that differs from the common opinion of the brothers who teach in our Churches. I do not wish to dispute the matter itself at greater length now. If, however, some think they can rightly exercise exclusion from the sacred mysteries in their own Church, let them enjoy their own judgement; we do not begrudge anyone this liberty. Indeed, when some years ago your Senate referred this matter to ours, we warned not only our own brothers but also those of Bern, Schaffhausen and Basel, that they should not be the authors of any plan by which the form of discipline and reform of morals then begun among you might be hindered. For we did not wish to claim any right or authority over other Churches. You are therefore right to write that all of us who hold the helm of the Zurich Church have always been devoted to concord and ecclesiastical peace, and not quick to rush into quarrels. That zeal certainly warns us not to be rashly the authors of any innovation for anyone, nor gladly to put our sickle into another's harvest, since we know that innovations are generally bound up with quarrels and contentions. As for what I recently wrote in my Lucas, I wrote it not for the sake of strife (from whose lust I have been most entirely free until now), but for the sake of preserving ecclesiastical peace. I have seen this peace disturbed for many years now by those who, by violently forcing excommunication upon people, have scattered by their importunity Churches that others had gathered and restored with labour. Indeed, it would be a long task to recount how many evils the Anabaptists have brought upon our century. You ask that, before the way is opened to contention, I should confer with learned and friendly men. I did not open the way to contention; but by whom and where it has been opened, everyone already knows well enough. But if anyone attacks me more insolently and compels me to write, I will see to it that everyone understands I am devoted to moderation, and that I do nothing without the authority and consent of our Church and of the most distinguished Senate. In our time men of outstanding learning and piety have often conferred about this matter, and they have always agreed that discipline is necessary in the Church (which we too still confess, indeed we urge and will urge it as long as the Lord grants us life), but that its method and form should be left free to each Church, so that it may use what builds up the Church and does not shake or overthrow it. We have also never concealed that the Lord's Supper is mixed with this matter, where the magistrate is Christian, with greater danger than benefit. You bid me consider how many grave inconveniences would follow if excommunication were removed from the Church and its use were not retained. But I think it no less necessary to consider, carefully and in good time, how great a division of minds and how dreadful a disturbance of affairs will arise if some wish to force upon all other Churches, even those unwilling and resisting, the form of discipline received among themselves, without any distinction. For us it seems sufficient if a discipline is instituted which the lawful magistrate administers, even if no exclusion from the sacred assemblies, from hearing the Word and from the use of the mystical Supper is carried out by certain men. I write these things rather freely, my brother, because the matter at stake here concerns not so much me as our Churches. I am not unaware who the chief actors are in this drama; I hope its outcome will be happy and serve the common building up of the Church. But I ask you, my respected brother, to take these things in good part, and to be persuaded about all of us that we think of nothing less than of causing trouble for your Churches or for others. I think your people are not unaware with what zeal and sincerity of mind we have so far embraced your Church, and we will not cease to love and embrace it in the future as well. Dr. Bullinger sends you greetings. Please give my greetings to Dr. Beza, Budaeus, Hessenhalt and the other friends and brothers in the Lord whom I hold in high regard. Farewell. At Zurich, the day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Son of God made manifest in the flesh, 1570.

units.la: Tui studiosissimus Rodolphus Gualtherus.
units.tr: Your most devoted Rudolf Gualther.

units.la: Ex literis ad generosiss. Comitem Ludouicum Vuitgensteinium 26. Augusti 1574.
units.tr: From a letter to the most noble Count Ludwig of Wittgenstein, 26 August 1574.

units.la: QVod autem inter media salutis externa disciplinam ecclesiasticam numeras, etsi per se nequaquam improbem, rogo tamen Excellentiâ tuam, ne ægre ferat, si de hac re aliquid dixero, de qua hodie inter multos controvertitur, & nisi quorundam ambitiosus rigor prudenti principum authoritate temperetur, turbas aliquando dabit maiores quam vt facile sedentur, & nouam in Ecclesias tyrannidem inuehet, Pontificia nihilò tolerabiliorem. Ecclesias absque disciplina consistere non posse, fatemur omnes, & vt ea sanctissimè instituatur atque seruetur omnino necesse est. De huius autem formula non inter omnes conuenit. Vestri homines præcipuum disciplinae caput in Exclusione à coena Domini constituunt: Adhæc exclusis certum tempus præscribunt, quo à communione abstinere debeant: vtque suam disciplinam tueantur Senatu ecclesiastico opus esse dicunt, cui omnis loci & ordinis homines, ipsi quoque
units.tr: As for your listing ecclesiastical discipline among the external means of salvation: although I by no means condemn it in itself, I nevertheless ask your Excellency not to take it amiss if I say something on a matter about which many now dispute. Unless the ambitious rigour of certain men is tempered by the prudent authority of princes, this matter will sometimes stir up greater disturbances than can easily be calmed, and will introduce into the Churches a new tyranny no more tolerable than the Papists'. We all admit that Churches cannot exist without discipline, and that it must be established and preserved most holily. But there is no agreement among all on its form. Your men make the chief point of discipline the exclusion from the Lord's Supper. Besides, they prescribe a fixed period for the excluded during which they must abstain from communion. And to defend their discipline they say there is need of an ecclesiastical senate, to which men of every place and rank, princes themselves included, must be subject.

units.la: principes, subijciantur. At ista eiusmodi sunt, vt de eorum veritate pij & cordati non temere dubitent. Etenim non absque causa quaeritur, an coena Domini, quae vt communionis & societatis Christianae symbolum sit, vtque fidei confirmandae seruiat, a Christo institura est, in vsum plane diuersum, adeoque Christi instituto contrarium, conuerti debeat? vt interim dissociationis & exclusionis organum & conscientiarum carnificina fiat? Deinde, annon cum Pauli regula hoc pugnet, qui vt quisque seipsum probet, non vt aliorum conscientias curiosius scrutemur, iusfit? Item, annon durum & iniquum sit, peccatorem, qui seria poenitentia tangitur, & quem iam proculdubio in gratiam receptum Christus ipse suo corpore & sanguine pascit, ab eius mensa arcere, imo prohibere, ne mortem Domini publice cum Ecclesia, cuius membrum germanum est, praedicet? Praeterea, annon monstri instar sit, duos in vno populo magistratus instituere? Aut enim politicus magistratus ab eorum cognitione excludetur, quae ad morum disciplinam spectant: aut vterque simul circa hanc occupabitur. Quod si illum excludamus a morum disciplina, id contra Dei leges faciemus, qui sua iudicia viris principibus credidit, & ijsdem vt malum e medio populi sui excindant, iussit. Sin vero illam his quoque committemus, vix vitari poterit confusio, & alter alterum impediet: aut saltem cessare debebit in hac parte politicus magistratus, donec causas eiusmodi Ecclesiasticus ad illum remiserit. Ita vero non habebit ille quod agat, nisi prius Seniores illi causas cognoscant, & huic de his decernendi potestatem faciant. Emergent ergo hinc nouae tyrannidis cornua, & paulatim cristas attollent ambitiosi Ecclesiarum pastores, quibus facile fuerit suos affectores in suas partes attrahere, cum ipsi inter hos primatum teneant. Et hoc me non absque ratione dicere intelliget Excellentia tua, si quae specimina vestri illi iam apud vos dederint, diligenter quaesieris. Etenim a coena abstinere per illos iussi sunt spectatae pietatis & probitatis viri, qui cur hoc iuberentur, nunquam rescire potuerunt: sed sufficiens responsum esse nouis illis alienae fidei dominatoribus vilum est, quod ipsi saluasua conscientia illos non possint admittere. Ergo ne propter morosi aut importuni pastoris conscientiam vir pius àsacro epulo abstinere, & in praedicando mortis Christo beneficio suum officium debet negligere. Tolerabilius multò Pontificij praesules agunt, qui cur nos profchismaticis & excommunicatis habeant, libere edicunt, neque nobis nos purgandi occasionem eripiunt. Quid ergo fore sperabimus, si quando regnum suum stabilierunt, cum hæ sint disciplinae istius primitiae, pro qua illi tantopere digladiantur? Mihi certè confulrius videtur, vt ministri intra suas metas sese contineant, magistratibus verò committantur quae ad morum & vitae disciplinam pertinent. Scio illos obijcere, Magistratus non semper officium facere, & proinde alio Senatu opus esse, qui illos in ordinem redigat. Ego verò hanc consequentiam nego, cum quod dicunt nullo exemplo Prophetico siue Apostolico probare possint.
units.tr: But these proposals are of such a kind that pious and sensible men do not rashly doubt their truth. For it is not without reason that one asks whether the Lord's Supper, which Christ instituted as the sign of Christian communion and fellowship, and to serve the strengthening of faith, ought to be turned to a use entirely different from it, and so contrary to Christ's institution, so that it becomes an instrument of separation and exclusion and a torture chamber for consciences. Next, does this not conflict with the rule of Paul, who bids each man to examine himself, not for us to scrutinise the consciences of others more curiously? Likewise, is it not harsh and unjust to bar from his table, or rather to forbid, a sinner who is touched by genuine repentance, and whom Christ himself has surely already received into grace and feeds with his body and blood, so that he may not proclaim the death of the Lord publicly with the Church, of which he is a true member? Furthermore, is it not monstrous to set up two magistracies in one people? For either the civil magistrate will be excluded from knowledge of those matters which pertain to the discipline of morals, or both will be occupied with them together. If we exclude him from the discipline of morals, we shall act against the laws of God, who entrusted his judgments to princes and ordered them to cut off evil from the midst of his people. But if we also commit this to them, confusion can scarcely be avoided, and each will hinder the other. Or at least the civil magistrate in this part must cease to act until the ecclesiastical men have referred such cases to him. Thus he will have nothing to do unless those elders first examine the cases and give him the power to decide upon them. From this, then, the horns of a new tyranny will emerge, and ambitious ministers of the Churches will gradually raise their crests, finding it easy to draw their supporters to their side, since they themselves hold the first place among them. Your Excellency will understand that I do not say this without reason, if you carefully inquire what examples of these men have already been given among you. For men of proved piety and integrity have been ordered by them to abstain from the Supper, and they could never learn why they were so ordered. Yet those new lords over another's faith have thought it a sufficient answer that they cannot admit them while their own consciences are safe. Therefore a pious man must not abstain from the sacred feast because of the conscience of a fussy or importunate minister, and must not neglect his duty of proclaiming Christ's benefit in his death. The Papist prelates act far more tolerably, who freely declare that they hold us as schismatics and excommunicates, and yet do not snatch from us the opportunity of clearing ourselves. What, then, shall we hope will happen if they ever establish their rule, since these are the first fruits of that discipline for which they fight so fiercely? It seems to me far wiser that ministers should keep themselves within their own bounds, and that matters belonging to the discipline of morals and life be committed to the magistrates. I know they object that magistrates do not always perform their office, and that therefore another senate is needed to bring them into line. I, however, deny this inference, since they can prove it by no example, prophetic or apostolic.

units.la: Ministrorum quidem est, principum ac iudicum vitia moresque corruptos corripere, eosdem officij admonere (quod olim Prophetas fecisse legimus) vt verò eosdem, si segnes esse pergant aut mali exempli auctores sint alij magistratui mulctandos aut excommunicandos subijciant, nuspiam me legisse memini. Prophetas certè nihil huius fecisse constat. De Apostolis non opus est dicere, quorum tempore magistratus Christiani nulli fuerunt. Quae causa fuit, vt in Ecclesijs necessariò Seniores constituerentur, qui morum disciplinae praeessent: quod hodie etiam fieri oportet sub tyrannis fidei persecutoribus. Alia longè est nostrarum Ecclesiarum ratio, quibus ex singulari Dei beneficio Principes Christiani dati sunt, qui esi suos naevos habeant, tamen eorum authoritatem ministri tueri, non ex illis publica spectacula facere debent. Rogo autem Excell. tuam, ut aliquando priuatim de tota hac causa cum D. Erasto, viro pietate & eruditione singulari praedito, conferat, neque eos audiat, qui optime meritum oderunt & persequuntur, adeoque ex ijs locis eiectum volunt, in quibus ipsi fortasis vix nidum inuenturi fuissent, nisi alij primam glaciem fregissent, inter quos istius viri eruditio & studium praecipue eluxit. Scripsit hic sub initium istius Tragoediae Theses aliquot, quibus totum hoc negotium complexus est. Probauit has D. Bullingerus cum toto nostro collegio. At confutationem earundem D. Bezainstituit: sed quod tanti viri pace dixerim, parum profecit. Nolim tamen apud vos nouas turbas excitari. Hoc potius opto, ut quae per nouatores aliquos inuecta est confusio, paulatim aboleatur. Quod facile fiet, si qui rectius & moderatius sentiunt, tuto per illos agere, & quod animo sentiunt, modeste proponere alijsque dijudicanda proponere possunt: Theologi vero a Reipub. gubernatione & bellorum consilijs atque aulicis negotijs ad suggestum & scholas remittantur: quae propria eorum arena & palaestra est, in qua se exerceant. &c.
units.tr: It is indeed the task of ministers to rebuke the vices and corrupt morals of princes and judges, and to admonish them of their duty, as we read that the prophets once did. But that they should subject such men to fines or excommunication, if they persist in sloth or are authors of bad example, so as to hand them over to other magistrates, I cannot recall reading anywhere. Certainly it is clear that the prophets did nothing of this kind. There is no need to speak of the apostles, in whose time there were no Christian magistrates. That was the reason why elders had necessarily to be appointed in the Churches to preside over the discipline of morals, which even today ought to be done under tyrants who persecute the faith. Our Churches stand in a quite different position, since by a singular benefit of God Christian princes have been given to them. Although these have their faults, ministers ought to defend their authority, not make public spectacles of them. I beg your Excellency to confer privately on this whole matter with Dr Erastus, a man endowed with singular piety and learning, and not to listen to those who hate and persecute a man who has deserved well, and who wish him driven out of places where they themselves would perhaps hardly have found a nest, had others not first broken the ice. Among these men the learning and zeal of this man have shone out especially. At the beginning of this tragedy he wrote several theses in which he embraced this whole business. Dr Bullinger approved them, together with our whole college. But Dr Beza undertook a refutation of them; yet, with respect to so great a man, I must say, it has achieved little. Still, I should not wish new disturbances to be stirred up among you. I would rather hope that the confusion introduced by certain innovators be gradually abolished. This will easily happen if those who think more correctly and moderately may act through them safely, and may modestly set forth what they think, and propose it for others to judge. As for theologians, let them be sent back from the government of the commonwealth, from the counsels of war and court affairs, to the pulpit and the schools, which is their proper arena and training ground, in which they should exercise themselves. Etc.

units.la: Rodolphus Gualtherus.
units.tr: Rodolphus Gualtherus.

units.la: Clariss. viro D. Thomae Erasto Doctori medico, D. meo honorando, & fratri charissimo. Heidelbergam.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Dr. Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, my honoured lord and dearest brother. At Heidelberg.

units.la: S. D.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: HOrreo sane ad commemorationem eorum quae narras de excommunicatoribus, verum ut ut res ceciderit, semper deteriora metui. Unde & illustriss. Principi scripsi, ne se huic aestuoso credat pelago. Ac mirum est homines istos Principi insinuasse, non tam meo consilio, quam Gualtheri nostri instigatione, ideoque non tam à me, quam à Gualthero omnia esse illa profecta, quae ad Principem Illustriss. sunt & scripta, & transmissa. Sanctè enim tibi affirmare possum, vtramque ad Principem epistolam à me esse scriptam: & deinde Gualthero, & Wolphio B. M. exhibitam, vt illi, si quid videretur addendum, adimendum, aut mutandum, liberè indicarent. At simpliciter approbarunt illi vtramque. Id quod non scribo, quasi non libenter audiam confratrum iudicia, & melioribus libenter cedam, atque acquiescam, sed quòd, per Dei gratiam, nunc in 51. Ministerij mei anno absoluto, ita res meas temperauerim semper, vt nunquam à quoquam pependerim, aut circumducendam me permiserim contra animi mei sententiam, citráque diuinae scripturae authoritatem. Pluribus D. Datheno expositi meam de excommunicatione sententiam. Vnde ille, & forte complices eius facilè potuerunt intelligere, me sentire, vt sentio, non in vllorum hominum gratiam, sed propter veritatem synceram confitendam, & affirmandam. Mihi quidem maximoperè necessarium videtur iugibus precibus rogare Dominum, vt ipse negotium hoc, satis alioqui periculosum, componere dignetur, efficereque, vt Princeps optimus emergat. Quod ipsi, & nobis omnibus concedere dignetur clementissimus Dominus. Cuius gratiae te, tuosque commendo. Salutant te nostri Gualtherus, Simlerus, Lauaterus, Hallerus, Funchius, Stuckius, & caeteri fratres tui amantissimi. Tiguri XI. Ianuarij ad lucernam, hora noctis IX. Anno, 1574.
units.tr: I shudder indeed at the report of what you tell me about the excommunicators, but however the matter has turned out, I have always feared the worse. For this reason I have also written to the most illustrious Prince, warning him not to trust himself to this stormy sea. It is remarkable that these men insinuated themselves with the Prince, not so much on my advice as at the urging of our Gualther, and that everything that was sent and written to the most illustrious Prince came not so much from me as from Gualther. I can solemnly assure you that I wrote both letters to the Prince myself, and then showed them to Gualther and to Wolphius, of blessed memory, so that they might freely point out anything that seemed to need adding, removing or changing. But they simply approved both. I do not write this as if I were unwilling to hear the judgements of my fellow ministers, or as if I did not gladly yield to better opinions and acquiesce in them. I write it because, by God's grace, now that the fifty-first year of my ministry is complete, I have always so ordered my affairs that I never depended on anyone, nor allowed myself to be led about against my own convictions and apart from the authority of Holy Scripture. I explained my opinion on excommunication to Dr. Dathenus at considerable length. From this he, and perhaps his associates, could easily have understood that I hold, as I do, not for the favour of any men, but in order to confess and affirm the pure truth. For my part, I think it most necessary to ask the Lord with constant prayers that he himself deign to settle this matter, which is otherwise dangerous enough, and bring it about that the excellent Prince comes through safely. May the most merciful Lord grant this to him and to us all. I commend you and yours to his grace. Our Gualther, Simler, Lavater, Haller, Funck, Stuckius and the rest of your most loving brothers greet you. At Zurich, 11 January, by lamplight, at nine in the evening, in the year 1574.

units.la: Bullingerus ex animo tuus.
units.tr: Bullinger, wholly yours.

units.la: Interpretatio eorum quae Germanicè scripta sunt pag. 363.
units.tr: Translation of those things which were written in German, page 363.

units.la: A Postoli sub Ethnico Magistratu vixerunt, qui tamen scelera non punituerunt, à quibus quisque Christianus abhorrere debet. Sed vt & Ecclesia poenam scelerum aliquam haberet: Admonitionem assumpsit, & exclusionem, quia gladio,quòd ipsis minimè committebatur,punire non poterant.Et hæc quidem caussa,apud eos excommunicationis fuit. Quia verò iam Christianus Magistratus, scelera ipsemet supplicijs coherceat, ideò excommunicatio non amplius necessaria erit.
units.tr: The Apostles lived under a heathen magistrate, who nevertheless did not punish the crimes from which every Christian ought to shrink. But so that the Church might also have some punishment for crimes, it took up admonition and exclusion, because it could not punish with the sword, which was not committed to them. And this was indeed the reason for excommunication among them. But since now the magistrate is Christian and itself restrains crimes by punishments, excommunication will no longer be necessary.

units.la: Potest etiam alia pœna, & cohercitio in Ecclesia Dei esse, quàm haberi pro Ethnico & Publicano. Quia Christus nihil aliud vult, nisi vt scelera puniantur. Atque adeò non perperam fiet, si & hoc quoque tempore aliud pœnae genus constituatur: vt ea nempe Magistratui committatur.
units.tr: There can also be another punishment and restraint in the Church of God, than to be regarded as a heathen and a tax collector. For Christ wills nothing else than that crimes be punished. And so it will not be wrong if, also in this age, another kind of penalty is established, namely that it be committed to the magistrate.

units.la: HAbemus, pie lector, doctissimorum virorum plures alias literas, quas hisce adiungere possemus, ne quis existimet,clarissimum illum virum & iudiciosissimū D. Thomam Erastum paucos habuisse in sua opinione suffragatores, & ad suas Theses scriptis defendendas impulsores. Verum prolixitatis euitandae gratia, ne volumen excrescerēt, multa alia omisimus, quæ huic instituto inseruire poterant. Quod si aduersariorum importunitas eò nos adigat, vt scriniola chartulis plena quæ de hoc argumento clarissimus ille vir suis haeredibus reliquit, euoluamus: intelligent Europæ Ecclesiæ, quàm erudita & pia huius sæculi ingenia supradictas Theses,tanquam verissimas probent & amplexentur. Interim, orandus est clementissimus Deus, vt per suum Christum nostræ salutis authorem, suas Ecclesias spiritu-sancto gubernare dignetur, pastorumque omnium animos ea modestia imbuat,vt omni tyrannide in consci-entias Christianorum sublata, Euangelicam doctrinam indesinenter propagare conentur omnes,qui à Deo vocati, Christiqué ministri volunt haberi, neq; hoc nomine tantoperè glorientur, vt contradicentem neminem pati velle videantur: quin potius depo-sito omni Pharisaico supercilio, & inquisitoria authoritate,alios etiam Dei seruos de rebus sacris in coetu Christianorum differentes, vti Paulus loquitur,prophetare, non inuitis animis permittant. Vale.
units.tr: We have, pious reader, several other letters from very learned men, which we could add to these, so that no one may think that that most distinguished and judicious man, Dr. Thomas Erastus, had few supporters of his opinion and few who urged him to defend his theses in writing. But to avoid prolixity, and so that the volume would not swell, we have left out many other things which could have served this purpose. If the importunity of our opponents should compel us to open the little boxes full of papers on this subject, which that most distinguished man left to his heirs, the Churches of Europe will understand how learned and pious the minds of this age are in approving and embracing the aforesaid theses as most true. Meanwhile, we must pray that most merciful God, through his Christ, the author of our salvation, deign to govern his Churches by his Holy Spirit, and imbue the minds of all ministers with such moderation that, with all tyranny over the consciences of Christians removed, all who are called by God and wish to be considered ministers of Christ strive unceasingly to spread the Evangelical doctrine, and do not glory so greatly in that name that they seem to wish to suffer no one who contradicts them. Rather, laying aside all Pharisaical arrogance and inquisitorial authority, let them also permit, not with unwilling minds, other servants of God who speak about sacred matters in the assembly of Christians to prophesy, as Paul puts it. Farewell.

units.tr: We ask the kind reader to pardon the errors that crept in during printing. The manuscript copy was full of crossings-out and marginal notes, which gave the corrector and the compositors considerable trouble from time to time, so the slips that got through deserve forgiveness. We have noted here only those errors that in some way obscured the sense. The rest, which are easy to see, we have left for the kind reader to correct. We ask that he receive everything in a fair and good spirit. Farewell.
